t.letreros de los martires@37.9,-2.5:
Out in the high north-east of Granada province, Huéscar feels a long way from the Alhambra and the beaches of the Costa Tropical. This is the altiplano, a broad upland of wheat fields, almond trees and pale badlands at around a thousand metres, ringed by mountains, with the great limestone hump of La Sagra rising to the north. The rock shelter called Letreros de los Mártires lies in this country, a dozen or so kilometres from the town.

Letreros, meaning signs or inscriptions, is a name that turns up across south-eastern Spain wherever shepherds found painted marks on rock and assumed someone had been writing. The paintings in this region are mostly schematic: stick-like human figures, animals, suns and zigzags in red ochre, made by farming and herding communities in late prehistory. They are part of the Mediterranean rock art group protected by UNESCO, and they are faint and small, so do not expect much from a glance. The real sense of the place comes from the setting, a great sweep of empty country where it is easy to imagine people tending flocks in exactly the same way.

Riding up here is wonderful if you like space. The roads across the altiplano between Huéscar, Galera, Orce and Castril are long, open and lightly trafficked, sweeping across plateaus and dropping into dramatic little river valleys lined with poplars. Toward La Sagra and the Sierra de Castril the tarmac narrows and climbs through pine forest. The surface varies from new to cracked and patched, and side winds can be strong on exposed stretches. This is a land of real extremes: summer afternoons are fierce, and winter mornings can be well below freezing.

Huéscar is the town to rely on for fuel, food and a bed, a market town of some eight thousand people with a solid main square. Galera, about twenty kilometres away, is worth a look for its cave houses dug into the clay hills, and nearby Orce is known for very ancient finds that put early humans in this basin over a million years ago. Coming here is a commitment of distance, but the reward is roads you will have almost to yourself.
t.abric de lambert@39.2,-0.3:
Cullera is not where most people would look for prehistory. It is a busy beach town at the mouth of the Júcar, with high-rise apartments along the sand, a lighthouse on the point and rice fields stretching inland toward the Albufera lagoon. But the town has a mountain at its back, a limestone outcrop crowned by a castle and a sanctuary, and in that rock there are shelters, including the one known as the Abric de Lambert.

The shelter belongs to the long chain of painted sites along Spain's eastern side that UNESCO inscribed together in 1998, and its presence here is a reminder that this coast was inhabited and travelled long before anyone built a holiday flat. The panels at sites like this are often faint and fragile, and access is usually restricted. What you can easily see is the mountain itself: the road up to the castle of Cullera and the sanctuary of the Virgen del Castillo climbs in tight hairpins and gives a superb view over the mouth of the Júcar, the beaches and the green and silver patchwork of the rice paddies.

Riding around Cullera is mostly flat. The roads across the Albufera rice country, through Sueca and Fortaleny, run along embankments and irrigation channels, straight-ish and easy, though crosswinds off the sea can catch you. The real hills begin inland, past Corbera and Favara, where the roads climb into orange groves and pine. In summer, traffic toward the beaches is heavy, particularly on weekends, and the town centre is better avoided at the height of the season.

Food is the big draw here. Sueca considers itself a capital of rice and holds a well-known paella competition, and almost any restaurant in this belt will cook you a proper rice dish at lunchtime. Order it for two and give it time; locals eat it at midday, not in the evening. Fuel and every other service are easy in Cullera itself. The light over the paddies at dusk, when the water turns pink and the herons drift home, is reason enough to linger before heading back.
t.abric de la penya@38.9,-0.7:
Moixent, or Mogente in Castilian, stands at the head of a corridor that has carried traffic between the Valencian coast and the interior of Castile for as long as anyone has been moving goods. The old road, the railway and now the motorway all funnel through here, between low limestone ridges with vineyards and olive groves in the valley floor. The rock shelter known as the Abric de la Penya sits in this landscape a few kilometres from the town, close also to Vallada.

This is serious archaeological country. Just outside Moixent lies La Bastida de les Alcusses, a large Iberian hilltop settlement from around the fourth century BC, where excavators found a small bronze figure of a mounted warrior that has become something of a regional emblem. The painted shelters are older still, part of the Levantine and schematic rock art traditions that UNESCO groups together along the Mediterranean side of Spain. They are small, protected sites, often visited by arrangement, and they reward a bit of reading beforehand.

For the bike, the interest lies off the main corridor. The roads south from Moixent toward Fontanars dels Alforins cross an upland wine plateau, a quiet, open landscape of vines and pine where the bends flow nicely and traffic is minimal. North and east, the lanes toward Vallada, Montesa and Xàtiva follow the valley with orange groves creeping in, while the roads up into the sierras on either side get tighter and steeper. Expect occasional broken tarmac and farm vehicles, and be ready for the wind that funnels down this pass.

Moixent itself is a modest town with bars and a fuel station or two on the old road, but Ontinyent, about eleven kilometres away, is the larger centre with every service. Xàtiva, a little further, is worth a detour for its enormous castle sprawling along a ridge above the town. The Alforins plateau has a growing number of small wineries; the reds here are generous. Spring is green and fresh, autumn brings harvest and red-gold vineyards, and summer heat in the corridor can be relentless.
t.cueva de las aranas del carabassi@38.2,-:
The Carabassí is one of the last stretches of wild-ish coast between Alicante and Santa Pola: a line of dunes held together by pine and marram grass, a long beach, and the sea glittering under the flight path of Alicante airport. In the low rocky ground behind it lies a small cave known for painted marks, the Cueva de las Arañas del Carabassí, close to the village of El Altet and a short hop from Santa Pola.

Its inclusion in the Mediterranean rock art inscription makes it something of an outlier. Most of the painted sites in eastern Spain are tucked away in inland gorges, but this one sits within sight of the sea, a reminder that coastal people were part of the same world of image-making. The marks themselves are modest and the site is protected, so treat it as a curiosity and context for the landscape rather than as a destination with a ticket office.

The riding here is coastal and flat, a different rhythm from the mountain loops further inland. The road along the coast between Santa Pola and Alicante runs past the dunes, salt flats and urbanisations, and it can be busy, particularly in summer. The Santa Pola salt pans, just south, are home to flamingos, and the sight of pink birds standing in the shallow lagoons with the airport traffic overhead is one of the odder pleasures of this coast. For better roads, head inland toward Elche and beyond into the hills of the Vinalopó valley.

Elche, a short ride away, holds the great Palmeral, a vast grove of date palms laid out by the Moors and protected by UNESCO in its own right. Santa Pola is a working fishing port, which means seafood: grilled fish, rice cooked in fish stock and the local caldero. Fuel, food and all services are everywhere along this coast, so logistics are easy. The best time to come is outside high summer, when the light is soft, the traffic thins and the dunes smell of warm pine resin.
t.barranco del cabezo del moro@38.9,-1.0:
Almansa is one of those towns you see from the motorway and do not stop at, and that is a mistake. Its castle is spectacular, a Gothic fortress built on a sharp limestone outcrop right in the middle of town, looking exactly like a child's drawing of a castle. Around it spreads a wide plain at about seven hundred metres, the meeting point of the Valencian, Murcian and Castilian lands, and a few kilometres out in the surrounding hills lies the ravine known as the Barranco del Cabezo del Moro.

The painted shelters in this area belong to the same broad family as those along the Valencian mountains, part of the UNESCO-listed rock art of the Mediterranean basin. They sit in quiet ravines, often protected by fencing, and the figures are small, red and easy to miss. The name of the ravine, like so many others in Spain that refer to Moors, says more about how later villagers explained old things in their landscape than about who actually made them.

Almansa's other claim to fame is a battle. In 1707, during the War of the Spanish Succession, the plain outside the town saw a decisive victory for the Bourbon side, which helped settle the Spanish crown on Philip V and led to the loss of the old Valencian legal privileges. There is a monument to the battle on the plain, and locals still talk about it.

For riding, Almansa is a good hub. The road north toward Ayora drops through a deep valley full of character, with bends and changing views, while the roads west and south across the plateau are fast and open. The surfaces on the main CM and N roads are good; smaller routes are rougher. Wind is a fact of life on the plain, and winter can be cold. The town has all services, plenty of fuel and some good places to eat, with gazpacho manchego, a hearty stew of game and flatbread, the dish to look for. Spring, with the plain green and wildflowers in the verges, is the time to come.
t.barranc de la penya blanca@38.8,-0.3:
Planes is a small village in the hills of the Comtat in northern Alicante province, crowned by a castle and looking out over a valley of olive and cherry orchards. The Barranc de la Penya Blanca, the ravine of the white rock, lies close by, among the folded limestone ridges between Planes, Benimarfull and the reservoir at Beniarrés.

This part of Alicante holds some of the richest rock art of the whole Spanish Mediterranean. Not only Levantine paintings, but also the much rarer Macro-schematic style, large symbolic figures in red painted by early farming communities, were identified in these ravines and are found almost nowhere else. The Pla de Petracos shelters near Castell de Castells are the best known example. The shelters in the Penya Blanca ravine are part of the same rich tradition. Visits to protected panels are usually possible only with a guide, often arranged through the Museu d'Alcoi or regional authorities.

The riding around Planes is fantastic. This corner of Alicante is a maze of narrow mountain roads through orchards and pine woods, with countless bends and little traffic. The roads linking Planes, Benillup, Gorga and Millena, or heading toward the Vall de Gallinera and the Vall d'Alcalà, are a joy, though narrow, sometimes poorly surfaced and with blind corners. The Vall de Gallinera, to the east, is famous for its cherry blossom in spring, when the terraces turn white. The Vall d'Alcalà is associated with Al-Azraq, a Muslim leader who rebelled against the Christian conquerors in the thirteenth century and is remembered in local history.

Planes has a bar or two, but for fuel and a full range of services, Muro de Alcoy, about eleven kilometres away, is the nearest larger town, with Cocentaina and Alcoy beyond. The local cuisine is mountain fare: rice dishes with rabbit and snails, olleta, a hearty bean and vegetable stew, and pericana, a mix of dried peppers and salted cod in olive oil. Spring and autumn are perfect; summer can be very hot in the valleys.
t.barranc de les coves abrigo l@38.9,-0.4:
Castelló de Rugat sits on the southern rim of the Vall d'Albaida, a broad valley in the south of Valencia province hemmed in by mountain ridges. On one side rises the long saw-toothed crest of the Benicadell, on the other the Serra de la Solana, and between them lies a patchwork of vineyards, olive groves and small towns with church towers. The Barranc de les Coves, the ravine of the caves, cuts into the slopes near Castelló de Rugat, Ràfol de Salem and Beniarrés, and its first shelter holds painted figures.

This ravine is part of the dense cluster of rock art sites around the Benicadell, where the mountains of the Comtat and the Vall d'Albaida meet. The paintings here, like those in neighbouring ravines, include the lively Levantine style as well as schematic marks, and they sit within the UNESCO inscription that covers more than seven hundred sites along Spain's Mediterranean side. Some panels are protected behind bars and best visited with a guide; the ravine itself, with its pines, cliffs and seasonal stream, is a pleasant place to walk.

Riding in the Vall d'Albaida is a real pleasure. The CV roads that cross the valley and climb over the passes to the Comtat are well surfaced and wind their way through vineyards and woods, with the Benicadell always looming. The pass between Beniarrés and Salem, or the road over to Muro, have lovely sequences of bends. The reservoir at Beniarrés, a stretch of turquoise water, makes a fine viewpoint. Traffic is light, but watch out for agricultural vehicles and the occasional cyclist group.

Castelló de Rugat is a small town with a bar, a bakery and a church, and it is known in the region for textile workshops. For fuel and more choice, Muro de Alcoy is around ten kilometres away, and Ontinyent and Albaida, the valley's main towns, are within easy reach. The area produces wine and olive oil, and local bakeries sell coca, a flat Valencian pastry, savoury or sweet. Spring brings green hills and wildflowers, and autumn offers harvest colours and mild weather.
t.cova de la petxina@39.0,-0.5:
Bellús is a small village in the valley of the Albaida river in southern Valencia, just upstream from where the river flows into a reservoir and then joins the Júcar. The old village was partly flooded by the reservoir, and the new one stands on higher ground. The Cova de la Petxina, the cave of the shell, is in the hills near the village, close to Guadasequies and Genovés.

The cave is known for prehistoric remains, part of a wider area rich in archaeological sites. The Cova del Parpalló, near Gandia, about thirty kilometres east, is famous for its thousands of engraved and painted stone plaques from the Upper Palaeolithic, and the Cova Negra near Xàtiva has yielded Neanderthal remains. Petxina adds to this long story of human presence, though it is a small and protected site rather than a tourist destination.

Xàtiva, a few kilometres to the south, is the big attraction nearby. Its castle stretches along a ridge above the town, with walls and towers climbing the hill, and the old town below has fountains, churches and palaces. Xàtiva was the birthplace of two Borgia popes, Callixtus III and Alexander VI, and it was burned by Philip V's troops in 1707 after the War of the Spanish Succession; as a result, the portrait of Philip V in the town museum hangs upside down. It is the kind of grudge that makes history feel personal.

The riding in this area is mixed. The valley floor is busy with roads and orange groves, but the hills on either side offer twisting roads toward the Serra Grossa, Quatretonda and the Valldigna. The road from Xàtiva south toward Bocairent and Ontinyent climbs gradually into the mountains. Watch out for traffic around Xàtiva and for farm vehicles in the groves.

Benigànim, about five kilometres away, is the nearest larger town, with fuel and food, and Xàtiva has everything. Xàtiva is known for its arròs al forn, rice baked in the oven with chickpeas, sausage and pork. Spring, when the orange blossom fills the air, is the best time to ride here.
t.abrigo del canto blanco@38.4,-1.4:
Jumilla is wine country, and you know it as soon as you arrive. The town sits in the north of the Murcia region, surrounded by a high, dry plateau of vineyards growing the Monastrell grape, which produces powerful, dark red wines. A castle tops the hill above the old town, and the bodegas on its outskirts welcome visitors. The Abrigo del Canto Blanco, the shelter of the white stone, lies in the hills about five kilometres away.

The Murcia region has many painted shelters, part of the UNESCO-listed Mediterranean rock art group. Around Jumilla, the sites include both Levantine and schematic paintings, and the area was evidently used by prehistoric communities who hunted in the mountains and later farmed the valleys. The shelters are small and protected; to see them, ask at the town's tourist office or museum, which can also tell you about the Iberian and Roman remains found in the area.

The riding around Jumilla is a mix of open plateau and mountain. The roads across the vineyards are long and gently curving, with wide views and little traffic, while the climbs into the Sierra del Carche or toward Yecla and the Sierra de la Pila are twistier and more fun. The Carche, a regional park, rises to over thirteen hundred metres and has roads that wind through pine forest. The surfaces are generally good on main roads, with gravel and patches on smaller ones. Summer heat is intense; spring and autumn are much more pleasant.

Jumilla has fuel, food and accommodation. The local cuisine is hearty: gazpacho jumillano, a stew of game and flatbread, and the region's famous wines. Many bodegas offer tastings, though obviously not for the rider. The town's Holy Week processions are well known, and in August the town holds a wine harvest festival with a wine battle. The castle, open to visitors, offers fine views over the plateau, and the Santa Ana monastery on the outskirts has been home to Franciscan friars for centuries.
t.abric del garrofero@39.1,-0.8:
Bicorp is a small village in the Canal de Navarrés, a valley in the interior of Valencia province walled in by rugged mountains and deep ravines. The surrounding Macizo del Caroig is one of the largest wild areas in the Valencian Community, a vast tableland of pine, scrub and gorges cut by the Júcar's tributaries. The Abric del Garrofero, the shelter of the carob tree, lies in the hills near Bicorp, Quesa and Navarrés.

This area is famous for one painting above all. In the Cuevas de la Araña, a short distance from Bicorp, there is a small figure of a person climbing a rope or ladder to collect honey from a hive, with bees swarming around. It is one of the most widely reproduced images of prehistoric art in the world and a key piece of evidence for honey gathering in prehistory. The village has a museum dedicated to the rock art of the area, and guided visits to the shelters can be arranged there. The Abric del Garrofero is another painted site in the same network, with its own figures.

The Canal de Navarrés is a beautiful area to ride, with roads that run along the valley floor between orange groves and then climb into the mountains on all sides. The road from Navarrés to Bicorp and Quesa climbs gently through olive and almond groves, with views of the Caroig massif. Heading south toward Enguera, or north-west into the Caroig toward Ayora, you get wilder, emptier roads through pine forest, with twisting climbs and descents. Surfaces vary; watch for gravel and for wild boar in the evening.

Navarrés has a lake and fuel, and Enguera, about thirteen kilometres away, is the nearest town of size. Quesa is known for the Charco Azul, a series of pools in the river where people swim in summer. The local cuisine includes gazpacho, the Manchegan-style stew, and rice with rabbit and snails. Spring and autumn are perfect for riding; summer brings heat and the risk of forest fires, which have hit this area hard in the past.
t.abrigo del melgar@37.8,-3.1:
Quesada is a white town at the foot of the Sierra de Cazorla, in the province of Jaén, surrounded by an ocean of olive trees. The groves stretch to the horizon in every direction, a landscape that makes Jaén the world's largest producer of olive oil. Behind the town, the mountains rise steeply, with pine forest and limestone cliffs, and the Guadalquivir river has its source not far away. The Abrigo del Melgar lies in the hills just outside the town.

The Sierra de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas is Spain's largest protected natural area, home to deer, ibex, wild boar and griffon vultures, with forests of black pine and deep gorges. Its foothills hold many rock shelters with prehistoric paintings, part of the UNESCO-listed rock art of the Mediterranean basin. The paintings around Quesada are mostly schematic, with stylised figures and symbols. The Cueva del Agua, a cave sanctuary near Tíscar, is a place of pilgrimage nearby, where a waterfall pours through the rock.

Quesada is the birthplace of the painter Rafael Zabaleta, one of the most important Spanish artists of the twentieth century, and the town has a museum dedicated to his work, with paintings of the local landscape and people. It is a quiet town with a pleasant centre and good views over the olive groves.

The riding around Quesada is wonderful. The road from Quesada up to Tíscar and on toward Pozo Alcón climbs into the mountains through pine forest, with hairpins, cliffs and views. The roads into the Sierra de Cazorla, toward Cazorla town, the Guadalquivir valley and the reservoir of El Tranco, are among the best in Andalucía, with endless curves and almost no traffic outside the summer holidays. Watch for deer and wild boar on the road, and for gravel in the corners.

Quesada has fuel and food. Local cuisine includes andrajos, a stew with pieces of flatbread, and, of course, excellent olive oil. Spring and autumn are perfect; summer heat in the valleys is intense, and winter can bring snow to the mountains.
t.la sarga abric i@38.6,-0.5:
Alcoy, or Alcoi in Valencian, is a city of bridges, built where three rivers meet in deep ravines, in the mountains of northern Alicante. It was one of the cradles of Spain's industrial revolution, with textile and paper mills powered by its rivers, and its streets have fine modernist buildings from that era. It is also famous for its Moors and Christians festival in April, one of the most spectacular in Spain, with parades, music and mock battles in honour of Saint George. The rock shelters of La Sarga lie in the hills about eight kilometres from the city, toward Ibi.

La Sarga is one of the most important rock art sites in the Valencian Community. Its shelters contain Levantine paintings of hunters and animals, as well as large Macro-schematic figures, a style unique to this region, with symbolic human figures and signs painted by the first farming communities around seven thousand years ago. The site is fenced off, and guided visits are organised by the Museu d'Alcoi, generally on certain weekends; check ahead.

The surrounding mountains are beautiful. The Font Roja natural park, south of Alcoy, protects a forest of oak, maple and yew on the north face of the Menejador mountain, unusual in this dry region. There is a sanctuary and a network of trails, and the old snow wells, where snow was stored to make ice, are a reminder of the region's history.

The riding around Alcoy is excellent. The roads that climb from the city toward Ibi, Banyeres or the Font Roja wind through pine forest and over passes, with good surfaces and great views. The road from Alcoy toward Penàguila and Benifallim, or over to the Vall de Guadalest, is a sequence of tight bends through mountains, with almost no traffic. In winter, it can be cold and occasionally snowy at altitude.

Alcoy, about eight kilometres away, has all services. Local specialities include olives stuffed in the Alcoy style, coffee liqueur known as licor café, and pericana. Ibi, nearby, is famous as the toy-making capital of Spain, with a toy museum.
t.cueva de la plata@37.9,-1.6:
Aledo is a tiny village on a rocky spur in the hills of Murcia, a place that punches well above its weight in history. In the eleventh century, it was a fortress on the frontier between Christian Castile and the Muslim taifa kingdoms, and the siege of Aledo in 1088 was a major episode in the struggle for the peninsula. A tower still stands above the village. The Cueva de la Plata, the silver cave, lies in the hills nearby, between Aledo, Totana and Alhama de Murcia.

The area around Aledo and the Sierra Espuña is rich in prehistoric sites, from Bronze Age settlements of the El Argar culture, which flourished in south-east Spain around four thousand years ago, to painted shelters in the ravines. La Bastida, near Totana, is one of the most important Argaric sites in Europe, a fortified hilltop town with massive walls. The Cueva de la Plata is part of this rich archaeological landscape, a small site rather than a visitor attraction.

The Sierra Espuña, just north, is a regional park with forests of pine that were replanted at the turn of the twentieth century to stop erosion, a pioneering project. The mountains rise to over fifteen hundred metres, and the park has old snow wells, where snow was packed into ice for the towns below.

The riding here is excellent. The road from Aledo into the Sierra Espuña winds through pine forest, with tight bends, steep sections and views of the plains of Murcia below. The road from Alhama de Murcia up to the park and over toward Mula is a local favourite with motorcyclists and cyclists. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel, cyclists and wild boar. Summer heat on the plain is intense, but the mountains are cooler.

Totana, about fourteen kilometres away, has all services, as does Alhama. Totana is known for its pottery, with workshops still producing large clay jars. Local cuisine includes rice with rabbit and snails and pastries such as the paparajote, lemon leaves dipped in batter, fried and dusted with sugar, but you do not eat the leaf. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.abric de la paella@38.8,-0.5:
Muro de Alcoy and Cocentaina sit side by side in the valley of the Serpis river, in the Comtat, a district of northern Alicante surrounded by mountains. Cocentaina is crowned by a castle with a tall tower, and below it lies an old town with a palace of the Counts of Cocentaina and a Franciscan convent. The Abric de la Paella, named after the paella pan perhaps because of its shape, lies in the hills between the two towns.

The Comtat is one of the richest areas in Spain for prehistoric art. The mountains around the valley hold dozens of painted shelters, with Levantine, schematic and Macro-schematic paintings. The Macro-schematic style, with its large symbolic figures, was first identified in this area and is found almost nowhere else, which makes the sites of the Comtat particularly important. The Abric de la Paella is one of these, protected and best visited with a guide; the Museu d'Alcoi and the local councils organise visits to some shelters.

Cocentaina is known for its All Saints Fair, the Fira de Tots Sants, held every year around the beginning of November and dating back to a royal charter of 1346. It draws hundreds of thousands of visitors and fills the town with stalls, livestock and food. Like Alcoy, Cocentaina also holds a Moors and Christians festival, with parades and costumes.

The riding around Muro and Cocentaina is excellent. The roads that climb from the valley toward the Vall de Gallinera, the Vall d'Alcalà, the Vall de Seta or over the Benicadell to the Vall d'Albaida are narrow and twisty, through orchards and pine forest, with little traffic. The road from Cocentaina toward Alcoy follows the valley and is busier. Watch out for gravel, agricultural vehicles and cyclists on the mountain roads.

Muro de Alcoy, about two kilometres away, and Cocentaina have fuel and all services. Local cuisine includes rice dishes with rabbit and snails, the Alcoy-style stuffed olives, and pastries filled with sweet potato or almond. Spring, with almond and cherry blossom, and autumn are the best times to ride here.
t.penon de los machos@39.2,-1.0:
Cofrentes is a village at the confluence of two rivers, the Júcar and the Cabriel, in the interior of Valencia province, and it has a curious mix of attractions. Above it stands a castle on a crag. Nearby rises the Cerro de Agrás, the only recently active volcano in the Valencian Community, a dark cone of basalt in a landscape of limestone. And just outside the village, the cooling towers of the Cofrentes nuclear power station send plumes of steam into the sky. The Peñón de los Machos, a rocky outcrop with painted shelters, lies in the hills between Cofrentes, Jalance and Jarafuel.

The Valle de Ayora-Cofrentes, the valley that runs south from here, is a fertile corridor between mountains, rich in prehistoric and Iberian sites. Painted shelters in the area hold Levantine and schematic art, part of the UNESCO-listed group. The name Peñón de los Machos, meaning rock of the billy goats, hints at the wild goats that still roam the cliffs. The site is protected and small, best visited with local information.

Cofrentes has thermal springs, and a spa has been operating here since the nineteenth century. The rivers offer boat trips through the gorges of the Júcar, and the reservoir of Embarcaderos is popular for kayaking. The castle on the crag above the village, with Muslim origins, can be visited, and the views over the confluence and the volcano are worth the climb.

The riding here is excellent. The road from Cofrentes south through Jalance, Jarafuel and Teresa de Cofrentes to Ayora follows the valley, with the mountains rising on both sides, and is fast and flowing. The road west toward Requena and the Cabriel gorge, and north toward Cortes de Pallás through the Júcar gorge, are spectacular, with tight bends, cliffs and reservoirs. Cortes de Pallás in particular is a twisty, remote route through a dramatic canyon. Surfaces vary; watch for gravel, and be careful on narrow sections.

Cofrentes has a fuel station and restaurants, and Ayora, about fifteen kilometres away, has more services. Local food includes gazpacho, the Manchegan stew, and honey from the mountains. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
Alginet sits in the Ribera Alta, the flat, fertile plain south of Valencia where the Júcar river spreads out among orange groves, rice fields and small towns. To the west, the plain meets the first hills of the interior, low ridges of limestone covered in pine and scrub. The Barranc de la Falaguera, the ravine of the fern, cuts into these hills near Alginet, Alfarp and Benifaió.

The ravine holds rock shelters with painted figures, part of the network of Levantine and schematic art that UNESCO protects along Spain's Mediterranean side. The Barranc de la Falaguera is one of the few sites close to the Valencian plain, showing that prehistoric communities used these hills as well as the more remote mountains. The site is protected and small.

The Ribera is the heart of Valencian citrus country. The orange groves stretch for kilometres, and in spring the scent of orange blossom, the azahar, fills the air. The towns are agricultural, with warehouses where oranges are packed for export across Europe. Alginet is also known for its Moorish-style tile-domed churches. The Albufera, the great lagoon south of Valencia, with its rice fields and fishing villages, is a short ride east.

The riding here is flat on the plain, through orange groves and villages, with a lot of local traffic and tractors. The roads into the hills to the west, toward Llombai, Catadau and the Serra de les Agulles, offer more interesting riding, with bends through pine forest and views over the plain. The road over the hills toward Montroy and Real, and on into the Hoya de Buñol, is a good loop. Watch out for gravel and agricultural vehicles on the smaller roads.

Alginet, about four kilometres away, has fuel and all services. The Ribera is the home of paella, and every town claims its own version; the classic Valencian paella is made with chicken, rabbit, green beans and garrofó, a large white bean. Spring, with the orange blossom, is the best time to ride here.
t.penya de benicadell@38.8,-0.4:
From almost anywhere in the southern half of Valencia province you can see it: a long, jagged ridge of grey limestone with a sharp tooth at its eastern end, standing on the skyline like a broken saw. The Benicadell, at 1,104 metres, separates the Vall d'Albaida to the north from the Comtat to the south, and the sharp summit, the Penya, is the mountain's signature. At its foot lie the villages of Beniarrés, Ràfol de Salem and Otos.

The Benicadell has been a landmark for as long as people have lived in this region. Its slopes and ravines are rich in prehistoric sites, with painted shelters in the Barranc de l'Infern and other ravines around the mountain. During the Muslim period, the area was fortified, and the ruins of castles still crown hilltops in the area. The summit is a popular hike, with a path that climbs from the Port d'Albaida or the Port de Salem, and the views from the top stretch from the sea to the mountains of the interior.

Otos, on the northern side, has turned itself into an outdoor gallery of sundials. Dozens of them, designed by artists, decorate the walls of houses in the village, each one different, and walking around to find them is a pleasant way to spend half an hour. Beniarrés, on the southern side, overlooks a reservoir on the Serpis, a stretch of turquoise water surrounded by olive groves.

The riding around the Benicadell is some of the best in the region. The two passes that cross the ridge, the Port d'Albaida and the Port de Salem, are short but twisty climbs with great views, and the roads along the foot of the mountain, through olive and almond groves, are lightly trafficked. The circuit around the mountain, via Beniarrés, Muro, Albaida and Salem, makes a fine half-day loop. Watch out for gravel, cyclists and occasional agricultural vehicles.

Muro de Alcoy, about six kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel and all services, and Albaida and Ontinyent are close. Local food includes the putxero, a winter stew, and the rice dishes of the area. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.las covachicas@38.2,-2.1:
The Sierra del Segura, in the far south of Albacete province, is a world of its own: deep valleys, rivers lined with poplars, terraces of olive and almond trees, and white villages that look more Andalusian than Castilian. Letur is one of the most beautiful, a village of Moorish origin built on a rock above a stream, with narrow alleys, arches and gardens watered by old irrigation channels. Las Covachicas, a group of shelters, lies in the hills nearby, between Letur, Socovos and Férez.

The Sierra del Segura is rich in rock art. Its shelters contain Levantine paintings of hunters and animals, and schematic figures, part of the UNESCO-listed Mediterranean rock art group. The name Covachicas, meaning little caves, is typical of how local people named these places. The sites are small and protected, and the local councils and tourist offices can provide information on visits.

Letur's old town is a protected historic site, and its layout reflects its Muslim past, with houses climbing the rock and paths descending to the gardens along the stream. The village is surrounded by water, with springs and waterfalls, unusual in this dry region. Nearby, the Taibilla and Segura rivers have carved deep valleys, and the reservoirs of the Cenajo and the Taibilla are popular for fishing and swimming.

The riding in the Sierra del Segura is superb. The roads that link Letur, Socovos, Férez, Elche de la Sierra, Yeste and Nerpio wind through the mountains with endless bends, climbs and descents, through pine forest and past olive terraces, with very little traffic. The surfaces are mixed, sometimes excellent, sometimes rough, with gravel and potholes. The road from Letur toward Yeste and the Segura valley is particularly good. In summer, it is hot in the valleys, and in winter, snow can close the higher roads.

Services are limited. Letur and Socovos have small shops and bars, and Socovos has fuel. Moratalla, about twenty-one kilometres away, is the nearest town of size. Plan fuel carefully. Local food includes the gazpacho of the region, cured meats, cheese and honey. Spring and autumn are the best seasons for riding.
t.cueva de las palamas@38.1,-1.8:
Cehegín, in the north-west of the Murcia region, is a town of two faces: a modern lower town, and an old town on a hill, with steep streets, noble houses and churches, declared a historic site. The Cueva de las Palomas, the cave of the doves, lies on the edge of the town, less than a kilometre from the centre, with the larger town of Caravaca de la Cruz about five kilometres away.

The Murcia region is rich in prehistoric sites, and the Cueva de las Palomas is one of many caves and shelters with traces of ancient occupation and art in the area, part of the UNESCO-listed Mediterranean rock art group. Close to Cehegín, the archaeological site of Begastri, on a hilltop, preserves the remains of a Roman and Visigothic town that was an important bishopric in late antiquity, with walls and buildings partly excavated.

Caravaca de la Cruz is one of the holy cities of Catholicism, with the right to celebrate a jubilee year, because of a relic of the True Cross kept in the sanctuary on its castle hill. The town is famous for its festival in early May, when the Caballos del Vino, horses dressed in elaborately embroidered mantles, race up the steep slope to the castle, each horse led by a team of runners holding onto it. It is wild, colourful and deeply rooted.

The riding around Cehegín is varied. The roads west toward Moratalla and the Sierra del Segura, or north toward Calasparra and the Segura river, offer good bends through hills, olive groves and pine forest, with little traffic. Calasparra is known for its rice, grown in terraced paddies along the river, with its own designation of origin. The roads south toward Bullas and Mula pass through vineyards. The surfaces are mostly good.

Cehegín has fuel and all services, as does Caravaca. Local food includes the rice of Calasparra, the wines of Bullas, and the sweets of Caravaca, such as the yemas, made with egg yolks. Spring and autumn are the best times to ride here; summer is hot.
t.abric de gontran@38.9,-0.7:
Head south-west from Xàtiva along the old road to Castile and you climb gently into a corridor between two mountain ranges, the Serra Grossa on one side and the Serra de Enguera on the other. The town of Moixent sits where the corridor narrows, with Vallada just downstream and the vineyards of Fontanars dels Alforins on the plateau beyond. The Abric de Gontran lies in the hills just outside Moixent.

The painted shelters of the area belong to the Levantine and schematic traditions listed by UNESCO, and they show how important this pass was even in prehistory, as a route between the coast and the interior. The shelters are small, protected and often require a guide to visit. They are part of a dense archaeological landscape that also includes Iberian settlements and Roman roads.

A few kilometres downstream, above the village of Montesa, stand the ruins of the castle that gave its name to the Order of Montesa, a military order founded in 1317 by the King of Aragon after the dissolution of the Templars, to defend the kingdom of Valencia. The castle was the order's headquarters until it was wrecked by an earthquake in 1748, and its ruins still crown the hill above the village. The village of Vallada, between Moixent and Montesa, has a pleasant old centre and a reputation for its pottery.

The riding is best off the main road. The A-35 motorway and the old N-430 carry most of the traffic through the corridor, but the roads that climb into the hills on either side, toward Enguera and the Caroig massif to the north or toward Fontanars and the Alforins plateau to the south, offer twisting roads with little traffic. The road from Moixent to Fontanars climbs through pine forest onto the plateau, with views back over the corridor. Watch out for the wind that funnels through the pass.

Moixent has fuel and food, and Ontinyent, about thirteen kilometres away, is the nearest larger town. The wineries of the Alforins plateau produce good reds. Local food includes the rice dishes of the area. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.port de penaguila abric ii@38.7,-0.4:
The Port de Penàguila is a mountain pass in the interior of Alicante province, on the road between Alcoy and the Vall de Guadalest, where the hills of the Comtat rise toward the Serra d'Aitana, the highest range in the province. The village of Penàguila, below the pass, is a small, ancient place huddled beneath a castle on a rocky crest, and Benilloba, Cocentaina and Alcoy are all close. The second shelter of the Port de Penàguila is one of several painted sites in the area.

The mountains around Penàguila hold numerous rock shelters with Levantine, schematic and Macro-schematic paintings, part of the UNESCO-listed group. The Macro-schematic style, with its large symbolic human figures, is unique to this part of Alicante and dates from the arrival of the first farmers, around seven thousand years ago. The shelters are protected and visits require a guide.

Penàguila is a surprise. Apart from its castle ruins and medieval streets, it has a romantic nineteenth-century garden, the Jardí de Santos, laid out by a wealthy family with fountains, statues and a labyrinth of hedges, an unexpected oasis in the dry mountains. The village is also known for its sausages and cured meats. The Serra d'Aitana, to the south, rises to over fifteen hundred metres, with the summit occupied by a military installation, but the slopes are open and the views are huge.

The riding here is excellent. The road over the Port de Penàguila, from Alcoy toward Benasau and the Vall de Guadalest, is a classic, with tight bends, steep climbs and views over the mountains. The roads toward Benifallim, Alcolecha and the Port de Tudons, the high pass over the Aitana, are some of the best in the region, with little traffic and great scenery. Surfaces are generally good, though there is gravel in places and cyclists are common. In winter, the higher roads can be cold and icy.

Cocentaina, about ten kilometres away, has fuel and all services, as does Alcoy. Penàguila and Benilloba have bars. Local food includes the mountain sausages, rice dishes and the pericana. Spring and autumn are perfect for riding.
t.barraac de la palla@38.8,-0.1:
Tormos and Sagra are tiny villages at the foot of the mountains in the north of Alicante province, at the point where the plain of the Marina Alta meets the hills. They are surrounded by orange groves and orchards, with the mountains of the Vall de Laguar and the Serra del Migdia rising steeply behind. The Barranc de la Palla, the ravine of the straw, cuts into the hills near Tormos, close also to Orba and the town of Pego.

The mountains of the Marina Alta are rich in rock art, part of the UNESCO-listed Mediterranean group. The shelters here include Levantine, schematic and Macro-schematic paintings, and the Barranc de la Palla is one of several sites in this area. They are small and protected. The Vall de Laguar, above Tormos, is also famous for its walking trails, particularly the Barranc de l'Infern, a deep gorge with thousands of stone steps built by the Moors to link the villages, often called the cathedral of hiking.

Pego, the nearest town, is set on the edge of a large coastal wetland, the Marjal de Pego-Oliva, a natural park with springs, rice fields and canals, home to many birds. Rice is grown here, and the area has a long tradition of fishing and hunting in the marsh. The town has a pleasant old centre with a fine church.

The riding around Tormos is excellent. The roads that climb into the mountains, toward the Vall de Laguar, the Vall d'Ebo and the Vall de Gallinera, are narrow, twisty and spectacular, with steep climbs, tight hairpins and great views over the coast. The road from Pego up to the Vall d'Ebo is a local favourite, climbing in a series of bends to a valley in the mountains. Surfaces vary, and some roads are very narrow. In summer, the coastal roads are busy with tourist traffic, but the mountains are quiet.

Pego, about five kilometres away, has fuel and all services. Local food includes the rice of Pego, cooked in many ways, and the fish of the coast. The orange groves blossom in spring, filling the air with scent. Autumn is also a good time to ride.
t.cejo cortado i@38.1,-1.5:
Mula is a town in the heart of the Murcia region, built on the slopes of a hill crowned by a sixteenth-century castle, with an old quarter of narrow streets, noble houses and churches. Around it, a dry landscape of hills, ravines and badlands opens out, with orchards and olive groves along the river. The Cejo Cortado, a name meaning the cut brow, refers to a rocky escarpment with prehistoric shelters about seven kilometres from the town, between Mula, Albudeite and Ricote.

The shelters of the Cejo Cortado contain paintings in the Levantine and schematic styles, part of the UNESCO-listed group, and they are among the most important in the Murcia region. The figures include hunters and animals. The site is protected, and visits can be arranged through the local authorities. The area around Mula is also rich in other archaeological sites, including the Iberian sanctuary of El Cigarralejo, whose finds are displayed in a museum in the town, with an important collection of Iberian sculpture and pottery.

Mula is famous in Spain for its drums. On the night of Holy Tuesday to Wednesday, thousands of people in the town beat drums through the night, a deafening and moving tradition that is part of a wider custom in this part of Spain. The nearby village of Ricote, in the Valle de Ricote along the Segura river, was the last stronghold of the Moriscos, the descendants of Muslims, before their expulsion in the early seventeenth century, and the valley still has the irrigation systems and orchards they created.

The riding around Mula is excellent. The roads that cross the hills toward Pliego, the Sierra Espuña, Bullas and the Valle de Ricote are twisting and scenic, through a dry landscape of ravines and pine forest, with little traffic. The road through the Valle de Ricote, along the Segura, is a beautiful ride through orchards and palm groves. The surfaces are generally good. Summer heat is intense, so ride early or late.

Mula, about seven kilometres away, has fuel and all services. Local food includes the rice dishes of the region and the sweets of Holy Week. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.abrigo de la fuente@38.0,-2.3:
Nerpio is about as remote as it gets in southern Spain: a village in the far south-west corner of Albacete province, deep in the Sierra del Segura, close to the borders of Andalucía and Murcia. It sits in the valley of the Taibilla river, surrounded by mountains, with terraced fields, walnut trees and pine forests on the slopes. The Abrigo de la Fuente, the shelter of the spring, lies in the hills about eleven kilometres from the village.

Nerpio has one of the largest concentrations of rock art in the Iberian Peninsula. Dozens of shelters with Levantine and schematic paintings have been found in the mountains around the village, part of the UNESCO-listed Mediterranean group. The Solana de las Covachas and the Abrigo del Molino de Juan Basura are among the best known. The village has an interpretation centre that explains the rock art and organises guided visits to some of the shelters. The Abrigo de la Fuente is one of these sites, in a landscape that has changed little in centuries.

Nerpio is famous for its walnuts. The walnut trees along the Taibilla river are centuries old, and the local walnuts are prized for their quality. The village has a pleasant centre, with a church and narrow streets, and the surrounding countryside is full of old farmhouses, mills and irrigation channels.

The riding to and around Nerpio is spectacular. The roads that wind through the Sierra del Segura, toward Yeste, Letur, Moratalla and Santiago de la Espada, are narrow, twisty and remote, with almost no traffic and stunning scenery: mountains, gorges and pine forests. The road from Nerpio toward Pedro Andrés and the source of the Taibilla is especially beautiful. The surfaces vary, with some rough sections. In winter, snow can close the higher roads, and the nights are cold.

Services are very limited. Nerpio has a small shop, a few bars and a fuel station, but the nearest town of size is Huéscar, about thirty-six kilometres away, or Yeste. Fill up before you head into the mountains. Local food includes walnut-based dishes, game, cured meats and cheese. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.hadrian s wall vallum between field boun:
Hadrian's Wall runs for about seventy-three miles across the north of England, from the Solway Firth in the west to the Tyne in the east, built on the orders of the Emperor Hadrian after his visit to Britain in 122 AD. At these coordinates, north of Hexham near the village of Acomb, the wall crosses the gentle farmland of the Tyne valley, and what survives here is mostly the Vallum, a great earthwork that ran parallel to the wall on its southern side.

The Vallum was a broad, flat-bottomed ditch flanked by mounds of earth, and it marked the southern boundary of the military zone. Its exact purpose is still debated, but it probably controlled movement into the frontier zone from the south, forcing traffic through official crossings at the forts. In many places, the Vallum is more visible than the wall itself, as the stone of the wall was robbed for buildings and roads over the centuries. Hadrian's Wall is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire site.

The best-preserved sections of the wall lie further west, around Housesteads, Vindolanda and Steel Rigg, where the wall rides the crags of the Whin Sill. Chesters, a Roman cavalry fort on the North Tyne, is a short distance from Acomb and has a fine bath house. Corbridge, a few miles east, has the remains of a Roman supply town.

The riding along Hadrian's Wall is excellent. The B6318, known as the Military Road, was built in the eighteenth century, partly on top of the wall, and it runs along the frontier with long straights, dips and crests, and wide views over the moors. It is a popular road with bikers, but it is also notorious for accidents, with blind summits and sudden dips, so ride carefully. The roads north into Northumberland National Park and Kielder Forest are quiet and scenic. Weather is a big factor: rain, wind and fog are common, even in summer. Remember that the UK drives on the left.

Hexham, about six kilometres away, has fuel and all services, and a fine abbey. Local food includes stotty cake, a flat bread, and pies. Late spring and summer are the best seasons.
t.abrigo de los cortijos@38.5,-1.6:
Hellín is a town in the south-east of Albacete province, on the edge of the dry plains of La Mancha, where the landscape breaks into hills and ravines on its way down to the Segura river. Its old town climbs a hill crowned by a castle, and its streets are lined with houses from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. The Abrigo de los Cortijos lies in the hills about nine kilometres from the town, toward Albatana and Tobarra.

The area around Hellín is one of the most important for rock art in Spain. The site of Minateda, south of the town, has a large shelter with hundreds of painted figures, including Levantine hunters and animals, studied since the early twentieth century. The Abrigo de los Cortijos and the other shelters in the area belong to the same UNESCO-listed group, and they show how important this transition zone between the plateau and the Segura was for prehistoric communities. The area is also rich in Iberian and Roman sites, including the Tolmo de Minateda, a fortified hilltop town that later became a Visigothic bishopric.

Hellín is known throughout Spain for its Holy Week drumming, the Tamborada, when thousands of people in tunics beat drums in the streets for days on end. It has been recognised as a festival of international tourist interest, and the sound is overwhelming. Tobarra, nearby, has a similar tradition.

The riding around Hellín is good. The roads south toward the Segura river, the Cenajo reservoir and the Sierra del Segura are twisty and scenic, through pine forest and ravines, with little traffic. The road toward Isso, Liétor and Ayna follows the Mundo river through a gorge, with spectacular views; Ayna has been called the Switzerland of La Mancha for its dramatic setting. The surfaces are mostly good. Summer heat is intense, so ride early.

Hellín has fuel and all services, as does Tobarra. Local food includes the gazpacho manchego, the hearty stews of La Mancha, and the sweets of Holy Week. Spring and autumn are the best seasons for riding here.
t.abric de la creu@38.8,-0.6:
Ontinyent and Bocairent sit close together in the southern part of Valencia province, in the upper valley of the Clariano river, surrounded by the mountains of the Serra de Mariola and the Serra Grossa. Ontinyent is a textile town with a fine old quarter on a hill above the river, crowned by the tall bell tower of the church of Santa Maria. Bocairent, a few kilometres away, is a medieval village perched on a rocky outcrop above a ravine. The Abric de la Creu, the shelter of the cross, lies in the hills between the two.

The mountains around Ontinyent and Bocairent hold many painted shelters, with Levantine and schematic art, part of the UNESCO-listed group. The Abric de la Creu is one of them, a small, protected site. Bocairent also has a stranger site: the Covetes dels Moros, a series of artificial caves carved into a cliff face, accessible only by climbing, whose origin and purpose are still debated, perhaps granaries or refuges. The village also has a bullring carved out of the rock and an old snow well.

The Serra de Mariola, to the south, is a natural park known for its aromatic plants, which have been used for centuries in medicine and to make herbal liqueurs. The mountain is also the source of several rivers, and its springs and fountains are a feature of the landscape. Ontinyent is known for its Moors and Christians festival in August.

The riding around Ontinyent and Bocairent is excellent. The roads through the Serra de Mariola, toward Banyeres, Alcoy and Agres, are twisty and scenic, through pine forest and over passes, with little traffic. The road from Bocairent toward Banyeres climbs gently through the mountains. The road from Ontinyent toward the Vall d'Albaida and the Benicadell is also good. The surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel and cyclists.

Ontinyent, about three kilometres away, has fuel and all services. Local food includes the rice dishes of the area, and the herbal liqueur of the Mariola, the herbero. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.cueva de la clau@38.9,-0.2:
Behind Gandia, the orange groves climb into the folded limestone hills of La Safor, and among the tiny villages there, Palma de Gandía and Ador sit almost touching each other at the foot of the slopes. Cueva de la Clau is one of the many rock shelters in the Valencian hills that form part of the UNESCO-listed Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula, a scattered collection of hundreds of sites where prehistoric people painted hunters, animals, dancers and abstract signs on limestone overhangs. I cannot tell you exactly what is on the wall here, and many of these shelters are protected or fenced, so treat it as a place to understand rather than a gallery to tick off.

What you can enjoy without any restrictions is the landscape. The Serra de la Safor and Mondúver rise behind the villages, with craggy limestone ridges, pine and scrub, and the smell of orange blossom in spring so thick it almost feels like weather. Below, the coastal plain spreads toward Gandia and the sea, a patchwork of citrus orchards and irrigation channels that the Moors laid out more than a thousand years ago.

The riding is lovely in a small-scale way. Narrow roads link villages like Alfauir, Ador and Villalonga, with tight corners, short climbs and quick descents. The road that winds past the Monastery of Sant Jeroni de Cotalba, near Alfauir, is a pleasant detour; the monastery was founded in the fourteenth century and has a mix of Gothic, Mudejar and later styles. Traffic is light apart from tractors and the odd cyclist, but surfaces can be dusty and patched, especially after rain. Summer heat is intense, so early morning rides, ideally from October to May, make more sense.

Gandia is only a few kilometres away and has everything: fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and the ducal palace of the Borgia family, who came from here before one of them became Pope Alexander VI. On the coast, Gandia's beach is long and busy in summer, and the local speciality is fideuà, a seafood dish like paella but made with short noodles, said to have been invented by fishermen here. A plate of it at a beachside restaurant after a morning in the hills is hard to beat.
t.solana del molinico@38.3,-2.0:
Socovos is the sort of village you only find by getting a little lost: a cluster of white houses below a ruined castle in the far southeast of Albacete province, where the plains of La Mancha give way to the tangled ridges of the Sierra de Segura. Solana del Molinico, close by, is one of the rock-art shelters in this corner of Spain that belong to the UNESCO listing for Levantine rock art. The word solana means a sun-facing slope, and many of these painted overhangs face south, catching the warmth on winter days just as they must have done when hunters and gatherers sheltered here.

The paintings in this region typically show small human figures with bows, deer, ibex and abstract patterns, painted in red ochre thousands of years ago. Many shelters are locked behind grilles to protect them from vandalism and the elements, and visits are often arranged through local town halls or interpretation centres, so ask in the village before setting out on foot. Even without seeing a painting, the walk through the scrub of rosemary, thyme and pine, with eagles circling above, gives you a feel for why people stayed here.

The roads in this area are a quiet treat. The route between Socovos, Férez and Letur twists through olive and almond groves, past rock walls and dry riverbeds, with very little traffic. Letur, a dozen kilometres away, is a gorgeous village of Moorish origin with narrow lanes, water channels and a waterfall right in the centre. Further west, the roads climb toward Yeste and Nerpio into deep pine forest. Surfaces vary; expect patched tarmac and gravel at the edges, and watch for livestock and hunters' vehicles in season. Spring and autumn offer the best conditions, as summer can be scorchingly hot and winters surprisingly cold at night.

For reliable fuel, food and lodging, the nearest town of any size is Moratalla in Murcia, about seventeen kilometres away, though villages here often have a bar and a small shop. In Socovos itself, look for a bar where you can order a coffee and a plate of local cheese or the hearty gazpacho manchego, a game stew served on flatbread that has nothing to do with the cold soup of the same name.
t.gabar@37.8,-2.1:
High in the north of Almería province, far from the beaches most people associate with the name, the Sierra de María rises in grey limestone above a plateau of almond orchards and cereal fields. Gabar is a point in the hills between the villages of María and Vélez-Blanco, part of a cluster of rock-art shelters in the Los Vélez district. This corner of Spain is famous for one painted figure in particular: the Indalo, a little stick man holding an arc over his head, found in the Cueva de los Letreros just outside Vélez-Blanco. It has become the emblem of the whole province, painted on doors and sold as a lucky charm, which is a remarkable career for a prehistoric doodle.

Vélez-Blanco itself is crowned by one of the most dramatic castles in Andalusia, a Renaissance fortress on a rock built for the Fajardo family in the early sixteenth century. Its marble courtyard was sold off in the early twentieth century and ended up in the Metropolitan Museum in New York, so what you see today is the shell, still imposing against the sky. María has a lovely shrine in the pines above the village and a botanical garden that introduces the plants of the Sierra de María-Los Vélez natural park.

The riding is excellent and empty. The road from Vélez-Rubio via Vélez-Blanco to María winds through dry hills, almond terraces and pine woods, with long views and very little traffic; beyond María, roads continue toward Orce and Huéscar across a high, bare plateau where the wind can be relentless. Winters are properly cold up here, with frost and occasionally snow, while summer days are hot but the nights are cool. Late February, when the almond trees blossom pink and white across the slopes, is unforgettable.

Vélez-Rubio, about fifteen kilometres away, is the main town of the district, with fuel, supermarkets, banks and restaurants, and a surprisingly grand baroque church for a place its size. María and Vélez-Blanco have bars and simple restaurants serving local dishes like migas, fried breadcrumbs with garlic and peppers, or hearty bean stews. If you are heading into the hills, carry water and a snack; distances between villages are longer than they look on the map.
t.zona 1@38.1,-2.4:
Nerpio is about as far from anywhere as you can get in mainland Spain. The village lies in the southwestern corner of Albacete province, close to the borders of Murcia, Granada and Jaén, in a high, wild landscape of limestone ridges, pine forest and deep river valleys. The area is known for two things: walnuts, which grow in huge old trees along the Taibilla river and are celebrated in local cooking, and one of the densest concentrations of prehistoric rock art in the Iberian Peninsula, part of the UNESCO-listed rock art of the Mediterranean Basin. The generic label Zona 1 points at the hills near the village, where rock shelters with painted figures are scattered across the cliffs.

Nerpio has an interpretation centre for its rock art, and guided visits to some of the shelters can be arranged there; the best-known sites, like the Solana de las Covachas, feature hunters, archers, animals and enigmatic figures painted in red and black. Even if you do not visit a shelter, the walk through the hills, with views over canyons and the scent of pine and thyme, is rewarding.

Getting here is a ride worth doing for its own sake. The roads from Yeste, Moratalla or Santiago de la Espada climb and twist through forested mountains, with tight bends, steep sections, and views over reservoirs and valleys. Traffic is minimal, but so are guardrails in places, and the surfaces can be rough or covered with gravel and pine needles. Weather can change quickly at this altitude, with cold winds and even snow in winter, while summer brings clear skies and dry heat. The local roads are popular with cyclists and hunters, so stay alert.

Nerpio has a few bars, a small shop and simple lodging, but do not count on finding fuel here at every hour. Yeste, about twenty-seven kilometres away, is a larger village with services, and Huéscar in Granada, close to forty kilometres, is the nearest town of over five thousand. Fill your tank before heading into the mountains and carry water and snacks. In Nerpio, try walnut cake or local lamb, and if you visit in autumn, you may catch the walnut harvest and festival.
t.abric mas de los perez@39.9,-0.7:
Between the Turia and the Palancia rivers, northwest of Valencia, the land rises into a maze of limestone mountains, pine forest and small villages that rarely see foreign visitors. The Abric del Mas de los Pérez is a rock shelter in the hills near Andilla, Viver and Alcublas, one of hundreds of painted sites in eastern Spain listed by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean Basin. These shelters were decorated by hunter-gatherers and early farmers thousands of years ago, and while some feature vivid hunting scenes, many are faint and hard to see without a trained eye. Respect any fences and signs, and never wet or touch the rock.

Andilla is a quiet village with a surprisingly large Renaissance church, sometimes called the cathedral of the mountains, and a few streets of stone houses. Viver, in the Palancia valley, is known for its springs and fountains, which supply water to the region, and for its almond and olive orchards. Alcublas, to the south, is a small agricultural village surrounded by vineyards.

The roads around here suit riders who like twisty, empty mountain roads. The route from Viver to Andilla climbs through forested hills with tight bends and steep gradients, and the road from Andilla to Alcublas crosses a high plateau with views over the surrounding sierras. Surfaces are mostly decent, but expect potholes, gravel and the occasional landslide. Weather is generally mild, though winter nights can be frosty and summer days hot. Late spring and early autumn are especially pleasant, with green hills and fewer cyclists than near the coast.

For fuel and services, Segorbe, about twenty kilometres away in the Palancia valley, is the nearest larger town. It is an old episcopal city with a cathedral, a medieval aqueduct and a famous bull-running festival in September, where horses guide the bulls through the streets. Viver has a few restaurants, and a fountain-side bench to rest on. Local specialities include olla de pueblo, a hearty stew of beans, pork and vegetables, and embutidos, cured meats from the mountains. The A-23 motorway runs through the Palancia valley, linking Valencia with Teruel and Zaragoza, if you need to cover distance quickly.
t.olula@38.8,-1.0:
Caudete and Almansa sit in a corridor of land where Castile-La Mancha, Valencia and Murcia meet, and for centuries this was frontier country, where kingdoms and armies passed and fought. Olula is a point in the hills near Caudete, linked on the rides with rock-art shelters in the surrounding sierras, part of the extensive UNESCO listing of prehistoric art in Mediterranean Spain. I cannot tell you exactly what survives at the spot, but the dry limestone hills with pine and holm oak, looking down over vineyards and almond groves, are typical of the places where prehistoric painters left their marks.

Caudete, about eight kilometres away, is a town of around ten thousand people, historically linked to Valencia although it now belongs to Albacete province, and its people still speak with a Valencian accent. The town is known for its Moors and Christians festival in September, with parades, music and gunpowder, and a sanctuary dedicated to the Virgin of Gracia. Almansa, to the northwest, is dominated by a spectacular castle perched on a limestone crag right in the middle of town, and it was the scene of a decisive battle in 1707 during the War of the Spanish Succession, a victory for the Bourbon side that changed the political history of Spain.

The riding here is a mix of open plateau and hill roads. The main roads, including the A-31 motorway, run through the corridor between Albacete and Alicante and are busy with trucks, while the smaller roads toward La Font de la Figuera, Villena and the Sierra de Salinas are quieter, with curves and climbs through pine forest. The climate is continental, with hot summers, cold winters and strong winds in the open, so plan for wide swings in temperature between morning and afternoon.

Caudete has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, and Almansa offers more services, including hotels and bike repair shops. Local food reflects the meeting of regions: gazpacho manchego, a hearty game stew with flatbread, alongside Valencian rice dishes and Murcian vegetables. Villena, a short ride south, has another impressive castle and a museum with the treasure of Villena, a collection of Bronze Age gold vessels and jewellery that is among the most important in Europe.
t.diosa madre@38.3,-2.5:
Some places on a map feel remote; this one actually is. The point named Diosa Madre, mother goddess, lies in the mountains of the Sierra de Segura, in the far southwest of Albacete province, roughly sixteen kilometres from Yeste and not far from the border with Jaén. The name suggests a painted figure interpreted by someone as a female deity, which would fit the rich rock-art heritage of this corner of Spain, but I cannot confirm what is on the rock, and many shelters here are fenced off or difficult to find without a local guide. The mountains themselves are the real experience.

The Sierra de Segura is a wild landscape of limestone peaks, deep river gorges and vast pine forests, where the Segura river, one of the most important in southeastern Spain, begins its journey to the Mediterranean. Villages are small and scattered, many clinging to hillsides or perched on rocky outcrops, and the population has declined for decades as people moved to the cities. Wildlife is abundant, including ibex, deer, wild boar, griffon vultures and golden eagles, and the forests smell of resin and wild herbs.

Yeste is the main village in this area, with a castle that once belonged to the Order of Santiago and a lovely old town. The Fuensanta reservoir, on the Segura below Yeste, is a beautiful stretch of turquoise water surrounded by forest.

Riding here is a pure pleasure for those who enjoy mountain roads. The roads from Yeste toward Segura de la Sierra and Siles, or north toward Elche de la Sierra, twist and turn endlessly through the forest, with steep gradients, hairpins and spectacular views over the valleys and reservoirs. Surfaces vary from excellent to rough, with gravel and fallen rocks after storms, and there are few guardrails. Traffic is very light, but watch for logging trucks and animals. Winters are cold, with snow on the heights; summers are warm but cooler than the plains.

Yeste has fuel, a few shops, bars and simple lodging, and it is wise to fill up there before heading deeper into the mountains. Segura de la Sierra and Orcera, on the Jaén side, offer more services. Local food includes ajo pringue, a rich pork and liver spread, and roasted kid, washed down with robust local red wine.
t.canada de la cruz@38.1,-2.7:
From these coordinates, the nearest villages are all more than twenty kilometres away, which tells you where you are: deep in the Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park, the largest protected area in Spain, a vast expanse of limestone mountains, pine forests and river valleys in the northeast of Jaén province. The Cañada de la Cruz is a high valley or drovers' pasture in the Segura mountains; cañada is the word for the traditional livestock routes and grazing grounds used by shepherds moving their flocks between summer and winter pastures, and this part of Spain has a long history of transhumance.

Segura de la Sierra, the closest village of note, is one of the most spectacular in Andalusia, a cluster of white houses beneath a castle on a rocky peak, with views over a sea of olive groves to the west and mountains to the east. The poet Jorge Manrique, whose verses on his father's death are a landmark of Spanish literature, is traditionally said to have been born here. The village also has a Moorish bath and a unique square bullring carved into the rock.

The riding in the park is some of the best in southern Spain. Roads like the one from Segura de la Sierra over the mountains toward Santiago de la Espada, or along the Guadalquivir valley toward the Tranco reservoir and Cazorla, offer endless curves, steep climbs and descents, and wonderful views of forests, cliffs and lakes. The roads are narrow and often without guardrails, the surfaces can be bumpy, and in autumn and winter there may be ice in the shade. Deer and wild boar often cross the roads, especially at dawn and dusk, so ride with care. Weekends can be busy with visitors, but weekdays are quiet.

Services in the mountains are limited, so plan ahead. Beas de Segura, about twenty-five kilometres away, is the nearest town with more than five thousand people and all services, and Orcera and Segura de la Sierra have fuel, shops and restaurants. Local dishes include game stews, trout from the mountain rivers, and the excellent olive oil of the region, which you will taste on everything from toast to salads. Carry water and warm clothing, as the weather can change quickly in the mountains.
t.barranc de les coves abric i@38.7,-0.6:
Ibi is the toy capital of Spain, a fact that surprises everyone who rides through this mountain town in the hills of Alicante. Since the early twentieth century, workshops here have produced dolls, tin toys and plastic figures, and the Valencian Toy Museum tells the story. The rock shelter named Barranc de les Coves Abric I lies in the hills between Ibi and Alcoy, in a ravine whose name simply means the gully of the caves. It belongs to the network of painted shelters of the UNESCO-listed Mediterranean rock art, and while I cannot tell you what is painted on its walls, the location, with sheltered limestone overhangs above a valley, is typical.

The hills around Ibi and Alcoy are among the greenest in Alicante, thanks to higher rainfall and altitude. The Font Roja natural park, between the two towns, protects a forest of holm oak, maple, ash and yew on the slopes of the Carrasqueta range, unusual in this dry region, and there is a sanctuary with a spring at the top. Alcoy, about nine kilometres away, is a former textile town built on steep ravines crossed by bridges, with modernist buildings and the most famous Moors and Christians festival in Spain, held in April with spectacular parades.

The riding here is excellent. The N-340 between Alcoy and Xixona, over the Puerto de la Carrasqueta, is a classic: a long, winding climb with hairpins, sweeping bends and views down to the coast and Alicante, popular with riders and cyclists alike. The roads around Ibi, Onil and Castalla wind through pine forests and almond groves, and the climb to the Font Roja sanctuary is short but steep. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel and cyclists, especially on weekends. Winters can be cold, with occasional snow; spring and autumn are perfect.

Ibi has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Alcoy has a full range of services. Local specialities include olleta alcoyana, a hearty stew of beans and pork, and the coffee liqueur called licor café de Alcoy. Xixona, at the bottom of the Carrasqueta, is famous for turrón, the almond nougat eaten at Christmas throughout Spain, and you can visit factories and museums to see how it is made.
t.cueva de las conchas@38.1,-1.8:
Cehegín's old town rises in a tight cluster of ochre houses and church towers on a hill above the Argos river, in the northwest of Murcia, and it is one of the best-preserved historic centres in the region, with narrow streets, noble houses and churches dating back to the sixteenth century. The Cueva de las Conchas, the cave of the shells, lies less than a kilometre from the town, and it is part of the rich network of prehistoric sites in this area, included in the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean rock art. I cannot vouch for what is painted or preserved there, but the name suggests archaeological finds of shells, perhaps used as ornaments or food in prehistoric times.

Just a few kilometres away, Caravaca de la Cruz is one of the holy cities of Catholicism, thanks to a relic of the True Cross kept in the sanctuary-castle at the top of the town, and every few years it celebrates a jubilee year that draws pilgrims from all over the world. In early May, the town celebrates the festival of the wine horses, where teams of men run up the steep streets to the castle alongside richly decorated horses, a spectacle unique in Spain.

The riding in northwest Murcia is excellent and underrated. The roads from Cehegín toward Calasparra, famous for its rice grown along the Segura, or west toward Moratalla and the Sierra de Segura, wind through hills, river valleys and pine forests, with very little traffic. The Gran Vía del Noroeste, a fast road, links the area with Murcia city, but the minor roads are where the fun is. The climate is dry and hot in summer, with cold nights in winter; spring and autumn are ideal, and almond blossom in February is spectacular.

Cehegín has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Caravaca, about five kilometres away, has more services. Local food is hearty and delicious: arroz con conejo y caracoles, rice with rabbit and snails, migas, and the sweet yemas de Caravaca, made with egg yolk and sugar. The Bullas wine region, a short ride east, produces robust reds from the Monastrell grape.
t.barranc del salt abric l@38.7,-0.4:
Benilloba is a tiny village in the Comtat, the mountainous district north of Alcoy in the province of Alicante, with fewer than a thousand people, a church and a cluster of stone houses among olive and almond groves. The Barranc del Salt, the waterfall ravine, cuts through the hills nearby, and its first shelter is one of the many painted sites in the region that are part of the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean rock art. The Comtat and the neighbouring Alcoià are particularly rich in this heritage, with all three main styles of prehistoric painting represented: Levantine, schematic and the older Macro-schematic, unique to this small area, with large, enigmatic figures.

The landscape is rugged and beautiful. The Serra de Mariola, a natural park to the west, is famous for its aromatic herbs, used to make liqueurs and medicines, and its springs, and the Serra d'Aitana, the highest mountain in Alicante province, rises to the south. The villages are small and quiet, and the terraced hillsides tell of centuries of farming in difficult conditions.

The riding here is a joy. The roads from Benilloba to Penàguila, Alcoleja and the Aitana range climb through forests and terraces with endless curves and steep gradients, and the road over the Port de Tudons, near Aitana, is a classic. The road toward Cocentaina and Muro follows the valley of the Serpis river, with gentler curves and views of the mountains. Traffic is light, but watch for cyclists, especially on weekends, and for gravel on the corners. The weather is milder than the high plateau, but winters can be cold and snowy on the heights.

Cocentaina, about ten kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and a castle on a hill overlooking the town. Its All Saints' Fair, held in early November, is one of the oldest in Spain, dating back to the fourteenth century. Local food includes hearty mountain dishes like olleta, a stew of beans and pork, and pericana, a mix of dried peppers, salt cod and olive oil. Alcoy, a short ride south, offers more services and a lively town atmosphere.
t.abrigo del milano@38.0,-1.6:
Bullas is wine country, and the vineyards of Monastrell grapes roll over the hills around the town in the northwest of Murcia, producing robust red wines under their own denomination of origin.
