The Abrigo del Milano, the kite's shelter, named after the bird of prey that circles over these hills, lies in the countryside between Bullas, Mula and Pliego. It is one of the many rock shelters in Murcia with prehistoric paintings, part of the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean rock art, though access to many shelters is restricted to protect them, so ask locally before trying to visit.

Mula, about ten kilometres away, is a historic town with a castle on a rocky hill, built in the sixteenth century, and a lively old town with churches and convents. In Holy Week, the town hosts the Noche de los Tambores, a night of drumming when thousands of people beat drums through the streets from midnight until dawn, a deafening and unforgettable experience. Pliego, to the south, is a small village beneath the remains of a Moorish castle.

The riding here is varied and enjoyable. To the south, the Sierra Espuña, a natural park of pine forests and limestone peaks, has some of the best mountain roads in Murcia, with tight hairpins and spectacular views, and the old snow wells, built to store snow for the city of Murcia before refrigeration. The roads around Bullas wind through vineyards and almond groves, and west toward Cehegín and Caravaca de la Cruz, the landscape becomes more mountainous. Traffic is light on the minor roads, but watch for farm vehicles and cyclists. Summers are very hot, often exceeding forty degrees, so ride in the morning.

Bullas has fuel, shops and restaurants, as well as a wine museum that explains the local wine-making tradition, and several wineries offer tours. Local food includes arroz con conejo, rice with rabbit, migas and grilled lamb. In October, the town celebrates its wine festival. Mula has more services and a museum with Iberian artefacts. The thermal baths of Mula, a short distance from the town, offer a relaxing break after a long ride.
t.abric del voro@39.1,-0.8:
The Canal de Navarrés is a wide valley in the interior of Valencia province, surrounded by limestone mountains and deep gorges, and the Abric del Voro lies in the hills between Quesa and Bicorp, two small villages in the heart of some of the wildest country in the region. It is one of the many rock shelters with prehistoric paintings in the area, part of the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean rock art. The valley's most famous site is close by: the Cuevas de la Araña near Bicorp, where a painting of a figure climbing ropes to collect honey from a wild bees' nest, surrounded by bees, is one of the best-known images of prehistoric art in Spain, often cited as one of the earliest depictions of honey gathering.

The landscape is rugged and beautiful, with gorges, pine forests, olive groves and orange orchards in the valley bottom. Quesa is known for its natural pools, the Charco Azul and other blue pools in the river, which are popular for swimming in summer, and Bicorp has an interpretation centre for the rock art, where guided visits to the shelters can be arranged.

The riding here is excellent. The roads from Navarrés to Quesa and Bicorp, and on to the Júcar gorge and the reservoirs of Tous and Cortes de Pallás, wind through gorges and over mountains, with steep climbs, hairpins and spectacular views. Traffic is light, and the surfaces are mostly good, though gravel and rockfalls are possible. The road from Bicorp to the Muela de Cortes, a high plateau, is particularly wild and remote. Summers are very hot, and forest fires are a risk; winters are mild in the valleys but cold in the mountains.

Navarrés, about eight kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Enguera, a bit further, is the nearest town with more than five thousand people. Quesa and Bicorp have bars and small restaurants serving local food, including arroz al horno, rice baked with pork and chickpeas, and gazpacho de pastor, a game stew with flatbread. The honey of the region is excellent, a fitting souvenir after seeing the ancient honey gatherer.
t.east halladale@58.3,-3.7:
Strath Halladale is one of the emptiest valleys in mainland Britain, and East Halladale is a scatter of crofts and sheep fields along it. The A897 runs up the strath from Helmsdale on the east coast to Melvich on the north coast, following the Halladale River for much of the way, and for long stretches you will see more deer than cars. It is single track with passing places, so the rules are simple: pull in to let faster traffic by, wave, and never park in a passing place.

All around lies the Flow Country, a vast rolling blanket bog that UNESCO added to its World Heritage list in 2024. From the saddle it can look like nothing much, a brown and olive moorland broken by pools that shine silver under the clouds. In fact it is the largest expanse of blanket bog in Europe, peat built up over thousands of years, locking away enormous amounts of carbon. In summer the pools ring with the calls of greenshank, golden plover and dunlin, and divers nest on the lochans. At Forsinard, a little way south, the RSPB runs a visitor centre in the old station on the Far North Line, with a boardwalk out onto the bog that is worth half an hour.

The river is a famous salmon water, and the strath carries the memory of the Clearances, when nineteenth-century landlords pushed families off the land for sheep. The ruins of old townships are still visible if you know to look for them.

The road itself is a joy if you take it on its own terms. The surface is mostly decent but patched, with cattle grids, sheep that wander without warning and occasional loose gravel on the bends. Weather comes in fast off the Atlantic and the Pentland Firth, and a dry morning can turn into horizontal rain by lunch. Long June evenings give you light almost until midnight; midges in July and August are a real nuisance whenever you stop and the wind drops.

Plan fuel carefully. There is nothing reliable in the strath itself, and the nearest town of any size is Thurso, about thirty kilometres away, with Helmsdale and the north coast villages as the other options. Carry water, snacks and a warm layer, and enjoy a silence that is hard to find anywhere else in Britain.
t.abric del rincon del tio escribano@39.9,:
High in the interior of Valencia province, where the coastal orange groves give way to limestone plateaus and pine forest, the village of Titaguas sits on the road towards the Rincón de Ademuz. Close by lies the Abric del Rincón del Tío Escribano, a rock shelter with prehistoric paintings, one of the hundreds of sites that make up the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula, listed by UNESCO in 1998.

Levantine rock art, as it is known, shows people and animals in action: hunters with bows, deer in flight, sometimes scenes of gathering or conflict, painted in red or black under overhangs that protected them from the weather. The figures are often small, sometimes only a few centimetres high, and they reward patience. Many shelters are fenced off for protection and can only be visited with a guide by appointment, so check with the local tourist office before turning up and expecting to see anything up close.

The neighbouring village of Alpuente has one of the more surprising histories in the region: in the eleventh century it was the seat of a small Moorish taifa kingdom, and its castle ruins and old town walls still hang over the valley. The area is also known for dinosaur trackways in the surrounding rocks, which gives the place a pleasingly deep sense of time.

The riding is the real reward. The CV-35 runs from Valencia up through Llíria and the Turia valley to Chelva and Tuéjar, then climbs onto the plateau through Titaguas towards Ademuz, and it is one of the most popular motorcycle roads in the Valencian interior, with good surfaces, flowing bends and long views over ravines and terraced hillsides. Side roads branching off it are narrower and rougher but have even fewer cars. Expect cold mornings at altitude, even in late spring, and strong sun by midday. Gravel can collect on the bends after storms, and wild boar and deer cross at dusk.

Fuel needs some thought. Titaguas is small, and the nearest large town listed is Utiel, around thirty-six kilometres away, though Chelva and Tuéjar on the main road are more practical stops. Village bars serve hearty food: try the local cured meats, olla serrana, or a simple plate of eggs and potatoes after a cool morning in the hills.
t.andragulla i@38.2,-2.0:
In the far north-west corner of the Region of Murcia, where the land climbs towards the mountains of Albacete and Jaén, lies Moratalla, a town of whitewashed houses piled up a hillside beneath a castle tower. Its countryside is surprisingly wild for Murcia: pine forests, rivers, gorges and limestone ridges, some of the greenest land in a famously dry region. The rock shelter of Andragulla is one of many painted overhangs scattered through these hills, part of the Levantine rock art sites inscribed together by UNESCO. Many are protected behind fences and need a guide; the tourist office in Moratalla can advise.

Moratalla has a lively calendar. During Holy Week its streets fill with drummers, the tamboradas, who play for hours on end in an almost hypnotic rhythm, and in July the town holds bull runs through its streets as part of its main fiesta. Nearby Caravaca de la Cruz, a few kilometres east, is one of the holy cities of Catholicism, home to a relic of the True Cross, and its May festival features the Caballos del Vino, where teams of men race richly decorated horses up the hill to the castle.

The riding is excellent. Roads climb west from Moratalla into the Sierra de Moratalla and towards the Albacete border, through pine forest, over passes and down into deep valleys with rivers and orchards. Bends are plentiful, surfaces are mostly good, and traffic is minimal outside holiday weekends. The area is one of the least populated parts of Murcia, so the feeling of space is real. Watch for gravel, especially after rain, and for wildlife, including wild boar and the occasional ibex on the rocks.

The climate is more extreme than on the coast. Summer days are hot and dry, winter mornings can be frosty, and spring and autumn are glorious, with almond blossom in late winter and golden light on the hills in October. Rain, when it comes, can be heavy and sudden.

Moratalla, about twelve kilometres away, is a town of eight thousand people with fuel, shops and restaurants, and Caravaca is larger still. Try the local rice dishes with rabbit and snails, or a hearty stew, followed by sweets made by nuns or local bakeries, and take a walk up to the castle for the view.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum between the fi:
Here the Wall is at its most dramatic. In the central sector of Hadrian's Wall, north of Haydon Bridge and Hexham in Northumberland, the Roman frontier runs along the top of the Whin Sill, a long ridge of hard volcanic rock that breaks the moorland into a series of north-facing cliffs. The Romans built their wall right along the crest, using the natural defences, and the result is a line of stone that rises and falls with the crags like the spine of a great animal. Behind it, to the south, runs the vallum, a broad earthwork ditch with mounds on either side that marked the military zone, still clearly visible across the fields.

The Wall was begun in the early 120s on the orders of the emperor Hadrian, running from coast to coast for about seventy-three miles, with forts, milecastles and turrets along its length. Housesteads fort, a short distance west, is the best-preserved of them all, and Vindolanda, to the south-west, has yielded the famous writing tablets, letters and notes that bring the soldiers and their families vividly to life. To the east lies Carrawburgh, with a small temple to the god Mithras standing in a boggy field.

The main road through the area, the B6318, is known as the Military Road. It was built in the eighteenth century by General Wade's successors after the Jacobite rising of 1745, and for long stretches it was laid right on top of the Roman wall, using its stones. It runs straight across the moors with steep dips and blind crests that can launch a careless rider, so take care. The views are wide and wonderful, the traffic usually light, though tourist coaches are common in summer.

Weather here can change in an instant. A sunny morning can bring sideways rain by noon, and fog sometimes rolls over the crags, so pack waterproofs and warm layers in every season. Sheep wander freely on the road, and the surface can be greasy with mud near farm entrances.

Hexham, about thirteen kilometres away, is the market town for fuel, shops and food, with a fine abbey to visit as well. Pubs and cafés near the Wall offer hearty meals and a warm fire.
t.balma de la fabriqueta@39.7,-0.6:
The Serra Calderona is the green ridge that rises north-west of Valencia, separating the city's plain from the valleys of the interior. It is a natural park of pine forest, cork oak and rocky hills, close enough to the city for weekend walkers and riders, yet surprisingly wild once you get into it. The rock shelter of Balma de la Fabriqueta lies near the village of Olocau on its southern side, one of the painted shelters that make up the Levantine rock art inscribed by UNESCO. Access to many of these sites is restricted or guided, so check with the local tourist office before trying to visit.

Olocau sits at the foot of the hills, a small village with an Iberian hillfort, the Puntal dels Llops, on a ridge above it. The fort was a watchtower for the Iberian city of Edeta, which stood where Llíria is today, and from its walls you can see over the coastal plain to the sea. Llíria, a few kilometres away, is a lively town known as the city of music, with two famous rival brass bands that each have their own concert hall, and it has Roman and Iberian remains, including a sanctuary and bath complex.

The Calderona is fragrant with pine and herbs, especially after rain, and in spring it is full of wildflowers. In summer the risk of forest fires is high, and access to some areas may be restricted on days of high danger. Autumn and winter are pleasant for riding, with mild temperatures and clear air.

The roads through the Calderona are a favourite with Valencia's motorcyclists. Twisty routes climb from Olocau and Marines over the ridge towards Gátova and Segorbe, with tight bends, steep climbs and fine views, and traffic is light on weekdays. Surfaces are mostly good, but gravel, cyclists and occasional animals call for attention. On weekends the roads are busier, and police checks are not unusual.

Llíria, about eight kilometres away, is the nearest larger town, with fuel, shops and restaurants, and Olocau has a few bars and a shop. The obvious food to try in this part of Spain is paella, cooked properly over a wood fire in many country restaurants at weekends, with chicken, rabbit and beans rather than seafood, as the Valencians insist it should be.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum between the b6:
East of Hexham, the Roman frontier crosses gentler country, a rolling landscape of fields, hedges and small woods north of the Tyne valley. Here the Wall itself has mostly disappeared, its stones long since recycled into farmhouses, field walls and the eighteenth-century Military Road that runs along its line. But the vallum, the broad ditch with mounds on either side that marked the southern edge of the military zone, survives in places as a clear earthwork across the fields, and walkers on the Hadrian's Wall Path follow it for miles. This section is part of the same World Heritage site as the dramatic crags further west.

Just south lies Corbridge, an attractive stone town on the Tyne. The Romans built a fort and then a town there, called Coria, where Dere Street, the main road north into Scotland, crossed the river. The remains of granaries, a fountain and streets can be seen at the Roman site just west of the modern town, and the museum displays finds such as the Corbridge Lion, a sculpture of a lion attacking a stag. Nearby, Aydon Castle is a fortified manor house from the thirteenth century, built to resist raiders in the troubled border country.

The riding here is pleasant. The Military Road runs fast and straight along the line of the Wall, with occasional dips and crests, while minor roads wander through the countryside to villages, farms and the Tyne valley. Traffic is moderate, heavier near Hexham and Newcastle, and the roads are generally good, though farm vehicles and mud are common. Weather in Northumberland is changeable, with frequent rain and strong winds, and winter can bring snow and ice on higher ground.

For a longer ride, head north into the empty hills and forests of Northumberland National Park, or east to the coast, with its castles at Bamburgh and Dunstanburgh. The Tyne valley also offers quiet roads following the river.

Corbridge, Prudhoe and Hexham all have fuel, shops and cafés, with Prudhoe the largest town nearby. Try a stottie, a large, flat bread roll from the north-east, filled with ham and pease pudding, or stop at a country pub for a pie and a pint after the ride.
t.munsary shielton@58.4,-3.3:
Inland from Wick, in the far north-east of Scotland, the land flattens into a vast, rolling expanse of peat bog, brown and gold, dotted with pools and lochans that reflect the sky. Munsary and Shielton are areas of this blanket bog, part of the Flow Country, which was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2024 as the largest expanse of blanket bog in Europe. Here, sphagnum mosses have built up peat over thousands of years, storing vast amounts of carbon, and the bog teems with life: insect-eating sundews, cotton grass waving white in summer, and birds such as golden plover, greenshank and dunlin nesting among the hummocks.

The land looks empty, but people have lived here for thousands of years. Just south of Munsary stand the Grey Cairns of Camster, two remarkable Neolithic chambered cairns, great piles of stones covering passages and chambers built around five thousand years ago. You can crawl inside along low passages to stand in the chambers, an eerie experience. The surrounding area is rich in standing stones, brochs and ancient sites.

Wick, the nearest town, was once the busiest herring port in Europe, with hundreds of boats crowding the harbour in the season. The heritage centre tells that story well. Wick also has Ebenezer Place, which holds the record as the shortest street in the world, and a distillery producing whisky with a salty, maritime character. To the south, the Whaligoe Steps descend a cliff to a tiny harbour, where women once carried baskets of fish up hundreds of steps.

The riding is open and lonely. Single-track roads with passing places cross the bog, with long straight stretches, gentle curves and huge skies. Traffic is minimal, but sheep, deer and the occasional tractor demand attention, and the surface can be rough. Weather is the main challenge: wind blows almost constantly across the open landscape, rain can arrive suddenly, and in winter the days are very short. Summer brings long days with light until late at night, though midges can be a nuisance when the wind drops.

Wick, about fifteen kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafés. There is little in between, so plan ahead. Try fresh seafood, smoked salmon or a fish supper, and a dram of the local whisky, once the riding is done.
t.summer palace@40.0,116.3:
The Summer Palace is the Qing court's idea of escaping the city, and even with the modern capital spread out around it, the idea still works. The core is Kunming Lake, a large artificial basin, with Longevity Hill rising from its northern shore and covered in halls, pavilions and the tall Tower of Buddhist Incense. The Qianlong Emperor shaped the garden in the mid eighteenth century, reportedly to celebrate his mother's birthday, and modelled parts of it on the scenery around West Lake in Hangzhou. British and French troops burned it during the Second Opium War in 1860, and the Empress Dowager Cixi rebuilt it later in the century, which is where the famous story comes from that she paid for it with money meant for the navy. The marble boat moored at the lakeshore, which cannot sail, has become the punchline of that tale.

The Long Corridor running along the shore is the thing to walk, painted with thousands of scenes from legends and novels on its beams. Go early, ideally right at opening, because by late morning tour groups fill it shoulder to shoulder. Winter brings a sharp, clean light and sometimes ice on the lake; spring has blossom and the sandy wind from the north; summer is hot, humid and crowded.

As for the riding, be realistic. The palace sits in Haidian district, northwest of the centre, inside the urban sprawl, and Beijing places strict limits on motorcycles, especially those not registered in the city and especially inside the inner ring roads. Check the current rules before you plan a route, and expect heavy traffic, electric scooters on every side and very little in the way of enjoyable corners until you head out toward the Western Hills. Once you do, the roads climbing toward Fragrant Hills and beyond into Mentougou get properly interesting, with switchbacks and temples tucked into the valleys.

Fuel, food and every other service are everywhere around the palace; this is a city of millions. There are noodle and dumpling places within a short walk of the gates, and the area near Peking University and Tsinghua to the east has cheap student food. Park legally, keep your helmet with you and give yourself half a day inside: the grounds are much bigger than they look on a map.
t.abrigo del engarbo@38.1,-2.6:
Deep in the Sierra de Segura in the northeast of Jaén province, close to where the Segura river is born, the Engarbo rock shelters hide a few small painted figures under limestone overhangs. They belong to the great serial UNESCO listing of Levantine rock art, prehistoric paintings found along the mountains of eastern Spain, with stylised humans and animals in red ochre that have survived thousands of years of sun, frost and goats. The shelters are modest and fragile, often fenced, and visits usually need to be arranged locally, so treat them as a reason to explore this remote corner rather than a guaranteed sight.

And remote it is. The area falls inside the Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park, one of the largest protected areas in Spain, a vast sea of pine-covered ridges, deep valleys and limestone cliffs. Black pine and Aleppo pine cover the slopes, griffon vultures circle overhead, and ibex and deer are common enough that you should ride the bends expecting one standing in the road. The Segura rises from a spring near Pontones and becomes the river that later waters the orchards of Murcia; up here it is clear and cold.

The roads are narrow, often single carriageway with crumbling edges, and twist relentlessly through the mountains. There are spectacular stretches over passes and past reservoirs, but also fallen rocks, gravel washed across bends after rain, and blind corners where a truck loaded with timber appears without warning. Plan for slower progress than the distances suggest. Spring and autumn are lovely; midsummer is hot in the valleys but bearable up high, and winter can bring snow above a thousand metres.

Services are scarce. Nerpio, Segura de la Sierra and Orcera are small mountain villages; Segura de la Sierra in particular is worth the detour for its castle perched on a crag and its whitewashed streets. For reliable fuel, plan around the larger towns, and Huéscar, about thirty kilometres away, is the nearest place of eight thousand people. Fill the tank whenever you see a station. Village bars serve grilled meat, migas and local olive oil of extraordinary quality, and the water from the mountain fountains is usually clean and cold.
t.fuensanta ii@38.2,-2.1:
Fuensanta II is the sort of name only an archaeologist could love, a numbered rock shelter in the hills of northwest Murcia where prehistoric painters left a handful of figures on the stone. It is one of the hundreds of sites grouped under UNESCO's listing of rock art in the Mediterranean Basin of the Iberian Peninsula, and the Moratalla area is unusually rich in them. The paintings are small, faint to the untrained eye and protected, so the real value of coming is to understand the landscape that drew people here thousands of years ago: springs, shelter and game in rough, broken country.

The town of Moratalla, a little under twenty kilometres away, climbs a hillside under the ruins of its castle, with narrow streets that are better walked than ridden. Its municipality is huge and mostly mountain, covered in pine and holm oak, cut by river gorges and dotted with farmhouses. Nearby Caravaca de la Cruz is a place of pilgrimage built around the relic of a holy cross, and it has its own jubilee years that fill the town with visitors. Its old centre and hilltop sanctuary are worth a slow look.

The riding is excellent if you like quiet mountain roads. Routes west of Moratalla toward Nerpio and the Albacete border wind through the Sierra de Moratalla with constant bends, short climbs and few cars. The scenery shifts between dry red earth, almond and olive groves on the lower slopes and denser pine woods higher up. Expect some broken tarmac, gravel in corners and occasional livestock. The heat in July and August is brutal at midday, so ride in the morning and late afternoon; spring is green and full of flowers.

Moratalla, with about eight thousand inhabitants, is the place to stop for fuel and food; Caravaca, with over twenty-five thousand, has more choice. Once you head deeper into the mountains, services thin out quickly, so leave with a full tank. Try local rice dishes, lamb, and the area's sweet pastries, and on a hot day ask about the river pools around the Benamor and Alhárabe, which locals use to cool off.
t.palmeral of elche@38.3,-0.7:
Riding into Elche from the dry hills of southern Alicante, the sudden forest of date palms feels like a mistake of geography, as if a piece of North Africa had been set down in Spain. In a sense it was. The palm groves were laid out in their present form during the Islamic period, when Arab settlers brought an irrigation system of channels fed by the Vinalopó river and arranged the orchards in walled plots, with palms on the edges and crops beneath. Tens of thousands of palms remain today in and around the city, the largest palm grove in Europe, and the Palmeral was added to the UNESCO list in 2000.

The most famous garden is the Huerto del Cura, where a palm with several trunks growing from one base, known as the Imperial Palm, gets photographed by just about everyone. Elche also gave the world the Dama de Elche, the mysterious Iberian bust found at La Alcúdia in 1897 and now in Madrid, and every August the Basilica of Santa María hosts the Misteri d'Elx, a sung medieval drama about the Assumption of the Virgin that UNESCO also recognises. In spring you will see palm fronds being blanched and woven for Palm Sunday, a craft for which the city is known across Spain.

As a riding stop, be honest with yourself. Elche is a city of over two hundred thousand, flat and busy, with roundabouts, delivery vans and the usual urban chaos. The rewards lie outside: the hills toward Aspe and Crevillente, the coastal road toward Santa Pola and its salt flats, where flamingos feed in the shallow lagoons. Summers are very hot and the air can be heavy with humidity from the sea, so early morning is the best time to move, and afternoons are best spent in the shade of the palms.

Practically, Elche has everything: fuel on all the main approaches, workshops, hotels, supermarkets. The city's shoe industry is famous, if you need new boots. Look for local rice dishes like arroz con costra, a baked rice with sausage and a crust of egg, and finish with dates or a glass of horchata. Parking near the gardens is easier on two wheels than four, but keep valuables with you.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum between the tr:
Just north of Hexham, the A road climbs out of the Tyne valley and meets the Roman frontier on a high, windy shoulder of Northumberland. Here, near Acomb, Wall and the crossing of the North Tyne at Chollerford, the line of Hadrian's Wall and its vallum runs across open farmland, sometimes visible as a low bank, sometimes followed by the road itself. Like every stretch of the frontier, it belongs to the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire, and this middle section is where the wall starts to feel serious, heading west into the wild central crags.

A little way along is Heavenfield, a quiet hillside with a wooden cross and a small church, where in 634 the Northumbrian king Oswald defeated the British king Cadwallon. According to Bede, Oswald raised a cross before the battle, and his victory helped establish Christianity in the north. It is a bleak but moving spot, with views across the valley and the wind singing in the grass.

The riding here is famous for one road in particular: the B6318, known as the Military Road, built after the Jacobite rising of 1745 to move troops quickly between Newcastle and Carlisle. Its builders used the Roman wall as a convenient source of foundations and stone, and in places the road sits right on top of it. Today it is a fast, rolling ride with long straights, blind crests and sudden dips, beloved by bikers and photographers alike. Be careful: the crests hide oncoming traffic, sheep wander freely, and the wind can be strong and gusty on the exposed sections. Low sun in the morning or evening is magical, but it can also blind you on the eastward and westward stretches.

Hexham, six kilometres away, is a market town of eleven thousand with fuel, supermarkets and the beautiful Hexham Abbey, whose Anglo-Saxon crypt was built by Wilfrid in the seventh century, partly with Roman stones from nearby Corbridge. Corbridge itself, a pretty village with a Roman town site on its edge, has good tea rooms and pubs. Pick up a Northumbrian pie, and if it is wet, do not be shy about warming up by a pub fire before continuing.
t.the flow country@58.4,-4.0:
Most people who first see the Flow Country think it is empty. It is not; it is simply flat, wet and enormous, and it takes a while to understand what you are looking at. Spread across Caithness and Sutherland in the far north of Scotland, this is the largest expanse of blanket bog in Europe, a landscape of peat built up over thousands of years, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2024. The surface is a patchwork of sphagnum mosses, cotton grass and heather, studded with countless small pools called dubh lochans that shine like broken mirrors when the sun comes out. Under your feet, the peat holds an extraordinary amount of carbon.

The birds are the stars. Greenshank, golden plover, dunlin and red- and black-throated divers breed here, along with hen harriers and merlins hunting low over the bog. At Forsinard, the RSPB has a visitor centre in the old railway station and a short boardwalk trail leading to an observation tower, which helps make sense of the scale. In the 1980s, tax incentives encouraged large conifer plantations on the bog, causing serious damage; decades of restoration work since then, including felling trees and blocking drains, are one of the great conservation stories of Britain.

Riding through the Flow Country is a unique experience. The roads are mostly single track with passing places, like the A897 through Strath Halladale, and they demand courtesy and patience: pull in to let others pass and wave thanks. The surface is often broken at the edges, and sheep and deer wander onto the road without warning. The wind can be relentless, and the weather can change from bright sunshine to horizontal rain in minutes. In summer, the light lasts almost all night; in winter, the days are short and dark.

Plan your fuel carefully. Thurso, nearly forty kilometres away, is the nearest town with full services, and petrol stations in the countryside are few and far between. Halkirk has a few amenities, but do not rely on finding fuel or food in the smaller hamlets. Bring warm clothing, rain gear and midge repellent, as the midges can be fierce on still summer evenings.
t.el pantanet@38.8,-0.6:
Few riders have heard of the Serra de Mariola, and that is a pity, because this little limestone range between Alcoi, Bocairent and Ontinyent is one of the most rewarding corners of inland Valencia. El Pantanet, near the village of Alfafara, is a small rock shelter with prehistoric paintings, one of the many sites in the UNESCO listing of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. As with most of its sisters, it is protected and access may be limited, but the hills around it reward the trip on their own.

The Mariola is famous for its aromatic plants: thyme, rosemary, sage, lavender and dozens of others, used for centuries in folk medicine and in herbero, a herbal liqueur made in the villages. On a warm day, the scent of the hills is intoxicating. The range is also dotted with old snow wells, deep stone pits where snow was packed in winter and turned into ice, then carried down to the coastal towns in summer for food preservation and cooling drinks. The village of Agres, with its sanctuary perched on the hillside, is a good starting point for walks up to the snow wells and the summit of the Montcabrer.

The riding is excellent. The roads that connect the villages of the Mariola, such as Alfafara, Agres, Bocairent and Alcoi, wind through valleys and over passes, with tight curves, steep climbs and fantastic views. Bocairent, a short ride west, is a dramatic village built on a rocky spur, with medieval caves carved into the cliff face. The roads are generally in good condition, with little traffic, but watch for cyclists and the occasional goat. Summer is hot, and winters can be surprisingly cold in the hills.

Ontinyent, five kilometres away, is a textile town of nearly thirty-eight thousand with fuel, shops and restaurants. Alfafara and Agres are small villages with a few bars and inns. Try the local dishes, such as olleta, a hearty bean stew, or arròs al forn, baked rice with chickpeas and sausage. Finish with a shot of herbero to settle the stomach before heading on.
t.barranc de frainos abric i@38.7,-0.3:
The mountains behind Benidorm are a world away from the high-rise hotels and the beaches. Inland from the Costa Blanca, the land rises quickly into a jumble of limestone ridges, the highest of which, the Serra d'Aitana, reaches over fifteen hundred metres, the roof of the province of Alicante. Between Sella, Benilloba and Relleu, deep in this rugged country, the Barranc de Frainos holds a rock shelter with prehistoric paintings, part of the UNESCO listing of Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. The sites here are small and fragile, and access is usually limited to guided visits, but the landscape is worth the journey.

The villages are small, white and perched on hillsides, surrounded by terraces of almonds, olives and cherries. In spring, the almond blossom turns the hills pink and white. Guadalest, a short ride south, is a dramatic village with a castle perched on a rocky spike, and the reservoir below is a striking turquoise. Alcoi, to the north, is an industrial town famous for its Moors and Christians festival in April, one of the most spectacular in Spain, with parades, music and mock battles. The Font Roja nature park, near Alcoi, protects a rare forest of oaks, maples and yews on a cool mountainside.

The riding is superb, with some of the best mountain roads in eastern Spain. The road over the Port de Tudons, between Sella and Alcoi, climbs through pine forests and over a pass, with tight bends and great views. The roads around Guadalest and Confrides are also excellent, with hairpins, cliffs and views of the sea. The surface is generally good, but watch for cyclists, who love these climbs, and for gravel and loose stones. In summer, the heat can be intense in the valleys, so ride early or late.

Cocentaina, about thirteen kilometres away, is a town of eleven thousand with fuel, shops and restaurants. Sella, Benilloba and Relleu are small villages with bars and a few restaurants. Try olleta alcoyana, a hearty bean and rice stew, or pericana, a dip of dried peppers, salt cod and olive oil, served with bread. Alcoi is also known for its café licor, a coffee liqueur.
t.cueva del nino@38.5,-2.2:
Ayna is a village of white houses clinging to the walls of a deep gorge carved by the Mundo river, in the Sierra de Alcaraz in the southwest of Albacete province. Its setting is so dramatic that it is sometimes called the Little Switzerland of La Mancha, and it was the backdrop for the cult Spanish film Amanece, que no es poco, a surreal comedy shot here in the late 1980s. A few kilometres away, in a rocky ravine, the Cueva del Niño holds something rare for this part of Spain: Palaeolithic paintings of deer, ibex and horses, much older than the Levantine figures painted later on the same walls. It is part of the UNESCO listing of Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula, and access is restricted to protect the paintings.

The Mundo river rises not far away, near Riópar, where it bursts out of a cave in a series of waterfalls called Los Chorros, spectacular after the spring rains. The sierra is covered in pine and oak forests, with limestone cliffs, gorges and caves, and it is home to ibex, deer, eagles and vultures. The air is fresh and fragrant with pine and wild herbs.

The riding is excellent, with winding roads through the mountains and gorges, steep climbs and descents, and very little traffic. The road into Ayna from the plain is a series of hairpins down into the gorge, with stunning views. The roads to Bogarra, Molinicos and Riópar follow river valleys and climb over passes, with tight curves and changing surfaces. Watch for gravel, fallen rocks and animals on the road. The weather is continental: hot in summer, cold in winter, with snow possible on the higher roads.

Ayna and Bogarra are small villages with bars and restaurants, but fuel is scarce, so fill up in Hellín, about forty kilometres away, or in Albacete. Try gazpacho manchego, a hearty stew of game meat and flatbread, or atascaburras, a mash of potatoes, salt cod and garlic. The local olive oil and cheese are excellent, and the honey from the sierra is delicious.
t.abric pedro mas@38.9,-1.1:
Almansa announces itself from far away: a castle perched on a limestone crag right in the middle of the town, its walls and towers silhouetted against the sky. The town sits at the eastern edge of La Mancha, where the high plateau meets the mountains of Valencia, and it was here, in April 1707, that one of the decisive battles of the War of the Spanish Succession was fought, when the Bourbon army defeated an allied force and secured the throne of Spain for Philip V. A monument on the battlefield and a museum in town tell the story. In the hills to the north, near Alpera, the Abric Pedro Mas holds prehistoric paintings, part of the UNESCO listing of Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. Nearby, the Cueva de la Vieja is one of the best-known Levantine sites, with archers, deer and goats.

The landscape around Alpera is open and dry, with fields of cereals, vineyards and almond trees, surrounded by rocky hills covered in pine and scrub. To the east, the Ayora valley leads into the mountains of Valencia, with deep gorges, rivers and the vast Caroig massif. Wind farms line some of the ridges, a sign of the strong winds that sweep across the plateau.

The riding is good, especially if you like empty roads and open landscapes. The roads around Alpera and Almansa are mostly straight, with some curves through the hills, and very little traffic. To the east, the road through the Ayora valley and over the mountains to the coast is more winding and scenic. The wind can be strong and gusty, especially on exposed sections. Summer is hot and dry, while winter is cold, with frost and occasional snow.

Almansa, about nine kilometres away, is a town of twenty-six thousand with fuel, shops and restaurants. Alpera, a small village, has a few bars and a visitor centre for the rock art. Look for ajo mataero, a rustic paste of pork liver, bread and spices, or gachas, a porridge of flour, garlic and pork. The local wines, especially the reds made from Garnacha Tintorera, are robust and full of flavour.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum between sunnyb:
Just east of the point where the A68 crosses the line of Hadrian's Wall, at Portgate, the Romans had a gateway through the frontier for Dere Street, the great road running north from York into Scotland. Today the A68 follows much the same course, and the wall and its vallum run east and west across the fields here, sometimes visible as a bank or a ditch, sometimes buried under the Military Road. A little to the east, the fort of Halton Chesters, known to the Romans as Onnum, lies under the fields, and like the rest of the frontier, this stretch is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire.

The countryside here is the rolling heart of Northumberland, with farmland, hedges, woods and scattered stone farms, and big skies that change from sun to rain in minutes. A short ride south, Aydon Castle is a remarkably well-preserved fortified manor house from the late thirteenth century, built for a wealthy merchant and fortified against the raids that plagued the border for centuries. Corbridge, nearby, has a Roman town site, once a supply base for the wall, with granaries, temples and a museum full of finds.

The riding is excellent, with the Military Road heading west along the wall, fast and rolling, with crests, dips and long straights. Heading north on the A68, the road dips and climbs over the moors toward the Scottish border at Carter Bar, with long, straight sections that rise and fall like a roller coaster, popular with riders. Watch for hidden dips, which can hide oncoming traffic, and for sheep, which wander freely. The weather can be cold, wet and windy, even in summer.

Corbridge, five kilometres away, is a pretty village with a few pubs, cafés and shops, and Hexham, about nine kilometres off, is a market town with fuel and supermarkets. Try a Northumbrian stotty cake, a flat, chewy bread roll filled with ham or bacon, or a plate of fish and chips. The local pubs serve real ales from small breweries, and a pint by the fire is the perfect end to a day on the wall.
t.renaissance monumental ensembles of ubed:
Úbeda stands on a ridge above an ocean of olive trees. In every direction, the province of Jaén rolls away in silver-green rows, millions of trees planted in geometric lines up to the horizon, and on this sea floats a town of honey-coloured stone that looks as if it had been lifted from Florence. In the sixteenth century, powerful local families who served the Spanish crown, above all Francisco de los Cobos, secretary to Emperor Charles V, poured their wealth into palaces and churches here, and the architect Andrés de Vandelvira gave them a Renaissance style of rare purity. Úbeda and its smaller neighbour Baeza were inscribed together on the UNESCO list in 2003.

The Plaza Vázquez de Molina is the heart of it: the Sacra Capilla del Salvador, built as a funerary chapel for Cobos, the Palacio de las Cadenas, now the town hall, and a row of noble façades around a long, quiet square. Walk it in the late afternoon, when the stone glows and the swifts scream overhead. The town also has a tradition of pottery, with workshops in the old potters' quarter still producing green-glazed ware.

Riding into Úbeda is a pleasure in itself. The roads across the olive country are smooth, generally quiet and full of long, flowing bends over the hills, and the views open wide on every crest. Eastward lies the Sierra de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas, Spain's largest protected area, where the riding becomes properly mountainous, with tight climbs through pine forest, deer on the road and the source of the Guadalquivir. It is one of the best motorcycling regions in Andalusia.

In summer, Jaén is brutally hot, often over forty degrees, so ride early and rest through the afternoon as the locals do. Spring and autumn are glorious. Fuel, food and lodging are plentiful in a town of thirty-five thousand. Order anything cooked in the local extra virgin olive oil, and if you are curious about the town's famous sons, the singer-songwriter Joaquín Sabina was born here, while the poet Antonio Machado taught in Baeza, a short ride away.
t.penon de santo espiritu@39.7,-0.3:
Behind the orange groves of the Camp de Morvedre, a few kilometres inland from Sagunto, the land rises into the Sierra Calderona, a low range of pine woods, scrub and red sandstone that separates the coastal plain from the dry interior. The Peñón de Santo Espíritu is a rocky outcrop in these hills above the village of Gilet, and it carries prehistoric rock art in the Levantine tradition, the style of painted hunters, animals and human figures found in shelters along the Mediterranean side of Spain and listed by UNESCO as the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. The paintings are fragile and often protected, so do not expect to wander up and touch anything.

The name comes from the Franciscan monastery of Santo Espíritu del Monte, founded in the fifteenth century in a quiet valley above Gilet and still home to a community of friars. Its gardens, cloister and pine-shaded surroundings make a peaceful stop, and the walks from there into the Calderona are fragrant with rosemary and resin. Valencians come here at weekends to escape the coast's heat and noise.

For riders, the Calderona offers short but satisfying roads: the climbs from Gilet and Serra up toward the Portacoeli monastery and over to the Turia valley are narrow, twisty and usually quiet on weekdays, with views back toward the sea. Watch out for cyclists on weekends, gravel on bends and the odd wild boar at dusk. Summer brings high fire risk, and some forest tracks can be closed.

Sagunto, seven kilometres away, is where to refill the tank and eat. The town's hilltop castle stretches along the ridge for nearly a kilometre, with layers of Iberian, Roman, Moorish and Christian walls, and the Roman theatre below was controversially restored. In 219 BC Hannibal besieged Saguntum, starting the Second Punic War. A plate of paella valenciana or arroz al horno in a village restaurant makes the perfect end to a hill loop.
t.cueva de los pucheros@38.2,-1.6:
North-west of Cieza, the Segura river cuts through a dry landscape of limestone ridges, almond and fruit orchards, and rice fields that look out of place in arid Murcia. The Cueva de los Pucheros, a rock shelter in these hills between Cieza and Calasparra, is one of the many sites in the region holding prehistoric paintings, part of the UNESCO-listed Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. Like most of these shelters, it is fragile and often protected by a fence, and access may require a guided visit arranged through the local authorities.

The Segura valley around here is an oasis. The river supports a narrow green strip of orchards, palm trees and reed beds, and Calasparra is famous for its rice, grown since the fourteenth century in paddies watered by the cold mountain river and protected by its own designation of origin. It is the rice to use for a proper paella or arroz con conejo. In late February and early March, the peach and nectarine orchards around Cieza burst into pink blossom, and the floración draws visitors from all over Spain.

The riding is excellent and underrated. The roads between Cieza, Calasparra and Moratalla wind through gorges and over dry hills with long sightlines, very little traffic, and good surfaces. Head north toward the Sierra del Segura for more serious mountain roads. Summer heat is fierce, so carry water and ride early, and watch for loose gravel on bends after storms.

Calasparra, around eleven kilometres away, has fuel, bars and restaurants, and the Santuario de la Virgen de la Esperanza, built into a rock cave above the river, is an atmospheric stop. Cieza, a larger town, has more choice. The river gorge between Calasparra and Cieza, known as the Cañón de Almadenes, is also popular for rafting, and its caves contain more rock paintings, a reminder that people have been living along this river for many thousands of years.
t.cavidad v@38.2,-2.2:
Nerpio is about as far from anywhere as you can get in mainland Spain. This village of around sixteen hundred people sits in the Sierra del Segura, in the far south-west of Albacete province, close to the borders of Murcia and Andalusia, and the surrounding hills are dotted with shelters containing prehistoric paintings. The numbered sites around here, Cavidad V among them, are part of the UNESCO-listed Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin, and the Nerpio area is one of the richest concentrations of Levantine art in Spain, with hunting scenes, archers and animals painted thousands of years ago.

Visits to the shelters are usually organised from the village's interpretation centre, and a guide is generally required because the sites are protected and sometimes hard to find. The paintings can be faint, and they show best in the right light, so it pays to plan ahead. The surrounding landscape is dramatic: limestone ridges, pine forests, deep river valleys, and terraced fields of walnuts, for which Nerpio is well known.

The roads in the Sierra del Segura are a motorcyclist's dream, if you like tight bends and few people. They twist through gorges and over passes, with long climbs and descents and an almost total absence of traffic. The surfaces vary from excellent to rough, and there may be gravel, rockfall or livestock around any corner. Winters are cold, and summer storms can be violent. This is the kind of place where you see more goats than cars.

Plan your fuel carefully: Nerpio is small, and the nearest reliable larger town is Moratalla, nearly thirty kilometres away by winding road, with Yeste another option. Food in the area is simple and robust, with lamb, game, and gazpacho manchego, a hearty stew made with flatbread. Spend a night in the village if you can, and look at the stars, which are spectacular in this remote corner of Spain, then ride out at dawn, when the light on the cliffs is warm and the valleys are still in shadow.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum between the ma:
Most people meet Hadrian's Wall in the wild middle section around Housesteads, where it rides the crags of the Whin Sill. Out here at the eastern end, a few miles from Newcastle, it is a quieter, more domestic affair, and that is part of its charm. Heddon on the Wall, four kilometres away, keeps one of the longest surviving stretches of the wall's full broad foundation on this side of the country, a solid run of masonry beside the road, and the ground around it preserves the vallum, the great flat-bottomed ditch with banks on either side that the Romans dug just south of the wall to mark the military zone. Begun under the emperor Hadrian in AD 122, the whole frontier ran from the Tyne to the Solway, and it is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage Site.

The road you will want is the B6318, the Military Road, which starts near Heddon and runs west toward Chollerford and beyond. It was built in the 1750s after the Jacobite rising, when General Wade's army had struggled to move between Newcastle and Carlisle, and the engineers simply laid much of it on top of the Roman wall, using the stones as foundation. That is why it runs so ruler-straight, rising and falling over the swells of the land like a roller coaster. Those blind summits are the hazard: there are hidden dips where oncoming cars disappear, and the road has a reputation for serious crashes, so overtake only with a clear view.

The Tyne valley below is green, wooded and gentle. Wylam, just down the hill, is where George Stephenson, the railway pioneer, was born in a cottage by the river, and the old wagonway along the Tyne is now a path. Northumbrian weather changes fast, and wind and rain can sweep in from the west in minutes even in summer, so pack waterproofs. On a good evening, though, the light over the fields is soft and long, the curlews call, and the line of the vallum shows clearly as a shadow across the grass.
t.the vallum between oatens bank@55.0,-1.9:
Look south of the road near Oatens Bank, just west of Heddon on the Wall, and you will see it: a broad, flat-bottomed ditch running across the fields, with a low mound on either side. That is the vallum, and it is one of the strangest and most debated elements of Hadrian's Wall. It runs parallel to the wall, a short distance to the south, along most of its length, and it seems to have marked the rear edge of the military zone, controlling access from the south rather than defending against attack from the north. Crossings were limited to causeways opposite the forts, which suggests a kind of customs line.

Here it is unusually well preserved, partly because the farmland around has been used as pasture rather than ploughed. On a sunny morning or late in the day, low light makes the earthworks stand out, and you can follow the line by eye for some distance across the countryside. The Hadrian's Wall Path runs nearby, and walkers pass through in summer heading east toward Wallsend or west toward Bowness-on-Solway.

The road through here is the Military Road, the B6318, which was built on the line of the wall itself, and you are riding on top of Roman stones for much of the way west. It is straight, undulating and exposed, with dips that can hide oncoming traffic and crosswinds that can catch you on the high points. Watch out for farm vehicles, walkers crossing, and sheep that have found a gap in the fence.

This part of Northumberland is rural and quiet, but you are never far from services. Prudhoe and Hexham, in the Tyne valley to the south, have fuel, pubs and shops, and Corbridge, with its Roman town and pleasant streets, makes a good lunch stop. Further west, the wall becomes more dramatic around Chesters, Housesteads and Vindolanda, and the Military Road runs on toward Greenhead and Carlisle, giving one of the finest historic rides in Britain.
t.port de confrides abric i@38.7,-0.3:
Inland from Benidorm, barely half an hour from the high-rise towers and the beach crowds, the mountains of Alicante rise steeply and the whole mood changes. The Port de Confrides is the saddle on the CV-70 between the Guadalest valley and the upland basin of Confrides and Benasau, with the long limestone wall of the Sierra de Aitana to the south. t.abrigo del pozo iii@38.2,-1.6:
The Segura river cuts through the north-west of Murcia in a series of gorges and green oases, and near Calasparra its banks hold a surprising treasure. A good plan is to combine a visit to the sanctuary with lunch in Calasparra and an afternoon ride through the gorges, stopping at viewpoints over the river. Evening light on the red cliffs and green rice paddies is magical.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum between the fi:
East of Carlisle, near the market town of Brampton, Hadrian's Wall crosses a landscape of rolling farmland, hedges and woods along the valley of the River Irthing. Here the wall and its vallum, the great earthwork ditch that ran behind it on the southern side, cross fields where the stone has mostly been robbed for farm buildings, but the earthworks remain clearly visible as long ridges and hollows in the grass.

The wall was begun around AD 122 on the orders of the emperor Hadrian, and ran about 73 miles from the Solway Firth to the Tyne. The vallum was a ditch with mounds on either side, marking a military zone behind the wall and controlling movement. Along this stretch, the wall originally was built of turf before being rebuilt in stone. A few kilometres east lies Birdoswald, one of the best preserved forts on the wall, and nearby the ruins of Lanercost Priory, founded in the twelfth century and built partly with stone taken from the wall.

The riding around Brampton is pleasant country stuff: narrow lanes between stone walls and hedges, gentle hills and occasional views across to the Pennines to the south. The roads are often damp, sometimes muddy from farm traffic, and sheep may wander onto them. To the east, the B6318, known as the Military Road, follows the line of the wall for many miles, built in the eighteenth century partly on top of the Roman foundations. It is fast, straight and undulating, with hidden dips that can surprise you, so ride with care.

Brampton, about five kilometres away, is a small market town with fuel, shops and pubs, and Carlisle, twenty kilometres west, has all services and a castle and cathedral worth visiting. The weather here changes fast, with rain and wind sweeping in from the west, so pack waterproofs even in summer. In late spring the hedges bloom white with hawthorn, and lambs fill the fields. Walk a little along the line of the wall and you will feel the scale of the Roman effort, and the loneliness of the soldiers stationed here.
t.abric de les finestres iv@38.8,-0.6:
Bocairent is a village built on a rock, its old houses clinging to a limestone spur above a ravine in the Serra de Mariola, in the south of the province of Valencia. Summer is hot in the valleys but cooler in the mountains, and winters can bring frost and occasional snow at altitude.

t.abric de la fos@38.9,-0.6:
The Vall d'Albaida is a broad valley in the south of the province of Valencia, between the Serra Grossa to the north and the Serra de Mariola to the south, and its towns grew wealthy on textiles. t.canaica del calar l@38.2,-2.2:

t.los grajos@37.9,-1.4:

t.cueva del peliciego@38.5,-1.3:
Jumilla is wine. The town has a castle on a hill and a Roman monument, the Casón, a late Roman mausoleum.

The roads cross the high plain through vineyards, with long straights and gentle curves, and climb into the surrounding mountains with more winding routes. Traffic is light, and the surfaces are generally good. The climate is continental, with hot summers and cold winters, and the light is bright and clear. The best seasons are spring and autumn, especially the harvest in September and October, when the vineyards are busy and the air smells of grapes.

Jumilla, six kilometres away, is a town of twenty-five thousand with fuel, shops and restaurants. Many wineries offer tours and tastings, though tasting should wait until the riding is over. t.izquierda e de santonje@37.8,-2.2:
The Indalo is everywhere in Almería: a little stick figure holding an arc over its head, painted on houses, sold as a souvenir and used as the symbol of the province. t.stone circle@55.0,-2.4:
Long before the Romans built their wall across northern England, people were raising stones on these moors. Pubs along the Wall serve hearty food and local ales. t.crooks roman temporary camp@55.0,-2.6:
The Roman army on the march built a camp every night: a rectangle of ditch and rampart, with tents inside, defended by sentries. t.ubeda@38.0,-3.4:

t.raco de la cova dels llidoners@38.8,-0.1:

t.arroyo de la fuente de las zorras@38.1,-:
