Yeste and Segura de la Sierra are also small. Village bars serve simple, hearty food: roast lamb, gazpacho manchego, which here is a game and flatbread stew rather than a cold soup, and local cheese and cured meats.

April, May and October are ideal, with green or golden hills and comfortable temperatures. Summer brings heat and the risk of forest fires, winter can bring snow to the higher roads. A ride through these mountains is a step back in time, through a landscape that has been inhabited, hunted and painted for thousands of years.
t.rio frio@38.1,-2.6:
Cold water is a rare luxury in southern Spain, and a stream called Río Frío promises exactly that. These coordinates lie deep in the Sierra de Segura, the vast mountain range that straddles the provinces of Jaén and Albacete and forms part of Spain's largest protected area, the Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park. It is a land of pine forests, limestone crags, deep river gorges and tiny villages, and the painted rock shelters scattered through these hills are part of the UNESCO listing of rock art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula.

Not far away, near Pontones, the River Segura itself rises from a spring before starting its long journey to the Mediterranean, and the Guadalquivir is born a little further south in the Sierra de Cazorla. The forests of black pine, some of them centuries old, are home to Spanish ibex, deer, wild boar and griffon vultures that circle over the cliffs. In spring the meadows are full of wild flowers, in autumn the smell of resin and damp earth fills the air.

Segura de la Sierra, about twenty-five kilometres away, is one of the most spectacular villages in the region, perched on a hilltop below a restored Moorish and Christian castle, with views over the valley of olive trees below. The poet Jorge Manrique is traditionally said to have been born there. Orcera, at the foot of the hill, is a small town with basic services.

The roads in the Sierra de Segura are a rider's dream: twisting, narrow, steep, with endless curves through forest and along gorges, and very little traffic. Surfaces vary from good to rough, and gravel, fallen rocks and animals are common hazards. Distances on the map look short, but the time needed is long, so plan for a slow pace and plenty of stops.

Fuel is scarce. Fill up in Orcera, Huéscar or one of the larger towns before heading into the mountains, and carry water and some food. Village bars serve simple meals, often with game, lamb or trout from the mountain rivers. Avoid midsummer if you can, when heat and fire risk are high, and winter, when snow can close the higher roads. In spring and autumn, a day in these mountains feels like a week anywhere else.
t.hadrian s wall between the road to garth:
The Emperor Hadrian visited Britain in AD 122 and ordered a wall built from coast to coast, and the soldiers who did the work left their marks in stone that still stands across the north of England. The section near Brampton, in Cumbria, lies toward the western end of the Wall, where it crossed gentler country toward Carlisle and the Solway Firth. Here the Wall was first built partly in turf and later rebuilt in stone, and the remains of turrets, milecastles and the ditch can still be traced in the fields. Hadrian's Wall is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire.

A few kilometres to the east lies Birdoswald, one of the best-preserved forts on the Wall, overlooking a loop of the River Irthing, and nearby is one of the longest continuous stretches of Wall, running across the open country with a fine view. Lanercost Priory, a beautiful ruined Augustinian monastery partly built with stone taken from the Wall, sits by the river near Brampton and is well worth a stop.

The riding in this area is quietly excellent. Roads wind through rolling farmland and moorland, with long views to the Pennines and the Scottish hills. The B6318, known as the Military Road, follows the line of the Wall to the east, built in the eighteenth century after the Jacobite rising using stone from the Wall itself, and it rolls and dips along the ridge with blind crests that can catch out the unwary. Watch for sheep, cattle, tractors and walkers crossing the road, and for the wind, which can be strong on the high ground.

Brampton, about two kilometres away, is a small market town with fuel, shops, cafés and pubs, and a distinctive octagonal moot hall in its centre. Carlisle, around sixteen kilometres west, is a city with a castle, a cathedral and the excellent Tullie House museum, where you can learn more about the Wall and the Roman frontier.

Weather in this part of England is changeable, with rain and wind common at any time of year. Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with long days and fewer crowds. Find a stretch of Wall away from the car parks, sit on a stone and look north across the empty land, the way a Roman sentry might have done on a grey afternoon nearly two thousand years ago.
t.abric de la penya banya@38.7,-0.5:
Somewhere in the limestone folds around Cocentaina, under an overhang of rock, people painted small figures thousands of years before anyone here had heard of Rome. The rock shelters of this part of Alicante belong to the great family of Mediterranean rock art that runs down the eastern side of Spain, recognised together by UNESCO, and the Abric de la Penya Banyà is one of these quiet, unassuming sites. Expect faded red pigment on pale stone, often protected behind a grille, and a short walk from the nearest track rather than a visitor centre.

The setting is the valley of the Serpis, closed in by the Serra de Mariola to the west and the long ridge of the Benicadell to the north. Cocentaina sits right at its heart, a town of around eleven thousand with a castle tower on a hill above and a counts' palace in the old centre. A few kilometres away Alcoy fills a tight knot of ravines with bridges and textile mills, and it is famous across Spain for its Moors and Christians festival in April, when the streets fill with costumed armies, gunpowder and brass bands. Locally made sugared almonds and the herbal liqueur of the Mariola hills are small, sweet souvenirs that travel well in a tank bag.

For a rider, this is excellent country. The roads climbing into the Mariola toward Agres, Bocairent or the high plateau behind Alcoy are narrow and twisting, with pine and holm oak, honey-scented scrub and views back over the terraced valley. The surfaces vary from fresh to patched, and in summer the heat comes up off the rock by late morning, so start early. Spring is the best season, when the almond blossom is done, the hillsides are green and the air smells of thyme and rosemary. Winter can bring frost on the higher shaded bends.

Cocentaina and Muro de Alcoy both have fuel, cafés and the kind of bar where a coffee and a slice of tortilla appear almost before you sit down. Water is worth carrying if you plan to walk to any of the shelters, as tracks are stony and shade is rare. Treat the art with patience: the figures are tiny, the light matters, and they reveal themselves slowly. Stand still for a minute, let your eyes adjust, and the little archers and animals begin to move.
t.coves roges abric i@38.8,-0.3:
Planes looks like a village that has been arguing with gravity for a thousand years and winning. Its houses climb a hill crowned by the remains of a Moorish castle, and the whole place overlooks a valley of olive and almond terraces that falls toward the Beniarrés reservoir. The Coves Roges, the red caves, lie in the broken limestone country around here, and the first of their shelters carries prehistoric paintings, part of the scattered rock art of the Valencian mountains. The colour in the name is not poetry: the rock itself is stained a warm iron red.

This corner is called the Vall de Perputxent, a small, folded world between the Serra de Benicadell and the Serra d'Almudaina. Settlements are tiny, from Benimarfull with a few hundred inhabitants to Beniarrés and Planes, and they still feel agricultural rather than touristic. Close to Planes, the Barranc de l'Encantà hides a cascade and a deep green pool, and the name, the ravine of the enchanted woman, comes from a local legend about a Moorish girl who appears by the water. On a hot day the pool is the most sensible place in the valley.

The riding is small-scale and very satisfying. Lanes wind between stone terraces and through olive groves, dropping into ravines and climbing out on tight, blind bends where you should always expect a farmer's pickup coming the other way. The reservoir road gives open water views and a slightly faster rhythm, and the climb toward the Benicadell ridge offers big vistas across the Vall d'Albaida. Gravel and dust collect on corners after storms, and goats occasionally take an interest in the tarmac. Late afternoon light turns the red rocks almost orange.

Practically, these villages are too small to count on fuel, so fill up in Muro de Alcoy or Cocentaina before heading in. Planes and Beniarrés have bars where locals will feed you without fuss, usually something with rice, beans or a slab of grilled meat, and the coffee is strong. Carry water if you walk to the shelters: the paths are short but steep and stony. And give yourself a few unhurried minutes at the top of Planes, by the castle, where the whole valley lies below and the only sounds are a church bell and a dog somewhere far away.
t.benizar v@38.3,-2.0:
Benizar is one of those places that only a handful of maps bother to name. It is a hamlet belonging to Moratalla, in the hilly north-west of the Murcia region, close to where the province meets Albacete and the first ridges of the Sierra de Segura begin. Around it, in the rock faces and gullies, archaeologists have recorded a cluster of painted shelters, and Benizar V is one in this series: a stone overhang with faint prehistoric figures, part of the Levantine rock art that runs along Spain's eastern mountains.

The land feels big and dry. Pine woods alternate with almond and olive groves, and patches of irrigated green follow the streams. Socovos, with its castle on a crag, lies just over the boundary in Albacete, and the Segura river cuts deep gorges to the west. In early spring the almond blossom drifts across the hillsides like snow; by July the heat is serious and the air hums with cicadas. Eagles are common, and at dusk you may see wild boar crossing the road, which is a good reason not to be riding fast after sunset.

The roads in this part of Murcia are one of the region's best-kept secrets for motorcyclists. They wind through the sierra with long, well-cambered bends and climbs that open onto wide views, and traffic is almost non-existent away from market days. Surfaces are generally decent, though the minor lanes to the shelters can be broken or gravelled. Distances between villages are long, and the landscape can be lonely in the best sense.

Moratalla is the place to refuel and eat. It is a town of about eight thousand built up a steep hill under a castle, with narrow streets that are more fun to walk than to ride. Nearby Caravaca de la Cruz is one of the holy cities of Catholic Spain, home to a relic of the True Cross and a jubilee year that draws pilgrims every few years, while Calasparra is known for rice grown in paddies along the Segura, a surprise in such dry country. In any of them you can get a proper lunch at a reasonable price. Carry water if you walk out to the shelters, tell someone where you are going if you leave the bike for long, and come in spring or autumn when the light is soft and the hills are kind.
t.barranc del xorquet@38.7,-0.1:
Ask a cyclist on the Costa Blanca about Coll de Rates and watch their face change. The pass road climbing from Parcent toward Tàrbena is a pilgrimage for professional teams in winter training, and it lies only a few kilometres from the Barranc del Xorquet, one of the ravines in the tangled limestone hills behind the coast. This is an area rich in prehistoric rock art: the shelters at Pla de Petracos near Castell de Castells hold some of the best examples of the so-called macro-schematic style, big abstract human figures painted in red thousands of years ago, and the ravines around here hide further sites.

The villages are tiny. Bolulla has a few hundred people and a ruined castle, Castell de Castells perches on its upland, and Parcent sits in the Jalón valley among vineyards and orange groves. Inland of the tower blocks of Benidorm, the landscape becomes another world: terraced almond and olive groves, cherry trees in the high valleys, dry ravines full of oleander, and mountains like the Serrella and Aitana closing the horizon. In February the almond blossom turns whole hillsides white and pink.

For riding, this is the good stuff. The roads are narrow, often freshly surfaced thanks to the cycling tourism, and they twist endlessly, with tight hairpins on the climbs and views opening to the Mediterranean on the way down. Share them politely with the cyclists, who come in big groups in winter and spring and expect to be passed with room. Blind bends are the norm, and a delivery van can appear at any moment. Wind can be strong over the passes, and the descents into the coastal valleys get warm fast.

Fuel is scarce in the hill villages, so fill up in Callosa d'en Sarrià or la Nucia before climbing in. Callosa is also the gateway to the Fonts de l'Algar, a chain of waterfalls and turquoise pools that make a fine cool break in summer, though they get crowded at weekends. Village bars in the hills serve robust mountain food, from rice dishes to stews, and the local orange juice is fresh and cheap. If you want to see the rock art, check access first, carry water and wear something better than riding boots for the walk. Then return to the bike, pick a road at random, and let the hills do the rest.
t.cova llarga@38.8,-0.3:
The Benicadell is the mountain that tells you where you are in this part of Valencia. Its long, sharp limestone ridge, topped by a distinctive rocky tooth, separates the Vall d'Albaida from the valleys of Alcoy and Cocentaina, and on clear days it is visible from the coast. The Cova Llarga, the long cave, sits on the southern side of this world, in the folded hills near Beniarrés, Terrateig and Planes, and it belongs to the scatter of small sites that record people living, painting and sheltering in these hills since prehistory.

The local geography is all ridges and pockets. Terrateig, with fewer than four hundred inhabitants, looks north over the Vall d'Albaida, a broad valley of vineyards, orange groves and old textile towns like Albaida and Ontinyent, which once made blankets for half of Spain. To the south, the Beniarrés reservoir holds the waters of the Serpis. Agriculture still shapes everything: terraces built by generations of hand labour, irrigation channels that go back to Moorish times, and stone huts in the fields where farmers once spent the night at harvest.

The roads here are made for unhurried riding. The climb over the shoulder of the Benicadell links the valleys with a string of tight bends and wide views, and the descents into the Vall d'Albaida flow nicely between the vines. Expect narrow lanes, rough edges, the occasional tractor and plenty of cyclists at weekends. Spring and autumn bring the best conditions; in summer, ride early and hide from the midday sun in a village bar. Watch for wind on the exposed passes and gravel washed out of field tracks after storms.

The small villages around the cave do not reliably have fuel, so plan on Muro de Alcoy, Albaida or Ontinyent. For food, the Vall d'Albaida is known for its hearty cooking, from rice baked in the oven to stews of beans and turnip, and for its sweets and pastries. A village bar will often have just one or two dishes of the day, which is usually a good sign. If you go looking for the cave on foot, take water, sturdy shoes and a sense of humour about paths that fork without signs. When you get back to the bike, look up at the Benicadell ridge, now familiar, and you will have a fixed point for the rest of the ride.
t.cantos de la visera i@38.7,-1.3:
Monte Arabí rises from the high plain north of Yecla like a ship run aground, a lonely mass of sandstone with flat top and fluted sides, and locals have told stories about it for centuries: Moorish treasure, enchanted caves, a hidden city. The real treasure is painted. The Cantos de la Visera shelters on its slopes hold prehistoric rock art, including Levantine figures of animals and schematic signs, and they belong to the great series of Mediterranean rock art sites listed by UNESCO. There are also strange carved holes and basins in the rock, whose purpose is still debated.

The country around is the altiplano of north-eastern Murcia, a high, open land of vineyards, almond orchards and cereal fields around six hundred metres up and more. Yecla is the town, some thirty-five thousand people, known across Spain for two things: furniture factories and wine. The Yecla appellation grows mostly Monastrell, a dark, sun-loving grape that makes rich reds, and the bodegas are scattered across the plain. Montealegre del Castillo and Fuente-Álamo, small towns over the border in Albacete, add castles and quiet squares.

For riding, this is wide country. The roads run straight for long stretches between vineyards, then kink over low ridges or swing around the base of a sierra. They are generally well surfaced and very lightly used, which makes them relaxing rather than technical, with big skies and the kind of light that photographers love at the end of the day. The wind across the plateau can be strong, and summer temperatures are high, though nights are cooler than on the coast. In winter, mornings can be frosty. The tracks around Monte Arabí itself are dirt and gravel, so leave a heavy road bike at the end of the tarmac.

Yecla is the place for fuel, a mechanic if needed, and food. Local dishes lean toward the hearty: gazpacho manchego, a game and flatbread stew that has nothing in common with the cold soup, plus rice, lamb and local sweets. Access to the shelters is regulated and sometimes guided, so check before you go and carry water, as there is little shade on the mountain. Afterwards, ride back across the plain in the evening, when Monte Arabí glows red behind you and the vineyards turn to long blue shadows.
t.the roman fort@55.0,-2.1:
Down by the North Tyne, where the river runs fast over stones under a canopy of trees, a Roman cavalry regiment once kept its horses and its very comfortable bath house. Chesters, the fort the Romans called Cilurnum, sat astride Hadrian's Wall near the village of Walwick, guarding the bridge that carried the wall across the river. It is one of the best preserved forts along the wall, with the headquarters building, the commander's house and the bath house still standing to knee or shoulder height, and the remains of the bridge abutment visible on the far bank.

The fort was preserved largely thanks to John Clayton, a nineteenth-century town clerk of Newcastle who bought up long stretches of the wall and its forts to protect them from stone robbers. The museum on site, a charming Victorian building, displays his collection of altars, inscriptions and sculptures, crowded together in the old style. Hadrian's Wall, built from AD 122 across the narrowest part of Britain, is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire listed by UNESCO.

The riding is one of the joys of the north of England. The B6318, the Military Road, runs west from here along the line of the wall. It was built in the eighteenth century by General Wade's successors after the Jacobite rising, partly on top of the wall itself, and it rises and falls over the crags with blind crests, sudden dips and long views. It is a fabulous road, but treacherous: the crests hide cars, sheep and walkers, the surface can be rough, and the weather changes in minutes. Summer weekends bring tourists, while autumn brings fog and wet leaves.

Hexham, six kilometres south, is the place for fuel, food and lodgings, a lively market town with a fine abbey. Acomb is a small village with a pub. The local food is hearty, from pies to fish and chips, and Northumberland lamb is excellent. A tearoom at the fort serves cakes and hot drinks, welcome after a cold ride. Walk down to the river and look across at the bridge remains; Roman engineers built them to last, and the river has been trying to wash them away ever since.
t.roman fort@55.0,-1.6:
Newcastle got its name from a castle built in 1080 by Robert Curthose, eldest son of William the Conqueror, but the hilltop he chose above the Tyne had already been used for centuries. Beneath the Castle Keep and the Black Gate lie the remains of Pons Aelius, a small Roman fort that guarded a bridge across the river near the eastern end of Hadrian's Wall. The name honoured Hadrian himself, whose family name was Aelius. Outlines of the fort are marked in the paving around the keep, and the Swing Bridge below crosses the river close to where the Roman bridge stood.

The wall ran east from here to Wallsend, where the fort of Segedunum has been excavated and has a museum and a viewing tower. Westward, its line follows the West Road out of the city, with fragments visible in suburbs like Denton and Heddon-on-the-Wall. Newcastle itself grew rich on coal, shipbuilding and engineering, and its quayside, crossed by a famous series of bridges, from the High Level of Robert Stephenson to the tilting Millennium Bridge, is the heart of the city's revival.

The riding is urban. Expect heavy traffic, one-way systems, bus lanes and cobbles on the steep streets of the old quayside. The Side, which climbs from the quay to the cathedral, is cobbled and steep, and in the wet it deserves care. Parking near the castle is limited, so it is easier to leave the bike on the edge of the centre and walk. Once out of the city, though, the A69 and the Military Road lead west along the wall into some of the best riding in England.

Fuel, food and every service are on hand. Newcastle's food scene ranges from traditional pies and pease pudding, a spread of split peas, to modern restaurants in the Ouseburn valley. The city's nightlife is famous, and its people, the Geordies, are known for their friendliness and humour. Climb the Castle Keep for a view of the bridges and the river, and look down at the lines of the Roman fort below. Two thousand years ago, soldiers here were watching the same river, probably complaining about the same weather.
t.barranc de les covatelles@38.7,-0.3:
Guadalest is a tiny village on a rock, entered through a tunnel cut in the stone, with a castle, a bell tower perched on a pinnacle and a view over a turquoise reservoir below. It is one of the most visited places in the province of Alicante, and it sits at the heart of a valley surrounded by mountains: the Aitana, the highest in the province at over fifteen hundred metres, the Serrella and the Xortà. The Barranc de les Covatelles is one of the ravines in this mountainous country, near Benimantell, Sella and Castell de Castells, with rock shelters that hold prehistoric paintings, one component of the World Heritage inscription for the rock art of the Mediterranean Basin.

The villages in this area are small, with a few hundred inhabitants each, and their life revolves around almonds, olives, cherries and, increasingly, tourism. Sella is a famous climbing destination, with limestone cliffs drawing climbers from across Europe, especially in winter. Benimantell, close to Guadalest, has restaurants serving mountain cuisine. The Aitana, whose summit is occupied by a military base, has forests of pine and holm oak, springs and snow pits, where snow was once stored to be sold as ice in the summer.

The riding is excellent. The roads around the Guadalest valley are twisty and narrow, climbing over passes with views over the mountains and down to the sea. The road from Guadalest toward Confrides and the Port de Tudons, a pass of over a thousand metres, is particularly fine, with long curves and few cars. Road quality is fair to good, but there are cyclists in large numbers, especially in winter and spring, and tourist coaches near Guadalest. Watch for gravel and goats. Summer is hot, while winter is mild, though the high roads can see frost and snow.

Guadalest and Benimantell have restaurants and shops, but for fuel, head to Callosa or Alcoy before setting out. Food here is mountain cuisine: olleta, a stew of beans and meat, embutidos, cured sausages, and pericana, a dish of dried peppers and salt cod. Local cherries, in season, are delicious. Visit Guadalest early in the morning, before the coaches, then ride into the mountains and leave the crowds behind.
t.abrigo del buen aire i@38.5,-1.3:
Jumilla country is dry, wide and honest. The town sits in the far north of Murcia where it bulges up towards Albacete, surrounded by limestone sierras, almond groves and vineyards of Monastrell grapes that make some of the most powerful red wine in Spain. A few kilometres outside town, in the folds of these hills, lie a group of small rock shelters known as the Abrigos del Buen Aire. They belong to the long chain of prehistoric painted sites strung along the eastern side of the peninsula that UNESCO lists together as the rock art of the Mediterranean Basin.

Do not expect a museum. These are shallow overhangs in the rock where people painted small figures, often schematic signs or stylised humans and animals, in red ochre. Many shelters are fenced to protect them, and some can only be visited with a guide arranged through the town, so treat the stop as a chance to stand in the landscape the painters knew rather than a guaranteed viewing. The setting does a lot of the work anyway: pale stone, esparto grass, the smell of rosemary and pine when the sun warms it, and a silence broken only by wind.

The riding around Jumilla is straightforward and pleasurable. The main roads to Yecla, Hellín and Cieza are broad and quick, with long sightlines across the plain, while the minor roads that climb into the sierras, towards Ontur or around the Sierra del Carche to the south, bring tighter bends and rougher surfaces. Dust and loose grit collect on the shoulders, and agricultural traffic is common at harvest time in September and October. Summer here is brutal; midday temperatures can be dangerous on a bike, so ride at dawn and hide in the afternoon like the locals do.

Jumilla itself, about seven kilometres away, has everything you need: several petrol stations, bars serving tapas and cold beer, and a castle on the hill above the old town with wide views over the vineyards. Many bodegas offer tastings, though that is a pleasure for the evening when the bike is parked. If you need a reason to linger, the monastery of Santa Ana del Monte on the hillside south of town is a quiet, shaded spot for a break. Carry more water than you think out here, and do not count on finding anything open between the villages after two o'clock.
t.barranc de l infern conj 4@38.8,-0.1:
There is a valley behind the Costa Blanca that most beach visitors never suspect, and the Barranc de l'Infern cuts right through it. Between the Vall de Laguar and the Vall d'Ebo, a river gorge drops deep into the limestone, and the old mule paths that zigzag down one side and up the other are among the most famous walks in the Valencian region, sometimes called the cathedral of hiking for the thousands of stone steps laid by the Moorish farmers who once worked these terraces. The set of rock-art shelters recorded under this name lies around the gorge, part of the wider prehistoric painted landscape of the Marina Alta.

The history of the valleys is not gentle. After the Christian conquest the farmers here remained Muslim in faith or in culture, and in 1609, when the Moriscos were expelled from Spain, the people of these mountains rose in revolt and made a last stand around the Vall de Laguar before being defeated and shipped away. The villages were later resettled, and the terraces, ruined farmhouses and dry-stone walls you see from the road are partly their work.

For riders, the area is a playground. The CV-712 from Pego climbs through the Vall d'Ebo and on towards Castell de Castells in a seemingly endless series of tight, cliff-edged bends, narrow and often patched but blissfully quiet. Close by, the Coll de Rates above Parcent is a local favourite with cyclists and bikers alike, a smooth climb with views down to the coast. On these roads you share space with goats, the odd tractor and climbers' vans, and the surface can carry gravel washed down from the slopes after storms, which hit hard here in autumn.

The hamlets nearest the pin, Murla, Vall de Ebo and Tormos, are tiny. You might find a bar in the square but do not count on fuel; Pego and Orba to the east, or Benissa and Dénia nearer the coast, are where to fill the tank. Spring is glorious, with almond blossom and wild flowers on the terraces, and autumn is good once the heat breaks. In midsummer the gorge becomes a furnace by late morning, so arrive early, take water, and if you fancy a walk down into the barranc, leave the boots on the bike and wear something you can actually climb steps in.
t.abric del gegant@38.8,-0.6:
Ontinyent is the kind of Valencian town that does not bother selling itself to tourists, which is part of its charm. It grew rich on textiles, and the old quarter of La Vila, perched above the gorge of the Clariano river, still has a fine bell tower that is among the tallest in the region. The Abric del Gegant, a rock shelter recorded among the prehistoric painted sites of eastern Spain, sits in the hills just outside town towards Bocairent, where the valley narrows and the Serra de Mariola begins to rise.

Bocairent, only a few kilometres away, is worth the detour. The village is piled up on a rocky spur, its streets tumbling down to a ravine, and in the cliffs nearby are the Covetes dels Moros, a honeycomb of man-made windows cut high in the rock whose original purpose nobody has fully explained. The Mariola is also full of old ice houses, the cavas de neu, where snow was packed in winter and sold as ice to the coastal towns in summer. The mountains smell of herbs; this is where local liqueurs and the herbal Herbero come from.

The riding is a big part of the appeal. The CV-81 links Ontinyent with Bocairent and Banyeres in a quick, flowing line, while the smaller roads over the Mariola, towards Agres and Alcoi, and the climb around the Benicadell ridge to the north are tighter, narrower and much more fun. The surfaces vary from silky to crumbling, and in winter the higher bends can be frosty in the morning; this is a cooler inland corner of Valencia, and fog can sit in the valleys. Late spring and early autumn are perfect, with green slopes and warm afternoons.

Practically, it could hardly be easier. Ontinyent is a sizeable town with several petrol stations, supermarkets and plenty of bars where a mid-morning almuerzo of a bocadillo and a coffee costs little and sets you up for hours. Locals swim in summer at the Pou Clar, a series of natural pools in the river gorge just below town, a lovely place to cool off on a hot day. If you are looking for the painted shelter itself, ask locally; access to many of these sites is restricted to protect the figures, and the experience is as much about the country they were painted in as the pigment on the rock.
t.queso@37.7,-2.2:
The far north of Almería surprises people who think the province is all desert and greenhouses. Up here, around the villages of María and Vélez-Blanco, you are in the Sierra de María-Los Vélez natural park, a range of limestone mountains covered with pine and holm oak, with snow in winter and cool nights even in August. The site recorded on the map simply as Queso sits in the hills south of María, among the cluster of prehistoric shelters for which this corner of Andalusia is known.

The most famous of them is the Cueva de los Letreros near Vélez-Blanco, where among the painted figures is the Indalo, a little stick man holding an arc over his head. It has become the symbol of Almería, painted on houses for luck and stamped on every souvenir in the province. Seeing the real thing, faint and red on the rock, is a quietly moving experience. Visits are arranged locally, so check before setting off.

Vélez-Blanco is dominated by its castle, a Renaissance fortress built in the early sixteenth century by the Fajardo family on a rocky crag above the town. Its marble courtyard was sold in the early twentieth century and ended up in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, where it has been reassembled. The castle still stands, its shell impressive and the views from its walls superb.

The riding is wonderful. To the west, the road continues toward Housesteads and the crags, where the scenery becomes even more dramatic. Stand among the altars, imagine the initiates gathered in the dim light for their rituals, and then walk to the site of Coventina's Well. It is a short stop, but one that stays with you, a glimpse into the religious life of the frontier.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum in wall mile 8:
Here, at the western edge of Newcastle, the Roman frontier starts to escape the city. Wall mile 8 lies around Newburn and Throckley, with Blaydon across the Tyne and the suburbs thinning into fields as you head west. The masonry itself has mostly vanished under roads, houses and farmland, but the line of the Wall and the great earthwork of the Vallum to its south can still be followed in hummocks, ditches and the occasional consolidated stretch of stone, most famously a little further west at Heddon-on-the-Wall, where a long run survives at nearly its full original width.

The Vallum is the part people often misread. It is not a defensive ditch facing the enemy but a broad flat-bottomed cut with mounds on either side, set behind the Wall, a controlled zone that marked off the military strip from the civilian country to the south. Together they made Hadrian's frontier from the 120s onwards, running from Wallsend to the Solway, and in this eastern sector it was built of stone from the start.

History did not stop with the Romans. In 1640 the Scottish army forced a crossing of the Tyne at Newburn and routed the English, one of the first real battles of the troubles that led to the civil wars. A few kilometres upstream lies Wylam, where George Stephenson was born in 1781, and the riverbanks here are thick with the memory of early railways and wagonways that carried coal down to the Tyne. Today the Tyne Riverside Country Park makes a calm green break between the industrial past and the modern city.

The riding is mixed. Getting out of Newcastle on the A69 or the old West Road is urban and busy, with lights, buses and speed cameras. Once past Heddon, though, you join the B6318, the Military Road built after the Jacobite rising of 1745, which runs arrow straight in places directly on top of the Wall's foundations. It rolls over crests and dips that hide oncoming traffic, so treat the long straights with suspicion. Westerly wind is common and can be strong on the higher ground.

You are in a city here, so fuel, food and parts are everywhere. Newburn and Blaydon have supermarkets and filling stations, and Newcastle has every kind of bike shop if something needs fixing before the emptier country further west.
t.the roman bath house to the north east o:
Brampton is the kind of small Cumbrian market town that riders pass on the A69 without a second look, which is a pity, because the country just north and east of it is some of the richest Roman and medieval ground on the whole Wall. The site of the Roman bath house lies close to the town, near the remains of an early fort on the Stanegate, and like most bath houses it sat outside the fort walls, where its furnaces and the risk of fire could do less harm. Little or nothing stands above ground, so come for the setting rather than the stones.

Bath houses were essential kit for a Roman garrison. Soldiers moved from cold rooms to warm to hot, scraping themselves clean with oil and a strigil, gambling and gossiping as they went. On a damp grey day in the north, with the wind coming off the Pennines, you understand why they bothered to build them in stone and keep the fires going.

Brampton itself has an octagonal Moot Hall in the market place and a long memory of the Jacobite rising of 1745. Bonnie Prince Charlie stayed in the town when Carlisle surrendered to his army, and after the rising was crushed, Jacobite prisoners were hanged on the Capon Tree on the edge of town, where a memorial still stands. Three kilometres away, Lanercost Priory, founded by Augustinian canons in the twelfth century, sits in a quiet meadow by the River Irthing; Edward I spent months there, ill, during his campaigns against the Scots.

For riding, avoid the A69 when you can. It is fast, busy with lorries and has more than its share of police attention. The minor road north-east past Lanercost to Banks and Birdoswald is the one you want: narrow, twisting, climbing onto the Wall with views across the Irthing gorge, and short enough that you can do it twice. Talkin Tarn, just south of town, is a glacial lake with a country park where a cup of tea by the water is easy to arrange.

Brampton has fuel, a supermarket, pubs and cafés, which makes it a sensible place to refill before the emptier stretch of the Wall heading east. Carlisle is fourteen kilometres away for anything bigger.
t.the section of stanegate roman road from:
Haltwhistle likes to call itself the centre of Britain, and on the road through the South Tyne valley it is easy to believe that this is where England quietly runs out of people. Just north of the town, the line of the Stanegate, the Roman road that linked Carlisle with Corbridge, crosses farmland on the flank of the valley. Little of it shows as more than a faint agger, a raised bank under the grass, but it is older than Hadrian's Wall, which runs along the crags a few kilometres to the north.

The Stanegate was the first frontier here. Under Agricola and his successors, the Romans built a string of forts along it, Vindolanda being the most famous, and only later decided to build a continuous barrier on the high ground. Standing on the old road and looking up at the dark wall of the Whin Sill, the volcanic dolerite ridge that the Wall follows, you see why the engineers made that choice. The ridge is a natural rampart, with cliffs facing north and long views across empty moorland.

This was also reiver country. For centuries after the Romans, raiding families on both sides of the border stole cattle, burned farms and settled feuds by force, which is why the area is scattered with bastle houses and pele towers, fortified farmhouses where livestock went downstairs and people slept above. Haltwhistle was raided so often that its church and older houses have a distinctly defensive look.

For riding, this is a crossroads. The A69 along the valley floor is quick but busy. Up on the B6318 Military Road you get long rolling straights and sudden dips, with the Wall itself appearing and disappearing on the ridge; Walltown Crags, Cawfields and the Roman Army Museum at Carvoran are all close. Southwards, the A689 climbs from the Tyne valley over the Pennines towards Alston, one of the finest moorland roads in England, high, bare and exposed. The wind can be brutal up there and fog rolls in quickly, even in summer.

Haltwhistle has fuel, a few cafés and pubs, and a small supermarket, which is useful because the country north of the Wall is very empty. Hexham, with its abbey and a proper market town's worth of services, is twenty-six kilometres east.
t.zhenwu temple and estuary docks@24.9,118:
In the Song and Yuan centuries, roughly a thousand years ago, Quanzhou on the coast of Fujian was one of the busiest ports on the planet. Arab, Persian, Indian and Southeast Asian merchants lived here, ships loaded silk, porcelain and tea for the Indian Ocean, and Marco Polo, who knew it as Zayton, described a harbour crowded with vessels. The Zhenwu Temple stands on a small rise by the estuary of the Jin river, where officials once made sacrifices to the god of the sea before the fleets sailed, and the old docks along the shore nearby are part of the World Heritage Site inscribed in 2021 as Quanzhou: Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China.

The temple is modest in size but rich in atmosphere: curved roofs with upturned eaves, incense smoke, stone steps leading up from the water's edge. From the terrace you look out over the estuary, which has silted and changed since the great days of the port, with mudflats, fishing boats and the modern city spreading along both banks. The other sites of the World Heritage group, scattered around Quanzhou, include mosques, Hindu temple carvings, Buddhist temples, bridges, pagodas and kilns, reflecting the extraordinary diversity of the medieval city.

Riding in China as a foreigner is complicated. You need a Chinese driving licence or a temporary permit, and importing a foreign bike requires special arrangements, usually through an agency. Many Chinese cities also restrict or ban motorcycles in their central districts, so check local rules for Quanzhou before planning a route. Traffic is dense, with electric scooters everywhere, and road manners can be very different from what you are used to.

If you do ride in Fujian, the countryside offers mountains, tea plantations and coastal roads. Anxi, in the hills north-west of Quanzhou, is the home of Tieguanyin oolong tea, and the roads through its terraced plantations are beautiful. The coast to the south has fishing villages, beaches and the island city of Xiamen.

Quanzhou is a big city with fuel and services everywhere. Its food is distinctive: thin rice noodles in rich broth, oyster omelettes, peanut soup and a huge range of seafood. Walking the old streets in the evening, with their temples, shops and noodle stalls, is a pleasure after a day on the road.
t.central e de santonje@37.8,-2.2:
The Indalo, a little stick figure holding an arc over its head, is now the symbol of the whole province of Almería, painted on houses, cars and souvenirs, and it comes from a rock shelter here in the hills around Vélez-Blanco. The Cueva de los Letreros, a few kilometres from this point, holds the original among other paintings of the Levantine and schematic styles, and the shelters of the Sierra de María are part of the World Heritage Site of Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula, inscribed in 1998. Santonje, as the area is called, is one of a cluster of sites in these mountains.

The paintings are in red ochre, small and often faded, showing humans, animals, hunting scenes and abstract signs. They were made by people living in the area thousands of years ago, from the Mesolithic to the Bronze Age. Seeing them requires effort: most shelters are reached on foot and some are fenced or open only on guided visits.

Vélez-Blanco itself is dominated by a Renaissance castle on a rock, built in the early sixteenth century by the Fajardo family. Its marble courtyard, a masterpiece of Italian Renaissance carving, was sold in the early twentieth century and now stands in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, leaving the castle with an empty space where its heart used to be. The village below has whitewashed houses and narrow streets.

The landscape is the high, dry country of north-eastern Almería, with the Sierra de María rising above plains of almond trees and cereal fields. The Sierra de María-Los Vélez Natural Park has pine forests, limestone peaks and wildlife, including ibex and birds of prey. Summers are hot, winters cold and sometimes snowy at altitude.

Traffic is almost absent once you leave the main road. The roads between Vélez-Blanco, María and Vélez-Rubio are scenic, and further afield, the routes into Granada and Murcia provinces offer more mountains. Vélez-Rubio, twenty-three kilometres away, is the place for fuel. Try migas, fried breadcrumbs with garlic and sausage, and the hearty stews of the region.
t.abrigo de zaen ii@38.2,-2.1:
Zaén is a quiet valley in the north-western corner of the Murcia region, in the municipality of Moratalla, where pine-covered sierras close in and the streams run clear and cold. The Abrigo de Zaén II is one of several painted rock shelters here, and like the others it belongs to the World Heritage Site of Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin, inscribed in 1998. Levantine art, found along the eastern side of the Iberian Peninsula, shows lively figures of humans and animals, often in scenes of hunting, gathering and, sometimes, conflict.

The figures in the Zaén shelters are small and faded, painted in red pigment on the rock face, and you need patience and good light to make them out. The setting, though, is lovely: a valley of farms, orchards and pine woods, with limestone cliffs above and the sound of water. It feels remote and untouched, far from the tourist coasts.

The wider area has much to offer. Caravaca de la Cruz, one of the holy cities of Catholicism, with a shrine housing a relic of the True Cross, is about half an hour's ride away. Every May the town celebrates the Caballos del Vino, when teams of men race horses decorated with embroidered cloaks up the hill to the castle. Socovos, nearby in Albacete province, has a castle on a rock above the village, and Letur is a beautiful village of Moorish origin with narrow streets and water channels.

The roads in this area are a delight: winding, quiet and scenic, through mountains, valleys and villages. The road from Moratalla to Nerpio, through the Sierra de Segura, is particularly good, with curves, climbs and views. Surfaces vary, and you may meet livestock, cyclists and farm vehicles. Summers are hot, especially in the valleys, and winters can be cold, with snow at higher elevations.

Moratalla, eighteen kilometres away, is the base for fuel and supplies. Buy bread, cured sausage and a wedge of local cheese there, and eat by a stream in the Zaén valley where the only interruption will be goat bells.
t.las cabritas@38.1,-2.3:
Nerpio sits at the edge of the world, or at least at the edge of Albacete province, a small village in the Sierra de Taibilla close to where Murcia, Granada and Jaén come together. Its walnuts are famous, grown in old orchards along the river, and the hills around it hold some of the finest Levantine rock art in Spain. Las Cabritas, the little goats, is a shelter just over a kilometre from the village, named after the animals painted on its walls, and it is part of the World Heritage Site of Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin.

The paintings around Nerpio include hunting scenes, animals and human figures, some remarkably detailed. The Solana de las Covachas, Cañaica del Calar and other sites are reached on foot, and guided visits are organised from the village. The rides that pass here include a figure known locally as the Mother Goddess, a reminder that the meaning of these images is still debated.

The landscape is wild and beautiful: limestone mountains, pine forests, deep valleys and the Taibilla river, which supplies water to much of Murcia through a famous canal system. The air is clean, the nights are dark and full of stars, and the silence is deep. In autumn, the walnut harvest brings the village to life.

Riding here means remote roads, many curves and very little traffic. The roads from Moratalla, Yeste and Letur are all scenic, with climbs, descents and views. Surfaces are variable, and some roads are narrow and twisty. Watch for animals, especially deer, wild boar and livestock. In winter, snow can close some roads.

Nerpio has a few shops and bars, but for reliable fuel you may need Moratalla, thirty-eight kilometres away, or Yeste, so arrive with a healthy tank. Lamb, game and walnut cakes appear on the menus, and the bars serve generous tapas with drinks. Spending a night in Nerpio, with a walk to the rock art in the morning, is the best way to appreciate this remote corner of Spain.
t.abrigo de los gavilanes@37.8,-2.0:
Gavilanes means sparrowhawks, and the name fits a shelter high on a limestone face above the dry country where Murcia meets Almería. The Abrigo de los Gavilanes lies in the hills west of Lorca, in an area scattered with painted shelters such as the Collado de la Cruz and Los Grajos, the jackdaws, and it is part of the World Heritage Site of Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. The figures are small, red and schematic, painted by communities who farmed and herded here thousands of years ago.

The country around is the high plateau of the Altiplano, with almond orchards, cereal fields, olive groves and bare limestone ridges. In February the almond blossom turns the hillsides white and pink, and in summer the land bakes under a fierce sun. The light is sharp and the air dry, and the sense of space is enormous.

Lorca, the main town of the area, is a historic city with a great castle, the Fortaleza del Sol, on a hill above the old town, and baroque churches and palaces. It is famous for its Holy Week processions, when rival brotherhoods, the Blues and the Whites, compete to produce the most spectacular parades, with horses, chariots and costumes. In 2011 an earthquake damaged many buildings, and the restoration has been a long effort.

The riding here is a mix of straight plateau roads and winding mountain routes. The roads between Lorca, Vélez-Rubio and the villages of the area are quiet and scenic, and further north, the Sierra de Espuña and the mountains of north-western Murcia offer more curves. Summer heat is a serious consideration, so ride early and late, and carry water.

Vélez-Rubio, nineteen kilometres away, is the closer fuel stop, and Lorca has everything from workshops to tapas bars. Murcian tapas are a cult of their own: try a marinera, a breadstick ring topped with Russian salad and an anchovy, with a cold caña. Then climb to the castle for sunset over the plain.
t.la risca i@38.2,-2.0:
Moratalla is a hill town that spills down a slope beneath its castle in the north-west of Murcia, a maze of steep, narrow streets, whitewashed houses and stairways. Around it lies a vast municipality of mountains, forests and valleys, and in the valley of Benizar, near the Río Benamor, is La Risca, a group of painted shelters that form part of the World Heritage Site of Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin. The paintings include human figures and animals, typical of the Levantine style, small and faded but full of life.

The Moratalla area is one of the richest in Murcia for rock art, with dozens of shelters in the surrounding hills. A visitor centre in the town can provide information and arrange guided visits. The landscape is beautiful, with pine-covered mountains, river valleys, orchards and terraces of almonds and olives.

Moratalla is famous for its September fiesta in honour of the Santísimo Cristo del Rayo, which includes bull runs through the streets, and for its tamborada at Easter, when hundreds of drummers fill the town with an extraordinary, relentless sound that goes on for days. The town's castle, a Christian fortress built on Moorish foundations, offers views over the roofs and the surrounding countryside.

The roads around Moratalla are a joy for riders, with curves, climbs and quiet villages. The road north towards Nerpio and the Sierra de Segura is especially scenic, and the routes west into Albacete and Granada provinces offer more mountains. Surfaces vary, and you may meet slow vehicles and animals. Summers are hot in the valleys but cooler in the mountains, and winters can bring snow to the higher roads.

Moratalla, twelve kilometres away, has fuel, places to sleep and a handful of good, plain restaurants. Order the rice with rabbit and snails, cooked over vine cuttings when they do it properly, and a bottle from Bullas or Jumilla, and let the drummers, if it is Easter, keep you awake.
t.la pena del castellar@39.9,-1.6:
Villar del Humo is a tiny village in the Serranía of Cuenca, the high, forested mountain country east of the city of Cuenca. Around it, sandstone outcrops rise from pine forests, and on their faces prehistoric painters left images of animals and people. The Peña del Escrito and La Peña del Castellar are among the most important shelters here, and they are part of the World Heritage Site of Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin. The paintings include deer, horses and human figures, some in the dynamic Levantine style and others more schematic.

The landscape is remote and quiet, with pine forests, red sandstone rocks, fields of cereals and scattered villages. The Serranía is one of the least populated areas of Spain, and you can ride for long stretches without seeing another vehicle. The air is clean, the nights are dark and the stars are bright.

Cuenca, about an hour's ride away, is famous for its hanging houses, built on the edge of a cliff above the Huécar gorge, and its old town is a World Heritage Site. The rides that pass here link it with the walled town, and the city makes a good base for exploring the region. Cardenete, nearby, has a castle and a Renaissance church.

The riding here is wonderful, with winding roads through forests and over hills, very little traffic and good views. The roads from Cuenca to Villar del Humo and beyond are quiet and scenic, and the Serranía offers endless options for exploration. Surfaces are generally fine, but watch for gravel, animals and occasional potholes. Winter can be cold and snowy, and summer hot during the day but cool at night.

Do not count on services. Villar del Humo is a hamlet of a few hundred people, so fill up in Cuenca or Motilla del Palancar, forty kilometres away. Cuenca's kitchen is shepherd and hunter food: morteruelo, a rich pâté of game and liver, and ajoarriero, a cod and garlic spread. Sleep in Cuenca and walk the gorge at dusk, when the hanging houses light up above the drop.
t.wanshou pagoda@24.7,118.7:
On a hill above the coast south of Quanzhou, in China's Fujian province, a slender stone pagoda has watched the sea for some nine centuries. The Wanshou Pagoda on Baogai mountain, near the town of Shishi, was built in the Southern Song dynasty and served as a landmark for sailors approaching the port of Quanzhou, then one of the busiest harbours in the world. Locals call it the Aunt Pagoda, after a legend that tells of a woman who climbed the hill every day to wait for her husband to return from the sea.

Quanzhou, known to Arab and European travellers as Zayton, was a great international port in the Song and Yuan dynasties, a city of merchants from Arabia, Persia, India and Southeast Asia, with mosques, Hindu temples and Christian churches alongside Buddhist and Taoist temples. Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta both wrote about it. The city and its related sites, including the pagoda, were listed by UNESCO in 2021 as Quanzhou: Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China. In the city, the Kaiyuan Temple with its twin pagodas, the Qingjing Mosque and the Islamic tombs on Lingshan hill are well worth visiting.

The view from the pagoda takes in the coast, the bay and the sprawling towns of Shishi and Jinjiang, now an industrial area known for its textile and shoe factories. The climate is subtropical, hot and humid in summer, with typhoons possible from July to September, and mild in winter.

Riding in China as a foreigner is complicated. A Chinese driving licence is required, and bringing in a foreign motorcycle involves extensive paperwork and usually a guided tour. Many Chinese cities restrict or ban motorcycles in their centres, and expressways are usually closed to them. For those who manage it, the coastal roads of Fujian, winding through hills, fishing villages and tea plantations, offer good riding, especially in spring and autumn.

Yongning, about five kilometres away, and Shishi have fuel and services; Quanzhou has everything. Fujian cuisine is light and fresh, with an emphasis on seafood and soups. Try oyster omelette, a local favourite, or noodles in a rich seafood broth, and drink a cup of Tieguanyin, the famous oolong tea grown in the mountains of Anxi, not far away.
t.penya escrita@38.7,-0.1:
In the folded limestone hills behind the Costa Blanca, far enough inland that the resorts feel like another country, a rock shelter called Penya Escrita holds prehistoric paintings. The name means something like the written rock, which is what the people of Tàrbena and Bolulla called it long before archaeologists arrived. The figures belong to the rock art of the Mediterranean Basin of the Iberian Peninsula, a UNESCO site made up of hundreds of shelters scattered from Catalonia down to Andalusia, painted by hunter-gatherers and early farmers thousands of years ago. They are small, faded and easy to miss, and they are best appreciated with patience rather than expectation.

The landscape around is the real attraction for most visitors. The Marina Alta and Marina Baixa meet here in a jumble of ridges, terraced almond groves, loquat orchards and tiny villages perched on spurs. Bolulla has a ruined Moorish castle on its hill. Tàrbena, higher up, was resettled by families from Mallorca after the expulsion of the Moriscos in 1609, and people there still speak with a Mallorcan accent and make sobrassada the island way.

The road you will remember is the one over the Coll de Rates between Parcent and Tàrbena. It climbs in a long series of well-surfaced hairpins and bends, with views back over the Jalón valley to the sea, and it is famous among cyclists, so on a winter weekend you will share it with whole teams training in the sun. Take it steadily, pass carefully, and stop at the top where there is a restaurant with a terrace over the valley. From Tàrbena the road down to Callosa d'en Sarrià and Bolulla twists through rock and pine, with the Algar waterfalls nearby offering cool pools in summer.

This part of Spain is at its best from October to May. In July and August the heat is serious, the hills are dusty, and the shade is thin. Spring brings almond blossom early, often as soon as January and February, when the valleys turn white and pink.

The villages are small and fuel is not guaranteed in them. Fill up in Callosa d'en Sarrià or La Nucia before you head up, and carry water, because the walk to the shelter is short but the sun here does not negotiate.
t.cova jeroni@38.8,-0.2:
Cova Jeroni belongs to that quiet tangle of valleys behind Pego and Dénia where the Marina Alta hides its oldest stories. The shelters in this part of Alicante, along the ravines of Famorca, Ebo and Gallinera, carry some of the finest prehistoric art in eastern Spain, and they are listed together with hundreds of others as the rock art of the Mediterranean Basin. Do not expect a visitor centre and a car park; expect a dirt track, a short walk, a rock overhang and a few ochre figures that reward a long look.

The drive in is half the point. From Pego, the road up to the Vall d'Ebo climbs a steep wall of limestone in a staircase of hairpins, with the rice fields and marshes of the Pego-Oliva wetland spread out below towards the sea. It is narrow, the surface is fair, and the views are wide enough to make you forget the next corner, which you must not. Once over the top, the valley opens into a high basin of olive and almond terraces with Vall d'Ebo at the centre, a village of a few hundred people with a bar on the square and a cave nearby, the Cova del Rull, full of stalactites.

Beyond the village, the Barranc de l'Infern cuts down towards the Vall de Laguar. It is one of the great walks of the region, thousands of old stone steps built by the Moors to link their mountain villages, and it gives a sense of how densely these empty valleys were once farmed. The Moriscos were expelled in 1609 and many villages never recovered their population, which is why the terraces now run up the hillsides with nobody to tend them.

The nearer villages of Adsubia and Villalonga are small; Pego is your place for fuel and for a proper lunch, a town of around eleven thousand with a lively centre and good arròs, the local rice dishes, cooked properly in a flat pan. In spring the air smells of orange blossom down in the plain and of rosemary and thyme up in the valleys.

Avoid the hottest months if you can. In winter the light is clear and gold, the roads are empty on weekdays, and the only traffic up the hairpins is a farmer in a battered pick-up who will wave you past.
t.abric del pontet@38.8,-0.6:
The Serra de Mariola is the green heart of the Valencia-Alicante borderlands, a mountain range of pine, holm oak and aromatic scrub that feeds the rivers Vinalopó and Clariano and perfumes the air with thyme and rosemary. The Abric del Pontet is one of its rock shelters, a small overhang with prehistoric paintings, part of the scattered UNESCO site that gathers the rock art of Mediterranean Spain. It sits between Bocairent, Alfafara and Ontinyent, and it is the kind of place that makes most sense as an excuse to explore the villages around it.

Bocairent is the star. Built on a rocky spur above a ravine, it has a medieval quarter of steep, narrow lanes, a bullring carved straight into the rock, and, on the cliff face across the gorge, the Covetes dels Moros: dozens of small windows cut into the limestone, opening onto chambers whose purpose nobody has fully explained. Granaries, refuges, a monastery? The guides will tell you the theories. In the hills above, the old snow wells of Mariola recall a trade that once sent compacted winter snow down to the coast in summer for medicine and ice cream.

The riding is excellent and varied. The road from Bocairent over to Banyeres de Mariola and on towards Alcoi winds along the flanks of the range with long views, good surface and little traffic. From Ontinyent the CV-81 runs fast through the Vall d'Albaida, while the smaller roads up to Agres and the Mariola sanctuary are tighter and more rewarding. Winter mornings here can be cold, at the altitude of these villages frost is common, while summer afternoons stay comfortable compared with the coast.

Mariola is also known for its herbal liqueur, herbero, distilled with a long list of local plants. Many families have their own recipe, and a small glass after lunch is local custom, though best saved for when the key is out of the ignition. The food leans to mountain dishes: hearty rice with beans and turnips, and the pilotes, big meatballs cooked in stew.

Ontinyent, five kilometres away, is a textile town of nearly forty thousand with fuel, workshops and plenty of places to eat. Bocairent has a station of its own on the main road too, and enough bars to fill an afternoon if the old quarter seduces you.
t.pla de petracos abric i@38.8,-0.2:
Pla de Petracos is one of the most important prehistoric art sites in Spain, and it looks like nothing much: a row of shallow shelters in the side of a ravine near Castell de Castells, in the high interior of the Marina Alta. What makes it special is the style. The paintings here are among the clearest examples of what archaeologists call Macroschematic art, large, bold, almost abstract human figures with raised arms and serpentine forms, painted by the first farming communities of the region in the early Neolithic. Elsewhere in the Valencian mountains you find Levantine hunting scenes; here you find something stranger and more symbolic. A short path and viewing platforms make the panels accessible, and the information boards help you see what the eye misses at first.

Castell de Castells itself is a small, sober village of a few hundred people in a high valley ringed by mountains. It feels a long way from the coast even though Calp and Benidorm are less than an hour away. Above it rises the Serra de la Serrella, and near the summit ridge of the Bernia, to the south, a natural tunnel pierces the rock, a classic walk if you carry boots.

Getting here is the fun part. The roads that thread through the Vall de Pop, the Vall d'Ebo and up from Benigembla follow the contours in endless loops, narrow and patched in places, with sheer drops and goats occasionally standing in the middle like they own the deeds. You will need to concentrate, and you will rarely get out of third gear, but the scenery of terraced ridges, crags and deep blue sky is relentless. On a weekday you may meet more cyclists than cars.

This is dry country with little shade. In summer, ride early, visit the shelters in the morning, and be somewhere cool by midday. In winter, when snow occasionally dusts the peaks, the light is so clear you can pick out individual trees on the ridges.

The village has a bar or two and sometimes a small shop, but do not count on fuel. Pego, about eleven kilometres as the crow flies but much longer by road, is the nearest reliable place to fill up, and the towns of the Jalón valley are the other choice before you climb into the mountains.
t.barranc d alpadull abric iii@38.8,-0.1:
Murla sits in the Vall de Pop, a broad valley of vines, oranges and almonds where the Girona river runs down from the mountains towards the coast at El Verger. The ravine of Alpadull cuts into the hills above, and in one of its shelters, the third along, there are prehistoric paintings, part of the great scatter of rock art across Mediterranean Spain that UNESCO lists as a single site. Like most of these shelters, it is better approached as a reason to wander a beautiful valley than as a spectacle in itself.

The Marina Alta was raisin country for most of the nineteenth century. Moscatel grapes grown on these terraces were dried and exported through Dénia to Britain and America, and the trade made the region rich for a while. You can still see the riuraus everywhere: long, low buildings with an open arcade along one side, where the grapes were laid out to dry and taken in when rain threatened. Many have been converted into houses or restaurants, and a few still store farm tools. The moscatel lives on in the local sweet wine, and in September the harvest fills the lanes with tractors and the smell of crushed fruit.

The roads through the Vall de Pop are a cheerful mix. The main road between Alcalalí, Xaló and Benigembla is smooth and gently curving, lined with wine bodegas offering tastings, and with a big Saturday market at Xaló that stops traffic in the village. Turn off into the side valleys towards Murla, Tormos and the Vall d'Ebo and the road narrows immediately, climbing in short bends through terraces and pine, with the occasional loose stone washed down after rain. The autumn storms here, the gota freda, can be violent, so check the forecast in October.

Murla has a fortified church, rebuilt from an older tower, that gives the village a stern look. Tormos, across the valley, is a tiny cluster of houses with a laid-back bar.

For fuel, head to Pego to the north or Ondara and the coastal towns to the east; the small villages here rarely have a station. There is food in Xaló and Alcalalí, and in winter you can sit outside in the sun at lunch, which is a strong argument for riding here in January.
t.albrigo de jutia i@38.2,-2.4:

Brampton is a small market town at the foot of the North Pennines, and just north of it, the line of Hadrian's Wall crosses the low country between the Irthing and the Eden. On this stretch, the stone wall itself has mostly vanished, robbed for building material over the centuries, but the line can still be traced in places through fields and hedgerows, along with the vallum, the great earthwork ditch the Romans dug just south of the wall. Its ruined church and cloisters stand in a peaceful valley, and the nave is still used as the parish church. Edward I stayed here for several months in 1306 and 1307 during his campaigns against the Scots, and the border wars brought frequent raids. Further along the Wall to the east, Birdoswald Roman fort sits on a bend of the Irthing, with one of the best surviving stretches of stone wall nearby.

Brampton itself has an octagonal moot hall on its market square and a church with stained glass windows designed by Edward Burne-Jones and made by William Morris's company. It's a pleasant place to stop, with bakeries, cafés and pubs.

South of Brampton, the road over Hartside Pass into the North Pennines, the A686, is one of the great motorcycling roads of northern England, climbing in long bends to over five hundred metres. The weather changes fast up there, so be ready for wind, rain and mist.

Brampton has fuel and services, and Carlisle, fourteen kilometres west, has everything. Try a Cumberland sausage or a slice of local cake with your tea.

Rudchester, known to the Romans as Vindobala, was the fourth fort along Hadrian's Wall counting from Wallsend at the eastern end. It sat astride the Wall on high ground west of Newcastle, with a garrison of around five hundred soldiers. Today, there is nothing to see above ground but fields and the bumps and hollows of buried walls, with a farm nearby. Excavations in the twentieth century found traces of a temple to Mithras just outside the fort, one of several on the Wall, where soldiers worshipped the god in a dark, cave-like building.

The new road, completed in the 1750s, followed the line of the Wall for long stretches, and in many places it was built directly on top of it, using the Roman stones as foundation and quarry. It is one of the great ironies of British history that the road built to defend the realm destroyed so much of the realm's most famous monument.

The weather is changeable, and the wind can be strong on the exposed ridges.

t.eight roman inscriptions in the roman qu:

Inland Valencia is a world away from the beaches on the coast. t.coves roges abric ii iii@38.8,-0.3:

t.derecho e de santonje@37.8,-2.2:

t.abric de tollos i o de la fuente seca@39:
This is the country of the honey-gatherer. t.penya roja o ulls de canals@38.7,-0.6:

t.the forth bridge@56.0,-3.4:

The sight of a train crossing slowly over the water, with the other two bridges standing beside it, is one of the great views of Scotland. t.hadrian s wall and vallum between the ro:
Around Haltwhistle the wall climbs on to the Whin Sill, a hard ridge of dark volcanic rock that runs across northern England like a spine, and the effect is among the most dramatic on the whole frontier. The wall rides the crest of crags, rising and falling over the rock, with a steep drop to the north and long views over moorland, and the Roman engineers made full use of the natural defence. The vallum, a broad flat-bottomed ditch with mounds on either side, runs in the valley to the south, and it marks the boundary of the military zone behind the wall.

The road in the title is the Military Road, the B6318, which runs close to the line of the wall for many miles. It was built after the Jacobite rising of 1745, when General Wade found that he could not move his army across the north of England quickly enough, and the road builders used wall stones as foundations, which tells you how the wall suffered. Today the Military Road is a fine, undulating ride with long straights and sudden crests, but it is narrow in places and busy on summer weekends, so take it easy and watch for walkers crossing.

Spring and autumn have the best light, and in summer the evenings are long and the heather turns purple. Haltwhistle, about three kilometres off, has a fuel station, shops, cafés and pubs, and Hexham, a larger market town further east, offers more choice. Try a pie and a pint in a local pub, or a cup of tea and a slice of cake at a village tearoom, and take a short walk along the wall before you ride on.
t.milestone house roman temporary camp and:
Long before the wall existed, the Romans ran a road across the narrow neck of northern England, the Stanegate, linking the forts of Corbridge on the Tyne and Carlisle on the Eden. It was built around AD 80, in the time of the general Agricola, and it served as the frontier line for a generation before Hadrian ordered the wall to be built a little to the north. Forts and fortlets sat along it, among them Vindolanda and the small post at Haltwhistle Burn, and temporary camps like the one at Milestone House show where troops stopped on the move.

The camp, like others in the area, was marked out by ditch and bank in a neat rectangle, and today its outline is a faint ripple in the grass. Milestone House takes its name from a Roman milestone that stood on the road, and the road itself is still partly followed by modern lanes. The wall and its famous crags lie a few hundred metres to the north, so a walk of an hour or two can take you across the whole system of frontier works, from the old road to the ditch, the wall and the vallum.

The surrounding countryside is high, open and windswept, with rough pasture, scattered farms and long views to the Pennines on one side and the Cheviots on the other. Haltwhistle stands in the valley of the South Tyne, and the nearby Haltwhistle Burn flows through a small wooded gorge. Curlews cry over the fields in spring, and the light changes constantly, from shadow to bright sun in minutes.

Riding here is open and enjoyable. The old Stanegate lanes are narrow, with farm gates and sheep on the road, while the main road along the valley is faster. Surfaces vary, with some rough patches and cattle grids, and in winter the high ground is icy. The best months are May to September. Weather can turn quickly, so pack waterproofs even on a sunny morning.

Haltwhistle, about two and a half kilometres away, is the nearest town of size, with fuel, shops, cafés and pubs, and Hexham has more. A plate of local Northumbrian lamb or a pasty from the baker is a good, plain lunch. Look for the information boards along the road, and spend a few minutes imagining the old road busy with carts, couriers and columns of marching men.
t.vindolanda@55.0,-2.4:
Vindolanda is the place where the Romans on the northern frontier start to sound like people. Haltwhistle, about six kilometres away, and Hexham have fuel stations, shops and cafés, and there is a tearoom at the site. Try a plate of local lamb or a Northumbrian pasty, and give yourself a couple of hours, since the site rewards slow looking.
t.shihu dock@24.8,118.7:
In the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, Quanzhou was one of the busiest ports in the world. Arab, Persian, Indian and Italian merchants lived in the city, which Marco Polo knew as Zayton, and ships loaded with silk, porcelain and tea left for the Indian Ocean. The port stood on the Fujian coast of southern China, at the mouth of the Jin river, and the whole system of temples, mosques, bridges, docks and kiln sites was listed by UNESCO in 2021 as Quanzhou, Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China.

Shihu Dock is one of the port facilities. It was a wharf on the bay where ships tied up, built in stone to withstand tides, and it remains a physical piece of that maritime story, a place where the port of the Song and Yuan dynasties can still be pictured. For a foreign rider, China is a special case, and Quanzhou is no exception. Foreign motorcycles are generally allowed only with temporary permits and a registered guide, and foreigners cannot ride a local bike without a Chinese licence, so independent riding is difficult and often not possible. Many cities restrict motorbikes inside central areas. It is far more practical to arrive by train, rent a bicycle or take a taxi, and make the visit a day of walking.

Baiqi and Dongyuan are small towns near the site, with shops and cafes, and Quanzhou itself, a city of several million in its wider area, has everything you could need, including fuel, hotels and some of the best food in Fujian. The climate is subtropical, with hot, humid summers and typhoons from July to September, and mild winters. October to December and March to April are the most pleasant times, with warm days and clear skies. Wander along the old streets, find a quiet courtyard and let the past catch up.
t.abrigo de d pedro mota@38.4,-3.4:

t.la higuera@38.5,-1.6:

t.covacha del barranc del diable@39.6,-0.3:

t.friso de los gitanos o abrigo del cazado:
Nerpio sits at about a thousand metres in the Sierra de Segura foothills, at the far south-west corner of Albacete province, in a high valley that feels closer to Andalusia than to La Mancha. It is an out-of-the-way place, with orchards of apples, almond and walnut trees in the valley bottoms and bare limestone peaks above. There is an eagle's nest somewhere above it, and the quiet is of the kind you can hear.
t.molino de las fuentes i@38.1,-2.3:
A mill is a good reason to remember how much of the old Spanish countryside ran on water. t.abrigo de zaen i@38.2,-2.1:

t.raco de gorgori abric i@38.8,-0.2:

t.molinos ii@37.7,-2.1:
Vélez-Blanco is a white town under a limestone wall, and the castle above it is one of the oddest in Spain. The Marquises of Los Vélez built it in the early sixteenth century, in a hurry to look both fortified and Italian, so the outside has round towers and the inside had a marble Renaissance courtyard that was later sold, piece by piece, and ended up in New York's Metropolitan Museum. Molinos II is one of the nearby mill and shelter sites, and I do not know what survives of it, but the valley is full of old irrigation and water works.

The A-317 and local lanes link up in loops, with generous bends and little traffic. The road surface is generally decent, though patches of loose stone appear after storms. Spring is glorious, with blossom and green slopes, and autumn is mild. Winter brings ice and sometimes snow, so check the forecast.

Vélez-Blanco has about two thousand people, and Vélez-Rubio, four kilometres away, is a bigger town of seven thousand with fuel, supermarkets and a handsome baroque church. Fill the tank there. The bars in Vélez-Blanco serve strong coffee and plates of local cured meats, and it is a perfect place for a slow breakfast with the castle on the skyline above. Early morning light on the pale rock is unforgettable.
t.rock art of the mediterranean basin on t:
Tuéjar, Chelva and Alpuente are small towns in the Serranía, the rugged highland of inland Valencia, where the rivers cut deep valleys between pine-clad ridges. It is a corner of the province that most visitors to the coast never see. The name on the stop refers to the UNESCO listing of 1998 for the rock art of the Mediterranean basin on the Iberian peninsula, and the paintings of Barranco de las Colochas, the ravine nearby, belong to it. A few kilometres away stands the Roman aqueduct of Peña Cortada, a long run of arches and rock-cut channels that carried water down the valley in Roman times and is still impressive.
