Surfaces vary, with some rough patches and rock spills after storms. Traffic is almost nonexistent, and you may ride an hour without meeting anyone. The air is scented with pine and rosemary, and in spring the hillsides are full of flowers. Summer is hot but the valleys are cooler, and autumn brings mushroom hunters into the woods.

Fuel is a concern. The villages here have a few thousand people at most, and the nearest sizeable town in the data is Utiel, about twenty-nine kilometres away, in a wine region known for the Bobal grape. Fill up before you commit to the hills, and bring water. For lunch, ask for a plate of local ham, a paella cooked over orange wood in the Valencian way, or a stew of mountain meat. A glass of cold water from a village fountain, which flows even in summer, is a quiet pleasure.
t.barranc de la falaguera abric ii@39.3,-0:
South of Valencia the land flattens into the Ribera, a plain of orange and persimmon orchards cut by irrigation ditches, and then, quite suddenly, it crumples into low hills. Alginet and Alfarp sit on this edge, with the Albufera lagoon and its rice fields a little to the east. I do not know what survives on this wall, and I would rather say so than guess.

This is not a dramatic ride, and it is not meant to be. The roads are small, flat and quick, between orange trees and drainage canals, with the smell of blossom in March and April that you can almost taste. Mopeds and tractors share the lanes, and the farm traffic is heavy at harvest. Once you leave the plain for the hills, the road climbs gently with a handful of bends, mostly easy, and views back toward the coast. Summer is steamy and hot, and a late October day is much kinder.

t.marmalo iv@39.9,-1.7:
Villar del Humo is a village of a few hundred people in the Serranía de Cuenca, a high land of pine forest, limestone gorges and sparse villages that lies between the cities of Cuenca and Valencia. Cañete, a walled town, has a small bar and a bakery, and it is a nice place to stop.

If you want something to remember, wait for the sunset. The pines turn orange, the hills go blue, and the sound of the forest settles.
t.la alamedilla@38.3,-4.0:
Nobody lives close to this point, and that is its main fact. It lies in the eastern Sierra Morena, in the wild border country between Córdoba and Jaén, where holm oak and cork oak cover steep, empty hills and the nearest villages, Mestanza, Baños de la Encina and Cardeña, are all more than twenty-five kilometres away. The ride titles link it with the mercury mines of Almadén, whose Royal Forced Labour Gaol and miners' hospital are part of a UNESCO listing shared with Idrija in Slovenia, but Almadén lies far to the north-west, and the connection is a routing choice rather than a neighbourhood.

The castle is one of the oldest and best preserved in Spain, with a ring of towers, and the village below has whitewashed houses. It is thirty-four kilometres away at least, so you need to plan for fuel. Fill up in Bailén or in Andújar, carry water, and check the weather.

Spring and autumn are the best times. Summer is brutal, with temperatures well above forty degrees by mid-afternoon, and winter nights are cold. If you stop, you will hear birds and wind and little else, and the smell of rock-rose and warm stone fills the air. It is a good place to eat a sandwich and look at an empty horizon.
t.old and new towns of edinburgh@56.0,-3.2:
Edinburgh is built on the remains of a volcano. The Castle sits on a plug of hard rock, and the ridge that slopes eastwards from it, the Royal Mile, carries the medieval Old Town on its back, a tall, dense, soot-dark jumble of closes and tenements that went up because the city was shut inside walls and could only grow upwards. In 1767 the council ran a competition for a plan to build a New Town on the open ground to the north, and the winning design by a young architect named James Craig gave the city a grid of Georgian terraces, squares and gardens. The contrast between the two halves, medieval and classical, is the reason UNESCO listed the combined area in 1995.

The coordinates fall on the western side of the centre, close to Princes Street Gardens and the West End, where the ground drops from the Castle rock to the valley of the Water of Leith. The Scott Monument, a vast Gothic spire to the novelist Walter Scott, stands further east along Princes Street, and the Dean Village, a former mill hamlet in the river gorge, is a short walk to the north-west. Arthur's Seat, a crouching volcanic hill with a view over the city, rises to the east, and on a clear day the Firth of Forth glitters to the north.

Riding in Edinburgh itself is a matter of patience. Trams run along Princes Street and cross the main roads, so keep wheels clear of the rails, which are slippery when wet. Cobbles, bus lanes and one-way systems fill the old town, and parking for motorbikes is available at marked bays at the edge of the centre. Petrol stations are scarce in the middle, so fill up on the outskirts. The best riding begins outside the city, over the Queensferry Crossing, the bridge opened in 2017, and into Fife, or south into the Pentland Hills and the Borders, where the roads climb across heather moors.

The weather can turn in a quarter of an hour, with a warm sun giving way to a cold wind and rain, and locals say you can have four seasons in a day. Summer evenings are very long, with light until after ten, and August is crowded with festival visitors. A bowl of cullen skink, a smoked haddock soup, in a pub off the Royal Mile makes a fine lunch.
t.chesters pike roman temporary camp@55.0,:
The country around Haltwhistle is where Hadrian's Wall is at its most dramatic. The Romans built it along the Whin Sill, a ridge of hard volcanic rock that rises in a long wall of crags above the farmland, and the ruins of milecastles, turrets and forts run along the top, making a line that climbs and dips like a stitched seam. Haltwhistle claims to be the centre of Britain, which no one can prove, and the town has a quiet, grey-stone high street. A Roman temporary camp, like the one at Chesters Pike, was a marching camp, where an army dug a ditch and raised a bank around a night's lodging, and left almost nothing behind. Often the only trace is a faint rectangle in the grass.

The Military Road, the B6318, runs along the line of the Wall and gives the area its best ride. It was built after the Jacobite rising of 1745, on the advice of General Wade, who wanted a way to move troops across England, and the builders took stone from the Wall for the road base, so the road still follows the line of the old frontier. It dips and rises like a roller coaster, with long straights, crests that hide the road, and views over the moors to the north. Wind, sheep and the occasional tractor are the main hazards, and the road is very exposed in winter.

On the way you pass Cawfields Quarry, where a lake sits below the crag with a milecastle on the edge, and Walltown Crags, a high point with a spectacular view. Housesteads Fort and Vindolanda lie a little to the east, and the latter has produced hundreds of wooden writing tablets with letters from Roman soldiers, including a birthday party invitation and a request for socks. They are among the most human objects from the Roman world.

Haltwhistle has some four thousand people, with fuel and a couple of cafes, and Hexham is the nearest big town. Take a waterproof and a warm layer, since weather changes quickly on the ridge. In clear weather the long light in the evening makes the crags glow, and it is the best time to be there.
t.hadrian s wall in wall mile 5@55.0,-1.7:
Wall mile 5 is in Newcastle, which means that the Roman frontier is under a bus route. The Wall began at Wallsend and ran west, and the antiquarians who surveyed it numbered every Roman mile from there, so mile five falls in Benwell, a hillside district of terraces above the Tyne. Here the old line is now more or less the West Road, a main road into the city, and a short way off the road you can find real Roman stone. A tiny temple dedicated to a local British god called Antenociticus stands in a small garden between modern houses, with its three altars copied in place, and the remains of the Vallum, the broad ditch south of the Wall, crosses a causeway nearby. The fort of Condercum stood on the hill above, with a fine view east down the river.

It is an odd and rather lovely mix: a few courses of Roman masonry, a street of Victorian houses, a school, and the city sprawling to the Tyne. On a clear day the view from the high ground sweeps over the river and the bridges, and the Roman soldiers who watched here would recognise the shape of the valley, if not the cranes. Nearby Newcastle has a long history with coal, shipbuilding and engineering, and the quayside is a cheerful place to walk, with seven bridges in a short stretch and a lively evening scene. Segedunum, the fort at Wallsend, has a tower you can climb and a reconstructed bath house, and it makes a good starting point if you are following the Wall.

The riding here is city riding, with buses, lights and parked cars, and the road surface is patched. The best part of the day lies to the west, where the Military Road runs along the Wall through open country, and the Tyne valley offers quiet lanes past Hexham and Corbridge. Come out of the city early, before the commuters, and aim for the sunlit crags. Fuel is easy, since Benwell and Whickham are suburbs with petrol stations, and the city centre is a short ride east.

Newcastle's weather is cooler and windier than in the west, and sea fog, called a haar, rolls in from the North Sea in spring and early summer. A bacon sandwich from a corner cafe is the local breakfast, and a pie and a pint in the evening finishes the day. Look at the temple, read the board, and think about how many people have walked past it without knowing.
t.the great wall@40.4,116.1:
The Great Wall is not one wall but many, built and rebuilt over two thousand years by different dynasties, and the section north-west of Beijing is the one most people picture. The stone and brick wall you see here was largely built by the Ming dynasty from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, when a strong frontier was needed against the peoples of the steppe. Watchtowers stand on the crest every few hundred metres, and the wall climbs and falls along the ridges of the Yanshan mountains, with signal towers on the high points that once passed warnings by fire and smoke.

The pass at Juyongguan and the fortified gate at Badaling guard the route that led from the capital to the plateau beyond. Badaling is the most visited part of the wall, reopened to the public in the 1950s and restored, and visitors from all over the world come here. It can be very crowded, especially on public holidays, so arrive early or choose a quieter, less restored section. The steps are steep and uneven, and the wind on the ridge is cold in winter. The hills around are rugged and bare, with scrubby slopes that turn gold in autumn.

Changping, with about 93,000 people some 26 km from here, is the closest town for fuel and food, and Beijing lies beyond it. Riding in China needs preparation: foreign visitors cannot normally ride a motorbike on a home licence, and Beijing in particular has restrictions on motorcycles. Most visitors will reach the wall by train, bus or hired driver, and the main expressway to Badaling is busy with coaches. Check what is possible for your own plans well in advance.

The best times are spring and autumn, when the air is clear and the colours are best, and the early morning, when the light is soft and the crowds have not yet arrived. Winter can be bright and cold, with a dusting of snow on the stone. Above Yanqing, the reservoir at Guanting and the surrounding hills add to the scene. Take water, sun protection and shoes with good grip, and give yourself time to walk away from the main stretch, where the wall runs on into quieter country along the crest.
t.cimbarrillo prado reches@38.4,-0.3:
The hills behind Alicante rise quickly. A few kilometres inland from the Costa Blanca, the flat coastal strip gives way to dry limestone ridges covered in scrub, pine, carob and almond, with deep ravines cut by streams that run only after heavy rain. These are the foothills of the Betic ranges, and in this part of the province the land climbs towards the sierras of Aitana and Mariola. El Campello, a former fishing town of about 26,000 people on the coast, is the closest sizeable place, and the nearby resort towns fill with visitors every summer, but the hinterland stays quieter and more rural.

People have lived in these hills for a very long time. The shelters and ravines of eastern Spain hold some of the most remarkable prehistoric art in Europe, the so-called Levantine rock art, in which small red and black figures of archers, hunters and animals are painted on rock walls. UNESCO listed the Mediterranean rock art of the Iberian Peninsula in 1998, and the Alicante province has several sites. The sites are fragile and often unmarked, and many are fenced or closed to protect the paintings, so do not expect a signed attraction. Ask locally, or at the nearest tourist office, before you go.

The ride inland is good. Roads from El Campello and Mutxamel wind into the hills past almond groves, small farmhouses and villages, with tight bends and some steep ramps. Some roads are narrow and the surfaces are patchy, so take care, especially after rain. In summer the heat is intense, with temperatures easily above 35 degrees, so ride early or late. Spring, when the almond trees blossom in white and pink, and autumn are the best times.

Fuel and food are easy near the coast, with stations in El Campello and Mutxamel, and fewer in the hills, so top up first. The nougat town of Xixona, home of the Spanish turrón, lies a short ride inland, and a stop at a shop to taste the hard and soft types is a pleasant detour. The Mediterranean light, the smell of pine and thyme and the sea glittering in the distance make a simple afternoon out of town.
t.abrigo del buen aire ii@38.5,-1.3:
Jumilla is wine country, and the hills around it hold one of the more unusual stretches of Spanish landscape. The town, a handsome place of about 25,000 people in the north of Murcia, lies on a high, dry plateau under the Sierra del Carche, and its name is on the label of bold red wines made from the Monastrell grape, a variety that thrives in poor, stony soil and fierce sun. Rows of low, gnarled bush vines stretch across the plain, with almond and olive trees and the odd fortified farmhouse, and the Carche range makes a dark backdrop to the north.

The rock shelters in this area belong to the Levantine rock art tradition, the red paintings of hunters and animals in small shelters that archaeologists place in the period after the last Ice Age. The Mediterranean rock art of the Iberian Peninsula was listed by UNESCO in 1998. The shelters are small, on cliffs and in ravines, and they are not easy to find. Many are protected by gates or are on private land, so it is best to ask at the museum in Jumilla before you set out. Do not touch or wet the paintings, which are fragile.

The landscape here is open, with big skies and long views, and the roads are generally good, with long straights and gentle curves between fields of vines. Summers are very hot, and winters can be cold, with frost and the odd fall of snow on the Carche. The best seasons are spring and autumn. In September the grape harvest is under way and tractors with trailers of grapes crowd the lanes, so ride with care.

Jumilla has fuel stations, supermarkets and many bodegas where you can book a tasting, and the town has a castle on a hill above the old quarter, which gives a good view over the roofs. Ontur and Albatana, smaller villages across the border in Albacete, are quiet and dusty places with little in the way of services. The local food leans on hearty dishes such as gazpacho manchego, a stew with flatbread and game, and on cheese and bread. A glass of local red with some cured ham is a good way to settle after a dusty ride.
t.prado del azogue@38.4,-0.3:
El Campello was a fishing village until quite recently, and it still has a working fish market on the seafront, where boats come in each afternoon and the catch is sold by auction. Today the town, with about 26,000 people, is one of the commuter and holiday towns on the coast north of Alicante, its beach lined with flats and its old harbour with small restaurants serving fresh fish and rice dishes. It is a nice place for a stop, with a long sandy beach and calm water, and in the summer evenings the promenade fills with families.

Inland, the land climbs steeply into the hills, and the contrast is large. The slopes above the coast are covered with the same pine, carob and almond that grow across the Alicante hinterland, and the view back towards the sea gives a feeling of how closely wild country and tourist coast sit together. Somewhere in the ravines and cliffs of this area are rock shelters with prehistoric paintings, part of a tradition of Levantine rock art that stretches along eastern Spain, listed by UNESCO in 1998. Because the paintings are delicate, access is limited and many are not marked, so check locally before you set out to look for any of them.

The riding between El Campello, Villajoyosa and Alicante is a coastal one, with the sea on one side and the hills on the other. Roads are busy in summer, with tourist traffic and many roundabouts, so early morning is much the best time. Villajoyosa, with its colourful houses along the seafront and the chocolate factories that have been in the town for generations, is a good stop on the way north. Inland roads climb towards the sierra with tight bends and good views.

Fuel is easy, as El Campello, Villajoyosa and Alicante all have plenty of stations, and the beach cafés will serve a coffee and a tostada in the morning. A local speciality is the arroz a banda, rice cooked in fish stock and served with allioli, and the nearby island of Tabarca, a short boat ride from Alicante, is known for its caldero fish stew. Take sun protection, as the light here is strong even in winter, and keep to the shade in the middle of the day.
t.cueva de los cascarones@38.3,-2.0:
This is the country of the upper Segura, where Albacete and Murcia meet, and it is among the least visited corners of southern Spain. The river cuts through limestone sierras, with pine forests, reedy banks and small terraced fields where almond and olive trees grow, and the villages, Socovos and Férez among them, are small, white and quiet. The scale of the land is bigger than its population, and in summer the cicadas are the loudest thing you will hear.

The caves and shelters of this region contain remarkable prehistoric art. Rock paintings in red and black, small figures of hunters, archers and animals in motion, are scattered through the ravines, and the area around Moratalla and Nerpio has some of the densest concentrations in the whole of the Levantine tradition. The paintings are thousands of years old, and UNESCO has recognised them as a group, listed in 1998 as the rock art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. Access to individual shelters is usually restricted, so ask at the visitor centre in Moratalla, which can tell you what is open, and never touch the paintings.

Moratalla itself, 14 km away, has about 8,500 people, a castle above the town and a tradition that surprises visitors: during Holy Week the townspeople beat drums day and night in a thundering procession called the Tamborada. It is the nearest sizeable place for fuel, food and rooms. Beyond it, roads wind through the sierras on twisty surfaces, with long climbs and some rough patches, and the nearest alternative fuel can be far, so keep the tank topped up.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons, as summer temperatures often pass 40 degrees and winter nights can bring frost. Take plenty of water and a map, since signal is weak in the valleys. The landscape has the dry, aromatic smell of rosemary and thyme, and the stars at night are exceptional. Local food includes migas, fried breadcrumbs with chorizo, and gachasmigas, a hearty winter dish, with a glass of the strong local wine. It is a place for those who like silence, and the road rewards patience.
t.abrigo i@39.0,-1.2:
Here the wide plains of La Mancha begin to tilt towards the coast, and the country turns into a patchwork of vineyards, cereal fields and low, pine-covered ridges. Alpera, Carcelén and Alatoz are small villages in the east of Albacete province, close to the border with Valencia, and the landscape has a high, windy character with big skies and few trees on the open ground. The Júcar river runs through a deeper, more broken country to the south, with canyons and reservoirs that give the otherwise dry terrain a green edge.

Alpera is the name that matters in the history of rock art. The painted shelter called the Cueva de la Vieja, near the village, is one of the great sites of the Levantine tradition, with dense scenes of people, deer, goats and bulls in red and black, and it is among the places that made this region central to the UNESCO listing of the rock art of the Mediterranean Basin in 1998. The paintings there are protected by gates and visits are controlled, so ask in Alpera before setting out. Other shelters in the area are small, hard to find and fragile.

The riding is relaxed and open, on roads that run across the plateau between fields, with gentle bends and the odd climb into pine woods. Wind is the main factor, and wind turbines on the ridges show how reliable it is. Summers are hot and winters can be bitterly cold, with frost and the occasional dusting of snow. Spring, with green fields, and early autumn, when the grape harvest begins, are the best seasons. The town of Almansa, with its castle on a rock above the plain, lies a short way north-east and was the scene of a famous battle in 1707 in the War of the Spanish Succession.

Ayora, about 17 km away, is the nearest town of 5,000 people, with fuel stations, shops and cafés, while Alpera and the other villages have little in the way of services. This is wine country, part of the La Manchuela area, where Bobal and other grapes are grown, and the local cuisine is hearty, with dishes such as gazpacho manchego, a rich stew served with flat bread, and local cheeses. Take cash, as small bars may not accept cards.
t.fuente serrano i@38.2,-2.2:
Nerpio is the kind of place that makes you check the map twice. It sits at the head of the Taibilla valley in the far south-west of Albacete province, on a high plateau more than a kilometre above sea level, in the Sierra de Segura, surrounded by mountains and reachable only by long and winding roads. The village is small, with about 1,600 people, and the countryside around it is a mix of cherry orchards, almond groves, pasture and pine forest, with limestone crags and the cold, clear water of the Taibilla river cutting through the valley floor.

For students of rock art, it is a celebrated place. The shelters of the Nerpio area hold what is one of the densest concentrations of Levantine paintings in all of Spain, with dozens of sites scattered through the ravines. Many are small shelters with figures of goats, deer, archers and hunters in red and black pigment. They belong to the UNESCO-listed Mediterranean rock art, and access is strictly controlled. Enquire in Nerpio itself, where local guides and the council may be able to arrange visits, and do not try to find sites by yourself, as the paintings are fragile and many are on protected land.

The riding to Nerpio is the real attraction. Roads wind up through the sierra, with long climbs, hairpins and fine views over the valley, and you are likely to share them with few other vehicles. The surface can be rough in places, and rockfall after heavy rain is possible, so take care. In winter the plateau gets cold and snow can close roads, while summer is warm and dry in the day with cool nights. Late spring, when cherry blossom is out, and October are particularly lovely.

Fuel is the concern. The nearest town of any size in the data is Moratalla, about 29 km away, and Yeste, a smaller place, is closer, so fill the tank and carry cash before you head up. Local specialities include cherries in season, goat dishes and the hearty mountain stews of the Segura country. The stars at night in this region are among the clearest in Spain, so if you stay in the village, look up.
t.barranc de les coves abrigo ii@38.9,-0.4:
The word barranc means a ravine, and the Barranc de les Coves is exactly that, one of the many steep valleys that cut into the limestone mountains of the Comtat and Alcoià in the interior of Alicante province. This is a green country compared with the dry plains farther south, with forests of pine and holm oak, terraced slopes of cherry, almond and olive, and clear streams in the bottom of the gorges. Roads in the area link small villages such as Beniarrés, Ráfol de Salem and Castelló de Rugat, each with a church tower and a cluster of white houses.

The shelters in these ravines belong to the Levantine rock art tradition, in which small human and animal figures were painted in red on the walls of rock shelters, possibly between six and ten thousand years ago, though dating is debated. The area around the Valls d'Alcoi has several important sites, and they are part of the group listed by UNESCO in 1998. As with other sites, the shelters are small, delicate and often closed, so check with the local museum in Alcoy or the nearest tourist office before planning a visit.

Alcoy itself is worth a visit. The industrial town, in a valley surrounded by hills, was a centre of paper and textile manufacture in the nineteenth century, and the modernist buildings from those days still stand. Every April it holds a festival of Moors and Christians, one of the largest in Spain, with mock battles and elaborate costumes. The nearby Sierra de Mariola, a natural park, is full of aromatic herbs, and a herbal liqueur called herbero is made from them.

The riding here is some of the best in the province, with twisting roads through the mountains, climbs with hairpins and long views. Surface quality varies, and in winter there can be ice on the higher roads. Muro d'Alcoi, about 10 km away with almost 8,000 people, has fuel and shops, and Alcoy is larger. Try olleta, a rich vegetable and bean stew, or a slice of coca, a flatbread with toppings, and finish with a café bombón, coffee with condensed milk. Spring and autumn are best, as summers get hot and winters can be chilly.
t.abric del barranco garrofero@39.1,-0.8:
Somewhere in the mountains south of Valencia there is a cave named for a spider, and it holds one of the most famous paintings of prehistoric Europe. The Cueva de la Araña, in the village of Bicorp, shows a figure climbing a rope or ladder of plant fibre on a cliff face, apparently collecting honey from a wild bees' nest, with bees flying around. It is a small, lively picture, thought to be several thousand years old, and it has become an emblem of the Levantine rock art tradition that UNESCO listed in 1998. The shelters nearby, among them the Barranco Garrofero, belong to the same landscape and tradition, and you should treat them as protected and fragile places.

This is rugged, rarely visited country. Bicorp, Quesa and Navarrés are small villages with fewer than three thousand people between them, set among the foothills of the Sierra de Martés and the Muela de Cortes, a limestone plateau cut by deep ravines and the green gorge of the Júcar river. The vegetation is scrubby Mediterranean forest of pine, kermes oak, rosemary and thyme, and carob trees, garrofero in Valencian, grow on the terraced slopes, which explains the name of the ravine. Griffon vultures circle on the thermals, and wild boar and mountain goats live in the hills.

The riding is delightful, with narrow, twisting roads that climb and fall, some with tight bends and rough patches, and few other vehicles. Rain can cause rockfalls, and summer heat is intense. Take plenty of water and keep the tank full, since services are scarce. Ayora, about 21 km away, is the nearest town of 5,000 people, and Navarrés has a few shops and fuel.

Local food reflects the interior: rice cooked with rabbit and snails, gazpachos with game, and honey from the wild thyme of the hills, which seems the right treat given the painting. Spring is best, when the hills are green and flowers are out, and autumn is also pleasant. Always ask permission before going onto farmland, close gates behind you, and respect any signs near rock art sites.
t.abrigo de la llagosa@38.1,-2.3:
The upper Segura valley, south of Nerpio, is a world of cliffs and reservoirs, and the place called La Llagosa lies in the middle of it. This is the Sierra de Segura, a limestone massif that forms part of one of Spain's biggest natural parks, the Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas, a UNESCO biosphere reserve. It is a land of pine forest and rocky ridges, where the Segura and its tributaries cut deep valleys, and the landscape is dotted with small villages like Yeste and Letur, whose white houses cluster on rocky spurs.

The shelters scattered through these hills belong to the Levantine rock art tradition. Artists using red and black pigment painted tiny, lively figures of hunters, archers, goats and deer, and the paintings have survived in sheltered overhangs for thousands of years. The Mediterranean rock art of the Iberian Peninsula has been on the UNESCO list since 1998. Visits to individual shelters are limited, and some are gated, so enquire at the local tourist information in Yeste or Nerpio before you plan a visit. Never touch the walls, and keep to paths.

Riding in this area is demanding in a good way. The roads are narrow and twisty, with lots of climbing and descending, and there are long stretches without a house or a station. Fuel is the crucial point: the nearest big town in the data, Moratalla, is 38 km away, and Yeste, with about 3,600 people, is closer and has some services, so fill the tank beforehand. Weather can change quickly in the sierra, and winter snow and ice can make higher roads treacherous. Summer is hot, but nights remain cool.

The Segura is clean here, and its reservoirs, such as the Taibilla and the Fuensanta, are used for fishing and swimming. Look for griffon vultures and, with luck, mountain goats on the crags. Local food leans on game, such as venison and wild boar stews, and on migas, with strong cheese from the mountain farms. This is a quiet, spacious part of Spain, best taken slowly, with a camera and a full water bottle.
t.abric del espolon del zapatero@39.2,-0.8:
The Cortes de Pallás area, in the interior of Valencia province, is one of the wildest places within an hour or two of the coast. The Júcar river has carved a deep canyon through the limestone, and the Muela de Cortes, a high plateau of rock and scrub, rises above it. Bicorp, Quesa and Millares are small villages on its edge, and the roads that link them are some of the twistiest in the region, with sections that cling to the sides of the gorge and open on huge views. Griffon vultures and golden eagles use the cliffs, and the pine woods are home to wild boar and roe deer.

The Espolón del Zapatero, the Shoemaker's Spur, is a rocky outcrop, and the shelter that carries its name belongs to the same family of Levantine rock art as the nearby sites. Small painted figures of animals and people decorate overhangs in these ravines, and the whole group is part of the UNESCO listing for Mediterranean rock art of 1998. Most shelters are fragile, and access is regulated, so ask at the local town halls or the regional heritage office before you go. Do not expect signs.

In the area, the great engineering fact is the reservoirs. The Júcar has been dammed for hydroelectric power, and the lakes, such as the Embalse de Cortes, give the country an unexpected green-blue colour among the dry hills. A road along the water gives views over the lake, and in summer people swim and kayak. The canyon was the scene of a huge flood in 1982, when the Tous dam failed downstream, which is still remembered in the Ribera region.

For fuel and supplies, plan ahead. Carlet, a town of about 15,000 people 23 km away, is the nearest place of any size in the data, and Millares and the villages have little. Riding is slow and rewarding, with bends and climbs, and the surface is patchy in places. Spring and autumn are best, as summers are hot. A meal of rice with rabbit and snails, or a local olla with sausage, and a glass of Valencian wine make a hearty lunch in one of the village bars.
t.barran de parets@38.8,-0.2:
The Vall d'Ebo is a pocket of mountains behind the Costa Blanca where the sea is only half an hour away, yet the villages look as if they belong to another century. Adsubia and Vall d'Ebo are tiny settlements of a few hundred people, in a landscape of steep ravines, terraces and bare limestone walls. The Valencian word barranc, a ravine, is on the map everywhere, and each one has its own name. The Barranc de l'Infern, the Hell Ravine, nearby, is a famed walk on a path of thousands of stone steps that the Moriscos, Muslim farmers, built to link villages. They were expelled in 1609, and the terraces and steps are a legacy of their work.

The rock shelters here belong to the family of Levantine paintings, with their small red figures of hunters and animals, which UNESCO listed in 1998. The area has several sites, including the Barranc de Parets, and they are small and fragile. Access is limited, so ask in Pego or Vall d'Ebo about what is open to visitors, and do not try to climb to shelters on your own. The cliffs here are unstable, and the paths can be dangerous after rain.

Below the mountains lies the Marjal de Pego-Oliva, a wetland natural park where the plain beside the sea is flooded for rice. In summer the paddies are bright green, and herons, egrets and many other birds feed in the shallows. Pego, a town of about 11,000 people seven kilometres away, is the centre of the area, with fuel stations, supermarkets and a market, and it is famous for rice dishes, among them arroz al horno, rice baked in the oven with sausage and chickpeas, and for oranges.

The riding here is very good. Roads from Pego climb into the hills with a sequence of bends and long views toward the sea, and the villages along the way are quiet. The surface is variable, and the roads can be narrow, with cyclists on weekends, especially in winter and spring when northern Europeans arrive. Late autumn and spring are lovely, with clear light, and summer can be very hot. Remember to fill up at Pego, as there is nothing in the valley.
t.chiquita@37.7,-2.2:
Almería is known for deserts and beaches, but its northern edge is a different country, a high, cold plateau of almond orchards and pine-covered sierras that the locals call Los Vélez. The town of Vélez-Blanco, with just over 2,000 people, lies under a castle on a rocky crest, and María and Chirivel are smaller places on the plateau. The region is protected as the Sierra María-Los Vélez natural park, and the air is clear, the sky enormous, and the nights cold, even in summer. In late winter the almond trees bloom pink and white on the slopes below the peaks.

Vélez-Blanco has two stories to tell. The castle, a Renaissance fortress built in the early sixteenth century for the Marquis of los Vélez, has a handsome interior courtyard, though the original marble patio was sold in the early twentieth century and is now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, a fact the locals do not forget. The other story is older. The Cueva de los Letreros, a rock shelter in the hills, holds paintings from the same tradition as the Levantine sites, among them a figure with raised arms that became the Indalo, the little stick-figure charm that you now see on car stickers and doorways across Almería. The cave is protected, and visits are arranged through the town.

The shelter listed as Chiquita belongs to the same landscape, and treat it with the same care: paintings of this kind are thousands of years old and fragile, UNESCO listed the group in 1998, and access should be arranged locally. The surroundings reward a slow ride. Roads on the plateau are quiet, with gentle bends and long views, and the wind can be sharp. Winter brings frost, and sometimes snow on the Sierra de María, so check the forecast.

Vélez Rubio, a bigger town of about 7,000 people ten kilometres away, has fuel stations and supermarkets, and a big baroque church, the Encarnación, with twin towers. The local food is hearty, with gurullos, a pasta-based stew, migas and almond sweets. Spring is the best time, with green slopes and blossom.
t.abrigo del paso@38.2,-1.6:
Calasparra is a rice town, which is not what most people expect of inland Murcia. The rice grown here, in terraced paddies along the Segura and Mundo rivers, was the first in Spain to receive a protected designation of origin, and it is prized for absorbing flavour without turning to mush, so paella cooks prefer it. The paddies shimmer green in summer and gold in autumn, with herons and egrets feeding in the flooded fields, and behind them rise bare limestone hills, so the effect is of a patch of Asia dropped onto a dry Spanish landscape.

The Segura here cuts through the Cañón de Almadenes, a narrow gorge with vertical walls, where the river runs green between cliffs and a sanctuary clings to the rock face. The Virgen de la Esperanza sanctuary, in a cave in the cliffs, is the most important pilgrimage site in the region, and the image is carried in a procession on feast days. A viewpoint above the gorge gives a fine look at the cliffs, and vultures and eagles often circle overhead.

The painted shelters of the Calasparra and Cieza area belong to the Levantine rock art tradition, part of the UNESCO listing of 1998, and the cliffs of the Segura valley are full of small overhangs where such paintings survive. As elsewhere, the sites are fragile and protected, access is limited and local advice is essential. The nearby town of Cieza, a larger place of about 35,000 people, is famous for its peaches and its spring blossom, when thousands of fruit trees come into flower together in February and March.

Calasparra, with about 10,000 people, is 11 km away and has fuel stations, shops and cafés. The riding is easy, on roads that follow the river and cross the dry hills, with the odd bend and good views, and in summer the heat is severe, so ride early. Try arroz con conejo y caracoles, rice with rabbit and snails, or a plain rice and vegetable dish, the best way to taste the local grain. Carry water, and stay out of the river after heavy rain, when the flow can rise fast.
t.las covaticas i@37.8,-2.0:
The name Las Covaticas means the little caves, and the whole area south of Vélez Blanco is a country of small hollows in the rock. The ground rises from the plain of Vélez Rubio to the long ridges of the Sierra de María, where pine forests and bare slopes meet wide sky, and the air at more than a thousand metres feels cool and thin. Vélez Rubio, a town of about 7,000 people 15 km away, is the largest place in the area, with a grand baroque church that seems too big for its surroundings. The Renaissance castle of Vélez Blanco stands nearby on its crag.

This part of Spain, the Altiplano de Los Vélez, has a long human history, and the cliffs hold many shelters that people used and painted long ago, among them the Cueva de los Pucheros. The UNESCO listing for the rock art of the Mediterranean Basin covers the painted ones, and access to any of them should be arranged through local museums and guides, as paintings are fragile and sites are protected.

The riding is open and quiet. Roads cross the plateau in long, gentle curves between almond and cereal fields, with the Sierra de María as a backdrop, and the surfaces are generally good. Wind is the main factor, and in winter ice can form on the higher parts, with snow now and then. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with mild days and clear light. The sky is notably dark at night, and the area is used for stargazing.

Vélez Rubio has everything a rider needs: fuel, supermarkets, bars and rooms. Local food is plain and hearty, with migas, stews of lamb and pork, and sweets made with almonds. Villages on the plateau often have a bar that serves a free tapa with each drink, in the tradition of Almería, so a stop for a beer or a coffee also feeds you. Keep an eye out for flocks of sheep and goats, which have right of way on many of the country roads.
t.mingarnao i@38.2,-2.3:
Everything about Nerpio feels remote, and Mingarnao pushes the feeling a little further. The shelter sits in the Sierra de Segura, where the road ends and tracks wander over limestone ridges, through pine woods and past small farms. A scattering of hamlets, such as Yeste, Letur and Nerpio itself, are the nearest signs of life, and the nearest big town in the data, Moratalla, is a long 38 km away. The sense of space is the point of coming here.

The rivers help explain the place. The Taibilla, the Segura and their tributaries have cut gorges through the rock, and in the bottoms of the valleys there are poplar groves, orchards and small irrigated fields, with water that is clear and cold. Letur is a village of whitewashed houses clinging to a rock above the Mundo river, with narrow lanes, a Moorish quarter and a small museum, and it is one of the prettiest places in the region. The Mundo, which rises nearby in the Calar del Mundo, has an extraordinary source: a cave that gushes out of the cliff, in the Cueva de los Chorros, with waterfalls and pools.

The painted shelters in this area are part of the Levantine rock art, listed by UNESCO in 1998. Because Nerpio is so rich in sites, a rule of thumb is to learn first and look second: visit the information point in Nerpio or Yeste, find out which sites are open, and hire a local guide if one is offered. Many shelters are closed with gates, others lie on private land, and the paintings can be damaged by even the slightest touch.

Riders will love the approach. Roads cross the sierra in tight bends with long climbs and sudden views, and traffic is almost non-existent. The surface can be rough, so take your time. Fuel is limited: fill up in Yeste or Moratalla, and carry some cash. Local cuisine uses game and mountain produce, so try venison or a stew of the season. Winter brings snow, while summer days can be hot and dry, with cool evenings.
t.abrigo de las canas i@39.2,-0.8:
Millares is a village of fewer than six hundred people in the interior of Valencia province, and the whole district feels like a place the twentieth century forgot to modernise. The land is a mix of limestone gorges, dry terraces and pine forest, with the Júcar river running through a deep canyon to the south, and the reservoirs of Cortes and Naranjero lighting the valley floor with turquoise water. The roads wind through small farming settlements, past carob and olive trees, and the silence is often broken only by the bells of a flock of goats.

The Cañas shelter is one of the small painted rock shelters that dot the ravines here, part of the Levantine rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998. Painted in red, these scenes of people and animals are among the earliest depictions of daily life in Europe, though the exact age and meaning are debated. The shelters are fragile, many are on private land, and access is controlled, so enquire locally in Millares, Bicorp or Quesa before planning a visit. If you are lucky you may meet a farmer who knows the paths, and who may tell you stories you will not find in a book.

The Júcar canyon is the great sight in this area. The river, held back by dams, fills long arms of the canyon with calm water, and the cliffs above are home to griffon vultures, golden eagles and Bonelli's eagles. The road along the gorge gives long views and tight bends, and is among the most beautiful in the province. Surface quality varies, with some patches of loose gravel and the odd rockfall after storms.

Fuel is a long way off. Turís, a town of about 5,300 people 22 km away, is the nearest place in the data, and the local villages may have little, so plan a full tank. In spring and autumn the weather is gentle, with clear light. The cuisine is rural: gazpachos with game, rice with rabbit, and sweets made with almonds and honey. Turís itself is known for its wine and for the huge cellar built in a modernist style, a surprise in a small town.
t.abric del sordo@39.0,-1.2:
Ayora sits in a broad valley between two mountain ranges, in the interior of Valencia province, and the land around it has a high, golden look in summer, with fields of cereal, vines and almond trees under big skies. The town, with about 5,500 people, has a castle and a handsome palace of the Counts of Cervellón, and it feels like a gateway to a quieter Spain. To the south, the Cabriel river has cut a long canyon through the limestone, the Hoces del Cabriel, a protected area with clear water, poplars and cliffs, listed as a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

Close by, at Cofrentes, there is a surprise. The Cerro de Agrás is an extinct volcano, one of the few in the Valencian interior, and a nuclear power station stands in the valley below it, which gives the landscape an odd mix of the ancient and the modern. Cofrentes also has a castle on a rock above the village and a hot spring spa. Not far from here is Alpera, home to a famous painted shelter, the Cueva de la Vieja, and the rock shelters in this district, including the Abric del Sordo, belong to the same Levantine tradition that UNESCO listed in 1998.

Treat any shelter as a protected place. Paintings of hunters, goats and bulls in red pigment have survived for thousands of years under overhangs, and they are fragile. Many sites are closed, and the ones that can be visited are handled by local guides, so ask in Ayora or at the council before setting out. Never touch, spray water or chalk the paintings.

The riding is relaxed and rewarding. Roads cross the valley between fields and follow the Cabriel, with gentle bends and the odd climb into pine forest, and traffic is light. In summer the heat is strong, and in winter frost can form on the roads in the morning. Spring is best, with the green of the cereal fields and wildflowers. Ayora has fuel stations and supermarkets, and the local food includes gazpachos, rice with rabbit and local sausages, and the bakeries make good almond sweets.
t.abrigo de la vinuela@38.1,-2.4:
Segura de la Sierra is a village that looks like a stage set, and it is real. It sits on a conical hill above the olive groves of the upper Guadalimar valley, crowned by a castle, with narrow lanes of whitewashed houses winding up to the walls, and from the top the view takes in miles of olives, pine-covered ridges and distant sierras. The castle was a stronghold of the Order of Santiago, the knightly order that held much of this frontier in the Middle Ages. It has a Moorish bath house, restored and open to the public, a bullring built into the rock, and a medieval keep.

The village lies in the Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park, the largest protected area in Spain, a UNESCO biosphere reserve with deep valleys, big forests of black pine and a rich wildlife. Red deer, mouflon and ibex live in the park, and the Guadalquivir, the great river of Andalusia, rises in the Cazorla mountains close by. Griffon vultures and bearded vultures can be seen over the crags. In the autumn the sound of rutting stags echoes in the woods.

The nearby shelters, including La Viñuela, belong to the painted rock tradition of the Levantine art, part of the 1998 UNESCO listing of the Mediterranean Basin rock art of the Iberian Peninsula. Sites of this kind are fragile, and the ones open to the public are managed by local guides, so ask at the village or in Nerpio, and never touch the walls or look for paintings without advice.

The ride is unforgettable. Roads from Orcera and Hornos wind through olive terraces and then climb into the pine forests with plenty of bends, and views of the plain below. Surfaces are mostly decent, with some rough patches, and traffic is light except in the hunting season and weekends. Fuel is a worry: Huéscar, about 39 km away, is the nearest town in the data, though Orcera and Santiago de la Espada have some services, so fill the tank. Spring and autumn are best, with clear air and colour. The local olive oil is excellent, and game stews and the regional dish of andrajos, a stew with flat dough, are good meals.
t.barranc de la falaguera abric iii@39.3,-:
The coordinates put you in the flat farmland south of Valencia, where the plain of the Ribera is a sea of orange trees. Alginet, a town of about 13,000 people, and its neighbours Benifaió and Alfarp are part of a landscape of citrus groves, irrigation ditches and tiled farmhouses, where the Júcar river has laid down rich soil over thousands of years. In spring, when the orange blossom is out, the scent of azahar fills the air and can be smelled from the road with the visor up.

The shelter named for the Falaguera ravine belongs to the world of Levantine rock art, which UNESCO listed in 1998, and its ravine lies in the hills rather than the plain, so the day's ride takes you from the groves into the folds of the interior. The paintings in these shelters, red figures of hunters, animals and scenes of daily life, are fragile, and the shelters are not signed, so enquire locally and do not expect to find them without a guide.

The ride across this part of Valencia is mostly easy. Flat roads cross the plain between orchards, with the odd crossing of the Júcar, and traffic is heavy near Valencia and on the motorways. The turn inland, towards Alfarp and the hills, brings gentle curves and views over the groves. The surface is generally good. In late summer the heat is intense and the humidity is high, so early starts are best, and autumn storms can bring heavy rain, with flooded roads in the lowest places.

Alginet has fuel stations, supermarkets and cafés, and the neighbouring towns have more. Valencia is only about 25 km north, with the huge Albufera lagoon, rice fields and the home of paella to the east. The authentic recipe uses chicken, rabbit and flat green beans, cooked over an open fire of orange wood, and arguments about the right way to cook it are a local sport. Horchata, a sweet drink made from tiger nuts, grown in the nearby huerta of Alboraya, is the proper cooler on a hot afternoon, served with fartons, a long sugar-glazed pastry.
t.abric de los gineses@39.1,-0.8:
Bicorp has about 650 inhabitants and a church, a main street, a bar or two and a long view across a valley of pine and carob trees, and that is the kind of place that makes an inland Valencia ride special. This is the so-called España vaciada, the emptied Spain, where villages have lost most of their young people over the last sixty years, and where the land has been returning to scrub and forest. The roads are quiet because the people are gone, and the effect on a rider is a gift: bend after bend with no traffic, the smell of rosemary and warm pine, and a sky as large as you will see in Europe.

The Abric de los Gineses is part of a group of painted shelters that give the district its renown, in the same tradition as the famous honey-gathering scene in the cave not far away. The paintings, in red, show small figures of archers and animals, and UNESCO lists the Mediterranean Basin rock art as a World Heritage Site, from 1998. The sites are fragile, so a visit must be arranged with local people, and the shelters themselves are often in difficult, steep terrain. Look at the displays in the nearest village to find out what is open.

The villages in the district are tiny, with Quesa and Navarrés at hand, and they repay a stop. A bar in Bicorp or Quesa is a place where the whole village seems to be present at midday, with the television on, the waiter chatting and the plate of the day on the counter. Local cuisine is rural and filling, with rice and rabbit, gazpacho with game, and olives and almonds from the nearby trees. Farmers still keep goats and sheep, and you may meet a flock on the road.

For fuel, plan carefully. Ayora, about 21 km away, is the nearest town of 5,000 people in the data, and Navarrés has a station and shops, but the smaller villages do not. Roads can be narrow, with sharp bends and patched asphalt, and fallen rock after storms is possible. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with comfortable days and fresh air. Carry water and a layer, and give the shepherds a wave.
t.cova fosca@38.8,-0.2:
The cave called Cova Fosca means the dark cave, and the name is as plain as the country around it, a series of pale limestone ravines in the interior of the Marina Alta. Vall d'Ebo, Adsubia and Pego lie at the foot of the mountains, with villages of a few hundred people, and a land of terraced slopes where the Moriscos, the Muslim farmers who stayed after the Christian conquest, grew grain, grapes and almonds until their expulsion in 1609. After that the valleys emptied, and the terraces stand as monuments to a vanished community.

At Pego, about five kilometres away, the mountains meet a wetland. The Marjal de Pego-Oliva is a natural park of marsh, reedbeds and rice fields, a remnant of the lagoons that once covered much of the coast, and it supports herons, ducks, fish and many migrant birds. Rice is grown here, and the harvest in September fills the area with combines and the smell of straw. Pego itself has about 11,000 people and a tradition of rice dishes, among them arroz al horno, as well as oranges and the cake called coca de llanda.

The shelters of this district, with their small red paintings of hunters and animals, belong to the Levantine rock art tradition, listed by UNESCO in 1998. They are protected and fragile, so always check locally about access, and treat the sites with care.

The riding is excellent. Roads climb out of Pego towards Vall d'Ebo with hairpins and long views over the marsh and the sea, then run along ridges and down into the villages, and the bends are consistently good. The road is narrow in places, with patched asphalt, and in winter and spring cyclists are numerous, as the Marina Alta is a popular training area. Summer is very hot, and autumn storms can be heavy. A rice dish at a restaurant in Pego after the ride is the natural conclusion.
The Guadalest valley is one of the most photographed places on the Costa Blanca, and it is easy to see why. A narrow rocky spur rises from the middle of the valley, topped by the tower and ruined walls of the castle of Guadalest, and the village clings to the rock below, reached through a tunnel cut in the stone. Beyond it, a reservoir with a startling turquoise colour fills the valley floor, and the great grey wall of the Sierra de Aitana, at 1,558 metres the highest peak in the province of Alicante, rises behind. The village itself is crowded with visitors in summer, and many of the shops sell souvenirs, but at dawn the view across the valley is quiet and fine.

The villages of the district, Castell de Castells, Benimantell and Bolulla, are small, between three and five hundred people, set in terraced slopes covered with almond, olive, carob and loquat trees. The loquat, called nispero, is the specialty of the lower valley around Callosa d'en Sarrià, whose harvest in spring is celebrated, and the almond blossom in February turns the slopes white. The Barranc de Miquel el Serril is one of the countless gullies that drain the mountains.

The rock shelters here belong to the Levantine painting tradition, part of the UNESCO site listed in 1998, and the area around Castell de Castells has several of them. Access is regulated and some shelters are closed, so ask at the local council or the museum in Castell de Castells before setting out, and do not touch the paintings.

The riding is among the best in Alicante province. The roads from La Nucia and Callosa climb through the hills with a sequence of bends, such as the Coll de Rates, a favourite with cyclists and bikers, and there are views of the sea far below. Weekends can be busy, and the narrow roads call for care. La Nucia, about 12 km away with almost 18,000 people, has fuel and shops. Try olleta, a stew of vegetables and beans, and the honey and almond sweets of the interior.
t.defended settlement and roman signal sta:
The South Tyne valley below Haydon Bridge is one of the best places in England to understand why the Romans chose this line. To the north rises the long whinstone crag, the Whin Sill, a hard dark rock that stands up in a series of cliffs facing north, and along its crest Hadrian's Wall once ran. South of it lies the valley, with the river, the old road called the Stanegate and a string of forts. A defended settlement and signal station here would have been part of this web, sitting on high ground where a fire or flag could pass news along the line in minutes.

The wall was built from about AD 122 and garrisoned for nearly three centuries, and its stones have had a long afterlife. When the military road was built across the country after the 1745 Jacobite rising, General Wade's engineers used the wall as a quarry and as a foundation, which is why the B6318 runs so straight across the high ground. The cliffs, the sheep and the hard sky make it feel like the end of the world, and in a sense, for the Romans, it was.

For motorcyclists the area is a delight, though not for technical riding. The roads are open, rolling and fast in places, with long views north over moor and forest. The B6318 has a line of dips and crests, and there are tight bends where it follows the crags. Sheep stray onto the road without warning, and the weather can flip from sunshine to hill fog in a quarter of an hour. Surfaces are generally good but frost-damaged in places, and in winter the high road is sometimes closed by snow.

Haydon Bridge is a small village with a pub and a shop; Hexham, fifteen kilometres to the east, is a handsome market town with an abbey, fuel, supermarkets and a good choice of cafes. The nearby fort at Vindolanda has given the world the Roman writing tablets, including a famous birthday party invitation, and its museum is worth the stop.
t.seatsides 2 roman temporary camp@55.0,-2:
Seatsides is a name on a map of fields, a spot where a Roman temporary camp is visible only as a faint square in the grass when the light is low. These camps were put up by marching armies, each night, with a ditch and a bank thrown around a regular rectangle, and some of them in the north of England survive as earthworks nearly two thousand years later. This one lies near Haltwhistle, in the Tyne Gap, the low pass that cuts between the Pennines and the Cheviot hills and has been the natural route from east to west across northern England since before the Romans.

The wall itself runs close by, along the edge of the Whin Sill crags at Walltown, where the Roman Army Museum tells the story of the soldiers who lived here. Haltwhistle claims to be the centre of Britain, a boast you can spot on shop signs, and it is a small, attractive town of stone houses on the South Tyne. Nearby Greenhead and Gilsland mark the point where the wall runs into Cumbria. The land is a mixture of rough grazing, wet pasture and sudden rocky outcrops, and curlews and lapwings call in the spring.

The roads here are open and often exposed, rising and falling over the ridges. Wind and rain sweep across the high ground, and sheep and cattle are regular obstacles. The A69 is a fast dual-carriageway-style route carrying plenty of lorries, while the smaller roads up toward the wall, notably the old military road, are much more fun. In winter the higher sections can ice up, and snow sometimes closes them.

Haltwhistle has a few thousand people and enough shops and cafes for a break, and it also has fuel, though it is wise to top up in Hexham or Carlisle before heading into the quieter hills. Pack a waterproof, because the weather here changes quickly. The best time for the wall country is late spring or early autumn.
t.tianloukeng tulou cluster@24.6,117.1:
The tulou of southwestern Fujian look like something dropped from the sky, huge round or square earthen fortresses sitting among tea terraces and bamboo, with roofs that curve like turned-up eaves. Tianloukeng is a cluster of them in Nanjing County, in the hills inland from Xiamen, and the group is probably the most photographed in the region because it can be seen as a whole: a square tulou at the centre, surrounded by round ones, set on a slope so the roofs stagger like a bowl of dumplings.

They were built by Hakka communities, who migrated south from the Chinese heartland over centuries and often found themselves unwelcome neighbours. The answer was architecture. A tulou has walls of rammed earth, sometimes more than a metre thick at the base, and a single heavy gate, so a whole clan could shut themselves in during a feud or a bandit raid. Inside, families lived in rooms on several storeys around a shared courtyard with a well and an ancestral hall. Some held hundreds of people. The Fujian Tulou were inscribed by UNESCO in 2008, and the Tianloukeng group was part of that listing.

Nothing about the surroundings is flat. The roads wind up through narrow green valleys, tight and steep, with villages along the way and old men selling tea at the roadside. Expect narrow lanes, delivery trucks and the occasional water buffalo, and wet roads in the damp season. Fog is common in the hills, and spring brings rain. Autumn is generally clearer. Note that motorcycles are subject to strict local rules in China, and foreigners usually cannot ride without a Chinese licence and registration, so check what applies to you before you plan to ride here.

There is no sizeable town right at the cluster, so plan to buy fuel and food at a county town on the way in. Local food is built around the hills: mushrooms, bamboo shoots, tea, and Hakka dishes such as braised pork and salted chicken. Many tulou still house residents, and some sell tea in the courtyard. Be a considerate guest, because this is a place where people live, not a museum with its own staff.
t.arroyo de martin perez@38.4,-0.3:
Behind the Costa Blanca's hotel towers there is a quite different country, dry, stony and mostly empty, and the Arroyo de Martín Pérez belongs to it. An arroyo is a gully that stays dry for most of the year, and here, on the hills inland from El Campello and San Juan de Alicante, it carries the water away when the rains arrive. Those rains, when they come, come hard. Autumn storms on this coast can drop a month's water in a few hours, and the gullies fill suddenly, so check the forecast before you go poking about dry beds.

The shelter here is one of the many small rock-painting sites of the Alicante hills, part of the Levantine art tradition that UNESCO lists as the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. The paintings are generally small, red and faded, and were made by hunter-gatherer and early farming people many thousands of years ago. The ride also touches the Palmeral of Elche, a huge grove of date palms laid out under Moorish rule and now itself a World Heritage site, which is a lovely contrast with the bare limestone.

The land around is carob, almond and pine on thin red soil, with Mediterranean scrub that smells of thyme when the sun is on it. Looking inland, the long blue wall of the Sierra de Aitana stands over everything, the highest summit in the province of Alicante. Looking the other way, you may catch the glint of the sea.

Riding here is easy to get wrong because the area is busy. El Campello, Mutxamel and San Juan de Alicante all have over twenty thousand people, so the roads near them are lined with roundabouts, villas and delivery vans, and traffic can be heavy at weekends. Once you turn off onto the minor roads into the hills, it quietens down at once, with tight bends and patchy tarmac. Early morning is by far the best time, partly for the light and partly because midday in summer is brutally hot.

Fuel is no problem here, with stations on every main road around the three towns. The coast, with its beaches and cheap cafes, is only a few minutes away, which makes this a good half-day.
t.inferior letreros@37.7,-2.1:
The Cueva de los Letreros is what most people mean when they say Vélez-Blanco, and the rock shelter at Inferior Letreros is part of the same story. Famous images in the main cave include a little figure with raised arms and a bow-like shape that locals have adopted as the Indalo, now the good-luck symbol of the whole province of Almería, painted on walls and sold on keyrings from the beaches to the mountains. The paintings belong to the Levantine tradition that UNESCO lists as the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula.

The village is a lovely place to arrive. Vélez-Blanco is small, about two thousand people, white houses climbing a hill under a square Renaissance castle built in the early sixteenth century by the Marquis of Los Vélez. The castle is a story of its own. Its beautiful marble courtyard was bought and shipped to New York in the early twentieth century, and now stands inside the Metropolitan Museum of Art, which leaves the shell oddly empty and the village mildly sore about it.

The country around is the Sierra de María-Los Vélez, a natural park of limestone ridges with pine forest, almond groves and wide, pale uplands, where the northernmost corner of Almería meets Murcia and Granada. Maimón, the highest peak, is above two thousand metres, and winter snow is not unusual. In summer, the area is hot but breathes far better than the coast, and evenings are fresh.

For riders, this is excellent territory, with quiet roads climbing from the valley into the sierra, with long views, bends of every radius and almost no traffic. Surfaces are mostly good, though patched and dusty near farms, and the wind on exposed ridges can be strong. Early spring and autumn are best. Velez-Rubio, three or four kilometres away, is larger, with about seven thousand people, and has fuel, bakeries and bars, so fill up there rather than trusting the smaller villages. María and Vélez-Blanco itself have cafes where you can sit with a view of the castle and wait for the heat to pass.
t.cueva de la mina@38.4,-0.3:
The Cueva de la Mina lies in the hills behind Alicante's northern suburbs, close enough to the coast that you can leave a beach town after lunch and be among rock and scrub within the hour. That gives it a particular pleasure: the contrast. One moment you are among apartment blocks and palm trees at El Campello, a former fishing village that has become a seaside town of twenty-six thousand people, and the next, you are on a narrow lane with the sea shrinking behind you and the sun pressing on the stones.

The cave belongs to the group of sites in the Alicante hills that carry traces of prehistoric people. Some of them, like the neighbouring Abric de Lambert on the same ride, contain Levantine-style paintings, small red figures that UNESCO protects as part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. I will not claim to know what is painted in this particular cave, so treat it as an invitation to look at the landscape that people have used for a very long time: dry limestone, caves, a bit of water, and views down the valley.

The country is typical of the Alicante interior, with carob and olive trees, wild rosemary and a lot of bare rock. From the heights, you can often see both the sea and the Sierra de Aitana, a long grey wall to the north. Summer is almost too hot for walking, with temperatures that push past thirty-five degrees by noon, so go in the cooler months or very early. In autumn, brief violent storms can wash gravel across the road.

Riding is a mixture of tight lanes and dull suburban approaches. Coming from the coast, expect roundabouts, and once off the main roads, narrow tarmac that can be broken at the edges. Local drivers are quick, but not unreasonable. Fuel is no trouble, with El Campello, San Juan de Alicante and Villajoyosa all within fifteen kilometres. Villajoyosa, with its brightly painted fishermen's houses and a chocolate-making tradition, is the best place to eat on the way back.
t.barranc del salt abric li@38.7,-0.4:
The Barranc del Salt is a ravine on the edge of the Serra de Mariola, a limestone massif in the north of Alicante province that is protected as a natural park. The shelter here is one of several along the ravine, and it carries rock art in the Levantine tradition, small red figures painted long ago and protected by UNESCO as part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. As elsewhere in this area, many of the images are faint, so approach it as a walk first and a picture-hunt second.

The Mariola is the real attraction for anyone who loves quiet country. It is famous for its herbs. Thyme, rosemary, mountain tea and dozens of aromatic plants grow on its slopes, and for generations local people have collected them to make an aniseed-flavoured herbal liqueur, the herbero, which you will see for sale in the villages. In the past, people also stored winter snow in great stone wells, the neveras, and sent ice down to the cities of the coast. A few of these round stone pits survive in the hills, and you may stumble on one.

The nearest settlement is Benilloba, a small village of under a thousand people, with Relleu and a few similar places not far away. For bigger supplies, Cocentaina, with over eleven thousand people, is the place, about ten kilometres off. It has a handsome palace of the old counts, a Saturday market and a lively medieval fair around All Saints, and fuel is easy to find there. Do not rely on a pump in the small villages.

The roads are the best part. The lanes climb through pine and oak with short, tight bends, then open onto terraced slopes of almonds and olives. Traffic is thin on weekdays, but at weekends, cyclists and walkers fill the lanes, so slow down on blind corners. The tarmac is usually decent but narrow, and in places broken by tree roots and washouts. Spring, when the hills are green and herb-scented, and autumn, with clear light and cool air, are the times to come. In July and August, the heat is intense and the rock holds it well into the evening.
t.cueva del queso@39.0,-1.2:
Alpera is a farming town of about two thousand three hundred people on the high, wind-swept plain of southern Albacete, where La Mancha slides toward the Valencian hills. It is famous in the archaeology books for the Cueva de la Vieja, a shelter with a dense frieze of Levantine paintings, among the most celebrated in Spain, and the Cueva del Queso, the Cheese Cave, is one of its neighbours. Together these belong to the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula, a UNESCO site since 1998. I do not know what the Cheese Cave holds in detail, so treat it as a place to look at the setting rather than a promise of a particular image.

The setting is a surprise if you think of Spain as coast and mountains. This is a high plateau, around the height of a decent hill in Britain, with vineyards, almond trees and cereal fields rolling to the horizon under a huge sky. The land is broken by low limestone ridges, outcrops and gullies, and the shelters are in those cuts. Almansa, a short ride away, has a castle on a rock that looks like it was drawn by a child, and it was the site of a decisive battle in the War of the Spanish Succession in 1707.

Riding here is open and fast. The roads run straight across the plain with long visibility, and there are some pleasing sweepers where they drop toward the Valencian side, with long views over vineyard and plateau. Traffic is light on the minor roads. The main danger is wind, which can blow steadily from the west and hit bikes hard at gaps and ridges, so keep a firm grip. Winters are cold at this height and frost can lurk on shaded bends, while summers are very hot.

For fuel and supplies, Alpera itself has enough people to have a pump, though a full range of services is in Almansa or Ayora. Carcelén and Alatoz are tiny and quiet. Alatoz leads you toward the gorges of the Júcar river, a spectacular detour if you have time. Take water in summer, as there is little shade.
t.abrigo del collado de la cruz@38.2,-2.3:
The Collado de la Cruz is a saddle in the wild Sierra del Segura, in the south-west corner of Albacete province, and the shelter here belongs to one of the richest regions of prehistoric painting in Spain. Nerpio, the village about three and a half kilometres away, sits at over a thousand metres and is surrounded by dozens of rock-art sites, in both the Levantine style and the later schematic style, which uses simple dots, lines and stick-like figures. The Levantine paintings are protected by UNESCO as part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula.

This is remote country, even by Spanish standards. Nerpio has under seventeen hundred people, and the next town of any size, Yeste, is more than twenty kilometres away. Between lie high valleys, pine forests, bare limestone ridges and the headwaters of the Taibilla, a river that supplies drinking water to a good part of the south-east. Winter here is cold, with snow on the tops and sharp frosts at night, while summer is dry but not as brutal as the coast. The air feels thin and clear, and the night sky is exceptionally dark.

For motorcyclists, this is the sort of place that justifies a long detour. The roads are twisting, narrow and nearly empty, with every sort of bend, from long sweepers across the plateau to tight switchbacks as they fall into valleys. Surfaces are mostly good on the main links but can be broken and gravelly on side roads, particularly after storms or winter. In some places, livestock wander across the road, and in the early morning you may share the tarmac with sheep.

Fuel is the main thing to plan. Nerpio is small, and I would not count on it, so fill up before you come. Yeste, with around three and a half thousand people, is the best bet nearby, and it also has food. Letur, a pretty whitewashed village to the east, is worth the stop for coffee and a view of its Moorish-looking lanes. Bring plenty of water, a warm layer in spring and autumn, and a willingness to go slowly.
t.barranc de famorca abric iii@38.7,-0.2:
Famorca is one of the smallest municipalities in the province of Alicante, a few dozen houses clinging to a slope in the mountains of the Marina Alta, and the ravine named after it is a deep cut in the limestone that holds several rock shelters with painted art. Abric III is one of them, in the Levantine tradition, small red figures that UNESCO protects with other sites across the eastern side of the country as the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. The nearest village, Castell de Castells, two kilometres away, has a famous neighbour: the Pla de Petracos, a major painted shelter with a visitor trail, which shows what the area offers at its best.

The country here is a surprise to anyone who knows Alicante only from the coast. A short distance inland from the resorts, the land rises into a maze of ridges and valleys, with terraced slopes of almonds, olives and cherry trees, small villages whose names still reflect Moorish origins, and big views toward the Serrella and the Sierra de Aitana, the highest peak in the province. In February, the almond blossom looks like a light fall of snow, and in autumn, the air is gloriously clear.

Riding here is a treat. The roads wind through the Vall de Castells and into neighbouring valleys in long climbing sweeps and tight switchbacks, with sudden views down gorges and over terraces. They are narrow, sometimes rough at the edges, and lightly used by anyone except local farmers and cyclists. Watch for gravel and for rocks that fall from the cuttings after heavy rain. The best seasons are spring and autumn. Summer is hot, and the roads can be busy near the beach-bound areas.

Do not expect fuel in Castell de Castells, which has fewer than five hundred people. The nearest place with more services is Pego, on the plain inland from Denia, about fifteen kilometres away, or the towns of the Guadalest valley and the coast. Plan ahead, carry water and enjoy the quiet.
t.coves roges abric iii@38.8,-0.3:
Beniarrés is the key to this corner of the Alicante hills, a small town beside a reservoir in the mountains between Alcoi and the coast, and the shelter called Coves Roges, the Red Caves, lies a few kilometres to the north-east above the village of Planes. The name is honest: the rock here is stained in warm rust tones, and one of the overhangs carries painted figures in the old Levantine manner, listed by UNESCO along with the other rock art of eastern Spain. A neighbouring shelter, La Sarga, is the better-known site in the district and is often visited together with this one.

The landscape is the Vall d'Alcalà and its neighbours, a district of narrow valleys threaded between steep limestone ridges. After the Christian conquest of the thirteenth century this was Moorish farming country for a long time, and the terraces, irrigation channels and clustered villages are still recognisably theirs. The whole population was expelled in 1609, and the valleys were repopulated by settlers from elsewhere, which is why you hear a surprising mix of place names, Arabic ones beside Catalan ones. Cherry trees blossom here in spring and fruit in early summer, and the slopes can look as if a fall of snow has settled on them.

The ride is the best reason to come. The lanes climb out of Planes, Beniarrés and the neighbouring villages through bends that come one after another, usually tight, sometimes with a short straight where the valley opens. Tarmac is narrow and patched, with loose gravel at the edges, and the cut-through roads between valleys are even rougher. Traffic is thin. Take it slowly, watch for cyclists and keep your eyes up for the views over terraced slopes to the high ridges of the Serra de Benicadell and Mariola.

Planes has fewer than eight hundred people, and Beniarrés, with about thirteen hundred, is only a little larger, so fuel is not a safe bet in either. Cocentaina, to the north-west, and Alcoi, to the south, are the proper towns, and both have plenty of stations and good places to eat. Beniarrés reservoir is a pleasant spot for a break, with shaded paths. In midsummer, the heat is fierce, so start early.
t.morciguilla de la cepera@38.3,-3.3:
Aldeaquemada means burnt village, which tells you something about the history of this lonely corner of Jaén, and the shelter named Morciguilla de la Cepera sits in the hills about ten kilometres away, in the Sierra Morena. That range forms the long dark edge between the high plateau of La Mancha and the Andalusian lowlands, and its slopes are some of the richest places in Spain for rock painting. Shelters here include both Levantine figures and the simpler schematic ones, and a number are protected as part of the UNESCO-listed rock art of the Iberian Mediterranean basin.

This is not the Andalusia of white villages and orange trees.
