It is dehesa country, an open woodland of holm and cork oak grazed by cattle, sheep and black Iberian pigs, with granite outcrops, scrub of rockrose and broom, and in spring a fierce yellow bloom. Red deer and wild boar live here, and in parts of the Sierra Morena the Iberian lynx has been reintroduced, though your chance of seeing one from a bike is vanishingly small. Birds of prey are another matter, and you will probably see a few kites or a vulture overhead.

For riders, it is lovely, quiet country. The roads wind gently through the oak woods, with long gradual bends and not many hard corners, and sometimes a few kilometres of rough or patched tarmac. Traffic is very light, with the occasional lorry carrying cork or livestock. A short way north lies the Despeñaperros pass, the historic gateway between Castile and Andalusia, a dramatic gorge where the road threads between towers of rock, and which makes an excellent detour.

Aldeaquemada has about five hundred people, and Montizón, a little larger, has around two thousand. Santisteban del Puerto, about twelve kilometres away, is the better bet, a town of nearly five thousand with a castle and fuel. Plan your tank carefully, as distances between services are long. In summer, temperatures soar and shade is scarce, so go in spring or autumn, when the countryside is green and the air is cool.
t.abric de la balsa calicanto@39.1,-0.8:
Bicorp is a village of just over six hundred people in the dry, broken country where the Valencian interior folds into the gorges of the Júcar and the Cabriel, and the Balsa Calicanto shelter lies about four kilometres from it. Rock art is at home here. In the same municipality, the Cueva de la Araña, the Spider Cave, holds one of the best-known scenes in Spanish prehistoric painting: a small figure climbing what look like ropes or vines to raid a wild bees' nest, honey bag in hand. It was painted by hunter-gatherers thousands of years ago, and it is part of the UNESCO-listed Levantine rock art. Many of the other shelters nearby are more modest, and Calicanto is one of those.

The landscape is rugged, with limestone cliffs and ravines, pine forest on the slopes, wild thyme and rosemary, and little cultivation except in the valley floors. The Hoces del Cabriel natural park lies not far to the west, with dramatic river gorges, and the Júcar's canyon cuts through the district too. Bee-keeping is still done here, and the honey is excellent, with thyme and rosemary flavours.

For riding, this is a rewarding, remote area. The roads are narrow and winding, with short climbs and drops between villages, and the occasional view over a gorge. Surfaces vary from smooth to rough, and the quietest lanes can have gravel and sections of broken tarmac. There is almost no traffic, but there are blind corners, so take care. Spring and autumn are best, as summers are hot and the winter nights are cold at this height.

You will not find fuel in Bicorp or in Quesa, a little farther away. Navarrés, with nearly three thousand people, about thirteen kilometres off, has the nearest services, and Enguera, a bit larger, is another good bet. Carry water, check the weather before heading into the ravines, and expect the final approach to the shelter to be on foot, on a path that may be rocky and steep.
t.abric del raco del condoig@38.8,-0.3:
When you stand in the valleys behind Planes, in the country between Alcoi and the coast, it is easy to forget how recently they were emptied. The Racó del Condoig shelter lies about five kilometres from Planes, in a landscape of dry-stone terraces, cherry and almond trees and narrow gorges. The paintings in the shelter belong to the Levantine tradition, listed by UNESCO with other rock art of eastern Spain, and they were made so long ago that the people who made them would have seen the Moors as impossibly modern.

The Moors, in fact, give this place much of its human character. In the thirteenth century, after King Jaume I took the region, a Muslim leader called al-Azraq, the Blue One, rose against the Christians from strongholds in these valleys, and for years the area was a battleground of castles and ambushes. The Muslim farmers stayed on for centuries as vassals, building terraces and irrigation channels, until the great expulsion of 1609 emptied the valleys almost overnight. Many villages were refounded with settlers from elsewhere, which is why the local names still mix Arabic and Catalan roots.

The riding follows the folds of the land. Roads climb out of Planes, Beniarrés and the neighbouring villages through bends that come thick and fast, with the best of them on the cut-through lanes between valleys. They are narrow and often patchy, with loose gravel on corners and the occasional stray goat. Traffic is almost absent, though cyclists like these hills too. Spring, when the cherry blossom is out, and early autumn are the best times, while midsummer afternoons are hot enough to make you rethink your plan.

Planes has fewer than eight hundred people and no certainty of fuel, so do not rely on it. Beniarrés, a little larger, has a reservoir with some shade and a small bar or two, but for proper services you will want to go to Cocentaina or Alcoi. Carry water, since the scrub is dry, and bring a torch for the shelter.
t.garganta de la hoz ix@38.4,-0.2:
Hoz is the old Spanish word for a gorge, and the Garganta de la Hoz, repeated in the name for good measure, is a cleft in the hills behind the Alicante coast, a dozen kilometres or so inland from El Campello and Villajoyosa. I will not pretend to describe this specific shelter in detail; what I can tell you is the country around it. The rock here is a pale limestone, worn into ledges and overhangs by wind and water, and wherever there is an overhang there is a chance that people have used it, as they have since the Stone Age. A few shelters in the district carry Levantine paintings, small red figures that UNESCO protects as part of the Mediterranean rock art of Spain.

The country is bone dry for most of the year, with carob, almond and wild olive, pine woods on the higher slopes and, in the gullies, oleander and reeds in the few places where water lingers. It is a good area for walkers and for birdwatchers. The shape of the hills hides the sea, so it comes as a pleasant surprise to reach a crest and see it glittering behind you.

For riding, the interest is variety. The coastal strip is crowded and slow, with roundabouts and apartment blocks, but the road into the hills quickly turns twisty and quiet, with climbs, hairpins and long views over scrub and rock. Surfaces vary, with patches of new tarmac next to stretches of broken surface, and in autumn, storms may leave mud and rocks on the road. Go early, as the midday sun is relentless, and expect the hills to be busy with cyclists at weekends.

Fuel is easy in El Campello, with over twenty-six thousand people, and Villajoyosa, with nearly thirty-four thousand. The latter is worth a stop, with its seafront of brightly coloured houses and a long tradition of chocolate-making. San Juan de Alicante is also close. Do not expect services inland.
t.cova alta abric i@38.8,-0.2:
The Vall d'Ebo is one of the quietest places in the Marina Alta, a high valley of fewer than four hundred people in the mountains behind Dénia, and the Cova Alta, the High Cave, stands above it on the slopes of the surrounding ridges. Castell de Castells is the nearest village, about three kilometres off, and Benimantell and Vall d'Ebo are the neighbours. The shelter carries painted figures in the Levantine style, protected with the rest of the region's rock art by UNESCO, and it is one of a group of caves that the rides tie together around the Port de Penàguila.

What strikes you here is how empty the land feels. The hills are steep, terraced in places with dry-stone walls, and clothed in pine, scrub and abandoned almond and olive groves. The villages are tiny, white-washed and mostly silent outside the weekend. Near Vall d'Ebo is one of the best-known walks in the region, the Barranc de l'Infern, a spectacular gorge reached by thousands of old stone steps cut by farmers who once used them to reach their fields. It is a reminder of how hard people worked this land.

The ride into the high valleys is a real pleasure. The roads climb steeply from the coast in tight turns, with big drop-offs and views over the Mediterranean, then run along ridges with long, flowing bends. They are narrow and rarely busy, but they can be rough in places, with broken edges and rubble after storms. Watch for goats, cyclists and the occasional tractor. The best seasons are spring and autumn. Summer brings intense heat, and winter evenings can be cold and misty on the ridges.

There is no reason to hope for fuel in Vall d'Ebo, Castell de Castells or Benimantell, which are all very small. Plan to fill up on the coast, in Pego or in one of the larger towns of the Guadalest valley, and carry water. The final approach to the shelter is on foot, so wear sturdy shoes, and pause on the way up to look back at the valley.
t.abrigo de los covachos@38.1,-2.3:
The Covachos, the little caves, are a short ride from Nerpio, a mountain village of about sixteen hundred people in the south-west of Albacete province, in the headwaters of the Segura river. The shelter is one of dozens in this district, which has one of the densest concentrations of prehistoric painting in Spain, in both the Levantine style and the later schematic one. UNESCO protects the Levantine sites as part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. What makes Nerpio special is that the paintings are scattered through a living landscape of farms, springs and sheep tracks, so you may find yourself looking at a thousands-year-old figure with a shepherd's dog watching from the next rock.

This is high country. Nerpio stands above a thousand metres, and the sierras around it, Segura, Alcaraz and Taibilla, are among the wildest in southern Spain. Pine woods cover the slopes, and the limestone cliffs are home to vultures and eagles. The sky at night is exceptionally dark and clear, and on a moonless night in late summer, the Milky Way is impressive. Winters are cold, with snow likely on the higher roads, and summer days, though warm, are rarely oppressive.

The riding is excellent, with empty roads through high valleys and forest, the surface mostly good but with the occasional broken patch or stretch of gravel. Bends range from long sweepers on the plateau to tight turns where the road drops into a ravine. Segura de la Sierra, a hill village in Jaén province about twenty-eight kilometres away, has a castle on a crag and a view that justifies the trip.

You cannot assume fuel at Nerpio. Fill up at Yeste, the nearest town of any size, with about three and a half thousand people, or even farther afield before heading into the sierra, and check opening hours. Letur, a pretty white village with Moorish-looking lanes, makes a good coffee stop. Take a jacket even in summer, as the evening cools quickly.
t.las covachas@37.7,-2.1:
Los Vélez is a district of its own, a high, dry corner of northern Almería where the province meets Murcia and Granada, and the title of its old masters, the Marquises of Los Vélez, still hangs over it. Las Covachas is a rock shelter about four kilometres from Vélez-Blanco and a bit more from Vélez Rubio, and it belongs to a rich local group of painted sites that includes the famous Cueva de los Letreros. The paintings are in the Levantine style, protected as part of the UNESCO rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. Other shelters have stronger images, so treat this as part of a pattern, not a highlight.

Vélez Rubio, a few kilometres away, is the bigger of the two towns, with about seven thousand people and a vast baroque church, the Iglesia de la Encarnación, which seems wildly out of scale for the place, a reminder of the wealth that once flowed here from wool, wheat and the marquises' estates. Vélez-Blanco has its castle, a Renaissance fortress on a hill, with a courtyard that is now in a New York museum.

The Sierra de María-Los Vélez natural park fills the skyline, a limestone range reaching more than two thousand metres at Maimón, with pine forest, almond groves and wide pale uplands. In late winter, the almond trees bloom pink and white, and the lower slopes can look as if they have been dusted with snow. Birds of prey are common, and in the evening, the light turns the limestone gold.

The roads here are delightful. They run through the valley in long, easy bends, then climb into the sierra with tight turns and big views, with almost no traffic. Surfaces are generally good, though dusty near farms, and the wind can pick up on exposed crests. Fuel is easy in Vélez Rubio, which has several stations, and María, with about fifteen hundred people, has the basics. Eat in Vélez-Blanco, where the bars serve decent local food. In summer, ride early or late, as midday brings real heat.
t.cortijo de la rosa@38.1,-2.4:
A cortijo is a farm in the Andalusian style, a cluster of whitewashed buildings around a yard, and the one named for La Rosa stands in the mountains of the Sierra del Segura, where Albacete, Murcia and Jaén meet. The shelter nearby, one of the many in the Nerpio district, lies about twelve kilometres from the village of Nerpio and a good deal farther from anything else. It carries paintings of the old Levantine kind, protected by UNESCO as part of the Mediterranean rock art of Spain, and the ride links it with another site at Benizar, in the Moratalla district across the border in Murcia.

This is some of the loneliest country in the south of Spain, and the beauty of the ride is in its emptiness. The land is a series of high ridges clothed in pine, with deep valleys, terraces of almond and olive in the more sheltered folds, and bare limestone above. To the east lies Moratalla, and to the south, the great Parque Natural de las Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas, which is the biggest protected area in Spain and the source of the Segura river. The sound of water in the gullies in spring is one of the pleasures of the place.

Segura de la Sierra, about twenty-eight kilometres away in Jaén province, is worth the detour. It is a village crowded on a hilltop below a castle, with narrow streets and a set of old Moorish baths, and the view across the Sierra from the walls is huge. The road there is a rewarding ride in itself, a long run of bends through forest.

Surfaces in this district are mixed. The main roads are generally good, but the side routes can be rough and patched, with gravel at the corners and the odd landslip after storms. Traffic is nonexistent. Nerpio has only sixteen hundred people, so fuel is uncertain. Yeste, about thirty kilometres off, is the nearest dependable stop, with food and a few shops. Winter brings snow and ice at this height, so check forecasts, and carry warm clothing in all seasons.
t.fuente del sabuco ii@38.2,-2.2:
Sabuco is the old word for the elder tree, and a fuente is a spring, so this shelter is named for the water that makes the place possible: the Elder Spring. Fuente del Sabuco II lies about eleven kilometres from Nerpio in the high country of south-west Albacete, and it is one of the many shelters of this district that hold paintings. The ride also links it to a site called Diosa Madre, the Mother Goddess, a name given by archaeologists to a type of schematic figure that appears across the prehistoric art of the Iberian Peninsula. The Levantine art of the region is protected by UNESCO as part of the Mediterranean rock art of Spain.

Why a spring? Because in this dry mountain country, water was everything, for people, animals, and, it seems, for ritual. Wherever the old painters worked, there is often a source of water nearby, and the places where springs emerge from the limestone were probably sacred. Today, the flow is gentle but steady, and the spot is a cool, shaded refuge in summer, with ferns and moss around the rocks and the sound of dripping water.

The mountains around Nerpio are wonderful riding country. The roads climb in long loops through pine woods and across high pasture, then drop into valleys with tight, well-banked turns. There is virtually no traffic, so you can set your own pace, though you should take care on the side lanes, where the tarmac can be broken and loose. Spring and early summer are lovely, with wild flowers and clear air, while in autumn the colours are soft and warm. Snow can close the high passes in winter.

For supplies, Nerpio has under seventeen hundred people, and I would not rely on it for fuel. Fill up at Yeste, with about three and a half thousand people, or at Letur, a smaller place, which has a bar and a view of its pretty whitewashed lanes. A few kilometres farther, you will find roadside springs where you can top up water bottles, but check that they are marked as drinkable. A hat and sun protection are useful, since the thin air and strong light at a thousand metres make sunburn easy.
t.barranc de famorca abric v@38.7,-0.2:
The Guadalest valley is the best-known inland stretch of the Alicante coast, and the village of Guadalest itself, with its castle perched on a pillar of rock and its bell tower on the cliff, is one of the most photographed places in the province. The shelter at Barranc de Famorca, Abric V, is not in the busy part. It lies about two kilometres from Castell de Castells and a few kilometres from Famorca, in the quiet valleys on the far side of the Serrella. Like the others in the ravine, it carries Levantine painting protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain.

What the guide books do not always say is how quickly the crowds fall away. Guadalest draws coachloads from Benidorm, but a few kilometres inland, in the valleys of Castell de Castells and Famorca, you can ride for an hour without seeing another vehicle. The mountains here are steep, terraced with centuries of dry-stone walls, and covered with a mix of pine, carob and wild olive. Almond trees bloom in February, and the slopes look dusted with snow.

The road from the coast to these valleys is a classic. It climbs out of Callosa d'en Sarrià, where medlars are the local fruit, passes the turquoise Guadalest reservoir, and then winds up through bends of every size to the high ground. Surfaces are generally good on the main route, but narrow and patchy on the side lanes. Traffic is heavy near Guadalest at weekends, with coaches and rental cars, so start early. Beyond the village, you will have the road to yourself.

Castell de Castells, with fewer than five hundred people, has a bar or two and a small shop, but fuel is uncertain. Fill up on the coast, at Callosa or Altea, or at Pego. Benimantell, nearby, is another tiny village. The Pla de Petracos, a famous painted shelter with a visitor trail, is close, and is worth the stop if you want a more structured introduction to the art. Take water and sun protection in all seasons.
t.barranc de la fita abric v@38.7,-0.2:
If you came here in February, you would find the slopes above Castell de Castells covered in almond blossom, white and pale pink against the grey rock. In April, the cherry trees follow. By June, the almonds and the first cherries are being harvested, the heat settles in, and the shelters in the ravine give welcome shade. By October, the first rains return, the air clears, and the whole valley looks newly washed. The shelter at Barranc de la Fita, Abric V, lies about three kilometres from the village and is a good excuse to see the valley in whichever season you choose.

It carries painted figures in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The paintings are small and faded, and are best seen in the low, slanting light of early morning or late afternoon, when the shadows bring out the colours. Along the same ravine, the ride passes a second site on the way. The Barranc de la Fita is a deep, narrow cut, and the walls of the gorge are grey and ochre, with ledges where goats can be seen climbing.

The mountains of the Marina Alta have a character all their own. They are steep and compact, with the sea always somewhere behind, and the villages are very small and quiet, many with fewer than five hundred inhabitants. The Serrella, the long ridge to the north, and the Sierra de Aitana, behind, keep the valleys sheltered, and the climate is mild in winter and hot, but not humid, in summer.

The roads here are among the best small-bike routes in Alicante province. They are narrow and twisty, with a wonderful variety of bends, and they rarely see heavy traffic. Surfaces are mostly good, but gravel gathers in the corners, and rocks occasionally fall from the cuttings. Cyclists are common, so be careful on blind curves.

Castell de Castells and Benimantell have only a few hundred people, so fuel is a matter for the coast, at Pego or Callosa d'en Sarrià. Vall d'Ebo, farther on, is tiny and silent. Carry water, and wear sturdy shoes for the walk.
t.los grajos iii@38.3,-1.4:
Cieza is a big town for this part of Murcia, with over thirty-five thousand people on the banks of the Segura, and its fame in Spain rests on fruit. In February, the peach and apricot orchards of the river valley burst into pink and white blossom, and visitors come from all over the region to see the hills turn soft with it. The name of the shelter, Los Grajos, means the jackdaws, or rooks, the black birds that nest in the cliffs, and the ride ties it to Maina and to the Abric de la Paella. The paintings belong to the Levantine tradition protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain, and Cieza has some of the most important sites in this part of the country.

The landscape is a surprise. Just beyond the orchards, the river has cut the Almadenes gorge through the limestone, a narrow cleft with walls of rock on either side, and the dry hills around are the colour of toast, dotted with pine, esparto grass and rosemary. The grass was once a major local industry, and esparto from Cieza was used for ropes, mats and baskets. Moorish farmers laid out the irrigation channels in the valley, and some of them still work.

The roads around Cieza are not the most famous in Spain, but they have plenty to enjoy. The main routes are fast and open, while the lanes into the hills climb through scrub and rock with plenty of tight bends and good views over the valley. Surfaces are variable, with occasional dust and gravel. Traffic is heavy near the town and negligible once you leave it. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and summer heat is fierce, with temperatures pushing past forty degrees in July and August.

Fuel and food are no problem in Cieza, and Abarán, with nearly thirteen thousand people, and Blanca, with about six thousand, are both nearby, in the lovely Ricote valley, where Moorish orchard terraces still line the river. Blanca is a good place to stop for a coffee on a terrace, with views over palms and orange trees.
t.cavidad vi@38.2,-2.2:
Nerpio is a village of sixteen hundred people at more than a thousand metres in south-west Albacete, and the area is among the richest in Spain for prehistoric painting. The shelter at Cavidad VI is one of dozens, in the Levantine tradition protected by UNESCO as part of the Mediterranean rock art of Spain, and the ride links it with a site called Las Cazuelas, the Cooking Pots, and a cave named for a Gypsy, Cueva del Gitano, a name that probably recalls a squatter or a shepherd rather than any famous event. The label Cavidad, meaning a cavity, tells you something about the people who numbered these places. They were archaeologists with a long list of holes in the rock.

The setting is high, thinly peopled mountain country. The Taibilla and Segura rivers rise nearby, in the Sierra del Segura and Sierra de Alcaraz, and the ground is limestone cut into long ridges and wooded gorges. Pine, juniper and holm oak cover the slopes, and in spring the meadows are full of wild flowers. Golden eagles and griffon vultures use the thermals along the ridges, and wild boar and roe deer are common but shy. After sunset, the sky fills with stars, and the cold comes down fast, even in July.

For a motorcyclist, the district has the perfect combination of emptiness, bends and views. Roads dip and climb through forest and across high plains, with long sweeping turns and, in the gorges, sharp bends with steep drops. They are mostly in good condition, though side roads can be rough and gravelly. You can ride an hour without meeting another vehicle, and the odd flock of sheep or goats is the main hazard. Spring and autumn are lovely; in winter, snow and ice make some roads impassable.

Fuel is the big question. Nerpio is small, and I would not count on a pump. Yeste, about twenty-three kilometres away, is the nearest village with services, and the town of Moratalla, in Murcia, with more than eight thousand people, is farther but reliable. Letur, a pretty village with Moorish lanes, is a good stop for a drink. Carry warm clothes, water, and a spare layer, since conditions can change quickly.
t.historic city of toledo@39.9,-4.0:
Toledo sits inside a tight loop of the Tagus, with a gorge on three sides and a fortified hill in the middle, and its position is the reason for much of its history. It was the capital of the Visigothic kingdom, a Muslim city for centuries, and then the seat of the Spanish crown until Philip II moved the court to Madrid in 1561. Christians, Muslims and Jews lived side by side here in the Middle Ages, and the old centre still holds a synagogue, a small mosque and a great Gothic cathedral within a few minutes' walk of each other. UNESCO listed the whole city in 1986. The painter El Greco made it his home, and his huge picture of the burial of the Count of Orgaz hangs in a small church near the old Jewish quarter.

Toledo is also a place of craft. Its steel swords have been famous since Roman times, and the shops sell blades and damascene work, the black steel inlaid with gold thread. Marzipan, in elaborate shapes, is the local sweet, and sold in every pastry shop. Roast partridge and stews of game are the city's traditional food.

The ride's other stops, Segovia with its great Roman aqueduct and the Paseo del Prado and Buen Retiro in Madrid, give you a sense of how it fits among the old royal cities. On a motorbike, the best approach is along the ring road, which circles the gorge on the far bank and offers one of the best views in Spain, with the city piled up on its rock. A viewpoint on this road, the Mirador del Valle, is where the postcards come from, and it is at its best in the late afternoon.

Inside the old town, the streets are steep, narrow and cobbled, with parts closed to traffic, so park at the edge and walk. Fuel is no problem in a city of over eighty thousand people. In summer, the heat in Toledo is intense, and in winter, a damp chill rises from the river, so spring and autumn are best. Cobisa and Burguillos de Toledo are quiet, small places nearby.
t.garganta de la hoz vi@38.4,-0.2:
Villajoyosa, the Joyous Town, is the first place to know in this stretch of the Alicante coast, and it is an easy one to love. Its seafront is a row of houses painted in bright colours, ochre, pink, blue and green, reputedly so that fishermen could pick out their own homes from the sea. A Moors and Christians festival every July commemorates the town's defeat of a Barbary pirate raid in 1538, with a staged landing on the beach and a lot of gunpowder. The town is also famous for chocolate, with old family factories that still make it, and you can buy a bar or a cup in the old centre.

The Garganta de la Hoz, about fourteen kilometres inland, is a cleft in the hills, and the sixth shelter of the ravine, Abric VI, belongs to the Levantine tradition protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. I cannot honestly describe what is painted here, and the figures may be too faded for a casual visitor to see, so treat it as a walk to a good place rather than a definite sight.

The landscape inland is pale limestone with carob, almond and pine, and the sea is never far away. On the crests, you can see the whole coast, with the high-rise towers of Benidorm to the north and the long blue line of the Mediterranean to the east. In autumn, brief fierce storms bring a flush of green to the slopes and send water roaring down the gullies.

The route inland from the coast is a good one, leaving the crowded coastal strip and quickly becoming a winding mountain road, with bends that tighten as you climb. Surfaces are variable, so watch for gravel and rocks after rain, and expect cyclists, especially at weekends. Early morning is the best time to ride, with soft light and cool air.

Fuel is easy at Villajoyosa, which has nearly thirty-four thousand people, and El Campello, with over twenty-six thousand, is the other nearby town. Cafes on the seafront serve fresh fish and rice dishes, a good reward after a day in the hills.
t.molinos i@37.7,-2.1:
Molinos means mills, and the name tells you how this corner of Almería was run. Above Vélez-Blanco, the sierra drops snow and rain on limestone that gives it back as springs, and for centuries the streams below were harnessed by grain mills, fulling mills and irrigation channels. Many were laid out under Moorish rule, and the system of acequias that still waters fields in the Los Vélez valley follows their pattern. The shelter at Molinos I, a bit under two kilometres from Vélez-Blanco, belongs to the rich cluster of painted sites around the town, in the Levantine tradition protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride also links it to the site known as Guijarral, a name that means pebbly ground.

It is a surprisingly green spot for such a dry province. Poplars and fruit trees follow the stream below the village, and on the slopes above grow almond trees, pine and the grey-green of thyme and rosemary. In late winter, the almond blossom turns the valley pink, and the mountain, Maimón, above two thousand metres, may still be capped with snow.

Vélez-Blanco itself is worth the time. A Renaissance castle, built in the sixteenth century by the Marquis of Los Vélez, stands on a crag above the village, with a robust, square outline that looks remarkably like a toy fort. The marble courtyard that once graced its interior now sits in the Metropolitan Museum in New York, a bit of local history that residents still mention with a shrug.

The riding in this district is first-rate. Roads leave the valley in long, climbing curves and rise into the Sierra de María-Los Vélez natural park, with big views, easy bends and almost no traffic. Surfaces are mostly good, with dust and gravel near farms, and the wind can be strong on the crests. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, while the middle of summer is hot and dry.

Fuel is available in Vélez Rubio, only a few kilometres away, with about seven thousand people, and the town also has bakeries, cafes and a big baroque church. María, a village of about fifteen hundred, is smaller but useful for a coffee. Carry water for the walk.
t.abrigo de vicent@39.2,-0.8:
For most of its length, the Júcar river in Valencia province runs through gorges, reservoirs and dry hills, and in the days before roads, the way to bring timber from the mountains to the coast was to float it. The woodsmen who did this were called gancheros, after the long hooked poles they used to push logs through rapids, and for centuries they took pine trunks down the Júcar and the Cabriel in spring floods, riding the logs and breaking jams. That trade ended in the twentieth century, but their memory is kept alive in villages like Millares and Bicorp. The shelter named for a man, Abrigo de Vicent, lies about five and a half kilometres from Bicorp, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain.

Bicorp's most famous site is the Cueva de la Araña, with its scene of a person climbing to a bee's nest, so honey and bees go with the district. Today beekeepers still work the thyme and rosemary slopes, and the honey, dark and aromatic, is for sale in village shops.

The landscape is steep. Limestone ridges, pine forest and deep ravines cut through the country, and the valley floors hold small farms of orange, almond and carob trees. The Cortes de Pallás reservoir and the dramatic Muela de Cortes plateau lie not far to the south. In the late afternoon, the cliffs glow orange and the air smells of resin.

For a rider, this is remote and rewarding territory. Roads are narrow and winding, with tight bends, steep drops and spectacular views, and they carry little traffic. The surface ranges from good to rough, with gravel and fallen rock after storms. Winter nights are cold, summer days are hot, and spring and autumn are best.

Fuel is far away. Bicorp, Millares and Quesa are tiny, with fewer than eight hundred people each, and the nearest sizeable town is Carlet, in the plain, about twenty-three kilometres away, with over fifteen thousand people. Fill up before you set out, carry water and a spare layer, and expect a walk to the shelter.
t.barranc del salt abric vi@38.7,-0.4:
Alcoi is the capital of this mountain district, a big industrial town in a basin between ranges, and its reputation rests on paper, textiles and fiesta. The town was a centre of paper-making for centuries, drawing on the water of its rivers, and in the nineteenth century, it became one of the first industrial cities in Valencia, with factories in the valley bottom and fine modernist buildings on the hill. Every April, it stages the most famous of the Moors and Christians festivals in Spain, with hundreds of costumed participants, mock battles, firecrackers and processions that last for days. The festival is dedicated to Saint George, and it commemorates the legendary victory of Christians over Muslims in the thirteenth century.

The shelter at Barranc del Salt, Abric VI, lies in the hills not far to the north-east, about four kilometres from the village of Benilloba, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. It sits among the pines and rock of the Serra de Mariola, and is accompanied on the ride by another site named Abric del Garrofero, the carob-tree shelter.

The Mariola is wonderful for walkers and has some of the best mountain scenery in the province, with limestone cliffs, beech and holm oak in the shadier gullies, and pine on the slopes. It is a refuge for birds, with eagles, kestrels and vultures overhead, and the aromatic plants give the air a clean, herbal scent. Local people collect them for teas and liqueurs.

The riding is a delight. Roads wind from the Benilloba side up into the hills with bends that range from gentle to tight, with big views over the valleys. Surfaces are mostly good but narrow, and cyclists are common, particularly on weekends. Autumn brings mushroom hunters, and cars parked along the verge. Take care in winter, when ice can persist in shaded bends.

Benilloba is small, with fewer than nine hundred people, so I would not rely on it for fuel. Cocentaina, about ten kilometres away, is bigger, with over eleven thousand people and plenty of stations, and Alcoi is larger still. In either, you will find good, simple food.
t.barranc de carbonera abric ii@38.8,-0.4:
Between the mountain ranges of northern Alicante and the plains of Valencia lies the Vall d'Albaida, a quiet and little-visited district of small towns, vineyards and orchards, and the shelter at Barranc de Carbonera, Abric II, is on its edge. It lies about two and a half kilometres from Otos, a village of five hundred people, and close to Ráfol de Salem and Bèlgida, which are about the same size. It carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain, and the ride links it to the Cova de la Catxupa, an even smaller site in the same area.

What you notice first is how many villages there are. The valley is dotted with settlements, each with its own church tower, its own square and its own festival, a result of centuries of Moorish and Christian farming. The terraces on the slopes are old, and the irrigation channels, the acequias, are in places still working. Cherry trees, almonds and olives grow on the higher ground, and in spring, the colours are lovely.

Albaida, the little capital of the valley, has an odd distinction: its museum of puppets, the Museu Internacional del Titella, houses puppets from all over the world and is a genuine delight, particularly for children. It is a pleasant place to stop for a coffee.

Riding in the Vall d'Albaida is gentle and pleasant. The roads are narrow, with lots of corners but no great gradients, and the surfaces are generally good. Traffic is light, and there are views over the plain to the sea on a clear day. In the hills, the lanes are rougher, with gravel and the occasional landslip. Spring and autumn are best, and the vines turn red in October.

Otos and the neighbouring villages are too small to count on for fuel. Muro d'Alcoi, about seven kilometres away, has nearly eight thousand people and is the safer choice, and Albaida and Cocentaina have more. Carry water, and wear sturdy shoes, since the last stretch is on foot.
t.garganta de la hoz v@38.4,-0.2:
El Campello was a fishing village a few decades ago, and the old port still has some of that flavour, with boats pulled up on the sand and a row of restaurants selling fish and rice. It now has over twenty-six thousand people, thanks to tourism and to the sprawl of Alicante, but it also has a surprisingly deep history. On the headland south of the beach, a small rocky islet, the Illeta dels Banyets, preserves the remains of a Bronze Age and Iberian settlement and of Roman fish tanks cut into the rock, a reminder that people have been exploiting this coast for thousands of years.

The Garganta de la Hoz, about fourteen kilometres inland, is a different world. This Abric V lies in the hills behind the coastal strip, in a landscape of pale limestone, scrub and pine, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. A neighbouring site on the ride is the Barranc d'Alpadull. I cannot tell you what is painted in this shelter, and the figures may be faint, so go for the walk and the view.

Hoz means gorge, and the landscape, a mix of dry gullies and ridge-tops covered in thyme, rosemary and dwarf palm, does look as if it was cut by water. The palm, the palmito, is the only palm native to mainland Europe, and its fan-shaped leaves have been used for centuries to make baskets and brooms. Look for the stumpy clumps among the rocks.

The ride from the coast climbs quickly into the hills and is a welcome change from the congested seafront. Roads are narrow and twisty, with a mix of smooth tarmac and rough patches, and gravel in the corners. Traffic is light, but cyclists are common, especially at weekends. Morning is best, before the heat builds.

Fuel is easy at El Campello and Villajoyosa, which has nearly thirty-four thousand people, and San Juan de Alicante is also close. There are no services in the hills, so carry water and a snack.
t.garganta de la hoz vii@38.4,-0.2:
Everyone in Spain associates the hills north of Alicante with one thing: turrón. The town of Xixona, in the valley behind the coast, has been making the almond-and-honey nougat for centuries, and the soft, oily version, turrón blando, and the hard, brittle one, turrón duro, are shipped across the country at Christmas. Almonds grow all over these slopes, and you will pass many groves on a ride. Whether you pick up a box from a factory shop or a roadside stall, it is the right souvenir for a rider with a pannier.

The shelter at Garganta de la Hoz VII lies about fourteen kilometres from the coast, in the hills behind El Campello and Villajoyosa, and the ride links it with El Pantanet, the Little Reservoir. It carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. I will not pretend to know what is on the wall, and the paintings may be hard to see, so treat the visit as an outing to a good place.

Water is scarce here, and the small reservoir is a reminder of how much effort has gone into keeping it. Alicante is one of the driest provinces in Spain, and for centuries farmers have built cisterns, channels and small dams to catch what rain falls, which is usually in a few violent bursts in autumn. The terraces of almond and carob that climb every slope were built for the same reason, to hold soil and water against the hill.

The roads in this district are a joy for a bike. They twist through the hills in tight bends, with views to the sea, and they rarely carry heavy traffic. Surfaces are mixed, and rain can wash gravel and mud across the road. Spring and autumn are best, and summer is hot, with temperatures that can top thirty-five degrees by noon.

Fuel is no problem at El Campello or Villajoyosa, both of which have plenty of stations, and San Juan de Alicante is also close. Bring water, a hat and a sense of curiosity.
t.cueva negra del bosque@39.0,-1.2:
Black Cave in the Wood is the translation, and while I cannot say which wood or why it is black, the name has the feel of something a shepherd said and a surveyor wrote down. The Cueva Negra del Bosque lies about five and a half kilometres from Alpera, on the high plateau where La Mancha begins to fold into the hills of Valencia, and it is one of the painted shelters of the district. It carries rock art in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain, and the ride links it with the Abric de Lambert, a site far to the east. Alpera is the best known name of the area, because of the Cueva de la Vieja, but there are other shelters scattered in the limestone gullies.

The wine of the district is a pleasure of its own. The plateau around Almansa and Alpera has its own appellation, and the local reds, made from the dark, deep-coloured garnacha tintorera grape, are strong and fruity. Vineyards stretch across the flat land in low bush vines, not trained on wires, and in October the leaves turn red and gold. Almond trees blossom in February.

It is a land of big skies. The plateau is high and open, with a scatter of pines, and the wind is a constant companion. Winters are cold and frosty, and summers dry and hot, with a harsh, bright light that bleaches the stone. In spring, the cereal fields are a startling green.

The ride is pleasant and unhurried. Roads run across the plain in long straights and then drop into a gorge or climb to a ridge with a flurry of bends. Surfaces are generally good, but patchy on minor lanes. The wind can be strong enough to push a bike sideways on exposed stretches, so keep a firm hold. Alpera, with a little over two thousand people, has fuel and bars, and Ayora, about seventeen kilometres away, with just over five thousand five hundred, is bigger. Carcelén and Alatoz are small and quiet, but have a coffee on offer. Bring water in summer, because there is little shade.
t.garganta de la hoz iii@38.4,-0.2:
Carob trees are the quiet workhorses of the Alicante hills. They are broad, dark and evergreen, with glossy leaves and long, leathery brown pods that hang in clusters in late summer, and in the dry terraces behind the coast, they thrive where little else will. The pods, called garrofas in Valencian, were once fed to mules, horses and pigs, and are now ground to make a sweet, cocoa-like flour and a thickening gum used in food. In the old days, a carob harvest was a family event, with branches beaten and pods gathered in sacks. Many of the groves are abandoned now, but the trees stand on, and you pass dozens on a ride.

Garganta de la Hoz III is a painted shelter in the hills about fourteen kilometres inland from El Campello and Villajoyosa, in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride links it with El Pantanet. I cannot describe what the wall holds, and the figures may be faint, so expect a pleasant walk and a modest reward.

The climate here is the gentlest in Spain for riders. Winters are mild, with daytime temperatures often in the high teens, and spring comes early. That makes the coast hills one of the best places for a ride in February, when northern Europe is frozen, and the almond trees are in bloom. Summers, by contrast, are hot, with temperatures above thirty-five degrees, so go early.

The lanes inland are narrow, twisty and quiet, with views over the terraces to the sea. The surface is mixed, with new tarmac and patches of rough, and gravel in the bends. After heavy rain, mud and rock may be washed on to the road. Cyclists are numerous on weekend mornings, so keep a little caution on blind corners.

Fuel is easy in El Campello, Villajoyosa and San Juan de Alicante, all within a short ride. Villajoyosa's seafront is a pleasant place for lunch, and the town has a famous chocolate tradition. There are no services in the hills, so take water.
t.barranc de famorca abric iv@38.7,-0.2:
From the high villages of the Marina Alta, the road drops to the plain of Pego, and the contrast is startling. Instead of terraces and rock, you find a flat, green country of rice paddies and orange groves, with the Marjal de Pego-Oliva, a protected wetland, in the middle. Reeds, pools and channels attract herons, ducks, and in winter, great numbers of migrating birds. Rice has been grown here for centuries, and the local rice dishes, cooked in paella pans over a flame, are among the best on the coast. The town of Pego, with about eleven thousand people, is the market town of the district and has fuel and good places to eat.

Abric IV at Barranc de Famorca lies about two kilometres from Castell de Castells, high above, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride links it with Pinós, a site in the same mountains. It is the sort of place you reach after a long climb through almond terraces and pine woods, with the sea left far behind.

The road between the two worlds is a joy for riders. From Pego, it climbs in long, rising bends through the foothills, passes villages of white houses, and then enters the narrow valleys of the Vall de Castells, where the curves tighten and the views open. The surface is mostly good, but narrow, with gravel and rock in places. Traffic is light, apart from cyclists at weekends, and early morning is the best time.

Castell de Castells, Benimantell and Vall d'Ebo have only a few hundred people each, so fuel is not to be counted on. Fill up in Pego, about fifteen kilometres away, or on the coast. Take water and a snack, and wear sturdy shoes for the walk.
t.cimbarrillo ma antonia ii@38.4,-0.3:
Rice is the soul of Alicante's cooking. Along this coast, the classic dishes are arroz a banda, rice cooked in a rich fish stock and served with garlic mayonnaise, and further inland, arròs amb costra, a baked rice with a crust of egg, from Elche. Fish and seafood from the local ports go into stews and grills, and the local sweet, the turrón of Xixona, is sold everywhere. After a day in the hills, a long lunch on the coast is the proper end to the ride.

The shelter at Cimbarrillo Ma Antonia II lies about twelve kilometres from El Campello, in the hills behind the coast, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride links it with the Abric del Voro, another site in the district. The name, with its mention of a woman, Antonia, suggests a local who gave her name to the rock, and the place has the feel of a spot known to shepherds for generations.

The landscape is dry and beautiful. Carob, almond and olive trees stand on terraces of pale stone, wild rosemary and thyme grow in the gaps, and the air smells of resin and warm earth. From the high points, you can see the sea in one direction and the long blue wall of the Sierra de Aitana in the other.

The roads inland from El Campello are a pleasant change from the crowded coast. They wind up through the hills in tight bends and long curves, with good views and light traffic. Surfaces vary, and gravel collects in the corners. Cyclists are numerous at weekends, so ride with care.

Fuel is easy in El Campello, Villajoyosa and San Juan de Alicante, and the coast has restaurants in plenty. Carry water, since there are no services in the hills.
t.los grajos ii@38.3,-1.4:
Before Cieza was Cieza, there was Siyasa. In the Middle Ages, when this part of Murcia was under Muslim rule, a fortified town stood on the hill above the Segura river, with a mosque, houses, a defensive wall and a castle, and it flourished from about the eighth to the thirteenth century. The ruins have been excavated and are now an archaeological site, with a few walls and foundations on the hillside, a reminder that the history of this valley goes much further back than the modern town. The ride also passes the Cejo Cortado, the Cut Ridge, a rocky outcrop in the same hills.

Los Grajos II, the jackdaw shelter, is about four kilometres from the town, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. It lies close to the gorge of the Almadenes, where the Segura squeezes between towering rock walls, and the area is one of the most important for rock art in the region.

The land is dry and beautiful, with pine and esparto grass on the hills and orchards of peach and apricot on the valley floor. In February, the blossom turns the valley pink and white. In summer, the heat is fierce, and the rock holds it well into the evening, so go early.

The roads around the town are a mix of fast main routes and narrow lanes into the hills, with tight bends and good views. Surfaces vary, with dust and gravel in places. Traffic is heavy near Cieza and light elsewhere. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Cieza, with over thirty-five thousand people, has fuel and food in plenty, and Abarán, with nearly thirteen thousand, and Blanca, with about six thousand, are close. The Ricote valley, with its orchards and Moorish irrigation channels, is a pleasant detour.
t.port de penaguila abric i@38.7,-0.4:
In Valencian, a port is a mountain pass, and the Port de Penàguila is one of the best known in this part of Alicante province. It crosses the Serra de Mariola's neighbouring ridges, linking the high valleys of the interior with the coastal side, and it has been a route for people, flocks and goods for centuries. The shelter at Port de Penàguila, Abric I, lies about four kilometres from Benilloba, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride ties it to Olula, another site in the district.

A pass is a good place for a painted shelter, because it is where animals and people move through the land. Whoever painted here may have watched the herds cross, or lain in wait for them. Passes are also viewpoints, and from the heights you can look over long folds of hills, terraced slopes and small white villages.

For a rider, a Valencian port promises curves. The road climbs in a series of bends, some wide, some tight, through pine and scrub, with views opening at every corner, and drops down the other side in the same fashion. The surface is generally good, but narrow, and cyclists are numerous at weekends. Rock and gravel can fall on to the road after rain, and ice can form in winter.

Benilloba has fewer than nine hundred people and may not have fuel to hand. Cocentaina, about ten kilometres away, has over eleven thousand and plenty of stations. Relleu and Sella are small villages, with a bar or two, and are pleasant for a coffee. Bring water, and a layer for the wind at the top. Mid-morning is a good moment to arrive, when the sun has cleared the ridge but the heat has not yet settled, and the valleys below are still hazy and soft. In autumn, when the first rains have passed, the air is washed clean and the view can run for fifty kilometres, with the sea a pale line on the horizon. Stop at a wide verge rather than on a bend, and give the cyclists room.
t.abric del zuro@39.1,-0.8:
In July 2012, a huge fire swept through the hills around Cortes de Pallás, not far from Bicorp, and burned tens of thousands of hectares of pine forest, one of the worst wildfires in the history of the Valencian Community. Fire is a fact of life in these dry Mediterranean mountains, and the landscape tells the story: the pines that regrow quickly from seed, the scrub that returns within a few years, and the gaunt grey trunks that still stand on some of the slopes. It is a sobering reminder that the beauty of this country is fragile.

The Abric del Zuro lies about three and a half kilometres from Bicorp, in the rugged hills where Valencia's interior begins, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride links it with the Abric de Seguili, another site in the same country. The shelters here stand among limestone cliffs and ravines, and the paintings are small and faded.

The district is rich in wildlife. Bonelli's eagles nest on the cliffs, and griffon vultures glide above, with wild boar, foxes and rabbits in the scrub. In spring, orchids, rockrose and wild thyme cover the slopes, and the air hums with bees.

For a rider, the roads are narrow, winding and almost empty, with steep climbs, tight bends and big views. Surfaces vary, with patches of gravel and rock. Spring and autumn are best, and in the heat of summer, an early start is wise. Winter nights are cold at this height.

Navarrés, with nearly three thousand, about twelve kilometres away, has the basics, and Enguera, about twenty-two kilometres off, with over five thousand, is larger. Fill up before you go, and carry water.
t.abrigo chorradores@39.2,-0.8:
Chorro is the Spanish word for a jet or spout of water, and a chorrador is a place where water spouts, so the name of this shelter suggests a spring or a waterfall that once poured from the rock nearby. It would have been a precious thing in this dry country, and probably explains why the painters chose the spot. The Abrigo Chorradores lies about two kilometres from Millares, a village of fewer than six hundred people in the rugged hills of inland Valencia, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride links it with a site called Barranco del Cabezo del Moro.

The neighbouring village of Dos Aguas, the Two Waters, gave its name to a noble title, the Marquis of Dos Aguas, whose palace in the city of Valencia has a famous carved alabaster doorway and now houses the national ceramics museum. It is a surprising link between a tiny mountain village and the grandeur of the city.

The country around is a mix of gorge, forest and farmland. The Júcar river runs nearby through a deep canyon, and the slopes are covered with pine, scrub and abandoned terraces. In spring, the hills are green and fragrant, and in autumn the air is clear.

The ride is a delight. Roads are narrow and winding, with tight bends, steep drops and views over the gorge, and they carry very little traffic. Surfaces are mixed, and rock and gravel may be present. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and midsummer can be very hot.

Fuel is far away. Millares and Dos Aguas are tiny, and the nearest sizeable place is Turís, in the plain, about eighteen kilometres off, with over five thousand people and a famous cooperative winery. Fill up before you go, and carry water and a snack.
t.barranc del salt abric v@38.7,-0.4:
A good day in this part of the Serra de Mariola might go like this. You leave early, when the air is cool and the light is low, and ride the lane from Benilloba up into the hills. The shelter at Barranc del Salt, Abric V, lies about four kilometres from the village, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride links it with Benirrama, in the Vall de Gallinera, a quiet valley to the east. You walk to the wall, look, and sit for a while with the view.

By mid-morning, you are ready for coffee, and Cocentaina, about ten kilometres away, is the obvious place. The town has a fine old palace, the Palau Comtal, once the seat of the counts of Cocentaina, and a pleasant old centre. Its market is a lively one, and the fair at the start of November, around All Saints, is among the biggest in the region. Fuel is easy there, with several stations.

The afternoon is for the heat, and for the shade of pine woods. Take a long lunch, or a siesta, and return to the road when the day cools. The lanes of the Mariola are best in the late afternoon, with warm light on the limestone and the smell of thyme and rosemary in the air.

The roads are narrow and twisting, with bends of every kind, and the surface is mostly good, though gravel collects in places. Cyclists are common, especially at weekends, and in autumn, mushroom pickers park along the verges. Benilloba itself is small, with fewer than nine hundred people, so I would not rely on fuel there. Relleu is another small village, good for a drink. Carry water, and wear sturdy shoes.
t.barranc del salt abric lii@38.7,-0.4:
The Barranc del Salt is one of the narrow ravines that cut into the limestone country of the Comtat, the inland county of Alicante province, with Cocentaina eleven thousand strong a short way down the valley and the small village of Benilloba closer still. The shelter that carries its name holds paintings in the Levantine style, red figures of hunters and animals daubed on the rock by people who lived here thousands of years ago. The shelters are marked on the map, but the last stretch is on foot, and the coordinates are good for the neighbourhood rather than the doorstep, so expect to walk and to look around.

Getting there is the part a rider will enjoy. The roads in this corner of the Valencian interior wind up out of olive and almond terraces into pine and holm oak, with short climbs, tight hairpins and the occasional farm track that is better left to the walkers. Surfaces are generally decent on the main local roads and rough where the tarmac gives up. Traffic is thin outside the weekends, when cyclists and day trippers from Alcoy and the coast come up to the Serra de Mariola, which rises nearby and is a natural park known for its wild herbs. Locals still gather them for the herbal liqueur that every bar in the region seems to keep behind the counter.

Cocentaina is the town to remember. It has fuel, cafes and a proper old quarter dominated by the palace and castle of the counts, the family that ran this valley in the late Middle Ages. Alcoy, just beyond, is where the Moors and Christians festival takes over the streets every April, a loud, costumed, gunpowder-fuelled affair that is worth planning a trip around if you like noise. Benilloba itself is small, so do not count on a petrol pump there.

Summer on this side of Spain is hot and shadeless, and the midday rock face radiates like a stove. Spring and autumn are the seasons to come, when the light is low and gold on the cliffs and the ravine still smells of thyme and resin. Bring water, because the walk up to a shelter has none, and go early enough that you are back at the bike before the heat settles in.
t.abrigos del pozo i y ii@38.2,-1.6:
Calasparra sits where the Segura river leaves the hills of the Murcian interior, and anyone who has ordered a paella with proper grains has probably eaten its rice without knowing it. The town has its own protected denomination for rice, grown in terraces watered from the river, and the pale fields in the valley are an odd and welcome sight in country otherwise made of rock and scrub. Eleven thousand people live here, which means fuel, a bakery that opens early and plenty of bars where lunch is not a negotiation.

Abrigos del Pozo are two rock shelters in this part of the river valley, and they belong to the Levantine rock art that UNESCO lists for the Mediterranean basin. The paintings are red, small and quite delicate, figures of hunters and animals that are older than any writing in the peninsula. The shelters are in the landscape rather than beside a car park, so plan on a short walk from wherever the track ends, and be ready for the possibility that access requires a booking or a guide. Check locally before you ride out, as these things change.

The riding around here suits a relaxed pace. The roads follow the contours of the Segura gorges, with long straights through almond and pine, then sudden bends where the river has carved a canyon too narrow for anything but a viaduct. The Almadenes gorge, a short distance away towards Cieza, is a dramatic cut through the limestone, and a good excuse for an hour of photography. Cieza, bigger at thirty-five thousand, is the place for a full tank and a lunch with more choice than Calasparra offers.

The sanctuary of La Esperanza, which stands above the town, is the local pilgrimage site and has views over the valley that are worth the short climb on a clear day. In winter the mornings are sharp and sometimes foggy in the river bottom, while July and August are brutally hot. The best months are April, May and October, when the rice fields are flooded and reflect the sky, and the roads belong to you and a few farm trucks.
t.abrigo de la cornisa@38.1,-2.3:
High above the Segura headwaters, the village of Nerpio feels more like a mountain outpost than part of southern Spain. It lies on the edge of the Sierra de Alcaraz and the Sierra de Segura, well over a thousand metres up, and the climate is the sort that sends locals indoors in January and has snow arriving early. The Abrigo de la Cornisa belongs to a cluster of painted shelters in the district, and the Nerpio area as a whole is known for having one of the richest groups of rock paintings in the country.

The paintings here were made in several waves, with older Levantine figures and later schematic signs, so a single cliff can carry images created thousands of years apart. The name of the shelter says it all: it is a cornice, an overhang in the rock wall, which protected pigments from rain for centuries. Visits are best arranged locally because the sites are sensitive, and the track in is often a walking path rather than a road.

The riding is the real prize. From Nerpio the roads fall away to the Taibilla river and climb through pine forest to open plateaus, with long views of pale mountains and very little traffic. Surfaces are patchy where the local councils have little to spend, so ride as if there might be gravel in every bend, which sometimes there is. Fuel is thin on the ground. Yeste to the north is the nearest place with something at all, while Moratalla, farther south and bigger at about eight and a half thousand people, is where you can be sure of a tank and a lunch. Do not leave Nerpio with a low light on the dash.

Autumn is when the area shows off, with oaks and poplars along the river turning gold against dark pine. Spring is fresh and green. Summer is bearable at this altitude, but the shadeless slopes still bake by afternoon, so start early and keep water on the bike. Nights are cold, even in July, if you are camping.
t.barranc d en grau@38.8,-0.3:
Marina Alta is the part of Alicante that most visitors know from the beach, but behind the coast the landscape rises into limestone ravines that feel closer to Mallorca than to a resort. The Barranc d'en Grau is one of those clefts, in the hills above Villalonga and the upper reaches of the Vall d'Ebo. The painted shelter in the neighbouring ravine is among a number of rock-art sites in the region, sharing the Levantine style with sites farther north: red figures of hunters, animals and symbols that were painted long before any Roman set foot here.

The Vall d'Ebo has a sad and fascinating recent story. In 1609 the Moriscos, descendants of the Muslims who had stayed after the Christian conquest, were expelled from the Kingdom of Valencia, and valleys like this one were emptied almost overnight. Terraces fell into disuse and some villages never really recovered, which explains why such an inland place is still so sparsely settled. The old irrigation walls and dry-stone terraces that climb the hillsides are a quiet reminder.

For a rider, the approach is one of the better short rides in the province. The road climbs from the coastal plain through almond groves and pine, with plenty of bends and some stretches where the guard rails are suspiciously short. Pego, down the valley at eleven thousand people, has fuel and food, and its marshland, a natural park of rice paddies and reed beds, makes a good contrast with the dry mountains above. Villalonga is smaller but does the job for coffee. Vall d'Ebo itself, with only a few hundred people, is a place to look at rather than to refuel in.

The best season is winter and early spring, when the almond blossom turns the valley white and the roads are free of tourist traffic. August is hot and crowded near the coast, and the shelters give almost no shade on the approach. Carry water and a map that does not depend on mobile signal, because reception in the ravines is patchy.
t.garganta de la hoz x@38.4,-0.2:
Behind the Costa Blanca, in the dry hills between El Campello and Villajoyosa, the coastal strip of hotels and apartment blocks gives way surprisingly quickly to scrub, limestone and abandoned terraces. The coordinates for Garganta de la Hoz X are a general pointer to a ravine in that country, and the name refers to a group of rock-art shelters, one of many cave sites listed by UNESCO among the Levantine paintings of the Mediterranean basin. The painted figures themselves are small, red and weathered, and very easy to pass by unless someone shows you where to look.

Do not expect a visitor centre. Sites like this often sit at the end of a walking track, on private or protected land, and some have restricted access to protect the paint. Treat the point as a place to start a wander, and ask locally before assuming you can climb in.

The ride here, though, is a pleasure of its own. The back roads in this part of Alicante province wind through carob, almond and pine, with short climbs and an abrupt drop to the sea on the far side. Traffic is heavy on the coastal road in summer and thins to almost nothing once you head inland, where the biggest hazards are cyclists in tight groups and the odd flock of sheep. Surface quality varies but is generally acceptable on the main local roads. Villajoyosa, with nearly thirty-four thousand people, has fuel, a seafront of brightly painted houses, and a chocolate-making tradition that it is justly proud of. El Campello is smaller but just as practical for a stop.

The hills are the place to be in the cooler months. In the middle of summer the sun is merciless and the stone gives off heat well into the evening. Late autumn, with the first rains, brings out the smell of wet pine and thyme, and the light over the sea in the afternoon is the kind that makes people stop the bike for no reason at all.
t.abrigo ii@39.0,-1.2:
Alpera is a small town on the plateau between Albacete and the Valencian coast, in the flat, windy country where La Mancha begins to tilt towards the sea. It is best known among archaeologists for Cueva de la Vieja, a shelter with one of the largest collections of Levantine paintings in the interior, and Abrigo II is part of the same group. The cluster of figures includes human forms, animals and symbols, painted in red and black, and the whole group is part of the UNESCO listing for the Mediterranean basin.

The landscape here looks plain at first, a patchwork of cereal fields, vineyards and almond plantations, with low limestone outcrops pushing up through the soil. On closer acquaintance, the rock outcrops turn out to be riddled with overhangs, and the paintings were made precisely because those shelters offered a dry, smooth wall in a country with few natural caves.

Roads in the district are straight and fast, with long visibility and little traffic. For a rider that means easy kilometres, though it is not high drama. Wind is the main enemy, blowing cold in winter and gritty in summer. Ayora, over in the Valencian side with about five and a half thousand people, is the nearest reasonably sized town for fuel and food. The big castle at Almansa, a short way along, commemorates the battle of 1707 that decided the War of the Spanish Succession in Spain, and the town makes a handy stop for lunch.

Fuel is not available at every village on the plateau, so take Ayora or Almansa as the safe choice. Water is not a problem in the villages, though out in the countryside there is none.

The best season is spring, when the cereal turns the plain green and wildflowers crowd the roadsides. Autumn brings a hazy gold, and in the vineyards the harvest is under way. Winter is cold and bleak and the frost can sit on the road until late morning, so check the surface before leaning into a bend.
t.barranc de famorca abric vi@38.7,-0.2:
Famorca is a tiny village in the mountains above the Guadalest valley, and the ravine below it, the Barranc de Famorca, has several painted shelters among its rocks. Abric VI is one of them, a small overhang with red Levantine paintings that form part of the UNESCO-listed rock art of the Mediterranean basin. The nearest places with more than a few hundred people are Castell de Castells and Benimantell, and for anything resembling a proper town you have to go to Pego.

The mountains here are the Serra d'Aitana and its neighbours, the highest range in Alicante province, with the main peak a little over fifteen hundred metres. They are surprisingly wild for a place so close to the Costa Blanca. Goats graze on the slopes, griffon vultures circle above the cliffs, and almond trees fill the valleys with blossom in late winter. The terraces were built by Moorish farmers who worked this country for centuries, and some are still tended.

The road to Castell de Castells and beyond is one of the best short rides in the region. It winds up through pine and terraces with hairpins, narrow sections and views of the long blue line of the Mediterranean in the distance. The surface is variable, generally decent but with the odd patch where winter rain has chewed the edge. Traffic is light, apart from cycling groups at weekends. The village of Guadalest, not far away, has a castle perched on a rock and is the busiest tourist stop in the area, so go early or late in the day if you want peace.

A few bars serve lunch, and the local speciality is a hearty stew that suits a cold day in the mountains. The seasons are straightforward: spring and autumn are lovely, summer is hot and busy near the coast, winter can bring frost and occasionally snow on the high ground.
t.barranc de famorca abric i@38.7,-0.2:
Famorca clings to the side of a mountain in the Comtat, a district of Alicante province where the roads are as steep as the villages are small. Abric I in the Barranc de Famorca is the first of a series of painted shelters in the ravine, and like its neighbours it shows Levantine red paintings, part of the UNESCO list for the Mediterranean basin. The shelters lie in a deep gully below the village, and getting down to them means a walk on a stony path.

What makes the whole area worth the climb is the geography. The Serra d'Aitana, its highest summit a little over fifteen hundred metres, rises to the north, and the Sierra de Serrella and Bèrnia fill the horizon to the east and south. Between them the valleys are terraced with almond, olive and carob, and in late winter the almond blossom turns whole hillsides pink and white. The air smells of rosemary and woodsmoke, and the silence is broken by sheep bells, dogs and the occasional motorcycle.

A good road runs from Callosa d'en Sarrià, a town known for its loquats, up the Guadalest valley, with the reservoir below and the castle of Guadalest on its rock above. The corners are tight and constant, the gradients steep, and the surface patchy in places. On a sunny weekend you will share the road with cyclists, who tend to climb in the middle of it. Midweek, and especially in winter, you can have the lot to yourself.

For fuel and a proper lunch, use Pego or the coast, since the mountain villages have little and sometimes nothing. Benimantell and Castell de Castells have small bars where a plate of local food and a coffee is cheap.

In summer the heat can be savage by midday, and the afternoon thunderstorms that sometimes form over the Aitana are sudden and heavy. October and March are probably the best months, with clear skies and a sharp light that picks out every terrace wall.
t.senda de la cabra@38.1,-2.4:
Senda de la Cabra, the goat path, is the kind of name a mountain gives to the only way across a slope. It lies in the high country of the upper Segura, near Nerpio on the border of Albacete and Murcia provinces, where the Sierra de Segura folds into the Sierra de Alcaraz and the rivers run cold and clear. The painted shelters of the area, Gabar among them, are part of the large group of rock-art sites in the Nerpio district, which includes some of the best-known Levantine and schematic paintings in Spain.

The village of Nerpio itself is high enough, over a thousand metres, to keep its cold snaps into spring. Segura de la Sierra, to the north-west, is the better-known village, a medieval castle town on a crag with narrow streets and views over a huge sweep of olive-covered hills. Both are small, with fewer than two thousand people each, and neither has a reliable pump, so you must plan your fuel. Huéscar, with just over eight thousand people and about an hour away, is the safe bet, or Yeste for a smaller option.

The roads between them are among the most rewarding in this part of Spain, and among the loneliest. They climb through Aleppo pine and black pine forest, cross bare ridges and drop into river valleys where the water runs under old stone bridges. Corners are open and fast in places, then tighten suddenly at a village or a river crossing. The tarmac is usually fine on the main routes but deteriorates on side roads, so a rider should treat each bend with respect.

Wildlife is a bonus. Mouflon, red deer and wild boar live in the forests, and golden eagles hunt over the ridges. In autumn the oak and poplar turn colour in the valley bottoms, and in spring the lower slopes are a carpet of flowers. Winter brings snow and ice at this height, and the roads can close with little warning.

To visit the shelters, enquire in Nerpio first. Access is controlled, and the walk from the road is rough in places.
t.garganta de la hoz viii@38.4,-0.2:
Eight shelters, ten shelters, more: the hills between El Campello and Villajoyosa have been counted and numbered by archaeologists, and Garganta de la Hoz VIII is one of those that earned a place on the UNESCO list of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin. The paintings are in the Levantine tradition, red figures on pale limestone, and they have survived on this dry hillside for thousands of years. The coordinates are approximate, and the shelter itself is hidden in the rocks some distance from any tarmac.

One thing that surprises visitors is how quickly the coast gives way to the interior. Ten minutes from the beach, the road is among pine and carob, and the roar of the resort towns is replaced by cicadas and the occasional tractor. The terraces on the slopes were built for almond, olive and vines, and abandoned as farming moved to the plains. Wild rosemary, thyme and gorse have taken over.

For motorcyclists, this is a good area for a leisurely half-day. The roads climb in a series of short bends, with sections of tight hairpin and others where you can open up. Surfaces are fair, and traffic is minimal inland, although the coast road in summer is a slow crawl behind caravans. Villajoyosa, with nearly thirty-four thousand people, and El Campello, with a little over twenty-six thousand, both have fuel and plenty of cafes. In Villajoyosa, the old centre by the sea, with its row of houses painted pink, ochre and blue, is worth a stroll, and the town's chocolate factories have been making sweets for well over a century.

Be careful about summer. Temperatures on the exposed slopes soar, and the stone keeps its heat long after sunset. The cooler months are far kinder, and in November the first rain brings out the smell of wet earth and a startling green in the gullies.

The walk to the shelter is not long but is rough, and some rock art sites in this area have restricted access, so ask in the villages before you set out.
t.hoyos i@37.7,-2.1:
Vélez-Blanco is a white village below a castle, and the hills around it hold some of the most celebrated prehistoric paintings in south-eastern Spain. Hoyos I is one of the painted shelters in the district, which sits in the Sierra María-Los Vélez, a natural park of limestone peaks on the northern edge of Almería province. The nearby Cueva de los Letreros is famous as the source of the Indalo, the little stick figure with an arc above its head that has become the symbol of Almería and appears on car stickers all over Spain. The shelter here belongs to the same tradition of painted art.

The castle in Vélez-Blanco is a Renaissance showpiece, built in the early sixteenth century for the Marquis of Los Vélez. Its marble courtyard was sold in the early twentieth century and is now installed in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, a story locals tell with a mixture of pride and irritation. The empty rooms at the castle are still worth a visit, and the views over the plain are wide.

Vélez-Rubio, a few kilometres down the valley, is the larger town, with seven thousand people and a baroque church of remarkable size for such a small place. It is the place to find fuel, a pharmacy and a long lunch. The roads here run through open country of almond and cereal, with the Sierra María rising to the west. The bends are gentle and the surface is mostly good, and traffic is light.

Climb into the sierra and the scene changes. Pine and cedar forests cover the slopes, and the road twists up in tight bends to viewpoints with long views over the dry plain. In winter the high ground can see snow, and in summer the plain is hot and dry. Late spring and early autumn are the best times for a ride.

Walking to the shelters is a matter of arranging a visit locally, since the sites are protected. Take water and a hat, as shade is scarce.
t.barranc de famorca abric ii@38.7,-0.2:
In the valley of the Famorca, the fold in the mountain that carries the name Abric II is a few paces along from its neighbours, and it shows how many people once used this ravine. Levantine paintings in red adorn the overhang, with the usual cast of hunters, animals and signs, and the whole series is part of the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean basin rock art.
