The place is remote, and the coordinates show the area rather than a place to leave the bike beside a sign.

Pinós is the name of the other shelter on this ride, and it points to a neighbouring Alicante town, Pinoso, in the drier hills to the south-west, where wine and marble are the local businesses. The two sites together make a ride that crosses Alicante from the green mountains of the north to the harsh interior.

The mountain section is the best of it. Roads climb between Callosa d'en Sarrià and the Guadalest valley, with hairpins cut into the hillside and long views of the Mediterranean in clear weather. On the way you pass the Guadalest reservoir, an improbable turquoise in a rocky bowl. The villages of Benimantell and Castell de Castells keep a few bars and a small shop. They don't have fuel, so fill at Pego or on the coast before you start.

The surface changes with the winter weather. After heavy rain you can find loose stones and mud on the bends, particularly on the shaded north-facing sections. In summer, temperatures are high, and the scent of pine resin and sun-warmed rock is strong. In February the almond blossom makes a delicate haze over the lower slopes, and in October the carob pods lie on the road and the first mist hangs in the valleys.

Treat any walk to a shelter with respect. Stay on paths, do not touch the paintings, and leave nothing behind. These images have survived for a very long time and are more fragile than they look.
t.abric del charco de la madera@39.1,-0.8:
The sign says Abric del Charco de la Madera, and the name suggests a pool, a charco, in a rocky gully near the village of Bicorp, in the highlands of the Valencian interior. This is the Canal de Navarrés and the Valle de Ayora-Cofrentes, a country of limestone ranges, river canyons and poor farming land, a long way from the Valencian beaches. The shelter holds paintings in the Levantine style, part of the UNESCO-listed group. The second stop on this ride, Penya Escrita, is a different site altogether, in the mountains of the Marina Alta far to the east, so treat the two as separate worlds.

Bicorp is a small village with about six hundred inhabitants, and nearby Quesa has a few more. Neither has a fuel pump you can rely on, so fill the tank at Ayora, which has over five thousand people, before you head into the hills. The Júcar river runs not far to the east, and the huge reservoir at Cortes de Pallás is one of the great hidden landscapes of the region, a flooded canyon with steep wooded sides and few roads.

The roads are the real draw for a rider. They climb out of the valleys in tight sequences, cross high passes of pine and holm oak, and drop to river crossings where the road narrows to one lane. The tarmac is not always smooth, and rocks can come down onto the road after heavy rain. Traffic is almost non-existent, which makes the sudden appearance of a tractor or a flock of goats all the more startling. In autumn, mushroom hunters park along the verges, and in winter the road can be icy on shady stretches.

The hills smell of resin and wild herbs, and the sky at night is full of stars. Spring is the best time to ride, with green slopes and mild weather. Summer is hot, with thunderstorms in the afternoon.

If you set out to find the shelter, take advice from the village first. The path is rough and the paintings are easily damaged, so leave them as you find them.
t.garganta de la hoz ii@38.4,-0.2:
Garganta de la Hoz II is another shelter in the same cluster of ravines inland from the Costa Blanca, in a rocky landscape between El Campello and Villajoyosa that is more austere than the coast would suggest. It is among the painted sites that were added to the UNESCO list in 1998 as part of the Mediterranean basin group, and the red figures on its wall are in the Levantine style that spread along Spain's eastern flank. The coordinates give you the district, but the shelter itself is up a track and a short climb, and will take a little finding.

I like this country for what it holds back. The roads here are not famous, and they do not make the guidebooks, but they are neat, twisting and almost empty. They climb from the coast through pine and carob, past old threshing floors and abandoned terraces, and the views open out onto the sea in the afternoon haze. The tarmac is mostly in good order, with the odd rough patch where winter storms have washed gravel across the road. Walkers and cyclists are the main company.

Villajoyosa has the big supermarket and the pumps, with nearly thirty-four thousand inhabitants, and El Campello, a seaside town of twenty-six thousand, is a good second choice. If you stop in Villajoyosa, look at the old fishermen's quarter and the Sunday market, and ask for a coffee at one of the cafes by the beach. In the hills themselves there is very little, so bring water and a snack.

In July and August this part of Alicante is hot and bustling, with beach traffic clogging the coast road. In spring the interior is green and the roads are quiet, and in autumn the sea stays warm enough to swim after a ride. Winter is mild but can be wet, and a sudden downpour can turn the dust on the road to a slippery paste.
t.abrigo de la hoz@38.2,-2.3:
Nerpio, in the south-east corner of Albacete province, sits at the end of a long run of mountain road, and the Abrigo de la Hoz belongs to the area's rich group of painted shelters. The name means the shelter of the gorge, hoz being the old Spanish word for a narrow river canyon, and the cliffs near the Taibilla river do indeed have a gorge-like feel. The paintings, in red, show the typical cast of animals and human figures, and they are part of the UNESCO listing for the rock art of the Mediterranean basin.

Nerpio is a long way from anywhere. The nearest town of any size is Moratalla, in the province of Murcia, a good forty kilometres away, with just over eight and a half thousand people, a castle, and a long tradition of drumming during Holy Week. Yeste, in Albacete, is closer and smaller. If you find the tank at half on the way in, fill it before climbing further.

The ride in is part of the reward. The roads wind up through pine and oak, with the Segura and the Taibilla below, and then come out onto high pastures where the horizon opens out. The bends come in long sequences, with a few sharp switchbacks, and gravel is sometimes washed onto the surface after storms. The cold is real here, even in spring, and a thermal layer is a good idea. Wild boar and deer cross the road at dusk, and in winter there may be snow on the heights.

The lack of traffic can be misleading, because logging trucks and farm machinery use the same roads and take up more than their share of the lane. Take it steadily and enjoy the quiet.

Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons, when the weather is mild and the colours are good. If you want to see the shelter, ask in Nerpio for advice about access and the state of the path.
t.cueva de jorge@38.2,-1.6:
The Segura river does something surprising near Calasparra. It runs between steep walls of limestone, pale and fissured, and in those walls people made their shelters long before anyone built a town. Cueva de Jorge is one of the painted sites in this stretch of the valley, and it forms part of the Levantine art listed by UNESCO. The cave is a small, rough opening high in the cliffs, and the paintings, in the usual red pigment, are modest but real.

Calasparra, with nearly eleven thousand inhabitants, is the closest town of any size and has the sort of services a rider appreciates: pumps, a bakery, a pharmacy and several bars. It is famous for its rice, grown in terraced fields beside the river and sold with a protected name that chefs value for its ability to absorb stock without turning mushy. A plate of rice with rabbit or vegetables is the dish to look for. Cieza, down the valley, has thirty-five thousand people and offers a still greater choice.

The riding is mostly gentle but has its dramatic moments. Roads follow the gorge, with views of the river far below, and cross it on old bridges. In the surrounding hills they climb through pine and esparto grass, with long straight sections and some fine open bends. Traffic is thin, apart from local farm vehicles. The surface is generally good, though some of the minor roads have seen better days.

The place can be uncomfortably hot in summer, with temperatures regularly into the high thirties, and the limestone reflects the glare. The river provides some relief, and the shade under the poplars along the bank is welcome. Spring brings blossom and green fields, and autumn the soft light that photographers like. Winter nights are cold, and mist can form in the gorge.

As with other sites in this series, access to the painted shelter is by foot, and local advice is the best guide to what is open and what is permitted.
t.barranc del salt abric lv@38.7,-0.4:
Four shelters along the Barranc del Salt are numbered in Roman numerals, and the fourth is the subject here. It lies in the folded limestone country between Cocentaina and Benilloba, a short way inland from Alcoy, where the foothills of the Serra de Mariola press up against the valley of the Serpis river. The painting is in the Levantine tradition, and the site is part of the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean basin rock art.

Cocentaina is an easy base. It has a population of about eleven and a half thousand, with fuel, supermarkets and a handful of restaurants around the old town. The great palace of the counts of Cocentaina overlooks the main street, and every autumn the town holds an important fair, the Fira de Tots Sants, which has been going for centuries and brings the whole valley in for food, livestock and noise. Behind it, the Serra de Mariola is a natural park covered in aromatic herbs, with a reputation for good walking and plenty of picnic sites.

On a motorcycle, the lanes leading into the barranc are narrow and often steep, and sections near the track are rough. The main roads up into the Serra de Mariola are better, with a mix of open bends and tight hairpins through pine and oak, and the views over the Comtat valley are wide. There are cyclists at weekends and a few hunters in the cooler months, but otherwise little traffic. A rider who is happy to take it slowly will find the surroundings absorbing.

Nature here is rewarding. Foxes and wild boar are common, and in the rocks you may spot a Bonelli's eagle or a peregrine. The smell of thyme, rosemary and pine resin is strong on a warm day, and in autumn the fungus hunters are out in the woods. Water in the barranc is scarce in summer, so bring plenty.

Spring is the best season for riding and for walking. Summer afternoons are hot and heavy, and in winter the mist can hang for days on the heights above the valley.
t.fuensanta i@38.2,-2.1:
Fuensanta is a place name that turns up all over southern Spain, a holy fountain, and the one on this ride lies in the mountains of the upper Segura, in the border country between Albacete and Murcia. t.cantos de la visera ii@38.7,-1.3:
Monte Arabí rises out of the plains of the Altiplano like an upturned boat, a long ridge of pale rock above a country of vines and cereal fields, and the Cantos de la Visera are among the shelters that gather round its flanks. The roads leading up to the Monte Arabí area are rough in places, and the last part to the rock is a track. Spring is the season to choose, with wild flowers in the fields and a soft light. Autumn is also good, and the grape harvest gives the roads a busy, cheerful feel. For the shelters, ask locally about access and follow the signs, because the paintings are delicate.
t.concejal i@38.1,-2.4:
Concejal is the name of a rock shelter in the sierra above Nerpio, a part of southern Albacete that most Spaniards have never visited. Nerpio sits at about a thousand metres or more, and the cold is a fact of life. The river Taibilla runs below, clear and fast, with trout and a few anglers, and the hills above are home to deer, boar and golden eagles. At night the sky is vast, and the Milky Way is easy to see.

Traffic is almost non-existent. In winter, the roads can be icy, and in spring, melting snow can leave mud and gravel on the bends. In autumn the leaves of the poplars along the river turn yellow, and the oaks go copper.

t.garganta de la hoz iv@38.4,-0.2:
The coast road at El Campello gives way almost at once to a dry, wrinkled interior, and Garganta de la Hoz IV is one of the numbered painted shelters tucked into those hills. Its figures are the familiar red ones of the Levantine tradition, an archer here, an animal there, in a group that forms part of the UNESCO listing of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin. If you ride, you will find that the best part of the journey is the contrast. In the morning you can have breakfast by the sea in El Campello, a fishing town grown into a seaside resort of about twenty-six thousand people, with fuel, cafes and a long beach. Within half an hour you can be on a quiet back road among carob trees, with a view of the sea shimmering below. The roads here are twisty and narrow in places, the surface is mixed and traffic is light. At weekends cyclists are everywhere, so give them room.

t.cimbarrillo ma antonia i@38.4,-0.3:
Cimbarrillo is a name that does not appear on tourist maps, and Ma Antonia, the woman or the farm it recalls, has been lost to anyone but the locals. The shelter, listed as number I, lies in the dry hills of the Alicante coast, between El Campello and Villajoyosa, in the same band of broken limestone as the Garganta de la Hoz shelters. Its red paintings are in the Levantine style and belong to the UNESCO listing for the rock art of the Mediterranean basin. As with many of these sites, the coordinates are an approximation, and the shelter will take some finding.

Here, in the hills, the land is dry and the only shade comes from carob and pine. Between the two lies a landscape of salt pans, orange orchards and bare mountains that shows how much water means in this corner of Spain.

The roads wind up from the coast through scrub, with views of the sea and a few sharp bends, and the traffic dwindles to almost nothing a few kilometres inland. The surface is mostly fair, and on weekdays you may meet only a cyclist or two. Walkers sometimes use the tracks, so watch for them on blind corners.

El Campello, about twelve kilometres away, has some twenty-six thousand people and all the fuel and food you could need, and its fish restaurants by the harbour are an honest choice for lunch. Villajoyosa, bigger still, has a colourful old quarter on the waterfront.

October and November are the best months, when the heat has gone but the days are still bright. Summer sun on the exposed slopes is punishing, and storms in autumn can bring heavy rain and loose gravel to the road. The walk to the shelter is brief, but a protected site deserves courtesy, so keep to the path.
t.west halladale@58.4,-4.0:
Forsinard is the name of a railway halt, but the country around it is what people come for. The Flow Country of Caithness and Sutherland is the largest expanse of blanket bog in Europe, a vast, treeless plain of peat, pools and sedge that rolls out to the horizon under a huge sky. It was added to the list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 2024 for its importance as a carbon store and a wildlife habitat. Midges, in summer, are the plague of the north and will find you the moment you stop.

The Kildonan Gold Rush, in 1869, brought hundreds of diggers to the next valley, and the story of the nuggets is still told locally. Late spring is the best time, when the birds are nesting and the long evenings give light until after ten.
t.abrigo del castillo de taibona@38.1,-2.4:
High in the south-east of Albacete province, where the Sierra de Segura meets the Granada highlands, the land turns to pine, juniper and bare limestone ridges, and the village of Nerpio sits in a basin about six kilometres from this stop. From Yeste or from Huéscar the roads climb through dry farmland into woods, with long, easy bends rather than hairpins, and surfaces that are fine but not always freshly laid. Cold nights arrive early here because of the altitude, and winter can bring ice and snow, so autumn and late spring are my choice, with sun on the rock and not much heat.

Nerpio is a small place, around sixteen hundred people, and it is the sensible spot for a coffee and a bocadillo, with a bar or two and a grocery for water. For fuel, count on Nerpio only if you check first; Yeste, about twenty-six kilometres away, is the larger bet, and Huéscar, thirty-nine kilometres off with some eight thousand inhabitants, is the sure one. The shelter is also a reminder of how long this land has been inhabited. The castle crowning the ridge is medieval and looks out over a landscape that sheep still graze, and the paintings below it come from a world that was already ancient by the time that wall went up.
t.inverness@57.5,-4.2:
Inverness is where the North Coast 500 starts and ends, the circuit that has turned the top of Scotland into a bucket-list road, and the sensible traveller treats the city as a place to arrive, wash, shop and sleep before heading out. It sits where the River Ness meets the Moray Firth, and for centuries it was the capital of the Highlands in practice, a market town at the junction of roads running north, west and south. The population of about forty-seven thousand makes it by far the largest settlement for a hundred miles in any direction, and that means all the fuel, tyres, spares and supermarkets you could want.

Before you leave, the city is worth a walk along the river, where the Ness Islands carry Victorian footbridges and tall trees, and the castle, a nineteenth-century building, looks over the water. Inverness is not ancient in appearance, because most of the old town was lost to fires and war, but it has a lively centre, a cathedral on the river bank and a big market. Culloden Moor, where the Jacobite army was destroyed in 1746, lies about ten minutes east, and it is a moving and quiet place; the visitor centre is a good short stop. Loch Ness, nearly twenty-three miles long, begins just to the south-west, and the Caledonian Canal that links it to the sea passes through the city.

The A9 is fast and busy for the first stretch, but once you leave it the roads narrow, and the single-track sections in the north and west need patience, passing places and a willingness to wave at campervans. Summer brings heavy traffic, midges and long light, with dusk past eleven in June, so book accommodation well ahead. Spring and September are quieter and often dry on the east side.

On the morning you set off, top up the tank and think about the distances, because the next large supply is some way on, and many stations in the north close early or on Sundays. Buy midge repellent, check your tyres and carry waterproofs, as Highland weather changes between two bends. Cullen skink or a fish supper makes a respectable first dinner, and the smoked salmon here is good.
t.hadrian s wall vallum between mill beck:
West of Newcastle, along the north bank of the Tyne, the line of Hadrian's Wall disappears under the suburbs and then pops up again in the villages of Heddon-on-the-Wall and Walbottle, and here, near the Mill Beck, the label points at something less famous than the Wall itself: the vallum. This was a great flat-bottomed ditch with mounds on either side, dug south of the Wall and running along its length, and it marked the rear boundary of the military zone. Nobody is entirely sure what it was for, but the usual view is that it was a barrier to control who approached the frontier from the Roman province behind it. Today, where it survives, it is a shallow, grassy trench, easy to miss unless you know to look for it.

Heddon-on-the-Wall, a village of about thirteen hundred people, has a stretch of the actual Wall, one of the longest in the east, with the foundation of a turret visible beside the lane. Newburn, a couple of kilometres away on the Tyne, is much bigger and has the fuel stations and shops, while Newcastle itself is just a few miles east. The land here is low and rolling, with farmland, hedgerows and the ridge of the Tyne valley behind, and from the higher fields you may catch the haze of the city.

For riding, the best road in the neighbourhood is the old Military Road, the B6318, which runs westward from Newcastle along the line of the Wall, though this stretch is nearer the city and busier. It was built after the Jacobite rising of 1745, when General Wade found he could not move troops quickly across the north, and sections of the Wall were quarried for its stone. The straight line beloved of the Romans is repeated by the road, with sudden dips and crests. Once you pass Heddon you start to feel the countryside open up.

Traffic is commuter-heavy on weekdays and the roads can be wet and greasy in autumn, with mud from farm vehicles. Bring waterproofs. A flask and a pasty are better than the village options, though there is a pub or two. The sensible time to come is a weekend morning in spring, when the light is clear and the lanes are empty enough to ride slowly.
t.hadrian s wall in wall mile 1@55.0,-1.5:
Wallsend, the name itself is the clue. This is the east end of Hadrian's Wall, on the north bank of the Tyne about five miles from the centre of Newcastle, where the Romans built a fort called Segedunum to guard the river and anchor the frontier. The label's Wall mile 1 is a reference to the first stretch of the Wall measured from here, and the fort and the short section of reconstructed Wall nearby are the real thing to see. Wallsend is a working Tyneside town of about forty-three thousand people, and Hebburn, on the other bank, has a similar shape; both were built around shipyards and mines.

Segedunum has been excavated and partly rebuilt, and its observation tower gives a view over the ground plan of barracks, granaries and the headquarters building, with the Tyne beyond. A reconstructed Roman bathhouse, built with the methods of the period, shows how the soldiers washed, and a stretch of the Wall runs from the fort towards the river. The museum is worth an hour, and it is better than you expect for a place so surrounded by housing. The fort stood here for around three centuries, and the garrison seems to have been a unit of auxiliary soldiers drawn from the provinces of the empire.

Riding is a city matter. From here you will take the A187 or the riverside road with its roundabouts, traffic lights and speed cameras, and the cobbled sections around the old shipyards are slippery when wet. The great cranes that once built liners and warships have mostly gone, but the memory of Swan Hunter remains in the street names. West along the north bank the road becomes the start of the Hadrian's Wall Path, one of Britain's national trails, and the Military Road runs towards open country. For a more rural ride, head west to the Tyne valley.

Fuel, cafes and shops are everywhere. The Tyne Tunnel and the Metro give easy ways in and out. Local food, pease pudding and a stottie cake, a flat round loaf, go together surprisingly well with ham, and the pubs along the river are friendly. Parking at Segedunum is free, which counts for a lot in the north-east, and bikes are easily accommodated. Arrive when it opens and you may have the tower to yourself.
t.markham cottage roman temporary camps 1:
Haltwhistle likes to call itself the centre of Britain, a claim measured with some creativity, and the town of nearly four thousand people is a good base for the middle section of Hadrian's Wall, where the frontier runs along the crags of the Whin Sill. The temporary camps in this label are Roman marching camps, the overnight enclosures that an army threw up with a ditch and a rampart each time it halted, and several are scattered across the fields south of the Wall. Almost all of them show only as faint rectangles in grass when the low sun catches them, and the ones near Markham Cottage fall in that category, so do not expect masonry or signs. What you get is a rare sense of how many soldiers once moved through this valley.

Aerial surveys and dry summers have revealed dozens of these camps in Northumberland, and they hint at the scale of campaigns long before the Wall was built, when the Romans were pushing north into Scotland and returning each winter. The Stanegate, a Roman road that ran between Corbridge and Carlisle, passes just south of here, and it was the frontier line before Hadrian ordered the Wall in about AD 122. To a historian that is the interesting layering: road first, then Wall, then ditch and vallum, then forts.

For a rider the area is a treasure, though the prize is the landscape. From Haltwhistle you can head east on the B6318, the Military Road, or along the lanes towards the crags, where long gradients and quick bends take you over the ridge with the Wall clinging to the edge. The surface varies, with some bumpy patches and the odd cattle grid, and sheep wander across without warning. Fog can sit on the ridge when the valley is clear, so check the sky. Spring and early summer give the best light, and the heather on the moors turns purple in August.

Haltwhistle has fuel and a handful of shops and cafes, and Hexham, twenty-odd kilometres east, has more of everything. The railway station on the Tyne Valley line is a useful sign that you are near civilisation. Bring a flask on the ridge, where there are few facilities, and note that the car parks at the main sites charge fees and sometimes limit bikes. Pasties and a pint of local bitter are the usual reward at the end of a day.
t.heart of neolithic orkney@59.0,-3.2:
There is a line of ancient monuments on the west Mainland of Orkney that together form what UNESCO calls the Heart of Neolithic Orkney: the chambered tomb of Maeshowe, the stone circles of Stenness and Brogar, and the village of Skara Brae on the Bay of Skaill. Here the coordinates fall between the two lochs, Stenness and Harray, on the narrow neck of land that separates them, and everything is within a few miles of Stromness, the ferry port on the southern side. Orkney as a whole is a set of green islands with almost no trees, huge skies and a wind that never really stops, and the monuments are about five thousand years old.

The first thing you notice is how open the country is. Without hills to speak of, the stones stand against the sky and you see them from a mile away, and the roads lie across the land in long, easy lines. The A965 and A967 are good, well-surfaced roads with a few gentle bends, little traffic outside the summer months, and views of the lochs that change with the light. The danger on Orkney is not the corners but the crosswinds, which can be strong enough to push a bike off line on exposed stretches. Rain comes in showers, and between them the air is washed and the colours are strong.

The Neolithic people here farmed barley and sheep, built houses of flagstone with stone furniture, and created ceremonial sites of astonishing precision. Orkney's flagstone splits so neatly that the builders had easy material. Later the islands were Norse, ruled by earls who left runes and sagas, and the Vikings left their mark inside the oldest tomb. The harbour at Stromness, with its flagged main street, was a stop for Hudson's Bay Company ships heading to Canada, and many Orcadians went with them.

Practical matters are simple. Fuel is available in Stromness and Kirkwall, which is the main town about fifteen miles east, and there are small shops and cafes along the road. Book Maeshowe in advance through the visitor centre at Stenness, because entry is by timed ticket, and the other sites are open air and free. The ferry from Scrabster or Aberdeen needs a booking in summer. The best months are May to September, but the midsummer light is the real prize, as it is bright past eleven at night.
t.cawfields roman temporary camp@55.0,-2.4:
Cawfields is a spot where Hadrian's Wall shows its best side. The Wall runs along the top of the Whin Sill, a hard volcanic dolerite ridge, and at Cawfields it follows a steep edge above a flooded quarry, with a milecastle, number 42, sitting in a dip and clear stone steps in its entrance. The quarry was cut into the crag in the nineteenth century, and the lake it left is a popular picnic spot. The temporary camp of the label lies nearby, a faint earthwork from the days of marching armies. It is not much to look at, so use it as an excuse to walk the Wall instead.

Whin Sill is a sheet of rock that was forced between layers of sedimentary rock about 295 million years ago, and it forms the ridge that carries not just the Wall but Bamburgh Castle and the Farne Islands on the coast. At Cawfields the dark rock breaks into columns, and its steep north face made a natural barrier that the Romans were wise to use. Walk up to the crest and you see the Wall disappearing in both directions, a stone ribbon over green hills, and the Pennines to the south. On a clear day, the effect is hard to forget.

Riding here means the Military Road, the B6318, which hugs the line of the Wall between Haltwhistle and Housesteads and gives a roller-coaster ride of dips and crests. It is a fast road with limited visibility on some crests, so keep your speed down, particularly in summer when walkers and cars cross it. Cattle and sheep graze beside it, and in winter it can be icy. A car park near Cawfields charges a fee and has toilets, and there is usually a small van selling coffee in high season.

Haltwhistle, under three kilometres away, has fuel and shops, and Hexham is the larger town about twenty-two kilometres east. Bring a waterproof, because the exposed ridge makes its own weather, and in a bad wind you will want to turn back before you reach the crest. Dusk brings out the barn owls over the fields, and the stone of the Wall turns golden. The Twice Brewed pub and the Vindolanda site, a little further east, make a good end to the day.
t.stones of stenness@59.0,-3.2:
At the southern end of the narrow neck of land between Loch Harray and Loch Stenness, four tall stones stand against the sky. They are all that is left of a circle that may have had twelve, laid out around 3000 BC, which makes it among the oldest stone circles in Britain. The tallest stone is over five metres, thin as a blade, cut from the local flagstone that splits into slabs, and the whole group has the stern, upright look of something that has stood a long time in the wind. Inside the circle are traces of a central hearth, and archaeologists have found bones of cattle from feasts.

The Watchstone, a single standing stone beside the causeway to the north, adds to the sense of a landscape arranged on purpose. Stenness and its neighbours are part of a ritual landscape that includes Maeshowe, about a mile east, and the Ring of Brogar further along the isthmus, and it seems that people travelled here from across the islands for ceremonies. In later centuries, local stories grew up around the stones. Some claimed that couples joined hands through a hole in one stone, now gone, to swear oaths, and one farmer in the nineteenth century smashed one stone and toppled another, and the local outrage was enough to stop him.

Riding to the circle is easy. The B9055 leaves the main road and runs beside the loch, flat and quiet, with a gravel pull-in beside the stones. The sky here is enormous and the wind stronger than you expect, so take care with your parking on soft ground and use a pad under the side stand. The stones are open, free to visit at any time, and the grass is cropped by sheep. Light in the evenings from May to August is spectacular, long and low, with colours on the water.

Stromness, about six kilometres away, has fuel, shops and a good harbour front with cafes, and Kirkwall, the main town, is further east. The Stenness area itself has a visitor centre for Maeshowe and a few places for a snack. Take a layer, because the lochside is often cool and breezy even on a bright day, and be prepared for brief showers that pass quickly. Birds are everywhere, with swans on the loch, curlews in the fields and oystercatchers calling over the grass.
t.maes howe@59.0,-3.2:
Maeshowe is a grass-covered mound in a field beside Loch Harray, about thirty-five metres across and encircled by a ditch, and inside it is the finest chambered tomb in northern Europe. Built around 2800 BC, it is entered by a long, low passage of huge single slabs, aligned so that around midwinter the setting sun shines straight down it and lights the back wall. The chamber itself is high and square, with corbelled walls that narrow towards the roof and side cells where the bones of the dead were laid. The precision of the masonry, with no mortar, is astonishing, and the stone slabs in the passage weigh several tonnes.

In the twelfth century, Norse crusaders broke in through the roof and sheltered inside from a storm, and they carved runic graffiti on the walls, the largest collection of Viking runes outside Scandinavia. Some are boasts about treasure, some are ordinary names, and one is a crude drawing of a dragon-like beast. The inscriptions link to the Orkneyinga Saga, the history of the earls of Orkney, and a few mention a hoard that, if it was ever there, had gone by the time modern archaeologists arrived in 1861.

Visiting is strictly regulated. You must book a timed ticket in advance through Historic Environment Scotland, and the tour begins at the visitor centre in Stenness, with a short shuttle or walk to the mound. Check the current arrangements, because they have changed in recent years. The passage is low, so you stoop, and the guides tell the story with warmth and humour. Midwinter is the most famous time, but the stone and the lamplight are impressive at any season.

Riding in is simple, on the A965 and B9055 along the loch, and bikes are easily parked at the visitor centre. The roads are quiet and well made, though wind is a constant factor and sheep sometimes wander. Stromness, a little over seven kilometres away, is the nearest place for fuel and a proper lunch, with the pier and the Pier Arts Centre. The bakeries sell the Orkney fudge and bere bannocks, a flat bread made from local barley. Late in the day, as the sun drops over the loch, the mound looks like a swelling of the earth itself.
t.ring of brogar@59.0,-3.2:
The Ring of Brogar is a perfect circle of standing stones on a flat spit of heather between the Loch of Stenness and the Loch of Harray, about a hundred and four metres across, ringed by a rock-cut ditch. Sixty stones are thought to have stood here originally, and twenty-seven remain, some of them toppled or broken, with the tallest about four and a half metres high. It was built perhaps four and a half thousand years ago, probably a little later than Stenness, and nobody knows precisely what it was for. The suggestions range from astronomy to gathering, and standing in the middle you can believe any of them.

The setting is the glory. The ring sits on an open peninsula called the Ness of Brodgar, with water on both sides and low hills in the distance, and you see it from the road long before you arrive. Lichens in grey, orange and pale green cover the stones, and many have been split by lightning, which has struck the circle repeatedly. Around it, burial mounds from the Bronze Age rise out of the heather, and the Ness of Brodgar has a scatter of mounds and a site excavated in recent years that revealed a large Neolithic building. Wind rattles the grass and the clouds move fast.

t.haltwhistle burn 4 roman temporary camp@:

When Hadrian's Wall was built a little to the north, the older forts gradually lost their purpose. The ground around is rich in history of other kinds. t.islamic tombs@24.9,118.6:

t.statue of lao tze@24.9,118.6:

t.the old city@24.9,118.6:

t.whistler@50.1,-123.0:

t.alicante@38.4,-0.5:

t.barranc del sord abric ii@38.7,-0.2:

t.john o groats@58.6,-3.1:

t.mcbride@53.3,-120.2:

t.vancouver british columbia@50.0,-122.7:

t.eastern qing tombs@40.2,117.6:

t.rannoch moor@56.7,-4.8:

The road itself is open and rolling, good for a relaxed pace but not for racing.
