The weather can change in minutes, and a day that starts in sunshine can end with horizontal rain, so a waterproof layer should live in the top box. In clear, still light, especially in the evening in late summer, the pools turn into mirrors and the whole moor glows.

A railway was built across the moor in the 1890s, floated on a raft of tree roots, brushwood and thousands of tonnes of earth because the peat swallowed ordinary foundations. The West Highland Line still runs this way, with a lonely station at Rannoch that has become a minor cult destination among walkers. The old drove roads and the West Highland Way also cross the moor, and you will often see walkers with huge packs trudging beside the A82.

Practical points matter here. Cafes are few, and in the colder months can be closed, so carry water and something to eat. Midges are a summer plague in still, damp weather, so leave the helmet visor shut when you stop. In winter, ice and snow can close or slow the road quickly, and the A82 across the moor is one of the first to feel it.
t.grantown on spey@57.3,-3.6:
Grantown-on-Spey was a planned town, founded in 1765 by Sir James Grant of Grant, who wanted a tidy settlement for weavers and a base for his estate. The pin lands in the centre of the town, on the river Spey in the Cairngorms National Park, with a wide main street, grey granite buildings and a neat square. It is the end of the Snow Roads, and it is a good one.

The ride that finishes here, from Blairgowrie over the Cairnwell, the Lecht and Tomintoul, covers some of the highest public roads in Britain. The A93 climbs to over six hundred metres at the Cairnwell, the highest main road in the country, and the A939 crosses the Lecht, with bleak moorland, heather and, in winter, deep snow. Snow gates close the roads in bad weather, so check conditions in the colder months. The surface is mostly good, the bends are open, and the views stretch for miles. Wind and rain can arrive suddenly, so bring layers even in summer.

Grantown is the heart of Strathspey, and the landscape around is a mixture of pine forest, moor and river. Ospreys nest at Loch Garten nearby, and red squirrels, capercaillie and crested tits live in the old Caledonian pinewood of Abernethy. The Spey itself, Scotland's second-longest river, runs fast and clear, and is famous for its salmon. This is also whisky country: the Speyside distilleries, including Cragganmore and The Glenlivet, are within a short ride, and the area produces a large share of Scotland's malt.

Fuel is available in Grantown, which has a few thousand people, and it is wise to fill up here before heading anywhere else, because the next big towns, Aviemore and Forres, are twenty and thirty kilometres away. The town has several cafes, bakeries and hotels, and a bowl of hot soup after the Lecht is a pleasure.

Walk down the main street in the late afternoon, when the light on the granite turns warm, and feel the quiet that has settled over the moor.
t.dunrobin castle@58.0,-3.9:
Dunrobin Castle stands on the shore of the Moray Firth just north of Golspie, and it is one of the most surprising buildings in Scotland, a fairy-tale pile of turrets and pinnacles that looks more like a French château than a Highland fortress. The seat of the Earls and later Dukes of Sutherland, it began as a medieval keep and was rebuilt in the 1840s in the Scottish baronial style by Sir Charles Barry, the architect of the Houses of Parliament. There are around 189 rooms, formal gardens that descend toward the sea, and a falconry display in summer. The castle even has its own railway halt, though trains stop there only occasionally.

It is also a place with a darker history. The Sutherland family owned vast estates, and in the early nineteenth century they cleared thousands of tenants from the glens of the interior to make way for sheep, in one of the most notorious episodes of the Highland Clearances. People were moved to the coast or forced to emigrate, and the memory is bitter. On the hill above Golspie stands a tall monument to the first Duke, visible for miles, which has been the subject of repeated calls for its removal. It is worth knowing the story as you ride past.

As the end of a ride from Durness, along the north coast, it makes a good finish. The route comes down the east coast on the A9, a road of fast, flowing bends along the sea cliffs, with views over the North Sea, past Helmsdale and Brora, and the traffic can be heavy with caravans and lorries in summer. Golspie, a village of about fourteen hundred, has a few shops, a café and a few other services, but treat fuel as something to sort out in advance, and top up in Brora or Dornoch, or anywhere along the A9 when you see a pump.

The weather is changeable, with rain and sea mist at any time, though long summer evenings give wonderful light, and the sun does not set until late. Midges come out on still evenings. The castle opens from spring to autumn and closes in winter, so check the dates, and the gardens are a pleasant place for a quiet walk after a long day on the road.
t.loch ness@57.3,-4.4:
There is nothing more mythical in Scotland than the great dark stretch of water at the end of this ride, and nothing quite so crowded in summer. Loch Ness fills the Great Glen, the geological fault line that slices Scotland in two from Fort William to Inverness, and it runs for about thirty-six kilometres. It is deep, cold and peaty brown, and holds more fresh water than all the lakes in England and Wales put together.

The coordinates fall on the north-west shore, near Drumnadrochit, a small village with a few cafes, shops and a pair of Nessie exhibitions that poke gentle fun at the whole business. The monster story goes back at least as far as the sixth century, when Saint Columba is said to have faced down a beast in the River Ness. Whatever you believe, the loch itself needs no monster to be impressive. Nearby Urquhart Castle, a ruin on a headland above the water, has been fought over for centuries and gives you the classic view down the glen.

The road is the A82, and it is busy. Coach parties, campervans and lorries share it, and the stretch along the north shore is winding and narrow in places, with plenty of blind bends and short overtaking opportunities. Treat it as a road for steady cruising, not racing. Weather matters here, as low cloud and drizzle can blot out the hills, though when the sun does break through the loch is dazzling and the birch woods along the shore turn bright gold in October.

Midges will find you from late spring to early autumn if you stop near the water on a still evening, so keep moving or wear a net. The bigger town of Inverness is about twenty-one kilometres to the north-east and has plenty of fuel, while Drumnadrochit has a pump or two on the main road if you are in a hurry.

Finishing here after a day from Rannoch Moor and Glencoe feels right: the landscape softens, the hills drop away and the great glen opens like a long final chord.
t.glasgow@55.9,-4.3:
Glasgow starts the A82 journey, and it is a city that deserves a look before you leave. The pin lands a little north of the centre, in the district of Cowcaddens and Garnethill, with the old tenements and the Mackintosh-designed art school on the hill. The Clyde, which built the city's wealth through shipbuilding, runs through the south, and the cathedral and Necropolis, a Victorian cemetery on a hill, lie to the east.

The ride north starts with an urban crawl and then, quite quickly, the world opens. The A82 follows the western shore of Loch Lomond, a narrow, winding road with bends and rock walls and slow traffic in summer, then climbs to Crianlarich and Tyndrum, crosses the bleak expanse of Rannoch Moor and drops into Glencoe, one of the grandest valleys in Scotland. The surface is mostly good, but wet weather is frequent, and the road can be busy with coaches and caravans. Early starts are the key.

Glasgow itself is a friendly, direct city with a lively music scene and a long industrial past. The Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, a red sandstone building in the west end, is one of the finest collections in Britain, and its free entry makes it a good stop. The city's food has improved greatly, and the old curry houses of the Pollokshields area are famous.

Fuel is no problem in the city, with stations on every major road, and it is wise to fill the tank before leaving, as stations become scarcer north of Loch Lomond. Tarbet, Crianlarich and Tyndrum have fuel and food, but the long section across Rannoch Moor has none.

Have a proper breakfast before setting off. A Glasgow breakfast, with square sausage and tattie scones, is worth the extra time, and the road will wait. Rain is likely at some point on this road, so a dry layer in the top box is better than hope, and Glencoe in mist can be as moving as in sun.
t.loch lomond@56.1,-4.6:
Loch Lomond is the largest lake in Great Britain by surface area, and its character changes sharply from south to north. In the south, around Balloch and Luss, it is wide and dotted with wooded islands; to the north it narrows into a long, steep-sided, Highland fjord overlooked by Ben Lomond. The loch lies inside the Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park, Scotland's first, created in 2002. Helensburgh, Balloch and Garelochhead are the nearest towns.

There is a geological point worth knowing. The Highland Boundary Fault crosses the loch here, and the chain of islands such as Inchcailloch follows it, which is why the south feels like Lowland Scotland and the north like the Highlands. The old song about the bonnie, bonnie banks has made the place famous well beyond Scotland, and walkers from Glasgow have been heading up Ben Lomond for generations.

The riding on the west shore is by the A82, and honestly it is a difficult road. It is narrow, twisty and busy, with several stretches where the limit drops and where the loch is hidden behind trees. It is a road to take at a measured pace, enjoying glimpses of water through the oaks rather than pushing for time. Coaches and campervans often slow the traffic, and Friday evenings and sunny Sundays can be congested. Early mornings are far better, with mist on the water and the road to yourself.

The woods here are old oak, birch and hazel, rich in ferns and mosses thanks to the damp Atlantic climate. Red deer and feral goats live on the hills. Luss is a pretty conservation village of stone cottages on the shore, handy for a coffee.

For fuel, Helensburgh and the towns of the Vale of Leven are the safest options, so fill up before you start the long northward run toward Tarbet and Crianlarich. Beyond Tarbet the road climbs toward Glen Falloch and the real Highlands, and fuel stops become much further apart, so plan accordingly.
t.whistler food@50.1,-123.0:
Whistler is a village built for pleasure in an old logging valley, and it knows it. The pedestrian village at the foot of Whistler and Blackcomb mountains, with its cobbled lanes, hotels and rows of restaurants, was planned in the late 1970s and took off when the two ski areas were developed, and then hit the world stage when the Winter Olympics came here in 2010. The Peak 2 Peak gondola, which links the two mountains across a deep valley, opened in 2008 and holds records for its span and height. In summer the ski slopes become mountain bike parks, and in winter the village is packed with skiers from around the world.

The food is the reason to pause. Whistler has a good reputation for its restaurants, from cheap noodle bars to expensive tasting menus, and a rider coming from Vancouver or Pemberton will have no trouble finding a plate. Bakeries and coffee shops line the village stroll, and the local craft breweries, such as the ones in the village, are a popular stop at the end of the day. The village's atmosphere is lively and international, with young people from around the world working a season. Prices are high, so it is not the cheapest meal on the route.

For a rider, Whistler is the midpoint of the Sea to Sky Highway, about a hundred and twenty kilometres from Vancouver, and the pivot of the ride. North of the village, the highway runs through the Pemberton valley, flat and fertile, with farms and potato fields, and then, at Pemberton, the road to Duffey Lake turns east and climbs into the mountains. The valley is also home to several lakes, including Green Lake and Alta Lake, where people swim and paddle in summer. The Whistler area has dozens of kilometres of paved lakeside trail, which is closed to motor vehicles.

Black bears are common around the village, particularly in spring and autumn, and they can be seen in the meadows or even on the roadside, so keep a distance. Fuel is available at several stations on the highway at Function Junction and in the village area, but the best time to fill the tank is before heading north toward Pemberton. The best months are June to September, when the roads are dry and the sun is warm, though thunderstorms can come in the afternoon. Winter brings snow and heavy traffic on the highway.
t.duffey lake road@50.4,-122.5:
The Duffey Lake Road is the part of British Columbia's Highway 99 that nobody forgets. It leaves Pemberton, in a flat green valley of farms and potato fields, and in less than an hour climbs into the Coast Mountains and drops into the dry interior, one of the sharpest changes of landscape in Canada. The road crosses Cayoosh Pass, a little over a thousand metres, and passes the shores of Duffey Lake, a long, green, glacier-fed water beneath towering peaks, and the trailheads for Joffre Lakes, three tiers of turquoise lakes beneath a glacier that have become some of the most popular walks in the province.

The riding is serious. From Pemberton the road rises through dense rainforest along the Lillooet River in a series of bends and straights, then climbs steeply in hairpins over Mount Currie, with gradients up to thirteen per cent in places. The descent on the east side, down Cayoosh Creek toward Lillooet, is even more demanding, with tight bends, loose gravel in places and long drops without guardrails. The road is paved but narrow, and logging trucks, RVs and tour coaches share it, so overtaking is hard and the pace is set by the slowest vehicle. Braking is the thing to watch on the long downhill, so use engine braking. The pavement can be damp or icy in shaded corners, even in summer in the early morning.

The scenery changes as you cross. West of the pass the forest is wet, with ferns and moss, while the east side is dry, with ponderosa pine, sagebrush and red rock, a rain-shadow landscape. Lillooet, at the end of the road, was the starting point, Mile 0, of the Cariboo Wagon Road in the gold-rush years of the 1860s, and the dry hills above the Fraser River hold some of the hottest weather in Canada in summer.

Fuel is the point to plan. There are no stations between Pemberton and Lillooet, a distance of around a hundred and thirty kilometres, and the road is slow, so fill the tank in Pemberton. Black bears and mountain goats are often seen, and there are few places to stop. The road can close for snow or slides in winter, and the pass can be icy from October. The best time is July to September, when the road is dry, but go early to avoid the crowds at Joffre Lakes.
t.almeria@36.8,-2.5:
Almería has a dry, bright, slightly North African feel that makes it unlike most Spanish cities, and the reason is simple: it gets less rain than almost anywhere in Europe. The city lies on a wide bay with the arid Sierra Alhamilla behind it, and the whole landscape is in shades of sand, ochre and pale grey. In summer it is hot and bright, in winter it is gentle, and the sea breeze keeps the air moving.

The great landmark is the Alcazaba, a huge Moorish fortress begun in the tenth century under Abd al-Rahman III, when Almería was one of the most important ports and silk centres of al-Andalus. Its walls climb the hill above the old town, enclosing gardens and ruined palaces, and the view across the bay is superb. The cathedral looks more like a fortress than a church, with thick walls and corner towers, because pirates raided this coast for centuries. Underneath the old town, a network of civil war air-raid shelters stretches for several kilometres and can be visited on a guided tour. If you stop for a drink, you may find a free tapa arrives with it, a local tradition that makes the city very kind to tight budgets.

For riders, Almería is the start of two quite different adventures. To the north, the Tabernas Desert is Europe's only true desert landscape, with eroded badlands and scorched canyons where spaghetti westerns were filmed in the sixties, and the roads there are fast and sweeping, with big views and little shade. To the east, the Cabo de Gata natural park offers volcanic headlands, empty beaches and white villages, with winding coastal roads. Fuel is straightforward in a city of nearly two hundred thousand, and you will want a full tank before heading into either area, since stations get sparse in the desert.

Carry plenty of water and start early, as summer heat here is relentless. The light in the morning and again late in the day turns the hills a warm gold, and that is when the place looks its absolute best.
t.tholos of el romeral@37.0,-4.5:
Just outside Antequera, a low grassy mound hides one of Europe's more unusual prehistoric chambers. The Tholos of El Romeral is a Bronze Age burial, roughly four thousand years old, built from carefully fitted stone slabs that rise in a corbelled dome above a long entrance corridor. Unlike its neighbours, the huge Neolithic dolmens of Menga and Viera, it uses a dry-stone technique closer to what you find in the eastern Mediterranean, so archaeologists argue about where the builders learned it. All three belong to the Antequera Dolmens Site, listed by UNESCO in 2016 partly because the landscape itself seems to be part of the design.

That landscape deserves a look. To the north-east rises the Peña de los Enamorados, the Lovers' Rock, a limestone crag whose profile looks like a face staring at the sky, and the monuments were built to align with it. The legend says a Christian girl and a Moorish boy leapt from the top rather than be parted. To the south lie the strange karst blocks of El Torcal, wind-carved limestone that looks like stacked plates. The plain between is farmland, olive and cereal, with a long, flat horizon.

The roads on this day out are mostly smooth, open and quick, with the occasional hill and curve as you come toward the Peña. Antequera itself has about forty-five thousand people, so it is a good place to fuel, and the town is known for its bread, molletes, and porra antequerana, a thick cold tomato soup, as well as its convents and baroque churches. Heat in summer is severe, often above forty, so choose the early morning or late afternoon. Spring brings green wheat and poppies, and winter days can be clear and cold.

The tholos site is small, and visits are free of drama, usually a short walk across a gravel car park and a dim entry corridor. Check opening times before you go, because the closing days can be awkward, and the dolmens at Menga and Viera sit a few kilometres away on the other side of town. Spend a few minutes inside, feel the temperature drop, and then ride back toward the sunlight.
t.blairgowrie@56.6,-3.3:
Blairgowrie is where the Perthshire farmland ends and the Highlands begin to show their hand. The town sits on the River Ericht, which comes tumbling out of Glenshee and, in the old days, turned the wheels of dozens of jute and flax mills; the stone mill buildings still line the river. Behind it the hills close in, and in front lies Strathmore, a broad, red-soiled plain that grows most of Scotland's raspberries. In July the fields are full of pickers, and you can smell the fruit from the road with your visor up.

Two odd things are within easy reach. Six miles south at Meikleour stands a beech hedge, planted in 1745, that is recognised as the tallest in the world and about as high as a six-storey building. It runs along the A93 for a third of a mile and is trimmed by crews on platforms only every ten years or so. North of town begins the A93 itself, the road that matters: up through Bridge of Cally, the Spittal of Glenshee and over the Cairnwell, one of the highest main roads in Britain, with the ski tows right beside the tarmac. Beyond is Braemar and Royal Deeside. The first miles run through wooded gorge and then open moorland, and the surface is generally good with a few frost heaves.

This is the start of the Snow Roads route, which links Blairgowrie to Grantown-on-Spey over the high ground of the Cairngorms National Park. In winter the Cairnwell section can close in snow, and gates are used, so check before a spring or autumn start. Even in May there can be snow on the verges. The weather up there changes fast; set off in sunshine and you can be wearing everything you own by the top.

You are in a town of almost nine thousand, which means fuel, shops and a good bakery or two on the high street. Fill up properly here. After Blairgowrie the next regular pumps on this road are a long way along, and the hills do not let you coast. Leave early and the glen will be quiet, with deer on the lower slopes and the occasional pheasant too dim to leave the tarmac.
t.zhenfu lou@24.6,116.9:
Hakka families in the hills of western Fujian built their homes as fortresses. The tulou, or earth buildings, are huge round or square dwellings with thick rammed-earth walls, sometimes three or four storeys tall, with a single gate and a courtyard in the middle where a whole clan once lived, shared a well, kept animals and worshipped ancestors. UNESCO listed a set of them in 2008, and the Hongkeng area near Yongding holds some of the best, with dozens of buildings scattered among tobacco fields, tea bushes and bamboo. Zhenfu Lou belongs to that cluster, a round tulou of the early twentieth century, and it stands out for the way its builders mixed traditional Chinese construction with Western decoration, including arched windows and columns inside.

The reason for such buildings is protection. Hakka people, a name that means guest families, migrated south from central China over many centuries and often settled on land that locals did not want, in mountains where bandits and feuds were common. A tulou could be defended, and if there was a siege the household had a well and grain stores inside. Today the walls are warm brown, streaked with age, and the roofs sweep outward in broad grey tiles. Some are still lived in, and you may see laundry hanging from the galleries and old men playing cards by the gate.

I cannot give much detail about riding conditions here. This is mountain country, with narrow roads that climb and fall between villages, bamboo groves and terraces. Surfaces in the county are usually paved, but landslides after heavy summer rain are common, and fog can settle in the valleys. Riding in mainland China with a foreign motorcycle is a complicated matter for visitors, requiring local licences, registration and often a guide, so plan well ahead and check current rules.

Yongding, the county seat, has the shops, fuel stations and guesthouses, and the villages near the tulou have simple restaurants where you can eat dishes like Hakka stuffed tofu, braised pork with preserved vegetables, and rice wine. Spring and autumn are comfortable, while summers are hot and wet, and winter mornings can be chilly in the damp hills.
t.drumnadrochit@57.3,-4.5:
Drumnadrochit is the village that Loch Ness made famous, and it is a place that has learned to live with its monster. It sits on the north-west shore, where Glen Urquhart opens out from the hills and meets the loch, about twenty kilometres from Inverness along the A82. The village has the practical things a rider needs, including fuel, shops, cafes and pubs, along with a couple of exhibitions devoted to Nessie, which treat the subject with varying amounts of seriousness. The first recorded report of a creature in the river Ness comes from a biography of St Columba written in the seventh century, which describes him telling a monster to turn back, and the modern fascination dates from the 1930s.

The loch is the real draw, and it is enormous. Loch Ness is about thirty-seven kilometres long and holds more water than all the lakes in England and Wales combined, with a depth of over two hundred metres in places. The water is dark with peat, which is why you can see nothing beneath the surface. A mile or two south of the village stand the ruins of Urquhart Castle, on a rocky headland above the water. It was fought over in the wars between Scotland and England, and in the end blown up by its own garrison in 1692 to keep it from Jacobite hands. It makes one of the most photographed ruins in Scotland.

The riding from here has options. The A82 along the loch is wide and quick but busy in summer with coaches, caravans and camper vans, so patience is useful. A better choice is to turn off west on the A831 to Cannich and onward to Glen Affric, a long glen of pine forest, lochs and mountains that many call the most beautiful in Scotland. The road narrows and twists, passing through remnants of the old Caledonian forest, and there are red deer, red squirrels and, with luck, golden eagles overhead. The surface is mostly good but narrow, with passing places on the upper sections.

Weather is quick to change, and a mild morning can become a cold wet afternoon without much warning. Midges are a fact of life from midsummer into early autumn, so carry a repellent. Beauly and Muir of Ord, a short ride north-east, have more shops and fuel, while Inverness has everything.

For a coffee, the village offers several options, and an early start gets you ahead of the coach tours.
t.dumfries@55.1,-3.6:
Dumfries calls itself the Queen of the South, and its great claim to fame is a poet. Robert Burns spent the last five years of his life here, from 1791 to 1796, working as an excise officer and writing some of his best songs, including A Man's a Man for A' That. He died in the town at the age of thirty-seven, and the house where he lived, in a street now named after him, is a small museum with his desk and letters. His mausoleum, a domed Greek temple in St Michael's churchyard, draws pilgrims on Burns Night every January.

The River Nith runs through the middle of the town, spanned by a medieval bridge, the Devorgilla, built in the fifteenth century and named for a lady who founded Balliol College, with a mill and weir beside it. Dumfries is a market town and the capital of the southwest of Scotland, with red sandstone buildings, an elegant main square and a long history of border conflict. J. M. Barrie, the creator of Peter Pan, went to school at Dumfries Academy, and he later said that the idea for Neverland grew out of games played in the town's gardens.

The South West Coastal 300, a long route around the Galloway coast, passes here. For riders, the roads that lead from the town are among the best in southern Scotland: the A710 coast road to the Solway shore, the quiet lanes through the Galloway hills, and the road toward Moffat and the Southern Uplands all offer gentle curves, long views and little traffic. The surface is variable, with some patched sections, and sheep wander freely on the open moors, so keep your speed under control.

Dumfries has plentiful fuel, supermarkets, pubs and cafes, and it is the main service town for the region. Locharbriggs, Lochmaben and the smaller villages around have fewer services. The best months are May to September, with long light evenings, though Scottish weather can change fast, and rain should always be expected. Midges can be a nuisance in damp, still weather. In winter, ice on the hill roads makes riding unwise. The Solway tides are among the fastest in Britain, so keep clear of the mudflats.
t.alnwick@55.4,-1.7:
Alnwick, pronounced Annick, is the town of a great castle and a great bookshop, and the combination seems entirely right. The castle, seat of the Percy family, the Dukes of Northumberland, for seven centuries, is the second-largest inhabited castle in England, with massive walls and towers above the River Aln. It has stood in for Hogwarts in the Harry Potter films and appeared in Downton Abbey, but its real history is of border wars with the Scots, and Hotspur, Henry Percy, the hot-tempered knight of Shakespeare's plays, was of this house.

The town below is a handsome market place of stone buildings, narrow lanes called wynds, and an old gateway, Bondgate Tower. The Alnwick Garden, created by the present duchess, has cascades, a treehouse restaurant and a poison garden with deadly plants. And Barter Books, in the old Victorian railway station, is a huge secondhand bookshop with open fires and model trains running overhead, where in 2000 the owners found a copy of the wartime poster Keep Calm and Carry On in a box of old books, sparking a worldwide craze.

The roads around are the draw for riders. The A1068 runs along the coast through Alnmouth, Warkworth and Amble, with views of dunes, castles and the North Sea, while the inland routes toward Rothbury and the Cheviot Hills are more twisting, over moorland with big skies. The Northumberland 250 route passes through. Traffic is light, apart from summer weekends at the castle, and the surface is generally good, though some of the hill roads are narrow and patched.

Alnwick has fuel, supermarkets, pubs and cafes, and it is the best base for the area. Shilbottle and Lesbury, nearby, are small. The best months are May to September, with long days, though the North Sea coast can be cool and misty, and sea fog, called a haar, rolls in without warning. Autumn is crisp and bright. In winter, snow closes the high roads, so choose your season. Sheep on the road are common, and the speed limits on moorland roads are strictly enforced.
t.braemar@57.0,-3.4:
Braemar is the kind of Highland village where the cold is part of the identity. It sits at about three hundred and thirty metres in the upper valley of the River Dee, ringed by the Cairngorm hills, and it holds a record for the lowest temperature ever measured in Britain, shared with another Highland site: minus 27.2 degrees Celsius, in 1895. Even in summer a night here can be frosty. By day, in good weather, the village is a pleasant cluster of grey stone buildings with a small castle, a few cafés and shops, and a steady stream of walkers heading for the hills.

The village is also famous for the Braemar Gathering, a Highland games held on the first Saturday of September, with caber tossing, hill racing, piping and dancing, which members of the royal family traditionally attend, since Balmoral Castle lies about fifteen kilometres down the valley. Braemar Castle, a seventeenth-century fortress later used as a Hanoverian garrison after the Jacobite risings, stands just outside the village, and it is run by the local community.

The riding is a main reason to come. From the south, the A93 climbs from Blairgowrie over the Glenshee pass, which at 665 metres is the highest main road in Britain, and descends into Braemar through a wild upland landscape of heather, grouse moor and bare hills. It is a fine road, with wide, open bends and good surface, but the weather can be fierce. Snow can come as early as October and as late as May, and the road is often closed in winter, with gates at both ends. In summer, the heather turns purple in August, and the long days mean you can ride into the evening. Watch for sheep, deer and slow-moving campervans.

Down the valley, the A93 follows the Dee through pine forest towards Ballater, with the river on one side and the Cairngorm foothills on the other. It is a lovely road, with a mix of open stretches and gentle bends, and you may see red deer, red squirrels and even golden eagles. Beyond the village, a narrow road runs to the Linn of Dee, where the river is squeezed through a rocky gorge, a good place for a short walk.

Braemar has a few cafés, a bakery, small hotels and some shops, and there is normally a small filling station, but it is wise not to rely on it. Ballater, about twenty-two kilometres to the east, is the nearest sure option. A hot drink and a slice of cake at a village café is the best response to the weather.
t.lecht pass@57.2,-3.2:
The Lecht is a bare, high saddle on the A939 between Tomintoul and Corgarff, and it has one of the stiffest gradients on the public roads of the Scottish Highlands. Signs warn of a slope of one in five on the approach, which means rising a metre for every five you travel. The summit, at 637 metres, is a wide, windswept moor with a small ski centre, fenced runs of snow and a few lonely buildings. Even in July the wind can cut through a jacket, and the temperature is often well below that of the valleys.

The road is old. It follows the line of a military road built after the Jacobite rising of 1745 to link the garrison at Corgarff with the north, part of a network that the government constructed to keep the Highlands under control. Corgarff Castle, a tower house later surrounded by a star-shaped wall, was used as a barracks, and it still stands near the road on the south side, a few kilometres from the pass. Nearby, the ruins of old iron and manganese workings at the Lecht mine recall the days when this empty land was a place of industry.

From a rider's point of view, the Lecht is an exciting stretch, though a short one. The climb from Tomintoul is steady, with long, open curves and a smooth surface, and the descent toward Corgarff is steeper and more twisting, with a couple of tight bends and a long straight at the bottom. Expect sheep on the road, and the occasional cyclist labouring up the climb. The road is on the Snow Roads route, and it is one of the first to close when winter comes, with snow gates at the bottom, so check conditions before you set out between November and April.

The land around is open moorland of heather and peat, with grouse and mountain hares, and, in the distance, the long, rounded shapes of the Cromdale hills. In late summer, the heather turns the hills purple, and the light on the moor is often wonderful in the evening. At the ski centre, a café sometimes opens in season, but you should not count on it.

Tomintoul has some services, but for a sure fill, head to Ballater, about twenty-one kilometres east, or Grantown-on-Spey. Bring warm layers and waterproofs, and check the forecast before you commit.
t.tomintoul@57.3,-3.4:
Tomintoul likes to call itself the highest village in the Highlands, and at around three hundred and fifty metres, it is certainly high enough that the winters bite. It sits on the edge of the Cromdale hills, between Speyside and the Cairngorms, in a wide, bare landscape of heather moor and rolling hills. The village was laid out in 1775 by the Duke of Gordon as a planned settlement, with a wide main street and a central square, and the plan can still be traced in its long, straight shape. It is neat, grey and rather windswept, and it has a certain stubborn charm.

The area around it is whisky country. The Glenlivet valley lies just to the south-west, where George Smith's distillery, licensed in 1824, was one of the first legal producers after a long period of illicit distilling, when smugglers hid stills in the hills and bribed or dodged the excisemen. The valley still has the feel of a quiet, secret place. Several distilleries in the district welcome visitors, and the Speyside Way, a long-distance footpath, has a spur that ends at Tomintoul. The area is also a designated Dark Sky Park, and on a clear, moonless night the stars are extraordinary.

The roads around Tomintoul are some of the best in Scotland. The A939 runs north to Grantown-on-Spey over moorland, and south over the Lecht toward Ballater and Deeside, with long, open bends, high views and surprisingly little traffic. The surface is usually good, though the weather can turn quickly. In winter, snow and ice make the road hazardous, and snow gates close it, so check before you ride from late autumn to spring. Summer brings the heather, and the evening light is soft and long. Watch for sheep, deer and the occasional tractor.

The countryside is a mix of high moor, small farms and pockets of birch and pine, with the River Avon, pronounced A'an, flowing through a deep glen close by. Wildlife includes red grouse, curlew, lapwing, red deer and, with luck, the odd golden eagle. The air is thin and clean, and smells of peat and heather.

Tomintoul has a few shops, cafés, small hotels and a small visitor centre, and a fuel pump has historically been available, though hours can be limited, so do not rely on it. Grantown-on-Spey, about sixteen kilometres north, is the safer place to fill up. A bowl of soup and a cup of tea at one of the village cafés is a good plan for a cold day, and a dram of local whisky, preferably after the ride, is almost obligatory.
t.abrigo de la rambla de pedro izquierdo@3:
A rambla is a dry riverbed that only runs after storms, and the Rambla de Pedro Izquierdo is one of many that cut into the limestone hills around Nerpio, in the remote south-western corner of Albacete. In a rock shelter above it, prehistoric people left paintings in the Levantine style, small, lively figures of people and animals, and the site is one of the many shelters around Nerpio that belong to the UNESCO-listed Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. Visits are normally arranged through the village, and a guide will know which shelters are accessible and when the light is right for seeing the faded pigment.

Nerpio lies in the valley of the Taibilla, a river whose water is famous across south-east Spain: the Mancomunidad de los Canales del Taibilla was set up to carry it to Cartagena and the Murcia coast. Up here, though, it is a clear mountain stream lined with poplars and walnut orchards, and the village is known for its walnuts, gathered in autumn from old trees that shade the terraces. Above the valley rise the Sierra de Taibilla and the Sierra de las Cabras, with pine forests, cliffs and griffon vultures circling on thermals.

The roads in and out of Nerpio are what bring riders back. From Moratalla in the south, from Yeste in the north or from Letur in the east, each approach twists through gorges and over passes, with long stretches where you will see nobody at all. Surfaces vary, and rockfall, gravel and goats are routine hazards, so ride with margin.

The practical side is simple: Nerpio is small, and fuel is limited, so arrive with a decent tank, ideally filled in Moratalla or Caravaca. The village bars serve hearty food, from gazpacho manchego to lamb chops grilled over vine shoots. Summer is hot by day and cool by night, and in winter frost is common. The best seasons are spring, when the almond trees and broom bloom, and autumn, when the walnuts fall and the poplars along the river turn gold.
t.los grajos i@38.3,-1.4:
The painted women of Los Grajos are among the most famous figures in Spanish rock art. In a shelter in the limestone hills just outside Cieza, prehistoric painters depicted a group of human figures, several of them women with wide skirts and raised arms, often interpreted as dancers, alongside animals and other motifs. The Los Grajos shelters are part of the UNESCO-listed Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula, and they are protected, so visits need to be arranged with the local tourist office in Cieza.

Cieza sits on the Segura river in the north of Murcia, a town of about thirty-five thousand surrounded by a sea of fruit orchards. Every year, from late February to mid March, the peach, nectarine and apricot trees bloom, and the valley turns pink and white. The town's history goes deep: on a hill above it lies Medina Siyâsa, the ruins of an Islamic town abandoned in the thirteenth century, with excavated houses and streets, and finds displayed in the town museum.

The Segura valley between Cieza, Abarán and Blanca is a narrow oasis between dry, bare mountains. Abarán is known for its norias, huge water wheels that lift river water into irrigation channels, a technology that goes back to Islamic times. Blanca, below a castle on a rock, sits beside a dramatic bend of the river.

For riders, the area offers a mix of valley roads through orchards and climbs into dry, rugged hills with long views. Traffic is light outside the towns, and the surfaces are generally good. Summer heat is intense, so ride early, and look for shade and water. Cieza has fuel, shops, bars and restaurants. Try the local fruit in season, and dishes like zarangollo, scrambled eggs with courgette and onion, a Murcian classic, best eaten with bread on a shaded terrace while the afternoon heat passes. Riders heading on toward the Sierra del Segura will find the roads get steadily wilder and emptier beyond Calasparra.
t.las cazuelas@38.2,-2.0:
Moratalla is the kind of hill town that looks as though it was poured down a slope: white houses tumbling below a castle tower, narrow lanes too steep for comfort, church bells echoing off the hills. Ten kilometres out, in the rugged country of north-west Murcia, the shelter of Las Cazuelas holds prehistoric paintings, part of the region's contribution to the UNESCO-listed Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin. The paintings are fragile and protected, and access is usually by guided visit, arranged in Moratalla or through the regional authorities.

The landscape is a striking mix of irrigated valleys, almond and olive groves, pine forest and bare limestone ridges, rising toward the Sierra de Moratalla and the Sierra del Segura. In spring, the almond blossom and the green of the young wheat make a soft contrast to the grey rock, and in summer the hills are baked gold and the air smells of thyme and pine resin.

Caravaca de la Cruz, thirteen kilometres away, is one of the five holy cities of Christianity, recognised by the Vatican, because of a relic of the True Cross kept in its basilica-fortress. Every few years, Caravaca celebrates a holy year that draws pilgrims from all over Spain, and every May, the Caballos del Vino festival sees teams racing richly decorated horses up the hill to the castle. Cehegín, nearby, has a well-preserved old town of steep lanes and noble houses, built on the site of an older Iberian and Roman settlement, and it is far less visited than it deserves.

Riding around Moratalla is about tight, twisting roads with almost no traffic, climbing into the mountains toward Nerpio, El Sabinar and the Sierra del Segura. Surfaces are generally good but can be rough in places, and gravel on bends is common after rain. Moratalla has fuel, shops and bars, and Caravaca has more choice. Try the local migas, lamb, and wine from the nearby Bullas region, made largely from the dark Monastrell grape that thrives in this hot, dry country.
t.abrigo de rosser@39.2,-0.7:
Near Bicorp, in the dry, folded hills of inland Valencia, one of the most famous images in prehistoric art was found in 1920: a figure clinging to ropes on a cliff, reaching into a hole surrounded by bees, a honey gatherer painted thousands of years ago in the Cuevas de la Araña. The Abrigo de Rosser lies in the same rugged area of the Canal de Navarrés and the Júcar gorges, one of many shelters with Levantine paintings in this region, and together they form part of the UNESCO-listed Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin. Bicorp has a small interpretation centre, and guided visits to some shelters can be arranged.

The landscape is wild and empty. The villages of Bicorp, Quesa and Millares are small, each with a few hundred inhabitants, and surrounded by pine forests, scrub, cliffs and deep ravines. The Júcar river cuts through limestone gorges to the north, dammed in places to form long, turquoise reservoirs like the one at Cortes de Pallás. Further north, on the Turia, natural pools such as the Charco Azul near Chulilla draw swimmers in summer, and closer to hand the Júcar and its tributaries hide quieter spots known mainly to locals.

Riding here is a real pleasure. The roads are narrow, winding and often almost empty, climbing over ridges and dropping into gorges with views that stretch for miles. Surfaces vary from good to poor, and gravel, rockfall and wild animals can appear around any corner. Summer is hot and fire risk is high, while winter can bring cold winds.

The nearest larger town is Carlet, about eighteen kilometres away, with Xàtiva and Requena also within reach. The small villages have bars and simple restaurants serving local food like gazpacho, rice dishes, and roast meats. Plan your fuel stops carefully and carry water, especially in summer, when the hills shimmer in the heat. Spring is the kindest season, with the scrub in flower and the ravines still holding a little water.
t.sunny rigg 2 roman temporary camp@55.0,-:
Haltwhistle likes to call itself the centre of Britain, and whether or not you believe the measurements, it sits at the very heart of Hadrian's Wall country. Just outside the town, on a gentle slope called Sunny Rigg, the outlines of two Roman temporary camps have been traced, rectangular enclosures with rounded corners where units on the march, or building the wall, pitched their leather tents behind a bank and a ditch for a night or a season. They are part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage Site, though on the ground you will see only faint lines in the grass, best appreciated from the air or in low evening light.

North of Haltwhistle, the wall reaches its most dramatic stretch, riding the crags of the Whin Sill, a hard volcanic rock that forms steep cliffs facing north. Cawfields, Walltown Crags, Steel Rigg and Housesteads are all close, and the Roman Army Museum at Carvoran gives an excellent introduction. The famous Sycamore Gap tree, a landmark beside the wall, was illegally felled in 2023, an act that shocked the whole country; the gap remains, now without its tree.

The riding around here is a mix of busy and quiet. The A69 through the Tyne valley is fast and carries a lot of traffic, while the B6318 Military Road, a few miles north, rolls across open moorland on the line of the wall, with blind summits that demand care. Minor roads north into the Northumberland National Park and toward Kielder Forest are narrow and empty, with cattle grids, sheep and wide views.

Haltwhistle is a small market town with fuel, shops, pubs and cafés, and Hexham, about twenty-four kilometres east, is larger. The weather is changeable, with wind and rain common, so carry waterproofs. Late spring and early autumn offer the best combination of light, weather and quiet trails.
t.the vallum between the road to garthside:
Brampton is a small red sandstone market town at the edge of the Pennines, and just north of it, where the land rises toward the Irthing valley, a stretch of the vallum runs across the fields near Garthside. The vallum, the great ditch and banks that ran south of Hadrian's Wall, is often clearer than the wall itself in this area, because the stone of the wall was carried off long ago to build farmhouses, churches and even a priory. It is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage Site, and it is best seen in low light, when the earthworks cast long shadows.

The priory is Lanercost, a few kilometres to the north-east, an Augustinian house founded in the twelfth century and built partly from Roman stones. Edward I stayed there for months during his campaigns against the Scots, and the ruined church and cloister are hauntingly beautiful. Nearby, Birdoswald fort stands above a bend of the Irthing, with a long, well-preserved stretch of wall and a visitor centre.

Brampton, with four thousand people, has fuel, shops, pubs and cafés, and a weekly market. Talkin Tarn, a glacial lake just south of town, set in a country park, is popular for walks and swimming. Further afield, the Bewcastle Cross, an Anglo-Saxon carved cross standing in a remote churchyard to the north, is one of the finest early medieval monuments in Britain.

The riding here is varied. The A69 runs east-west along the valley and is busy, but the minor roads north toward Bewcastle and Kielder are narrow, quiet and often unfenced, crossing moorland where sheep wander freely. South, the Pennines rise steeply, and the A686 from Penrith to Alston over Hartside is one of the best motorcycle roads in England, climbing in a series of bends to a summit with views across the Eden valley to the Lake District.
t.castellon de los machos@39.9,-1.7:
High in the Serranía de Cuenca, among pine woods and sandstone outcrops near the village of Villar del Humo, prehistoric hunters painted figures on the rock shelters thousands of years ago. The site called Castellón de los Machos is one of a cluster in this area that belongs to the vast UNESCO listing of rock art of the Mediterranean Basin of the Iberian Peninsula, which covers hundreds of painted shelters from Catalonia to Andalusia. The images here are small, reddish and stylised, and finding them takes patience and good eyes.

This is deeply rural Spain. The nearest villages, Villar del Humo and Cañete, have only a few hundred residents each, and the wider region has been emptying for decades. That leaves a landscape of rolling plateau and deep valleys, juniper and pine forest, red earth and scattered farms, where the loudest noise is often wind in the pines. In autumn, mushroom hunters comb the woods, and you may meet deer, wild boar or griffon vultures circling above the cliffs. Villar del Humo takes its name, according to local tradition, from smoke rising from the charcoal burners who once worked these forests.

The roads through the Serranía are a quiet treat: narrow, mostly well surfaced and almost empty, with long flowing bends through forest and occasional tight sections where they drop into river valleys. The ride north to the old fortified town of Cañete, and further on into the hanging rocks and gorges around the city of Cuenca, is excellent. Be aware of gravel on corners, livestock, and the occasional hunting party in season. Winters on the plateau are cold and can bring ice and snow, while summer afternoons are hot but much more bearable than down on the plains.

Fuel is the main thing to plan. There is no large town nearby, and the dependable option is to fill up in Cuenca or another sizeable town before heading in. Village bars serve simple meals; try morteruelo, a rich game pâté, or ajoarriero, a cod and garlic spread, with crusty bread. Carry water when visiting the shelters, which often involve a walk on rough paths.
t.barranc de l infern conj 3@38.8,-0.1:
Hikers in the Marina Alta speak of the Barranc de l'Infern with a mix of affection and fear. This dramatic gorge between Vall de Ebo and Fleix carries a path of thousands of stone steps built by the Moriscos, the converted Muslims who farmed these valleys until their expulsion from Spain in 1609. Rock shelters along the ravine hold prehistoric paintings, some of which belong to the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean rock art, and the cliffs themselves are spectacular, with layers of grey and orange limestone glowing in the late afternoon sun.

The surrounding valleys, the Vall de Laguar, Vall d'Alcalà and Vall de Ebo, are tucked behind the busy Costa Blanca coast, yet feel a century away from its high-rises. Terraced almond and olive groves, cherry orchards and little white villages cling to the slopes, and the air smells of pine and wild herbs. The cave of the Rull near Vall de Ebo is worth a stop if you want something cooler than the sun-baked gorge. Many places here still carry Arabic names, a reminder of the people who built the terraces and the long stairway.

For a rider, these valleys are a playground. The roads through Vall de Ebo, Vall d'Alcalà and the climb over the Coll de Rates between Parcent and Tàrbena are known for their tight hairpins, panoramic balconies and smooth tarmac, and they are hugely popular with road cyclists, so expect groups of them on every climb, particularly on winter weekends when teams train here. The roads are narrow and blind in places, with gravel on corners and the occasional stray goat. Spring is glorious, with almond blossom in February and wildflowers later, while summer is hot.

Murla and the other villages are tiny, so plan your fuel in Pego, a town of eleven thousand, or along the coast. Village bars serve coffee and bocadillos, and Pego has proper restaurants, with rice dishes from the nearby marsh, which was historically a rice-growing area. If you plan to walk part of the gorge, take water, good shoes and give yourself plenty of time, and remember those steps go up as well as down.
t.hadrian s wall in wall mile 2@55.0,-1.6:
Most people picture Hadrian's Wall striding across lonely Northumberland crags. Wall mile 2 is the other end of the story: an urban stretch in the east of Newcastle upon Tyne, where the wall ran from the fort at Wallsend, Segedunum, westwards along the north bank of the Tyne towards the bridge and fort at Pons Aelius, beneath today's city centre. Very little of the wall itself is visible here; terraced houses, roads and shipyards have long since swallowed it. But you are standing on the first miles of a frontier that once ran coast to coast for about eighty Roman miles.

Newcastle's own history is layered right on top. The castle keep that gave the city its name sits on the site of the Roman fort, and the Tyne's bridges, from the famous green arch of the Tyne Bridge to the tilting Millennium Bridge, tell the tale of an industrial city that built ships, locomotives and coal fortunes for the world. At Wallsend, Segedunum has a reconstructed bathhouse, a section of rebuilt wall and a viewing tower over the fort's excavated foundations, and it is a good place to start a journey westwards.

Riding in Newcastle is city riding, with busy junctions, bus lanes, speed cameras and plenty of traffic, especially around rush hours and match days at St James' Park. The reward comes once you escape west along the Tyne valley, where the B6318 military road shadows the wall through open moorland with long straights, dips and crests, and the scenery grows wilder with every mile. Weather can be bracing even in summer, with strong westerly winds and showers that blow through in minutes.

Fuel, food and accommodation are plentiful everywhere around here. The Quayside is the place for a break, with cafés, pubs and the Sunday market, and if you are in the mood, a stottie cake, a dense, flat local bread, makes a good filling sandwich. The Hadrian's Wall Path begins at Wallsend too, so you may well meet walkers setting off on their week-long trek to the far end at Bowness-on-Solway.
In the heart of Valencia's old town, a Gothic building with crenellated walls and gargoyles looks more like a castle than a market, and that was rather the point. The Lonja de la Seda, the silk exchange, was built in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries when Valencia was one of the richest cities in the Mediterranean, and it was meant to show the power of its merchants. Its great hall, the Sala de Contratación, is one of the masterpieces of late Gothic architecture, with slender columns that twist like palm trunks up to a ribbed vault. It was listed by UNESCO in 1996.

The architect Pere Compte designed the main hall, and the building also includes a tower that served as a prison for debtors, a courtyard with orange trees and a hall where the city's maritime tribunal met. Inscriptions on the walls urge merchants to honesty and fair dealing. Directly opposite stands the Mercado Central, a vast modernist market hall with a glass dome, where you can buy fresh fish, fruit, ham and spices, and nearby the church of Santos Juanes and the cathedral, with its octagonal bell tower, the Miguelete, complete the picture of a city that has always been busy and proud.

Riding in Valencia is city riding: dense traffic, scooters everywhere, numerous traffic lights and a ring of motorways. The old centre has restricted traffic zones and limited parking, so leave the bike at the edge or in a public car park and walk in. The surrounding region offers excellent riding, with the Albufera lagoon and rice fields to the south, the mountains of the interior to the west, and the coast to the north and south, though summer traffic can be heavy along the coast.

Fuel stations are plentiful around the city. Valencia is the home of paella, which locals traditionally eat at lunchtime and never with chorizo, and of horchata, a sweet, cold drink made from tiger nuts, served with fartons, soft pastries for dipping. In March, the Fallas festival fills the city with giant satirical sculptures, fireworks and noise, which are then burned on the final night.
t.barranc de mastec@38.7,-0.5:
Between Cocentaina and Alcoy, in the hilly interior of Alicante province, a small ravine called the Barranc de Mastec holds rock shelters with prehistoric paintings, part of the UNESCO listing of rock art of the Mediterranean Basin. This corner of Spain is particularly rich in it, with styles ranging from the naturalistic Levantine figures of hunters and animals to the strange, abstract macro-schematic art that seems unique to these valleys. The ravine is surrounded by terraced olive and almond groves, pine woods and limestone crags.

Cocentaina is a pleasant town with a castle on the hill above it, a palace of the Counts and a medieval quarter, and it hosts one of the oldest fairs in Spain, held every autumn. Alcoy, next door, is an industrial city built on ravines and connected by spectacular bridges, famous for its Moors and Christians festival in April, when thousands parade in elaborate costumes and fight mock battles in the streets with gunpowder and noise. Around them rise the mountain ranges of Mariola and Font Roja, both natural parks, with forests of holm oak, pine and maple, aromatic plants used in herbal liqueurs, and springs.

The riding here is excellent. The roads around the Serra de Mariola, through villages like Agres, Alfafara and Bocairent, wind through the mountains with beautiful views and light traffic, and the climb to Font Roja through the forest is a favourite. Further south, routes towards the coast cross the mountains via passes with tight bends and dramatic drops, linking the interior with Benidorm and the Marina Alta. Both Cocentaina and Alcoy can fill your tank and your stomach. Cooking up here is mountain food: olleta, a hearty stew of beans, rice and vegetables, and pericana, a dish of dried peppers, salted cod and olive oil. Alcoy is also known for its stuffed olives and for herbero, a herbal liqueur made in the Mariola mountains. Bring water if you plan to walk to the rock shelters.
t.barranco de las colochas abrigo i@39.6,-:
West of Valencia, the river Turia leaves the mountains through a series of deep gorges, and around the villages of Gestalgar, Sot de Chera and Chulilla, the landscape turns dramatic: limestone cliffs, pine-covered slopes and the river winding green below. In a side ravine near Gestalgar, the Barranco de las Colochas shelters a handful of painted panels that UNESCO counts among the Mediterranean rock art of Iberia. The figures are faint, but the setting is worth the effort on its own.

Chulilla, a few kilometres upstream, has become famous among rock climbers, who come from all over the world to climb its limestone walls. The village, crowned by the ruins of a Moorish castle, is the starting point for a walk through the Turia gorge that crosses two suspension bridges, known as the hanging bridges, built over the river for the construction of a canal. Sot de Chera, a tiny village in a side valley, has a geological park with rock formations and a river beach where locals swim in summer. The surrounding hills are covered in pine and holm oak, with rosemary, thyme and lavender scenting the air.

The roads here are twisting and narrow, following the river and climbing over the hills, with little traffic but plenty of gravel, sharp bends and sometimes loose rocks. Routes link Chiva, Gestalgar, Chulilla and Bugarra, with views of the gorges, and further west the roads climb into the Serranía, a high, sparsely populated region with pine forests and stone villages. Summer heat is intense, and storms can bring flash floods in autumn, when the region can receive torrential rain in a short time.

Fuel is available in Chiva and other larger towns along the main roads, while small villages may have limited services. Gestalgar and Chulilla both have places to eat, where the menu runs to paella valenciana, which here traditionally includes chicken, rabbit and beans, and gazpacho manchego, a hearty stew of game and flatbread. Bring water and sun protection, as the walks to the shelters often involve exposed paths.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum between st osw:
North of Hexham, where the land rises above the Tyne valley, the B6318, the military road built in the eighteenth century partly on top of Hadrian's Wall, runs straight across open country, and here, near the hamlet of St Oswald's, the remains of the wall and the vallum, the great earthwork that ran along its southern side, are clearly visible in the fields. The vallum was a broad ditch flanked by mounds, marking a military zone, and its scale still impresses. This stretch is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site.

The name St Oswald's recalls a battle fought here in 634, when Oswald, the Christian king of Northumbria, defeated the Welsh king Cadwallon at Heavenfield. According to tradition, Oswald raised a wooden cross before the battle, and a small church and a cross now mark the site, standing alone on the hillside with wide views across the valley. A few kilometres west, at Chollerford, the Roman fort of Chesters guards the crossing of the North Tyne, with a well-preserved bathhouse beside the river and a museum full of inscriptions and carvings.

The B6318 is a classic motorcycle road, running west from Newcastle to Greenhead, with long straight sections, sudden dips and crests, and views across the wild landscape of the wall. It can be fast and fun, but beware of hidden dips, livestock, slow tourist traffic and strong crosswinds on exposed stretches. The road becomes more dramatic further west, where the wall climbs along the crags of the Whin Sill. Weather can change quickly, with rain and wind sweeping across the hills even in summer.

Hexham, a market town of around eleven thousand, has pumps, pubs and cafés, as well as a beautiful abbey with a Saxon crypt. Corbridge, a few kilometres east, is a pretty village with tearooms and the remains of a Roman town. Try a pub lunch of pie and peas or a plate of local lamb, and if you are lucky, a slice of stottie cake, the local bread, with ham and pease pudding.
t.barranc d alpadull abric i@38.8,-0.6:
The painted shelter of Barranc d'Alpadull sits in the folds of the Serra de Mariola, the limestone massif that rises between Bocairent, Alfafara and Agres in the inland corner where Valencia, Alicante and the old kingdom's hill country all meet. It is one of the many small overhangs in eastern Spain that carry Levantine rock art, the group of sites inscribed together by UNESCO as the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin. Do not expect a museum. These are faint, reddish figures under a lip of stone, usually fenced, often hard to read unless the light is low and raking, and part of the pleasure is simply knowing that hunters drew here thousands of years before anyone thought of building a road up this valley.

The road, when it comes, is good fun. The range has been a herb pharmacy for centuries, and the local liqueur, herbero, is still made from a long list of plants gathered on these slopes.

Bocairent, a few minutes away, deserves more than a glance. t.cavidad ii@38.5,-1.6:
South of Hellín the land opens into the dry, high steppe of southern Albacete, a country of esparto grass, almond terraces and bare limestone ridges, and it is in these ridges that the small painted cavities of the area hide. Hellín itself, seven kilometres away and a town of around thirty thousand, is where everything practical happens. t.barranc de bolulla@38.7,-0.1:
Bolulla is barely a village, a few hundred people tucked into a valley of the Marina Baixa behind Benidorm, and the ravine that carries its name cuts into the limestone hills just outside it. The mountains here are steep and close together, terraced for centuries with olives, almonds and loquats, and their caves and shelters hold traces of prehistoric painting that place this corner of Alicante within the wider family of Mediterranean rock art. What you see on the ground is a dry, rocky gully scented with pine and wild herbs, with the ruined castle of Bolulla perched on a ridge above, a reminder of the Moorish centuries when these valleys were densely settled.

From Callosa d'en Sarrià and Polop the routes climb into the sierras through tight, often narrow bends, and some of the best roads on the whole Costa Blanca start within a few kilometres of here. The climb to Castell de Castells is quiet and technical, and the nearby Coll de Rates, between Tàrbena and Parcent, is well known to cyclists for its steady gradient and the view down to the coast and the Montgó massif. Watch for cyclists in winter, when teams and amateurs from northern Europe train on these roads in large numbers.
