t.cueva del gitano@38.3,-2.3:
Some places are remote on the map and remote in the gut, and the country around the Cueva del Gitano is both. It lies in the Sierra de Segura on the southern fringe of Albacete province, in the municipality of Nerpio, where the mountains of Albacete, Murcia, Jaén and Granada all run into one another. This is one of the richest areas for prehistoric rock art in Spain, with dozens of painted shelters along the valley of the Taibilla river and its side ravines, and the Cueva del Gitano is one of the smaller sites in that dense cluster. The art is faint, the walk can be rough, and the setting does most of the talking.

The roads to get here are a joy if you like quiet tarmac and plenty of bends. From Yeste or from the Murcian side through Moratalla, the routes climb into pine-covered mountains and then wind along limestone valleys, rarely straight for more than a few hundred metres. The surface is generally fine but narrow, with fallen rocks after storms and the odd herd of goats on the move. You can ride for half an hour and meet two cars. In winter, snow and ice can make the higher sections dangerous, and in summer the heat is real, though it is gentler here than down on the plain.

Nerpio is known for its walnuts, which grow in groves along the river, and for a village life that has changed little in many decades. Yeste, slightly larger, has a castle above the town and an old quarter of narrow streets. Both are small, and while they have the basics, services can be limited, especially on Sundays and in the afternoon siesta hours.

Fuel is the thing to plan. The larger town of Moratalla in Murcia is nearly forty kilometres away, and there are long gaps between pumps across these mountains, so fill up when you can and carry the habit of topping off at every opportunity. Water from village fountains is usually drinkable, but carry your own anyway. The reward for the effort is solitude, dark night skies, the scent of resin in the warm afternoon air, and the sense of riding through a corner of Spain that has quietly kept its own rhythm.
t.canalejas de abajo@38.2,-2.4:
Canalejas de Abajo is a name on the map rather than a place with a church and a bar: a scattering of farms and old cortijos in the upper valley of the Taibilla river, south of Nerpio, in the mountains where Albacete, Jaén and Granada meet. The Sierra de Segura and the Sierra de las Cabras rise all around, high limestone country cut by deep valleys, and the region is known among archaeologists for its painted rock shelters. The Abrigo del Sabinar and others along the same valley hold some of the most important prehistoric paintings of the Spanish south east, drawn on the soft overhangs that the river and the wind have shaped.

This is a land of transhumance. For centuries shepherds drove their flocks along drove roads between the summer pastures of these mountains and the winter grazing of the Andalusian lowlands, and you will still see the old stone pens and huts dotted across the slopes. The valleys are dotted with sabinas, the slow-growing juniper trees that give some of the shelters their names, and the high meadows are bright with wildflowers in late spring.

The roads are narrow and winding, following the contours of the valleys and climbing over ridges with long views across the mountains. The road south from Nerpio towards Santiago de la Espada in Jaén is one of the great quiet rides of the region, all bends and empty space, though the surface can be patchy and gravel collects on the inside of corners. Snow and ice are serious hazards in winter, and in summer the afternoons can bring sudden thunderstorms that turn the tarmac slick within minutes.

There is no town of five thousand people anywhere close, which tells you everything about how remote this corner of Spain is. Nerpio, about seven kilometres away, has the basics, while Yeste and the villages of the Sierra de Segura further west are the other options. Fuel stations are few and far between, so a full tank before entering these mountains is not optional. Carry water, snacks and a basic tool kit, and let someone know your route. In return you get some of the darkest night skies in Spain, the smell of juniper and pine, and roads where an hour can pass without another vehicle.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum between the fi:
Just west of Chollerford the road climbs onto higher ground and the Wall begins to show itself, first as a hump in the fields, then as a ditch and earthwork running alongside the tarmac. This is the central sector of Hadrian's Wall, built from the 120s on the orders of the emperor Hadrian to mark the northern edge of Roman Britain, and the stretch around Carrawburgh is one of the most atmospheric. The vallum, a broad ditch flanked by mounds on the southern side of the Wall, is especially clear here, and it shows the Roman frontier was not just a wall but a whole military zone, with forts, milecastles, turrets, roads and earthworks.

At Carrawburgh lie the remains of the fort of Brocolitia, and just outside it, the small temple of Mithras, a mysterious cult popular among Roman soldiers. The temple, with replica altars standing in the boggy ground, is one of the most evocative places on the Wall. Nearby, a spring dedicated to the water goddess Coventina yielded thousands of coins and offerings when it was excavated in the nineteenth century.

The road you are riding, the B6318, is known as the Military Road, and it has its own story. It was built in the middle of the eighteenth century, after the Jacobite rising of 1745, to allow troops to move quickly between Newcastle and Carlisle, and in places the builders used the Wall itself as foundations and quarried its stones for the road. The result is a long, undulating ribbon of tarmac, with blind crests and dips that hide oncoming traffic, so take care, especially on summer weekends when the road is busy with visitors.

The landscape is open and wild, with rolling hills, moorland, and long views north towards the Cheviots and Kielder forest. The weather can change quickly, with wind, rain and fog sweeping across the hills, so pack warm and waterproof clothing even in summer. Hexham, about eleven kilometres away, is the nearest larger town, with an abbey, a busy market and all the services you need, including fuel. Haydon Bridge and Acomb have pubs and basic shops, but services along the Wall itself are sparse, so plan your stops in advance.
t.walwick fell roman temporary camp@55.0,-:
Roman armies on campaign dug in every night. Wherever they halted, soldiers threw up a rectangular earth rampart and ditch around their tents, and on Walwick Fell, a short way west of the North Tyne, the faint outline of one of those temporary camps survives in the rough pasture. You need a keen eye and low sunlight to make it out, but its presence is a reminder that the Wall was built, maintained and defended by thousands of men who lived and worked in these hills, sometimes under canvas, sometimes in stone forts.

The best known of those forts is Chesters, just down the hill by the river. Its remains include one of the finest Roman bathhouses in Britain, set on the riverbank, and the abutments of a Roman bridge that once carried the Wall across the North Tyne can still be seen on the opposite bank. A short distance to the west, at Limestone Corner, the Roman builders tried to cut the Wall's northern ditch through a band of hard whinstone and gave up, leaving huge split blocks lying where they fell, with wedge holes still visible. It is one of those places where you can almost hear the swearing.

The riding around here combines the Military Road along the Wall with the quiet valley roads of the North Tyne. Heading north from Chollerford, the road follows the river through Wark and Bellingham towards Kielder Water, the largest reservoir in England, surrounded by a vast forest and some of the darkest skies in the country. The roads are narrow but well surfaced, with gentle bends, rolling hills and little traffic. Sheep wander freely on some of the moorland roads, so ride with caution.

Hexham, about eight kilometres away, is the nearest larger town, with a fine medieval abbey and a good range of shops, cafes and fuel stations. Chollerford has a hotel and a small village, and Acomb, Wall and Humshaugh have pubs. The North Tyne valley is green and gentle, with old stone villages, river meadows and pockets of woodland, in contrast to the bare uplands of the central Wall. In late summer, the heather turns the moors purple, and the evenings are long and golden, perfect for a slow ride home.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum between the fi:
West of Birdoswald the Wall changes character. The central crags fall behind, the River Irthing loops through its gorge below, and the frontier runs across gentler farmland towards Banks and Hare Hill, where one of the tallest surviving fragments of the Wall still stands, patched by later hands. Here too the vallum, the great earthwork south of the Wall, can be traced across the fields, and the remains of turrets at Banks East and Pike Hill sit right beside the road. It is a quieter stretch than the famous sections further east, and all the better for it.

Birdoswald fort, perched on a spur above the Irthing, has some of the best-preserved defences on the Wall, and nearby at Willowford the Romans built a bridge across the river, whose abutment can still be seen. A short distance west lies Lanercost Priory, founded in the twelfth century by Augustinian canons, and built in part from stone taken from the Wall. Its ruined church, with its tall west front, is one of the most beautiful in the north of England, and the nave is still used as the parish church. Edward I stayed here for several months in 1306 and 1307, during his last campaign against the Scots, already ill and close to death.

The riding here is a pleasure, with narrow lanes running along the Wall, through small villages and farmland, and climbing onto the edge of the moors to the north. The roads are generally good but narrow, with sharp bends, steep hills and occasional cattle grids. Traffic is light, and the views are wide and open. The weather can be wet and windy at any time of year, and the lanes can be muddy after rain, so take care.

Brampton, about eight kilometres away, is a small market town with fuel, shops and pubs, and its octagonal Moot Hall stands in the centre of the market square. Haltwhistle, to the east, claims to be the centre of Britain and is another good place for supplies. Carlisle, the largest city in the area, is about twenty two kilometres away, with its castle, cathedral and all the services you could need. The Lake District and the Scottish borders are both within easy reach, offering more challenging riding for those who want to extend the trip.
t.barranc de l infern conj 2@38.8,-0.1:
Local walkers call it the cathedral of hiking, and once you have seen the Barranc de l'Infern you understand why. This deep limestone gorge, between the Vall de Laguar and the Vall d'Ebo in the mountains behind Dénia, is crossed by an old Moorish mule path that descends and climbs again by thousands of stone steps, carved and built into the rock walls over centuries. The route, a classic day walk, is spectacular and exhausting, with the gorge narrowing at its deepest point to a passage between towering walls. The gorge also holds prehistoric rock art in its shelters, and the sites grouped as Conjunt 2 are among them, part of the wider family of Mediterranean rock art protected by UNESCO.

The valleys around the gorge are a world apart from the busy coast just a few kilometres away. The Vall de Laguar is a cluster of small villages, Campell, Fleix and Benimaurell, perched on terraced slopes, with cherry orchards that bloom white in spring and almond and olive trees. The Vall d'Ebo, to the west, is a high, quiet valley, with a cave, the Cova del Rull, full of stalactites and stalagmites, that is open to visitors.

The roads into these valleys are narrow, steep and winding, with tight hairpins, sheer drops and fine views over the mountains and the coast. The road from Pego up to the Vall d'Ebo is especially dramatic, climbing in a series of bends from the coastal plain into the hills, with the marshes and rice fields of the Marjal de Pego-Oliva spread out below. Surfaces are generally good, but gravel, fallen rocks and walkers on the road are common hazards, and cyclists are numerous in winter. Traffic is light, apart from weekends.

The villages have limited services, with small shops, bars and a few restaurants, so fill up in Pego, about seven kilometres away, a town of over eleven thousand people, or in the larger towns on the coast. The local food includes rice dishes, such as arroz al horno, and coca, a kind of flatbread with toppings, and the cherries of the Vall de Laguar are famous in season. Summers are hot, so the early morning is the best time for riding and walking, and winters are mild, making this a good destination for off-season rides.
t.raco del pou@38.8,-0.2:
The Safor is the fertile coastal strip around Gandia, and behind it rise abrupt limestone hills, the Serra de la Safor and its neighbours, where the orange groves give way to pine, scrub and terraces of olives and almonds. Racó del Pou, a sheltered corner in these hills between Villalonga and the Vall d'Ebo, is one of the many rock shelters of the region that hold prehistoric paintings, part of the Mediterranean rock art group listed by UNESCO. Like most of them, it is modest and protected, but the walk up and the view over the hills to the sea are reason enough to come.

Villalonga, the nearest town, lies at the foot of the mountains on the river Serpis, and it marks the end of the Via Verde del Serpis, a former railway line converted into a path for walkers and cyclists, which runs up the river gorge towards Alcoi through tunnels and over bridges. The gorge, with its rushing water, cliffs and the ruins of medieval castles perched on the rocks, is beautiful, and the old line was built in the nineteenth century to carry coal from the port of Gandia to the textile mills of Alcoi. The Serpis gorge is also home to otters, kingfishers and other wildlife.

Gandia, on the coast, was the home of the Borgia family, who rose to become dukes and popes, and their palace, the Palau Ducal, is open to visitors. Saint Francis Borgia, a duke who gave up his title to become a Jesuit, was born there. The coastal plain is covered in orange groves, and in spring the scent of orange blossom fills the air, a sweet, heady perfume that is one of the great sensory experiences of the Valencian coast.

The roads into the hills from Villalonga are narrow, steep and winding, with tight bends, few barriers and fine views. They are quiet, apart from cyclists, who come in large numbers in winter to train on the climbs, and the occasional tractor. Villalonga, a town of about four thousand people, has basic services, and Pego and Gandia have fuel and everything else. The local food includes fideuà, a dish similar to paella but made with short noodles, invented, according to tradition, by a ship's cook in Gandia. Summers are hot, winters are mild, and spring and autumn are perfect for riding.
t.sierra de alfaro@38.7,-0.3:
The Sierra de Alfaro is a long limestone ridge in the mountains of northern Alicante, between Castell de Castells, Benimantell and Planes, a rugged, empty landscape of rock, scrub and pine, with terraced valleys and small villages tucked into its folds. Its slopes hold several shelters with prehistoric paintings, and the area is part of one of the richest regions for rock art in Spain, with Levantine, schematic and the unique macroschematic styles found nowhere else. The ridge is also crossed by walking trails, and the views from the top over the mountains and the sea are wide.

To the south lies the valley of Guadalest, one of the most visited places in the province, with its castle perched on a needle of rock and a village reached through a tunnel in the stone. Benimantell, just below, is a quieter village with restaurants serving traditional mountain food. Above the valley rises the Serra d'Aitana, the highest mountain range in the province of Alicante, with its summit at over fifteen hundred metres, crowned by military installations, and its slopes are home to the Safari Aitana and the snow wells that once supplied ice to the coastal towns. The Guadalest reservoir, turquoise and surrounded by mountains, is a striking sight from the road above.

The riding in these mountains is outstanding. The road from Callosa through Guadalest to Confrides and on over the Port de Confrides, a pass through the mountains towards Alcoi, is a classic, with flowing bends, steep sections and dramatic views. The minor roads around Castell de Castells, Famorca and Planes are narrower and quieter, with tight bends, rough patches and almost no traffic. Cyclists are common in winter, and walkers in spring and autumn, so stay alert on blind bends.

Services are limited in the villages, with small shops, bars and restaurants, and fuel is not available everywhere, so fill up in Callosa, Cocentaina, about fifteen kilometres away, or the larger towns on the coast. The local food is hearty, with olleta, a stew of beans, meat and vegetables, and pericana, a dish of dried peppers, salted cod and olive oil. Summers are hot, but the mountains are cooler than the coast, and winters can be cold, with occasional snow on the higher ridges.
t.bewcastle roman fort@55.1,-2.7:
Bewcastle is one of the loneliest places in Cumbria, and it has been for a very long time. Roman soldiers built an outpost fort here, about ten kilometres north of Hadrian's Wall, on a plateau whose shape the walls followed, giving it an unusual six-sided plan. It was a forward base for scouts watching the tribes beyond the frontier, and it was linked to the Wall at Birdoswald by a road. Later, a medieval castle was built into one corner of the old Roman defences, and its broken walls still stand above the beck.

The real treasure is in the churchyard of St Cuthbert. The Bewcastle Cross, carved in the late seventh or eighth century, has lost its head, but the shaft still stands where it was raised, covered in vine scrolls, chequer patterns, figures of Christ and John the Baptist, and a runic inscription. Along with the Ruthwell Cross across the Solway, it is counted among the finest surviving pieces of Anglo-Saxon sculpture anywhere, and seeing it out in the weather, in a field at the end of the world, is part of its power.

Getting here is half the fun. From Brampton the lanes climb north through Lanercost, Banks and Roadhead into open moorland, narrowing to single track with passing places, cattle grids and gates. The surface is mixed, with gravel and moss in the middle of the lane, and blind crests where you meet a farm truck at the worst moment. The rewards are huge skies, curlews in spring, the edge of Kielder Forest on the horizon, and almost no traffic. This was the heart of the reiver country, the debatable borderland where families like the Armstrongs and Elliots answered to nobody, and the emptiness still feels slightly lawless.

There is nothing in the way of services. Brampton, thirteen kilometres south as the crow flies but further by road, is a pleasant little market town with fuel and cafés; Carlisle is the big supply stop. Fill up before you head north, carry water and something to eat, and do not rely on phone signal. The church is usually open, and there is a small exhibition about the site nearby. In mist the moors close in fast, so allow time to get back down before dark.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum between banks:
North-east of Brampton, the Wall climbs out of the Irthing valley and runs along a ridge past the hamlet of Banks, and here you can see something many visitors miss: not only the Wall itself, but the vallum, the great earthwork ditch with banks on either side that the Romans dug just south of it. The vallum marked a military zone, a controlled strip where civilians could not wander freely, and seeing its long straight line beside the stone curtain makes the frontier feel less like a wall and more like a whole system of control.

At Banks East there is a well-preserved turret, and a little further along is Pike Hill, where a signal tower stood at an angle to the Wall, older than the Wall itself, placed to talk to stations on the Stanegate road behind. Down by the river, Lanercost Priory was founded by Augustinian canons in the twelfth century, and its builders helped themselves to Roman stone; you can spot it in the walls. Edward I stayed at Lanercost for months in his final year, ill and still planning campaigns against the Scots.

The road from Brampton through Lanercost and Banks towards Gilsland is a narrow, hedged lane that climbs and dips with the land, with a few tight corners, sudden steep pitches and splendid views north over the Cumbrian fells and the forests towards Bewcastle. It is popular with walkers on the Wall Path and with cyclists, so ride it gently and watch for people stepping out at stiles. In autumn the trees along the Irthing turn copper and the light is lovely in late afternoon.

Brampton, a few kilometres away, is a friendly market town with fuel, a couple of decent cafés and an octagonal moot hall in the square. Carlisle is the big service centre if you need tyres or parts. Lanercost has a tearoom by the priory, which is a happy place to sit with a scone, and there is usually water and toilets for walkers along the path. Further east, Birdoswald fort is one of the best places to see a long length of Wall, and well worth the extra miles.
t.hadrian s wall and associated features b:
This is the stretch of Hadrian's Wall that everyone pictures: the stone curtain running along the crest of the Whin Sill, a hard dolerite ridge that ends in sheer north-facing crags, with lakes like Crag Lough and Greenlee Lough glinting below. Housesteads fort is close by, clinging to the hillside with its barracks, granaries and famous communal latrines, and the Wall dips and climbs over each crag in a way that seems almost reckless as engineering. The Sycamore Gap tree, which stood in a dip in the ridge for generations, was felled in an act of vandalism in 2023, and the loss is still felt locally.

The landscape here is open grazing land, big and windswept, with drystone walls, scattered farms and the dark line of Kielder Forest to the north. Skylarks sing over the rough grass in summer; in winter the place can be bleak and very beautiful. The Wall is a World Heritage Site, and between Chesters, Housesteads and Vindolanda, where the famous wooden writing tablets came out of the waterlogged ground, you could easily spend a whole day reading Roman life from the stones.

The B6318, the Military Road, runs just south of the Wall and is the main artery. It was built after the 1745 Jacobite rising so that government troops could move quickly between Newcastle and Carlisle, and in places its builders laid it right on top of the Wall's foundations. It is a fabulous road to ride, with long rolling straights over crests, dips that hide oncoming cars and a few sharp bends. Its reputation for accidents is well earned, so treat every crest as a blind corner. Farm vehicles and tourists pulling into car parks add to the fun.

Haydon Bridge and Haltwhistle are the nearest villages with fuel, and Hexham, a handsome abbey town, is the main centre about fourteen kilometres away. The Twice Brewed area on the Military Road has a pub and visitor centre at The Sill, which is useful for coffee, toilets and information. Weather moves fast up on the Sill: plan for sunshine and squalls in the same hour, and keep a layer handy even in summer.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum in wall mile 7:
It takes a little imagination to find the Roman frontier in Benwell, a suburb on the western hill of Newcastle, but it is there, tucked between semi-detached houses and bus stops. Wall mile 7 counts the distance from the Wall's eastern end at Wallsend, and in this part of the city the Romans built a fort called Condercum on the high ground above the Tyne, with fine views up and down the river. Most of it now lies under roads and housing, yet two small survivals make the detour worthwhile.

The first is the vallum crossing on Denhill Park, the only place along the whole frontier where you can still see a stone causeway carrying a road across the vallum ditch, with the remains of a gateway that controlled traffic into the military zone. The second, a few minutes away, is the little temple of Antenociticus, a local god known only from here, its foundations and replica altars sitting in a garden plot surrounded by modern homes. The juxtaposition is wonderful: Roman soldiers made offerings on this spot, and now people walk their dogs past it.

Riding in this corner of Tyneside is urban riding, honestly described. The West Road, which follows the line of the Wall out of the city centre, is busy, stop-start and lined with shops, buses and speed cameras. The appeal is in what comes next: within twenty minutes heading west you are out past the ring road, the houses fall away and the B6318 Military Road begins its long roll towards the Pennines. Benwell makes a good first or last Roman stop on a Wall ride, a reminder that the frontier ran right through what became a great industrial city.

Fuel, food and everything else are close at hand, with supermarkets and filling stations along the main roads. Newcastle itself is worth an evening for the Tyne bridges, the Quayside and the Great North Museum, which holds many of the finds from along the Wall, including inscriptions and altars that make the bare stones on the ground suddenly speak. Park thoughtfully in the residential streets and keep an eye on your bike; it is a city, after all.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum from east town:
Heddon-on-the-Wall announces its pedigree in its name, and just east of the village, on the slope down towards Newcastle, you find the longest surviving stretch of the Wall in the eastern sector. It is a section of broad wall, built to the original specification of about ten Roman feet thick, before the builders further west were told to save time and stone by making it narrower. Standing beside it, with fields falling away towards the Tyne, you get a strong sense of the scale of the project: this curtain once ran unbroken for eighty Roman miles.

The vallum is visible here too, a long shallow trough with low banks that runs parallel to the Wall through the fields, and on a low sun in winter or late evening the earthworks show up beautifully. Down in the valley, the village of Wylam is the birthplace of George Stephenson, the railway pioneer, and the cottage where he was born in 1781 still stands beside the old wagonway along the river. It is a pleasing coincidence that two great feats of engineering, separated by sixteen centuries, sit within sight of each other.

Heading west from Heddon, the B6318 Military Road begins in earnest. Built in the 1750s for troops chasing Jacobites, it runs dead straight for long stretches, rising and falling over ridges with views opening north to the Cheviots on a good day. The early miles are open farmland with long sightlines, and it is tempting to wind it on, but hidden dips can conceal cars and tractors, and local police know the road well. Rain and low cloud can arrive quickly from the west. East of Heddon, the A69 and the city traffic take over.

Newburn and the western suburbs of Newcastle are a few kilometres away and have all the fuel and food you could want. Heddon itself has a pub and a small shop, convenient for walkers starting the Wall Path. If you are heading west, it is worth knowing that the services thin out quickly beyond here until Corbridge and Hexham, so top up on the edge of town rather than waiting.
t.quanzhou emporium of the world in song y:
Medieval travellers called it Zaitun, and to Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta it was one of the greatest ports in the world. Quanzhou, on the coast of Fujian facing Taiwan, flourished under the Song and Yuan dynasties as a hub of maritime trade, where Arab, Persian, Indian and Southeast Asian merchants lived alongside Chinese traders, and ships left laden with silk and porcelain. In 2021 UNESCO inscribed a group of sites as Quanzhou: Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China, including temples, mosques, tombs, kilns, bridges and docks that together tell the story of this cosmopolitan city.

The coordinates fall near the coast south-west of the city, close to the Anping bridge, a stone causeway more than two kilometres long built in the twelfth century across a tidal estuary, and still crossed on foot today. In the city itself, the Kaiyuan temple with its twin stone pagodas, the Qingjing mosque, one of the oldest in China, and the Islamic tombs on Lingshan hill, where two companions of the Prophet are said to be buried, show the mix of faiths that trade brought. A statue of Laozi carved from a single rock sits on Qingyuan mountain, smiling gently over the city.

Riding here comes with serious caveats. Many Chinese cities restrict or ban motorcycles in central areas, and foreign riders need a Chinese driving licence and often an organised tour to ride legally. The roads around Quanzhou are busy, with heavy traffic, electric scooters, trucks and buses, and the coastal plain is densely built up. Out in the hills of inland Fujian, among tea plantations and the round earthen tulou houses of the Hakka, the roads are quieter and more scenic. The best seasons are autumn and spring; summer brings heat, humidity and typhoons.

Fuel and services are everywhere in this prosperous region, and Jinjiang, the nearest large town, is a centre of the shoe and textile industries. Quanzhou's food is a highlight: oyster omelettes, noodle soups and the beef broths of the old town, with tea from the hills of Anxi, home of the famous Tieguanyin oolong.
t.abric de la cocina@39.3,-0.7:
The Abric de la Cocina, the kitchen shelter, is a rock overhang in the gorges of the Valencian hinterland near Dos Aguas, and on its walls prehistoric painters left scenes of archers, animals and geometric signs. It is one of the sites of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula, inscribed by UNESCO in 1998, which covers hundreds of shelters along the eastern side of Spain with paintings showing hunting, gathering, dancing and warfare, with lively human figures in red and black. Excavations at the shelter also revealed tools and pottery, showing that people lived here over thousands of years.

Not far away, at Bicorp, the Cuevas de la Araña hold one of the most famous images of Levantine art: a figure climbing ropes or vines to collect honey from a wild bees' nest, surrounded by bees, one of the earliest depictions of honey gathering in the world. The landscape here is rugged and dry, with deep gorges cut by the Júcar river and its tributaries, pine forests, scrub and cliffs, and the villages of Millares and Dos Aguas perch on the slopes.

The roads through this part of Valencia are wonderful for riders: narrow, winding and mostly empty, climbing over ridges and dropping into gorges, with spectacular views. Expect broken edges and the odd pothole, and in July and August the gorges cook like ovens. The road from Dos Aguas to Millares and on to Bicorp is a favourite, with endless curves and little traffic. Come in March, when the almond blossom has gone and the hillsides smell of rosemary, or in crisp, clear November.

Turís, fourteen kilometres towards Valencia, is the nearest dependable filling station, and the villages have bars serving tapas and local dishes. Try the Valencian specialities: paella, of course, made the proper way with rabbit, chicken and beans, but also gazpacho manchego, a hearty stew of game and flatbread that has nothing to do with the cold soup. The rock shelters can usually be visited with a guide, so check in advance with the local tourist offices. Carry plenty of water in summer, when the gorges trap the heat and temperatures soar.
t.benirrama abric i@38.8,-0.2:
In the Vall de Gallinera, a long, narrow valley in the mountains of northern Alicante, the Benirrama shelter is one of a cluster of rock art sites, part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin World Heritage listing. The valley is particularly rich in macro-schematic art, a distinctive style found only in this region, with large, abstract human figures and symbols painted in red, and the nearby Pla de Petracos is the most famous site of this style. Benirrama itself is also the name of a ruined Moorish castle on a hill above the valley.

The Vall de Gallinera is famous for its cherries, and in spring the valley is white with blossom, while in early summer the trees are heavy with fruit. The villages are small and quiet, and the landscape is a mix of terraced fields, olive groves and rocky mountains. The area was home to Moorish communities until their expulsion in 1609, and the ruined castles and abandoned villages are reminders of their presence. To the east, the Marjal de Pego-Oliva is a coastal wetland, home to many birds.

The roads through the Vall de Gallinera and the neighbouring valleys are a joy for riders: narrow, winding and quiet, with endless curves and views. The road from Pego through the valley and over the mountains to Planes is a classic, and the Coll de Rates, a short climb further south, is famous among cyclists. Cyclists love these climbs too, so expect lycra round blind corners, and a dusting of gravel after storms. February, when the almond trees blossom, is magical.

Pego, seven kilometres away, is a market town with fuel, shops and restaurants, and the villages of the valley have small bars and restaurants. The cherry season, from May to June, brings markets and festivals, and the fruit is sold at stalls along the road. Try the rice dishes of the region, such as arroz al horno, baked rice with sausages, chickpeas and potatoes, and the local olive oil. The Pla de Petracos shelter is well signposted and easy to reach, with an information panel explaining the paintings.
t.abric de les torrudanes@38.8,-0.2:
In the Vall d'Ebo, a small valley in the mountains of northern Alicante, the Abric de les Torrudanes is a rock shelter with prehistoric paintings, one of many in the area that form part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin World Heritage listing. The paintings include human figures and animals in the Levantine style, and the shelter's location, on a cliff above the valley, offers views over the mountains. Nearby, the Cova del Rull is a show cave with stalactites and stalagmites.

The Vall d'Ebo is also the starting point for one of the most famous walks in the region, the Barranc de l'Infern, a deep gorge with a route of thousands of stone steps, built by the Moorish inhabitants to connect their villages and fields, sometimes called the cathedral of hiking. The village itself is small and quiet, with whitewashed houses and a church, and the landscape around is a mix of terraced fields, olive and almond groves, and rocky mountains.

The roads in and out of the Vall d'Ebo are narrow and winding, with tight curves and steep climbs, and they are a delight for riders who enjoy technical roads. The road from Pego to the Vall d'Ebo climbs steeply with hairpins and views over the coast, and the road on to the Vall d'Alcalà is quieter still. Grit washes onto the bends after rain, and goats occasionally wander onto the hairpins. The cool months from October to April are the most comfortable for riding here.

Pego, five kilometres away, has a filling station, shops and restaurants, and the village of Vall d'Ebo has a couple of bars and restaurants. The Cova del Rull show cave has a café and guided tours, and it is a cool refuge on a hot day. Try the local olive oil and almonds, and the hearty mountain dishes of the region, such as olla, a stew of meat, beans and vegetables. If you have the legs for it, the walk down into the Barranc de l'Infern and back up the stone steps is unforgettable, but bring water, as there is none on the route.
t.abrigo del sabinar@38.2,-2.2:
The Abrigo del Sabinar lies in the remote mountains of north-western Murcia, near Moratalla, where the Sierra de Segura and the Sierra del Taibilla meet, and its paintings of human figures and animals, including deer and goats, are among the finest examples of Levantine rock art in the region. The shelter is part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin listing, and the area around Moratalla and Nerpio is particularly rich in painted shelters. The landscape is wild and rugged, with pine forests, limestone cliffs and deep river valleys, and the villages are few and far between.

Nearby Caravaca de la Cruz is one of the holy cities of Catholicism, home to a relic of the True Cross, and it holds a jubilee year every seven years, attracting pilgrims from all over Spain. Its annual festival in May includes the Caballos del Vino, a race of horses decorated with embroidered cloaks, up the steep street to the castle. Moratalla, a town of narrow streets and white houses below a castle, is famous for its drumming during Holy Week.

The roads in this corner of Spain are among the best and least known in the country, winding through mountains and valleys with little traffic and spectacular scenery. The road from Moratalla to Nerpio, through the Sierra de Segura, is a classic, with endless curves, climbs and descents, and the roads on to the Sierra de Cazorla offer more of the same. The tarmac is patchy in places, and summer temperatures in these sierras can be fierce, so April, May and October make the most sense.

Moratalla, twenty-six kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Caravaca de la Cruz, a little further, has more. The villages have bars and simple restaurants serving local dishes, such as lamb, rice with rabbit and snails, and migas, fried breadcrumbs with sausage. Carry water and fuel, as services are scarce in the mountains. The rock shelters can be visited with a guide, and the interpretation centres in Moratalla and Nerpio explain the paintings and organise visits.
t.fuente del sabuco i@38.2,-2.2:
High in the Sierra del Taibilla, in the borderland hills between Moratalla and Nerpio, the shelters of Fuente del Sabuco hold Levantine paintings of hunters, archers and animals, part of the rich rock art of this remote corner where Andalusia, Murcia and Castilla-La Mancha meet. Nerpio and Moratalla between them hold a remarkable number of painted shelters, making this one of the key centres of rock art in Spain, and an interpretation centre in the village explains the paintings and organises visits. The shelter is part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin World Heritage listing.

Nerpio sits in the valley of the Taibilla river, surrounded by mountains covered in pine and holm oak, and it is famous for its walnuts: the valley's ancient walnut trees, some of them centuries old, produce nuts that are highly prized. The village is small and quiet, with white houses and narrow streets, and the landscape around is a mix of terraced fields, orchards and wild mountain slopes. Golden eagles and griffon vultures soar over the cliffs, and the night skies, far from any city, are spectacular.

The roads here are narrow, winding and almost empty, a paradise for riders who enjoy remote mountain roads. The road from Nerpio over the mountains to Yeste, with its castle, and on to the Sierra de Segura, is a classic, and the road south to the Andalusian border is equally rewarding. Surfaces vary, with rough patches and gravel, and the weather can change quickly in the mountains, with summer thunderstorms building fast over the peaks. May and early October are the sweetest months.

Fuel is scarce in these mountains, so fill up in Moratalla, Yeste or Caravaca de la Cruz before heading into the hills. The villages have a few bars and restaurants serving mountain food, and the walnuts of Nerpio are a must. Carry water and warm clothing, as the nights can be cold even in summer. The interpretation centre in Nerpio explains the rock art of the area and organises guided visits to some of the shelters.
t.l tello i cama del pastor@37.8,-2.1:
In the mountains of northern Almería, near the village of Vélez-Blanco, the Cueva de los Letreros holds a small painted figure that has become the symbol of the province: the Indalo, a human figure holding an arc over its head, which locals paint on houses as a good luck charm. The rock shelters around Vélez-Blanco, including the one known as Tello I or Cama del Pastor, the shepherd's bed, are part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin listing, with paintings ranging from Levantine scenes to schematic signs. The landscape is dry and rugged, with the limestone mass of the Sierra de María rising above.

Vélez-Blanco itself is a white town below a magnificent Renaissance castle, built in the early sixteenth century by the Marquis of Los Vélez. The castle's marble patio was sold in the early twentieth century and now stands in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, a fact the town has never quite forgiven. The Sierra de María, a natural park, is covered in pine forests and home to wildlife, including ibex and birds of prey.

The roads here are a pleasure for riders, winding through mountains and valleys with little traffic. The road from Vélez-Rubio through Vélez-Blanco to María and on into the Sierra de María is a classic, with climbs, curves and views, and the roads towards Granada and Murcia offer more of the same. Surfaces are generally good, and the dry climate means good riding conditions most of the year, though summer can be very hot.

Vélez-Rubio, twenty-two kilometres off, is the place for petrol, and Vélez-Blanco has bars and restaurants serving local dishes, including migas and lamb. The castle can be visited, and the interpretation centre in the village explains the rock art and organises visits to the Cueva de los Letreros. Look for the Indalo painted on houses and sold as souvenirs throughout the province. The Sierra de María natural park has a visitor centre and walking trails, and the pine forests are a cool refuge on a hot summer day.
t.abric de tortosillas@39.0,-1.2:
The Abric de Tortosillas lies in the mountains near Ayora, in the inland valley of Ayora-Cofrentes in Valencia, and its paintings of human figures and animals are part of the rich rock art of this region, part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin listing. Nearby, at Alpera in Albacete province, the Cueva de la Vieja holds one of the most famous Levantine panels, with dozens of figures, archers, deer and goats, and an interpretation centre in the village. The landscape here is dry and mountainous, with pine forests, cliffs and the valley of the Júcar river.

Ayora is a small town below a ruined castle, with a long history as a frontier between the kingdoms of Valencia and Castile, and it is known for its honey, produced from the rosemary and thyme that grow on the hillsides. The valley of Ayora-Cofrentes, to the north, follows the Júcar through gorges and past the spa of Cofrentes, and the dam at Cortes de Pallás forms a large reservoir in a dramatic canyon.

The roads here are a joy for riders, winding through mountains and valleys with little traffic and spectacular views. The road from Ayora to Cofrentes and on to Cortes de Pallás, through the canyon of the Júcar, is a favourite, and the roads towards Almansa and Requena offer more of the same. Surfaces are generally good, and the dry climate means good riding conditions for most of the year.

Ayora, thirteen kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try the local honey and the hearty mountain dishes, such as gazpacho manchego and rice with rabbit. Carry water in summer, when temperatures soar. The interpretation centre in Alpera explains the rock art and organises visits to the Cueva de la Vieja, and the castle in Ayora offers views over the valley. The canyon of the Júcar at Cortes de Pallás can be explored by boat, an unusual way to see the dramatic landscape.
t.the vallum between the field boundary so:
Not every stretch of Hadrian's Wall is the dramatic crag-top masonry of the postcards, and this is one of the quieter parts: a section of the vallum, the great ditch-and-mound earthwork the Romans dug behind the wall, running across farmland near Brampton in Cumbria. The stone wall here was largely robbed out long ago for farms and churches, so what survives is often a long, soft hollow in the grass, a line you only notice once someone points it out, and then can't stop seeing.

The vallum is something of a puzzle. Built just south of the wall in the 120s, it was a flat-bottomed ditch about six metres wide flanked by banks, and it seems to have marked the rear edge of a military zone, controlling who could approach the wall from the Roman side. Crossings were only at the forts. Grazing sheep, field walls and a few centuries of ploughing have softened it, but in low evening light the shadows bring the line out across the fields.

For riders this is lovely country. The Irthing valley and the hills towards Gilsland roll gently, with narrow lanes between drystone walls and hedges, short steep climbs and blind crests that demand some respect. Watch for gravel washed onto bends, mud from tractors, and sheep who regard the road as theirs. A few miles east, Lanercost Priory, founded in the twelfth century and partly built from Roman stone, makes a superb stop, and Birdoswald fort beyond it shows you what one of the wall's garrisons looked like.

Brampton is a small market town with an octagonal Moot Hall in the square, a couple of cafes, pubs and a fuel station; Edward I's sick body rested nearby on his last campaign against the Scots in 1307. Carlisle, about twelve miles west, has everything else, from bike shops to the castle and cathedral. Weather here comes in from the west and changes quickly, so even on a bright day keep waterproofs handy. On a fine evening, though, with the Pennines purple to the south and the Scottish hills hazy to the north, it is hard to imagine a nicer place to be on a bike.
t.hadrian s wall in wall mile 0@55.0,-1.5:
Wall mile zero is where Hadrian's Wall began, or ended, depending on which way you are riding, and it is in the most unlikely setting you could imagine: Wallsend, on the north bank of the Tyne, among terraced streets and the cranes of what was once one of the great shipbuilding rivers of the world. The town's name says it all. Here stood Segedunum, the easternmost fort of the wall, and its foundations have been laid bare beside the road, with a viewing tower that lets you see the whole plan at once, barracks, headquarters and gates, like a diagram on the ground.

A short stretch of wall has been reconstructed nearby, together with a Roman bath house, which gives a sense of what the frontier actually looked like before it was robbed for building stone. From here the wall ran some seventy-three miles west to Bowness-on-Solway, built in the 120s on the orders of the emperor Hadrian, who wanted, in his biographer's words, to separate Romans from barbarians.

The other history here is industrial. The Swan Hunter yards built ships for more than a century, including the liner Mauretania, which held the Blue Riband for crossing the Atlantic for twenty years. Shipbuilding has largely gone, but the scale of the river and its quays still impresses, and the Tyne bridges upstream in Newcastle, especially the Tyne Bridge and the tilting Millennium Bridge, are worth a look on the way through.

As a ride start, it is urban and slow at first. You will deal with traffic, roundabouts, bus lanes and a fair bit of stop-start before the city releases you westwards. The reward is the B6318, the Military Road, which General Wade built after the 1745 rising and which runs straight along the line of the wall for miles further on, roller-coastering over the crests with wide northern views. Wallsend has fuel, shops and plenty of cafes; Newcastle has everything else, including a famously lively evening. Grab a stottie, the local flat bread roll, before you go.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum between the fi:
Around Haltwhistle the wall country becomes the landscape everyone imagines: the Whin Sill, a long ridge of hard volcanic dolerite, rears up in a series of cliffs facing north, and the Romans used it as a ready-made rampart, running their stone wall along the very top. Between the crags and the road the vallum ditch runs across the fields as a broad, clear trench, and from any high point you can see the whole military system laid out: crag, wall, road and ditch side by side.

Walltown Crags, a few miles east of here, has some of the highest-standing wall on the whole frontier, climbing and dropping along the ridge in a way that looks almost impossible to build. Close by, at Carvoran, the Roman Army Museum explains how the garrisons lived, and Thirlwall Castle, a fourteenth-century tower built from Roman stone, stands ruined above the Tipalt Burn. Vindolanda, further east, is where the famous wooden writing tablets were found, including a birthday party invitation from one commander's wife to another.

The riding is superb. The B6318 Military Road is straight in plan but heaves up and down over the ridges like a wave, with blind crests that hide oncoming cars, so hold back a little and do not trust the far side. There are no hedges, the views go for miles and the wind can be strong and gusty on the exposed tops. Sheep wander freely in places. The A69 in the Tyne valley to the south is the faster, duller alternative. In summer, walkers' cars cluster around the car parks; on a weekday in May or September the road is wonderfully empty.

Haltwhistle, which proudly claims to be the centre of Britain, is a small stone town with a fuel station, a few cafes and pubs and a supermarket; it is your nearest reliable supply, as the Military Road itself has almost nothing. Hexham with its abbey is the bigger town further east. Weather can turn from sunshine to horizontal rain in the time it takes to put on gloves, so pack accordingly, and be careful on the wet cattle grids.
t.ming tombs@40.3,116.2:
North of Beijing, where the plain meets the first ridges of the Jundu mountains, thirteen emperors of the Ming dynasty lie buried in a broad valley chosen for its perfect feng shui: mountains behind, a gentle slope, water in front. The first to be buried here was the Yongle emperor, the ruler who moved the capital to Beijing and built the Forbidden City in the early fifteenth century; his tomb, Changling, is the largest and best preserved, with a magnificent hall supported by enormous columns of nanmu wood. UNESCO lists them with the other imperial tombs of the Ming and Qing dynasties.

The approach is along the Sacred Way, a long avenue lined with stone statues of animals, lions, camels, elephants and mythical beasts, some standing and some kneeling, and of military and civil officials, all carved in the fifteenth century to guard the route to the tombs. Walking it under the willows is a peaceful experience, far from the noise of the city. Dingling, the tomb of the Wanli emperor, was excavated in the 1950s, and visitors can descend into the underground palace, a series of vaulted stone chambers. The excavation was a mixed blessing: many of the artefacts were damaged by poor conservation, and during the Cultural Revolution the remains of the emperor and his empresses were destroyed. Since then, no other imperial tombs have been opened.

The landscape is pleasant, with orchards of persimmons and apricots, reservoirs and wooded hills. The Great Wall at Badaling and Mutianyu is not far away, and the roads through the mountains north of the tombs wind through valleys and over passes.

Riding a motorcycle in Beijing, however, is complicated. Foreigners need a Chinese licence and properly registered vehicle, and motorcycles face significant restrictions within the city, particularly bikes with non-Beijing plates. Organised motorcycle tours with local guides and permits are the realistic option for visitors. The roads to the tombs from the city are busy multi-lane highways, while the country roads further north are quieter and more scenic. Changping, six kilometres away, has fuel and all services. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; summer is hot and humid, and winter is cold, dry and windy.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum in wall mile 9:
Nine Roman miles west of the wall's starting point at Wallsend, the frontier is already climbing out of the Tyne valley, and here on the edge of Newburn and Heddon-on-the-Wall you can still find it in the fields. Emperor Hadrian ordered the wall in AD 122, a stone barrier across the narrowest part of northern Britain from the Tyne to the Solway, and behind it the army dug the Vallum, a broad ditch flanked by earth mounds that marked the military zone from the civilian south. On this stretch the Vallum is often easier to read than the wall itself, a long shallow trough running through the grass, especially when the evening light comes in low and picks out every bump.

At Heddon, a short ride west, a consolidated length of the broad wall survives at its full planned thickness, and it is the first proper chunk of masonry you meet heading out of Newcastle. Most of the rest round here went into farmhouses, churches and, famously, the Military Road. After the Jacobite rising of 1745, when government troops could not get an army across from Newcastle to Carlisle quickly enough, General Wade's engineers built a road straight along the line of the wall and used it as foundation and quarry. That road is the B6318, and it starts just beyond Heddon.

Which is good news for the ride. The Military Road is one of the great English motorcycling roads: dead straight in long sections, it rises and falls over every ridge like a roller coaster, with blind crests that hide tractors and walkers, so treat it with respect. Further west it runs alongside the best of the wall and the Whin Sill crags. Here at the eastern end you are still on the urban fringe, with Newburn, Throckley and the A69 close by. Newburn has its own place in history too: in 1640 a Scottish army forced the Tyne crossing here and went on to occupy Newcastle, one of the opening blows of the conflicts that led to the Civil War.

Practically, everything you need is within a few minutes. Newburn and the villages along the A69 have fuel, shops and takeaways, and Heddon has a pub with the wall almost at its door. If you are heading west, fill the tank here; between Heddon and Haltwhistle the choice thins out quickly.
t.hadrian s wall between walltown quarry e:
Of all the places where Hadrian's Wall still behaves like a wall, Walltown is one of the most dramatic. The masonry rides the crest of the Great Whin Sill, a sheet of hard dark dolerite that pushed up through the surrounding rock about three hundred million years ago and then weathered into a line of cliffs facing north. The Roman engineers simply put their wall on top of the cliff, so the stones rise and fall with the crags, dipping into gaps the locals call nicks and climbing out again. Stand up there on a windy day and look north towards the empty country of Northumberland and you understand exactly why they chose the line.

The quarry is a later chapter. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries the same tough whinstone was quarried for road stone, and the quarrymen took away a good chunk of the crag and the wall with it. When the work stopped the hole was landscaped into a small country park with a pond, reeds and picnic tables, and it makes a good place to leave the bike and walk west along the best-preserved stretch. Just down the road at Carvoran is the Roman Army Museum, and nearby the ruins of Thirlwall Castle were built partly of stones taken from the wall.

The riding is the Military Road, the B6318, at its finest, though here it runs a little south of the crags. It is long, straight in sections and full of dips and crests that hide oncoming traffic until the last moment. In summer you will share it with campervans and walkers crossing to footpaths, so keep your speed honest and watch the lay-bys. Westwards it drops towards Greenhead and the A69; eastwards it heads past Cawfields and Housesteads, where the wall views get even better. Wind is the constant up here, often strong enough to push a bike across the lane.

Haltwhistle, a few kilometres away in the South Tyne valley, has fuel, shops, cafés and a station, and it likes to call itself the centre of Britain. Brampton to the west also has fuel, and Hexham is the nearest bigger town if you need a proper supply run. Facilities at the quarry park are basic, so bring water and expect the weather to change at least twice before you get back on the bike.
t.kulangsu@24.4,118.1:
Kulangsu, or Gulangyu, is a small island across a narrow strait from the city of Xiamen, and the first thing to know is that you will have to leave your motorcycle behind: no motor vehicles are allowed on the island apart from a few electric service carts. You get there by ferry, and that is part of the charm. Once on the island, the noise of the city disappears, replaced by the sound of footsteps on narrow lanes, birdsong and, quite often, piano music drifting from an open window. Kulangsu is known as the island of pianos, with a long tradition of music and a piano museum.

After the Opium Wars, Xiamen was opened to foreign trade, and in 1903 Kulangsu became an international settlement, where consulates, churches, schools and the mansions of foreign merchants and wealthy Chinese returning from Southeast Asia were built. The result is a remarkable mixture of styles: colonial verandas, Art Deco villas, Chinese courtyards and buildings that blend all of them together, set among banyan trees, bougainvillea and gardens. The island was added to the World Heritage list in 2017. Sunlight Rock, the highest point, offers views over the island, the strait and the skyline of Xiamen.

Xiamen itself is a pleasant coastal city with a relaxed atmosphere, a university campus by the sea and the Nanputuo temple at the foot of the hills. Riding in the city, however, is complicated: like many Chinese cities, Xiamen restricts motorcycles in much of the urban area, and foreign riders need a Chinese licence and properly registered vehicle. The better riding lies inland, in the mountains of southern Fujian, where roads wind through tea plantations and forests towards the earthen tulou, the great round communal houses of the Hakka and other communities, which are also a World Heritage site and make a fine destination for a day or two.

Fuel, food and accommodation are plentiful in Xiamen. On Kulangsu itself, the lanes are full of small cafés, guesthouses, shops selling dried seafood and pastries, and stalls offering fish balls and oyster omelettes, a local speciality. Go early in the morning or in the evening to avoid the crowds of day visitors, who can make the main lanes very busy at weekends and holidays.
t.cueva de la vieja@39.0,-1.2:
In 1910 a local man led researchers to a shallow shelter above the plain of Alpera in Albacete, and the paintings they found there became some of the best known examples of Levantine rock art in Spain. The Cueva de la Vieja shows archers with feathered headdresses, women in long skirts, deer and goats, all painted with a sense of movement that still feels immediate. The nearby Cueva del Queso holds more figures. Both are part of the UNESCO listing for the rock art of the Iberian Mediterranean, and guided visits run from the village, so check times with Alpera's tourist office.

The shelter looks out over the Corredor de Almansa, a broad, high valley that has carried roads and armies between the Meseta and the coast of Valencia for centuries. In 1707 the Battle of Almansa, a few kilometres south, was a decisive moment in the War of the Spanish Succession. Today the corridor is lined with wind turbines, vineyards and almond orchards, and the Almansa castle, perched on a single rock, can be seen from far away.

Alpera itself, a village of about two thousand three hundred people, sits at the foot of the Sierra del Mugrón, and the climb to the shelters is a short walk up the hillside with wide views. The air here is dry and clear, and in spring wildflowers fill the margins of the fields.

Riding around Alpera mixes long, open roads across the plain with more interesting stretches into the hills. The road west to Carcelén and Alatoz crosses quiet farmland with very little traffic, while the route toward Ayora drops into the Valencian hills with better corners and more relief. Summer heat is strong, and wind on the high plain can be tiring. Winter mornings are often frosty, as this is high country at around seven hundred metres or more.

For fuel and food, Alpera has the basics, and Almansa, about twenty kilometres south, is a sizeable town with everything you need. Ayora, the nearest town of five thousand, lies seventeen kilometres east in the Valley of Ayora-Cofrentes. t.poyo inf de la cimbarra@38.4,-0.3:
Ten minutes inland from the beaches of El Campello and the high rises of the Alicante coast, the country changes completely. The hills behind San Juan and Mutxamel climb toward the bulk of the Cabeço d'Or, a limestone mountain whose name means the head of gold, and in its folds are small rock shelters with prehistoric paintings, among them the Poyo Inferior de la Cimbarra. Busot, the village at the foot of the Cabeço d'Or, is known for the Canelobre caves, a huge cavern with a vault high enough that concerts are held inside. Aigües, nearby, was once a spa and sanatorium town, and its abandoned grand building still looks down from the hill.

Roads climb out of the urban sprawl into twisting, sometimes narrow lanes through the hills, with good views back to the sea and over the Alicante bay. Surfaces vary from smooth to patched, and gravel in corners is common. Weekends bring cyclists in numbers. Further inland, Xixona, home of turrón, the almond nougat Spain eats at Christmas, is a short ride away, and the road beyond it toward Alcoy has some of the best corners in the province.

t.abrigo del mediodia i@38.7,-1.3:
North of Yecla, where the Murcia region meets Albacete, the land rises into a series of isolated limestone hills above a wide, dry plain of vineyards and almond groves. The rock shelters scattered through this country, including the Abrigo del Mediodía, are part of the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean Iberian rock art. Traffic is very light, surfaces are generally good, and you can see weather coming from a long way off. Wind can be strong. The road from Yecla toward Jumilla, another wine town, runs through vineyards and offers a good loop.

t.los paradores@37.8,-2.0:
The far north of Almería province is not the desert most people imagine. Around Vélez-Blanco and María the land rises into the Sierra de María-Los Vélez Natural Park, a range of limestone peaks with pine and holm oak forest, high plains of cereal and almond and villages that can see snow in winter. Los Paradores is one of the rock art sites in this area, part of the UNESCO listing of the Mediterranean Iberian rock art, and the region holds one of the most famous painted shelters in Spain, the Cueva de los Letreros, home of the Indalo, a stick figure holding an arc over its head that has become the symbol of Almería.

Vélez-Blanco is a white village below a dramatic Renaissance castle built by the first Marquis of Los Vélez in the early sixteenth century. Fuel and food are best found in Vélez-Rubio, a town of seven thousand with a baroque church that seems far too big for it, and Vélez-Blanco has bars and small restaurants. t.abrigo de las canadas ii@38.1,-2.4:
Nerpio is about as remote as mainland Spain gets. The village sits in the far southwest corner of Albacete province, in the Sierra de Segura, where the mountains of Andalusia, Murcia and Castilla-La Mancha meet, and the rock shelters scattered around it make up one of the richest concentrations of prehistoric art in the region. The landscape is magnificent and harsh: limestone ridges, deep river valleys, pine forest and, in the valley around Nerpio, terraces of walnut trees that the village is known for. Some are well maintained, others narrow and broken, and the distances between villages are long. Visits to the rock art are organised from Nerpio, often with a guide, and require some walking over rough terrain. The shelters are fenced to protect the paintings. The village itself has bars and a few places to eat, serving hearty mountain food such as stews, lamb and cured meats. Winters are cold here and snow is possible, while summers are warm but fresher than the plains below. Come in May or October if you can, when the light is soft and the terraces are green.
t.abric de tollos ii o de cambriquia@39.1,:
Bicorp is famous for a single painting. In the Cuevas de la Araña, a short walk from the village, a figure clings to ropes on a cliff, reaching into a hole surrounded by bees: one of the oldest known depictions of honey gathering in the world. The Abric de Tollos, also called Cambriquia, is another of the painted shelters around Bicorp, in the deep gorges of the Valencian interior, one of the World Heritage rock art sites of the Spanish east.

Bicorp and its neighbour Quesa are small villages in the Canal de Navarrés, a valley west of Xàtiva surrounded by rugged hills and canyons. The Júcar and its tributaries have cut deep ravines through the limestone, creating pools and waterfalls. Near Quesa, the Charco Azul and other natural pools in the river are popular swimming spots in summer, and Bicorp has an interpretation centre explaining the rock art. The hills are covered with pine, scrub and rosemary, and wild boar and mountain goats live here.

The riding in the Canal de Navarrés and the surrounding hills is excellent and quiet. Roads climb and twist through the mountains, with good surfaces and very little traffic, and the views over gorges and valleys are dramatic. The road west from Bicorp toward the Júcar, and the routes through the Sierra de Enguera, are especially good. Watch for gravel and occasional rockfall, and take care in summer, when the heat can be intense.

Fuel and services are limited in the villages. Navarrés, about ten kilometres away, is a bigger village with more facilities, and Enguera, twenty one kilometres away, is a town of five thousand with fuel and shops. Xàtiva, further east, is a historic town with a castle and everything you might need. In the villages, look for the inland version of gazpacho, a hot dish of torn flatbread and game, and rice cooked over vine cuttings.
t.cova del mansano@38.7,-0.1:
Every cyclist in Europe seems to know the Coll de Rates, and that is a good hint for motorcyclists too. The climb starts in Parcent, a few kilometres from the Cova del Mansano, and winds up the mountainside in a long sequence of smooth, well surfaced bends to a pass with a view over the whole Vall de Pop and the sea beyond. The rock shelter itself sits in the hills around Jalón, Alcalalí and Parcent, a short walk from the road, and its paintings belong to the same World Heritage group as the other Levantine shelters of the coast.

The Vall de Pop, also called the Jalón valley, is a broad valley of vineyards, almond and orange groves, between the mountains of the Marina Alta. Jalón, or Xaló in Valencian, is known for its wine cooperative and bodegas, selling local moscatel and red wines, and for its large Saturday market, a rastro where everything from antiques to vegetables changes hands. Alcalalí has a medieval tower in its centre, and Parcent is a quiet village at the foot of the Coll de Rates.

Riding here is a joy, but share the roads. The Coll de Rates and other climbs are full of cyclists, especially in winter, when professional teams train on the Costa Blanca. Take care on blind bends and give them room. Beyond the pass, the road continues to Tàrbena and on into the mountains toward Callosa d'en Sarrià and Guadalest, with more bends, views and quiet villages. The surfaces are generally excellent, and traffic is light outside the main valley.

Fuel is available in Jalón and in Benissa, nine kilometres away, a town of thirteen thousand with all services. Restaurants in the valley serve good local food, and the bodegas are worth a stop if you are not riding afterwards. Spring is the best time to visit, when the valley is green and flowers are blooming; summers are hot, but the mountain air is fresher than the coast.
t.las casas de las ingenieros il@38.2,-2.3:
Water from these mountains ends up in the taps of Cartagena. The Taibilla river, which rises in the hills above Nerpio, feeds the canals of the Mancomunidad de los Canales del Taibilla, built in the twentieth century to supply towns across Murcia and beyond, and a name like the engineers' houses hints at how much that project marked the valley. Las Casas de los Ingenieros II is a rock shelter near Nerpio, one of the many painted sites in this remote corner of the Sierra de Segura.

The valley around Nerpio is a green oasis in dry mountains. Walnut trees line the river terraces, and the village is known for its nuts, sold in sacks in autumn. The surrounding ridges are covered with pine and juniper, cliffs rise above the valley, and the sky is huge. Letur, to the north, is a village with a Moorish layout of narrow alleys, arches and streams running through the streets, and Yeste, to the northwest, has a castle and a big reservoir nearby.

Traffic is minimal, and you can ride for an hour without meeting another vehicle. The route east toward Moratalla crosses high, wild country, and the road north toward Yeste and Letur follows valleys and ridges. Rockfall and gravel are common, and in winter snow and ice can close higher roads.

Yeste, about twenty kilometres away, is bigger than Nerpio. Fill up before entering the sierra and carry water and food. In Nerpio and Yeste, bars and restaurants serve mountain food, lamb, game, stews and cured meats, and the local walnuts appear in desserts.
t.cueva del esquilo@38.2,-2.1:
The border between Albacete and Murcia runs through a tangle of mountains here, and the villages of Socovos, Férez and Letur sit among them like small islands.
