Like most of the rock art in the region, it is protected and best visited with local guidance; the town halls and tourist offices of the surrounding villages are the place to ask.

Letur is the jewel of the area: a village of Moorish origin, built on a rock above a gorge, with narrow lanes, arches and water channels that still carry springs through the streets. Socovos has the ruins of a castle that belonged to the Order of Santiago, which held much of this frontier land after the Christian conquest in the thirteenth century. The Segura river and its reservoirs lie to the north and east, and the Cenajo reservoir, a long blue lake among pine forests, is a fine sight from the road.

The roads here twist through pine covered mountains and deep valleys with very little traffic. Some sections are narrow and steep, others wide and flowing. The route from Moratalla toward Socovos and Letur is particularly good, with views over the mountains and valleys. Watch for gravel, especially after storms, and for animals on the road. Weather can change quickly, and in winter the higher roads can be icy.

Moratalla, sixteen kilometres away in Murcia, is the nearest town of size, with fuel, food and lodging, and a castle above its old streets. Calasparra, further east, is known for its rice, grown in terraced paddies along the Segura and protected by its own denomination; a rice dish here is a must. In the villages, expect simple bars and restaurants with local food, including lamb, game and stews. April, May and October bring the kindest weather, with green slopes and cool mornings.
t.hadrian s wall@55.0,-2.4:
North of Haltwhistle the land rises in a series of dark ridges, and along their crest runs the most dramatic surviving stretch of Hadrian's Wall. Built from AD 122 on the orders of the emperor Hadrian, the wall ran some seventy three miles from the Tyne to the Solway, with forts, milecastles and turrets along its length, and here, between Walltown Crags and Birdoswald, it climbs and drops along the edge of the Whin Sill, a band of hard volcanic rock that forms natural cliffs facing north. The wall is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage Site.

The landscape here is wild and open, with moorland, crags and loughs, small lakes in the hollows, and big skies. Sheep graze up to the wall, and curlews and lapwings call in spring. The weather changes fast, and a sunny morning can turn to rain and wind in minutes. Walking along the wall, you feel the scale of the Roman achievement and the remoteness of the frontier.

The B6318, the Military Road, runs along the wall, laid out by the army in the years after the Jacobite rising of 1745, when the government needed to move troops between Newcastle and Carlisle quickly, and long stretches sit right on top of the Roman stones. It is straight in places but has blind crests and dips that hide oncoming traffic, so take care. Sheep on the road are common, and the road can be busy with tourists in summer. The Roman Army Museum at Walltown and the fort at Birdoswald are both worth a visit.

A few miles east, toward Steel Rigg, the wall dips into Sycamore Gap, whose famous tree, a landmark for generations, was illegally felled in 2023, causing national outrage. The stump and its fresh growth still draw visitors.

Haltwhistle, four and a half kilometres away, is a small town that claims to be at the centre of Britain, with fuel, shops and cafés. Hexham, twenty kilometres east, has more services and a fine abbey. In the pubs, try a pint of local ale and a hearty pie, and bring waterproofs: the weather here is rarely kind for long.
t.corbridge@55.0,-2.0:
Two thousand years ago, Dere Street, the Roman road heading north into Scotland, crossed the Tyne here, and a town grew up around a supply base just behind Hadrian's Wall. Coria, now called Corbridge Roman Town, was a bustling place with granaries, temples, workshops and a main street, and its remains, managed by English Heritage, are among the most important Roman sites in Britain. The museum displays finds including the Corbridge Hoard, a chest of armour and equipment, and the Corbridge Lion, a sculpture of a lion attacking a stag.

The modern village of Corbridge is a handsome place of stone houses, a market square, a medieval church with a defensive pele tower, and a seventeenth century bridge over the Tyne, which was the only bridge on the river to survive the great flood of 1771. The village has a range of independent shops, cafés and pubs, and it is a popular stop for walkers and visitors to Hadrian's Wall.

The riding in the Tyne valley is pleasant, with roads winding along the river and climbing into the hills on either side. The A69 runs along the valley as a fast main road, but smaller roads offer more interest, rising onto ridges where the whole dale opens below. North of the river, the roads climb toward the wall and the moors, with open views and quiet roads. The weather can be changeable, and the roads can be wet and muddy, especially in winter.

The town's position on the river has shaped its whole story. After the Romans left, the site of Coria became a quarry, and its dressed stones turn up in Hexham Abbey and in the walls of local farms. In the Middle Ages Corbridge was rich enough to be a target, burned by Scottish raiders more than once, which is why the vicar's pele tower beside the churchyard has walls so thick. Today the Tyne here is a broad, clear salmon river, and in autumn you may see fish leaping at the weirs upstream.

Corbridge has a small range of services, and Hexham, four and a half kilometres away, has more, including fuel and a fine abbey. Tea rooms around the square do a fine scone, and the pubs pour ales from Northumberland breweries. The Roman town is open to visitors, and the museum is well worth a visit.
t.nether denton roman fort@55.0,-2.6:
Before Hadrian built his wall, the Romans controlled northern Britain with a line of forts along a road called the Stanegate, which ran from Corbridge to Carlisle, and Nether Denton was one of them. The fort, on a hill above the River Irthing near Gilsland, is now marked only by faint earthworks around the small church of Nether Denton, which stands on the site. It is a quiet place, with only rooks and sheep for company.

The Irthing valley is green and wooded, with farms, villages and the river winding through. Nearby, Lanercost Priory, an Augustinian priory founded in the twelfth century, was built partly with stone from Hadrian's Wall, and its ruins and church are well worth a visit. Gilsland, a few kilometres east, is a small village near one of the best preserved stretches of the wall, and Birdoswald Roman Fort, nearby, has a museum and the remains of a large fort.

The riding here is pleasant, with quiet country roads winding through the valley and climbing onto the moors. The A69 runs along the valley to the south, a fast main road, but the smaller roads are more interesting, with views over the valley and the hills. The roads can be narrow and muddy, with sheep and tractors, and the weather can change quickly.

The Stanegate forts were in some ways the first draft of the frontier. When Hadrian decided to build a continuous barrier a few kilometres to the north, the soldiers stationed in places like Nether Denton were among those who supplied the labour, and the wall followed the high ground while the old road kept to the valley. Walking up from the river you can still see why this hill was chosen: it commands the crossing and looks far along the Irthing in both directions.

Brampton, seven kilometres away, is a small red sandstone market town with fuel, a few cafés and an octagonal Moot Hall in its square, and Carlisle, twenty one kilometres away, has everything else, including a castle that has faced the Scots for nine centuries. The fort itself is on private land, but the church and the views can be enjoyed from the lane.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum between the b6:
Out at the eastern end of the frontier, the Wall leaves the moors behind and runs through gentle farmland toward Newcastle, and most of what survives here is not stone but earth: the vallum, a broad ditch flanked by banks that the Romans dug just south of the Wall along almost its entire length. Between the Tyne and the Military Road, near Heddon-on-the-Wall and Rudchester, the vallum can be traced in the fields as a long hollow, and the Wall itself lies largely under the road or as low courses in the grass. Its purpose is still debated, but most scholars see it as a boundary marking the military zone, controlling who could approach the Wall.

The B6318, the Military Road, follows the line of the Wall west from Heddon, built straight over its foundations in places. It is a fast road, with long straights and sudden dips, and it is popular with bikers, so expect company on sunny weekends and watch your speed. The surrounding country is rolling farmland with woods and hedges, and the views stretch south over the Tyne valley.

Down in the valley, Wylam is the birthplace of George Stephenson, the railway pioneer, and his cottage beside the old wagonway is a National Trust property. Prudhoe has a medieval castle above the river. The Tyne here is a broad, peaceful river, and the riverside paths are popular with walkers and cyclists.

At Heddon-on-the-Wall, a substantial stretch of Wall survives above ground, and further west the fort of Rudchester lies under fields. The Wall at Heddon is a good place to start a journey westward, as the landscape becomes wilder and the remains more impressive. The weather can be changeable, and the roads can be wet and slippery.

Prudhoe, seven kilometres away, has fuel and services, and Newcastle, not far east, has everything. Corbridge and Hexham, further west, are attractive towns with pubs, cafés and shops. In the pubs, try a pint of local ale and a stottie, a flat bread roll typical of the North East, filled with ham and pease pudding.
t.roman quarry inscription on queen s crag:
The Wall needed millions of dressed stones, and the Romans quarried them close to where they were needed. On Queen's Crags, a ridge of sandstone north of the Wall near Housesteads, they left a calling card: an inscription cut into the rock face, one of several known Roman quarry inscriptions along the frontier, recording a soldier or unit at work. It is a small, weathered thing, hard to find without directions, but it is a direct link to the men who cut the stone for the Wall.

Queen's Crags lies just north of the line of the Wall, across a boggy valley from the dramatic ridge of the Whin Sill. To the south is Housesteads, the best known fort on the Wall, perched on a slope with views over the countryside, and Broomlee Lough, a small lake below the crags. Local legend says that King Arthur and his knights sleep in a cave beneath Sewingshields Crags, a little to the east, waiting to be awakened by someone who blows a horn and cuts a garter with a sword. Another story says that the queen of the name, Guinevere, threw a stone at Arthur from these crags, and that it lies in the fields still.

The landscape here is wild and open, with moorland, bogs, crags and loughs, and big skies. It is one of the most remote parts of the Wall, and walking out to the crags involves crossing rough, wet ground. Curlews, lapwings and skylarks fill the air in spring, and the light on the crags in the evening is lovely.

The roads nearby are few: the B6318 runs along the Wall to the south, and minor roads lead north into the forests and moorland of Northumberland National Park. The Military Road is fast and fun but has blind crests and dips, and sheep wander onto it. The weather can change quickly, and fog and rain are common.

Haydon Bridge, eight kilometres away, is a small village with a shop and a pub, and Haltwhistle and Hexham have fuel and services. Housesteads has a café and a museum. Bring waterproofs and good boots if you plan to walk to the crags.
Rivers move, and the Irthing at Willowford proves it. When the Romans built the Wall here, they carried it across the river on a bridge, and the massive stone abutment of that bridge survives on the east bank, now well away from the water, because the river has shifted west over the centuries. Nearby, the earthwork outline of a Roman temporary camp, one of many marching camps built by units on campaign or on construction duty, lies in the fields. Temporary camps were ramparts of turf and ditches thrown up for a few nights or weeks, and their faint shapes are often best seen from the air or in low winter light.

A short walk along the Wall from Gilsland brings you to the bridge abutment, past a good stretch of Wall and a turret. Across the river, the Wall climbs steeply to Birdoswald, one of the best preserved forts on the frontier, with a museum and a café. The Irthing gorge below is wooded and beautiful, with the river running over rocks and the sound of water everywhere.

Gilsland is a village split between Cumbria and Northumberland, with a long history as a spa: its sulphur springs drew visitors in the nineteenth century, and the poet Walter Scott met his future wife here. Poltross Burn milecastle, at the edge of the village, is one of the best preserved milecastles on the Wall. Thirlwall Castle, a ruined medieval tower built with stone from the Wall, stands a little to the east.

The roads around Gilsland are quiet, narrow and winding, with farmland and moorland, and the B6318 runs nearby. The roads can be wet and muddy, and sheep are common. The weather here can be wild, with strong winds and rain from the west, but on a fine day the views over the Irthing valley and the Pennines are superb.

Haltwhistle, eight and a half kilometres away, is where to fill the tank and find a meal, and Brampton, ten kilometres away, has more. Carlisle, twenty five kilometres away, has everything. Gilsland has a pub and accommodation, and Birdoswald has a café.
t.roman signal station on mains rigg@55.0,:
On a low ridge south of the Wall, near the village of Low Row, the foundations of a Roman stone tower sit in a field with a commanding view up and down the Irthing valley. The signal station on Mains Rigg belonged to the system of the Stanegate, the road that ran from Corbridge to Carlisle before the Wall was built, and it allowed messages to be passed between forts by fire, smoke or flags. From here, on a clear day, you can see for miles: west to Carlisle, east toward the Pennines and north over the Wall.

The Irthing valley here is a lovely mix of farmland, woods and river, with the moors rising to the north and the Pennines to the south. It is quiet country, with small villages and farms. Talkin Tarn, a small glacial lake near Brampton, is a popular spot for walking, rowing and picnics, and the woods around it are full of birds.

The riding here is gentle and pleasant. The A69 runs along the valley as the main road, fast and busy, but the minor roads that branch off it are quieter, winding through farmland and villages with good views. The roads can be narrow, with high hedges and tractors, so take care. North of the valley, roads climb onto the moors, with wide open views and few cars.

Brampton, nine kilometres away, is a market town with fuel, shops and cafés. Carlisle, twenty three kilometres away, has everything, including a cathedral, a castle and the Tullie House museum, which tells the story of the Wall and the Border reivers.

The signal station is on private land but can be viewed from a footpath. The weather here can be wet and windy, so bring waterproofs. Spring and early summer are lovely, when the hedgerows are full of flowers and the lambs are in the fields.
t.grindon school roman temporary camp@55.0:
Marching soldiers did not sleep in the open. Every night on campaign, a Roman army dug a ditch and threw up a rampart around its tents, and the faint outlines of these temporary camps are scattered across Northumberland, some dating from the conquest of the north, others from the building of the Wall. The camp near the old Grindon school, close to the Stanegate a little north of Haydon Bridge, is one of these. You will need a good map and a low sun to make out its banks.

The country around here is a mix of farmland and moorland, with the South Tyne valley to the south and the Wall to the north. Haydon Bridge, on the South Tyne, is a village with an old stone bridge, and Langley Castle, a restored fourteenth century tower house now a hotel, stands to the south. Newbrough and Fourstones are small villages along the Stanegate.

The roads here are quiet and pleasant, with gentle curves, farmland and views. The B6318 runs along the Wall to the north, and the A69 runs along the valley to the south. The minor roads in between are narrow and winding, with sheep and tractors, and they can be muddy. The weather can be changeable, with rain and wind common.

Haydon Bridge, six kilometres away, has a shop and a pub, and Hexham, thirteen kilometres away, has filling stations, shops and somewhere to eat. Vindolanda has a café and a museum. The camp itself is in a field and best seen from the road or a footpath.
t.baeza@38.0,-3.5:
Baeza is a town of honey-coloured stone set on a ridge above a sea of olive trees. From its edge, the view drops over the Guadalquivir valley to the dark line of the Sierra Mágina, and in every direction the hills are covered with orderly rows of olives, millions of them, the source of more olive oil than almost anywhere on earth. The town's Renaissance palaces, churches and squares, together with those of neighbouring Úbeda, make up a World Heritage site.

In the sixteenth century, Baeza and Úbeda were wealthy towns, and their nobles and clergy hired some of the best architects of the Spanish Renaissance to build palaces, churches and public buildings in the new Italian style. In Baeza, the Plaza del Pópulo with its Lions' Fountain, the cathedral, the old university and the Jabalquinto Palace, with its extravagant Gothic façade studded with stone points, are highlights. The poet Antonio Machado taught French here for several years in the early twentieth century, and his classroom in the old university has been preserved.

The riding around Baeza is excellent. The roads through the olive groves are winding and hilly, with good surfaces and little traffic. Head south towards the Sierra Mágina, or east towards Cazorla, where the roads climb into the mountains of the Sierra de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park, the largest protected area in Spain. These are great motorcycling roads, with tight bends, steep climbs and spectacular views. Summer is very hot, so ride early or late in the day. Spring and autumn are ideal.

The olive harvest takes place from November to January, and the whole region is busy with workers, tractors and mills. Many mills offer tastings and tours, and the oil is excellent, especially the early harvest oils with their green, peppery taste. In the evening, the stone of Baeza glows golden in the sunset, and the narrow streets are pleasant to wander.

Baeza has fuel, restaurants and accommodation. Úbeda, a few kilometres east, is larger and equally beautiful. In the bars, tapas are often free with a drink, and you should try local specialities like andrajos, a stew of flatbread and hare, or simply bread dipped in fresh olive oil.
t.maina@37.7,-1.5:
Maina is an obscure name on the map in the Murcian hills north-west of Totana, where the Sierra Espuña rises above the valley of the Guadalentín. It refers to a rock shelter or painted site in the dry limestone country, part of the cluster of prehistoric art sites around here included in the World Heritage listing of Levantine rock art. As with many such places, there is often little to see without a guide, but the landscape around it is worth the ride.

The Sierra Espuña is a green island in a dry region, a mountain range covered with pine forests that were planted in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries to stop erosion and flooding. Today it is a regional park, with walking trails, viewpoints and old snow wells, the pozos de nieve, where snow was packed into deep stone pits in winter and sold as ice in the towns during summer. The highest peaks rise to over 1,500 metres, and the views from the top stretch to the sea.

The riding is very good. The roads that climb into the Sierra Espuña from Alhama de Murcia and Totana are twisting and steep, with hairpins, good surfaces and views over the forests and valleys. The road through the park itself is narrow and requires care, but traffic is light. The surrounding countryside is dry and hilly, with almond and olive groves, and the roads between the villages are quiet and fun. Summer is very hot, so spring and autumn are best.

Totana is known for its pottery, especially large earthenware jars called tinajas, once used to store oil and wine. The sanctuary of Santa Eulalia, the town's patron saint, sits in the hills just outside town, with a church decorated with colourful frescoes. Aledo, a tiny village on a rocky spur, has a medieval tower and a strange history as a Christian outpost deep in Muslim territory during the Reconquista.

Totana, about twelve kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Alhama de Murcia and Lorca are larger towns nearby, with Lorca's castle and baroque churches worth a visit. Try local specialities like michirones, a spicy stew of broad beans, or a plate of grilled lamb chops with a glass of Jumilla wine.
t.abrigo de la ventana i@38.2,-2.2:
High in the Sierra de Segura, where Albacete, Murcia and Jaén meet, the Taibilla river cuts a deep valley through limestone mountains, and the cliffs and shelters along its banks hide some of the finest prehistoric paintings in Spain. The Abrigo de la Ventana, the window shelter, is one of them, near the village of Nerpio, and it is part of the World Heritage site of Levantine rock art.

The shelters around Nerpio, including the famous Solana de las Covachas, contain hundreds of figures: archers, hunters, animals, and scenes of daily life, painted in red and black. The art is remarkable for its movement and detail. Nerpio has an interpretation centre, and guided visits are available to some of the shelters, which are protected by fences. The walk to the shelters is part of the experience, through pine forests and along the river.

This is remote country, and the riding is spectacular. The roads from Moratalla, Yeste or Caravaca to Nerpio wind through mountains and valleys, with tight bends, steep climbs and descents, and views over forests and gorges. The surfaces are generally good, but some roads are narrow and twisty, and traffic is very light. In winter, snow can fall at higher elevations, and summer can be hot in the valleys, though the mountains are cooler.

Nerpio is a small village known for its walnuts. The trees grow along the river, and some are centuries old, with huge trunks. The village has a church, a few bars and restaurants, and a peaceful atmosphere. The surrounding mountains are home to wild goats, deer, eagles and vultures, and the rivers are clean and clear.

Nerpio, about twelve kilometres away, has a shop, bars and a place to sleep, but do not rely on finding fuel there. Moratalla, about twenty-five kilometres away, is the nearest larger town with more options. Try local dishes like gazpacho manchego, a hearty stew of flatbread and game, or trout from the river. And buy a bag of walnuts before you leave.
t.cueva del encajero@37.8,-4.0:
Olives, and then more olives. Riding west out of Jaén towards Torredonjimeno you cross one of the most single-minded agricultural landscapes in Europe, a rolling grid of grey-green trees running over every hill to the horizon, broken only by white farmhouses and the occasional oil mill. Somewhere among these low hills near Villardompardo, the Cueva del Encajero is a small rock shelter with traces of prehistoric painting, one of the many scattered sites that make up the World Heritage listing of rock art in Spain's Mediterranean basin.

Do not come expecting a show cave with lights and a gift shop. Sites like this are modest, often fenced and sometimes accessible only with a local guide, and the paintings themselves, schematic figures in reddish pigment, can be hard to make out. What they offer is a sense of how long people have been living on these ridges, long before the Romans planted the first olive groves here and long before the Moors and Christians fought over the castles that crown the towns.

The castles are worth a look. Torredonjimeno has the remains of one in its old centre, and Martos, a few kilometres south, sits beneath a dramatic rock with a fortress on top. Jaén itself is overlooked by the castle of Santa Catalina, now partly a parador, from where the view over the olive sea and the Sierra Sur is tremendous. The cathedral in Jaén, a Renaissance masterpiece by Andrés de Vandelvira, is one of the grandest in Andalusia.

As riding goes, the countryside here is a gentle roller-coaster of quiet, well-surfaced roads through the groves, easy to string together into a loop. Things get more interesting towards the south, where the Sierra Sur de Jaén offers steeper, twistier roads and real mountain scenery. Summer heat can be oppressive by late morning, and in the harvest months from November onwards, tractors and trailers loaded with olives are everywhere, sometimes dropping fruit and mud onto the tarmac.

Torredonjimeno, about five kilometres away, is a solid little town with fuel, bars and shops. Torre del Campo and Jaén are close too. In the bars, order a pipirrana, a Jaén salad of tomato, pepper, egg and tuna, and dip your bread in the new oil if it is harvest time: bright green, grassy and almost spicy.
t.cerro de la caldera@38.3,-3.3:
The Sierra Morena marks the end of Andalusia, the hilly rampart that the old road from Madrid had to cross before dropping into the Guadalquivir lowlands. Cerro de la Caldera, a hill near Aldeaquemada in the north-east of Jaén province, sits in the heart of this frontier, in a quiet landscape of holm oaks, cork oaks, rockrose scrub and sandstone outcrops. Rock shelters in these hills hold schematic and Levantine paintings, and the area is part of the wider World Heritage listing of Iberian rock art.

The history here is thick with battles and journeys. Just to the west lies the gorge of Despeñaperros, the dramatic pass that carried the road and later the railway between Castile and Andalusia, with rock towers and steep walls rising above. Not far south, at Las Navas de Tolosa, a Christian coalition defeated the Almohad army in 1212, a turning point in the Reconquista. In the eighteenth century, King Charles III settled colonists from Germany and Flanders in new towns across the Sierra Morena to make the road safer, and Aldeaquemada was one of these planned settlements.

Near Aldeaquemada, the Cascada de la Cimbarra is a fine waterfall where the Guarrizas river drops through a gorge of quartzite, especially impressive after winter rains. The surrounding hills are wild and empty, home to deer, wild boar, eagles and, with luck, the Iberian lynx, which has made a comeback in the Sierra Morena thanks to conservation efforts.

The riding is quiet and enjoyable. Roads between Aldeaquemada, Santisteban del Puerto and Navas de San Juan run through the hills with gentle curves and good surfaces, and traffic is minimal. The old N-IV through Despeñaperros, now partly bypassed by the motorway, is a fun road in its own right, with tight bends and spectacular rock scenery. Summer is very hot, so ride in the morning or evening, and keep an eye out for wildlife on the roads at dusk.

Aldeaquemada is a tiny village with limited services. Santisteban del Puerto, about thirteen kilometres away, and Navas de San Juan have fuel and basic shops. La Carolina, on the main road, is a larger town with more options. In autumn and winter, the deer rut fills the hills with the roars of stags, an extraordinary sound in the stillness of the evening.
t.barranc de beniali abric l@38.8,-0.2:
The Vall de Gallinera is one of those valleys that seems to exist slightly outside time. Running east to west in the mountains of northern Alicante, it holds eight tiny villages strung along a single road, terraced slopes of cherry trees, and above them limestone ridges cut by steep ravines. The Barranc de Beniali is one of those ravines, and in a shelter on its walls prehistoric people painted figures that are now part of the World Heritage site of Levantine rock art. The valley next door, the Vall d'Ebo, is just as wild, and its Cova del Rull is a show cave full of stalactites.

This was Muslim country for centuries after the Christian conquest. The Moriscos, Muslims forced to convert, lived in these valleys until their expulsion in 1609, when the whole population was deported to North Africa. The rebellions and the emptying of the villages left a deep mark, and the remains of Morisco villages and terraces can still be found on the slopes. Later settlers from Mallorca and elsewhere repopulated the area.

The riding is fantastic. The road through the Vall de Gallinera from Pego up to the Port de Salem and beyond is narrow and winding, with tight bends, good views and very little traffic. The roads through the Vall d'Ebo and the Vall de Laguar are even more extreme, with steep climbs, hairpins and dramatic drops. Surfaces are generally good but narrow, so take care on blind corners. Spring is the best time, when the cherry trees blossom in a cloud of white, usually around March and April.

The landscape is a mix of terraced orchards, pine woods and rocky slopes, with the smell of wild herbs in the air. The mountains are home to eagles, wild boar and goats, and the views from the passes stretch down to the coast and the sea. In early summer, the cherries ripen, and the villages sell them by the roadside.

Pego, about nine kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel and shops. Villalonga and Adsubia are smaller villages with basic services. Pego also has a marshland nature reserve, the Marjal de Pego-Oliva, rich in birds. The local food is rustic and hearty, with dishes like olleta, a bean and vegetable stew, and the cherries are famous across Spain.
t.morro carrascal@38.7,-0.3:
Inland from Benidorm, barely half an hour from the tower blocks and beaches, the mountains of the Alicante interior rise steep and empty. Morro Carrascal is a rocky height in this country, near the villages of Benilloba, Sella and Benimantell, where the sierras of Aitana, Serrella and Mariola come together. Shelters in these mountains hold prehistoric paintings in both the Levantine and the older Macroschematic styles, and they belong to the World Heritage listing of Iberian rock art.

The landscape here is dramatic. Aitana, the highest peak in the province at over 1,500 metres, dominates the skyline, and the valleys below are terraced with almond and olive trees. The villages cling to hillsides, with white houses, narrow streets and churches. Guadalest, just to the south, is perched on a rocky outcrop with a castle and is one of the most visited villages in Spain, so expect crowds in summer. Penàguila, to the north, is quieter, with a castle and a beautiful garden.

The riding is exceptional. The CV-70 from Benidorm through Polop, Benimantell and over the Port de Confrides to Alcoy is a classic motorcycle road, with endless bends, climbs and views. The roads through Sella and over the Puerto de Tudons are equally fun, with tight hairpins and spectacular scenery. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel, cyclists and tourists in rental cars. In winter, snow can fall on the higher passes.

The area has a long history. The Moors terraced these mountains and built castles on the peaks, and many villages still have Arabic names. After the expulsion of the Moriscos in the seventeenth century, the villages were repopulated, and agriculture continued to be the main activity until the twentieth century. Today, many villages are partly abandoned, but some are reviving with rural tourism.

Benilloba, about seven kilometres away, has limited services. For fuel, Cocentaina and Alcoy to the north, or Callosa d'en Sarrià to the south, are the best options. The mountain villages are known for their olleta de blat, a stew with wheat and pork, and for local sausages and cheeses. Stop in a village bar for a coffee and a slice of torta, and enjoy the views before tackling the next pass.
t.los sacristanes@38.2,-2.4:
Los Sacristanes is a name given to a group of painted shelters in the empty uplands near Nerpio, in the south-western corner of Albacete province. It sits on the high, pine-covered ground between the Taibilla valley and the headwaters of the Segura, a place so thinly populated that the nearest town of any size is the better part of an hour away. The paintings here, like those across this region, belong to the World Heritage site of Levantine rock art, and they are best seen with a local guide from Nerpio's interpretation centre.

The country is high and wild. Much of it lies above a thousand metres, with forests of black pine and maritime pine, open ridges of juniper and stone, and deep ravines where streams run in spring and often dry up by late summer. Cortijos, isolated farmhouses, are scattered across the land, many abandoned when people left for the cities in the mid-twentieth century. Winters are cold, with snow and frost, and summers are hot but fresher than the lowlands.

The riding is for those who like solitude. Roads from Nerpio towards Yeste and Santiago de la Espada, deeper into the Sierra de Segura, wind through forests and over ridges, with tight bends, steep gradients and almost no traffic. Some roads are narrow and the surfaces vary, with gravel and potholes on minor routes. Fuel is scarce, so plan carefully. The Sierra de Segura, in Jaén, is part of the largest protected natural area in Spain, with dramatic limestone peaks and gorges.

Yeste is a beautiful village with a castle overlooking the valley, and Segura de la Sierra, further west, is perched on a hilltop with an imposing castle and views over the mountains. Both are well worth the ride. The region was a frontier between Christian and Muslim kingdoms for centuries, and the castles are reminders of that turbulent past.

Nerpio, about six kilometres away, is the nearest village, with a few bars and a small shop. Yeste, about twenty-five kilometres away, has more services. Carry water, snacks and fuel, and enjoy the silence. At night, the sky here is extraordinarily dark and full of stars.
t.throp roman fortlet@55.0,-2.6:
Throp is a farm name on the edge of Gilsland, in the narrow gap where the River Irthing slips between the northern Pennines and the moors that roll north towards the Scottish border. A small Roman fortlet stood here, close to the Stanegate, the road that ran along the valley before the Wall was built, and it is one of the many features that make up the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site. Not much remains to see, but the setting is classic Wall country.

Within a short ride you have some of the best Roman remains on the whole frontier. Birdoswald, perched above a meander of the Irthing, has the longest continuous surviving stretch of the Wall, a fort with well-preserved gates and granaries, and a farmhouse built over part of it. Below the fort, at Willowford, the Wall crosses the river, and the remains of the Roman bridge abutment show how the river has shifted since. Poltross Burn milecastle, near Gilsland station, is one of the best preserved, with traces of the steps that led up to the wall walk.

The riding here is quiet and enjoyable. The A69 between Carlisle and Newcastle is the main road, fast and busy, but the B6318, the Military Road, runs parallel to the Wall further north and is a fantastic ride, with long straights, sudden dips and crests and stunning views. It was built in the eighteenth century by General Wade after the Jacobite rising of 1745, partly on top of the Wall itself. Be careful: the road has blind summits and dips that hide oncoming traffic, and sheep wander freely. Minor roads around Gilsland are narrow, steep and twisty.

The Irthing valley is green and wooded, with the river cutting through sandstone gorges. The moors to the north are wild and empty, home to curlews, lapwings and skylarks in spring. In winter, the weather can be harsh, with snow and strong winds.

Haltwhistle, about eight kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafés. Brampton, about eleven kilometres away, is another small market town with services. Carlisle is the nearest city. The tea rooms at Birdoswald and in Gilsland are popular with walkers and riders alike, and there is nothing better after a cold ride than a pot of tea and a scone with jam and cream.
t.new lanark@55.7,-3.8:
Coming down the steep, wooded road from Lanark into the gorge of the Clyde, you see New Lanark all at once: a cluster of tall, plain sandstone mill buildings and tenements packed onto the riverbank at the bottom of the valley, with the water rushing past. It is one of the most remarkable industrial villages in Europe, founded in 1786 by David Dale and the inventor Richard Arkwright to harness the river for cotton spinning, and later turned into a social experiment by Dale's son-in-law, Robert Owen. It is a World Heritage site.

Owen believed that people were shaped by their environment, and that better conditions would make better workers and a better society. He refused to employ young children in the mills, opened the first infant school in Britain, provided healthcare and a village shop that sold goods at fair prices, and created the Institute for the Formation of Character, a community centre for education and recreation. His ideas influenced the cooperative movement, trade unions and early socialism. The mills continued to operate until 1968, and the village has since been restored, with a visitor centre, a hotel and a roof garden on one of the mills.

The Falls of Clyde, just upstream, are a series of waterfalls that powered the mills, with Corra Linn the most spectacular. A nature reserve protects the woodland along the river, home to peregrine falcons, otters and badgers. The walk from the village to the falls is beautiful, especially after heavy rain, when the water thunders through the gorge.

The riding around here is good. The roads in the Clyde valley wind through orchards, woods and villages, with gentle curves and good views. Head south into the Southern Uplands for more open, wild landscapes, with roads like the Dalveen Pass and the Mennock Pass to Wanlockhead, the highest village in Scotland, climbing through bare, rolling hills. Weather can be changeable, so be prepared for rain.

Lanark, just over a kilometre away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and its market town atmosphere is pleasant. The road down into New Lanark is steep and has tight bends, so take it slowly. The village has a café and a hotel restaurant where you can have a hearty Scottish lunch, perhaps a bowl of Cullen skink or haggis with neeps and tatties.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum in wall mile 1:
Heddon-on-the-Wall is aptly named. Just west of Newcastle, on a ridge above the Tyne, the village sits right on the line of Hadrian's Wall, and at its eastern edge is the longest surviving stretch of the broad wall still visible in the east, a section of thick, solid masonry about a hundred metres long, complete with the foundations of a medieval kiln built into it. Wall mile 10 is the stretch around here, counting westward from Wallsend, and it is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site. South of the wall, the vallum, a huge ditch flanked by earth mounds, can still be traced across the fields.

This is where the Military Road, the B6318, begins its run west across Northumberland, and for many riders it is the true start of a Wall journey. The road follows the line of the Wall closely, often sitting right on top of its foundations, with the vallum visible beside it. The first few miles are rolling farmland, with views south over the Tyne valley, and the road gets wilder and more spectacular as you head west towards Chollerford and the crags of the central section. Watch for dips and crests that hide oncoming traffic, and for cyclists, walkers and slow-moving tourists.

The Tyne valley below has a rich history of its own. At Newburn, just downstream, a Scottish army defeated English forces in 1640, during the Bishops' Wars, a prelude to the English Civil War. A few kilometres upstream at Wylam, George Stephenson, the railway pioneer, was born in 1781 in a small cottage that still stands beside the old wagonway, and the village has a small railway museum. The Tyne valley was the cradle of the railways, and the early wagonways carried coal from the pits to the river.

The landscape is gentle here, with farmland, woods and the river winding through the valley. The view from Heddon over the Tyne and the hills to the south is lovely, especially in the evening light.

Newburn, about one and a half kilometres away, and the outskirts of Newcastle have fuel, shops and restaurants. Heddon itself has a pub and a few services. Wylam and Corbridge, further west, are pleasant villages with cafés. Newcastle, just east, is a lively city with famous bridges over the Tyne and a great nightlife, if you fancy a night out after the ride.
t.the roman fort and associated civil sett:
Bowness-on-Solway is where Hadrian's Wall ends, or begins, depending on which way you are walking. This quiet village on the southern shore of the Solway Firth sits on top of the Roman fort of Maia, the second largest on the Wall, and its civilian settlement, which together make up the site on the label, part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site. Almost nothing of the fort survives above ground, as much of the stone went into the houses, church and farm buildings of the village, but you can find Roman stones reused in walls if you look closely.

The village is the western terminus of the Hadrian's Wall Path, a long-distance trail that runs eighty-four miles from Wallsend on the Tyne, and walkers arriving here often stop at a small shelter on the shore to celebrate or collapse. From the shelter, called the Banks Promenade, you look out over the Solway towards Scotland, which is very close here; at low tide, it once was possible to wade across at certain fords, a fact the Border Reivers knew well.

The church of St Michael, built partly from Roman stone, has an interesting story: its bells were stolen by Scottish raiders in the seventeenth century, who dropped them in the Solway while escaping. The villagers retaliated by stealing bells from Scottish churches across the water, and those bells are still said to hang in the church today. Every new minister of the Scottish parishes is supposed to ask for them back, and is refused.

The riding to Bowness is flat and scenic, along narrow lanes beside the salt marshes, with views over the firth and the hills of Scotland. The roads can flood at high tides, so check tide times and follow warning signs. Little traffic, huge skies and a sense of being at the end of something make this a memorable ride, especially in the evening light.

The nearest towns with services are Carlisle and Wigton, inland, or Silloth, along the coast. Annan and Eastriggs, nearer on the map, are across the water in Scotland, a long way round by road via Gretna. The pub in Bowness, popular with walkers, is a good spot for a pint and a hearty meal.
t.chapel rigg roman temporary camp@55.0,-2:
West of Haltwhistle, the land rises gently to the watershed between the Tyne and the Irthing, a broad, windy saddle of rough pasture known as the Tyne Gap, where rivers flow east to the North Sea and west to the Irish Sea. Chapel Rigg Roman temporary camp is one of several marching camps here, where Roman soldiers on the move dug a rectangular ditch and rampart for a night or a season, the earthworks now barely visible as low ridges in the grass. It is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site.

The camps make sense once you see the lie of the land. This gap is the easiest route across northern England, and the Romans used it for the Stanegate road, and later the Wall, both of which run nearby. Close by is Walltown Crags, where the Wall climbs along the top of a dramatic line of cliffs formed by the Whin Sill, a band of hard volcanic rock that runs across Northumberland. At Carvoran, below Walltown, the Roman Army Museum tells the story of the soldiers who served on the Wall, with reconstructions, films and artefacts.

Thirlwall Castle, a ruined medieval tower house built partly from Roman stones, stands above the Tipalt Burn near Greenhead, a reminder of the violent centuries when the Border Reivers raided back and forth across this land. Its name comes from the gap in the Wall through which raiders passed, the thirled or holed wall.

The riding here is excellent. The Military Road, B6318, runs along the line of the Wall from Greenhead eastwards, with long straights, steep dips and blind crests, and views over the crags and loughs. The A69 is faster but less interesting. Minor roads into the moors to the north and the South Tyne valley to the south are quiet and twisty. Beware of sheep, walkers and changeable weather.

Haltwhistle, about six kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafés. Greenhead, a small village nearby, has a tea room and a pub. Brampton and Hexham are larger towns with more options. The Roman Army Museum at Carvoran has a café, and the view from Walltown Crags at sunset is worth the short walk from the car park.
t.limestone corner roman temporary camp@55:
Limestone Corner is the most northerly point on Hadrian's Wall, and it is famous for a job left unfinished. The Romans dug a defensive ditch in front of the Wall along most of its length, but here they hit a band of hard whinstone, and after cutting some of the huge blocks free and splitting others with wedges, they simply gave up. The blocks still lie where they were left, some with the holes for the wedges visible, nearly nineteen centuries later. Nearby, the earthworks of a Roman temporary camp, where troops on the move once pitched their tents behind a ditch and bank, are part of the same Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site.

The B6318, the Military Road, runs right past, and the corner is a good place to pull in and take a short walk along the ditch. The views from here stretch north over rough grazing and moorland towards the Cheviots and the Scottish border, and south over the Tyne valley. On a windy day, which is most days, you understand why the soldiers stationed here were not always keen on their posting.

Just to the east lies Chesters, one of the best-preserved Roman cavalry forts in Britain, with a bathhouse on the bank of the North Tyne. To the west, the Wall climbs towards the crags of the central section, with Housesteads and the great cliffs of the Whin Sill. Carrawburgh, a short way west of Limestone Corner, has the remains of a temple to Mithras, a mysterious Persian god popular with Roman soldiers, with replicas of its altars in place.

The riding here is a highlight of any trip in northern England. The Military Road is a roller-coaster of dips and crests, long straights and sudden bends, with constant views. It demands respect: the dips hide oncoming traffic, sheep wander onto the road, and in summer it is busy with tourists. Ride it early in the morning or in the evening, when the light is low and the road is quieter.

Hexham, about nine kilometres away, has fuel, shops, restaurants and a fine abbey church with a Saxon crypt built partly from Roman stones. Acomb and Chollerford are smaller villages with pubs. The George Hotel at Chollerford, beside the bridge over the North Tyne, is a well-known stop for walkers and riders.
t.the vallum and early roman road between:
From the Military Road near Sewingshields, look south and you will see a long, straight scar running across the moorland: two mounds and a ditch, keeping pace with the Wall a short way behind it. That is the vallum, the great earthwork the Romans dug along the south side of the frontier to mark a military zone, and running alongside it here are traces of an early Roman road. This stretch near Housesteads is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site, and it is one of the places where the full layout of the frontier, wall, ditch, vallum and road, is easiest to read in the landscape.

Housesteads, just to the west, is the most famous fort on the Wall, perched on the edge of the Whin Sill escarpment with views over the moors. Its remains include barracks, granaries, the commander's house, a hospital and the best-preserved Roman latrines in Britain, with seats over a channel of running water. Further east, the Wall runs along the top of Sewingshields Crags, a wild, lonely stretch where legend has it that King Arthur and his knights sleep in a cave beneath the castle that once stood there, waiting to be woken.

To the north, Broomlee Lough and the other loughs, small lakes held in hollows between the ridges, reflect the sky and are home to waterfowl. South, the land falls away to the South Tyne valley, and Vindolanda, the fort famous for the wooden writing tablets found there, lies just a few kilometres away. The tablets, letters and documents written in ink, include a birthday party invitation from one officer's wife to another and give an extraordinarily intimate glimpse of Roman life on the frontier.

The riding here is wild and exposed. The Military Road climbs and dips along the line of the Wall, with views that stop you in your tracks. The weather can change quickly, with mist, rain and strong winds sweeping across the moors, and the road can feel very remote. Minor roads to the south, towards Bardon Mill and Haydon Bridge, are narrow and steep.

Haydon Bridge, about six kilometres away, has fuel and basic services. Hexham and Haltwhistle are the nearest larger towns. The National Trust café at Housesteads is welcome on a cold day, and there is a popular pub at Twice Brewed, a short ride west, where walkers and riders swap stories over a pint.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum between cheste:
The North Tyne comes down from the Kielder hills and the empty moorland of the border, and at Chollerford it passes beneath an old stone bridge on its way to meet the South Tyne near Hexham. Just west of the bridge, the Wall strides away uphill from Chesters fort, and this stretch, with the Wall and the vallum running together across farmland and woods, is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site.

Chesters, the Roman Cilurnum, is one of the most enjoyable sites on the Wall. It was a cavalry fort, guarding the crossing of the North Tyne, and its remains include the headquarters building with a strongroom beneath it, barracks, the commander's house and a bathhouse down by the river, one of the best preserved in Britain, with niches in the changing room walls that may have held clothes. Across the river, on the east bank, the massive abutment of the Roman bridge still stands. The site was preserved and excavated by John Clayton, a nineteenth-century Newcastle town clerk who bought up large stretches of the Wall to protect them, and the small Clayton Museum displays his collection of altars and inscriptions.

Just east of the river, Brunton Turret is one of the best-preserved turrets on the Wall, standing to an impressive height, with a section of the broad wall joining a narrower one, evidence of changes in plan during construction.

The riding here is lovely. The Military Road crosses the North Tyne at Chollerford and continues west towards the crags, while the roads north up the North Tyne valley towards Bellingham and Kielder are quiet and scenic, through woods, farmland and moorland. Kielder Water, the largest reservoir in England, and the vast Kielder Forest offer remote, winding roads with very little traffic. Dark sky enthusiasts come here for some of the best stargazing in Europe.

Hexham, about eight kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Acomb, a small village nearby, has a pub. Chollerford has a hotel and a café. The North Tyne is a famous salmon river, and you may see anglers casting from the banks as you cross the bridge.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum and their asso:
Gilsland is a village with a split personality. The boundary between Northumberland and Cumbria runs right through it, along the Poltross Burn, so the houses on one side are in one county and those on the other in another. Hadrian's Wall runs through it too, and the stretch of Wall, vallum and associated features around the village is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site. The Wall here crosses the narrow gorge of the burn and the railway line, with a milecastle right next to the old station.

In the nineteenth century, Gilsland was a spa, with a sulphur spring that drew visitors to a large hotel, and the village had a reputation for romance. Walter Scott is said to have proposed to his future wife, Charlotte Carpenter, at the Popping Stone, a rock beside the River Irthing just outside the village, in 1797. The stone is still there, though the original has been chipped away by souvenir hunters, and the story is told with pride.

The River Irthing winds through a wooded gorge below the village, with sandstone cliffs and pools, and the walk along the river is lovely, especially in autumn. The moors to the north are wild and empty, stretching towards the Scottish border and the Bewcastle Fells, a remote area with few roads and a famous Anglo-Saxon cross in the churchyard at Bewcastle, one of the finest surviving from the period.

For riding, Gilsland is a crossroads. The B6318 passes through the village, and minor roads lead north into the moors towards Bewcastle, narrow and twisting, with gates, cattle grids and sheep. The roads are quiet, but care is needed on the steep and narrow sections, and the weather can be harsh, with snow in winter and strong winds year-round.

Haltwhistle, about eight kilometres away, and Brampton, about eleven kilometres away, are the nearest towns with fuel and services. Gilsland has a pub, a tea room and a few B&Bs. If you have time, ride up to Bewcastle and see the cross, then loop back through the moors; the empty roads and big skies make it one of the most memorable rides in the area.
t.seatsides 1 roman temporary camp and sec:
Haltwhistle likes to call itself the centre of Britain, a claim based on being halfway between the north and south coasts of the island, and while other towns dispute it, nobody disputes that it is the best base for exploring the central section of Hadrian's Wall. Just north of the town, on the rough ground below the crags, Seatsides 1 Roman temporary camp is one of several marching camps where Roman troops on the move dug defences for a night or longer, and the label includes a section of the vallum nearby. It is all part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site.

The camps are best seen from the air, as faint rectangles in the grass, but on the ground you can sometimes make out the low ridges of the ramparts. Nearby, Cawfields, a former quarry now a picnic site with a small lake, has a fine stretch of the Wall climbing over the crags, with a milecastle perched on the slope. Great Chesters fort, a short walk west, is a quieter, less excavated site with an altar still standing in its ruins.

Haltwhistle itself is a small market town with a long history. In the reiving centuries it was a lawless place, and several of its old houses are fortified bastles, with thick walls and living quarters above a ground floor where livestock could be secured during raids. The parish church of the Holy Cross is one of the finest in Northumberland. South of the town, the South Tyne flows through a wooded valley, and roads lead up towards Alston and the North Pennines, an area of outstanding natural beauty with high moors and remote villages.

The riding here is varied and excellent. The Military Road runs just north of Haltwhistle, with dramatic views over the crags. The A689 from Alston to Brampton, and the roads over the North Pennines towards Weardale and Teesdale, include some of the highest and most scenic roads in England, with long climbs, sweeping bends and huge views. Hartside Pass, on the A686 near Alston, is a favourite with riders. Be prepared for changeable weather and strong winds on the high ground.

Haltwhistle, under four kilometres away, has fuel, shops, cafés and pubs. Haydon Bridge and Hexham are further east. On a fine evening, the walk up to Cawfields and along the Wall is a perfect way to end a day in the saddle.
t.the vallum and a british settlement betw:
There is a stretch of Hadrian's Wall that everybody has seen in photographs: the Wall riding the crest of the Whin Sill like a stone ribbon, plunging into dips and climbing again, with a long, dark lake, Crag Lough, beneath the cliffs. This is it, near Steel Rigg and Once Brewed, and the site on the label, the vallum and the remains of a native British settlement, lies just to the south in the shadow of the crags. It is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site, and it is a reminder that people lived here long before the Romans and kept living here while the soldiers watched over them.

Along the crags, Sycamore Gap was for generations home to one of the most famous trees in England, a lone sycamore standing in a dip in the Wall, seen in films and on countless postcards. In September 2023 it was illegally felled overnight, causing national outrage. The stump remains, and seedlings from the tree are being grown and planted elsewhere, but the gap feels emptier now.

The Sill, a national landscape centre at Once Brewed, has exhibitions about the geology, wildlife and history of the area, and a green roof you can walk on. South of the road, Vindolanda, the fort famous for its writing tablets, is still being excavated every summer, with volunteers digging in the trenches. The Roman Army Museum and Housesteads are a short ride away in either direction.

The riding here is spectacular. The Military Road runs just south of the crags, with views of the Wall and the loughs, and the minor road from Once Brewed down to Bardon Mill and the South Tyne valley is steep and twisty. In summer, the area is busy with walkers and tourists, so parking can be tricky. Early mornings and evenings are the best times to ride and walk, when the light is soft and the crowds are gone.

Haltwhistle, about seven kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafés. Haydon Bridge and Hexham are further east. The pub at Twice Brewed is a popular stop, with its own brewery, and there is a youth hostel at The Sill. Walk from Steel Rigg along the crags to Sycamore Gap and back, about an hour, for one of the finest short walks in Britain.
t.sunny rigg 1 roman temporary camp@55.0,-:
Haltwhistle sits in the Tyne Gap, the low cleft where the South Tyne and the old Carlisle road squeeze between the high moors of the north Pennines and the Whin Sill ridge, and that gap is the reason the Romans cared about this ground. A temporary camp is exactly what it sounds like: a ditched and banked enclosure thrown up for a night or a few weeks by an army on the march or on building duty, then abandoned. Most were ploughed flat long ago and now show only as crop marks or faint corners in a pasture, so go in expecting a field, not a ruin. What you get is the story, and the story is good.

Hadrian's Wall was begun around AD 122, and the legionaries who built it needed somewhere to sleep while they quarried, hauled and laid stone along this stretch. Camps like this one are the scaffolding of that effort. A few minutes away the real thing is easy to find: the Wall itself, the ditch-and-mound system called the Vallum behind it, and the forts and milecastles strung along the ridge towards Housesteads and Vindolanda. The Roman Army Museum near Greenhead is the sensible rainy-day stop, and Walltown Crags is where the Wall climbs most dramatically.

For riding, the lanes around Haltwhistle are narrow, hedged and often bumpy, with the occasional cattle grid and a fair number of sheep with opinions. The Military Road, the B6318, runs along the line of the Wall further east and is the classic run, though it gets busy with walkers' cars on summer weekends. Go early, or in the long light of a June evening, and the ridge views north into Northumberland are enormous. In winter the same moorland can ice over without warning, so treat any shaded dip with respect.

Haltwhistle has a few thousand people, a main street with cafes and a bakery or two, and petrol, so it is the natural place to top up and eat before you head out. The town likes to call itself the centre of Britain, a claim based on some creative measuring between the coasts, and it will cheerfully tell you so. If you need a bigger shop or a wider choice of fuel, Hexham is about twenty-four kilometres east along the A69, and Brampton and Carlisle lie to the west.
t.a mhoine hope loyal@58.4,-4.4:
There is a particular silence on the A836 above Altnaharra, and this stretch of it is the best place to notice it. The road here is single track with passing places, running north from Lairg toward the Kyle of Tongue, with Loch Loyal laid out beside it and the four-peaked ridge of Ben Loyal standing over the water. Hope is the other half of the name, Ben Hope, the northernmost Munro, which you will have glimpsed already as a long flat-topped wall to the north-west.

The name A' Mhòine means the moss or the peat bog, and that tells you most of what you need about the ground. This is northern Sutherland at its barest: blanket bog, lochans, grey granite, and a skyline with hardly a building in it. Ben Loyal is sometimes called the Queen of Scottish mountains because of its sharp, elegant profile, and it earns the title best in low evening light. Golden eagles and red deer are common enough here that locals do not remark on them. Midges, by contrast, get remarked on constantly between June and September, so keep your visor down when you stop.

The people are the quieter part of the story. The glens to the east, Strathnaver especially, were cleared of their tenants in the early nineteenth century to make way for sheep, and the ruins of the old townships are still there in the heather, with signposted trails. Further on, the village of Tongue has Castle Varrich on its small hill above the water, a ruined medieval tower once held by the Clan Mackay, and the causeway across the Kyle was only opened in the early 1970s, replacing a long detour round the head of the inlet.

Fuel is the thing to plan for. There is nothing up here but moorland, and the sensible rule is to leave Lairg with a full tank, or to treat Thurso on the north coast as the next sure thing in the other direction. Passing places are for passing, and also for letting the camper vans behind you go by; a wave helps. The surface is generally decent but narrow, and in rain or the first frosts of October you will want to leave yourself more room than the map suggests.
t.frontiers of the roman empire@55.0,-2.6:
The Wall comes into its own here, at the Irthing gorge, where the line runs along a high shelf above the river and you can see why the Romans picked it. Birdoswald fort, known to them as Banna, sits right on that edge, with a long view down the valley and the ground falling away to the water. The coordinates land you at the fort and the stretch of Wall that runs from it, near the village of Gilsland on the Cumbria and Northumberland border.

What is unusual here is the sequence you can read in the ground. In the west the first Wall was not stone but turf, built in the 120s, and parts of that turf rampart were later replaced in stone when the engineers got round to it. At Birdoswald you can still follow the changeover, and the fort's granaries and the long Wall running east and west make the fort one of the better places to understand how the system hung together. Down by the river, the abutments of a Roman bridge show where the Wall crossed the Irthing, and the river itself has since wandered off and left them stranded, which gives you a quiet lesson in how long two thousand years is.

On a bike the approach is a country lane with a few blind corners, narrow enough that you need to listen for anything coming the other way, and the surface can be patchy after winter. It is a good road for a steady, unhurried pace and a bad one for being clever. Come in the morning if you can, before the car park fills and while the dew still sits on the fort walls, and bring a layer, because the wind off the moor is rarely shy.

Gilsland has a long history as a modest spa village, and Sir Walter Scott is said to have met his future wife here in the late eighteenth century, a bit of local lore the village is fond of. Fuel is a different matter: this is a thinly settled corner, so fill the tank in Brampton or Haltwhistle, both a few kilometres off, or in Carlisle if you want a wider choice. The inscription as a World Heritage site came in 1987, and it covers the whole frontier rather than one fort.
t.skinsdale@58.2,-4.1:
Nobody lives in Skinsdale to speak of, which is more or less the point. The glen lies in the east of Sutherland, an empty fold of moorland and burn between the coast at Brora and Helmsdale and the great open bog country to the north-west, and the nearest towns of any size, Golspie, Brora and Dornoch, are all over twenty kilometres away. A road passes through this part of the country, but the glen itself is a place you look into rather than ride through.

What surrounds it is the Flow Country, the largest expanse of blanket bog in Europe, a wet, quaking mat of sphagnum moss that has been building for thousands of years and holds a great deal of carbon. In 2024 it was inscribed as a World Heritage site, which surprised some people who had always thought of it as wasteland. On a still, bright day it is anything but: pools shine like dropped coins, golden plover and greenshank call over the heather, and the smell is a mix of peat, bog myrtle and wet wool. In the right months you may see dragonflies hovering over the lochans.

The history here is as stark as the land. Nearby, in the Strath of Kildonan, a minor gold rush took place in 1869, when prospectors washed gold from the Kildonan Burn and a short-lived tented settlement sprang up, still remembered locally as Baile an Òir, the town of gold. It is a lovely, slightly absurd episode for a place that now has more deer than people.

The riding in this part of Sutherland is about space: long single-track and narrow two-lane roads, big gradients that you see coming for a mile, and plenty of places to pull in. The surface is mostly good, but sheep wander and the odd frost heave appears in spring. Pack a waterproof even on a clear morning, because the weather in this part of the Highlands changes its mind quickly, and take a flask if you can, because the cafes are few.
t.statue of mani in cao an temple@24.8,118:
Hidden in the hills behind the coast of Fujian is a small stone temple with a figure that should not exist. Cao'an is the last surviving Manichaean temple in the world, and its main statue shows Mani, the third-century Persian prophet who founded a religion that once stretched from Spain to China, in the form of a serene Buddha-like figure with long white hair and eyebrows. It was carved in the fourteenth century, during the Yuan dynasty, from a single piece of local stone, and its identity was recognised only in the twentieth century, when scholars matched it with texts.

Manichaeism taught that the world was a struggle between light and darkness, and it travelled along the Silk Road to China, where it was banned in the ninth century and survived in southern ports, such as Quanzhou, under the guise of other faiths. The temple, which sits on a hillside near Jinjiang, was built against a rock face, with a small roofed hall in front of the statue. The incense, the Chinese inscriptions and the surrounding woods give it a quiet, slightly secret feel, and the local people still treat it as a Buddhist shrine.

The temple is part of the Quanzhou heritage, listed by UNESCO in 2021 as an emporium of the world in Song and Yuan China, and nearby Shihu Dock was once a stop for ships in the sea trade. Quanzhou, known to Arab and Italian traders as Zaytun, was one of the world's biggest ports in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, and people of many faiths lived there, leaving mosques, temples and tombs.

Riding in this part of the Fujian coast is a matter of crowded expressways and busy local roads, with scooters, vans and heavy trucks sharing the lanes, and the hills around the temple give a little relief, with narrow lanes through lychee and tea trees. The wet months are the summer and early autumn, when typhoons can reach the coast, and spring and late autumn are better. Jinjiang, a large industrial city, is around seven kilometres away and has fuel and food in abundance. Fujian cooking is lighter than Sichuan, and oyster omelettes and fish balls are a local speciality. Bring a rain layer, and be quiet at the temple.
t.site of shunji bridge@24.9,118.6:
The bridges of Quanzhou were as astonishing as its port. In the Song dynasty, when the city grew rich on trade with Arabia, India and South-East Asia, its builders spanned the estuaries with long stone bridges set on huge foundations of boulders and oyster shells, and some of them are still standing. The Shunji Bridge, whose site is on our list, belongs to this tradition, and what remains is a place beside the river where engineers once solved a problem that seemed impossible: how to build a stone bridge across a tidal estuary with strong currents.

The best-known example is the Luoyang Bridge, built in the eleventh century, with piers shaped like boats to cut the current and oysters planted on the foundations to bind the stone together, which is a clever use of biology. The city's wealth also paid for the Kaiyuan Temple with its twin stone pagodas, the Qingjing Mosque from the early eleventh century, and the Temple of the Heavenly Empress, dedicated to Mazu, the goddess of sailors. A medieval Chinese ship, found buried in the mud in the 1970s, is displayed in the maritime museum. The city's heritage was listed by UNESCO in 2021.

The area is not obviously scenic today, because the coast has silted up and Quanzhou is now a busy modern city of nearly two million people, with factories, expressways and a dense network of roads. Riding is therefore a matter of patience, and the quiet moments come in the old streets around Kaiyuan Temple, where lanes lined with camphor trees and shops selling sweets and tea give a taste of the older city. In summer it is hot and humid, with typhoon risk, and the best months are October to December.

Fuel and food are no problem in a city of this size, and Quanzhou is known for its street snacks, including oyster omelettes, peanut soup and noodles with seafood. The tea from nearby Anxi, the home of Tieguanyin oolong, is a good thing to buy. Allow time for the maritime museum, and look carefully at the stone, because the little marks of the workers' hands are still visible.
t.colmenas@37.7,-2.1:
Vélez-Blanco is a white town under a limestone crag in the north of Almería province, with a Renaissance castle on the rock above it and the pine-covered Sierra María rising behind. The Colmenas label sits less than a kilometre away, in country of dry slopes, almond groves and scattered farms. I cannot tell you what exactly stands at the pin, but the area is known for its rock art, shallow shelters in the limestone painted thousands of years ago, which are part of the Levantine art of the Spanish Mediterranean recognised by UNESCO.

The famous image from this district is the Indalo, a small figure holding an arc above its head, taken from a painting in the nearby Cueva de los Letreros, and now the symbol of all Almería, seen on stickers and doorways from the coast to the hills. The castle itself, built in the early sixteenth century for the Marquis of los Vélez, is worth a visit for its fortified outer walls. Its Renaissance courtyard, with fine marble carving, was sold and removed in the early twentieth century, and it now stands in the Metropolitan Museum in New York, an odd fact to repeat over lunch.

Out on the bike it feels quiet and open. The roads between Vélez-Blanco, Vélez-Rubio and María are in generally good condition and have very little traffic, with long views over high plains, and the corners are gentle, shaped by the landscape rather than the engineers. At about a thousand metres the air is clear and cooler than the coast, and the Sierra María-Los Vélez Natural Park offers walking and birdwatching. Wind can be strong on the exposed sections, and winter brings frost and the occasional snow, so check conditions from December to February.

For fuel, the nearest sizeable town is Vélez-Rubio, about five kilometres away, with seven thousand people and several stations; Vélez-Blanco is smaller and may not have one. Both towns have bars serving coffee and tapas, and Almería province is one of the places where a drink still comes with a free small plate. Spring is the best season, when the almond blossom is out in February and the hills turn green; summer is hot and dry, and the best riding is early morning or evening.
t.cueva ambrosio@37.8,-2.1:
Cueva Ambrosio belongs to the high, empty north of Almería province, on the dry plateau where Andalusia runs into Murcia, fifteen or so kilometres out of Vélez-Blanco. This is a landscape of broad, pale fields, almond and cereal farms, low limestone ridges and long skylines, with the pines of the Sierra María to the south and almost nothing built on the horizon.

Archaeologists know the cave as a site of the Solutrean period, the Upper Palaeolithic, roughly twenty thousand years ago, when hunters here worked fine leaf-shaped stone points and, in some places, painted or engraved signs on the walls. Ambrosio is regarded as an unusually early example of such art in this part of Spain, much older than the rock paintings of the shelters nearby, which come from a later and quite different tradition. I cannot say what you will be able to see at the entrance, and access to sites like this is often managed or restricted, so ask in Vélez-Blanco before planning a walk.

For a rider the pleasure is solitude. The roads out of Vélez-Blanco toward the north are quiet, sometimes narrow, often with stretches of rough patching, and you may see no other vehicle for half an hour except a farmer's pickup or a flock of sheep. Corners open out with the land, and the wind is a constant companion, pushing sideways on exposed sections and carrying a smell of thyme and dry earth. The altitude, about a thousand metres or a little more, keeps the summer heat down, but the nights are cold and the winters can bring frost, even snow, so start late and keep a layer in the bag in spring and autumn.

There is nothing at the site itself, so the practical side starts before you leave. Vélez-Rubio, about twenty kilometres away, has seven thousand people and several stations, and is the best place to fill the tank and eat. Vélez-Blanco and María, up in the hills, are smaller but have bars serving coffee and local dishes, in particular migas and lamb, and the almond sweets of the area. Good months are April, May and October; in July the plateau can be punishingly hot and shadeless, and there is little water along the way, so carry some.
t.tejera@37.7,-2.1:
A tejera is a tile works, a kiln where roof tiles were baked from local clay, and the name is common across the dry south-east of Spain. The Tejera on your map is near Vélez-Blanco, about two kilometres from the village, in the country that falls away from the Sierra María towards the plain, where red soil, almond terraces and clumps of pine and juniper make up the view.

The range behind is a natural park, the Sierra María-Los Vélez, covering more than twenty thousand hectares of limestone mountains, with its highest summit, Maimón, at about two thousand metres. The park is quite unlike the green north of Spain, dry and sunny with a rocky skeleton showing through, but it holds a surprising mix of life, with golden eagles and eagle owls, Spanish ibex on the cliffs, and in spring a carpet of wild flowers, thyme and rock roses, giving the air a sharp scent. Walking trails climb from the villages, and the views from the ridge stretch across Almería, Murcia and Granada.

The two Vélez towns were once part of a lordship that the Marquises of los Vélez ran from the castle in Vélez-Blanco, and Vélez-Rubio, a few kilometres down the road, grew bigger and richer thanks to farming. Its parish church, the Iglesia de la Encarnación, is one of the largest and most ornate baroque churches in the province, and quite out of scale with the surrounding dry hills. It is worth a look inside if the doors are open.

On a motorcycle the area is enjoyable and uncrowded. The road between Vélez-Rubio and Vélez-Blanco, and the one climbing towards María, offer easy, flowing bends with long views, and the traffic is local, with an occasional tractor or goat flock. At nearly a thousand metres the air stays fresh, but nights are cold in spring and autumn and winter brings frost and the occasional snowfall. The wind blows hard across the plateau and can be a nuisance on the open stretches. Come in April and May or September and October, and if you must come in July, ride before eleven.

Vélez-Rubio, with seven thousand people, is the town for fuel, supermarkets and bars, and Vélez-Blanco has a couple of restaurants where lamb and migas, fried breadcrumbs with peppers and sausage, are on the menu. Ask for a tapa with your drink, as is the custom in Almería.
t.barranc dels garrofers@38.8,-0.3:
Between the towns of Alcoy and Gandia, the mountains of the northern Alicante province fold into a tangle of narrow valleys, and the barranc, the ravine, of the carob trees is a dry gully among them, a few kilometres from the villages of Planes and Beniarrés. The carob, or garrofer in Valencian, is a dark, leathery tree that has grown here for centuries, and its long brown pods were once used as animal feed and sweeteners. The land is rugged limestone, laced with terraces now mostly abandoned and covered in pines and rosemary.

Rock shelters line the ravine, and the Abric del Garrofero, like others in this country, belongs to the prehistoric painting tradition that spread through the Mediterranean mountains of Spain. Alicante has some of the most important sites, with schematic figures, deer, goats and archers, and the group is protected by UNESCO. As with all such sites, access can be restricted, so ask in the village.

The valleys also carry a Moorish past. After the Christian conquest of the thirteenth century the Muslim population stayed on, farming terraces and building irrigation channels, until the expulsion of the moriscos in 1609 emptied the valleys. Some villages here, such as those of the Vall de Gallinera, are famous for their cherry orchards, which blossom in late winter and cover the slopes in white. The Beniarrés reservoir, a long green lake, fills one of the valleys. Alcoy, the main town of the area, is known for its April festival of Moors and Christians, with elaborate costumes and mock battles.

The riding is engaging.
