The CV roads through the Serra de Mariola and the valleys wind through pine and oak woods with plenty of bends, steady climbs and good views towards the sea, which glitters in the distance on a clear day. The Coll de Rates, on the road down to the coast, is a classic viewpoint above Callosa d'en Sarrià. Traffic is light, except near Alcoy at weekends, and surfaces are variable, so watch for gravel after rain. Winter can bring frost and fog, and summer is hot, so ride in spring or in the autumn.

Muro d'Alcoi, with eight thousand people, is the nearest town of any size and has fuel and cafes, and Cocentaina and Alcoy are bigger. Xixona, a short drive away, is the home of turrón, the almond nougat eaten at Christmas, and the local anise liqueurs and cherry spirit make a good gift.
t.abrigo de las enredaderas@38.2,-1.6:
Where the Río Segura squeezes through the sandstone and limestone ridges of northern Murcia, between Calasparra and Cieza, the valley turns into a canyon of orange and grey rock with narrow green strips of reeds and orchard along the water. The Abrigo de las Enredaderas, a rock shelter, lies twelve kilometres or so from both towns, in dry hills of pine, rosemary and esparto grass that smell sharply of resin on a hot day.

Shelters like this one hold some of the oldest images in the region. The paintings in this part of Murcia belong to the Levantine tradition, small red figures of deer, goats and hunters, made by prehistoric people thousands of years ago, and the whole group is protected by UNESCO as Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin. Several shelters are in the care of the regional government and may be fenced; others are hard to reach and unmarked, so ask at the tourist office in Calasparra before wandering into the scrub. Do not touch the walls, because the oils on a hand do real damage.

The towns have their own stories. Calasparra is known for its rice, grown in terraced paddies fed by the cold Segura water and protected by its own designation of origin, which is not what you expect to find in a dry corner of south-eastern Spain. Just outside the town the sanctuary of the Virgen de la Esperanza clings to the rock above the river, reached by a winding road. Cieza, larger and busier, is famous for its fruit: in February and March, thousands of peach and apricot trees bloom pink and white across the valley, a spectacle that draws visitors from across the region.

The riding is varied. Roads follow the river through the gorge of Almadenes with a sequence of bends, narrow bridges and a fine view of the cliffs, while the high plateau roads are quiet and wind-scoured. Summers are fierce, with temperatures over forty degrees, so ride at dawn and carry water. Spring and autumn are best. Calasparra, with some ten thousand people, has fuel and bars, and Cieza, with thirty-five thousand, has all you could want, including good small bakeries and a pleasant old quarter. Sunday afternoons are quiet, and many places close for a long lunch.
t.abrigo de las canadas i@38.1,-2.4:
High up in the Sierra del Segura, where the province of Albacete meets Granada and Jaén, the village of Nerpio sits at around eleven hundred metres in a country of oak, pine and bare limestone. The Abrigo de las Cañadas, a rock shelter, lies about twelve kilometres from the village among its dry gullies, in one of the most thinly settled corners of Castilla-La Mancha.

Nerpio is famous among archaeologists for the sheer number of its shelters. More than a dozen painted sites have been found in the municipality, and the paintings, small red figures of deer, goats, archers and strange abstract signs, are among the richest of the Levantine tradition, thousands of years old and recognised by UNESCO as part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. Some shelters are fenced and the local council runs guided visits, which is the best way to see them, and you should ask in the village before going on foot, as many paths cross private land and are poorly marked.

The setting suits a motorcyclist who does not mind solitude. The roads here are small, often narrow, and can be rough in patches, with long climbs and quick descents between pine woods and open pasture. Traffic is almost nonexistent, but so are services, and mobile coverage can disappear, so tell someone where you are going. The river Taibilla runs through the valley and feeds a reservoir that supplies water to much of Murcia. The light at altitude is clear and hard, nights are cold even in summer, and snow is possible from November to March, closing minor roads for days.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Nerpio has about sixteen hundred people and it is wise to ask whether the pump is open, but the dependable choice is Huéscar, thirty-odd kilometres away across the hills, a town of eight thousand with several stations and a pleasant old centre. Yeste, to the north-east, is another possibility. For food, expect mountain dishes: roast lamb, game, local sausages and gachas, a thick flour porridge from the days when shepherds lived on very little. Come in late spring or early autumn, when the days are warm and the pines smell strong, and the hills are quiet except for the sound of sheep bells.
t.twice brewed roman temporary camp@55.0,-:
The Twice Brewed inn gives its name to a stretch of Northumberland where the Roman frontier is at its most dramatic. Here the Great Whin Sill, a hard sheet of dark volcanic rock, breaks in a long line of cliffs facing north, and the Wall runs along the very edge of it, rising and falling like a stone roller-coaster. Haltwhistle, five kilometres off, is the nearest town, and Hexham lies a good deal further east.

The Romans liked to build on a crag. A soldier on the Wall here had the whole of the empire's northern edge in front of him, wet moorland and empty hills, and the plain to the south behind. Temporary camps like the one on your map were the overnight bases of marching armies. They are only earth banks and ditches, thrown up in an afternoon, laid out in neat rectangles, and left behind, and many survive as faint outlines in grass, best seen in low evening light or after a dusting of snow. Vindolanda, the great fort and settlement a short distance away, is where the famous wooden writing tablets were found, letters and lists in ink, among them an invitation to a birthday party. Sycamore Gap, a dip in the crags with a single tree, became famous after it appeared in a Hollywood film, and the tree was felled in the autumn of 2023, a sad loss to local people.

The road, the B6318, is the Military Road, built in the 1750s after the Jacobite rising of 1745 to move troops across the country, and it uses much of the Wall's stone as its foundation. It is straight where the Romans were straight, and then it rolls over sharp rises and dips where it follows the crags, with blind summits and sudden dips. Sheep and cyclists share it, and the surface is patched. In the summer the car parks fill by ten, and in winter ice and snow can close it, so go early on a weekday.

The area is the heart of a dark sky park, one of the best places in England to see the stars, and the visitor centre at Once Brewed explains it. The inn serves hearty food and local ale, and the car park is a good base for walking. Fuel is at Haltwhistle, with nearly four thousand people, or at Hexham, a larger town of eleven thousand, so fill the tank beforehand.
t.knockcross roman temporary camp at grey:
The Solway Firth is shallow and wide on its Scottish side, and between Annan and Gretna the land is flat and green, with sheep and cattle, field boundaries lined with hawthorn, and long views across the water to the Lake District hills. The coordinates take you east of Annan, in Dumfries and Galloway, about five kilometres from the town, and you are standing on a landscape where the Romans once built a temporary camp, a marching camp whose banks and ditches are now more cropmark than earthwork, and visible mostly from the air.

Roman armies marched through Scotland from the first century, and Annandale was one of their roads to the north. The camps that line it were built for a single night, then abandoned, and the farmers have long since ploughed most of them flat. It is a matter of faith more than sight, but it is worth knowing that the same low ground has carried soldiers, drovers and now lorries for two thousand years.

The region has more recent and stranger stories. At Eastriggs, a few kilometres east, the First World War cordite factory known as HM Factory Gretna was one of the largest in the world, nine miles long, and the women who worked there handled a paste the workers called the Devil's Porridge, which has a museum today. Near Gretna, in 1915, the worst rail accident in British history happened at Quintinshill, when troop trains and an express collided and some two hundred and twenty people died. Gretna Green, just over the border, was famous for runaway marriages, because Scottish law allowed couples to wed without parental consent, and you can still be married at the old blacksmith's shop. Annan, a small river town, was the birthplace of no less a figure than the essayist Thomas Carlyle, who went to school there.

The riding is flat and unhurried. The B721 and the minor roads between Annan and Gretna run straight between hedges, with a few bends and speed limits dropping through villages, and the A75 and the nearby motorway carry heavy traffic. In wind and rain the firth feels bleak, but in clear, still evenings the sunsets over the water are splendid. Spring and early autumn are best, though midsummer midges can be bothersome. Annan, with nearly nine thousand people, has fuel, a supermarket and cafes.
t.maiden way roman road from b6318 to 450m:
Where Cumbria meets Northumberland in the valley of the river Irthing, the Wall climbs out of a wooded gorge on to open ground, and a Roman road called the Maiden Way ran north from the Wall towards Bewcastle and south towards Kirkby Thore, linking the frontier to the supply routes of the interior. The coordinates sit near Birdoswald and Gilsland, with Brampton ten kilometres to the west and Haltwhistle thirteen to the east.

Roman roads are not glamorous when you find them. A raised strip of gravel across a field, a line of stones in a hedge, or a long straight lane where the surface has not changed for two thousand years: these are what remain, and a good map or a local guide helps you see them. The Maiden Way was a military road, built to move troops and supplies between the forts, and its name is old and uncertain. It was always more important than it looks, because the Wall was never intended to be a barrier alone, but a controlled line, with gates, patrols, and roads behind it.

Close by, the fort of Birdoswald, which the Romans called Banna, stands on a spur above a bend in the Irthing, and from it you can see a long stretch of Wall in good condition and the point where it changes from turf to stone. Gilsland has a quieter claim to fame. In 1797, Walter Scott met his future wife Charlotte there when it was a small spa, and the village still has a sulphur well. To the north, the Bewcastle Cross, an Anglo-Saxon carved stone of the seventh or eighth century, stands in a remote churchyard, and it is among the finest early Christian monuments in Europe.

The road along the Wall here is the B6318, the Military Road, and it dips and climbs through farmland, with long, open straights and some tight kinks. Nearby lanes are narrower and often rough, and in winter the moors can bring snow, ice and fog. The remote feeling is part of the charm, but it does mean services are scarce, so carry water and a map. Fuel is at Brampton, a town of four thousand people, or at Haltwhistle, and both have cafes and bakeries. Spring and early summer bring curlews and lapwings on the fields.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum between the ro:
Between Hexham and Haydon Bridge, the river Tyne runs through a wide green valley, and on the ridge to the north the line of Hadrian's Wall can be traced across fields and woods in a series of ditches, banks and stretches of masonry. The coordinates place you near the old Roman station of Chesters, ten kilometres from Hexham, where the Wall crossed the North Tyne on a bridge whose stone abutments you can still see on the riverbank.

The man who saved much of this landscape was John Clayton, a nineteenth-century lawyer from Newcastle who bought several farms along the Wall to stop the stones being carried away for walls and barns. His house at Chesters stands beside the fort, and his collection of Roman finds is on display in the museum. Chesters is the best preserved fort for cavalry, with the bath house on the riverbank still standing to shoulder height, and a visit gives a good picture of life in a garrison. Alongside the Wall runs the Vallum, the great ditch to the south, and between the two you can walk over the field and feel the scale of the scheme.

Hexham itself has a fine abbey, built in the twelfth century on the site of a church founded in 674 by Saint Wilfrid, and its crypt, made of Roman stone from the old fort at Corbridge, survives from that time. The town has a market, an old gaol and a pleasant mix of shops and cafes. The ride on your map also leads to Durham, whose cathedral stands above the river Wear, and it is worth the trip if time allows.

The riding in the Tyne valley is mostly pleasant. The A69 is fast and busy, while the old road along the Wall, the B6318, is narrower and more scenic, with dips, farm entrances and sudden changes in the surface. Lanes on the south side of the river, through villages like Acomb and Haydon Bridge, are quieter and have good views. In winter, ice lingers in shaded dips, and in summer the road can be crowded with walkers and cars.

Hexham has eleven thousand people and is the place to refuel and eat, with a decent choice of pubs and tea-rooms. Haydon Bridge, a smaller village on the South Tyne, has a few shops and a good bakery. The best season for a visit is early autumn, when the light is clear and the bracken turns copper.
t.housesteads fort@55.0,-2.3:
Of all the forts on Hadrian's Wall, Housesteads is the one that most people picture. It stands on the edge of the Whin Sill, high above the moors, with long grey walls running along the ridge on either side and an enormous view in every direction. The Romans called it Vercovicium, and from the road it takes about ten minutes to walk up the hill from the car park and museum to the gate, with the wind in your face.

The garrison were auxiliary troops, not Roman citizens, recruited in the provinces, and Housesteads was held for long periods by a unit of Tungrians, soldiers from what is now Belgium, who must have found the climate here a shock. About eight hundred men lived here at times, with granaries, a hospital, a commander's house and a set of barrack blocks, and the remains of all of these can be seen. The famous communal latrine, a stone-lined bench over a drain with a channel of running water, is one of the best preserved in Britain and always attracts a crowd. Outside the walls, a village grew up, with shops, taverns and homes for the soldiers' families, and its foundations lie on the slope below. The fort is owned by the National Trust and managed by English Heritage, and there is a charge for entry and for parking.

For riders, the approach is the thing. The B6318 runs close to the fort, a narrow, undulating road with dips, crests and bends, patched and sometimes rutted. It is a road for riding slowly, because sheep wander across it and walkers cross at the car park. The Wall path above is among the best day walks in England, with Crag Lough, a small lake under the cliff, and the line of crags rising and falling in front of you. Weather changes fast: a bright morning can bring cloud and drizzle, and the wind on the crags is strong. Bring a warm layer even in July.

There are no services at the fort apart from a cafe by the car park, so buy fuel beforehand. Haydon Bridge, seven kilometres away, has about fifteen hundred people and a few shops, and Haltwhistle, a little farther, has fuel and more choice. Hexham, fifteen kilometres to the east, is the larger centre. Summer weekends are crowded, so aim for an early start or a weekday in spring or autumn, when the fort is quiet and the moors are purple with heather in late August.
t.red house roman camp@55.0,-2.2:
A few kilometres west of Hexham the South and North Tyne have long since joined, and the valley widens into a level green floor of fields, hedges and small woods, with the Wall's ridge just visible to the north. The Red House Roman camp lies in this farmland, about five kilometres from Haydon Bridge, Acomb and Hexham, on the Roman road known as the Stanegate, which ran across the neck of Britain from Carlisle to Corbridge.

The Stanegate is older than the Wall, and for a time it was the frontier itself, a road with forts a day's march apart, and when Hadrian began his great barrier in about 122 AD it stayed in use as the supply line behind it. Camps beside it were built by marching soldiers and used for training, and they are only low banks and ditches in fields today. I cannot say what remains visible at this particular spot, so treat it as a window onto a landscape that the Romans organised carefully, with the road, the forts and the fortified line to the north working together.

The valley has plenty of later history. Corbridge, a little to the east, grew out of a Roman supply town and has a fine Saxon church built partly of Roman stones, as well as a large excavated site with granaries and fountain bases. Aydon Castle, a thirteenth-century fortified manor house, stands on a ridge above the village and is a well-preserved example of the houses built to withstand Scottish raids. The whole region was a border land for centuries, with peel towers in every village.

On the bike, the quiet lanes between Acomb, Fourstones and Haydon Bridge are very pleasant, with gentle bends, stone walls and cattle in the fields. The A69 is the fast road nearby, and the old road along the south side of the river carries less traffic and has more character. In spring the hedges are white with blossom, and in autumn the woods turn golden. Winter brings fog and frost in the valley bottom, so the best riding is after the sun has risen high.

Hexham, seven kilometres away, has everything you need, including filling stations, supermarkets, a fine abbey and a Saturday market that has been held for centuries. Acomb and Haydon Bridge are smaller but have pubs and shops, and the Northumberland pubs are known for hearty, generous food, with Sunday roasts and local ales.
t.badaling@40.4,116.0:
Badaling is the part of the Great Wall that most of the world has seen, and for good reason. The Ming dynasty rebuilt and strengthened the wall here in the sixteenth century, at a pass in the mountains northwest of Beijing, to guard the approach to the capital through the Juyong Pass. The wall climbs steeply over the ridges, with watchtowers at intervals, and the view from the top, with the line of stone snaking away over bare hills, is as epic as the photographs suggest. Restored in the 1950s, it was the first section opened to visitors, and later received many foreign leaders, including Richard Nixon in 1972.

The popularity has a price. On weekends and national holidays, thousands of people crowd the steps, and the experience can be slow and noisy. Go early on a weekday, ideally in spring or autumn, and walk beyond the first towers, where the crowds thin out. Summer can be hot and hazy, while winter, cold and crisp, gives the clearest views, with snow on the walls and almost no one around.

The area lies in the Yanqing district of Beijing, and the nearest large town is Changping, about twenty-four kilometres away, with plenty of fuel and food. The road from Beijing follows the Jingzang expressway, a fast, modern highway, which is closed to motorcycles, as in much of China. Foreign riders will need to arrange touring through a licensed operator, since independent riding is heavily restricted. Parking is organised, and the approach is mostly by coach or train.

Many visitors combine Badaling with the Ming Tombs, the burial ground of thirteen emperors in a valley near Changping, reached by a Sacred Way lined with stone animals and officials. It is a fine pairing: one monument for defence, the other for the afterlife. The Temple of Heaven, in the city itself, is a third part of the same imperial story. Dress in layers, wear proper shoes, and bring water.
t.el laberinto@38.2,-1.6:
Calasparra is a rice town, which sounds odd until you see the terraces beside the Segura river, flooded and green in summer, with herons wading between the plants. The rice here has its own protected designation, and it is the base for paella in much of Spain. The river has carved a deep gorge, the Almadenes canyon, on its way through the hills, and in the rock above the water, hidden among limestone cliffs, there are shelters decorated with paintings made thousands of years ago. El Laberinto is one of them, part of the rock art tradition of the Mediterranean basin, listed by UNESCO.

The shelters are scattered across the hills around Calasparra and Moratalla, and they hold paintings in red and black: schematic figures, animals and abstract signs, some of them quite small. They are not signposted like a museum, and many are protected by fences or locked gates, so enquire in town before you go. Respect the signs and never touch the rock, because even a fingerprint can damage pigment that has lasted millennia.

Above the town stands the Sanctuary of the Virgen de la Esperanza, built on a rock ledge in the seventeenth century, and the pilgrimage that visits it each year is a major local event. Calasparra has fuel and good restaurants where rice is cooked in broth over a flame. Cieza, to the east, is famous for its peach blossom in February, and Abarán has vineyards and fruit orchards along the Segura.

The riding is a pleasure in spring and autumn. Roads follow the river through gorges and orange groves, and climb into dry, scrubby hills with pine and esparto grass, with the sun hot and the views long. Summer is brutally hot, with temperatures above forty degrees, and the shaded gorge is the only sensible place to be. Winter nights can be cold, and the sky is crystal clear. After dark, you can hear the frogs in the rice fields and smell the damp earth.
t.abric de la monja@38.8,-0.6:
Ontinyent sits in the Vall d'Albaida, in the south of Valencia, a town of about thirty-eight thousand people with a long textile tradition that goes back to wool, blankets and, more recently, home textiles. The Clariano river runs through it, and the hills around are wrinkled limestone, covered in pine, holm oak and wild herbs. In the shelter of those hills, small rock overhangs, called abrics here, carry paintings made by prehistoric people, and the Abric de la Monja is one of them, part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998.

These are not grand monuments. Most of the shelters are small and in remote spots, requiring a walk along a ravine path, and the paintings are often faint, small figures in red that take a moment for the eye to pick out. Some sites are fenced or signposted, others are hard to find, and all are fragile. Look, photograph without flash, and leave everything as it is. The local tourist office can tell you which sites are open and how to reach them.

Not far to the east rises the Serra Mariola, a natural park with an aromatic carpet of thyme, rosemary and mountain tea, which is the base of a local herbal liqueur, the herbero. The nearby towns of Banyeres de Mariola and Cocentaina have castles and old centres that suit a lazy afternoon. In Ontinyent itself, fuel and lunch are easy, and bars serve arròs al forn, rice baked in the oven with potatoes, ribs and morcilla.

The roads that wind through the Vall d'Albaida and up into the Mariola are enjoyable, with gradual climbs, rock walls and long views over terraced slopes of olives and almonds. Surfaces are generally good. Heat in July and August is fierce, so ride early, while March to May and October to November are best. Almond blossom in late winter gives the valleys a pale, drifting beauty, and the smell of pine resin after rain lingers in the air.
t.penyo de les carrasques abric ii@38.7,-0:
Cocentaina lies in the green hollow of the Comtat, a valley in the Alicante hills, with its palace and castle watching the Serpis river from the edge of town. Above and to the east rise limestone crags, among them the Penyó de les Carrasques, named for the carrasca, the holm oak that clings to dry slopes here. A rock shelter in the cliff, Abric II, preserves prehistoric paintings, part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin listed by UNESCO in 1998. As elsewhere in this tradition, the figures are small and fragile, and access can be restricted.

It is a landscape of ravines and terraces, where generations have cut stone walls into the hillsides for olives, almonds and cherries. Walking in this region, you find that every ridge has a ruin, a spring or a shelter. The smell of the place is wild thyme, pine and warm limestone. Benilloba, the nearest village, is tiny, with a few hundred inhabitants, and reaching the shelter often means walking a rough track, so wear proper boots and carry water.

Cocentaina has fuel and is known for its Fira de Tots Sants, a big fair held every year in November, and for its Moorish and Christian heritage. The city of Alcoy, a short ride up the valley, is an industrial town with fine Modernista buildings and a spectacular festival of Moors and Christians each April. Food is robust: olleta, a bean and vegetable stew, and sweet pastries with almonds, along with the local chocolate.

On a bike, this is a rewarding area. The roads wind through the valleys and over passes toward the Costa Blanca, with open corners, gentle gradients and dramatic views of the mountain ridges, and traffic is light outside the holidays. Summer heat is intense, so go early, and in the evening the light on the crags is a deep gold. Spring wildflowers and autumn colours make those seasons the best, and winter nights can be bitterly cold on the high ground.
t.abrigo de la fuente del sapo@38.2,-2.4:
Nerpio sits high in the Sierra del Segura, in the southwest of Albacete, about eleven hundred metres up, and it feels like an outpost of the Andalusian mountains that happens to be in Castile-La Mancha. The village is small, with roughly sixteen hundred people, and the countryside around is a deep, rumpled landscape of pine forest, rock outcrops and tiny cultivated valleys. More than forty rock shelters with paintings have been found in the area, making Nerpio one of the richest places for prehistoric art in Spain, with paintings in red showing animals, hunters and abstract signs.

The Abrigo de la Fuente del Sapo, the Shelter of the Toad's Spring, is one of them, and it belongs to the wider tradition of rock art of the Mediterranean Basin listed by UNESCO. The names of the sites, like Fuente Serrano and Cañadas, tell you that water was the draw then as now. A small interpretation centre in the village is the best place to find out which shelters can be visited and how to get to them, as many lie along rough tracks or paths.

The mountains are the real reward. This is the headwater country of the Taibilla and Segura rivers, a land of black pine, juniper and cliffs, with wild boar, mountain goats and golden eagles. Honey, game and trout are on local menus, and the villages are hospitable. The nearest bigger town on the list, Yeste, is about twenty kilometres away, and there is little in between, so fill the tank beforehand. Nerpio has basic services, but do not rely on them late in the day.

Riding here means winding country roads, steep, narrow and often empty, with long views across forested ridges. Surfaces vary, with patches of gravel, and wildlife on the road, especially at dusk. Winters are cold and snowy at this altitude, and spring and autumn are glorious. Summer days are warm and the nights cool, perfect for stargazing, since there is almost no light pollution.
t.covacha de l aigua amarga@39.7,-0.4:
The Serra Calderona runs between Valencia and Castellón like a green ridge behind the coast, and Náquera sits on its southern flank, a village of nearly four thousand people with views across the Camp de Túria orchards. A short way into the hills, a ravine with the name Aigua Amarga, bitter water, opens beside the Covacha de l'Aigua Amarga, a small shelter with prehistoric paintings, part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998. The figures are modest and the shelter is small, so it is a place for a patient look.

Calderona natural park is a mix of pine forest, scrub of rosemary, gorse and kermes oak, and sandy ridges where the soil turns red after rain. The smell of resin in the heat is strong, and cicadas drown out everything in July. Higher up lies the Carthusian monastery of Portaceli, founded in the thirteenth century, and nearby are the remains of Roman and Moorish workings. To the east, the plain is a quilt of orange groves, and at Puçol the citrus blossom perfumes the air in spring.

Valencia is thirty kilometres south, so the hills are the green lung of a big city, and you will share the roads with cyclists, hikers and city dwellers on Sunday outings. Puçol, with about nineteen thousand people, has fuel and supermarkets, and the coast at Sagunt, with its great hilltop castle and Roman theatre, is a short ride away. A bowl of paella cooked over orange wood in a country restaurant is part of the experience.

The roads in the Calderona wind up and down through pine woods, with decent surfaces and plenty of bends, and they are popular with bikers, so expect company at weekends. Wildfires are a real risk in summer, and some tracks are closed in the dry season. Spring and autumn are best, with wildflowers and cooler air. Early mornings give the clearest views to the Mediterranean.
t.lavadero tello iii@37.8,-2.1:
Los Vélez is a corner of Almería that most visitors to the coast never see: a high, dry country of pine forest, almond groves and pale limestone peaks, with the Sierra de María rising above two thousand metres. The Lavadero Tello, the washing place at Tello, is on the edge of that mountain land, near María and Vélez-Blanco, and the shelters of the area hold some of the most famous paintings in southern Spain. At the Cueva de los Letreros, near Vélez-Blanco, a small figure with outstretched arms holding a rainbow-like shape is the Indalo, adopted as the symbol of Almería and painted on houses across the province.

The paintings belong to the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula, listed by UNESCO in 1998. As elsewhere, shelters are small and delicate, and access is managed, so ask locally before you go. Vélez-Blanco itself is dominated by a Renaissance castle built in the early sixteenth century by the Marquis of Los Vélez, with a famous courtyard that was sold and shipped to Paris in 1904, and is now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, while a plaster copy stands in the castle.

María is a tiny town of around fifteen hundred people, and Vélez-Blanco has about two thousand. Fuel and supplies are best bought in Vélez Rubio, about twenty kilometres away, which is the bigger local centre. The area is known for its bread, game, hams and almonds, and in February the almond blossom is a sight. The Sierra de María-Los Vélez natural park protects the pine and juniper woods and a rich flora.

For riding, the mountain roads are a delight: smooth, quiet, with long open bends and views over the plateau. Wind can be strong on the ridge, and winter brings snow and ice. In summer, days are hot and dry, but evenings are cool at altitude. Late spring and autumn are most pleasant, and the star-filled skies at night are some of the clearest in Spain.
t.al patro@38.8,-0.2:
The Vall d'Ebo is one of those valleys that history has emptied. In 1609 the Spanish crown ordered the expulsion of the Moriscos, the descendants of the region's Muslim population, and in the mountains of the Marina Alta, many villages lost almost everyone overnight. Some Moriscos resisted in the high cliffs of the Muela de Cortes before the end came. Vall d'Ebo today has barely three hundred inhabitants, and its terraced fields, built by Morisco farmers for irrigation, are still visible as stone steps climbing the hillsides.

Al Patró lies in this broken limestone country, with a rock shelter that is part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art tradition listed by UNESCO in 1998. A famous neighbour is the Penya Escrita, a cliff with schematic paintings that can be reached on a short walk. In this tradition, sites are small, delicate and sometimes remote, so take local advice, wear sturdy boots and respect any fencing. The ravines are hot in summer and filled with the scent of thyme and pine.

Pego, the nearest sizeable town, with about eleven thousand people, lies below the hills on the edge of the Pego-Oliva wetlands, where rice is grown in flooded fields and birds nest in reeds. It has fuel, restaurants and a Saturday market. Villalonga, a bit closer, is smaller. In the villages around, you will find simple, hearty food: rice dishes, local oranges, almonds, and honey, and the coffee is strong.

The riding here is first class. The roads from the coast climb into the mountains in a series of bends, with tight corners and long rock walls, and the views of the Mediterranean from the ridges are dramatic. Traffic is light, except in summer when coastal visitors venture inland. Look out for cyclists, who love these climbs, and for loose gravel on the corners. Spring and autumn are lovely, and the air after rain smells of damp earth and wild herbs.
t.guijarral@38.3,-2.5:
Spain's largest protected area is the Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas, and it spreads across a long stretch of wooded mountains in Jaén and Albacete. The Guijarral lies on its northern edge, in country close to Yeste, Segura de la Sierra and Orcera, where black pines and holm oaks cover steep slopes and rivers cut gorges between. Here, among rock walls, shelters preserve paintings, part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998, and the sites of the area, such as Zona 1 and the Collado de la Cruz, tell of hunting peoples who lived in these mountains long ago.

The scenery is grand. The Segura river, dammed in places, runs blue-green through forest, and the Guadalquivir has its source in the same range, a modest spring in a forest clearing. Wildlife is plentiful, with red deer, mouflon, wild boar and lammergeier vultures, and the park is known for its dawn chorus. Segura de la Sierra is a spectacular village on a hilltop with a castle and Arab baths, worth the climb.

Yeste, with around three and a half thousand inhabitants, is the main town in the area, and there are small shops and fuel stations in Orcera and Yeste. The nearest large towns lie far away, so plan your fuel and food carefully. Local products include olive oil from the Sierra de Segura, game, cured meats and honey, and the restaurants serve hearty mountain dishes such as gazpacho manchego and migas.

The roads here are among the best for riding in southern Spain: winding, scenic and often deserted, with long climbs and drops through forest, and views over gorges and reservoirs. Surfaces are generally good, though watch for rockfall and wildlife. Hot summer afternoons are best avoided, and winter snow can close the higher roads. Autumn brings colour and the roaring of the stags in the rut, an unforgettable sound.
t.cueva del tio labrador@37.7,-2.0:
Vélez-Rubio is a larger and busier place than its neighbour Vélez-Blanco, with seven thousand people, a lively main street, and a church that is a surprise in a town this size. The Church of the Encarnación, begun in the eighteenth century, has twin towers and a massive Baroque façade, usually described as the largest Baroque church in Almería, and its bulk dominates the roofs. It is a good place to start before riding up toward the mountains, because the fuel stations here are the nearest reliable ones for a long way.

The Cueva del Tío Labrador lies in the hills above Vélez-Blanco, ten kilometres from that town, in the Sierra de María-Los Vélez natural park. Like other shelters nearby, it belongs to the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin, listed by UNESCO in 1998, and the paintings are small and delicate. Access to many of the shelters is controlled, so check with the park office or the local tourist office before you set off, and never touch the rock.

The park is a high plateau of pines, junipers and almond groves, with limestone peaks, one of them above two thousand metres. The air is dry and clear, and the sky at night is brilliant. Wildlife includes ibex, foxes and eagles, and the spring flora is rich, with orchids and aromatic herbs. Almond blossom in February turns the valleys pink and white. The local food is simple and good: migas, game, cured ham and bread baked in wood ovens.

The roads in the Sierra are quiet and a pleasure for a motorcycle: smooth surfaces, long, open bends and long views across the plateau, with little traffic outside holidays. Winters are cold, with frost and occasional snow, and summers are hot, though the nights are cool. Wind can be strong on the exposed sections. Spring and autumn are the nicest seasons. On a clear morning you can see the distant mountains of the Sierra Nevada to the southwest.
t.haltwhistle burn 1 roman temporary camp@:
Haltwhistle likes to call itself the centre of Britain, a claim measured, by one method or another, from the farthest tips of the island, and it does sit in the narrow waist of the country, between the North Sea and the Irish Sea. The town, with about four thousand people, lies in the South Tyne valley, just south of Hadrian's Wall, and it is a good base for exploring the central section of the frontier. Haltwhistle Burn, a stream tumbling to the Tyne, gives its name to a Roman fort on the Stanegate and to the temporary camp near the coordinates, a square of banks used by soldiers on the march.

Temporary camps are among the stranger Roman remains, because they were built to be abandoned. A legion on campaign would dig a ditch and a rampart each evening, pitch tents inside and move on the next morning, so these camps were used for a night or a few weeks. Surviving earthworks, often low and grassy, show up best in low sun. The camp here belongs to the broader frontier landscape that UNESCO listed in 1987.

Walltown Crags and Cawfields, a few kilometres to the north, are the real attractions: dramatic sections of wall on the edge of the Whin Sill, a hard, dark ridge of dolerite, with steep drops and wide views. The Roman Army Museum at Greenhead, close by, tells the story of the soldiers' lives. Haltwhistle itself has fuel, shops and pubs, and Hexham, farther east, is a larger market town.

Riding here is great. The B6318, the Military Road, runs along the line of the wall, built by General Wade in the 1750s after the Jacobite rising of 1745, partly using stones from the wall itself, and it has long, straight sections and sharp dips, with views over moorland and crags. Sheep wander onto the road, and weekends bring cyclists and walkers. Spring and early summer are lovely, and in winter the road can be icy and exposed. The weather changes fast on the high ground, so bring waterproofs.
t.hadrian s wall and associated features b:
Midway along Hadrian's Wall, the land rises into a dramatic line of crags, and here the wall perches along the edge of the Whin Sill, a hard, dark rock that stands like a cliff over green pastures. The coordinates fall around the heart of this stretch, near Crag Lough, Steel Rigg and Housesteads, where the wall rises and dips over the ridges like a stone rollercoaster. Roman engineers followed the natural line of the escarpment, and from the top you can see for miles across moor and farmland, with the Cheviot hills blue in the north.

This is the best-known part of the wall, and one of its great pleasures is how much remains. Housesteads, the fort perched on the ridge, still shows its granaries, its hospital and its communal latrine, while Vindolanda, a short distance south, has given the world its wooden writing tablets, with birthday invitations and complaints about the weather and the beer. The wall, part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire listing, was begun in AD 122, and soldiers manned it for nearly three centuries.

Nearby is a famous dip in the ridge, Sycamore Gap, where a single tree once stood in the hollow of the crags, a favourite for photographers, until it was cut down in 2023 in a shocking act of vandalism. A shoot has since grown from the stump. The landscape remains superb with or without the tree. Pennine Way walkers pass along the same ridge, so be considerate on narrow paths.

Haltwhistle, about seven kilometres away, is the nearest town with services, and Hexham is farther east, a bigger town with an abbey. Fuel is scarce on the high road, so fill up before you set out. The Military Road, the B6318, follows the wall across the hills, with straight sections and sudden dips, and views over the crags. It can be busy in summer and treacherous in winter, with ice and fog, and the wind is strong on the ridge. Pack waterproofs even on a bright day.
t.roman fort@55.0,-1.4:
At the mouth of the Tyne, on a rise above the river, stands a reconstructed Roman gateway that looks surprisingly new. It belongs to Arbeia, the Roman fort at South Shields, which supplied the soldiers along Hadrian's Wall and was built, strategically, to guard the entrance to the river. Ships unloaded grain and other goods here, and the stores were carried along the Wall's line, so this was the logistical heart of the frontier. Reconstructed buildings, including the gatehouse, a barrack and a commander's house, show how it looked, and the museum holds finds from the site.

South Shields is a town of about eighty-four thousand people, with a working harbour, a long beach and a lively market. The Shields Ferry crosses the river to North Shields in a few minutes, and the view of fishing boats and container ships is wonderful. The novelist Catherine Cookson was born in the town, and her story is told locally. The seafront has amusements, ice cream and a famous tradition of fish and chips, so a bag of those on the sea wall is the thing to do.

Further along the coast, the Souter Lighthouse at Whitburn, the first in the world designed to be powered by electricity, stands in red and white stripes, and the Marsden Rock, a sea stack, is a short ride south. Hadrian's Wall began at Wallsend, across the river, where another fort, Segedunum, has an excellent museum and a viewing tower. Fuel and food are easy in any direction.

Riding around Tyneside is mostly urban, with dual carriageways, bridges and the Tyne Tunnel, which charges a toll. Escape west along the Tyne valley or south along the coast for quieter lanes. Weather is changeable, with cool sea breezes even in summer, and the haar, the sea fog, can roll in suddenly. Early spring and autumn are best for clear days, and winter can be bleak, but the harbour has a stark beauty.
t.fiag@58.2,-4.6:
Fiag lies in the empty country of central Sutherland, in the far north of Scotland, where one road, the A836, runs between Lairg and the north coast through miles of peat bog, heather and lochs. Loch Fiag and its bridge are close, a small, quiet water set among low hills, and the ridge of Ben Klibreck rises to the north, a rounded mountain above nine hundred metres. This is part of the Flow Country, a vast blanket of peatland that is one of the largest in Europe, and the habitat is home to golden plovers, greenshank, red-throated divers and, now and then, an eagle overhead.

The road is the main reason to come. It is mostly single-track with passing places, and it runs through a land with almost no trees or houses, so the sense of space is huge. Surfaces are generally good, but there are blind crests and rough patches, and sheep and red deer wander onto the road. Learn the passing-place etiquette: pull in on the left, or opposite the oncoming vehicle, and wave a thank you. Weather can change from sun to rain and wind in minutes, and midges in summer are legendary.

Services are extremely thin. Lairg, the nearest village, has fuel and a few shops, while Altnaharra, farther north, is a tiny place with a hotel. Fill the tank, carry waterproofs and spare layers, and keep a phone charged, because mobile signal is patchy. The Crask Inn, an isolated hostelry beside the road, has become a favourite stop among travellers, though I would phone ahead for opening times.

History here is a story of clearances. In the early nineteenth century, many tenants were evicted to make room for sheep, and the ruins of their houses still dot the glens. Today the population is tiny, but the land holds a strong, proud sense of identity. Late spring and early summer, when the days are long and the bogs bloom with cotton grass, are the best times. In winter, snow can close the road, and the nights are long and dark.
t.oliclett@58.4,-3.2:
Caithness is the flat northeastern corner of mainland Scotland, a country of big skies, peat and flagstone, and Oliclett lies in it west of Wick, among scattered farms and low fields. The soil is thin and the wind is constant, and the trees that grow bend away from the sea. But beneath it, the county is thick with prehistory: chambered cairns, standing stones and broch ruins by the hundred. The Grey Cairns of Camster, near Lybster, are among the oldest, built over five thousand years ago, and you can crawl into one of them along a low passage.

The label on this stop belongs to a family of ancient sites that connect Caithness to Orkney, where the Ring of Brodgar stands, and to the far west of Sutherland. People travelled by sea in the Neolithic, and the same designs of tombs and circles appear across these northern lands. Standing in the flat fields here, you feel the long human presence in a landscape that seems empty.

Wick, about ten kilometres away, is the main town, with just over seven thousand people, fuel stations, supermarkets and pubs. In the nineteenth century it was the busiest herring port in Europe, and Thomas Telford designed the planned district of Pulteneytown for the fishermen. The Wick Heritage Museum tells the story. The town has what Guinness recognises as the world's shortest street, Ebenezer Place, only a couple of metres long. Old Pulteney, the distillery, has a long maritime link.

For riders, the A99 and A9 are the main roads, fast and open, with strong crosswinds, and there are quieter back roads between the farms. John o' Groats and Duncansby Head are an hour away, and Dunnet Head, the northernmost point of mainland Britain, is close by. In summer, the evenings are very long, and in June it hardly gets dark. Spring brings wildflowers on the cliffs, and autumn brings storms, so keep a close eye on forecasts.
t.el corral de silla abric l@39.8,-1.0:
The Valencia hinterland hides one of Europe's oldest art galleries in the cracks of its limestone. Corral de Silla is one of the rock shelters of the Mediterranean Basin rock art, a group of sites in eastern Spain that UNESCO listed in 1998. The paintings are in the Levantine style, small, lively figures of archers, deer and wild goats in red or black pigment, and are thought to be thousands of years old, with the exact dates still debated by specialists. The surrounding country is the Serranía, the highland interior of Valencia province, a region of pine forests, almond groves, dry stone terraces and deep ravines carved by the Turia river and its tributaries. Near Chelva stand the arches of the Roman aqueduct of Peña Cortada, carrying water across a gorge that is dramatic enough to make you stop.

Narrow, curving roads rise and fall through limestone country, with sudden views over reservoirs and ridges, and traffic is light except in August and on spring weekends. The surface is generally good, though patched, and hairpins are tight enough to be fun without being frightening. The heat in midsummer can be fierce, so start early and carry water, and cold nights in winter bring ice to the higher bends.

Tuéjar, Chelva and Alpuente are small, with populations of a thousand or two, so do not count on a petrol station in each one; the larger towns on the main route, such as Requena or Llíria, are safer. Bars in the villages serve strong coffee and good bocadillos. The best seasons are spring, when the hills are green and the almonds bloom white in late winter, and autumn, when the light is golden and the vine leaves turn.
t.panal@37.7,-2.1:
The north of Almería province is a different Spain from the sunburnt beach coast to the south. Here, around Vélez-Blanco and Vélez-Rubio, the land lifts to a high, cold plateau of almonds, cereal and pine woods, and the Sierra María-Los Vélez natural park rises above it, a rough limestone ridge with its summit above two thousand metres. Panal is a rock shelter in those hills, a short distance from Vélez-Blanco, and it belongs to the group of paintings recognised by UNESCO as the Mediterranean Basin rock art. Here the paintings are of the schematic kind, simple red signs and figures, rather than the lively hunting scenes found further north.

What the visitor notices first is the nature. The park is dry, but it is rich: Aleppo pine and holm oak cover the slopes, rosemary and thyme grow in the rocks, and golden eagles and Bonelli's eagles hunt over the cliffs. In spring, the ground is alive with small orchids. The smell, after a shower on a warm day, is resin and herbs. Nights are cold even in summer, and the stars at this height are brilliant.

The riding is worth the journey. Roads climb gently from the plateau into the sierra and wind through the forest with a good mix of bends and straights. Traffic is thin, and surfaces are generally good on the main routes, rougher on the narrow forest tracks. Vélez-Blanco, under three kilometres away, is a small town with a handful of bars and restaurants, and Vélez-Rubio, a little larger with seven thousand people, has the fuel, supermarkets and pharmacy that a small village cannot offer. Spring and autumn are the best times, with mild days and clear light, and the almond blossom in February is a bonus.
t.hoyos ii@37.7,-2.1:
Above the whitewashed roofs of Vélez-Blanco stands one of the most unexpected castles in Spain. It was built in the early sixteenth century for the first Marquis of Los Vélez, Pedro Fajardo, on a rocky spur, with a severe Gothic exterior and a Renaissance courtyard of astonishing delicacy inside. In the early twentieth century the owners sold the marble courtyard, which was taken down stone by stone and shipped abroad, and it now stands, reassembled, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. A later restoration left the castle itself with plain rooms, but it remains a splendid sight from the road.

Hoyos II is a small rock shelter in the country around the town, in the Sierra María-Los Vélez, and belongs to the same family of painted shelters that UNESCO protects across the Spanish Mediterranean. These Almerian sites are often schematic, a few lines in red ochre, and they are among the oldest evidence of human presence in this high dry land. Much of the interest is in the context: sheltered rock faces under overhangs where prehistoric people sat out the weather, with fine views of the plateau.

Riding in the Los Vélez country is a quiet joy. The roads are mostly empty, with long straights across the plateau, then looping climbs into the hills with a good surface and grand views of rolling fields and distant peaks. Wind can be strong on the open ground, and in winter ice may linger in shaded corners. Spring is the best time, when the almond blossom is out and the fields are green, and autumn brings clear air and soft light on the stone villages.

Practical services are easy to find. Vélez-Blanco has a small selection of bars and restaurants and a visitor office near the castle, and Vélez-Rubio, a few kilometres further, has fuel, banks and shops. Lunch might be a local stew with a glass of wine from the nearby hills. Plan to arrive early if you want to visit the castle, and wear sturdy shoes if you want to walk to the shelters, because the paths are rocky and the sun is hot.
t.barranc de carbonera abric i@38.8,-0.4:
The Vall d'Albaida is the quiet valley south of Xàtiva where the Valencian hinterland starts to climb towards the mountains of Alicante, and Otos, Ráfol de Salem and Bèlgida are tiny villages scattered among its folds. The Barranc de Carbonera is one of the ravines that cut into the limestone slopes, and the shelter in it is part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art group that UNESCO inscribed in 1998. The Peñón de los Machos, another painted rock nearby, is on the same ride. The paintings belong to the Levantine tradition, red figures of people and animals painted on the walls of small overhangs in the cliffs.

The country is classic Valencian highland, a mosaic of terraced fields of olives, almonds and carob, patches of pine and holm oak, and bare ridges where wild thyme and rosemary perfume the air. The Serra del Benicadell rises to the south, a long limestone crest of just over a thousand metres, and the villages at its foot are quiet, whitewashed and cheerful. After rain the ravines fill with the sound of water, and in spring the terraces are full of wildflowers.

For a rider the area is very rewarding. Narrow roads wind among the villages with a good rhythm of bends and short climbs, with little traffic, a fair surface and the occasional hairpin where the road climbs out of a barranc. Summer is hot, and the shady roads under the pines are welcome. The Vall de Gallinera, a little to the south, is famous for its cherry blossom in late winter, which covers the terraces in white, and makes an excellent detour in the right month.

The villages themselves are small, with populations of a few hundred, and while you can usually find a bar, fuel is not guaranteed. Fill up in Albaida or Ontinyent, which are larger, before heading into the hills, and carry water in summer. Spring and autumn are the best times to ride, and the locals will cheerfully send you to a restaurant serving rice dishes cooked over orange wood, which is more than worth the detour.
t.abric del cinto de la ventana@39.3,-0.7:
South-west of Valencia the Júcar river has carved a long, winding gorge through the limestone, and the country on either side is some of the most rugged in the region. The Macizo del Caroig, a high limestone massif of pine and scrub, rises to more than eleven hundred metres, and the villages of Millares and Dos Aguas are small places tucked into the valleys at its foot. The Abric del Cinto de la Ventana is a rock shelter in the nearby cliffs, and belongs to the Mediterranean Basin rock art group listed by UNESCO in 1998, the red Levantine paintings painted by prehistoric hunters.

The land is hard and wild. Pines cover the slopes, with outcrops of grey rock, and the ravines hold small streams that flow in spring and run dry in summer. The reservoirs of the Júcar at Cortes de Pallás are close by, turquoise in colour, and their shores are good for a swim in hot weather. Golden eagles and Bonelli's eagles nest on the cliffs, and the nights are loud with owls. The smell in the afternoon is pine resin and rosemary, and the silence is almost complete.

For a motorcyclist the hinterland of Valencia is a splendid area. Roads here are narrow and winding, with a succession of bends climbing out of the Júcar valley and dropping into the ravines on the other side. Traffic is almost nonexistent except at weekends, when cyclists and other motorcyclists come out from Valencia. The surface is usually fair, though patches of rough tarmac and gravel occur on minor roads, and sharp bends can hide behind rock outcrops.

Millares and Dos Aguas are small villages with only a few hundred inhabitants, so do not rely on finding fuel there. Montroy, a larger place, has petrol, and the big towns of Buñol and Chiva are within reach. Carry water in summer, and bring layers for the high ground. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and the locals will direct you to a bar with a plate of rice and rabbit in the traditional style of the interior.
t.abric de la pareja@39.3,-0.7:
The Júcar gorge below Dos Aguas is the sort of scenery that makes Spanish interior roads famous among riders. A deep valley of red and grey rock, pine and oak, it carries the river towards the sea, and the villages along it, Millares and Dos Aguas among them, are old and small. The Abric de la Pareja is a rock shelter in the cliffs nearby, and its name, the Couple, refers to a pair of painted figures. It is part of the Levantine rock art that UNESCO lists among the Mediterranean Basin sites, and its paintings are among the best examples of how prehistoric hunters pictured themselves.

The village of Dos Aguas has another claim to fame. The village gave its name to the Marquis of Dos Aguas, and the family that held the title of Marquis of Dos Aguas built a palace in Valencia that now holds the national ceramics museum, with a lavish alabaster doorway. The village is quiet, with a church and a few bars, and a fine view of the surrounding cliffs. In late winter, the almonds bloom white in the valley, and the hills are patched with green.

The riding on these roads is excellent. The valley road twists beside the river with a succession of tight corners and short straights, with views across cliffs and woods, and the high roads that climb out onto the plateau are a pleasure, lined with pines. There is little traffic during the week, though weekends bring motorcycles and cyclists from Valencia. The surface is mostly good, though some stretches are rough, and rock falls are possible after heavy rain.

Alborache, a larger village, has a few bars and shops. Carry water and sun protection in the summer, and layers for the evening. Spring is the best season, with green hills and mild weather, and autumn brings clear air and good light.
t.coves roges abric ii@38.8,-0.3:
The Serpis river runs through the green, folded country of the Comtat, west of Alcoi, and its valley is one of the prettiest in the Valencian interior. Planes, Benimarfull and Beniarrés are small villages in the hills, farming olive and almond and cherry, and the old Moorish heritage is easy to find in the narrow streets and the names. The Coves Roges, the Red Caves, are a series of rock shelters in the nearby cliffs, and they hold paintings that are part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998. Abric II is one of them, and the red paint on the rock is faint but clear.

The Moorish past is lively in the region. In the thirteenth century, after the Christian conquest of the Valencian kingdom, the Muslim population here rose several times under a leader called al-Azraq, who held castles in the valleys nearby, and the revolts lasted decades. Alcoi, the big town to the west, commemorates those struggles each April with its Moors and Christians festival, a three-day spectacle of costumes, parades and gunpowder that is famous across Spain. The villages around keep similar festivals on a smaller scale.

For a rider, the Comtat is a hidden delight. The roads follow the contours of the valleys with a good succession of bends, climb over low passes with views over terraced slopes, and drop to the Serpis river with its old bridges. Traffic is thin, and the surface is generally good. In summer the heat is fierce in the afternoon, and the shade of the cherry and almond trees is welcome. In winter the mornings can be frosty on the higher roads.

Planes has a few hundred people and a handful of bars, and there is little fuel in the villages, so fill up in Alcoi or Cocentaina before heading into the hills. The local cooking is mountain food, with stews of beans and vegetables and rice dishes. Spring and autumn are the best times, with mild days and clear skies, and the cherry blossom in February is a reward for the early rider.
t.abric del ciervo@39.3,-0.7:
Not every deer on a cave wall is the same animal. The Abric del Ciervo, the Shelter of the Stag, is another of the small rock overhangs in the cliffs above the Júcar country west of Valencia, named for a painted deer that the first people to describe it picked out among the fainter marks. It belongs to the red Levantine art that UNESCO recognised in 1998 as part of the Mediterranean Basin group, and it sits a few kilometres from Millares and Dos Aguas, in a terrain of broken limestone and pine that rewards anyone who enjoys finding things the hard way.

The nearest sizeable village on the map is Alborache, on the road towards the Hoya de Buñol, and that direction is the interesting one for a day's plan. Buñol, a few kilometres further, is a quiet industrial town under a castle for eleven months of the year and then, on the last Wednesday of August, it hosts the Tomatina, in which tens of thousands of people throw ripe tomatoes at each other for an hour. It sounds like a joke and in fact has a long rulebook. Come on any other day and the town is a pleasant surprise, with a ravine park, a river and a bar serving a decent plate of paella.

The country between here and the coast is a patchwork of dry hills, citrus plantations in the lower valleys and pine woods higher up. Water has always been the currency, and the old irrigation channels, the acequias, still run beside the roads in places, which is why a village can be a green island amid ochre rock. Spring is a good moment, because the orange blossom drifts up the valleys on warm days and you can smell it from the saddle.

On two wheels the roads here are lively and quiet at once. They bend through the hills in long, steady curves and climb over small passes with a short run of tight corners at the top, and they are mostly well surfaced, though loose stones wash onto the carriageway after storms. Weekends bring a few cyclists and other riders from the city, but weekdays are almost empty. Fuel is a matter of planning rather than worry: the villages are tiny, while Chiva and Buñol have stations and supermarkets. Take water in summer, and be ready for the walk to the shelter, which is over uneven rock and best done in the cool hours of the morning.
t.cueva de la arana abrigo i@39.1,-0.9:
Bicorp is a small village in the folds of the Valencian interior, west of Xàtiva, in a country of pine, scrub and deep ravines that falls towards the Júcar and the Sierra de Martés. The Cueva de la Araña, the Spider Cave, is one of the most famous rock art sites in Spain, and the main reason to come. It is thought to be several thousand years old, and it is one of the finest and most human images of the Levantine rock art, listed by UNESCO in 1998.

The honey gatherer gives the place a charm that survives the distance of time. You can picture the person on the rope, the smoke, the hum of the bees, and the cliff behind. The country is still full of wild bees, and thyme and rosemary honey is sold in the villages. The landscape is rugged and quiet, a mix of limestone gorges, pine forest and terraced fields, with eagles overhead and wild boar in the woods. The smell, especially on warm days, is of resin and herbs.

Riding in the hinterland of Valencia is a joy, with narrow roads that wind through the mountains with a good succession of bends, climb to viewpoints over wooded valleys and descend to small villages. Traffic is almost nonexistent, and the surface is mostly fair, though minor roads may be rough. The shelter itself is reached by a walk, and regulations are in force, so enquire in advance. In summer the heat is strong, and the early morning is the best time.

Carry water, particularly in summer. A plate of rice with rabbit and snails, the traditional dish of the area, is a fine reward after a day on the road. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with mild days and clear light.
t.cueva de apolinario@38.5,-3.3:
Sierra Morena is the long, dark range that separates the plains of La Mancha from the valley of the Guadalquivir, and the high-road gateway between them is the gorge of Despeñaperros, a few kilometres to the east of Aldeaquemada. The name means something like the pass where dogs are thrown off the cliff, which tells you how the Castilians felt about it. The Cueva de Apolinario is a rock shelter in these hills, and belongs to the painted shelters of the Sierra Morena, with figures that experts date back several thousand years. The area also holds the rock art of the Mediterranean Basin, as protected by UNESCO.

It is a refuge of the Iberian lynx, one of the rarest cats in the world, which has been reintroduced in the area, and the area is also known for its deer, wild boar and black vultures. The rivers run clear in spring, and the light on the hills is soft and gold in the evening.

For a rider, the Sierra Morena is a delight. Roads wind through the oak forest with a good succession of curves, climb to passes with long views, and drop into valleys with small villages. Traffic is thin, and the surface is generally fair, though the roads near the main route are busier, with lorries. In summer the heat is intense, and in winter fog and frost are possible on the higher ground.

Úbeda and Baeza, a long ride south, are the famous Renaissance towns of Jaén, listed by UNESCO and a splendid place to end the day. t.barranco de la mortaja i@38.5,-1.6:
Hellín is a sizeable town of thirty thousand in the south-east of Albacete province, a dry, open country of hills, almond groves and stony plains that belongs more to Murcia than to La Mancha in feeling. The Barranco de la Mortaja is a ravine in the sandstone hills near the town, and the shelter that gives this stop its name belongs to the rock art of the Mediterranean Basin, a group of sites that UNESCO listed in 1998. The surface is generally good, and traffic is thin outside the town. In summer the heat is intense, and the wind can blow strongly across the open land. t.coves de la vila@38.8,-0.3:
Planes sits in a cleft of the green hills above the Serpis river, in the Comtat, and the village of Beniarrés a few kilometres away is known for its reservoir, which fills the valley floor with a long, quiet sheet of water. For motorcyclists the roads of the Marina Baixa are a famous playground. t.abrigo del mojao@37.8,-2.0:

t.poyo medio cimbarra@38.4,-3.4:

t.abric de la gleda@38.8,-0.3:

t.barranc de la magrana@38.8,-0.2:

t.barranc de galistero@38.7,-0.2:

t.la sarga abric ii@38.6,-0.5:
La Sarga is a deep, rocky ravine that cuts into the hills north of Alcoi, and it is one of the most important rock art sites in eastern Spain. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear air and mild temperatures.
t.sunny rigg 3 roman temporary camp@55.0,-:
Sunny Rigg is a name that sounds like a farm, and that is more or less what it is, a stretch of rough pasture on the high ground just north of Haltwhistle, in Northumberland, where archaeologists have found the faint outline of a Roman temporary camp. These camps were built by marching armies at the end of each day's journey, with a ditch and a rampart thrown up around the tents to protect them overnight, and they were abandoned the next morning. Most survive only as shallow earthworks or crop marks seen from the air, which is why the places are so evocative: they record a single night of an army's life on the march, two thousand years ago.

The Wall itself runs close by, along the line of the Whin Sill, the hard dark rock that forms the crags of the central sector. It was begun around AD 122 under the emperor Hadrian, and for nearly three centuries it marked the northern limit of Roman Britain. Haltwhistle is a small market town that claims to be the centre of Britain, and the nearest big sights, Vindolanda, Housesteads and the Roman Army Museum at Carvoran, are within a short ride. The Tyne Gap, the valley that carries the road and railway between Newcastle and Carlisle, runs close by.

The riding around is a delight. Narrow lanes climb the ridge from the valley, with views across the moors to the Pennines, and the military road, the B6318, follows the Wall's line for miles with long, straight sections and sudden crests. Sheep stray onto the road, and the surface can be rough after winter. In winter the high ground gets snow, and strong wind can make the exposed ridge uncomfortable.

Haltwhistle has fuel, a supermarket and a few cafés, and Haydon Bridge, to the east, is smaller. The nearest large towns are Brampton and Hexham. The best season is late spring, when the lambs are in the fields and the moors are green, and early autumn, when the heather is purple on the tops.
t.carvoran roman fort and hadrian s wall a:
A Syrian archer unit once garrisoned this hilltop. Carvoran was the Roman fort at the junction of the Wall with the Maiden Way, a road that ran north towards Scotland, and at one time the cohors I Hamiorum, an auxiliary unit raised in the city of Hama in Syria, was stationed here, men who had marched or sailed across the empire to guard a wet, windy ridge in Northumberland. A bronze grain measure found at Carvoran, the Carvoran modius, carries a long inscription that mentions the emperor Hadrian, and it gives a glimpse of how the garrison was supplied. The fort is mostly a grassy platform now, but the position, on a ridge with views over the Tyne Gap, shows why it was chosen.

Next to the site, the Roman Army Museum tells the story of the soldiers who served here, with good displays of weapons, armour and daily life, and some well-made models. It also has a short film about the Wall that is worth the time. The Wall itself runs just to the north along the line of the Whin Sill, a dark crag that stands out against the sky, and Walltown Crags and the Cawfields are a short ride in either direction.

The weather changes quickly, and a clear morning can turn into drizzle by noon. Wind is common on the ridge.

For a rider the road is a pleasure. The military road, the B6318, runs along the line of the Wall with long straights and rises, and the quieter lanes towards Haltwhistle and Greenhead are narrow, steep and twisting. Expect sheep on the road, gravel at the junctions and drivers in a hurry to get to Hadrian's Wall car parks. Haltwhistle, a few kilometres away, has fuel, a supermarket and a café or two, and Brampton and Haydon Bridge are further. The best months are May to September, and winter days can be icy.
t.hadrian s wall between the cam beck and:
The Cam Beck is a small stream that tumbles out of the hills and runs down towards the Irthing, and the Wall crosses it near Banks, in a stretch where the line is still very clear. Here the Wall's visible remains run along a ridge, with the green bank of the Vallum behind, the long ditch that the Romans dug on the south side to mark the military zone. The label gives the place as the stretch between the Cam Beck and Newtown, in the east of Cumbria, and the walk there is among the easiest on the whole line, with open fields and distant views of the Pennines. The nave still serves as the parish church, and the ruined cloister stands beside it, with the green of the lawn and the curl of the river. King Edward I stayed at Lanercost for months in 1306 and 1307, running his government from the priory while he prepared for another campaign against the Scots. Brampton, three kilometres away, has fuel, a supermarket and cafés, and Wetheral and Scotby are further. May to September is the best season, and autumn is lovely.
t.burnhead roman temporary camp@55.0,-2.5:
The Stanegate is the Roman road that came before the Wall, and Burnhead lies close to its line. t.the vallum between cockmount hill and wa:
The vallum is the strangest part of Hadrian's Wall, and the one that nobody fully understands. It is a great flat-bottomed ditch, with a mound on each side, running along the south of the Wall for its whole length, and it was dug soon after the Wall was begun. The usual explanation is that it marked the back edge of the military zone, a boundary that civilians were not meant to cross except at controlled crossings, but nobody knows quite what it was for. Between Cockmount Hill and the village of Walltown, the vallum is clear and well preserved, a green trench in the field that you can follow with the eye for a long way.

The Whin Sill rises here as a line of crags, with the Wall running along the top, and the view from the highest point takes in the Tyne Gap, the Pennines and the Cheviots. A former quarry, now a country park, holds a wildflower meadow. Nearby Thirlwall Castle, a ruin from the fourteenth century built with stone from the Wall, recalls the Scottish raids that struck this country for centuries.

The land has a bare, big-sky look, with fields and moor stretching to the horizon. Lapwings, curlews and skylarks nest here in spring, and the wild flowers in the quarry attract butterflies in summer. The air is clean and cold, and clouds throw moving shadows across the hills.

Riding here is excellent. The roads climb from Greenhead in a series of steep bends to the ridge, and the lanes along the line of the Wall have long views and good surfaces. Traffic is moderate in summer, with walkers crossing at parking places, and low in winter. Haltwhistle has fuel, a supermarket and cafés, and Haydon Bridge and Brampton are farther. In winter, snow and ice can close the roads, so check the forecast.

The countryside is stony and bare.
