The surface is generally good, but summer heat can be fierce, so start early and bring water. Winter and early spring are the best seasons, when the hills turn briefly green and the temperature is easy. On windy days, the coastal side picks up grit and the odd tumbleweed.

Mazarrón is a town of over thirty-five thousand people, about ten kilometres away, so fuel, supplies and food are easily found. The coastal strip at Puerto de Mazarrón has a long beach, and a short drive away the Bolnuevo erosions, strange wind-sculpted sandstone pillars, are among the most photographed sights on this stretch of coast. Fuente Álamo, a smaller town, lies in the other direction and has its own services, though Mazarrón is the better bet.

If you go inland, remember that hillside caves in Spain are protected sites, and the rock art inside them can be damaged easily. Look rather than touch, follow any signs and keep to the paths, and the place will still be here for the next rider. The light on the hills at evening, turning the stone red and then purple, is the real reward.
t.molino de capel i@38.2,-2.0:
Moratalla stands at the north-west corner of Murcia like a lookout post, and the highlands behind it feel far from the coast. The town is crowned by a medieval castle and its streets run down a steep hillside, and the municipality covers a huge area of pine forest, ravines and rock shelters, many of them holding prehistoric paintings that now sit on the World Heritage list. The Molino de Capel, a watermill name from a rural spot in the hills near the Albacete border, belongs to that scattered countryside, where old farms, mills and caves sit in a landscape of rosemary, thyme and holm oak.

The riding here is a reward for those who like to wander. The roads leave Moratalla and climb into the sierras in a series of curves, past dry stone terraces and almond groves, with long views over the Segura basin. The surface varies, and some minor roads are narrow with few barriers, so keep your speed measured. In summer the heat is dry and strong, and in winter nights can drop below freezing. Late April to June and September to October are the best months, when the hills smell of herbs and the sky is clear.

Moratalla, with about eight and a half thousand people, is the town for fuel, a shop and a meal, about fourteen kilometres from the site. Socovos, across the border in Albacete, is much smaller but has a castle on a crag that is worth a look. Local food is hearty, with lamb and game, rice dishes and thick stews, and mountain honey is a regional pride.

A word on the shelters themselves. Many are fenced, some are open, and all are fragile, so approach quietly and do not touch the painted surfaces. The figures, mostly small hunters, animals and strange stick-limbed people, were made thousands of years ago by those who shared this valley. There is something humbling about standing in the same shade they sought.
t.prado del tornero i@38.1,-2.3:
Nerpio is the place the road seems to forget. It lies in the far south-west of Albacete province, tucked against the Sierra de Segura and the Murcian border, in a high valley where the headwaters of the Taibilla and other streams gather. It has fewer than two thousand residents and one of the densest clusters of prehistoric rock paintings in Spain, dozens of shelters scattered through the surrounding crags. These are part of the Levantine and schematic traditions, painted in red and black, and covered by the same World Heritage listing as the painted caves of the Levante coast.

The approach is the main event. Whichever direction you come from, the roads climb through pine forest and over high, bare plateaux, with long straights and then a series of tight, rising bends as you drop toward the valley. The surface is mostly decent, but remote roads can have gravel and potholes, and the distances are greater than they look. There is very little traffic, and the sense of isolation is strong. Winter brings snow and frost, and even in spring the mornings are cold, so layers are essential. Summer is dry and clear, with brilliant light.

Prado del Tornero I is a short distance from the village. Nerpio has a few basic services, including a bar or two, but do not take it for granted, and arrive with a full tank. Yeste, about twenty-four kilometres away, is the next bigger town, and Moratalla is a long way further. The villages here serve the local farms with a few shops and one or two simple restaurants.

When you visit the shelters, go with a local guide if you can, because many are hard to find and the experience is much richer with someone who knows the stories. Respect the signs, keep to the paths, and above all do not touch the paint. You will be rewarded with the sort of silence that only a mountain village can offer, and a sky so clear that the stars at night seem close enough to count.
t.barranc de frainos abric ii@38.7,-0.3:
A barranc is a ravine in Valencian, and the country behind Alicante is full of them, deep cuts in the pale limestone where the winter rains drain toward the sea. This one lies in the foothills of the Aitana range, near the villages of Benilloba and Sella, and hides a rock shelter with prehistoric paintings, protected under the same World Heritage banner as the painted caves of the whole Spanish Levant. The interior of Alicante province is quite different from the coast, with almond and olive terraces, pine forest and little white villages tucked into the folds, and the air smells of pine resin and thyme.

The riding is pure pleasure. The roads climb out of the coastal plain in tight curves and then run along ridges with big views toward the sea, and Aitana itself rises to over fifteen hundred metres, the highest point in the province. Weekends are busy with cyclists, especially on the road that links Alcoy and the coast, so keep your speed measured and look well ahead. Autumn and spring are the best seasons, with clear light and mild temperatures. Summer is hot and dry, though the higher roads are cooler, and fog can drift in from the sea.

Cocentaina, about thirteen kilometres away, is a town of over eleven thousand people with fuel, food and an old quarter dominated by a fine palace of the counts. Its autumn fair, around All Saints, is a long-standing tradition that draws visitors from all over. Benilloba and Sella are tiny, so opening hours are a gamble. Alcoy, not far off, is known for its Moors and Christians festival in April, a riot of costumes and gunpowder, and for its marzipan and almond sweets.

If you plan to visit the shelter, check access locally, as some are closed or require permission. The most valuable thing you can bring is care. Stay on the path, leave no trace, and let the quiet of the ravine do its work, with a distant dog barking and the swallows swooping overhead.
t.tabla de pochico@38.5,-0.3:
Villajoyosa, the Vila, is one of those towns that makes a bad first impression only on the way in. The approach is lined with apartment blocks, but the old seafront is a long row of houses painted in bright colours, ochre, pink, blue and green, said to have helped fishermen find their own door from the sea. Behind the harbour the church stands fortress-like, built with walls designed to withstand pirate raids, and the whole place smells faintly of the sea and, oddly, of chocolate, because the town is home to one of Spain's best known chocolate makers, founded in the nineteenth century. The Tabla de Pochico lies in the hills a few kilometres inland, in the scrubby, rocky land that rises behind the coast.

The riding here is a study in contrasts. Along the coast the road is busy and crowded, particularly in summer, with traffic crawling between resort towns. But turn inland and the character changes quickly, with narrow roads climbing among terraced slopes, carob and almond trees, and dry stone walls. The Puig Campana, a sharp-toothed mountain of about fourteen hundred metres with a famous notch in its summit, dominates the horizon, and the roads around it are twisty and rewarding. Go in spring or autumn, and start early to avoid the traffic and the heat.

Fuel and food are easy. Villajoyosa has nearly thirty-four thousand people and El Campello over twenty-six thousand, and both have plenty of stations and restaurants. On the seafront you can order fresh fish and rice dishes, and a visit to the chocolate factory shop is almost compulsory, with a small museum attached.

If you find the rock shelters, remember that they are protected and fragile, and some require permission to visit. The hills here are dry, and the scrub can be flammable in summer, so do not leave anything burning and heed the fire warnings. Take a moment at the end of the day to watch the sunset over the Puig Campana, turning the whole mountain a deep rose.
t.cueva sima de la serreta@38.2,-1.6:
Calasparra is rice country, which surprises people who think of Murcia as parched and brown. The rice grows in terraced paddies fed by the clear, cold waters of the Segura, and the short-grain variety grown here has protected status and a reputation among Spanish cooks as the best for paella and slow rice dishes. Just upstream, the river squeezes through the Almadenes gorge, a narrow cleft between limestone walls where vultures soar and the water runs deep green. The Cueva-sima de la Serreta lies in the dry hills above, near the border with Cieza, in a land of rock and pine.

The roads are a mix of fast valley highway and winding country lane. Between Calasparra and Cieza the surface is smooth and the curves are open, passing through orchards, rice fields and the pine-covered hills of the Sierra de la Pila. Spring is the best season, when Cieza's peach trees flower in a sea of pink, one of the great sights of the region, and the whole valley looks fresh and bright. In summer, the heat is fierce, with temperatures that regularly exceed forty degrees, so ride early or late. Autumn is calm and clear.

Calasparra has nearly eleven thousand people and Cieza over thirty-five thousand, so both offer fuel, food and plenty of places to stay. Calasparra's sanctuary, built into a cliff above the river, is a place of pilgrimage with a striking position, and a short walk from the road. Cieza has an old Moorish quarter and a river promenade, and its local fruit, peaches and apricots, are sold in season at roadside stalls.

If you plan to visit the cave, remember it is a protected site and access may be limited. The rock art in Murcia is part of the UNESCO listing, and it is fragile. Pick a calm evening, find a spot with a view of the gorge, and watch the vultures circle in the rising air. The silence broken only by wings and wind is something that stays with you long after the ride.
t.marmalo i@39.9,-1.6:
The Serranía de Cuenca does not advertise itself, and that is half its appeal. Marmalo lies in the south-eastern corner of Cuenca province, where the high limestone plateau begins to break up into pine-covered ridges and gorges as it falls toward the Cabriel river and the border with Valencia. Villar del Humo, a village of only a few hundred people, is the nearest settlement of any note, and the shelters around it hold Levantine rock paintings, small, vivid figures of hunters and animals in red, a tradition UNESCO lists among Europe's major rock art. Marmalo I is one of several sites here, and there are more nearby.

The riding is on quiet roads through big, empty country. Pine forests roll away in every direction, broken by small farms, dry stone walls and the occasional sheepfold, and the Cabriel cuts a deep green gorge through the landscape, a river famous for its clear water and for being one of the last wild rivers in this part of Spain. The altitude is around a thousand metres or more, so mornings are cold even in summer and winter brings frost and snow. The roads are mostly narrow and winding, with patches of rough surface, and there is almost no traffic, so a breakdown here would be a long wait.

Plan your fuel carefully. Villar del Humo has only a few hundred people and Carboneras de Guadazaón, about thirteen kilometres off, has a bit under a thousand, so neither is a safe bet, and the nearest reliable towns are some distance away, Cuenca to the north-west and the Requena area to the east. Fill the tank at the last big town, carry water and tell someone where you are going. Phone signal is patchy.

In return, you get skies of astonishing clarity and the sound of the wind in the pines. Autumn is superb, with mushrooms in the woods and golden light, and spring brings wildflowers and birdsong. Approach the shelters quietly, keep to any marked paths, and leave the paintings untouched.
t.abrigo de los cerricos@38.1,-2.3:
Above the Taibilla valley, Nerpio's higher ground belongs to goats, vultures and wind. The Abrigo de los Cerricos lies a couple of kilometres from the village, among the limestone crags and pine slopes of the Sierra de Taibilla, where the Spanish ibex clambers over the rocks and griffon vultures ride the thermals above. It is exposed terrain, with strong gusts on the ridges, and clouds can drop quickly onto the high ground. Weather is changeable, so carry a waterproof jacket even in July, and in winter be prepared for ice. The surface is mostly good, but patched in places, and the nearest garage is far away.

Nerpio, about one and a half kilometres off, is the nearest village, with a bar or two and a few shops. Yeste, a market town, is twenty-five kilometres away and offers more services, and Moratalla, the larger town, is a long drive of nearly forty kilometres. If in doubt, fill up in Yeste. If you can, linger in the evening. The vultures return to their roosts, the light turns amber on the cliffs, and the smell of wild thyme drifts on the air. It is easy to see why people painted here, because the place invites you to look.
t.las casas de las ingenieros i@38.2,-2.3:
The name points to engineers, and in this corner of Albacete the likeliest explanation is water. Other shelters in the area carry the names of the people who first recorded them, a reminder of how recently some of these sites were noticed.

The ride takes you through an empty, beautiful country. The road from Nerpio runs through fields of cereal and almond, then climbs among rock outcrops and wooded hillsides, with long views south toward the Sierra de las Cabras. The surface is variable, with smooth sections giving way to potholes and loose gravel on the edges, and the bends are open but sometimes blind. Spring wildflowers, in April and May, are a high point, and autumn light is warm and golden.

Yeste, nineteen kilometres off, is a larger town with more shops and a petrol station, and Moratalla is the major centre, a longer drive. Fill up before you leave and carry water.

Visitors tend to come for the rock art, but the valley's greatest asset is its quiet. You will hear sheep bells, the wind in the pines and a distant tractor, and not much else. Park off the road, walk a short way up the slope and let the silence settle. Look for the shelters only with guidance and respect, because the paintings are very old and cannot be replaced.
t.fuente del sauco@38.3,-2.1:
The Fuente del Sauco is the elder-tree fountain, a small spring that gave its name to a shelter in the hills between Letur and Socovos in the south of Albacete. Water is the story of this country. Socovos has a castle perched on a crag, with views across the valley. In spring the almond blossom fills the hillsides, and in autumn the leaves turn gold along the river.

The nearest dependable source is Moratalla or one of the larger towns on the main roads, so fill up beforehand, especially if you plan to stay out all day. Water is welcome here, and the local springs and streams are clear, but carry your own to be safe.

Take a short walk along the river if you can. The Mundo's water is cold and pure, and in summer people swim in its deep pools. The shade of poplars and willows on the bank is a relief after the hot dry hills, and the sound of running water is a constant companion. At dusk, swallows skim the surface and the cliffs turn a deep orange.
t.abrigo grande de minateda@38.5,-1.6:
The Abrigo Grande de Minateda is the big one, the name says so, and for once the name is accurate.
