Hunters, deer, goats and strange, elongated human figures were drawn here over thousands of years, and the site is covered by World Heritage protection. The country around it is dry, broken and beautiful, a land of badlands, gullies and flat-topped hills that looks almost like another continent.

The riding around Hellín is quiet and open. Long, smooth roads cross semi-arid plains of cereal and almond, with big skies and distant ridges, and there are few villages, so you can ride for long stretches without meeting much traffic. To the south the land drops toward the Segura valley, and the roads to Cieza and the gorge of Almadenes pass through dramatic canyon scenery. Summer is very hot, and the best seasons are spring and autumn, with mild days and clear light. Winter mornings can be cold, with frost on the plain.

Hellín is a proper town of nearly thirty-one thousand people, about nine kilometres away, so fuel, food and accommodation are easy to find. It is famous for its Holy Week drumming, the Tamborada, during which thousands of drummers fill the streets with thunder through the night and day, a tradition recognised internationally. If you are here in that week, the noise is unforgettable, although rooms are scarce. Albatana, a small village, is the other nearby settlement.

At the site, take time to look carefully. The paintings are faint and sometimes hard to distinguish from natural stains, and a short pause often reveals an animal or figure you missed at first glance. Respect the fences and signs, and keep your hands to yourself. The landscape is not dramatic in the usual sense, but its stillness is a form of drama, and by the end of the afternoon it grows hard to leave.
t.cueva de la feliceta@38.4,-0.3:
Behind the resort towns of the Costa Blanca, a short ride inland, the land rises into dry limestone hills where almost nobody goes. The Cueva de la Feliceta is one of several prehistoric painted shelters in the hills above El Campello, a coastal town of over twenty-six thousand people about fourteen kilometres away, and one of several painted shelters in the same tradition. The surrounding country is scrub, pine and terraced almond groves, with the sea glinting in the distance and the sound of cicadas in summer.

The roads here are a surprise. From the coast they climb quickly into the hills in a run of bends, passing through small villages such as Busot and Aigües, with views over the bay of Alicante and, on clear days, the island of Tabarca. Busot is home to the Cuevas de Canelobre, a vast cave with towering stalactites and a huge central chamber, open to visitors and impressive enough to have been used during the Civil War to hide aircraft engine production. It is a cool refuge on a hot day. The roads can be busy with cyclists, especially at weekends, so ride with care, and in summer heat start early.

El Campello and Villajoyosa are both large enough to offer fuel, restaurants and shops, and Alicante is not far. In the hills the villages are small and the services limited, so take what you need from the coast. Fresh fish, rice dishes and good bread are easy to find at the seafront and the old fishing quarter of El Campello keeps some of its seafaring character.

The hills have an austere beauty, with pale rock, grey-green scrub and a light so strong it bleaches colour at midday. The best hours are early morning and late afternoon, when the shadows lengthen and the land warms to gold. In autumn, after the first rains, the whole landscape smells of wet earth and herbs. Treat the shelter with respect, as with all such places, and leave it as you found it.
t.tenada de cueva moreno@38.3,-2.1:
A tenada is a farm shed for livestock, the kind of low stone building that marks old transhumance routes, and the cave that goes with it is a local hollow in the limestone near Letur and Socovos in the south of Albacete province. This is the dry, hilly outer edge of the Sierra del Segura, where the pine woods give way to open scrub and cereal fields, and the horizon is a series of pale ridges. The label also links to the Letreros de los Mártires, a set of painted marks in a nearby shelter, which hints at the density of prehistoric art in this district.

Riding here is gentle and undemanding. The roads between Letur, Socovos and the surrounding hamlets run through olive and almond groves and over modest passes, with long, open bends and little traffic. The surface is mostly sound, though some farm tracks that look inviting on a map are rough. Socovos stands on a hill topped by a castle of Muslim origin, with a small village clustered below, and the road up to it gives a fine view across the valley. Summers are very hot and dry, and the best months are April, May, September and October.

Letur has about twelve hundred inhabitants and Socovos nearly two thousand, enough for a shop, a bar and perhaps a petrol pump, but not enough to rely on. Moratalla, twenty-one kilometres away, is the larger place, with eight and a half thousand people, a hillside castle and the full range of services, so fill up there or in Hellín. The Mundo and Tus rivers carve small gorges through this country, and a stop beside running water is a welcome change from the dry hills.

You may see griffon vultures wheeling overhead, and in the evening the hills turn gold and then violet. If you stop at a shelter, keep your voice low and your hands in your pockets, as the paint is very old and very thin. Bring plenty of water, a hat and patience, because this is a country that rewards slow travel.
t.marmalo v@39.9,-1.7:
Autumn is the season for this part of Cuenca, when people with baskets disappear into the pine woods in search of mushrooms. Marmalo V is another of the painted shelters scattered around Villar del Humo, a village of fewer than four hundred people on the south-eastern flank of the Serranía de Cuenca, where the high plateau breaks into forested ridges and the Cabriel river gathers its strength. The ride takes in the church tower of San Martín in Teruel as well, a long way off but tied to this one by a thread of Spanish rock art and old villages, so think of this stop as one chapter in a longer story.

What strikes you here is the sheer quiet. Between the villages, the landscape is a deep green carpet of pine, with the occasional clearing for a field or a sheepfold. The road twists through woods and along ridges, with a surface that ranges from good to rough, and traffic is rare enough that a passing car is an event. The air smells of resin and warm needles. Three of the great rivers of Spain, the Tagus, the Júcar and the Cabriel, rise within a day's ride of each other in these uplands, and the water you cross here is on its way to either the Atlantic or the Mediterranean, depending on which valley it chooses.

With so few people about, fuel and food need planning. Villar del Humo and Carboneras de Guadazaón, which has nearly a thousand inhabitants, offer little beyond a shop and a bar, so it makes sense to fill the tank in a larger town before you arrive. Mornings are often cold even in summer, and snow falls in winter, sometimes enough to close minor roads. The wild boar are numerous, so watch for them at dusk, and in the villages the hunting season is a serious matter.

The shelters are reached on short walks, and the paintings of hunters and animals are small, delicate and easily missed. Go slowly, look at the shapes in the rock, and give the place a little silence. It is not a landscape that shouts; it asks you to lean in.
t.hadrian s wall in wall mile 6@55.0,-1.7:
Wall mile 6 is not a place name but a measurement, since the Romans divided Hadrian's Wall into numbered miles counting from the east, and the sixth mile falls at Benwell, now a western suburb of Newcastle. Here, between terraces of Victorian houses, the remains of the Roman fort of Condercum once looked out over the Tyne valley, and you can still see a stretch of the Wall's foundation, the base of a turret and the remains of a small temple dedicated to a local god, Antenociticus, one of the few such temples to survive along the frontier. The fort stood on a ridge above the river, a good place to watch for trouble and a good place to be seen.

Newcastle riding is a city business. The roads around Benwell are busy, with traffic lights, buses and tight junctions, and the Roman line is mostly buried below the streets. The old Military Road, which follows the Wall westward, begins to open into a more rural route within a few miles, and in the Tyne valley the scenery becomes quite lovely, with woods, farmland and wide views. Weather can shift quickly, with wind and showers blowing in off the North Sea, so pack waterproofs even in summer.

Fuel and food are no problem. Benwell is only a few minutes from the city centre, and Blaydon-on-Tyne, with nearly fifteen thousand people, is a short ride to the west, famous for the Blaydon Races, immortalised in a Geordie song. Newcastle was founded by the Romans as Pons Aelius, the bridge of Hadrian, and it has bridged the Tyne ever since. Today seven bridges span the river within a short distance, and the iconic Tyne Bridge, opened in 1928, is the one on all the postcards.

If you have a spare hour, find the temple remains, which stand in a small enclosure beside a suburban street. They are modest, but there is something remarkable about an ancient shrine tucked between modern houses, a little island of the second century in the middle of a twenty-first century street. Then ride west, out of the city and into the Wall country.
t.lees hall roman camp@55.0,-2.5:
Haltwhistle likes to call itself the centre of Britain, a claim measured with some creativity, and it is certainly the middle of Hadrian's Wall country, a small market town on the South Tyne where the river valley narrows between the Pennines and the Wall crags. Lees Hall Roman camp is one of the temporary camps the army threw up while building the Wall or on campaign, a rectangle of bank and ditch now softened by grass. These marching camps were quick, practical affairs, ploughed flat in many places, and what survives is mostly a faint earthwork seen best in low evening light.

The ride into this country is among the best in England. The old Military Road, now the B6318, follows the line of the Wall along the high ridge, rising and falling in long, bold sweeps with wide views north into Northumberland's empty moorland and south toward the Tyne valley. It is a surprisingly fast road in places, with blind crests and tight bends, so respect the limits and the sheep. Weather is changeable, and the ridge catches the wind, so bring layers. Spring and early autumn are best, with long light and quieter roads, while summer weekends bring caravans and coach parties.

Haltwhistle, a mile and a half off, has under four thousand people and the fuel and food the area needs, including a couple of decent pubs and bakeries. Hexham, over twenty kilometres east, is the bigger town. Haltwhistle also holds a fine collection of fortified farmhouses called bastles, built in the sixteenth century for protection against Border reivers, the raiders who plagued the frontier for centuries. Near Greenhead, a few kilometres west, the Roman Army Museum explains how the garrison lived, and the crags at Walltown give the best views.

If you want a quiet moment, stop where the Wall climbs a ridge and look back over the valley. The scene would have been recognisable to a Roman sentry, with the hills rolling away and the sky enormous. Then listen. On a still evening you will hear only curlews, the wind in the grass and, perhaps, a distant sheep complaining.
t.hadrian s wall between the track to cock:
The stretch of Wall near Cawfields is where the whole thing makes the most sense, because the Romans used the landscape. Here the Great Whin Sill, a hard ridge of dark dolerite, rises in a line of crags along the north, and the Wall runs along the top of it, looking down over a drop on one side and a long slope on the other. Close to Cockmount Hill, the Wall and its southern ditch, the vallum, are both visible, and the milefortlet at Cawfields is one of the best preserved on the line, a square enclosure with a gateway still standing. Nearby, an old quarry has filled with water to make a small, dark lake at the foot of the crags.

The road that runs beside it, the B6318, is the Military Road, built after the Jacobite rising of 1745 so that troops could move across the country. General Wade's engineers laid it along the Wall, and in places they used the Wall's stones for the foundations, which is why long stretches of the Roman work have vanished. It is a splendid road for riding, with long straights, blind crests and bold bends, and it follows the ridge for miles. Wind is the main challenge, and the weather can turn from sun to rain in minutes. Sheep stray onto the road, so slow for the crests.

Haltwhistle, three and a half kilometres away, has the services you need, including fuel and a choice of cafes. Haydon Bridge, farther east, is much smaller, and Hexham, twenty-five kilometres off, is the nearest town of any size. The nearby fort of Great Chesters, known to the Romans as Aesica, was one of the main garrison posts in this central sector.

Pause on the crags and look both ways. To the north, the land falls away into empty moorland, once barbarian country, and to the south the green valley of the Tyne lies calm and farmed. It is easy to see why a frontier was drawn here, and equally easy to feel the loneliness of the men who patrolled it.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum between the fe:
East of the crags the Wall country softens into the Tyne valley, a green landscape of meadows and woods, and near Corbridge you meet something the Wall itself never had: a town. Corbridge Roman Town, known to the Romans as Coria, grew up at the crossing of the River Tyne and the great north road, Dere Street, and served as a supply base for the army and a market for the civilians who followed it. The granaries and fountain survive, and a museum holds finds such as the famous Corbridge Lion, a sculpture of a lion devouring a stag. The label puts us on a stretch of Wall and vallum near Herd Hill, a few kilometres north-east.

The ride is lovely. From Corbridge a road follows the Wall westward along the Tyne's north bank, past farms and woodland, with views over the river valley. Narrower lanes lead north into quiet farmland and moorland, where the surface is rougher and the traffic almost nil. The valley is at its best in May, with hawthorn in flower, and in October, when the beeches turn gold. Note that fords and flooded lanes can occur after heavy rain, so take care. A few kilometres west, at Heavenfield, a small church marks the place where King Oswald raised a wooden cross before winning a battle in 634, an early moment in the Christian history of Northumbria.

Corbridge has about three thousand people and a good village centre with shops, cafes and a petrol station nearby, while Acomb is smaller. Hexham, seven kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town, with just over eleven thousand people and an abbey of great age, whose Saxon crypt was built with stones taken from Roman buildings. A coffee and a slice of cake in the abbey grounds is a fine way to spend a morning.

When you stand on the Wall here, notice how low it is, and how often it has been robbed for farm buildings. Roman stones were useful, and the people of the valley used them for a thousand years. The same stones are in churches and barns, and in walls that now mark field boundaries.
t.roman aqueduct to great chesters from th:
The Romans were obsessed with water, and even on this bleak ridge they went to extraordinary trouble to bring it to their fort. The fort of Great Chesters, called Aesica in Roman times, stood on a crag high above the Haltwhistle Burn, with no spring close enough to supply a garrison of several hundred men and their animals. So the engineers built an aqueduct, an open channel that ran for about eight kilometres, following the contours of the land from a stream to the west, and delivered a steady flow into the fort. It was no great arched structure with spans of stone, but a simple ditch, and its beauty lies in the precision of the gradient. You can still trace the channel as a shallow line in the grass.

The country is high, open and often empty. A short ride from Haltwhistle brings you onto the ridge, where the Military Road runs in long straights across the moor, with sudden dips and crests and the occasional blind bend. Sheep graze the verges and sometimes the road, and the wind sweeps unimpeded. In clear weather the view stretches for miles across Northumberland, and in poor weather the cloud comes down, and the place feels austere.

Haltwhistle, four kilometres away, has fuel, food and shelter, and it is a pleasant market town with old stone houses. Haydon Bridge is much smaller, and Hexham is more than twenty kilometres off. At Chesterholm, to the east, the Vindolanda fort has yielded an extraordinary collection of wooden writing tablets, including a woman's invitation to a birthday party and a soldier's request for more socks and underpants, which bring the garrison to life in a very human way.

Walk out and look for the channel. It takes a moment to see, but once you do, the engineering begins to emerge. The Roman Army was not just a fighting force, it was an organisation of surveyors and builders. Out here in the wind, you can sense how much effort went into keeping a few hundred soldiers supplied with something as ordinary as water.
If the Wall was the barrier you could see, the vallum was the barrier you were not supposed to cross. This is a great flat-bottomed ditch, about six metres wide, with mounds of earth on either side, and it ran along the south of the Wall for most of its length, forming a kind of military zone behind the frontier. Nobody is quite sure of its purpose, though the usual theory is that it marked the rear boundary of the area and controlled the movement of people and goods. At Benwell, within Newcastle, the vallum has one of its best-known features, a stone causeway that allowed the road to cross the ditch near the fort gate, a neat piece of Roman engineering that came to light in the twentieth century.

The setting is suburban, with Victorian terraces and bus routes, and the Roman line is hidden beneath streets and gardens. Riding is a city affair, with traffic lights and one-way streets, so allow extra time, and avoid the rush hours. The route west along the river gives a gentler start, and within a few kilometres the city loosens into the valley of the Tyne, with fields and woodland. Rain falls often here, and the road surface in the city is patched and sometimes greasy.

Benwell is only a short ride from the centre of Newcastle, and Blaydon-on-Tyne, three kilometres west, has nearly fifteen thousand people. Fuel stations are plentiful. For a bite, the neighbouring streets hold plenty of cafes and takeaways, and the city's food scene is lively, from pie and peas to Chinese and Indian restaurants. A short ride away, the Quayside has bars and a view of the great bridges.

Walk the short stretch where the vallum survives, and you can see it as a hollow in the ground, edged by grassy banks. The effect is quiet and slightly eerie, like a scar on the landscape. It is not a thing that makes for a postcard, but it has a kind of stubborn dignity, and it reminds you that the Roman frontier was much more than a wall.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum from throckley:
Heddon-on-the-Wall is the place where the Wall comes up out of the suburbs and stands in the open. Here, west of Newcastle, a stretch of the Wall's foundation and lower courses survives beside the village, one of the few places in the east where it rises above knee height, and it is of the so-called Broad Wall type, wider than the narrower version built later in the sequence. The Romans changed their plan during construction, and here you can read the evidence in stone. Beside it, the vallum shows as a shallow ditch, and a short walk takes you along the line toward Throckley.

The riding in this part of Tyneside is mixed. The roads are busy around Newburn and Throckley, with traffic and roundabouts, but a short ride west along the Tyne valley brings you to quiet lanes, fields and woods. The village of Wylam, a few kilometres off, was the birthplace of George Stephenson, the railway pioneer, and the engine Puffing Billy was built at the nearby colliery. The cottage where he was born is a National Trust property and sits beside an old waggonway, now a footpath. Weather is changeable, and spring is a good time, with green fields and blossom.

Newburn, with over forty-one thousand people in its larger urban area, and Heddon, with about thirteen hundred, are both close, and fuel and food are easy to find. Newburn was the site of a battle in 1640, when a Scottish army defeated an English one at the ford over the Tyne and went on to occupy Newcastle, a turning point in the build-up to the English Civil War. It is a quiet spot now, with a riverside path and a park.

On the Wall at Heddon, you can touch the stones. They are rough and cold, and each carries the faint marks of the mason who shaped it. A short distance away, the sound of traffic fades, and you can hear birds. There is a good bench, and a fine view over fields toward the river. It is a quiet way to meet the Roman Empire.
t.the vallum between the road to steel rig:
Steel Rigg is the place everyone photographs. The crag rises steeply from the road, with the Wall running along its top and dipping into a gap known as Sycamore Gap, where a single tree stood for generations in a perfect V of the hills, until it was felled one night in September 2023. The loss caused shock across the country, and the stump now sprouts new shoots. The vallum, the great ditch and mounds south of the Wall, runs beside the road at the foot of the crags, and here it is clearly visible, a long straight hollow in the field, with the mounds standing on either side.

The road to Steel Rigg leaves the Military Road at the Once Brewed visitor centre, near a pub with the delightful name of the Twice Brewed Inn. The Military Road itself is a gem for riders, undulating over the ridge with wide views, long curves and little protection from the weather. On a clear day it is glorious, and on a wet day it is bleak and exposed. The area is also a designated International Dark Sky Park, one of the best places in England to see the stars, so a night stay brings a bonus.

Haltwhistle, about four kilometres away, has the nearest fuel and a range of shops, and Haydon Bridge, with fewer than sixteen hundred people, is smaller and farther. Hexham, twenty kilometres east, is a handsome market town with a fine abbey. Houses along the Military Road are few, so plan on carrying water and a snack, because you may not meet a cafe for miles. A short walk from the road to Steel Rigg leads along the crag to Crag Lough, a dark lake beneath cliffs.

Walk along the top of the crags in the late afternoon, when the shadows lengthen and the light turns gold. The Wall rises and falls over the ridge like a stone serpent, and the views north stretch to the horizon. It is easy to feel small here. The wind, the open sky and the sense of two thousand years of footsteps give you a feeling that few places can match.
t.hokgkeng tulou cluster@24.7,117.0:
This is the Hakka country of southwestern Fujian, the hills of Nanjing and Pinghe counties, where villagers built vast earthen fortress-homes called tulou. The ones near Hukeng and Tianloukeng are among the finest, and they are set in valleys of terraced tea, bamboo groves and rice paddies in a green so deep it looks artificial after rain. Each tulou is a ring, square or sometimes oval of rammed earth walls up to a metre or more thick, three or four storeys tall, with one big gate and a single courtyard in the middle where families kept a well, a shrine and animals.

The point of the design was defence and community. Hakka families, migrants from the north, were often outsiders in an area where clan feuds and bandits were real concerns, and a tulou could hold a hundred or several hundred relatives behind a locked door. Rooms were divided identically, kitchens on the ground floor, storage above, bedrooms higher, so it was egalitarian in a way that still surprises visitors. Many are still inhabited, with washing lines hung from the galleries, and some of the families now sell tea and small snacks to visitors.

The riding in this part of Fujian is hill-road riding. The tarmac is generally good but narrow, with tight bends climbing from valley to valley, forest on both sides, and a damp, cool microclimate. Fog and drizzle are common, especially in spring, so pay attention to wet leaves and sudden patches of mud. Local traffic includes motor scooters, small trucks and tour minibuses, and visitor numbers rise during Chinese holidays, so pick a weekday if you can, in autumn or early spring.

The coordinates for this point do not come with a mapped nearby town, so plan fuel, food and lodging in the nearest county centres before you enter the valleys. In China, fuel stations are common on main roads but thin in the hills, and foreign riders face significant licence and registration issues, so check the rules ahead of time. Local restaurants serve Hakka dishes, such as braised pork with preserved vegetables and stuffed tofu, plus strong tea, and the best way to enjoy a tulou is to buy a cup and sit in the courtyard for a while.
t.anping bridge@24.7,118.4:
Five li, that is the old name for it, because the Anping Bridge was reckoned to be five li long, a little over two kilometres, which made it the longest bridge in China for centuries and the longest beam bridge of its kind anywhere in the medieval world. It crosses what used to be a tidal inlet at Anhai, in Jinjiang county south of Quanzhou, and it was begun in the twelfth century under the Southern Song, when this coast was making its money from trade with Arabia, India and Southeast Asia. Local merchants and monks put up much of the cost, and the work went on for the better part of two decades.

Much of the bridge survives as built, long granite slabs, some weighing many tonnes, resting on stone piers with pointed ends. Along the walkway there are pavilions, stone guardian figures in the form of soldiers, and a small pagoda. At low tide you look down on mudflats and fish traps, and on a clear day the whole thing looks like a thin grey ribbon pulled across the bay. The silting of the inlet over the centuries has left the bridge standing partly over fields and houses, so you come off one end into a village rather than a river.

As for the ride, the approach is flat and ordinary, a Fujian coastal plain of small factories, fish ponds, temples with swooping roofs, and a constant dribble of scooters and trucks. Roads are wide in places and narrow in others, and junctions come without much warning. It is not for racing. Early on a spring or autumn morning the light is soft and the heat has not yet built, and you may have the bridge nearly to yourself, apart from the old men who walk it as exercise.

The closest settlement on the list is Neikeng, a small place, so for fuel and a proper meal plan on Jinjiang, about eighteen kilometres away, which is a big manufacturing city with everything you need. Quanzhou is just beyond, and its old quarter is worth a half day for the temples, mosques and street food. The local specialities include seafood noodles, peanut soup and sweet fried dough, so eat before you ride. Check licence and permit rules for foreign riders in China ahead of time, and keep to the walkway rather than climbing on the railings.
t.garganta de la hoz i@38.4,-0.2:
Behind the beaches and high-rises of the Costa Blanca, a few kilometres inland from Alicante and El Campello, the land rises quickly into dry limestone hills, scrub and almond terraces. This is the beginning of the Betic ranges, and the area is cut by ravines, barrancos, which carry water only after heavy storms and have carved gorges in the soft rock. Garganta de la Hoz is the name of such a gorge, a narrow cut in the hills, and the I suggests that more than one point on the ride lies along it. I do not know this particular spot well enough to describe it in detail, so I will describe the country around it.

The landscape smells of thyme, rosemary and pine resin in the sun, with Aleppo pines on the hillsides, carob and olive trees in the terraces, and cliffs where eagle owls and Bonelli's eagles nest. Nearby, the cave of Canelobre at Busot has a huge cathedral-like chamber with stalactites, and the hill villages of the Alicante interior, such as Xixona, are famous for turrón, the almond and honey nougat sold at Christmas across Spain. The sea is visible from many of the ridges, a deep blue strip beyond the white towns.

For a rider the interior is a delight. The roads from El Campello and Alicante climb into the hills with tight bends, hairpins and views, and they are quiet in the winter and spring, when the Costa Blanca tourists are fewer. Surfaces are generally good, though gravel washes onto the corners after rain, and the occasional cyclist or tractor is a hazard. Summer is hot, with temperatures often above thirty-five degrees, and busy on the coast, so the best seasons are autumn through spring. When the rain comes, it can be violent, and dry stream beds fill rapidly, so avoid crossing flooded roads.

El Campello, a coastal town of about twenty-six thousand people some fourteen kilometres away, has fuel stations, supermarkets, workshops and a fine selection of seafood restaurants along the sea front. Alicante, a short ride south, has everything else. Try arroz a banda, rice cooked in fish stock, or a plate of fried squid, and a coffee in a harbour café. Carry water on any walk in the hills, wear a hat, and keep to marked paths, since the ground is rocky and the sun strong.
t.barranc de les coves abric ii@38.7,-0.6:
Ibi is the first thing to understand here, because the town sits so close that the rock shelter feels like its back garden. Ibi is a place that makes toys, and has done for generations; the whole Hoya de Castalla and the neighbouring town of Onil grew a tinplate-and-plastic industry that once filled children's bedrooms across Spain. Before the factories, Ibi was known for something colder: snow and ice gathered from the high ground of the Sierra de Mariola and stored in pits for the summer. A town that lives on cold in a region that bakes is a good story to carry up the hill.

The shelter itself belongs to the Mediterranean rock art of the Iberian peninsula, the painted tradition in red and black that UNESCO listed in 1998 and that clings to rock overhangs all down the eastern side of Spain. The figures are small, lively and mostly pared down to a few strokes. Do not expect a cave mouth with a ticket office. These are shallow abrigos under limestone ledges, reached by track or path from where the tarmac stops, and the bike stays behind.

The riding is the Valencian interior at its most civil. From Ibi the road runs north into dry hills of pine, carob and almond, with the long wall of Mariola on one side and Alcoy's valley ahead. Corners are tidy, gradients modest, and the surface good enough that you spend more time looking at terraces than at the tarmac. Spring is the season to come: the slopes go green and the almond blossom has only just gone. In July the same hills are bleached and the middle of the day is for the shade of a bar in town.

Fuel and food are easy because you are close to real towns. Ibi, at about twenty-four thousand people, has pumps and a proper choice of lunch, and Alcoy, under nine kilometres away, has much more. Water is the thing to carry if you plan any walking, because the shelters are dry places and there is no tap at the end of the path.

One thing worth knowing before you go is that these painted sites are fragile and some are fenced. Look, photograph without flash, never touch the rock and never wet the paint to see it better, which people have done to their lasting regret. The quiet is part of it: a ledge, a view across scrub, and an archer a few thousand years older than any town you rode through.
t.abric de las sabinas@39.1,-0.8:
Bicorp is the village to head for, and it is worth the ride for the name alone. It is a small place in the Canal de Navarrés, the inland Valencian country where the hills fold into one another and nobody has ever made a postcard of them. This is also the country of the famous Cuevas de la Araña, the Spider Cave near Bicorp, where a painted figure on a rock face is shown gathering honey from a crevice with ropes or vines. Of all the Levantine paintings, that scene is probably the one most often reproduced, and it reminds you that the people who painted these walls were gatherers and hunters with a keen eye for small domestic tasks.

Abric de las Sabinas takes its name from the savin junipers that cling to this sort of dry limestone. The shelter lies in a landscape of gorges and ridges cut by little rivers heading towards the Júcar, with Quesa to the north-east and Navarrés to the east. If you have an eye for botany, the smell alone is worth stopping for: wild thyme, rosemary and pine resin warmed in the afternoon sun.

The riding is quiet, narrow and remarkably empty. Roads here connect villages of a few hundred people, and you can go several minutes without seeing another vehicle apart from a farm van or a cyclist training on the climbs. The corners are tight enough to keep you busy but rarely nasty, though the surface can be patchy where the road was patched after a storm. Take the afternoon light from the west if you can; it lights up the rock face and makes the scrub glow.

On practicalities, be sensible. Bicorp is tiny and Quesa not much bigger, so do not count on fuel in either. Navarrés, at nearly three thousand people, is the nearest place likely to have a pump and a few cafés, and Ayora, a little over twenty kilometres away, is the larger town for anything serious. Fill the tank before you leave the main road.

Walk the last stretch with respect. The shelter is old, fragile and not designed for visitors, and the best manners are the ones you would use in a church: quiet voices, no touching, nothing taken home.
t.barranc de les coves abric iv@38.7,-0.6:
Alcoy is the town that explains the surroundings here, and it deserves an hour of your time even if you came for the painted rock. It sits in a deep valley fed by three rivers, and in the nineteenth century it became one of Spain's early industrial cities, making paper and textiles from the waters that tumbled off the Mariola and Font Roja hills. The old factories are still visible in the streets, and the town centre has handsome modernista buildings from the time when the industrialists wanted everyone to know they had arrived.

Alcoy is also known for its April festival of Moors and Christians, a vast and noisy affair of processions, costumes and gunpowder that commemorates a medieval battle for the town. Every Valencian town has its version, but Alcoy's is considered the grandest. If you are riding in late April, check the dates, because rooms fill and the centre is closed to traffic.

The shelter marked here is Abric IV in a cluster of painted overhangs in a barranc, a dry ravine, in the hills between Ibi and Alcoy. These are examples of the Levantine rock art tradition: small red figures, often archers or animals, painted under overhanging limestone by prehistoric hunters. They belong to the Mediterranean Basin group that UNESCO inscribed in 1998. The paintings are not showpieces and you should not expect a visitor centre; they are modest, weathered and easy to walk past.

The road in from either town is a pleasant, medium-tempo ride through pine and scrub, with enough bends to keep the day interesting and enough straight to let you look around. Early in the morning is the best time, when the air is cool and the light is low and warm on the slopes. Summer afternoons can be punishing, and the tarmac gets hot enough to soften at the edges.

Fuel and food are no problem. Alcoy has all the services of a city of sixty thousand, with plenty of pumps, bakeries and bars serving the sort of cheap, solid lunch that suits a rider. Ibi is the other option on the way back. Bring water for the walk, as there is no source at the shelter.
t.barranc de les coves abric iii@38.7,-0.6:
Most places on a route have one personality. This one has two, because the ride runs between the toy town of Ibi on one side and Alcoy on the other, and the stop itself sits between them in a dry barranc of pine and rock. It is the third of a series of painted shelters here, small overhangs with faded red figures that belong to the Levantine tradition of eastern Spain.

That tradition is one of the great puzzles of European prehistory. The paintings show slim human figures, many with bows, hunting deer, ibex and wild cattle, and occasionally something more mysterious like a ceremonial dance or a gathering. No one can be sure exactly when they were made; the dating is argued over, and the answers run from the end of the Ice Age's aftermath through the early farming period. What everyone agrees on is that they were painted in the open air by people who knew these hills better than any of us ever will. UNESCO placed the group on the World Heritage list in 1998, which is why you will find the shelters signposted and sometimes fenced.

Getting here is a pleasure. The road from Ibi winds up through terraced slopes where old almond and olive trees are slowly being reclaimed by pine, and the gradients stay gentle. There are a handful of bends where you need to pay attention, mostly where the road crosses a dry stream bed, and the surface is generally good. Traffic is thin outside the weekends, when cyclists and walkers arrive from Alcoy and Alicante. October and March are the sweet months, with dry roads, cool air and clear views toward the Mariola ridge.

For fuel and lunch go back to Ibi, a town of around twenty-four thousand, or on to Alcoy. The hills between have a couple of village bars, but nothing you should plan around. Take water for yourself and a hat; the shelters sit in sun for most of the day.

Treat the paintings as you would a very old book left on a shelf: look, take a photograph without flash, and leave the rock alone. They have lasted thousands of years because few people have bothered them.
t.hondares@38.2,-2.0:
Hondares is a word on a map that barely registers, and that is exactly why people come. It lies in the high, dry country where the province of Murcia gives way to Albacete, between the Sierra de Segura foothills and the Segura river, which has carved a long valley here before it spills into the Fuensanta reservoir. Moratalla, the nearest real town, is about twelve kilometres away, and in this part of Spain that counts as close.

Moratalla municipality has one of the densest concentrations of prehistoric rock art in the country. The painted shelters here, together with the many others across the Mediterranean side of Spain, make up the group UNESCO recognised in 1998. The figures are mostly in red, small and delicate, and they show people, animals and hunting scenes. Moratalla has also been settled since the Bronze Age, and later the Romans and Moors left their marks. Its Holy Week is famous for the tamborada, in which hundreds of drummers fill the town with a sound you can feel in your chest, if you happen to be passing in spring.

The riding between Moratalla, Socovos and Férez is the kind of back-of-beyond roads that motorcyclists dream about. It is empty, curvy and lined with pine forest, with the occasional view over a reservoir the colour of a bruise. The surface is generally fine, though there are patches where frost has broken it up. Winter can bring ice at height, and summer is fierce, so spring and autumn are the best times. Early morning light on the red soil is something to see.

You will need to plan. Fuel is available in Moratalla, a town of around eight and a half thousand, but not in the smaller villages around, so fill up there. Socovos has a small shop and bars where you can get coffee, but keep your tank full. Take water, too, since the countryside is dry and the shelters have no facilities.

The shelters here are cherished by local archaeologists, so please leave them as you find them.
The Benicadell range is the thing that dominates every view here, a pale limestone ridge that rises above 1,100 metres between the Vall d'Albaida and the Comtat. The shelter marked here lies at the base of it, among villages that most Valencians have heard of but few have visited: Ráfol de Salem, Castelló de Rugat and Beniarrés, all within four kilometres of one another. This is quiet country of orchards, olive terraces and little hamlets with a church and a bar.

The painted shelters in this barranc belong to the Levantine tradition of rock art, with its small, nimble red figures of hunters and animals. The tradition is old, much older than the Romans or the Moors, and the best minds in archaeology still argue about exactly how old. UNESCO included the group in its World Heritage list in 1998, covering hundreds of sites along Spain's Mediterranean side. This one is a small piece of that larger picture, and part of its charm is that it is so unassuming.

Beniarrés has a reservoir on the Serpis river, a calm sheet of water in a crease of the hills which is a good place to eat a sandwich and watch birds. Ráfol de Salem is crowned by a ruined castle that sits above the village on a rocky knoll; it is a short, steep detour if you fancy it. There is Moorish history everywhere in this part of the country, from terraced irrigation to place names that begin with Beni, meaning sons of, in the old Arabic fashion.

The roads connecting these villages are the draw for a rider. They are narrow, quiet and bendy, with surfaces that range from smooth to tired, and the gradients are gentle except where the Benicadell pushes the road upward. Morning is cool, midday is hot and quiet, and evening light on the ridge is magnificent.

For fuel, the nearest larger town is Muro del Alcoy, about ten kilometres away, with Alcoy beyond. Castelló de Rugat is big enough for a bar and a bakery, but do not count on a pump in the smaller villages. Carry water if you plan to walk.
t.cueva de los mosquitos@38.4,-0.3:
Alicante is the city that everybody knows, but the hills behind it are the part you can have to yourself. This shelter lies in the dry interior north of the city, between El Campello on the coast and the towns of Mutxamel and San Juan, in a landscape of marl, pine and abandoned almond terraces. It is a long way from the seafront.

The name suggests a cave full of mosquitos, which tells you something about the damp spots in an otherwise parched region. The painted sites in this part of Alicante province belong to the Levantine tradition, tiny red figures of hunters and animals that UNESCO recognised in 1998 as part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin. They lie scattered through the barrancs, and finding them is as much a matter of local knowledge as anything else.

The coast below has history too. At El Campello you can visit the remains of an Iberian settlement on a tiny island called the Illeta dels Banyets, which was inhabited from the Bronze Age onward, and the town is a working fishing and holiday place with a harbour and a long beach. A bit further, the old city of Alicante is crowned by the Castle of Santa Bárbara, and the road to Xixona leads to the home of turrón, the nougat that fills Spanish Christmas tables.

For riders the interest here is the afternoon loop: leave the coast, climb through the hills on narrow country roads, and drop back down with the sea shining ahead. Corners are mostly short and tidy, the surface is often coarse in the local fashion, and cyclists are everywhere on weekends. Avoid the middle of the day in summer; the heat is intense and the hills hold it. October through April is ideal, and the sunsets over the plain are wonderful.

Fuel and food are no trouble. El Campello is the nearest large town, with plenty of pumps and seaside restaurants serving rice dishes and grilled fish. Bring water for the walk.
t.cova de reinos@38.8,-0.1:
Vall d'Ebo is one of those places where history has left obvious scars. In 1609 the Moriscos, the descendants of Spain's Muslim population, were expelled from the kingdom of Valencia, and valleys like this one were suddenly emptied. The Vall d'Ebo was resettled, but never fully recovered, and today it is home to fewer than four hundred people. The village stands in a deep bowl of mountains with terraces cut into the slopes, and it feels as though it belongs to another century.

The Cova de Reinós lies close by, in a dry landscape of limestone and pine above the town of Pego. The area has several painted shelters belonging to the Levantine tradition of rock art, the one listed by UNESCO in 1998. Their red figures, many of them archers and animals, were painted by hunting peoples long before the Moors ever came. Together the paintings and the empty terraces suggest how many layers of human life have passed through the same valley.

Below, Pego sits at the edge of a huge wetland, the Marjal Pego-Oliva, where rice has been grown for centuries and herons and other birds gather in winter. It is a good contrast to the dry mountains above. If you have time, take the Vall de Gallinera road north of Ebo; in late winter its cherry trees come into bloom, and the valley turns white.

The road to Vall d'Ebo leaves Pego and climbs through a narrow gorge before opening into the valley, with plenty of tight bends and little traffic. It is the sort of road where you slow down because you want to, not because you must. The surface is mixed, so keep an eye out for gravel on the corners after rain. Mornings are best, with cool air and good light.

Fuel is available in Pego, which has over eleven thousand people and all the usual services. Vall d'Ebo has a bar or two but no pumps that you should rely on. Eat in Pego, where the rice dishes are worth the stop, and bring water for any walking.
t.abrigo del mal paso@39.2,-0.8:
The Júcar is the river behind this stop, though you cannot see it from the shelter. Millares is a village of about five hundred people in the broken hill country of inland Valencia, not far from where the great river runs out of the mountains and into the reservoir at Tous. The country around is a labyrinth of gorges, ravines and small plateaux, cut by the Júcar and its tributaries, with pine woods on the slopes and bare limestone on the tops.

The name Mal Paso, bad step, appears all over Spain on any path with an exposed or awkward crossing, and here it is a reminder that this is walking country rather than a place for easy roadside viewing. The shelter belongs to the Levantine tradition, in which tiny red figures were painted under rock overhangs, and the label also mentions the Barranco Garrofero, named for the carob tree, garrofer in Valencian, which grows wild across the region. Carob pods were once an important animal feed and are still collected in some places.

The ride in is one of the nicest in the area. The road follows the river valley, goes through a few short tunnels, and climbs up toward Millares through terraces of oranges and olives. Corners come in a rhythm, some tight, some open, and the surface is generally smooth with the odd rough patch. Traffic is light except on weekend afternoons when cyclists and canyoners arrive. Spring is magnificent: the hillsides are green, the air smells of thyme and orange blossom, and the reservoir gleams.

You will need to think about supplies. Millares has a bar and probably little else. Turís is about eighteen kilometres away and, with five thousand people, has fuel and a proper selection of shops. The area is famous for wine, particularly from the Turís cooperative, and for the tomatoes of nearby Buñol, which every August become ammunition in the Tomatina.

Take water for the walk and wear sturdy shoes. The paths are dry and stony, and the shelter itself is exposed to the afternoon sun.
t.barranc de l infern conj 3 abrigo iil@38:
Three centuries of travellers have called this ravine Hell without anyone quite agreeing why. The Barranc de l'Infern is a narrow gorge in the Vall de Laguar, in the Marina Alta of Alicante province, and it is best known today for a footpath that follows the ravine up and down a long staircase of stone steps said to number thousands, built by the Moriscos as a pack route between villages. Along the walls, in sheltered places, are several clusters of rock paintings, and this is the third group, numbered as a conjunto, with a painted shelter that belongs to the Levantine tradition.

Those paintings are small, red and quite weathered, and some of the figures are hard to read without patience. The shelters were recorded by archaeologists who numbered each group, which is why you will see labels such as Conjunto 3 and abrigo III in the listings. They are part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula, inscribed by UNESCO in 1998.

The ride up is a classic of the Marina Alta. From the coast you climb through orchards of orange and loquat toward Pego or Orba, then up into dry, steep country where the villages cling to the slopes. Murla, with about five hundred people, sits close by, and the road toward the ravine is narrow, twisting and often empty. Corners are tight and some are blind, so go carefully and expect gravel on the edges. A late afternoon ride in spring or autumn, when the light is long and the air smells of rosemary and warm stone, is as good as riding gets.

Fuel is available in Pego, a town of eleven thousand, about seven kilometres away, and nothing larger exists nearby. Fill the tank before climbing, because the villages above have little beyond a bar and a small shop. Bring water, sturdy shoes and a hat if you plan to walk.

The ravine path is steep, can be slippery after rain, and gets hot, so go early.
t.cueva del humo@38.1,-1.8:
Cehegín is the sort of town that most travellers drive past on the way to somewhere more famous, which is good news for anyone who prefers a quiet table. It stands on a hillside above the Quípar river in the north-west of Murcia, only a few kilometres from Caravaca de la Cruz, and its old centre is a tangle of steep lanes, baroque houses and small churches. The place has a long history, with Roman, Moorish and Christian layers, and the narrow streets of the upper town reward a slow walk.

The cave named here, Cueva del Humo, is an easy one to find on a map, since it lies less than a kilometre from the town centre. Smoke caves are common in Spain, and the name most often points to a cave where shepherds lit fires or where smoke rises from a vent. The country around Cehegín has an extensive prehistoric record, with painted shelters in the Levantine and schematic traditions scattered through the hills, so this stop is one of the more accessible entries in the series. Check on the ground what is open and what is fenced before you go in.

Caravaca de la Cruz, the neighbouring town, is a pilgrimage centre. It holds a relic said to be a fragment of the True Cross, and it has been a holy city with jubilee years since the Middle Ages. In early May it hosts the Caballos del Vino, a festival in which teams of horses, decorated in embroidered cloth, race up a hill carrying skins of wine. If you are riding through at the start of May, the town is packed, and rooms vanish early.

The ride in this part of Murcia is a good one. Roads across the Quípar valley and into the Sierra del Gavilán are well surfaced, with moderate corners and long views over fields of almond and cereal. The area also lies near the Bullas wine zone, which makes red wine from the monastrell grape and is worth a bottle. Summer is hot and dry, and spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Cehegín has sixteen thousand people, so fuel, food and shops are plentiful, and there is no need to worry about supplies.
t.barranc de l infern conj 5@38.8,-0.1:
The thirteenth century left more traces in these mountains than people realise. When James I of Aragon took the kingdom of Valencia from the Muslim rulers, he met stubborn resistance in the valleys of the Marina Alta, and the leader of that resistance was a man called Al-Azraq. He held fortresses in the Vall de Gallinera and the surrounding hills for years, fighting two campaigns against the Christians before the region finally submitted. The Barranc de l'Infern, a deep ravine near the old Moorish villages, would have been part of the world he knew.

The fifth group of rock shelters in the ravine lies much further back in time, in a different story altogether. These are Levantine paintings, red figures on limestone, that archaeologists have numbered as conjuntos along the gorge. They belong to a tradition that UNESCO recognised in 1998 and that extends from Catalonia to Andalusia, along the mountains of the eastern Spanish seaboard. The people who painted them were hunters, and later perhaps early farmers, and the animals they drew are the same ones that still, in small numbers, inhabit these hills.

For a rider the approach is the draw. Roads here are narrow, steep and often empty, with a surface that varies from fresh tarmac to patched and cracked. The corners are tight enough to demand your attention, and some of the hairpins turn through terraced fields where almond and olive trees stand in rows. Murla is the closest village, small and quiet, and the larger town of Pego lies about seven kilometres away down the hill.

Weather matters. The summer sun is intense, and rain turns the limestone slick, so aim for spring or autumn, preferably in the morning when the air is cool and the light is low. If you walk any of the ravine, take water, good boots and a hat, and leave early enough to be back before the afternoon heat.

Fuel is in Pego, a town of eleven thousand people, and the villages up the valley are very small. Carry a little spare range if you can.
t.la hoz de vicente@39.5,-1.5:
The Cabriel is one of the few rivers in Spain that still runs clean and fast through a deep canyon, and the Hoz de Vicente stands on its upper stretch, where Cuenca meets Valencia. The Hoces del Cabriel are a natural park of limestone gorges, pine woods and river flats, with kingfishers, otters and, on the rock faces, griffon vultures. The Hoz de Vicente shelter is one of the painted places of this wild corner, a Levantine rock art site listed within the UNESCO group of the Mediterranean Basin.

The nearest village is Villargordo del Cabriel, a small place of about seven hundred people on the Valencian side. Around it lies the wine country of Utiel-Requena, where the bobal grape has been grown for centuries on red soil. The wine is dark, fruity and sometimes underrated, and the cooperatives and family bodegas welcome visitors. A glass of rosé from bobal, dry and berry-scented, suits a warm afternoon.

Riding here is quiet and open. The high plateau is a landscape of vineyards, pine woods and wide skies, with straight stretches broken by sudden descents into the river valleys. Surfaces are good on the main roads and rougher on minor ones, and in places the road drops into gorges with hairpins that demand attention. There is little traffic and few places to stop, so ride with a full tank and a bit of patience.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Villargordo has little beyond a bar, and the nearest sizeable town is Utiel, with twelve thousand people, about twenty-eight kilometres away. Fill up there before heading into the park, and bring water. Summer is hot and the gorges trap the heat, while winter nights can be properly cold. Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with clear light and comfortable days.

The shelter is not a place for crowds. Keep voices low, stay on the path and photograph without flash.
t.barranc de la cova negra@38.8,-0.2:
Cherry trees are the secret of this valley, and for a few days in late winter and spring they turn the slopes white. The Vall de Gallinera, which lies just north of the Vall d'Ebo, is a long, narrow valley of small villages, with Adsubia among them, filled with terraced fields that the Moors once irrigated with great skill. Its cherries are among the best in the region, and the blossom draws visitors who come to walk the terraces and take photographs.

The Barranc de la Cova Negra, Black Cave Ravine, is one of the painted gorges of this part of Alicante province, and the label also refers to the neighbouring Barranc de Carbonera. The Levantine shelters here, with their small red figures, are part of the tradition recognised by UNESCO in 1998, and they are scattered across the cliffs and side ravines. Some are hard to reach and hard to see, and a walking guide is helpful if you want to find them.

The valley also has history. The castle of Alcalà, above the village of the same name, was a stronghold of the Muslim leader Al-Azraq in the thirteenth century, and its ruins still look out over the valley. After the expulsion of the Moriscos in 1609, many villages here were abandoned, and the terraces fell out of use. The cherry trees are one of the ways the valley has found new life.

The riding is delightful. The road from Pego climbs through orange groves and then into steeper country, with a series of hairpins up to the valley floor, before winding along the valley past one small village after another. Surfaces are generally fine, traffic is very light, and the bends are the kind that suit an unhurried rider. In the cherry season the verges are busy with walkers, so go slowly.

Pego, with eleven thousand people, is the nearest town for fuel and food, about eight kilometres away. Adsubia has a bar and little else. Bring water for walking.
t.covacha picayo abrigo l@39.6,-0.3:
Hannibal is the name that should come to mind as you ride toward this part of the Valencian coast. In 219 BC the Carthaginian general besieged the Iberian city of Saguntum, now Sagunto, just north of Puçol, and the eight-month siege that followed set off the Second Punic War. The city fell, and Rome declared war. The castle that crowns the hill at Sagunto today is a long, thin fortress with Roman, Moorish and medieval layers, and its Roman theatre has been restored to a degree that some people find controversial but nobody finds dull.

The Covacha de Picayo lies in the hills behind Puçol, a coastal town of nineteen thousand, in the foothills of the Sierra Calderona. It is a small painted shelter, one of the Levantine sites in the Mediterranean rock art group that UNESCO listed in 1998, and it belongs to a scatter of marks left by hunters on the edge of what is now one of Spain's most intensely farmed coastal plains.

Between the sea and the hills, the land here is a huerta, a patchwork of orange groves and market gardens watered by channels that go back to the Moors. The mix of history is remarkable: in a single morning you can see an Iberian settlement, a Roman theatre and a monastery. The Mercedarian monastery on the hill of El Puig, a few kilometres south, marks the place where in 1237 the Christian army of James I won the battle that opened the way to Valencia.

The riding is easy rather than exciting. The coastal roads are busy, but a short climb inland puts you on quieter lanes among citrus and carob, with the Calderona ridge ahead. Roads here are generally well surfaced, and the corners are mild. Choose a weekday, avoid the beach traffic of summer weekends and aim for the soft light of spring or the cool clear days of November.

Puçol itself has fuel, bars and shops, and the coast has no shortage of paella. Bring water for the walk.
t.barranc del sord abric i@38.7,-0.2:
Aitana is the mountain you can see from nearly everywhere in this part of Alicante, and at 1,558 metres it is the highest in the province. The village of Benimantell sits in its shadow, a tiny place of fewer than five hundred people with white houses and a view that ends in blue haze. The shelter named here, Barranc del Sord, belongs to the Tabla de Pochico group, a scatter of Levantine paintings in the hills of the Marina Baixa that form part of the UNESCO-listed rock art of the Mediterranean Basin.

It is a strange thing to ride from the beach resorts of Benidorm, with their high-rise towers, into this country in half an hour. Within minutes the road leaves the coastal plain and enters the Guadalest valley, with its turquoise reservoir, its terraced almond and olive groves, and the dramatic rock on which the castle of Guadalest stands. The village is a tourist favourite, with a string of small museums, and gets busy at weekends. Go early.

The road beyond Benimantell climbs steadily toward the passes of the Serra d'Aitana and the interior. Here the riding is at its best: long, sweeping bends, clean surfaces, big views of terraced slopes, and almost no traffic once you pass the last villages. Spring turns the valley pink with almond blossom, while autumn gives clear skies and cool air. In winter the highest parts can be icy, and fog sometimes pours up from the coast.

Callosa d'en Sarrià, down the valley, is known for its nísperos, the loquats that ripen in spring, and the fruit stalls beside the road are a signal that you are in the right area. The Algar waterfalls near Callosa are a pleasant place to cool off in summer, though they get crowded.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Benimantell has none that you should rely on, and the nearest larger town is La Nucía, about fifteen kilometres away, which has pumps and shops. Fill up there or on the coast, and take water for the walk.
t.marmalo ii@39.9,-1.6:
There are places in Spain that sound like names from a fairy tale, and Villar del Humo is one of them, the Village of Smoke. It is a hamlet of about three hundred and fifty people in the Serranía of Cuenca, where the pine forest begins to thicken and the Cabriel river carves gorges through the limestone. Marmalo is the name of the ravine nearby, and its painted shelters are among the major Levantine sites of inland Spain, listed with the UNESCO group of 1998.

Why is there so much rock art in a region so far from the sea? The answer, as far as anyone can say, is that the gorges of the Cabriel offered shelter, water and game, and prehistoric hunters probably followed the river as a corridor between the high plateau and the coast. The Marmalo shelters, with their groups of red figures, are within a short walk of the road, and the paintings have been well studied. The work of conservation is ongoing, so look for signs and observe any restrictions.

Villar del Humo itself is the base. It has a few bars, a small shop and a handful of houses whose tiled roofs and wooden balconies speak of old mountain life. The region is sparsely populated, and the sense of space is part of the pleasure. Pines, junipers and the odd holm oak cover the hills, and in the evening the smell of resin and thyme drifts through the open window of a parked bike.

The riding is a good, honest mix. Roads connecting these villages are narrow, with tight corners in the gorges and long rolling sections on the plateau. Surfaces are patchy in places, and some gravel is common near the edges. Weather matters here, since winter can be bitterly cold, with snow on the heights, while summer afternoons are hot. Late spring and early autumn are the most reliable seasons.

Supplies need planning. There is no large town nearby, and the nearest big centres, Cuenca and Requena, are some way off. Fill up before you leave the main road, carry water, and bring something to eat.
t.cueva moma@39.2,-0.8:
Bicorp's name appears on the map of rock art mainly because of its famous spider cave, but the Cueva Moma sits a few kilometres south-west of the village and has its own quiet claim to attention. It is a Levantine painted site in the dry highlands of the Canal de Navarrés, in the middle of inland Valencia, where the hills are steep, the villages small and the roads wander.

The country here is shaped by water, even though it looks dry. The Júcar river runs a little to the south, cut into deep canyons and dammed in several places, and the Muela de Cortes, a flat-topped plateau that is now a natural park, rises to the south. Springs and small streams feed fields of oranges, olives and cereal in the valley floors, while the slopes are covered with pine, rosemary and the small, tough oaks known as carrasca. Griffon vultures patrol the cliffs, and in the evening you may hear the call of an eagle owl.

Riding between Bicorp, Quesa and Navarrés is an exercise in unhurried pleasure. The road follows the hills with many bends, mostly gentle, and the surface is generally decent. Traffic is light, but you may meet farm tractors and cyclists, so keep to your side on blind corners. Spring is lovely, with wildflowers and bright green fields, while autumn brings clear skies and softer light. Midsummer is hot, and the middle of the day is best spent in the shade of a village square.

Bicorp is a tiny community of fewer than seven hundred people, and its services are limited to a bar and a shop or two. The nearest larger town for fuel and supplies is Carlet, over twenty kilometres away, though Navarrés may also have a pump. It is wise to arrive with a full tank and a bottle of water.

These shelters are rarely visited, and they have survived for that reason. Treat them gently.
Taking a bearing on the Barranc de l'Infern is easy because the map labels it with such confidence, and the name itself has a long history. In local usage infern means a deep, hot, difficult gorge, and in a Mediterranean summer that description is fair. The ravine lies in the Vall de Laguar, a small valley in the Marina Alta of Alicante province, with a rim of terraced slopes and a floor of limestone and boulders.

The second shelter in the sixth group is part of a series of Levantine painted sites that line the walls of the gorge. They are, like all such sites, delicate, and the paintings of red figures are partly eroded. What is remarkable is how much life the area supports. The limestone supports Aleppo pine and holm oak, rosemary, thyme and the dwarf palm, the palmito, which is Europe's only native palm and grows wild on dry slopes along this coast. The cliffs shelter Bonelli's eagles, and kestrels hang over the terraces.

Rainfall is low, but when it comes it comes violently, and the gorge can rush with water that disappears within an hour. That is one reason the paths into the ravine can be dangerous in wet weather, and why local people tend to avoid it during storms. The terraces that climb the slopes were built by Moorish farmers who dug irrigation channels and grew almonds, vines and figs, and the pattern still shapes the view.

Reaching the area by motorcycle is a pleasure. Narrow roads climb from Pego or Orba through villages and orchards, with a lot of short, tight bends and frequent views over the valley. Surfaces are mostly decent, but potholes and gravel appear on the edges, and a vehicle coming the other way will often be a van. Take your time. Best conditions come in spring and autumn, when the days are clear and the heat is modest.

Murla, a village of five hundred people, is the closest place, while Pego, seven kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Carry water.
t.barranc de l infern conj 1@38.8,-0.1:
Nobody builds a gallery in a ravine called Hell without a reason, and the first group of paintings in the Barranc de l'Infern shows what the reason probably was: shade, shelter and a view of whatever walked up the valley. This is conjunto 1 in the numbering archaeologists use, one of several clusters of Levantine rock art in the Vall de Laguar, in the mountains of the Marina Alta, and it is part of the UNESCO-listed Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin.

If you want to see the best rock art of this district, ask in Castell de Castells, a village of fewer than five hundred people a few kilometres to the north-east. Near it, the Pla de Petracos is a large painted shelter with a dense mass of figures, and it is the best-known site in the area. Seen together with the smaller Barranc de l'Infern groups, it shows how several periods of painting overlap. Humans and animals appear in Levantine style, while later abstract signs in a more schematic style cluster alongside.

The geology explains the choice of shelter. This is a landscape of Cretaceous limestone, folded and fractured over millions of years, and rain has hollowed the softer layers of the cliffs into overhangs that stay dry in a storm. They face different directions, and some catch the low sun of winter. That is why a single ravine can hold six groups of paintings.

The ride into the district is demanding and rewarding in equal parts. Narrow roads wind up from Pego or Orba, past terraces of almond, carob and olive, and short, steep ramps lead into the hill villages. Surfaces are usually serviceable but grit gathers on the bends, and you should expect agricultural traffic. Mornings in spring or autumn, when the air is cool and the colours bright, are the best moments.

Fuel is in Pego, about seven kilometres from the ravine, which has eleven thousand people and all the usual shops. Murla and the other villages have a bar and little else. Bring plenty of water, wear boots and start early, because the sun in the ravine is intense and the stones hold the heat long after noon.
t.marmalo iii@39.9,-1.6:
A map of the Serranía de Cuenca looks like a crumpled green blanket, and the best way to understand it is to ride across it. Marmalo, the painted ravine near Villar del Humo, is in the south of this region, where the pines open into fields and the drainage heads toward the Cabriel river. This is the third shelter in the group, and a good excuse to plan a whole day around the surrounding country.

Start in Cuenca or Requena, fill the tank and set out early. From Cuenca the road runs south-east across a high, empty plateau of cereal, juniper and pine, at heights around a thousand metres. The bends are slow and wide, the views are big, and the traffic is so light that you may go half an hour without meeting a car. Wind is common on the open stretches, and in winter this country can be bitterly cold, with frost on the tarmac at dawn. Summer afternoons are hot and dry, and a hat and water are essential if you walk.

The shelters themselves are small, and the paintings are small too. They show human figures, with the slim, elongated bodies that mark the Levantine style, and animals, mostly deer and wild goats, in red pigment that has faded to a rusty brown in places. They are among the pieces of inland Spain's rock art that UNESCO recognised in 1998, and local authorities have put up signs and protective fencing at many of them. Please follow the instructions on the boards.

Villar del Humo is a village of three hundred and fifty people, and it is the place for a coffee and a bocadillo. There are few other services in the immediate area, and the nearest big towns, Cuenca and Requena, lie well over forty kilometres away. A full tank on leaving them is the sensible approach.

Late afternoon is lovely here. The sun drops behind the pines, the air smells of resin and warm stone, and the quiet is almost total. If you are staying nearby, it is a good time to sit still.
t.barranc de l infern corij 4@38.8,-0.1:
The farmer's calendar explains this country better than any history book. In late winter the almond trees of the Marina Alta bloom white and pink, in spring the carob pods begin to swell, and in early summer the loquats and cherries ripen on the lower slopes. In August the muscat grapes are laid out to dry in the sun, and by autumn the oranges are turning and the olives are ready. The Barranc de l'Infern, where this fourth group of painted shelters lies, sits in the middle of that cycle, in the Vall de Laguar and its neighbouring valleys of Alicante province.

The muscat of Alexandria grape is the speciality of the area, grown on narrow terraces, many of them built by Moorish farmers. After harvest the bunches are traditionally dried in a riurau, an open-fronted porch built onto the farmhouse so that the sun and wind can reach the fruit, and you will see these structures beside many farms. The raisins of the Jalón valley were once sent in barrels to northern Europe, and some are still exported. The sweet wine that comes from the same grape has its own character, tasting of honey and orange peel.

The painted shelter itself belongs to the Levantine tradition recognised by UNESCO in 1998, with red figures of hunters and animals on limestone walls. The people who made them lived by a different calendar, following game and seasons on foot, but it is not hard to imagine them watching the same hills.

For motorcyclists the valleys are a treasure. The roads climb through terraces to the villages, with short, sharp bends, steep gradients and some stunning views. The best season is spring, when the almond blossom and the green of the new growth give the valley its brightest look, and the second best is autumn, when the air clears and the colours deepen. Winter can be mild enough for riding, though occasional fog and ice appear at height.

Murla, the nearest village, has barely five hundred people, and Pego is the town for fuel and food, about seven kilometres away. Pack water and a snack if you plan to walk.
t.letreros@37.7,-2.1:
There is a little figure on a postcard from Almería that you will see on car stickers, jewellery and shop signs across the province, and it started here. The Indalo, a stick-like man holding an arch above his head, is the symbol of Almería, and it comes from a painting in the Cueva de los Letreros near Vélez-Blanco. The painted figure, called the Brujo or Sorcerer, was found in the early twentieth century, and local people adopted the shape as a good-luck charm and a mark of local pride.

The cave is more of an overhang than a cavern, set in the limestone cliffs of the Sierra de María-Los Vélez natural park, with a view over a broad valley of almonds and cereals. The paintings are in red, and some are in a faded white, and they show human figures, animals and signs, in a mixture of Levantine and schematic styles. They are part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin group, listed by UNESCO in 1998. A fence protects the cave, and you may have to arrange a visit through the local tourist office.

Vélez-Blanco is a lovely small town of about two thousand people, with a Renaissance castle on a hill above it. It was built in the early sixteenth century for the Marquis of los Vélez, and its inner courtyard is a marvel of carved marble. In the early twentieth century the courtyard was sold and shipped to America, and it now stands in the Metropolitan Museum in New York, a story that still annoys local people. A copy has been installed in the castle in its place.

The riding is excellent. The road from the Murcia side climbs steadily into the sierra, with long open bends, big views and a lot of empty country, where eagles and kestrels patrol the cliffs. The Sierra de María rises to over two thousand metres, so snow is possible in winter, and summer days can be warm even at height. Spring and autumn are perfect.

Vélez-Rubio, four kilometres away, is larger, with seven thousand people, and has fuel, shops and bars. Eat a plate of migas or lamb stew and look out for the local almond sweets.
t.covacha picayo abrigo ii@39.6,-0.3:
The Sierra Calderona is the wooded ridge behind Valencia's northern suburbs, and it is the best surprise on this coast. It is a natural park of pine, holm oak and rosemary, with low summits, deep ravines and a sense of space that is hard to believe so close to a large city. Wild boar wander the slopes, along with foxes, genets and a growing population of birds of prey, and in spring the slopes are full of orchids and cistus flowers.

The second Covacha Picayo shelter lies in this country, a short distance from Puçol, in a landscape of small hills and dry watercourses. It belongs to the Levantine group of painted sites, listed with the UNESCO Mediterranean Basin rock art in 1998, and it shows how far the tradition extended beyond the high mountains. These hunters were also coast dwellers, within reach of the sea.

Look for the signs of later human use as well. The area was once important for charcoal burning, for lime kilns, and for sheep. Stone huts and terraces dot the hills, and in the middle of the range stand the ruins of the Cartusian monastery of Portacoeli, founded in the Middle Ages and now a quiet historic site. The Calderona was also the hideout of bandits in the nineteenth century, a story that local people still enjoy telling.

On a bike you can explore the lower slopes by small roads that run inland from Puçol and Sagunto. They are narrow, with plenty of bends, mostly good tarmac, and a gentle climb, but they are popular with cyclists at weekends, so allow for them. The light is best in late afternoon, when the pines glow and the sea is visible beyond the plain. Spring and autumn are the ideal seasons, and summer is fierce.

Puçol is a town of nineteen thousand people, so petrol, supermarkets and cafés are close at hand, only three or four kilometres away. Bring water if you intend to walk, and mind the fire restrictions that apply in dry months in the natural park.
t.la sarga abric iii@38.6,-0.5:
Alcoy sits among mountains on every side, and every road out of it is a good one. To the north-west lies the Sierra de Mariola, a natural park of aromatic herbs, whose thyme, rosemary and mountain tea are used in the local liqueur. To the south is Aitana, and to the east the long ridge of the Serra de Penàguila. The Barranc de la Sarga, where the painted shelters lie, cuts through the hills a few kilometres from the town, and its rock art has been studied since the early twentieth century.

The paintings at La Sarga are among the best known in the region, and include both Levantine and schematic styles. Archaeologists consider them an important site for understanding how different painting traditions overlapped in this part of Spain. Abric III is one of several shelters in the ravine, and the whole group is part of the UNESCO listing of 1998. Details of access change, so ask at the tourist office in Alcoy or look for local information boards.

The best way to enjoy the country is to ride a loop. Leave Alcoy by the road toward the Font Roja natural park, where an enormous holm oak forest clings to the northern slopes of the mountain and gives the air a cool, damp smell. Continue through the villages of Penàguila and Benifallim, then loop back past Banyeres de Mariola, with its Moorish castle. The roads are a mix of broad, fast curves and tight bends, with surfaces that range from smooth to rough. Spring and autumn are beautiful, with clear air and good light.

Alcoy has sixty thousand people, and you will find fuel, pharmacies and plenty of cafés. The town is famous for its mountain liqueur, called Herbero, and for almond sweets. A coffee in a café in the main square, watching the town go about its business, is a good way to finish the day.

Take water if you plan to walk, and remember that conditions in the ravine can be hot and dry.
