Hadrian's Wall in its central section does what a good border should: it picks the best ridge in the country and sits on top of it. The wall was begun in AD 122, under the emperor Hadrian, and it runs for about eighty Roman miles, roughly 117 kilometres, from the Tyne to the Solway. In the middle stretch, between Haydon Bridge and Haltwhistle, it follows a line of crags called the Whin Sill, a hard, dark volcanic rock that breaks the Northumbrian moors into a series of cliffs, so that the wall looks as if it grew out of the stone.

The Roman camp marked here is a reminder that this was an army frontier. The legions built temporary camps wherever they stopped, with turf ramparts and a ditch around them, and traces of those camps are scattered through the Northumberland countryside. Some are visible as faint rectangles in the grass, only clear when the light is low. A short distance south of the wall, the Vallum, a deep ditch with mounds on either side, ran for the whole length, and its purpose is still debated.

The best road for the wall is the B6318, the Military Road, which runs just behind it. It was built after the Jacobite rising of 1745, to help move troops across the country, and the builders used stones from the wall itself for the foundations. The road runs up and down in long, straight sweeps, with fine views north into the empty moorland of Northumberland National Park. Traffic is moderate, and in summer there can be slow caravans and cyclists, but in spring and autumn it is a delight. Fog and sudden rain come off the moor, and the wind on the crags is serious.

For a break, the fort at Housesteads, a few miles away, is the best-preserved on the wall, with a hospital and a communal latrine you can still make out. Vindolanda, the fort south of the wall, has wooden writing tablets, including a birthday party invitation, found in the waterlogged soil.

Haydon Bridge is small, and Hexham, twelve kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets and cafés. Fill up there. Wear layers, and bring waterproofs.

Camboglanna is the Roman name of the fort at Castlesteads, and the sound of it has a ring that the present quiet farmland does not. Little survives above ground, because the site was built over by a country house and gardens in the eighteenth century, but the line of the wall and the vallum, the great ditch behind it, can be traced across the fields nearby.

The western end of Hadrian's Wall is different from the high crags of the central section. Here the wall was originally built of turf rather than stone, because there was no suitable rock near the surface, and only later was it rebuilt in masonry. The landscape is gentler, with wooded valleys, red sandstone, small farms and the broad flat plain of the Solway to the north. The lower, softer land made the wall a less dramatic thing, but it is a more peaceful one.

Brampton is the town to know, a small market place with an octagonal moot hall and a few good pubs, and nearby is Lanercost Priory, a ruined Augustinian house founded in the twelfth century and built partly from stone taken from the wall. Edward I stayed at Lanercost for months in 1306 and 1307, in the final stage of his campaign against the Scots. Birdoswald, a few miles east, is the best of the forts on this stretch, set on a cliff above the Irthing.

Surfaces vary, with mud and gravel after wet weather, and on single-track lanes you need to look well ahead. Spring is lovely, with blossom and lambs, and autumn has a lot of golden light.

Brampton has four thousand people and offers pumps, shops and cafés, and Carlisle, fourteen kilometres away, is the large town for everything. Carry a waterproof, because rain is common.

Haltwhistle likes to call itself the centre of Britain, a claim based on measurements that no one outside the town quite trusts, but which has produced a very good tourist sign. Roman marching camps look like nothing, and yet they tell you almost everything about how the legions worked. At the end of each day's march, the soldiers dug a ditch, threw up a rampart of turf and put up their leather tents inside, in a regular plan. The camps at Coesike West, two of them side by side, were built on the moorland north of Hadrian's Wall, and they probably date from the period of campaigns in the north, before or around the time the frontier was fixed. They are only low banks and ditches now, but from the air or in low light the outline is clear.

The ground is often wet, and the grass has the pale colour of winter even in summer. Skylarks sing overhead in spring, and curlews call from the rushes. North of the wall the country opens into a high, empty plateau, the same kind of land that the Roman soldiers must have seen as hostile.

It helps to know that this part of the world has been fought over for two thousand years. After the Romans came raiders from the north, then the Border reivers of the sixteenth century, who stole cattle across the line between England and Scotland. The bastle houses, strong stone farmhouses that can still be found in these valleys, were built so that families could shelter from them.

The roads across this district are quiet and sometimes narrow, with cattle grids and open sections where the wind can be strong. Surfaces vary, and rain and fog can arrive fast. The Racó de Sorellets is tucked between Castell de Castells and Vall d'Ebo, and to reach it you cross some of the most rugged ground in northern Alicante. This is the country of the Serrella and its neighbours, a jumble of ridges and ravines that the sea breeze hardly reaches, where goats still graze and the villages cling to the sides of the valley. Pego sits ten kilometres away on the plain, and the gap in character between the two is startling.

There is a rhythm to the ride. The roads rise out of the coastal plain in slow bends, pass through pine and holm oak, and reach plateaus with long views that on clear days show the sea like a line of blue paint. Surface quality is usually fine, though in the narrow places you have to share the tarmac with the occasional tractor, and the afternoons in summer can feel merciless. The best month, in my view, is November, when the heat has gone and the air has that washed brightness.

The valley's history is the story of the Moriscos. When Philip III ordered their expulsion in 1609, the Vall d'Ebo and many neighbouring places lost almost their entire population, and the fields went wild, so the terraces you pass are a record of what was once a dense farming landscape. The rock shelters belong to a far earlier chapter of human life, to hunters and herders of the post-glacial world, but they share the same sense of people having left something behind.

Fuel and food are the practical points. Pego is the sure place for both, with bakeries, restaurants and a long tradition of rice cooking, while Castell de Castells and Vall d'Ebo offer a coffee and little else. Murla, a little further out, is quiet as well. Fill the tank before the climb, carry water, and leave room in the schedule for the unexpected pause when a view demands it.
t.cejo cortado ii@38.1,-1.5:
Mula does not announce itself to motorcyclists, which is a pity, because the roads around it are among the most enjoyable in inland Murcia. The town of nearly seventeen thousand sits on the river that bears its name, below the long grey wall of the Sierra Espuña to the south, and its old quarter climbs a hill capped by a castle. Cejo Cortado, seven kilometres from the centre, is a small crag in dry hill country where a shelter holds prehistoric paintings, the kind of place you find by following a farm track and reading the contours.

Come in spring, when the almond blossom is long gone but the broom and the wild thyme are out, or in October, when the heat finally releases its grip. In July and August the whole district bakes, the pavement turns soft by afternoon and shade is rare. The roads here are open and sunny, mixing long rolling stretches with short bursts of tighter bends where they cut through the foothills, and the surface is generally sound. Take care at the field crossings, where tractors drop mud on the asphalt.

Mula has a quiet culture of its own. Its Holy Week is well known in the region, a theatrical affair of drums and processions, and the local cooking is a good example of the Murcian huerta with its vegetables, peppers, rice dishes and, in season, wonderful apricots from nearby orchards. A short ride takes you to Albudeite or Ricote, the latter lying in a valley of orchards that kept a Morisco population longer than most. The Ricote valley has a sleepy charm and a few places to eat, though not all will be open on a weekday afternoon.

Fuel is easy: Mula itself has several stations on the roads in and out, and the larger Murcia lies a short ride east. Water is a more serious question, because the hills around the shelter are dry, so carry more than you think you will need. If you are visiting the paintings, take some care, as the shelters are fragile and the best approach is quietly and in small groups.
t.arco ii@38.2,-1.6:
Sometimes the best way to read a landscape is to follow the water. East of Calasparra the Segura has cut its path through red and grey rocks, and the country on either side rises into a dry upland of pine, esparto grass and rock. Arco II lies in that district, a short walk from Cueva de las Cabras, and a rider arriving by the back roads feels the kind of silence you only get in places with very little to sell.

The roads are the easy part. Broad, empty and warm, they run between farmland and barren slope with few buildings and not much traffic, and you will often find that your only company is a kestrel hovering over the verge. The corners are open and obvious, which is good for sightseeing, and the surface is decent, though in places gravel from field tracks lies in the bends. Spring and autumn are best, because midsummer is genuinely hot and the light flattens everything into a white glare by noon.

Calasparra lies eleven kilometres away and is the place to refuel, eat and top up water. Its fame is its rice, grown with water from the river on terraces below the town, and in a bar you can usually order a dish of it with rabbit or vegetables for what feels like very little money. Cieza and Abarán, a little further, are fruit towns with long histories of cultivation, and Cieza in February has a spectacular bloom of peach trees that can turn the valley pink.

The shelters in this region belong to the Levantine tradition, small red paintings under natural overhangs which were drawn by people who hunted and gathered here after the ice age. They are protected, and some sit on private land or require permits, so ask locally before heading off on foot. The Segura valley has been a route for thousands of years, and you can imagine them walking the same line from the sea to the mountains, looking out over the same wide valley.
t.cueva de la arana abrigo ii@39.1,-0.9:
Bicorp lies at the edge of a green fold in the Canal de Navarrés, and the Cueva de la Araña is less than seven kilometres from it, up in the limestone gullies where the hills drop into the Barranco de Bicorp. This is the cave that put the Valencian interior on the map of European prehistory. A painted figure on its wall, climbing what look like ropes or tendrils towards a honeycomb while insects swarm around, is among the best-known pictures of honey-gathering anywhere, and rock-art textbooks tend to reproduce it.

The road is the standard approach: a narrow, twisting lane from the village that climbs and descends through pine and scrub for a few kilometres and then runs out at a parking area. Take it slowly, because the bends are tight and the surface can be broken, and be careful with gravel and loose stones at the edge. The best time is early on a cool morning in spring or autumn. By midday in summer the rock radiates heat and the hillside smells of resin and dust.

The rest of the district repays exploration. Navarrés, fifteen kilometres away, is the largest town nearby, with a fair spread of shops and a long history of farming on the plain of the Canal. Quesa, further up a side valley, is very small but pretty. Enguera has more services, and Ayora, eighteen kilometres to the west, has fuel as well as a good market. In the evenings, you can eat in a bar and watch the sun go down over a landscape that has hardly changed since the paintings were made.

Visiting the cave itself requires some planning. Access to the paintings is restricted, and the shelter is protected with a grille and managed by local authorities, so check ahead for opening arrangements and guided visits. The honey scene is not large, and it reveals itself slowly when your eyes adjust, so give it time. Afterward, stop for a jar of local honey and think about how long human beings have been climbing cliffs for sweetness.
t.pla de petracos abric vii@38.8,-0.2:
The first impression of Petracos is of tilted rock. Limestone strata lie across the plateau like a book dropped on its side, with caves and ledges under the edges, and the shelters tucked beneath them hold paintings that have lasted thousands of years because the overhang keeps the rain off. The plateau is a short distance above Castell de Castells, which gives you a village for coffee and a starting point for exploring the valley.

If you arrive in the late afternoon, the light on the cliffs turns orange and the shadows deepen, and the whole scene feels as though the clock has been turned back. You may hear sheep bells somewhere below, or a hoopoe in the pines. The approach roads are narrow, with a few tight hairpins and one or two blind bends, and the surface is mostly good, so a relaxed ride suits the place. In July and August go early or late, because midday is hard on both rider and bike.

There is a gentle comedy in the way these shelters are numbered. Archaeologists, faced with a cliff that has eight or ten painted overhangs, simply count them in the order they were found, so Abric VII is no more distinctive than its neighbours until you look closely and find a few faded figures, a little line of dots, a bow. It is a reminder that rock art is not a collection of masterpieces but the leftover marks of ordinary people over a very long time.

Pego, eleven kilometres away, has the fuel and the shops, and the wetland of the Marjal de Pego-Oliva lies below it, a natural park of rice fields and reeds where herons and purple gallinules breed. If you have time, try a local arròs al forn, a baked rice dish that is a regional favourite. Back on the plateau, remember to drink water and to respect any fencing. Even the most careful touch can damage fragile pigments.
t.raco de sorellets abric ii@38.8,-0.2:
Vall d'Ebo is one of those places that history has swept clean. In 1609, when the crown expelled the Moriscos, this valley lost almost all of its inhabitants, and the villages had to be resettled with newcomers from elsewhere, so the terraces and irrigation channels you see on the hillsides were built by people whose descendants were sent away. The Racó de Sorellets is on the heights nearly five kilometres from the village, in a landscape of cliffs and ravines where the shelter walls carry much older marks than any of that.

Close by is the famous Barranc de l'Infern, a gorge with a stepped trail that walkers love, and the roads that lead there are the finest riding in the district. They twist up from Pego through orange groves and almond terraces, the gradient steadying as the valley narrows, and the surface is decent but sometimes patchy where rockfalls have been cleared. Vall d'Ebo is a few kilometres away along a slender road with a series of tight bends and a long view of the sea.

In the other direction, Murla lies in a quieter pocket of the hills, with a small square and a couple of bars, and the village of Castell de Castells is around four kilometres off. All are tiny, with fewer than five hundred inhabitants each, so do not plan on finding fuel on a Sunday. Pego, ten kilometres away, is where to fill up, with restaurants and supermarkets, and its nearby marshes, the Marjal, are a bird-watcher's reserve where the rice is grown.

The shelters here are of the Levantine type, with small red figures that appear under the cliff edge. They tell of people who ranged across the hills in a world with forests of pine and oak where today there is scrub. Do not climb on the rock and do not use chalk or water to highlight the images, which can destroy them. A walk to the shelters, followed by a long lunch in Pego, is a fine day's programme.
t.abric de las cabras@39.3,-0.7:
The Millares country belongs to the Júcar, the long river that cuts through the limestone of inland Valencia and fills the reservoir at Tous before spilling out onto the orange-growing plain. Millares itself has fewer than six hundred people and sits in a landscape of gorges, ravines and dry hills, with Dos Aguas nearby in a similar fold of the land. The Abric de las Cabras is in the hills a few kilometres from the village, a rock shelter whose name suggests the animals that still use these slopes.

The ride in is a pleasure. From Turís or Montroy, the road rises from irrigated fields and orange groves through citrus, then carob and almond, then pine and scrub as the valley narrows, with bends that tighten and open in a pleasing sequence. The surface is usually good, but expect narrow stretches and occasional gravel, and give a wide berth to any cyclist you meet. Summer is hot and the best months are April, May, October and November.

Local history has a long reach. The Júcar was a boundary and a corridor, and the hills here were part of a Muslim agricultural economy that used terraces and irrigation channels, many of which are still working. Dos Aguas has a name that refers to the meeting of two streams, and the Valencian aristocratic family that took the title built one of the most extravagant Baroque palaces in Valencia city, a bit of Rococo exuberance that has nothing in common with this quiet village. Rock shelters like the one here are the oldest layer of the story, painted by hunters.

Fuel is an issue to plan. Millares and Dos Aguas are small and unlikely to have pumps, so Turís, with about five thousand people, thirteen kilometres away, is the reliable stop, and Montroy has a few more services. Both have bars and shops, and the villages on the way offer simple lunches of paella and local sausages. Take water and a map, because mobile signal in the gorges can be patchy.
t.abrigo del atajo ii@39.2,-0.8:
A shelter called Atajo, shortcut, tells you something about how people used these hills: as a place to cut across, between valleys, on foot and with animals. The Abrigo del Atajo II is two kilometres from Millares, in the same Júcar country where limestone has been carved into canyons and the villages cluster around springs. Dos Aguas is a little further, and Bicorp is just over the ridge, so you could string together several small places in one day.

It would be wrong to promise a dramatic ride. The roads here are plain and pleasant, with a few hairpins as they climb out of the valleys, and they tend to run through citrus, then scrub, then pine. Surface quality varies, so keep your speed measured, particularly after heavy rain, which sends gravel across the bends. Local drivers know the bends and take them fast, so keep to your side. In winter the early hours can be near freezing, while in high summer the gorge becomes a heat trap.

What makes the area interesting is the layering of use. Prehistoric hunters left their paintings under overhangs, and later farmers built terraces and stone huts, called barracas or casetas, that are still scattered over the hills. The villages have been shrinking for generations, so that today places like Millares are quiet, with an air of waiting. Carob trees, once an important crop for animal feed, still stand in the old terraces.

Turís, eighteen kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size and has fuel and supplies, and it lies on the edge of the Ribera, the fruit-growing plain. Bicorp has a few bars and could provide a break. Take food and water, because the walk to a shelter can be dry, and watch for snakes on warm days. Be gentle with the site, which has survived thousands of years by being left alone.
t.lavadero tello iv@37.8,-2.1:
Vélez-Blanco has a castle that has been in two countries. Built in the early sixteenth century by the first Marquis of los Vélez, it was a Renaissance palace of white marble inside a fortified shell, and in 1904 the owner sold the marble patio, which was shipped in crates to Paris and then to New York, where it is now in the Metropolitan Museum. The castle's empty courtyard remains in the village. Lavadero Tello is sixteen kilometres away, in the Sierra María-Los Vélez natural park, where red-and-gold hills, almond groves and pale limestone peaks rise above the plains of Almería and Granada.

The Cueva de los Letreros, near Vélez-Blanco, is the reason this area has such a famous name in prehistoric art. Its paintings include a figure with raised arms holding a rainbow-like arc, known as the Indalo, which has been adopted as the symbol of the province of Almería and appears on stickers on bumpers across Spain. The shelter you reach here belongs to the same cluster of painted sites in the hills.

The road to this district is among the best in Almería. Sierra María rises to over two thousand metres at Maimón, and the roads approach through pine forests and rock, with long smooth curves and big views. The surface is mainly good, though there are patches of rough tarmac, and the area is dry and exposed so wind can be a factor. In winter snow falls on the high ground. Spring is beautiful, with wildflowers, and autumn is clear and warm.

Vélez-Rubio, with about seven thousand people, twenty-two kilometres away, is the town where you should buy fuel and food, and it has a famously grand Baroque church. Vélez-Blanco and María, a village of around fifteen hundred, offer more modest services. Local cooking features lamb, game, cured meats and almond sweets, and the high plains are known for their bread and honey. Take water if you intend to walk to the shelter, and mind the sun.
t.benizar ii@38.3,-2.0:
If you are in Moratalla in Holy Week, you will hear it from far off: the drums. The town's tamborada, in which hundreds of people in tunics beat their drums in unison through the streets, is one of the most distinctive Easter traditions in Murcia, and it gives this stony, high country a pulse that outsiders do not expect. Benizar is a small hamlet in the municipality, eleven or twelve kilometres from the town, and the shelter lies in the broken hills near Socovos, where the border between Murcia and Albacete wanders across ridges and dry ravines.

This is the north-west corner of the Region of Murcia, a part that most visitors skip on the way to the beaches, and it is a joy to ride. The road from Moratalla towards Socovos undulates through pine and holm oak, with the Segura river somewhere out of sight, and the bends are long, smooth and mostly empty. The surface is generally fine, and you can go hours without seeing another motorcycle. Heat in summer is dry and hard, and in winter the high ground can be bitterly cold, so the shoulder seasons are best, and an early start is wise in August.

Moratalla has a castle on a crag over the town, a handsome old centre of steep streets, and a reputation in the region for solid country cooking, lamb above all. It is also the place to buy fuel, as Benizar and the other hamlets are too small for pumps. Socovos, seven kilometres off in Albacete, has fewer than two thousand people and will give you a bar and a coffee, while Férez, further north, is smaller still.

The shelter belongs to a wide scatter of rock art across the Segura uplands, where Levantine paintings in red sit near later schematic signs in similar overhangs. Most are small, many are fenced, and all of them depend on being left alone. Wear boots, bring more water than seems sensible, and keep your voice down; sound carries in these ravines, and goats and griffon vultures will tell you if you are making too much of it.
t.abrigo del molino juan basura o molina c:
Nerpio sits on a high plateau of the Sierra del Segura, in the south-west corner of Albacete province, at about a thousand metres above the sea, and the climate matches the height: hot dry summers, cold nights, and winters when snow arrives early. The Abrigo del Molino de Juan Basura lies less than two kilometres from the village in the valley of the Taibilla, and it is one of the sites that make Nerpio a name among specialists. In few other places in Spain can you find so many painted shelters within a short walk of a single village.

The ride is for those who like to go a long way for nothing in particular. From Moratalla or from Yeste the road climbs onto a high, empty country of pine, juniper and cereal fields, with the bends opening out and the traffic almost nonexistent. You may share a stretch with a flock of sheep or a lone tractor, but little else. Take care in winter, when ice can persist on the shaded sections, and in spring, when meltwater washes gravel across the road. Autumn is the best time, with warm days, cold nights and the oaks and poplars along the river turning.

What is remarkable about Nerpio is its density of prehistoric art. Specialists have recorded dozens of painted shelters in the district, in the Levantine tradition and in the later schematic style, and some of the scenes are crowded with animals and people caught in the middle of an action. The name of this one points at a mill, and many of the sites sit near water, mills and springs, which suggests that the people who painted here chose the same places as the farmers who came after them.

You should plan the practical side carefully. Nerpio is a village of around sixteen hundred people, and fuel is not something to count on, so fill up in Yeste, about twenty-five kilometres away, or in Moratalla, further still. Bars in the village serve simple food, and they are a good place to ask about access to the shelters, as some are reached only by tracks that turn difficult in wet weather. Carry water and be careful with any flame in the dry months.
t.raco de gorgori abric ii@38.8,-0.2:
Spring comes early to the Vall de Castells. By late January the almond trees on the terraces turn pink and white, and the whole valley is brushed with blossom while the peaks above still hold the cold. The Racó de Gorgorí, a ravine corner in the hills above Castell de Castells, is worth seeing in that season, when the air is crisp and the rock paintings seem to belong to a landscape waking up.

The road is the pleasure. It climbs out of the coastal plain among citrus and loquat trees, then through almond and olive terraces, and the corners get tighter as the valley narrows. Surface quality is good in most places, but be watchful in the bends where goats and farm vehicles use the road. Behind you the sea appears and disappears between the ridges, and ahead the long wall of the Serrella lies against the sky. January mornings can be sharp at this height, so carry a warm layer even when Alicante itself is in shirt sleeves.

Walkers will find a classic Mediterranean mountain flora: rosemary, thyme, kermes oak, the dwarf fan palm known as palmito, and the aromatic scrub that gives the hills their smell on a warm afternoon. The shelter belongs to the cluster of Levantine sites in this corner of the Marina, and the paintings are small, so patience and good raking light matter more than a good camera. A morning visit tends to be kindest.

For the practical side, Pego, thirteen kilometres away, is the sensible place for fuel and a meal, with Callosa d'en Sarrià an option on the way up. Vall d'Ebo and Benimantell are the nearest villages, both tiny, with a bar and a church each and little more. If the weather turns, the valley road stays rideable, but the barrancos can run suddenly after heavy rain, so do not cross any dry riverbed that looks questionable.
t.abric de trini@39.2,-0.7:
The Júcar country has a way of making you feel that you have taken a wrong turn and then rewarding you for it. The Abric de Trini lies about six kilometres from Millares, in rough limestone hills cut by ravines, and the lanes that lead to it give you something of that feeling, with villages that seem to have been left behind and views across empty slopes of pine and rock. Carlet, nineteen kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, in the flat fruit-growing country of the Ribera Alta, and it could hardly be more different.

The ride is rewarding if not demanding. Corners are gentle, with some tighter groups where the road drops into a barranco, the surface is variable, and traffic is almost nonexistent. Gravel can be a problem near field entrances and in the bends after rain, and cattle grids or loose chippings appear where you do not expect them. In summer the heat is fierce, and in winter it can be cold and clear, so the best months are April and October, when the pines smell of resin and the light is soft.

Millares, Bicorp and Quesa are the villages nearest, and all have fewer than a thousand inhabitants. They have bars, but you should not expect to find fuel, which means a visit to Carlet or Navarrés before you set off. It is worth knowing that Bicorp is the village associated with the Cueva de la Araña and its honey-gatherer, so this whole district has long been on the map of people who study rock art, and the shelters around here form a loose family.

The shelter itself, like others in the region, was painted by hunters who lived in these hills in the millennia after the ice age, and it has the typical modest scale of the tradition. Do not expect a gallery; expect a few red marks that take a minute for your eyes to organise into an animal or a person. Take water, wear boots, and tell somebody where you are going, because mobile signal drops out in the gullies.
t.pla de petracos abric iv@38.8,-0.2:
Eagles hunt on the cliffs above Petracos, or so local naturalists say, and you may well see kestrels and griffon vultures riding the thermals along the limestone edge in the middle of the day. Bonelli's eagle lives in the mountains of Alicante, though it is shy and hard to pin down. The plateau itself is a rough mosaic of kermes oak, pine, rosemary and the spiny scrub that rustles when the wind moves, and in spring there are small orchids in the damper spots. The shelters are tucked under the lip of the rock, four kilometres or so from Castell de Castells.

The road in comes by way of Callosa d'en Sarrià and the Guadalest valley, and it is one of the most enjoyable climbs in the province. Tight at first, with hairpins, it settles into a long series of curves that let you enjoy the rising views. The surface is mostly good, and cyclists use it often, so take care on blind bends. In summer, ride early to avoid the heat, and in winter be alert for damp and cold on the shaded side of the valley.

In this part of Alicante you are in the wrong place if you want to be alone with a famous painting, and in the right place if you like context. Petracos is a plateau with shelters in a group, and the experience is cumulative: one overhang with a few faint marks, another with a clearer figure, a third that is mostly stain. The sum is a feeling for how often and for how long these walls were used. The people who painted them left no names, only a repertoire of archers, animals and signs.

For fuel and food, go to Pego, eleven kilometres away, which has stations, restaurants and shops, and a famous rice-growing wetland nearby. The villages on the plateau have a bar and little more, and the nearest ones, Castell de Castells and Vall d'Ebo, are worth a short stop simply for the quiet.
t.port de confrides abric iii@38.7,-0.3:
Fog sometimes fills the valleys below the Port de Confrides while the summit shines in the sun, and when that happens the effect is like standing on the shore of a white sea. It is a lovely sight in autumn and winter, and it is a good reason to check the forecast before you set out. The Port de Confrides is a pass on the road between the Guadalest valley and the Alcoi plain, in the shadow of Aitana, and the shelter lies a short way from it, in the rough hillside of barrancos and scrub that falls towards Benimantell.

The ride over the pass is one of the best in the province for a rider with time. From the Guadalest side the road climbs in a series of steady bends, with views of the reservoir and the Serrella, and then crosses the high ground with a grand view of Aitana ahead. The descent towards Alcoi is faster and more open. The surface is good, there is little traffic, and it is usually pleasantly cool at the summit even in August, though the wind can be sharp.

The villages on the inland side have a long history. Sella has the remains of a castle above the houses, and Penàguila, a little further, has another castle and a quiet square, both relics of the frontier between Christian and Muslim lands in the thirteenth century. Benilloba is a typical small village of the Alcoià with a bar or two. None of these has fuel you can count on, and Cocentaina, thirteen kilometres away, is the town for filling up, with a historic centre built around the palace of the Counts of Cocentaina.

The paintings in the shelters around here are in the typical style of the Valencian shelters, with small red figures under a natural roof of rock. Respect the fences and walk gently. The terraces that climb the slopes around you are a more recent record, made by farmers who cleared stones by hand and stacked them into walls; the Moors left irrigation, and later generations left almonds and olives. Take water, as the barrancos are dry for most of the year.
t.andragulla ii@38.2,-2.0:
Moratalla is a big, rough municipality, with a rugged interior of pine ridges, rocky gullies and scattered hamlets, and Andragulla is one of those hamlets, twelve kilometres from the town. The shelters are in the folds of the hills south of the village. The surrounding country is one of the least known parts of Murcia, and it is a joy for a rider who likes silence, because the roads are narrow, winding and almost deserted.

Think of the ride as a series of small climbs and drops, with long views across the ranges and the bends tight enough to keep you busy. Surfaces vary from smooth to patchy, and the odd stretch is unpaved, so a bike with a little ground clearance is an advantage. In summer the heat is severe and the pines smell of resin, in winter there can be snow on the higher ground. Autumn is the sweet spot, with clear air and the first rain bringing out the smell of the earth.

Moratalla has the fuel, along with a handful of bars and shops. Caravaca de la Cruz, sixteen kilometres away and with about twenty-six thousand people, is a much bigger town and a place of pilgrimage. Its castle-sanctuary holds the Vera Cruz, a relic believed to contain a fragment of the True Cross, and every year in early May the town holds the Festival of the Wine Horses, in which teams of decorated horses race up the hill to the castle, a tradition now on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage. If you are passing in that week, book rooms early.

The shelters here belong to the same rock-art tradition as the others in Moratalla. Many are small, some are on private land, and several are fenced, so ask in Moratalla about access before setting out on foot. Take plenty of water and a hat, and keep off any painted surfaces. You may share a stretch of track with a flock of sheep.
t.barranco de la cueva ii@38.4,-0.3:
This is the dry hinterland of the Costa Blanca, in the stretch between El Campello and Villajoyosa, where the sea is never far but you can easily forget it. A few kilometres inland the hills turn to scrub, rock and abandoned terraces, with barrancos that run dry for most of the year and then flood in a night after a storm. The Barranco de la Cueva is one of those ravines, and the shelter in it belongs to the scatter of painted rocks found across the mountains of Alicante.

The towns on the coast are worth knowing. Villajoyosa has a seafront of tall houses painted in bright colours, said to have been chosen so that fishermen could recognise their homes from the sea, and it is the home of a chocolate factory that has been making bars for generations. El Campello is a working fishing town with a long beach, and Sant Joan lies on the edge of Alicante's urban sprawl. All three have fuel, and Alicante itself, with its castle on a rock, is a short ride south.

Inland, the roads wind up through almond and carob terraces and pine woods to little villages such as Relleu and Busot. The bends are tight and often rough on the surface, and in summer the temperature climbs fast. Spring, autumn and early winter are the right times, when you can ride in a T-shirt in the sun and a jacket in the shade. Near Busot, the Cuevas de Canalobre are a well-known cave with a huge chamber that can be visited.

A ride to Elche, on the plain to the south-west, is a worthwhile addition, as the town has a palm grove that UNESCO listed in 2000, with more than two hundred thousand palms planted by the Moors for dates and irrigation. The mystery play of Elche, performed every August, is also on the intangible heritage list. Take water to the shelter, and be careful about fire, since the pine woods dry out by mid-summer.
t.l esmoladora@38.8,-0.3:
The Serra de Mariola is a mountain of herbs. Its slopes smell of thyme, rosemary, sage and a score of other aromatic plants that people have gathered for centuries to make teas, liqueurs and remedies, and the natural park that protects it has become a favourite of walkers who like to crush a leaf between their fingers. L'Esmoladora lies a little way east of that range, in the hills between Planes and Beniarrés, a country of terraced slopes and small reservoirs that spreads out towards the plain of Alcoi.

Planes is a very small village with the ruins of a Muslim castle on a rock above it, and Benimarfull, a few kilometres away, is smaller still. Beniarrés has a reservoir on the river Serpis, created in the twentieth century by a dam, and the water turns the whole valley a green that is rare in this dry region. The three villages together give you a pleasing circuit, with narrow roads, little traffic and farms hidden among almond and olive trees.

Riding is the main attraction. Corners are tight but short, the surface is generally decent, and the views change at every bend, from olive groves to pine woods to the pale cliff of the Mariola. In the afternoon, you may meet cyclists. Spring brings flowers and the sound of water, autumn a hush and golden light. In summer, the shade is a gift, and in winter the high ground can be cold and misty.

Fuel can be bought at Muro d'Alcoi, with about eight thousand people, twelve kilometres away, and Alcoi, a bit further, is a bigger industrial town famous for its Moors and Christians festival in April, when the streets fill with parades, mock battles and gunpowder. Cocentaina is close as well. The shelter is part of a family of painted sites around the Serpis valley, and the paintings are small. Take water, and do not be tempted to touch.
t.benizar iv@38.3,-2.0:
Water tells you where to look in this country. Benizar is a hamlet in the municipality of Moratalla, and the ravine below it is one of the many seasonal streams that run down towards the Segura, dry for most of the year and a torrent for a day or two after heavy rain. The shelters on its sides are small hollows in the rock, shaded in the afternoon and warm in the morning, which is just what you would want if you were a hunter looking for somewhere dry to sit and paint.

The road is quiet and the riding is good. It passes through pine and juniper, with bends that are long and open, and the traffic is almost entirely local. A farm gate or a loose dog is a bigger hazard than another vehicle. In summer the afternoons are brutal, so start early and plan to be somewhere shaded by two. In spring the hillsides are bright with rock roses and the ravine bottoms hold a little green, while in autumn the first storms can leave mud and gravel across the bends.

Socovos, seven kilometres away in Albacete, is a pleasant place for a coffee, and Férez, a smaller village to the north, has an old church and a view over the valley. Moratalla, with its castle, is twelve kilometres off and has the fuel, so fill the tank there. None of the hamlets in between can be trusted to have a pump, and the nearest cash machine is likely to be in Moratalla too, so plan accordingly.

The paintings are in the Levantine style, with small red figures, and nearby are other shelters such as the Abrigo de la Ventana and the Abrigo de Zaén, so you could spend a day tracing the line between them. Take water and a hat, move slowly, and remember that these walls have survived because for most of their history nobody paid them any attention. The best way to repay that luck is to leave no mark of your own, not even a fingertip on the pigment.
t.los rumies@38.2,-1.6:
The name Los Rumíes looks like the Arabic word rumi, which was once used across the Muslim world for Romans, then for Christians, and the Spanish landscape is full of names like it, left behind by eight centuries of Andalusi presence. The place lies in the dry hills north of the Segura valley, near Calasparra, and the rides that visit it also pass through the wider district of the Abrigo Grande de Minateda, one of the most famous painted shelters in the whole Levantine tradition. The rock art of this corner of Spain is substantial and varied.

The ride is across Murcia's high interior, a country of terraced farmland, pale limestone and low pines, with roads that are mostly broad and empty. Corners are long and open, with only the occasional tight bend where the road drops into a ramblas, the dry watercourses that fill suddenly after a storm. Summer is very hot and winter can be cold at night. Spring brings flowers and a green flush on the slopes, but autumn, when the heat has gone and the air is clear, is better.

Calasparra, eleven kilometres away, is the place for fuel and for a meal, and Cieza, thirteen kilometres, has more services. The Segura gorge near Calasparra, the Cañón de Almadenes, can be seen from a path along the cliff and is one of the most impressive bits of landscape in the region. In Cieza, the ruins of Medina Siyâsa, an Islamic town of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, are a reminder of how long Muslim families farmed the valley.

The shelters here, like most, are small and fragile. Some are fenced, some are on private ground, and the paintings are usually faint, so go with realistic expectations and ask locally first. You will find figures of deer, goats and hunters, in red and sometimes black, and there are places where the paint has run in thin lines down the rock.
t.andragulla iv@38.2,-2.0:
Not every part of Murcia is beach and orchard. In the north-west, the Region meets the Sierra and the high steppe of Albacete and Granada, and the land becomes a country of pine, rock and sheep, with a climate of hot summers and hard winter frosts. Andragulla lies in the municipality of Moratalla, twelve kilometres from the town, and the shelters in its folds are part of the north-west's rich collection of painted rock.

A day in the area could be built around wine. Bullas, an hour to the south-west by road, is the centre of a small denomination whose reds are made from the monastrell grape, a variety that thrives in poor, dry soils, and the vineyards on the slopes around it are an attractive sight in autumn. Cehegín and Caravaca lie on the way, with old towns and churches. Caravaca, sixteen kilometres away, is the larger, with a castle sanctuary that is a centre of pilgrimage.

The riding is a pleasure. Roads between the villages twist through pine and rock, with views over valleys and up to the long ridges, and the surface is mostly good. Take it easy on the descents, where loose stones from the slopes can be a hazard, and give yourself time. April, May, October and November are best. In summer, start at dawn.

Fuel is available in Moratalla, as well as in Caravaca, which has about twenty-six thousand people and more of everything. Socovos, to the north, is smaller. Bring water, a hat and sturdy shoes if you are hiking to a shelter, and leave no trace.

It helps to hold the whole picture in mind. The shelters of Moratalla, the old castle above the town, the pilgrimage at Caravaca and the vineyards at Bullas are different centuries laid on top of each other in one high, dry corner of Spain, and a rider with a free day and a full tank can touch most of them. Leave the schedule loose; the roads here reward wandering.
t.pla de petracos abric v@38.8,-0.2:
Each of the Petracos shelters has its own character, and the fifth is neither the largest nor the best known. It is a place for people who have already looked at the others and want to understand what was repeated. Hunting, for instance: the Levantine painters were fascinated by it, and the art of this region is full of archers, goats, deer and boars, drawn with a quick, clear line. Over time, other peoples came to the same walls and added their own signs, which look very different, abstract and geometric, and the Pla de Petracos is one of the few places where you can see both side by side.

The plateau lies above the Vall de Castells, four kilometres from the village of Castell de Castells, and the road up from the coast is one of the finest in northern Alicante. It leaves the orange groves of Callosa d'en Sarrià, climbs through almond terraces and then runs along the valley with views of the Serrella. The bends are tight in places but open in others, and the surface is mostly good. Cyclists use the road a lot, so expect to share it. Early autumn, when the heat has eased and the air is clear, is the best time.

Vall d'Ebo is another few kilometres away and has a history that is a little haunting: after 1609, when the Moriscos were expelled, the valley was almost empty, and the terraces were cultivated again by settlers from other regions. Pego, eleven kilometres off, has fuel, cafés and the wetland of the Marjal. The villages on the plateau offer a coffee at best.

When you visit the shelters, remember that fences and signs are there for good reason, and that a drop of water or a touch of a hand can damage pigment that has survived millennia. Take a hat, plenty of water and good shoes.
t.la risca iii@38.2,-2.0:
Spend a day riding in a ring and you begin to understand a place. From Moratalla, one good loop runs north to Socovos, on to Férez, then swings east through the folded hills to Letur and returns by a different line, and La Risca lies on the Moratalla side of it, twelve kilometres out of town. This is a tour of a landscape in which the Segura and its tributaries have carved gorges through pale limestone, and between the gorges are plateaux of pine, almond and cereals.

The roads on such a loop are among the best in the south-east for a rider who likes quiet. Curves are long and flowing with the occasional tight hairpin where a road descends to a river, the tarmac is generally well kept, and the traffic is thin enough that you can ride in the middle of the lane through the corners. Be careful on descents after rain, when gravel washes out of the side gullies, and take layers in spring and autumn when the mountain air can be sharp.

Letur is the star of the loop. Its old centre, with narrow, twisting lanes and whitewashed houses, preserves the plan of an Andalusi village, a maze built for shade and for defence, and it hangs above a deep ravine with views over the surrounding hills. Férez and Socovos are quieter and have bars where you can sit with a coffee, and Moratalla has the largest range of shops and the fuel. Fill the tank before you set out, as the villages cannot be relied upon.

The shelter at La Risca belongs to the rock art of the Moratalla uplands, painted in the Levantine style, and like others it is small and protected. Ask in town about access, stay on the path and avoid touching the rock. Late afternoon, with the low sun on the cliffs and swifts overhead, is a fine time to be there.
t.la risca ii@38.2,-2.0:
Some of the best meals in the Segura uplands are served in places that have no sign. A bar in a Murcian hill village will put out a plate of migas, the fried breadcrumbs with garlic and chorizo that shepherds have eaten for centuries, or a stew of lamb with potatoes and peppers, and it will be a great deal better than the price suggests. La Risca, in the municipality of Moratalla, is a hamlet of scattered farms twelve kilometres from the town, and the shelter lies among the fields in a pocket of the hills, where the cortijos, the old farmhouses, stand in clumps of almond and olive.

Farms in this country were self-contained. Each had its threshing floor, its well or spring, its bread oven, and its flock of sheep or goats, and some are still in use. As the young went to the cities, many were left to crumble, but some have been restored as rural lodgings, a development that has brought some life back to the countryside. If you are staying overnight, a casa rural near Moratalla can be a good base, though it is wise to book in advance for Holy Week and for the weekends of the Caravaca festival in early May.

For riders, the roads here are twisting and quiet, with views over folds of pine and rock. The surface is variable, so keep a steady pace, and watch for livestock and for farm machinery in the bends. Fuel is at Moratalla, where there are also supermarkets and bars. Socovos and Férez, to the north, are smaller. Try to be out of the high ground before dusk in winter, when temperatures drop fast.

The rock shelter itself, with its small red paintings, is part of the Levantine tradition that covers the east of Spain. It is protected and often fenced, and you should check locally before setting out.

If you want to understand the place beyond the plate and the paint, the thing to do is to talk to someone who farms. The people of these hills know which springs fail in August, which slopes hold the first frost, where the foxes den and where the old paths cut across. The paintings suggest that people have been paying that kind of attention here for a very long time, and a conversation over a coffee, however halting your Spanish, brings the whole landscape into focus.
t.raco de gorgori abric iii@38.8,-0.2:
From the ridge tops above Castell de Castells you can have the sea and the tower blocks of Benidorm in view on a clear day, and the contrast is almost comic: a village of a few hundred people, goats and almond terraces, and not much more than twenty kilometres away a skyline of glass. The Racó de Gorgorí lies in the hills above the valley, and from the coast a good road climbs to it by way of Callosa d'en Sarrià and the Guadalest valley. A rider who does this in a morning will have made one of the most abrupt changes of scene in Spain.

On the way, Guadalest is hard to miss. The village stands on a pinnacle of rock above a turquoise reservoir, with a ruined castle and a bell tower on the very top, and it is one of the most visited places in the province, so go early or in winter. Its charm survives the souvenir shops if you are willing to walk beyond them. The road from there towards Benimantell and Castell de Castells climbs through pine and carob, with bends that tighten and release in a way that makes you glad of a light bike.

Benimantell and Bolulla are tiny villages, and the springs and waterfalls of the Algar, in nearby Callosa, are a cool relief in summer. Pego, thirteen kilometres away, is the nearest town with a full range of services, and Callosa d'en Sarrià, with its loquat orchards, has fuel on the way up. In the village bars you can find simple food, and local almonds and honey.

The shelter is small and protected, and its paintings, as in many Levantine sites, are in red. Try to arrive in the morning, wear sturdy shoes and bring water.

Late in the day the view repays the climb. The light turns the limestone orange, the shadows of the Serrella lengthen across the valley, and the sea, which has been a pale smudge all afternoon, becomes a bright line. It is a good moment to stop talking about archaeology and simply sit. The ride back down in the dusk should be taken slowly, with your lights on early, because goats and the occasional boar cross these roads at that hour.
t.fuente serrano ii@38.2,-2.2:
Most of the water that Cartagena drinks was once rain on the mountains of the Sierra del Segura. The Taibilla river rises in the high country near Nerpio, and a long chain of canals, tunnels and aqueducts carries it, through a public body created in the 1920s, to taps across Murcia and parts of Alicante and Albacete. It is a good thing to know when you stand beside the dry streambeds of Fuente Serrano, seven kilometres from Nerpio, where the springs seem to have a purpose beyond the paintings in the rock.

The shelter lies in the broken uplands to the south-east of the village, in country of pine, juniper and cereal fields, where the road narrows and the traffic disappears. The riding is quiet and comfortable, with bends that curve gently across the plateau and a surface that is mostly good, though rough in patches. At this altitude, about a thousand metres, the nights stay cool in July and the winters are cold, so check the forecast between November and March.

The rock art around Nerpio is one of the largest concentrations in Albacete, with Levantine and schematic paintings grouped near springs and watercourses. That pattern, with art close to water, suggests that these shelters were used by people who lived in these hills for part of the year and knew where the springs were. It is a pleasing thought when you are standing next to a spring.

Nerpio is a village of fewer than seventeen hundred people, and fuel is not guaranteed, so fill up in Yeste, twenty-five kilometres away, or in Moratalla. There are bars in the village and a handful of places to stay. Take water for the walk, and be careful on the tracks, which can be muddy after rain.

The scale of the country is what stays with you. From the high ground you look across a patchwork of pine woods, bare ridges and small cultivated hollows, with hardly a roof in sight, and you realise that this is what most of inland Spain looked like for most of its history. A rider who stops the engine and listens will hear sheep bells, a distant tractor, and maybe the wind in the pines, and that is all. It is a good place to eat a bocadillo slowly.
t.zona 2@38.1,-2.4:
A label like Zona 2 tells you that someone with a clipboard and a map divided this country into sectors, and numbered them, and then walked every one. That is how the rock art of the Sierra del Segura was found: slowly, valley by valley, by teams who recorded dozens of shelters around Nerpio and the high country towards Jaén. The Zona 2 stop is seven kilometres from Nerpio, in hills of pine and juniper at a bit over a thousand metres, and it is a good example of the way this part of Spain hides things in plain view.

It is also a good base for a large ride. To the south, Huéscar, a town of eight thousand on the high plateau of Granada, has the fuel, thirty-eight kilometres off. To the north-west, Segura de la Sierra, a village of white houses clustered around a castle on a crag, sits in the Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas natural park, which is the largest protected area in Spain. Yeste, twenty-seven kilometres to the north, has the nearest bigger services in the opposite direction.

The roads are quiet and the corners are generous, with long views across the highland. The surface is mostly good, but gravel and potholes can appear after winter, and the cold in January is real. In spring the hills are green and the rivers run, and in autumn the poplars along the valleys turn gold. Summer is dry, bright and hot in the afternoon.

Nerpio has a handful of bars and a couple of places to stay, but do not rely on it for fuel. Carry water, and take care of the paintings, which have lasted this long because the sector was hard to reach.

It is worth thinking about scale before you set out. On the map, these places look close, but the roads are slow and winding, and a loop from Nerpio to Huéscar and back by the mountains is a full day, not a morning. Start early, keep your lunch simple, and stay out of the high ground after dark in winter, when ice makes the descents unpleasant and there is nobody to flag down. Mobile coverage is patchy, so leave word with someone about where you are heading.
t.abrigo del idolo@38.1,-2.3:
Shelters collect names the way villages collect nicknames. The Abrigo del Ídolo lies barely a kilometre and a half from Nerpio, and it carries the name of a figure that someone once thought looked like an idol, which tells you less about the figure than about the person who named it. Across the district you will find shelters called after mills, springs, farms and the families who worked them, and the whole collection reads like a gazetteer of the people who walked these hills before the archaeologists arrived.

Nerpio itself sits on a high plateau of the Sierra del Segura, at about a thousand metres, and the approach from Yeste or Moratalla is a long climb through pine and juniper to open farmland. The roads are good, quiet and winding, and the corners wide enough to enjoy at a gentle pace. In winter, ice and snow can close the higher sections, and in summer the afternoons are dry and bright. The most comfortable months are May, June, September and October.

What makes Nerpio special is that the shelters are close to the village and to each other. Within a few kilometres there are many painted walls, some Levantine, with red hunters and animals, others schematic, with abstract signs, and walking between them is like leafing through a book whose pages are cliffs. Some are fenced and some are easy to miss, and a local guide or the tourist office in the village will save you time.

Fuel is not something to count on in Nerpio. Yeste, twenty-four kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable village with services, and Moratalla, farther off, has more. The village has bars where you can eat well and cheaply, and the water in the fountains is cold and good. Take care at the shelters, wear boots, and let the paintings be.
t.molino de las fuentes ii o de sautuola@3:
Sautuola is a name that matters in this story. Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola, a landowner from Cantabria, was the man who in 1879 recognised that the bison on the ceiling of Altamira had been painted by people of the Ice Age, and he was laughed at for it, and he died without seeing himself proved right. A shelter near Nerpio carries his name alongside that of a mill, which is a rather lovely thing to find in a village in Albacete, some seven hundred kilometres from Santillana. It sits less than two kilometres from the village.

The argument that Sautuola started never really ended. Levantine art, the art of the Mediterranean side of Spain, came to light in the early twentieth century, and it provoked its own long quarrels about age, style and meaning. Is it Palaeolithic, like Altamira, or much later, made by hunters and early farmers after the ice age? The consensus now leans to the later date, though debate continues, and each new dating technique gives new arguments. Standing at a Nerpio shelter, you are part of a conversation that has been going for a century and a half.

The ride is the same as for the other Nerpio shelters: climb from Yeste or Moratalla onto the plateau, with the road winding through pine and juniper, and enjoy the quiet. Take care in winter, when ice lingers in the shade. The mill in the name is a reminder that water here was valuable, and that small streams once drove grinding stones for the whole district.

Yeste, twenty-six kilometres away, has the nearest fuel, and Moratalla is further. Nerpio's bars serve plain mountain food, and the village is a pleasant place to rest. Carry water, avoid touching the rock, and take your time, because the paintings give up their details slowly.
t.arco i@38.2,-1.6:
The Segura valley around Calasparra and Cieza has been a corridor for as long as people have walked through southern Spain, and the sites known as Arco I and Arco II are two of the shelters that belong to it. Cieza lies thirteen kilometres to the east, and it is a town with a long past: before the Christians took it in the thirteenth century it was Medina Siyâsa, a walled Islamic city of some importance, and the ruins of the old quarter have been excavated on the hill above the river. The town's museums are a useful stop, and Cieza has fuel, shops and cafés.

Cieza was also, for much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, a centre for esparto grass, the tough, wiry plant that grows on the dry slopes here and was twisted into rope, baskets, sandals and mats. The hills around you were once harvested by hand, and the tradition is remembered in the town. It is a modest, humane piece of history, the kind that helps you understand why this dry country supported so many people.

On the road, the pleasure is in the open space. The roads run across low ridges and down into the valley with a mix of straights and long bends, there is little traffic, and the warm, clear light turns the hills a soft ochre. Take care at junctions with field tracks, where gravel and dust accumulate, and be careful of the midday heat in summer. April, May, October and November are the best times for a ride.

Calasparra, eleven kilometres to the west, is the other possible fuel stop. Its rice, grown on terraced fields watered by the Segura, is celebrated across Spain, and there is a sanctuary of the Virgin of Hope clinging to the cliff above the river. As for the shelter, it is small and protected, so ask locally before you go, take water, and tread gently.
t.pla de petracos abric viii@38.8,-0.2:
There is a trick to Petracos, and it is to look at the walls in the order that the rock gives them to you. The eighth shelter is at one end of the plateau, where the cliff curves and the shade falls early, and what you notice first is not paint at all, but the way the rock has weathered into smooth bowls and thin ledges. Water has done this over thousands of years, and the painters used the hollows that it made. Without the erosion there would be no shelters, and without the shelters no art, and the whole thing is a kind of collaboration between stone and people.

Four kilometres from Castell de Castells, the plateau sits at the head of a valley that has seen a great deal. In 1609 it was almost emptied of its Morisco inhabitants, and the farms and terraces were rebuilt by newcomers over the next decades. Later, in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the villages shrank again as people moved to the coast and the factory towns, and today the area is quiet and half-forgotten, which is why the paintings survive.

Ride up from Callosa d'en Sarrià, through the almond and olive terraces, and enjoy the shape of the road: tight at first, then rolling, with the sea behind you and the Serrella ahead. The surface is generally good, although a few patches of tarmac are broken and some corners carry gravel. In winter, mornings can be icy. For fuel, Pego, eleven kilometres off, is the place, with a supermarket and bars, and Murla and Vall d'Ebo are tiny.

Look after the shelters. Keep to the paths, do not climb on the rock, and carry water, because the plateau offers little shade. A good pair of boots and a hat will make the visit much more comfortable.
t.barranc d alpadull abric ii@38.8,-0.6:
Bocairent is a strange and beautiful town, and the hills around it are among the lesser-known gems of Valencian inland. It sits on a rocky spur above a gorge, with a medieval quarter of steep, narrow streets and a baroque church, and in the cliffs below the town are cave dwellings called the Covetes dels Moros, hollows cut into the rock that have been used as homes, storehouses and shelters for centuries. Beyond the town, in the Serra de Mariola, there are also old stone ice-houses, the neveres, in which snow was packed in winter and sold in summer. The Barranc d'Alpadull lies only three and a half kilometres away.

The Serra de Mariola is a natural park known for its aromatic and medicinal plants, and walkers come to gather thyme, rosemary, sage and lavender, or to follow trails through holm oak and pine to springs. The air has a clean, herbal smell, particularly after rain, and in spring the slopes are full of flowers. Wildlife includes foxes, wild boar and a good population of birds of prey.

Roads in the district are enjoyable. They climb out of the Vall d'Albaida through terraced slopes, wind past old farms and cross the saddles of the sierra, with bends that are neither too tight nor too fast. Surface is generally good, traffic is light apart from weekends, and the views of the Mariola are splendid. Autumn is lovely, with golden light and cool air. Winter can be cold and misty, and summer afternoons are hot.

Ontinyent, six kilometres away and with nearly thirty-eight thousand people, is the nearest large town and has all the fuel and services you need, as well as a long tradition of wool and textile production. Alfafara and Agres are villages with a bar or two. Take water for any walk to the shelter, and respect the paintings.
t.cueva de la arana abrigo iii@39.1,-0.9:
Honey is one of the oldest sweet things that people ever stole, and the most famous painted honey-gatherer in the world is on a wall a few kilometres from here. The Cueva de la Araña is in the hills above Bicorp, in the Canal de Navarrés, and its scene shows a figure on what look like ropes or vines, reaching into a cleft where bees have made their nest, with insects around him and a bag or container on his arm. It is more than a picture of honey. It is a rare view of ordinary life in the age of the hunters, and for that reason, it appears in nearly every book on rock art.

The honey tradition has never died. The scrub-covered hills of inland Valencia, with their rosemary, thyme, orange blossom on the plains and wild flowers in the spring, give some of the most fragrant honey in Spain, and beekeepers still bring their hives into the area in season. In the villages you can often buy a jar from a producer. It makes a good souvenir and it fits in a pannier.

The ride to Bicorp from Navarrés or Enguera runs through a green and rocky landscape, with a narrow road, tight bends in places and very little traffic. Take care with gravel and loose stones, and with farm vehicles at blind corners. It is best on a cool day in spring or autumn, when the climb to the cave is easy and the pines smell of resin. Summer afternoons are hot and heavy.

Fuel is available at Navarrés, about fourteen kilometres away, and at Ayora, eighteen kilometres off. Bicorp and Quesa are tiny, with a bar apiece. Access to the cave itself is controlled, and it is essential to enquire about visiting arrangements beforehand. Take water and be respectful of the paintings.
t.abriga de los idolos@38.1,-2.3:
Nerpio is a small village that looks like it has been there for ever, with white houses, a church, a few bars and a plaza where old men sit in the sun, and it is worth getting to know before heading out to the shelters. Its position on a high plateau, at around a thousand metres, makes it cool in summer and cold in winter, and the village has a long tradition of mountain farming: cereals, almonds, sheep and, in the valley bottoms, fruit trees. The Abrigos de los Ídolos are under a kilometre and a half from the plaza.

Local food is straightforward and good: lamb, game, cured meats, stews, migas and gachas, a thick, comforting dish made from flour. In autumn there may be wild mushrooms. The bars in the village are the place to try them, and the owners are generally happy to talk about the area and to recommend what to see.

The road in from Yeste or Moratalla is a pleasure. It climbs through pines and junipers, across open plateau and down into valleys, with smooth bends and little traffic, though the surface can be rough in patches. Winter snow and ice can make the road dangerous, and spring brings meltwater and gravel. Autumn is the best time, with warm days and cool nights.

Fuel is not guaranteed in the village, so fill up in Yeste, twenty-four kilometres away, or Moratalla. Take water to the shelter, and as ever, keep your hands off the paintings.

Nerpio rewards a night's stay more than a quick stop. In the evening the plaza fills with neighbours, the light turns gold on the whitewashed walls, and the sky, with almost no light pollution, shows more stars than most Europeans ever see. A rider who arrives at four in the afternoon, walks to the shelters in the soft light and then eats in the village will have a better day than one who rushes through between two other places. The nights are cold at this height even in summer, so bring a jumper.
t.hornacina de la pareja@38.1,-2.3:
A hornacina is a niche, a small hollow in a wall, the kind you find in a church for a statue. The Hornacina de la Pareja, the niche of the couple, is a small shelter near Nerpio, a kilometre and a half from the village, and the name suggests that someone once saw a pair of figures in the paint. You should treat that as a clue to how fragile and ambiguous these images are: a couple to one eye, a stain and a couple of lines to another.

Small shelters like this make up most of the Levantine art in this part of Spain. Not every site is a gallery, and many are merely a little overhang where a few figures were painted, perhaps by a hunter on a single visit. Seen in that light, the Nerpio district is less a museum than a record of lives, with thousands of small acts of painting scattered across a landscape.

The ride in is the same as for the neighbouring shelters, with a quiet climb from Yeste or Moratalla on roads that wind through pine and juniper. The surface is fine, the bends are gentle, and the air at a thousand metres is fresh. Watch for ice in winter, and for sheep and tractors at any time.

For fuel, Yeste is about twenty-four kilometres away, and Moratalla farther. Nerpio has bars and a few rooms, but no sure pump. Take water, wear good shoes, and try not to leave any trace of your visit.

There is a lesson in the modesty of these places. A few red lines under a ledge of rock, no bigger than a hand, can take longer to read than a vast mural, because you have to supply the rest: the person who stood here, the day of the week, the reason for stopping. Standing in front of one in the thin mountain air, with a kestrel working the slope below and the village bell carrying faintly up the valley, you find that the gap in time is smaller than you thought. Give it ten quiet minutes before you take out the phone. On the way back, the road from Nerpio drops into the valley in a long series of open bends, and the light at the end of the afternoon is the best you will see all day. Ride it slowly, with the sun at your back, and stop at the first bar in the next village for something cold.
t.benizar iii@38.3,-2.0:
Four shelters called Benizar, numbered one to four, do not make four attractions. The numbers come from a survey, in which an archaeologist walked along a cliff and gave each painted overhang a label in the order in which it was reached, and the result is a list like a row of rooms on a corridor. Benizar III is one of them, in the hills of Moratalla about twelve kilometres from the town, and it is best treated as a piece of a larger site, a stretch of wall that was used repeatedly, not a gallery you can tick off.

What the numbers mean in practice is that you can cover several in one walk. The overhangs lie within a short distance of one another, and the paintings are small, in the Levantine style, with red figures of archers and animals. Bring patience, because the paint is faded, and good light makes a great difference. In the morning the sun lights the cliff at a low angle and the figures appear more clearly. By noon the same wall can look blank, which is a lesson in why people who study rock art are so often seen sitting quietly with a flask.

The road to Benizar crosses pine and juniper country, with long, easy bends and almost no traffic. It is a good road for a relaxed rider on a bike that is happy at a steady pace, and a poor one for anyone in a hurry, because tractors, sheep and the occasional dog appear at the corners. April, May, October and November are the best months. In July, start before the heat has built, and in winter check for ice in the shady cuttings.

Socovos, seven kilometres away in Albacete, has a bar where you can get a coffee and a sandwich, and Férez is smaller still. Moratalla has the fuel, the shops and the castle, and you should fill the tank there before heading out. Do not touch the rock, take your rubbish with you, and leave the place as you found it.
t.benizar i@38.3,-2.0:
The names on the map around Moratalla tell the story of who was here before. Benizar begins with Beni, from the Arabic banu, the sons of, and the same prefix turns up all over the Spanish east: Benimantell, Benilloba, Benimarfull, Beniarrés. They are the names of the clans who farmed these valleys when this was part of al-Andalus, and who gave their ancestors' names to villages that have outlived the families. Benizar I is the first of four shelters in the hamlet's surroundings, about twelve kilometres from Moratalla, in a landscape of limestone ridges, pine and scrub.

The ride from Moratalla runs north across the high country towards Socovos, over low passes with long views and few other vehicles. The bends are broad and easy to read, and the surface is generally good, though some stretches are patched. Spring is lovely, with wildflowers and a green haze on the hills, and autumn is warm and clear. In July the heat is intense. In winter, check for ice in the shade.

Moratalla, a town of about eight and a half thousand, is the sensible place to buy fuel, and its castle is worth a visit. Socovos, in Albacete, is a pleasant village of nearly two thousand people with a bar or two, and Férez is smaller. The Moors left more than names in this area. The terraces, springs and water channels that sustain the villages are of Andalusi origin, and some are still in use.

The shelter belongs to the older layer of the landscape, the Levantine paintings of hunters and animals, and is small and fenced. Take water, treat the site with care, and enjoy the quiet.

It is worth noticing how much of the vocabulary of Spanish riding country is Arabic. Alfafara, Albocàsser, Alcoi, Almadenes, the word acequia for an irrigation ditch, even the word aceituna for the olive, all come from the language of the people who lived here for eight centuries, and a rider with a map and a little curiosity can read the history of a district in its place names, as clearly as in the paint on its rocks.
t.abric del charco negro@39.2,-0.7:
On 20 October 1982, after days of torrential rain, the dam at Tous on the Júcar gave way. The flood that followed swept down the Ribera, drowned fields and towns, and forced the evacuation of tens of thousands of people, and it remains one of the great disasters in the modern history of the Valencian country. The reservoir was rebuilt with a larger spillway, and today it is a calm sheet of water, but the people of Carlet and the neighbouring villages have not forgotten. The Abric del Charco Negro lies some way upstream, in the hills above Millares, where the Júcar and its tributaries cut through limestone.

Charco means a pool, and the name suggests a dark one, probably in the barranco below the shelter, where water lingers in the shade after rain. It is a reminder that in this country water is both the blessing and the danger. The same ravines that hold a pool in spring can run with a torrent in autumn, and it is wise to avoid any dry riverbed if there is heavy cloud in the hills.

The road to the shelter is a quiet and winding one, with bends that follow the contour of the valley, a mix of good and patchy surface, and a good deal of gravel at the verges. Traffic is minimal. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, as summer is hot and winter cold in the shade. Millares, Bicorp and Quesa are tiny villages with a bar each.

Carlet, nineteen kilometres away, is a town of about fifteen thousand people in the orange country of the Ribera Alta, and it has all the fuel and supplies you need. If you are there at the right time, the smell of orange blossom in spring is unforgettable. Bring water for the walk to the shelter, and treat the paintings with care.
t.cortijo de sorbas i@38.3,-2.1:
Sorbas is the name of a town in Almería, famous for its gypsum caves, and it is also the name of a cortijo, a farmhouse, in the hills south of Letur in Albacete, which is a coincidence that has confused more than one traveller. Cortijo de Sorbas is a shelter in a rough, dry upland that belongs to the municipality of Letur, about twelve kilometres from the village, and the ride that visits it also includes sites such as Los Sacristanes and the Cueva del Gitano.

Letur is the town to know. It stands on the edge of a deep ravine, a cluster of whitewashed houses along narrow, twisting lanes, with a plan inherited from the Moors who held it until the thirteenth century, and its lanes are worth an hour on foot. It has bars, a couple of viewpoints and a setting that is hard to beat. From there, the road to the Cortijo winds through pine and juniper, with the surface ranging from good to rough, and the bends tighter than you might expect.

This is the northern edge of the Sierra de Segura, and the landscape has the feel of the high Meseta cut by rivers. Spring is the time for wildflowers, and the autumn brings clear air. In summer the heat is dry and hard, and in winter snow can close the higher roads. Take care with gravel and loose stones, particularly after rain.

Fuel is at Moratalla, twenty-one kilometres away, which has a full range of services. Socovos, fourteen kilometres off, is smaller. If you are going to the shelter, make sure to carry water, wear boots, and ask locally about access, because some sites lie on private land and are reached by tracks across farms. Be courteous, close any gates you open and leave the paintings alone.
t.lavadero tello ii@37.8,-2.1:
In the early 1980s a skull found at Venta Micena, near the village of Orce in Granada, caused a minor sensation: it was said to belong to the oldest human in Europe, perhaps a million and a half years old. The claim was fiercely disputed, and many specialists now believe that the skull is from a horse, but the Orce basin is still one of the key places for early human presence in Western Europe, with stone tools and remains of ancient animals. The area lies not far from Vélez-Blanco, and it is one of the reasons why the northern Almería and Granada highlands have such a deep sense of the past.

Against that background, the shelters of Lavadero Tello are recent, a few thousand years old at most. The place lies in the Sierra María-Los Vélez natural park, sixteen kilometres from Vélez-Blanco, with a landscape of pine woods, white limestone and almond terraces that rise towards the peak of Maimón at over two thousand metres. It is not a desert, as most people imagine Almería to be, and in winter the peaks hold snow.
