The ride is one to savour. The roads from Vélez-Blanco and Vélez-Rubio climb through the pines in long, easy bends, with the plains of Granada and Murcia stretching away in the distance. The surface is mostly good, and the traffic is light. Wind can be strong on the exposed ridges, so hold the bars firmly. Spring and autumn are the best times, as the summer sun is intense and winter brings snow and ice.

Vélez-Blanco has a Renaissance castle on a crag, and Vélez-Rubio, seven thousand people and twenty-two kilometres away, has a grand Baroque church and the best range of services, including fuel. María, with about fifteen hundred people, is nearer and quieter. Local food includes roast lamb, game, migas and almond cakes. The shelters are protected, so ask locally before you go, carry water, and be careful with the paintings.
t.esbardal de miquel el serril abric ii@38:
Castell de Castells sits in a valley with running water in it, which in dry Alicante counts for a good deal. Springs, small pools and irrigated terraces give this corner of the Serrella a green freshness that comes as a surprise in such country. The Esbardal de Miquel el Serril is a rocky outcrop and shelter a kilometre and a half from the village, in a landscape of cliffs, pine and almond, and it is one of the closest shelters to Castell de Castells, with Benimantell four kilometres away.

The name Miquel el Serril looks like a person's nickname, and it suggests a farmer who once worked the land below. It is an example of how local people record their history in place names, and it is worth asking in the village whether anyone remembers who he was. People in the valley are generally friendly and glad to talk about their home.

The road in is one of the best in the province. From Callosa d'en Sarrià, it climbs through loquat and citrus, then through almond and olive terraces, past the village of Guadalest with its castle on a rock, and on to Benimantell and Castell de Castells. The bends are tight, the views are wide, and the traffic is mostly local. Guadalest is crowded in summer, so go early. In winter, frost can linger on the shady bends.

Fuel is at La Nucia, twelve kilometres away, or in Callosa d'en Sarrià, on the way up. Benidorm, with its towers, is not far, but a world away. Bolulla, with fewer than four hundred people, has a bar, and so does Castell de Castells. The paintings in the shelter are small, so go with patience, and treat the site with care. Take water for the walk, because the slopes above the village have little shade, and watch your footing on the loose limestone, which rolls underfoot after a dry spell and turns greasy after rain. A short visit in the early morning, followed by a long breakfast in the village, is a fine way to spend the first half of a day.
t.abrigo del atajo i@39.2,-0.8:
Valencian paella, the real one, contains no seafood. It is a dish of the interior, cooked over an open fire of orange wood in a wide, shallow pan, with rice, chicken, rabbit, flat green beans, a large white bean called garrofó, tomato, saffron and olive oil, and in some places snails. The coast got involved later. A rider who is tempted by a plate of it on the road to Millares should look for a bar that cooks to order and takes forty minutes, since the quicker ones tend to rely on the freezer.

The Abrigo del Atajo I, two kilometres from Millares, lies in the hills of the Júcar, in country that is dry, rugged and quiet. Millares and Dos Aguas are small villages, and Bicorp is a short ride further. The road to Atajo is narrow and winding, with a good surface in places and a poor one in others, and the views over the pine woods are lovely. Be careful of gravel, wild boar and farm vehicles, and avoid the middle of the day in July and August.

Turís, with five thousand people and eighteen kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel, and it is an agricultural centre of orange groves and vineyards. A little further, Montroy has a handful of shops. The villages near the shelter will have a bar, and some may serve food, but it is best to arrange meals in advance.

The shelter is small and part of a group of painted sites in this valley, and you should ask locally about access. Take water and wear good shoes.

There is a particular pleasure in this part of the Júcar country at the end of the day. The light comes in low and gold across the pines, the heat finally drains out of the stone, and from a bend in the road you can look down a long fold of hill to a village roof and a thread of smoke. Take your helmet off, listen to the engine tick as it cools, and let the cicadas finish their shift. When the sun goes behind the ridge, the temperature falls quickly, so put a layer on before you set off for the last stretch home.
t.andragulla iii@38.2,-2.0:
Bats live in cavities, and so do eagles. The rocky country around Andragulla, in the municipality of Moratalla, is full of holes: overhangs, clefts, small caves that the survey of rock art calls cavidades, and each of them is a home for something. Bats roost in the dark ones, swifts and choughs nest in the cracks, and on the highest cliffs a golden eagle or a Bonelli's eagle may build a nest of sticks. The shelters with painted figures are only the human part of a much larger story of life in the rock.

The hills here are covered in Aleppo pine, with rosemary, thyme, juniper and the tough esparto grass in the open ground. In spring, orchids and rock roses appear, and the air smells of resin and herbs. Wild boar, foxes and rabbits live in the scrub, and in the evening you may hear owls. It is a landscape that has been used by people for a very long time but never overwhelmed by them, and the paintings fit within it.

Getting here is an easy ride from Moratalla, twelve kilometres away, by quiet roads with long bends and little traffic. The surface is generally good, with some rough patches. Caravaca de la Cruz, sixteen kilometres off, has fuel, shops and a famous castle sanctuary, and Socovos is a smaller place to the north. Moratalla itself has the sensible services, including fuel.

Come in spring or autumn. Summer is hot and dry, with the risk of forest fires, and winter nights are cold. Take water, a hat and good shoes, and treat the shelters with care. Never light a fire or leave rubbish.

The most useful thing you can bring is time. These hills do not reward a quick look, because the paintings are small, the rock is complicated and the wildlife keeps its own hours. Sit still for a quarter of an hour at the foot of a cliff and the place changes: a lizard emerges on a warm ledge, a pair of choughs wheel overhead, a faint trail on the slope turns out to belong to a family of boar. Moratalla's hills are a landscape that opens to patience, and a motorcycle, with its small footprint and its ability to be parked and forgotten, is a good way to arrive at it.
t.arroyo tiscar@37.8,-3.0:
The Tíscar valley lies on the eastern side of the Sierra de Quesada, in the province of Jaén, where the olive groves of the plain give way to limestone ridges and pine. Arroyo Tíscar, the stream that gives this stop its name, runs through a narrow gorge, and the valley is known for a half-abandoned hamlet of the same name, with a ruined castle and a sanctuary, where springs gush from the cliff. It is a dramatic, slightly eerie place, a long way from the busy roads of Andalusia.

The area is rich in rock shelters with prehistoric paintings, part of the group of Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998. The painted figures are small and delicate, in red or brown, and the shelters are fragile, so access is controlled in many places. I cannot tell you exactly what the paintings at this particular shelter show, and it is best to ask in Quesada or Huesa about guided visits rather than try to find them alone. What you can do easily is look at the landscape the painters knew: steep rock, water, scrubby forest and the open valley below.

The riding in the area is a joy. The roads leave the olive sea and climb into the Sierra de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas natural park, the largest protected area in Spain, with long curves, hairpins and views over ridges. The surface is mostly fair, with some patched sections, and traffic is very light away from the main towns, so you can go at your own pace. In summer the heat is fierce, and in winter frost and even snow are possible on the higher roads, so the best seasons are spring and autumn.

Huesa, five kilometres away, is a small town of nearly three thousand people and should have fuel and a bar or two. Quesada, a little farther, is larger, and it is the home of the painter Rafael Zabaleta, whose museum is worth a visit. The food of the region is based on olive oil, bread, wild game and the rich stews of the mountains, and a plate of migas, fried breadcrumbs with chorizo, is a good way to start the day.

Take water and a map, because mobile signal can fade in the gorges.
t.benirrama abric ii@38.8,-0.2:
The Vall de Gallinera is a narrow valley in the mountains of northern Alicante, where eight small villages hang on the slopes among cherry trees, and Benirrama is one of them. The valley lies inland from the Costa Blanca, only an hour or so from the tourist beaches, yet it feels like another century. Terraced slopes, stone walls, irrigation channels and a thin, quiet road follow the Gallinera river, and in late winter and spring the cherry blossom covers the hillsides in white.

Benirrama, Abric II, is one of a group of rock shelters in the barrancs, or ravines, around the valley that hold prehistoric paintings, part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998. I do not know the details of what is painted here, and as a rule such shelters are small, fragile and best seen with someone who knows them, so enquire locally. The landscape itself tells a story, with its limestone cliffs, caves and the sound of water in the gullies.

The valley has a medieval history that is worth knowing. After the Christian conquest of Valencia in the thirteenth century, this was the heartland of a Muslim revolt led by al-Azraq, who held several castles in the mountains for years against King James I. The Moorish population stayed on in the valley for another three hundred and fifty years, until the expulsion of the Moriscos in 1609, after which the land was resettled, and the terraces and irrigation systems that you see today are part of that inheritance.

The roads are narrow, steep and twisting, with many tight bends, and they require care, especially in wet weather or when a farm vehicle comes the other way. The surface is fair but patchy, and there is almost no traffic. It is one of the more rewarding small roads of the region, with a very different feel from the coast. Adsubia and Vall d'Ebo are tiny villages with little more than a bar, so plan fuel and food in Pego or Villalonga, the latter being a town of nearly four thousand people.

Local food is simple and good, with rice dishes, orange juice and cherries in season, and the raisins and sweet muscat wine of the Marina Alta. Spring and autumn are the best seasons to ride.
t.zona 7@38.1,-2.4:
Nerpio sits at over a thousand metres in the south-west corner of Albacete, in the hills where the Taibilla river runs between pines and cliffs, and it is one of the highest villages in the province. The air is dry, the winters are cold and the sky at night is full of stars. The surrounding Sierra de Segura country is rough and sparsely populated, and for riders coming from the plains of La Mancha the landscape is a surprise, with long ridges and deep, wooded valleys.

The municipality of Nerpio is known among archaeologists for the number of rock shelters in its cliffs that contain prehistoric paintings, belonging to the Mediterranean Basin rock art tradition that UNESCO listed in 1998. Zona 7 is one of the numbered areas used to catalogue them, and I cannot say what is painted in it. As a rule, the paintings are small, fragile and sometimes hard to find, so ask in the village about guided visits and the local interpretation centre rather than wander the cliffs alone.

The roads in the area are a pleasure for those who like quiet and curves. The route up from Yeste climbs through pine forest in a succession of bends, with good views and almost no traffic. The surface can be patchy, with the odd rockfall and stretch of gravel, and the weather turns quickly, so go prepared, especially in winter, when snow and ice are real risks. In summer the hot afternoons are tempered by the altitude.

Nerpio has about sixteen hundred people, with a few shops and bars, but for reliable fuel you should plan on Yeste, a town of some thirty-five hundred, about twenty-seven kilometres away. The cooking of the region is shepherd's food, with migas, stews and roasted lamb, and the honey and cheese of the sierra are worth buying.

The ride links Zona 7 with the Cueva de las Palamas and with the Renaissance town of Úbeda, an unusual trio of landscapes. Late spring and autumn are the most comfortable seasons, with clear air and gentle temperatures. Bring layers, since mountain mornings can be cold even in May.
t.cavidad ii@38.2,-2.2:
Most of the water that comes out of the taps of Murcia and Alicante begins life high in the hills around Nerpio. The Taibilla river rises in the Sierra de Segura and flows through the valley here, and a network of canals and reservoirs named after it carries drinking water hundreds of kilometres to the dry south-east coast. That might sound a dull thing to dwell on, but it is part of why the valley is so green: pine, juniper and holm oak on the slopes, poplar and willow along the river, and in the valley floor small plots of vegetables and fruit trees watered by old irrigation channels.

Cavidad II is one of the rock shelters of the Nerpio area, about eight kilometres from the village. The sandstone and limestone cliffs of the district are pocked with overhangs, and in a number of them prehistoric people left paintings, which are part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998. I cannot tell you what this one shows, and I would rather say so than guess. As a general rule these sites are fragile, and visits are best arranged through the local rock-art interpretation facilities, which can also tell you which shelters can be visited and how to behave around them.

The riding around Nerpio is gentle mountain riding, not alpine. Roads follow the river, climb to small passes through pinewoods and open out onto rolling plateaux with long views. The curves are comfortable, the surface is sometimes broken at the edges, and there are very few other vehicles, apart from the occasional tractor or flock of sheep. A cold wind can blow across the high ground, even on bright days, so keep a layer in the pannier.

Nerpio itself has about sixteen hundred people and a handful of bars, shops and guesthouses, but fuel is better planned at Yeste, a larger town some twenty-seven kilometres away. Trout from the river and lamb from the hills are the local pride, and in the autumn mushrooms appear on menus. If you are lucky enough to be here on a still evening, the sound of the river and the smell of wood smoke make a good argument for staying the night.

Spring has the best water in the river and the freshest green, and autumn the best colours.
t.cavidad iii@38.2,-2.2:
There is a particular quiet in the high country of south-west Albacete that is hard to describe to anyone who has only ridden the coast or the motorways. Nerpio sits more than a thousand metres up on a rolling plateau, and the land around it is pine forest, scrub and rock, with long views to ridges that fade blue in the distance. At night the sky, free of city light, is dense with stars. Cavidad III, one of the Nerpio rock shelters, lies about eight kilometres from the village in this empty, open country.

As in other shelters in the area, the cliff here holds prehistoric paintings from the Mediterranean Basin rock art tradition, which UNESCO listed in 1998. I do not know what this particular cavity contains, so I will not pretend to, but I can say that the paintings of this region are usually small, red or dark and sheltered under overhangs, which is why they have survived thousands of years. Cavities like this one were chosen by people who lived on the move, hunting and herding, and it is easy to imagine them looking out over this valley from the same ledge.

For a rider the main thing to know is that weather up here is serious. Winters are cold, with snow and ice on the road from December to March, and even in spring and autumn the mornings can start near freezing and warm quickly. Summers are hot but the altitude keeps nights cool. The roads are quiet and the surface mixed, some good, some broken at the edges, and the bends are open and easy to read. A rockfall or a flock of sheep can appear around any corner, so ride within sight.

Nerpio has the basics, with some small shops and bars, but for fuel and a wider choice of food, Yeste is the nearest town of any size, with about thirty-five hundred people. The region's cooking is a hearty shepherd's tradition, with roasted lamb, stews with wild herbs and migas, fried crumbs with garlic and peppers, and the bread is good. Honey and cheese from the sierra make a fine picnic.

Go in late spring or early autumn and start early, so you are on the road when the light is low and golden.
t.barranc de beniali abric v@38.8,-0.2:
Beniali is another of the little hamlets of the Vall de Gallinera, tucked into the folds of the Alicante mountains between Villalonga and the head of the valley. The name looks Arabic and is, as with many place names here: the Beni- prefix means sons of, and recalls the clans who farmed these valleys during the centuries of Muslim rule. That legacy runs through the valley in the terraces cut out of the hillside, the irrigation channels, and the old way of growing fruit and almonds on thin soil.

The barranc, or ravine, gives its name to this stop. Abric V is one of several rock shelters in the gorge that contain prehistoric paintings, part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998. I cannot say what this shelter shows. The tradition here, as elsewhere in eastern Spain, is of small, red figures painted under overhangs, and in some places the shelter walls have been fenced to protect the paintings from touching and weather, so read the signs and keep to the paths. A local guide or the valley's tourist office can give far better detail than I can.

The valley's cherry blossom is its best-known spectacle, normally in late February or March, when the slopes turn white for a couple of weeks and the roads fill with visitors on weekends. In summer, the heat in the barrancs can be fierce, with the smell of pine and dry thyme, and autumn brings a softer light with wood smoke from the villages. Winter is mild, but it can be damp.

The road through the valley is narrow and winding, with many tight bends and some steep gradients, and it demands attention more than speed. The surface is mostly sound, and traffic is light except at blossom time. Villalonga, about five kilometres from the shelter, is a town of nearly four thousand people with fuel and places to eat, and it is a sensible base. Adsubia and Vall d'Ebo are tiny, and services there are limited, so carry water and a little food.

The ride continues to the Abric de Gontrán and, on another day, to Pinós, so it offers a pleasant spread of small mountain roads. Try the local rice dishes baked in the oven, or a sweet orange from the valley's groves if the season is right.
t.alhambra@37.2,-3.6:
The Alhambra is a red fortress on a hill, and inside its walls is the most delicate architecture in Europe. The Nasrid rulers of Granada, the last Muslim dynasty in Spain, built and rebuilt it from the thirteenth century, and in the fourteenth century they made it a palace city, with courtyards, fountains and rooms covered in carved plaster and glazed tile, all lit by the sun reflecting from water. The Court of the Lions, with its twelve stone lions holding up a fountain, and the Hall of the Ambassadors with its wooden dome are the most famous, though many visitors say they remember the small, quiet courtyards best.

The story ends in 1492, when Boabdil, the last Nasrid sultan, handed Granada to the Catholic monarchs, who made the city a Christian one. The Emperor Charles V later built a Renaissance palace inside the walls, a round courtyard inside a square block, which sits oddly against the Moorish rooms but has its own dignity. In the nineteenth century the American writer Washington Irving lived here for a few months and wrote his Tales of the Alhambra, and so helped to bring it back into fashion.

Granada lies at the foot of the Sierra Nevada, whose snow-capped ridge, with Mulhacén at nearly 3,500 metres the highest peak on mainland Spain, rises behind the city. In winter you can ski in the morning and walk in the Alhambra gardens in the afternoon, which is a luxury few cities offer. The ride from Granada north to Baeza crosses olive country, with mountains rising on the right and long, gentle bends.

The practical side needs thought. Tickets for the Nasrid palaces are timed and sell out well in advance, so book before you travel, and bring identification. The city has a low-emission zone and a complicated one-way system, so use a car park near the Alhambra hill or leave the bike on the edge of the centre. The streets around the Albaicín, the old Moorish quarter, are narrow, steep and cobbled.

Granada is a city of nearly a quarter of a million, so there are petrol stations and restaurants everywhere. The bars still serve a free tapa with each drink, a tradition that makes an evening cheap and generous.

Visit in spring or autumn, when the gardens are lovely and the heat is bearable.
t.cavidad i@38.2,-2.2:
The Nerpio area has been lived in, in one way or another, for a very long time, and the people who live there now seem to know it. Cavidad I, one of the shelters that archaeologists numbered in this district, lies about eight kilometres from the village of Nerpio, up on the plateau where the pines give way to farmland. The tradition of keeping sheep and goats on these hills is old, and the tracks that the flocks use to move between summer and winter pasture have shaped the paths you will find.

The shelters of the Nerpio region are among the more numerous in the Albacete province, and they belong to the Mediterranean Basin rock art tradition listed by UNESCO in 1998. As with the other sites in the area, I cannot say what is painted in this cavity, and I would not want to mislead you with a guess. The paintings, in general, are small and in red or black, and they are protected from the weather only by the overhang, so a few seasons of vandalism or careless touching can do lasting damage. t.fuensanta iii@38.2,-2.1:

t.caliphate city of medina azahara@37.9,-4:
In the middle of the tenth century, Abd al-Rahman III, the first Caliph of Córdoba, decided that the capital needed a palace city, and he built it a few kilometres to the west, on the lower slopes of the Sierra Morena. In the civil war that followed the collapse of the caliphate around 1010, the city was sacked and abandoned, and the stone was carried away for other buildings in Córdoba and Seville. The site lay forgotten under fields until excavations began in the early twentieth century, and work continues. The Salón Rico, the great reception hall, has been restored with its rich carved plaster, and its horseshoe arches and floral patterns show the height of caliphal art. t.zona 3@38.1,-2.4:

Córdoba was once the biggest city in Europe, or so people say, and it is easy to believe when you stand inside the Mezquita. The great mosque was begun in 785 by Abd al-Rahman I, on the site of a Visigothic church, and it grew over two centuries until it held a forest of columns, hundreds of them, in red-and-white striped arches that seem to run on forever. t.canaica del calar lii@38.2,-2.2:

t.cova alta abric iii@38.8,-0.2:
The pin sits in the folded limestone country behind the Costa Blanca, in the Marina Alta, a short ride from Castell de Castells, which has fewer than five hundred inhabitants and a church that looks too large for it. t.the menga dolmen and the viera dolmen@37:
Antequera sits in the middle of Andalusia like a coin in a pocket, and the two great dolmens stand on its northern edge, barely more than a kilometre from the centre. Menga and Viera were built more than five thousand years ago by farming people who dragged enormous blocks of stone into place, and Menga is one of the biggest megalithic chambers in Europe, with a roof of slabs that weigh many tonnes each. You walk into a long corridor of stone, with a mound of earth above, and the scale of it hits you before any explanation does.

What makes Menga strange is its orientation. Most such tombs face the sunrise, but Menga points at a limestone mountain called the Peña de los Enamorados, a rock whose outline looks like the face of a sleeping man in profile. People have told a legend about two lovers from rival faiths for centuries, but the builders, who could not have heard it, were already looking at that same shape. Viera, a few steps away, is straighter and lined up on the rising sun at the equinoxes. In 2016 the dolmens, together with the nearby El Romeral tholos and the mountains of the Peña and El Torcal, were listed by UNESCO as a single site.

It is a gentle landscape after the mountains around Ronda, with wide bends, long straights and a very open sky. The wind can be strong on the plain, and in July and August you will be riding in heat that begins at ten in the morning. Spring and autumn are the right seasons, with green wheat in March and low evening light in October.

The town is a proper stop. With more than forty thousand people, it has several petrol stations and plenty of cafés, and the local dishes are worth the time: the dense bread called mollete for breakfast, the thick cold tomato and cod soup called porra antequerana for lunch, and bienmesabe, a cake of almonds and sweet cream that is probably best saved for the afternoon. Parking beside the dolmens is easy for a bike. Visits are managed by the site, so check ahead whether a timed slot is needed, and plan on about an hour.
t.antequera dolmens site@37.0,-4.5:
A visitor's centre, some car parks, a long low mound and a view across a plain of wheat: the Antequera dolmens site does not look like much from the approach road, and then you step inside Menga and your sense of proportion rearranges itself. This stop is the formal gateway to the complex, a mile or so from the old town, and from here you can see the shape of the landscape that the prehistoric builders chose, with the strange rocky mountain called the Peña de los Enamorados rising to the northeast.

The first thing to know is how old it all is. Menga, Viera and the tholos of El Romeral were put up in the Neolithic and Copper Age, which is to say well before Stonehenge reached its final form and long before Rome. Menga's capstones, each of enormous weight, were brought from a quarry some distance away and set on huge uprights, and a deep shaft inside the chamber has never been fully explained. El Romeral, a couple of kilometres off, is different again: a corbelled chamber of small stones, like a beehive, with a second tiny room at the back.

Riding here is easy but not boring. From the Ronda side you drop out of the sierra onto the high plain of the Antequera depression, a crossroads where the main routes between Málaga, Granada, Córdoba and Seville have met for two thousand years. Roads are straight and fast in the valley, with limestone ridges standing up on the horizon, and the El Torcal range to the south, with its stacked rock towers, is worth a detour in good weather. Antequera is a big enough town, with more than forty thousand people, to have all the fuel, food and car-parking you could want. Try a late breakfast with the local mollete bread, olive oil and tomato, and if you have time walk up to the Moorish fortress, which looks over a cluster of churches and baroque towers. Take water to the site in summer, because there is little shade between the entrance and the chambers, and look into a ticket slot for the day before you arrive.
t.canaica del calar li@38.2,-2.2:

t.barranc de beniali abric iv@38.8,-0.2:
Between the villages of Vall d'Ebo and Adsubia the land buckles into narrow gorges, and Barranc de Beniali takes its name from a village a short way to the north, Benialí, which gives its name to the valley that cuts through the hills there. A string of small villages lines the road. The Moors lived here until the early seventeenth century, when the Spanish crown expelled the Moriscos, as the Muslims who had converted were called, and whole valleys here were suddenly emptied. Settlers from elsewhere were brought in to take over the fields and the terraces.

In summer it is hot, in winter it is gentle, and in autumn the air has the smell of damp earth and cut almond branches. Fuel is not available in the hills. Villalonga, close by, has around four thousand people and probably offers a pump and a baker, but for dependable fuel and a proper lunch you should head for Pego, nine kilometres away, a town of eleven thousand at the foot of the mountains and next to a huge wetland full of rice paddies and waterbirds. Carry water and wear walking shoes if you plan to climb to the shelter, because the slopes are stony.
t.barranc de la cova jeroni abric i@38.8,-:
Few countries have as many painted rock shelters per square kilometre as eastern Spain, and the stretch between Tàrbena, Vall d'Ebo and Pego is one of its richest zones. Rain falls rarely but hard, and the ravines fill and empty in a few hours. t.mingarnao ii@38.2,-2.3:
Nerpio is a high village in the far southwest of Albacete province, about eleven hundred metres above sea level, and Mingarnao is one of the names scattered across the countryside around it. The pin lies three kilometres out, in the folded limestone of the Sierra de Taibilla and the Segura headwaters. The shelter, Mingarnao II, is one of dozens in the Nerpio area that make up a notable concentration of rock paintings. Several have been found here, and some show Levantine figures and others show later schematic signs, a mixture that makes the area unusual.

Nerpio feels remote, because it is. The road from Letur and Moratalla climbs for a long time through pine forest, with passes at around a thousand metres and not much traffic, and the surface changes with the weather: in winter the shady corners are slick with frost, and in spring meltwater washes grit across the lanes. The scenery is huge and empty, with mountains in layers going off to the east. Few places in Spain offer such a calm road with so little to disturb you but an occasional farm truck.

The altitude is the quiet character of the place. Cold winters, short springs and high-summer evenings that call for a jumper make Nerpio an unusual place for the south of Spain. Apple, cherry and almond trees grow on the terraces, and people here are used to making the most of a short season. Wild boar, deer and golden eagles live in the forests, and at dusk the sky over the high plateau is full of swifts and kites.

Nerpio itself has about sixteen hundred people, so you can probably find a bar for coffee and a simple lunch, but planning for fuel is another matter. The reliable options are Yeste, twenty-two kilometres to the north, a town of about three and a half thousand, or Huéscar in Granada province, further south and east. Fill the tank before climbing up from either side, carry water, and keep in mind that mobile signal is patchy in the folded country between the villages.
t.abrigo de la fuente de montanoz ii@38.1,:
Montañoz may sound like a village, but as a place name it belongs to a spring and a stretch of hillside south of Nerpio, up where the Segura headwaters break the land into steep slopes. The shelter called Abrigo de la Fuente de Montañoz II is one of many in the district, ten kilometres from Nerpio, and it belongs to the extraordinary group of painted overhangs that make this part of Albacete one of the most important rock art regions in Spain. Some of the paintings around here are in a distinctive style, with stylised human figures, and the UNESCO listing of 1998 covers several.

The very name of the shelter includes a fountain, and that reminds you why people were here. In dry country, a spring is a magnet for animals and so for hunters, and a rock overhang next to a spring is the ideal place for a camp. Take that thought with you when you look at the slope: the shelters are not isolated curiosities but part of a landscape people used for thousands of years, a mosaic of water, shade and game.

The ride from Nerpio is a hill road of the unfussy sort. Corners are broad and the gradient is moderate, the surface is mostly intact, and you pass through pine woods, then bare ridge, then into a hollow of cultivated fields with an old farmhouse or two. Wind comes through the passes, particularly in March, and the temperature can fall five or six degrees in the shade. Winter snow is fairly common, so choose between late spring and early autumn.

You are a long way from large towns here, and the facts should shape your plan. Yeste is almost thirty kilometres away and Segura de la Sierra, a hill village with an Arab castle and a famously photogenic setting, is about the same. The big town in the neighbourhood is Huéscar, thirty-six kilometres off, which has fuel and shops. Start with a full tank, carry water and something to eat, and treat the paintings with respect: no touching and no chalk.
t.barranc de bil la abric ii@38.7,-0.2:
Only two kilometres from the village of Castell de Castells, the Barranc de Bil.la runs through a limestone landscape that has been farmed in terraces for centuries and left to scrub in recent decades. Abric II is the second shelter in the series catalogued along the ravine, and sits close enough to the village that you can plan a morning walk from the square without ever going near a map. Castell de Castells itself is a village of fewer than five hundred people in the Marina Alta, on the northern slopes of the Serrella, and it is better known to the archaeologists than to the tourists because of the Pla de Petracos, a famous painted site close by.

The paintings of the region represent two traditions. Levantine art consists of small red figures, deer, bulls and archers, made by hunters around six or eight thousand years ago, and schematic art, which is more abstract and appears later. The UNESCO listing covers both. The ride up from the coast is among the best excuses to see them, because the road leaves the tourist belt behind in the first twenty minutes. Villages of white houses with blue shutters give way to hillsides of cherry and almond trees, then to open limestone ridges.

The roads here are twisting and narrow, graded to suit tractors more than touring bikes, and they crawl in a series of hairpins up the mountainside. They are well maintained, though, and there are few cars. Spring is the loveliest time, when the almond blossom has gone and the cherry trees of the neighbouring Vall de Gallinera flower in white sheets. Summer is hot and dry; autumn brings the first heavy rain, which sometimes washes stones onto the road.

The nearest place for petrol and a big supermarket is Pego, fourteen kilometres away on the plain, where the town sits beside a wetland of reeds and rice fields. Keep water in your bag for the walk, and remember that the rock shelters are fragile and should be admired from a distance.
t.barranc de la fita abric ii@38.7,-0.2:
Fita is the Valencian word for a boundary stone, and many a ravine in this part of Alicante province bears the name because the line between two villages once ran along it. The Barranc de la Fita lies less than three kilometres from Castell de Castells, and Abric II is one of three catalogued shelters along it. They belong to the same family of rock paintings as the nearby Pla de Petracos, one of the most significant sites in the region, and share in the UNESCO designation of 1998. Whether this one holds a recognisable painting I cannot say, and it is not what you come for by motorbike.

What you come for is the road to Castell de Castells, which is the kind of road that makes a long detour seem a good idea. It leaves the Guadalest valley, with its toy-like castle and its turquoise reservoir, and crosses high bare country to a village huddled around its church. Along the way the road dips into a deep gorge, then rises in a series of hairpins, with limestone ridges to either side and the sea a blue strip far to the east. The Serrella range, about 1,300 metres at its highest, gives you a feeling of real mountains only a short drive from the beaches.

The Moriscos, the converted Muslims who made up most of the population here until their expulsion in 1609, built the terraces and irrigation channels that still shape the valley. Their descendants did not return, and the villages were repopulated by settlers from other parts of the kingdom, which explains the odd mix of Valencian dialect and Arabic names. It is the sort of history that you only grasp slowly, by looking at the walls and the way the water is led across the slope.

Services are modest. Bring water and sturdy shoes. In the middle of summer the heat on the south-facing slopes can be fierce, and the best time to walk is early in the morning.
t.molino de capel il@38.2,-2.0:
Sitting in the high interior of Albacete, the Molino de Capel is a mill name, and the shelter marked Molino de Capel II lies in the countryside near the Río Segura, fourteen kilometres from Moratalla across the border in Murcia. Rivers are the vital organs of this dry land. The Segura, which rises in the Sierra de Segura in Jaén and runs over four hundred kilometres to the Mediterranean at Guardamar, is thin and green at its edges and brown and tired by the end of its course, but here in the headwaters it is still lively.

The painted shelters of Moratalla and its surroundings are some of the best-known in Spain. The area has an unusual density of Levantine art, with scenes of hunting and gathering, and the whole group is part of the Mediterranean rock art that UNESCO recognised in 1998. A few of the Moratalla shelters have viewing platforms and a visitor centre in the town. Molino de Capel II is not one of the famous ones, as far as I know, and the paintings there, if any are visible, are for people with time and good boots.

Riding here has a quiet, northern character, though the sun is southern. The roads follow the river valley, with gentle bends and long views over irrigated orchards, and on the heights above you meet pine forest and rough grazing land. Traffic is very light. In summer, early morning is wise, because the temperature in the valley can pass forty degrees, while in winter the ridges are sometimes dusted with snow and the road shadows hold ice well into the day.

Moratalla is the town to aim for. It has about eight and a half thousand people, a castle on a conical hill and a reputation for a Holy Week festival in which hundreds of drummers play through the night. You will find fuel, supermarkets and several simple restaurants serving rice and local lamb, and the old streets are good for a wander before you set off again. Take water and a map, because mobile reception drops out in the narrow valleys and the tracks to the shelters are not marked on most road atlases.
t.abrigo del cerro de barbaton@38.3,-2.1:
Barbatón is a hill, and the Cerro de Barbatón a rounded bump of limestone that rises above the farmland between Letur and Socovos, in the south of Albacete. The shelter at its foot, catalogued as the Abrigo del Cerro de Barbatón, is twelve kilometres from Letur and fourteen from Socovos, which tells you right away that this is rural country with long distances between villages. The paintings in the region belong to the Levantine rock art that UNESCO recognised in 1998, and they include some of the finest and best preserved in Spain.

Letur is the place to spend an hour. It is a small town of about twelve hundred people spread along a ridge above the Río Mundo, and its centre is a maze of narrow lanes lined with whitewashed houses with wooden balconies, which keep the layout that they had when the town was Moorish. The Mundo, one of the Segura's main tributaries, rises in a spring cave in the Sierra de Alcaraz and cuts a rugged valley that is a delight to ride beside. You can tell what a Moorish origin means when you look at the details: narrow alleys that shade each other, little squares where the wind does not reach.

The roads in this corner of the Sierra are of the unhurried sort. They twist along the valleys, climb over low passes, and cross the river on narrow bridges, and at every turn you see farmland in small plots, with olives, almonds and a little irrigated vegetable ground. Sheep and goats graze on the hillsides, and shepherds still use some of the old tracks. Spring and autumn are the kindest seasons. The summer heat is fierce, and winter can bring frost to the shaded bends.

Neither Letur nor Socovos is large, and a dependable stop for fuel is Moratalla, twenty-one kilometres from the pin, a town of about eight and a half thousand with several garages and shops. Letur has a bar or two and some simple food, usually lamb or migas, a dish of fried breadcrumbs that is a staple across inland Spain. Take enough water for a walk, and be careful on the loose gravel of the farm tracks.
t.cueva del reloj@37.8,-3.1:
A cave with a clock in its name: nobody can tell you for certain why, but El Reloj, the shelter above the Quesada countryside in the province of Jaén, has been given that name since long before the archaeologists arrived. It lies four kilometres from the town of Quesada, on the western edge of the Sierra de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas, Spain's largest protected area. The area is thick with painted shelters, among them Cueva del Reloj, Las Covachicas and La Alamedilla, which appear together on the route and which belong to the rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998.

Jaén is olive country in a way that is hard to imagine until you see it. In every direction the slopes are covered with regular rows of trees, a grey-green carpet that stretches to the horizon, and the province produces more oil than most countries. Quesada, a town of about six thousand people, is also known as the birthplace of the painter Rafael Zabaleta, who painted the working people of the olive lands in a strong, simple style, and whose museum is in the town.

The ride towards Cazorla is a pleasure. The road from Úbeda climbs gradually through olive groves, then turns into the foothills, where pine takes over and the bends tighten. Beyond Quesada, the road toward Huesa and Hinojares crosses wide open rolling country with little traffic. In summer the temperature is brutal, regularly above forty degrees in the afternoon, and in winter the mountain roads can be icy. Spring and autumn are the right times, when the oil harvest starts in November and the roads fill with tractors and trailers.

Quesada is large enough to have fuel stations, shops and bars, and Huesa, a few kilometres away, is a smaller town of about two and a half thousand. Cazorla, thirty kilometres or so to the east, is the gateway to the natural park, with its narrow streets and Renaissance fountain. For the shelter itself you need good shoes and water, and a willingness to follow a local walker if you can find one.
t.concejal iii@38.1,-2.4:
Concejal is the sort of name that makes you wonder who the councillor was, and nobody now seems to know. The shelter called Concejal III is seven kilometres from Nerpio, on the high, scrubby plateau of the Sierra del Segura, in a district that has produced one of the largest collections of rock paintings in the whole Iberian Peninsula. The numbering tells you there are several at the same location, and the UNESCO listing of 1998 covers the Nerpio group, whose figures include goats, archers and curious, stylised human forms.

What strikes you about the Nerpio basin is its height. At about eleven hundred metres it is cooler and drier than the coast, and the vegetation is closer to Castile than to Andalusia: junipers, holm oaks, thorny scrub and, in the damp bottoms, poplars along the streams. In winter the plateau is cold, and in summer the evening air is fresh enough to wear a jacket. The high ground is part of the headwaters of the Segura, and many small rivers rise within a few kilometres of the village.

On the bike, your task is to enjoy the emptiness. The roads from Nerpio to Yeste and to Huéscar are narrow and bendy, with few villages in between and no particular hurry, and in autumn the oaks turn bronze and the light through them is lovely. Livestock, tractors and the odd hunter's pickup are the main traffic. The weather can change fast, and a clear morning can end with a thunderstorm at four in the afternoon. Check the forecast, particularly in spring.

Nerpio has some sixteen hundred inhabitants and a few bars where you can have a coffee or a plate of lamb, but treat fuel as a planning issue. The nearest large town is Huéscar, thirty-nine kilometres away, in the province of Granada, and Yeste to the north is about twenty-six. If you walk to the shelter, take water and avoid the hottest hours, and stay on the paths.
t.zona 9@38.1,-2.4:
Zona 9 is not a place name at all, just a number, and that is a clue to how much rock art there is around Nerpio. Archaeologists divided the district's cliffs and gullies into numbered zones to keep track of them, and the nine or so zones listed on these routes cluster about seven kilometres from the village, along a dry valley in the Sierra del Segura. The shelters there belong to the group UNESCO listed in 1998 as the rock art of the Mediterranean basin on the Iberian Peninsula. If you do not read Spanish the label will tell you nothing, so the landscape has to do the talking.

It does so quietly. The valley floor is a mix of cereal fields and fallow, with juniper and holm oak on the slopes, and cliffs of pale limestone rise above them in broken bands. Water is scarce in summer and the sky is huge. At night, with so little light pollution, the stars are some of the best in southern Spain, and the high plateau is increasingly used by amateur astronomers. A rider who stays in Nerpio for the night will find the sky worth ten minutes outside the front door.

The roads that lead here are slow and rewarding. From Yeste you climb the plateau on a road that shuffles through pine forest and past farmland, with frequent but not severe bends, and there is a run of about twenty kilometres where you may not meet another vehicle. The surface is generally fine but loose gravel is common at the edges. Temperatures vary: below freezing on winter mornings, thirty-five in July, and sharp winds in March and April.

Services need planning. Nerpio has a few bars and shops but the nearest big town is Huéscar, thirty-eight kilometres from the pin, with proper fuel, a market and a good selection of food. If you are riding from the north, Yeste is closer to twenty-seven. Take water, a hat and a spare layer, and do not rely on your phone for navigation once you leave the village.
t.zona 6@38.1,-2.4:
Zona 6 sits seven kilometres from Nerpio, in a stretch of country where the numbers of the rock art catalogue replace the poetry of place names. It is part of the group of shelters in the Nerpio basin, the territory of the upper Taibilla river, and the whole group falls inside the UNESCO listing of the Mediterranean rock art of the Iberian Peninsula. The routes that visit it also take in the town of Úbeda, which is a long way off in the province of Jaén and a very different sort of heritage site.

Úbeda and Baeza, a pair of Renaissance towns in the olive country, are on the UNESCO list in their own right, and a day that takes in both paintings and palaces suits anyone who likes to see how human culture has been written on the land at different scales. The contrast is the interesting part. In Nerpio the evidence is a few brown strokes of pigment on a rock wall, made by people about whom we know nothing but their art. In Úbeda it is carved stone, coats of arms and an ostentation of wealth from the sixteenth century. Both are the work of people who wanted to leave a mark.

Riding between the two is a long day, with the Sierra de Segura in the middle. Roads in the Sierra are good, with many bends and few cars, and the landscape rises in pine-clad folds above the Guadalquivir's upper valley. Weather deserves respect. Snow closes some roads in January and February, and in summer you want to be on the move by eight in the morning.

For fuel and supplies go to Huéscar, thirty-eight kilometres away, or to Yeste, a smaller town almost twenty-seven kilometres in the opposite direction. Nerpio has bars and a few shops, and a lunch of local lamb or gazpacho manchego, a stew in spite of its name, is a good end to a morning. Carry water and tell someone where you are going if you plan a walk to the shelter.
t.abrigo de jesus galdon@39.2,-0.8:
Bicorp is a village of about six hundred people in the interior of Valencia province, and it is famous among archaeologists for the Cueva de la Araña, whose painting of a person climbing a rope to reach a wild bees' nest is one of the best-known images of Levantine art. The shelter marked Abrigo de Jesús Galdón is a few kilometres from Bicorp, in the same dry, rugged country of limestone ridges and pine, and it belongs to the same tradition. The honey-hunting scene is also part of the reason that this rock art is protected by UNESCO, which listed it in 1998.

The country around Bicorp is little visited and strangely empty. It sits between the Júcar and the Cabriel rivers, in a district of reservoirs, canyons and cork oaks, and its villages are spaced a long way apart. Quesa, six kilometres away, and Millares, farther on, are both small, and the road that connects them winds along valleys of almond and olive. The whole district has the feel of an area that people left, and you meet more goats than cars.

Roads here are narrow, curving and not always well marked. Some of the best are the minor ones that follow the rivers, with sections of fresh asphalt alternating with old patched surface, and you should be ready for gravel on the bends. In spring the hills are green, in summer they are brown and hot, and in autumn mushroom hunters appear in the pine woods. The sun is intense, and the rock walls hold the heat until after dark.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Bicorp, Quesa and Millares are tiny, and the nearest big town is Carlet, twenty-two kilometres off towards the plain, in the middle of the Ribera orange country. Fill the tank before you start and carry water, because the shelters are in dry country with no shade. Bicorp has a few bars, and a plate of rice with rabbit and snails, a local classic, is a satisfying way to end a day on the road.
t.barranco de las colochas abrigo ii@39.6,:
The Turia river runs from the Teruel highlands down to Valencia, and between Chulilla and Gestalgar it passes through a country of cliffs, pines and small orchards that feels a world away from the city at its mouth. The Barranco de las Colochas is a side ravine on this stretch, about three kilometres from Gestalgar, and the shelter listed as Abrigo II is one of the painted rocks in the series along it. They belong to the Levantine art listed by UNESCO in 1998, and the Turia valley is among the areas where it was first noticed.

The gorge at Chulilla, a little way upstream, is the place most visitors come for. Its sheer walls of limestone, the clear green pools called the Charco Azul and the suspension bridge across the canyon draw climbers from across Europe, and in winter, when the Valencian plain is damp and grey, the cliffs sit in sunshine. Chulilla is a few kilometres from here, topped by a ruined castle. The valley has a mild climate, with orange and olive groves on the lower slopes and pine woods above, and spring brings a delicate smell of orange blossom.

For a motorcyclist the valley is a short escape from Valencia. The CV-35 from the city runs up along the Turia through Riba-roja, Benaguasil and Casinos, with fast, easy bends at first and then, past Gestalgar, increasingly narrow and twisting stretches. Cyclists and weekend riders from the city use it heavily on Sundays, so the best moments are weekdays and early mornings. Take care in the shaded bends in winter, when damp and a little frost can combine on the road surface.

Gestalgar itself has about seven hundred people, a bar or two and a handful of places to eat, and for fuel the nearest large town is Chiva, eighteen kilometres off. Chiva is near the Ricardo Tormo circuit at Cheste, where the MotoGP season traditionally ends, and its pumps are well used to motorcyclists. Bring water for any walk, because the slopes are stony and shade is rare.
t.cortijo de sorbas ii@38.3,-2.1:
The cortijo is a farmhouse of the south, and the one that gives this shelter its name is probably nothing now but a few walls and a threshing floor on a hillside. The Cortijo de Sorbas II lies twelve kilometres from Letur and fourteen from Socovos, in the dry limestone country on the borders of Albacete and Murcia, where the Segura and its tributaries cut deep valleys. The painted shelters here, part of the Mediterranean rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998, are spread in the folds of the hills, and their exact locations are often kept quiet to protect them.

Sorbas is another name that stands out, because the better-known Sorbas is in Almería, with its gypsum karst and its caves. The Albacete one is a modest farm name, and it points to the way families moved across the south of Spain in search of land. What links them is the terrain. The countryside is limestone, and limestone means caves and overhangs, and where there are overhangs, people left their mark.

The riding between Letur and Socovos is pastoral. A narrow road follows a stream through a gorge, comes out on a high plateau of cereal fields and juniper, and then drops again to a village with a Moorish tower. Surfaces are patchy and you should expect the occasional farm vehicle, but there is almost no through traffic, and on a Tuesday in May you may feel you own the road. The seasons are sharp: pale yellow stubble in July, cold nights in October and the first snow on the ridges in December.

Fuel is a long way off. Moratalla, twenty-one kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town, with petrol stations and a few restaurants, and Socovos, a village of nearly two thousand, may have a pump but is not worth relying on. If you stop in Socovos for lunch, expect plain, good country cooking. Carry water, because most of the springs on the map are dry in summer.
t.zona 4@38.1,-2.4:
The thing about Zona 4 is that it sounds like a military sector, and in some ways it is, because it is a piece of ground that archaeologists have mapped and numbered for the sake of order. It lies about seven kilometres from Nerpio, in the same dry valley as its neighbours Zona 5, 6, 8 and 9, in the Sierra del Segura. The paintings of the area belong to the Levantine tradition protected by UNESCO since 1998, and they are known for their variety, with hunting scenes, animals and human figures that appear to dance.

The ride that includes Zona 4 also visits Úbeda, and the pairing is worth thinking about on the road. Úbeda is a Renaissance town in the olive plains of Jaén, an hour or more to the south-west, built in the sixteenth century by a small group of rich families who commissioned architects from Italy and Spain. It is a showcase of palaces, churches and plazas in golden stone. The painters of Nerpio worked on a more modest scale, but they, too, had a sense of composition.

The best of the ride is the stretch between Nerpio and Yeste, a road through high pine forest that is unusually quiet. The bends are medium and the gradients modest, and the scenery reminds you of the Alps in miniature, with long slopes of dark trees and open meadows. Wildlife is plentiful, with Spanish ibex on the crags, and if you stop for a moment in the early morning you may see deer at the forest edge. Cold winds can sweep across the plateau in the afternoon, so keep a windproof layer in the pannier.

For fuel, Huéscar is the place, thirty-eight kilometres away, and Yeste is the alternative at twenty-seven. Nerpio has shops and bars of a basic sort, and a lunch of lamb and migas is likely to be hearty. Do not underestimate distances in this part of Spain, and bring water for any walk to the shelter.
t.cavidad vii@38.2,-2.2:
Nerpio's numbered Cavidades are a series of rock cavities scattered over the hills east of the village, and Cavidad VII lies seven or eight kilometres away from it, on the borders of the Sierra del Segura. The paintings in the shelters of this district form one of the largest and most varied groups in Spain, with Levantine figures and later schematic marks, and they fall within the UNESCO listing of 1998. Cavidad VII is on a route with the Cueva de la Plata and the Cueva del Peliciego, both of which are better known.

What do people see in this landscape? To a modern eye it is bleak, a high plateau of rock, juniper and thin pasture. To a prehistoric hunter it was a larder: deer, ibex, wild boar, rabbits and partridges, plus water in the springs and shelter in the overhangs. The animals that appear on the walls were the ones that mattered most to survival, and the people who painted them were closely observing the animals on which their lives depended.

The road to the shelter is the stuff of motorcycling daydreams, if your daydreams involve empty country. It climbs through pine forest on a surface that varies between smooth and rough, with bends that follow the contours and long straight stretches across the plateau. The altitude gives it a freshness in summer, but also winter ice. If the forecast is for snow, stay away. In spring the air has the scent of broom and wild thyme, and the sky is wide and blue.

Services are limited. Nerpio has a few shops and bars, and Yeste, twenty-three kilometres from the pin, is the nearest larger town, with fuel and food. Moratalla, twenty-nine kilometres off, is bigger still. Pack water and a spare layer, and plan the day so that you are back on a paved road by dusk, because the unlit tracks can be dangerous.
t.prado del tornero iii@38.1,-2.3:
Nerpio's village centre is only six hundred metres from this pin, so the shelter named Prado del Tornero III sits almost within earshot of its church bells. It is one of several in the Prado del Tornero group, with neighbours II and others in the same area, and it forms part of the exceptional collection of rock art around the village, covered by the UNESCO listing of 1998. For once the walk from bike to shelter is short, which is a kindness in this hard country.

There is a hidden thread that links this remote village to the coast. The Taibilla, the stream that rises in the mountains above Nerpio, has been dammed and piped since the early twentieth century to supply water to Murcia, Alicante and Cartagena, and a public body called the Mancomunidad de los Canales del Taibilla has run the system for decades. The cool snows of the high Sierra thus end up as tap water in towns on the hot Mediterranean plain. It is a good reminder that the sparsely settled interior carries the weight of the crowded coast.

The ride to Nerpio is the real event. Approaching from Yeste, the road crosses a high plateau of pine, juniper and dry meadow, then descends gently to a broad basin ringed by hills. The surface is decent and the bends are generous, which makes for a relaxed rhythm. The only sounds are the engine and the wind, and once in a while a lorry carrying timber. Cold is a factor from late October onward. Fresh snow is possible through March, and in the village you will see woodpiles stacked against many walls.

The village has about sixteen hundred inhabitants, so you can expect bars, a bakery and a basic shop, which makes it a useful base. Fuel is less certain, and the safer places are Yeste, twenty-four kilometres away, and Huéscar to the south-east. A good meal in Nerpio might include game stew, local lamb or a plate of the chickpea and spinach dishes that come out in Lent. Carry water, and use the village as your starting point for walking, because the shelters are best visited on foot.
t.cueva del clarillo@37.8,-3.1:
To understand this part of Jaén, you need to remember that it was a border. For two and a half centuries after the great Christian victory at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212, the frontier between Castile and the Muslim kingdom of Granada ran through the mountains to the south and east of here, and the towns of Quesada and Cazorla were fortified outposts. Castle towers still crown hills all over the province, and the old name for the area, Adelantamiento de Cazorla, tells you that it was ruled for a long time by the archbishops of Toledo as a military lordship.

The Cueva del Clarillo lies less than three kilometres from Quesada, in the dry limestone hills at the foot of the Sierra de Cazorla. Like its neighbours Las Covachicas and the shelters near Cerro de la Caldera, it carries prehistoric paintings, protected under the UNESCO listing of 1998, and the area is one of the southernmost for Levantine art. The idea that a frontier region should also hold some of the oldest human art is one of those coincidences of geography that make Spain such a rich country to travel in.

The roads are an unalloyed pleasure. From Úbeda and Baeza the A-315 climbs gently through olive plantations that fill every slope with grey-green order, and then the land begins to tilt upward and the first pines appear. Bends tighten as the road enters the foothills, and you can see Cazorla's cliff and castle from a distance. In winter, the high road over the sierra is sometimes closed by snow, and in July the temperature on the plain regularly passes forty degrees, so the best weeks are in spring and from mid-September.

Quesada, with about six thousand people, has fuel and a decent choice of bars and shops, and Cazorla, eleven kilometres away, is bigger and busier, with its cobbled streets, a Renaissance fountain and a castle above. In both you can eat well on a modest budget, with dishes based on olive oil, wild asparagus and game. Carry water for the walk to the shelter, and keep your helmet and jacket in the shade when you park.
t.el corral de silla abric li@39.8,-1.0:
A small group of villages in the Valencian interior goes by the name Los Serranos, and Tuéjar, Chelva and Alpuente are part of it. It is a country of mountain ridges, pine forest and river gorges, where the Turia and its tributaries have cut deep valleys, and where, because of its remoteness, many farms and hamlets have been abandoned. El Corral de Silla II is one of a series of painted shelters in the area, three kilometres from Tuéjar and about six from Chelva, and as with all the shelters on these routes it forms part of the Mediterranean rock art protected by UNESCO since 1998.

Chelva is worth the time. It is a village of about two thousand with a historic centre of narrow streets, a baroque church and the remains of Moorish buildings, and the stone is the colour of dry bread. Nearby, and a little way along the road to Alpuente, are the remains of a Roman aqueduct and a series of ravines with swimming holes. Alpuente has a striking Moorish heritage, because in the eleventh century it was the capital of a small independent kingdom, one of the many that arose after the break-up of the caliphate of Córdoba.

The riding here is a revelation for anyone who thinks of Valencia as flat. From Utiel, the capital of the Bobal grape country, the road climbs through vineyards and almond groves to the pine forests of the sierra, and then through a series of narrow curving valleys. There is little traffic, the surface is generally good and the scenery changes every few kilometres. Autumn is lovely, with the vine leaves turning red and gold, and the cold nights bring early frosts.

For fuel, Utiel, twenty-nine kilometres away, is the closest sizeable town, and the right place to fill up. Chelva has bars and a couple of restaurants where you can eat a plate of rice, a stew or grilled meat with a glass of local wine. The shelter itself needs a walk, and the slopes are loose and dry, so wear boots and bring water.
t.cueva colora@38.3,-2.1:
Letur is a village that photographs well, especially as you come in along the valley of the Río Mundo and see the cluster of white houses on its rock. The Cueva Colorá lies about twelve kilometres from it, in the dry hills toward Socovos and Férez, and it is one of a group of shelters that includes the Cueva del Gitano and the Cueva de la Plata, all of them within the area that UNESCO listed in 1998 as Mediterranean rock art.

The name Colorá means coloured, and it points to the reddish stain on the rock face, whether from iron oxide in the stone or from the paintings themselves. In this country red is the colour of everything: the soil, the clay roof tiles, the pigment on the shelters. Early painters used iron-rich ochre mixed with a binder, and in a few places it has survived for six thousand years or more, which is a better record than most modern paint.

For riders, the little roads of this corner of Albacete are an acquired taste. They are not spectacular in the way that the Alpine passes are, but they have a feeling of space and silence that is rare in Europe. A typical stretch rises over a low pass of pine, descends into a valley of olive and almond, crosses a stream on a narrow bridge, and climbs again. The tarmac is patched and occasionally rough, but traffic is almost absent, and you can ride at a gentle pace and stop wherever you like. The best months are April, May, September and October.

Fuel is a long way off. Letur has about twelve hundred people and a bar or two, Socovos and Férez are smaller or similar, and the nearest sizeable town is Moratalla, twenty-one kilometres away, which has pumps, shops and restaurants. Letur is a sensible place for a coffee and a slow walk through the lanes of the old Moorish quarter. Carry water for the shelter walk, since the paths are stony and exposed.
t.manolo vallejo@37.8,-3.0:
The upper valley of the Guadiana Menor lies on the south-eastern side of the Sierra de Cazorla, in a country of olive terraces and open pine, and the name Manolo Vallejo, a person's name, sits there in the list of shelters like a marker for a family farm. The shelter is about five kilometres from Huesa, a town of some two and a half thousand, and seven from Hinojares, and it belongs, like its neighbours, to the Levantine rock art of the Mediterranean arc, recognised by UNESCO in 1998. Its siblings on the route, Poyo Medio Cimbarra and Cerro de la Caldera, are in the same district.

You are on the doorstep of a very big park. The Sierra de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas is the largest protected area in Spain and the second largest in Europe, covering some two thousand square kilometres of mountains, forests and reservoirs. It is also the birthplace of the Guadalquivir, which rises from a spring high in the sierra and flows through Andalusia to the Atlantic at Sanlúcar de Barrameda. Thousands of visitors come in the summer to walk its gorges and watch for ibex, red deer and griffon vultures, and in October the stags' autumn roar is one of the great wildlife sounds of Spain.

The riding is outstanding, with some of the best roads in Andalusia in or near the park. The road through the sierra from Cazorla to the Tranco reservoir and on toward Segura de la Sierra is a bendy, climbing, scenic route, with forest to either side and views over the water. Closer to Huesa the land opens out, with gentle bends and long straights through olives. Summer is hot, winter can be cold with some snow, and the ideal months are May, June and the first half of October.

Fuel is at Quesada, eight kilometres away, or at Huesa, where there is a smaller choice of services, and Cazorla has more. All three have bars and restaurants where you can eat a hearty dish of mountain stew, ham or game. Bring water for walking, and respect the park rules if you head into the protected zones.
t.barranc de la fita abric i@38.7,-0.2:
Even in a dry year the Guadalest valley is surprisingly green, with fruit trees and water in the channels, and the road that climbs from Callosa d'en Sarrià up to the village of Guadalest is a classic of the Costa Blanca hinterland. A little to the west of it, in the Marina Alta, the Barranc de la Fita carries a series of painted shelters of which Abric I is the first, less than three kilometres from Castell de Castells. Its figures form part of the rock art of the Mediterranean arc of Spain, listed by UNESCO in 1998.

Water is the thread of the area. The Fonts de l'Algar, near Callosa, are a set of waterfalls and clear pools that make a good swim on a hot day, and the reservoir at Guadalest, an intense turquoise, supplies the coast. The old village of Guadalest itself stands on a rock crowned by a castle and a bell tower, and its small square is crowded with visitors from the beach resorts. Beyond it, the road toward Castell de Castells and Tàrbena is quieter, with olive and almond terraces and views of the sea far below.

You can make a fine loop of it. From Benidorm or Altea, follow the CV-70 inland to Guadalest, then take the narrow road over the Serrella foothills to Castell de Castells, and return by the Coll de Rates, a famous climb from the Tàrbena side, with long bends and a viewpoint over the Jalón valley. The surface is mostly good, and there are some stretches where the road has been widened. Cyclists are everywhere, so give them room.

Castell de Castells and Benimantell do not have fuel, so fill the tank in Callosa d'en Sarrià or in Pego, fifteen kilometres from the shelter. Local food is simple and good, with rice dishes, olive oil and a sweet wine made from muscatel grapes, and the villages along the road have small bars that open for lunch. Take water on the walk to the shelter, and look out for the lizards that bask on the rocks.
t.zona 5@38.1,-2.4:
Segura de la Sierra is the nearest big name to this stretch of the Sierra del Segura, and although it lies nearly thirty kilometres from the pin, it gives its name to a natural park of more than two thousand square kilometres that covers the mountains around Nerpio. Zona 5 lies seven kilometres from Nerpio, in the same dry valley as the other numbered zones, and belongs to the cluster of rock-art shelters listed by UNESCO in 1998. The paintings here are found at the foot of cliffs facing south, which catch the winter sun.

Segura de la Sierra itself is an extraordinary village, perched on a rock crowned by a castle that was held by the Order of Santiago in the Middle Ages. The Moors left a bathhouse, the Baños Árabes, below the village, and the Christians added a church and a town hall. The village has fewer than two thousand people, many of them elderly, but its streets are lively in summer when visitors come to see the castle and the views over a sea of olive trees stretching to the horizon.

Between Nerpio and Segura de la Sierra the country changes slowly, from the high, dry plateau of the Taibilla into the deeper forested valleys of the Segura headwaters. Roads are narrow but in good order, and the best section is the descent from the plateau into the olive lands, a succession of long, well-banked curves with a view that opens at every bend. In spring the hillsides are bright with broom, and in autumn the colours soften to gold and bronze.

Remember that fuel is scarce. Nerpio may have a pump but it is not something to rely on, and the safest source is Huéscar, thirty-eight kilometres away in Granada province. Yeste, almost twenty-eight kilometres off, has fuel too. A day in this country needs planning, because distances look short on the map and are long on the road. Take water, snacks and a warm layer, and tell someone your route.
t.abrigo de la ventana ii@38.2,-2.2:
A window in the rock gives the shelter its name, and the Abrigo de la Ventana II lies about twelve kilometres from Nerpio in the high country of the Sierra del Segura, where limestone cliffs are pierced by natural openings and hollows. It is the second of two shelters of that name, and it appears on a route with the Diosa Madre, the Mother Goddess, which is the title that archaeologists have given to a rock painting that they interpret as a female figure. The whole group belongs to the Mediterranean rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998.

The wildlife around here is worth the attention of any rider who looks at more than the road. The Sierra del Segura is among the best places in Spain to see Spanish ibex, a sturdy wild goat with sweeping horns, and in the early morning you may see them on the cliffs. Mouflon, introduced for hunting, live in some of the woods, and so do red and roe deer. Golden eagles, griffon vultures and the occasional bearded vulture are overhead, and the forests hold wildcats and genets that you will almost never see.

The riding is open, easy and fairly empty. Roads cross the plateau in long straights with gentle bends, with forest and meadow alternating, and drop at the edges into steep gorges. The surface can be rough in places, particularly after winter, and cattle sometimes graze on the verges. The cold is a factor from October to April, and the thaw can leave gravel on the road. In summer the air is dry and the sun strong, but the altitude keeps the nights cool.

Fuel is the issue to plan for. Nerpio is nearly twelve kilometres away and has limited services, and the sensible choices are Huéscar, 36 kilometres, or Moratalla, 25. In the village you can eat well on lamb, bean stew and migas. Always carry water, and leave the shelter untouched, because even small marks can damage the paint.
t.cova alta abric ii@38.8,-0.2:
On a clear day in this corner of Alicante you can see the long pale ridge of Aitana, the highest mountain in the province at about 1,558 metres, and the sea beyond it, which is a surprising combination for a country of rock shelters and mule tracks. Cova Alta II lies three and a half kilometres from Castell de Castells, in the high limestone country of the Serrella and Aitana massifs, and the name means high cave, which tells you what to expect: a climb. It is the second of the Cova Alta shelters, with Abric III and others nearby, and it forms part of the Mediterranean rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998.

The valley of the Castells river is quiet, and much of its charm is the lack of a destination. Villages are small, the roads are narrow, and the tourist crowds go to the coast. The people who live here earn their living from almonds, olives and a few cherry trees, supplemented by visitors who come to walk. In the village of Castell de Castells the main attraction is a plaza with a couple of bars, and the biggest event of the year is the village festival in late summer, when the population swells.

Riders will like the road. The CV-715 climbs from the Guadalest valley to a pass, then drops through a series of hairpins to Castell de Castells, and continues toward Tàrbena and the Coll de Rates. It is a narrow road with a few rough patches, but it is perfect for a slow, rolling ride. Cars are rare, cyclists are frequent, and in spring the roadsides are yellow with broom and white with rock rose. Beware of heat in summer and of fog on the heights in winter.

Fuel is the main thing to sort out, because Castell de Castells, Vall de Ebo and Benimantell are all tiny. Pego, twelve kilometres away, is the nearest proper town, and the coastal towns of the Marina Alta have everything else. A packed lunch is a good idea, since opening hours in the villages are unpredictable. Water is essential for the walk to the shelter, and good shoes are better than riding boots on the scree.
t.zona 8@38.1,-2.4:
The little town of Huéscar, thirty-eight kilometres from this spot over the border in the province of Granada, has a story that Spaniards tell with a grin. According to a local legend, in 1809, during the Napoleonic wars, the town council declared war on Denmark, mistakenly thinking that Denmark was an ally of Napoleon, and forgot to declare peace. The war, so the story goes, lasted for a hundred and seventy-two years, until a peace treaty was symbolically signed in 1981 by the mayor and the Danish ambassador. Historians doubt the details, but the town celebrates it anyway.

Zona 8 is in a different spirit altogether. It lies seven kilometres from Nerpio, in the high dry valley that is home to the numbered rock-art zones, and it forms part of the Mediterranean rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998. The paintings in the Nerpio basin include some striking figures, including stylised human forms with raised arms, as well as deer, goats and abstract signs. Zones 4, 5, 6 and 9 are all nearby, and a walker who has the time can compare their styles.

The road from Nerpio toward Huéscar crosses a bare, rolling plateau with a few farms and the occasional shepherd. It is a big-sky kind of ride, with long views, gentle bends and a feeling of space that is rare in Western Europe. In late afternoon the shadows lengthen and the hills turn violet. The surface is generally good, with a few patched sections, and you may go an hour without seeing another vehicle. Snow can close the road in winter, and fog sometimes lingers in the hollows.

Fuel is the obvious thing to arrange in advance. Huéscar has several stations, a sizeable market and a good variety of bars, and is the place to stock up before returning to the sierra. In Nerpio you can expect a modest meal of lamb, beans and bread. Carry water, because the shelter walk is exposed, and make a note of your route, because mobile signal is patchy.
t.barranco segovia@38.3,-2.1:
The Río Mundo is the Segura's most dramatic tributary, and it rises from a cave, the Cueva de los Chorros, near Riópar in the mountains of Albacete, in a burst of white water that bursts from the rock. By the time it passes Letur, thirty or so kilometres downstream, it has become a calm, green river in a steep-sided valley. The Barranco Segovia is a dry ravine on the south side of this area, some twelve kilometres from Letur and thirteen from Socovos, and the shelter named after it forms part of the rock art of the Mediterranean arc, protected by UNESCO since 1998. Its neighbours on the route, the Cueva de la Plata and the Cueva del Gitano, are in the same district.

Socovos, the nearer village, has a Moorish castle on a hill above the houses, and its streets are stepped and narrow. It was a frontier town in the Middle Ages, held in turn by Muslim and Christian lords, and its old walls still show the patchwork of repairs. The surrounding countryside is a quilt of cereal fields, olive groves and scrub, with limestone outcrops poking through, and is dotted with ruined farmhouses.

Riding here has an old-fashioned quality. The roads are not fast, and the scenery is a slow unfolding of small valleys, low passes and farming villages.
