A typical day might pass three tractors, one shepherd and a cyclist. The surface is variable, so keep your speed within the range at which you can stop for gravel or a pothole. In late spring the cereal fields are green and the poppies are out, and in October the stubble is gold.

Moratalla, twenty kilometres from the pin, is the sensible place for fuel and supplies, and Socovos and Letur have bars where you can have a coffee. Water is crucial for the walk to the shelter, and so is a hat. In July and August the heat is fierce, and the best time for walking is early morning. Remember that the paintings are vulnerable, and take only photographs.
t.prado del tornero ii@38.1,-2.3:
Forget the idea of a single village, because Nerpio is a municipality of scattered hamlets, farms and fields across a basin of the Sierra del Segura, and the shelters of Prado del Tornero are right at its edge. Prado del Tornero II, six hundred metres from the village, is the second of its group and belongs to the unusual concentration of rock paintings that makes the Nerpio district one of the great sites of Spanish prehistory, covered by UNESCO's 1998 listing. You can walk to it from the village in a few minutes, which makes it ideal for a short stop between legs of a long ride.

A base in Nerpio makes sense for a three-day exploration. The village has a few places to sleep and a handful of bars, and from it you can ride in several directions: south to Huéscar and the Granada plateau, north to Yeste and the valley of the Segura, east toward Letur and Moratalla, and west into the heart of the Sierra de Segura. Each direction offers its own mood. The north is forested and green, the south is open and dry, the east is a land of gorges and old castles, and the west is wild.

Season matters a lot. Nerpio is high and cold, with frost on many mornings from November to April, and snow is possible at any time in winter. Spring is short and bright, with flowers in May. Summer days are hot and dry, with cool nights. Autumn is probably the best, with golden poplars along the streams and a sharp clarity to the light. Whenever you come, carry layers and waterproofs, because the weather in the mountains changes quickly.

Fuel is the thing you must plan for. Nerpio is a small place, and Yeste, twenty-four kilometres away, has the nearest dependable station. Huéscar is farther and Moratalla farther still. Eat in the village, where you can expect hearty mountain food, and carry water on every walk. The shelter is easy to reach, and there is no need to hurry.
t.barranc de beniali abric ili@38.8,-0.2:
Every February the cherry trees of the Vall de Gallinera come into flower, and the valley that runs just north of the Beniali ravine turns white for a week or two, which is the best reason I know to ride in this corner of Alicante in winter. Barranc de Beniali, Abric III, is the third shelter catalogued along the ravine, five or six kilometres from Villalonga and Vall d'Ebo, and it belongs to the Mediterranean rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998. Its paintings, if you find them, are small and in dull reds.

The valley has a darker chapter. When the Moriscos were expelled from the kingdom of Valencia in 1609, the villages of the Vall de Gallinera and Vall d'Ebo lost almost their entire populations, and the Moorish terraces and irrigation channels had to be handed over to settlers from other regions. Some of the villages never fully recovered, and you can still read the history in the stone: mosque towers converted to bell towers, Arabic place names, and the neat, stepped fields that were built by people who knew how to move water.

Riders get the benefit of that engineering. The roads here follow the contours of the valleys in a long series of bends, and every village is a small knot of white houses and a church, with a bar in the square. Between them the land is a patchwork of cherry, almond and olive, with pine on the heights. The roads are narrow, with a good surface in most places and some rough patches after heavy rain, and the traffic is almost entirely local. Weekends in February and March are busier, when visitors come to see the blossom.

For fuel, Villalonga is a village of about four thousand and may have a pump, but the sure option is Pego, nine kilometres off, which also has supermarkets and a good market. Vall d'Ebo and Adsubia are tiny. A walk up to the shelter needs water and stout shoes, and a hat in the warmer months. In the villages, a plate of rice, a bowl of broad beans or a slice of coca, the local flatbread, makes a simple lunch.
t.toledo@39.9,-4.0:
Toledo sits inside a nearly closed loop of the Tagus, a granite gorge that makes the old city a natural fortress, and the first sight of it from the ring road is one that few riders forget. The Carretera de Circunvalación runs around the opposite bank, and its lay-bys and viewpoints, especially the Mirador del Valle, give the classic view: the Alcázar and cathedral on the skyline, the Alcántara bridge below, and the river shining in the gorge. El Greco painted that same view in the early seventeenth century, with stormy skies, and it is not hard to see why.

The city was the capital of the Visigothic kingdom, and later, for centuries, of Castile, and its reputation as a place where Christians, Muslims and Jews lived side by side, however imperfectly, is the source of its nickname, the city of three cultures. Its synagogues, mosques turned churches and Gothic cathedral are all within a few minutes' walk of each other. Toledo steel, which made the swords of kings, is still forged, and shops along the narrow lanes sell blades and damascene jewellery. The marzipan, mazapán de Toledo, is the sweet to try, made with almonds and sugar and sold in boxes in every pastry shop.

Riding in the old town is not a good idea. The lanes are steep and narrow, paved with slippery stone, and cars are restricted, so you should park outside the walls and walk. There are large car parks near the Puerta de Bisagra, and on the south bank, with a bank of escalators that lifts you up the hill. The roads that approach from Madrid and Aranjuez are mostly wide and fast, and the hills to the south, the Montes de Toledo, offer a quieter ride through holm oak and cork forests where deer and even a few lynx live.

The city has more than eighty thousand people, with fuel stations on all the main roads. In summer the heat is ferocious, and the best time to walk the old streets is early morning or late evening. A meal of partridge or venison stew, followed by marzipan, is a Toledan pleasure that costs more in tourist season, so look for the places a little off the main squares.
t.concejal ii@38.1,-2.4:
The word concejal means town councillor, and one can imagine a long argument about who was allowed to graze animals where, which would explain a field name like this. Concejal II is the second of a numbered series of shelters about seven kilometres from Nerpio, in the high basin of the upper Taibilla, among the dry valleys of the Sierra del Segura. They are part of a group of paintings listed by UNESCO in 1998, and they are set at the foot of south-facing cliffs, so that sun lights the walls on winter mornings.

If you want a sense of what this country was like for the first farmers, look at the soils. The basin of Nerpio has thin, stony earth, short summers and cold winters, and yet it was settled very early, perhaps because water and pasture were reliable. The tradition of cereal growing and sheep keeping goes back thousands of years, and the oldest local families still tend sheep. In spring the meadows have a scatter of wild tulips and narcissi, which come up after the snow.

Between Nerpio and Huéscar the road passes a landscape that feels more like Castile than Andalusia, with limestone hills, juniper and treeless plains, and a sky that can be intensely blue. There are not many bends, but each is well judged, and the ride gains its character from the sense of space. In the afternoon the wind picks up, and a loaded bike can feel it. Check the forecast for snow from November to April, and for storms in summer.

You will need fuel from Huéscar, thirty-nine kilometres away, or Yeste, twenty-six, because the village of Nerpio, with about sixteen hundred people, is not a reliable stop. Carry water, snacks and a layer of warm clothing, and take care with the mobile signal, which disappears in the hollows. The shelters are best visited early in the day, when the light is soft and the rock is cool.
t.cavidad iv@38.2,-2.2:
Cavidad is the archaeologist's word for a hollow, and the numbered Cavidades near Nerpio are a series of small shelters scattered across the plateau, seven or eight kilometres from the village. Cavidad IV is on a route with the Cañada de la Cruz and Las Cazuelas, the Little Pots, a name that suggests rounded hollows weathered into the rock. They belong to the cluster of rock paintings that UNESCO listed in 1998 as part of the Mediterranean arc, and which in Nerpio includes some of the most varied figures in Spain.

The word cañada is worth a note, because it means a drove road, one of the ancient routes used by shepherds to move their flocks between summer and winter pastures. Spain has some hundred and twenty thousand kilometres of such tracks, protected by medieval law and still marked on maps, and the powerful guild of sheep owners, the Mesta, once controlled them. In the Sierra del Segura the flocks moved up to the high meadows in June and returned to the lowlands in autumn, and a few families still follow the pattern. If you meet a flock on the road, stop, switch off and let it pass.

The plateau between Nerpio and Yeste is an excellent place for riding at an unhurried pace. The road is narrow but well made, climbing gently through juniper and pine, with generous bends that need no braking. The altitude means cool air and a clear sky, and in the evening the light goes gold and long. Wildlife is plentiful, with deer and boar crossing at dusk, so be alert after sunset. In winter the road can be icy, especially in shaded hollows, and gritting is limited.

Fuel is a question of planning. Yeste, with about thirty-six hundred people, is twenty-three kilometres away and has the nearest dependable pumps, and Moratalla is further. Nerpio has shops and bars for lunch and coffee. Carry water for any walk, wear sturdy shoes, and respect the paintings, which are fragile and sometimes protected by fences.
t.abrigo de los sabinares o ventana de los:
The sabina is the Spanish juniper, a tough, aromatic tree that grows on the high limestone plateaus of the interior, and the Abrigo de los Sabinares, also called the Ventana de los E, lies in a country where junipers cover the slopes in dark green clumps. The shelter sits eight kilometres from Nerpio, in the high basin of the Sierra del Segura, and it is one of the cluster of painted rocks that UNESCO listed in 1998 as part of the Mediterranean arc. Its neighbours on the route, the Cueva de los Pucheros and the Abrigo de la Fuente, are in the same district.

Juniper wood has a long human history. Its resin is rich in oils that resist rot, and builders used it for roof beams in old farmhouses, some of which are still standing after four or five hundred years. The wood is aromatic and used for carving, and the berries, dark blue in autumn, are used as a flavouring and as the main ingredient of gin. In the Nerpio district the junipers are slow-growing and ancient, and some are said to be centuries old.

The roads here are the pleasure of the high plateau. They run straight and then bend, climbing gently over passes and dropping into basins, and the juniper scrub lines the verges. The air is dry and fragrant, especially after rain, and the light has a hard clarity. There is little traffic. Ride carefully in winter, because the plateau gets heavy frost and the occasional fall of snow, and in summer, when thunderstorms build in the afternoon.

Services are limited, and fuel is the main issue. Nerpio is eight kilometres from the shelter, and Yeste, twenty-seven kilometres away, is the nearest reliable town, with Huéscar thirty-eight kilometres to the south. A basic lunch is possible in Nerpio, and it will probably include lamb or game. Carry water and a map, and do not rely on the phone. The walk to the shelter is moderate but exposed.
t.barranc de la fita abric iii@38.7,-0.2:
A barranc in this part of the Marina Alta is a dry ravine that carries water for a few hours after a storm, and the Barranc de la Fita has three shelters numbered along it. Abric III is the last of them, at the same spot as Abric I and Abric II, less than three kilometres from Castell de Castells. They are part of the Mediterranean rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998, and the density of such sites in a small area is one of the reasons the region is of such interest to archaeologists.

A different thing to know about this country is that it grows muscatel grapes. In the Jalón valley, a few kilometres to the north, the vines are trained on low trellises and the grapes are dried in the sun to make raisins or pressed for a sweet wine, and in September the valley smells of ripe fruit. Villages such as Parcent, Jalón and Lliber hold harvest festivals, and the roads are full of tractors. The slopes of the Serrella above are less cultivated, covered with pine and scrub, and the contrast between the cultivated valley and the wild mountain is striking.

For riding, the Coll de Rates, between Tàrbena and the Jalón valley, is the highlight. It is a long, steady climb of regular bends, and the views over vineyards and the sea are splendid. Between Tàrbena and Castell de Castells the road is quieter and more twisting, and it continues to Guadalest. The surface is generally good, with some narrow sections. Early morning is the best time, since the heat builds quickly in summer, and the roads fill with cyclists on weekends.

Fuel is in Pego, fifteen kilometres from the shelter, or in the coastal towns. Castell de Castells has a bar and a shop, but no pumps. Take water for the walk, and expect little shade. A lunch of rice with local vegetables and a glass of muscatel wine is a fine way to end the day.
t.birdoswald roman fort and the section of:
Birdoswald stands on a bluff above the River Irthing in Cumbria, almost at the point where Hadrian's Wall leaves the flatter country near Carlisle and begins to climb into the harder, wilder ground of Northumberland. The Roman fort here was called Banna, and it was one of the larger forts along the wall, home to a cohort of auxiliary soldiers. What makes it special is that you can walk along a stretch of the wall that stands tall, with the original facing stones and the line of the turrets still visible, and look out over a steep wooded gorge where the Irthing cuts through red sandstone.

The nearest towns are small ones. Brampton is about nine kilometres away and Haltwhistle about the same, both under five thousand people, so there is petrol and a few shops in each, but for supermarkets and bigger fuel stops, Carlisle is the sensible place, about twenty-four kilometres off. The road to the fort is a minor one, narrow in places, so take it gently, and watch for sheep, cattle grids and the occasional tractor.

The riding in this part of the world is a quiet pleasure. The B6318, the Military Road, runs on the line of the old Roman military way along the wall itself in the central sector, but near Birdoswald the roads wander through rolling farmland with hawthorn hedges, small stone bridges, and long views north to the Scottish Borders and south to the North Pennines. Corners are gentle, surfaces vary from good to patched, and the wind can be sharp even in summer. Rain is likely at any time and the Cumbrian light changes quickly.

The wall was begun around AD 122 on the orders of the emperor Hadrian and ran for about eighty Roman miles from the Tyne to the Solway. It was not only a defensive line but a way of controlling movement, taxing trade and showing that Rome had arrived. Soldiers were stationed along it for nearly three centuries, and the fort's story runs into the post-Roman period too, with evidence of timber halls built over the old buildings after the legions left.

If you stop, take time at the visitor centre if it is open, and note that opening times vary with the season and the managing organisation. A walk along the wall to the west is a gentle half hour, and a flask of tea is a sensible thing to carry.
t.great chesters roman fort and hadrian s:
Great Chesters, known to the Romans as Aesica, sits high on the Whin Sill ridge in Northumberland, the dark dolerite crag that Hadrian's Wall uses as its backbone for much of its central length. The fort is small, a modest rectangle of grassy banks and a few stone foundations in a field, and it is easy to drive past without noticing, which is part of its appeal. What you get is the setting: a wide skyline, the wall visible as a rough stone line running east and west, and the sort of silence that only comes from a long way from any town.

Haltwhistle is the closest settlement, about two and a half kilometres away as the crow flies, a small market town with a few shops and a petrol station. Hexham, about twenty kilometres or so from here, is the larger town with the bigger supermarkets, an abbey and plenty of cafés. In this part of the country the villages are small and spaced out, so it pays to top up in one of the towns before a long afternoon on the moor roads.

The riding is the best reason to come. The Military Road, the B6318, was built after the 1745 Jacobite rising so that troops could move quickly across the country, and it runs straight and rolling along the line of the wall, with a series of crests that give views north over the Northumberland National Park and the empty moorland beyond. The old road builders even used the Roman wall as a quarry, which is why so much of it vanished. Surfaces are mostly good but the road is fast and straight enough to tempt people, so keep an eye out for speed cameras and the occasional police presence, as well as farm traffic and lambs near the verges in spring.

The weather up here is changeable, with clouds rolling in from the west and the wind often strong enough to bother a light bike. Visibility can drop quickly in low cloud, and in winter the road can ice over. The best conditions are on a clear morning in late spring or early autumn, when the light picks out every ridge and the sheep are the only traffic.

Take a minute to stand by the field, look east along the wall, and think about the soldiers posted here, many of them recruited from distant parts of the empire, stuck on a cold escarpment with a long view and little else to do.
t.edinburgh@56.0,-3.2:
Edinburgh climbs a volcanic spine from the Firth of Forth, with the Castle on its crag at one end and Holyrood Palace at the other, and the Royal Mile running between them down the ridge the glaciers left behind. It is a city that makes you look up: tall tenements, black stone, turrets, spires and, on a clear day, the green hump of Arthur's Seat rising out of the middle of the town like something the builders forgot to level. The old town and new town together form a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with the Georgian grid of the New Town contrasting sharply with the medieval jumble of the Old.

For a motorcyclist it is a city of two halves. The centre is a challenge, with cobbles, tram works, buses, bus lanes and a one-way system that seems to be designed by someone who disliked the idea of arriving. Parking for motorbikes is reasonably good, with designated bays in the centre, but be prepared for rain, wind and a surface that can be slick in the wet, especially the cobbled streets around the Grassmarket and the old town. Edinburgh is famously windy, and bridges across the Forth can be tricky on a blowy day.

Practicalities are easy. With nearly half a million people, the city has all the fuel, food, coffee and bed you could want, and the outskirts such as Colinton offer a quieter, leafier base. The Water of Leith walkway runs through a wooded gorge into the heart of town and is a pleasant place to unwind, while the Dean Village, with its stone mills and bridge, looks more like a hidden hamlet than a corner of a capital.

Edinburgh has a long literary and scientific history, from Robert Louis Stevenson and Walter Scott to the Enlightenment philosophers who made the city a centre of European thought in the eighteenth century. The Festival in August fills every pavement and doubles the price of everything, so if you are planning a stay then, book early. The food is better than the old stereotypes suggest, though a pie and a pint is still a perfectly decent lunch.

Heading south from here, the Pentland Hills and the Borders open up quickly and give a very different picture, so the city is both a destination and a gateway.
t.coesike east roman temporary camp@55.0,-:
The Romans were a marching people, and every night on campaign they dug in. Coesike East is one of those night camps, a temporary enclosure of banks and ditches thrown up by a column on the move, probably around the time the frontier was being organised, long before anyone thought of building a wall. Nothing much stands above ground now. What survives is a faint rectangle in rough pasture, visible mostly to people who already know what they are looking for, or to aerial photographs in low winter sun. I would be lying if I said there was a monument to see here, so treat it as a reason to be in this particular corner of Northumberland rather than a sight in itself.

The corner is lovely. You are on the high ground south of the South Tyne, with Haydon Bridge about six kilometres away in the valley and Hexham, the real town with the supermarkets and the fuel, some thirteen kilometres off. Acomb lies to the east. Haydon Bridge is a village of a thousand-odd people with a couple of shops and cafés, and it sits on the river with a handsome old bridge, but if you need serious petrol, take it in Hexham rather than assuming.

The roads in this country are what make the stop. They climb out of the valley onto moorland with the Pennines blue to the south, and the lanes are narrow, hedged or walled, and sometimes unfenced across open fell, so sheep appear around corners with total confidence. Gradients are modest but the exposure is real, and wind comes off the moor with a sharp edge. Surfaces vary from smooth to broken at the edges, and frost lingers late in the shaded dips. Early morning in May, with lapwings and curlews calling over the fields, is about as good as northern England gets.

Not far to the north runs the Stanegate, the road the Romans built before the wall, linking Carlisle with Corbridge, and many of the forts and camps around here belong to that earlier frontier line. Understanding this makes the landscape click: the wall was a later, grander idea, but the real military life of the area was the road and its stopping places.

Bring a flask, wear something windproof, and if you do get off the bike for a look at the field, remember it is working farmland, so keep to the gates and tracks.
t.haltwhistle burn roman temporary camps 2:
Haltwhistle Burn is a small stream that cuts down toward the South Tyne just east of Haltwhistle, and the name is one of those wonderful northern English mouthfuls that seems to have been in use forever. Here, beside the burn, the Romans left a cluster of temporary camps, several overlapping enclosures that show how often armies returned to the same convenient ground. Alongside them lies a fort on the Stanegate, the military road that predates Hadrian's Wall. The camps are low earthworks in pasture, best appreciated in slanting light and with a little imagination.

Haltwhistle, about two kilometres away, bills itself as the centre of Britain, a claim that rests on some measuring of the island's extremes and is mostly good for a laugh and a postcard. It is a small town with a long main street, a petrol station, a couple of bakeries and pubs, and a railway station on the line between Newcastle and Carlisle. For anything bigger, such as a large supermarket or a garage that can fix a puncture, the nearest option is Hexham, about twenty-two kilometres east.

The riding here is gentler than on the high stretch of the Military Road a little farther north, and a lot quieter. The Stanegate itself survives in places as a lane, running along the south side of the valley, with the Tyne glinting below and the wall's line visible on the ridge across the water. What you get is rolling farmland, hedges, small woods, hay meadows in June, and a fair amount of rain. Cattle grids and sheep are the main hazards, plus mud on the road after farm vehicles pass.

There is a different kind of history in the valley too: coal and lead were mined in the nearby hills, and the railway came in the nineteenth century, linking this empty-feeling country to the industrial towns on both coasts. Old stone barns and farmsteads are scattered through the fields, many of them built with stone robbed from the Roman remains. It is an old English habit, reusing what the Romans left.

A pleasant way to spend an hour is to take a walk beside the burn, listening to the water and the birds, and then ride back along the valley road to Haltwhistle for a pie and a cup of tea before moving on.
t.skara brae@59.0,-3.3:
Skara Brae is the oldest house you will ever walk past on a motorbike, or at least the oldest complete set of them. On the Bay of Skaill, on the west coast of Orkney's Mainland, a group of Neolithic stone houses lies half buried in the grassy dunes, built roughly five thousand years ago and lived in for several centuries. A great storm in the winter of 1850 stripped the turf from a mound and exposed the walls, and what was uncovered astonished everyone: stone beds, stone dressers, hearths, and cupboards still in their original places, because the settlers had built with slabs rather than timber, and there was no timber to rot. The site forms part of the Heart of Neolithic Orkney, along with the Ring of Brodgar and the Standing Stones of Stenness a few miles away.

Orkney as a whole is a gift to riders who like open space. The islands are low and green, with a coastline of red sandstone cliffs, and there are almost no trees to break the wind, which comes in from the Atlantic with very little to stop it. The roads are narrow, mostly well surfaced and quiet, with long straights and gentle curves, passing places on the minor lanes, and sheep and cattle that regard the tarmac as theirs. Traffic is light except around the main sights in summer, when coaches and campervans arrive in pulses. Be ready for sudden showers, strong crosswinds on exposed stretches, and sea mist, which can arrive within minutes in summer.

Stromness, the nearest town, about ten kilometres away, is a handsome grey-stone port with a flagstoned main street, a harbour full of small boats, and the ferry terminal for Scrabster on the Scottish mainland. It has a few shops, cafés, a museum and fuel, though with fewer than two thousand people it is not a place with many choices, and Kirkwall, the main town, is the better stop for supermarkets and a wider range of services.

Orkney's other pleasures are everywhere: the fudge and cheese, the beer, the seafood, the smell of seaweed on the wind and the calls of oystercatchers and curlews in the fields. Remember that the visitor centre and the site have set opening hours and charge entry, and in the middle of summer the car park can be busy.

Come in late afternoon, when the day trippers have gone, and the sand and sky go the colour of old pewter.
t.bean burn 2 roman temporary camp@55.0,-2:
Bean Burn is another of those names that sounds as if it belongs in a children's book, and the Roman camp here is one of the less visible members of the frontier zone along Hadrian's Wall. A temporary camp was a rough overnight enclosure for a column of soldiers, thrown up with a ditch and a bank and abandoned the next morning, and Bean Burn 2 is one of a family of such camps scattered across the moors south of the wall. If you go looking for stone, you will be disappointed. What you will find is open moorland, with a wide sky and the quiet that belongs to a place where the nearest road is a single-track lane.

Haltwhistle is about five kilometres away and Haydon Bridge about nine, so help is close, but the large fuel and supermarket stop is Hexham, roughly eighteen kilometres away. It is worth filling up there before heading into the uplands, because the road network is thin and the villages small.

The roads here form part of one of England's best-kept secrets for motorcyclists. South of the wall, between the South Tyne and the Allen valleys, minor roads climb onto heather moor with long open views, dropping into hidden valleys with a farmhouse and a cluster of sycamores. The gradients are fair, the bends are broad and the surface is mostly decent, though cattle grids, sheep and sudden dips filled with water are part of the game. Cyclists and walkers on the Pennine Way and the Hadrian's Wall Path share the area, so keep your speed sensible near the junctions.

The landscape belongs to the Northumberland National Park's southern fringe, a country of curlews, lapwings and red grouse, with skylarks overhead in spring and wheatears on the walls. In late summer the heather turns purple and the moors smell of honey. In winter the same roads can be bleak, icy and closed by snow, so check conditions before setting out.

Understanding the camps is a small pleasure: they remind you that the army was a moving thing, and that the famous wall was only one part of a system of roads, forts and camps that held the northern frontier in place for centuries.
t.trevelez@37.0,-3.3:
Trevélez is one of those places that people tell you about long before you see it. It hangs on the southern slope of the Sierra Nevada at around fifteen hundred metres, among the highest villages in Spain, below the bulk of Mulhacén, which at 3,479 metres is the highest peak on the Iberian mainland. The village is split into three barrios, one above the other, with whitewashed flat-roofed houses that look from the road like a staircase of sugar cubes. Above them is a valley of terraced orchards and chestnuts, and the cold, clear river that carries the snowmelt down toward the Mediterranean.

What made the place famous is ham. The cold, dry mountain air is ideal for curing, and the hams of Trevélez, hung in the drying sheds for many months, are sold throughout Spain under a protected name. Stop at any of the small restaurants in the lower barrio and you can eat it sliced thin with bread and olive oil, along with the local trout, and the usual mountain dishes of the Alpujarra. It is sensible to carry cash, and to remember that in winter the village gets real cold, with snow some years.

The Alpujarra has a deep history. After the Christian conquest of Granada in 1492, many Muslims retreated to these valleys, and their way of building, with flat clay roofs and narrow terraced lanes, is still visible in every village. They were then driven out after a revolt in the 1560s, and the region was repopulated by settlers from the north. The terraces and the irrigation channels, called acequias, which carry the meltwater, are a heritage from that earlier period.

The riding to get here is memorable. From the Órgiva side the road climbs the valley through Pampaneira and Capileira, and the final approach to Trevélez is a long series of bends above steep drops, with a very uneven surface in places and rock fall after rain. Take your time. The road is narrow, and coaches and locals in small vans use it fast. Tank up beforehand in Órgiva, or the larger towns on the plain, because fuel in the high villages is something you should never take for granted. Bérchules and Busquístar are small villages a few kilometres on in either direction, with simple bars for a coffee.
t.gredos mountain weekend high point@39.8,:
Toledo does not look like a high point until you see it from the right side, and then it looks like exactly that. The city stands on a granite hill, almost encircled by a deep loop of the Tagus, and the river has cut a gorge round the base that makes it look like a castle on a stone throne. The road in from the north, through Cobisa and the olive and cereal land near Layos, runs over the dry plateau of the meseta and gives no hint of what is coming until the walls and the Alcázar appear over the edge of the ridge.

That is why the stop is worth making, even for riders who have no interest in monuments. For centuries Toledo was a meeting place of Christians, Muslims and Jews, and the old centre still has a synagogue, former mosques and a vast Gothic cathedral within a few streets of each other. It was the capital of Spain's court until the 1560s, and later it became famous for its steel, so the swords and daggers sold in the shop windows have a long pedigree. Local specialities include marzipan, made in convents and shops, and game stews, and a plate of partridge is typical of the Montes de Toledo to the south.

The streets in the old town are narrow, steep, cobbled and often one-way, and riding in them is hard work, especially in crowded summer months. Park outside the centre, where there is a lot of space near the river, and walk up. The best view of the whole city is from the road on the far side of the Tagus, which loops around the hill, and if you have a camera, the late afternoon light turns the stone gold. Doing that loop road is a small pleasure in itself, with a few bends and a smooth surface.

The city has fuel in plenty, with around eighty thousand inhabitants, and the ring road has stations. In midsummer, afternoon temperatures can be extreme, so aim for morning or evening, and carry water because the shade is sparse on the plateau around the city.
t.lanjaron@36.9,-3.5:
Lanjarón is the front door of the Alpujarras, and the first thing it offers is water. The springs that rise from the Sierra Nevada above the town are among the best known in Spain, and the mineral water bottled here is sold across the country. The town has a spa tradition that goes back centuries, with a grand old bathing house and a long main street of cafés, shops and hotels, and a public fountain where you can taste the water for free. It is cold and light, with a faint mineral tang.

Every year on the night of Saint John, the twenty-third of June, the town celebrates the Fiesta del Agua, a huge water fight in which everyone on the main street throws water at everyone else, with buckets, hoses and water pistols. It is both a tradition and a joke, and visitors are not spared. If you are in town on that night with a motorbike, move it well out of the way and keep your phone dry.

Above the town stand the ruins of a Moorish castle, a reminder that this region was one of the last strongholds of Muslim Spain. After the fall of Granada in 1492 the Alpujarras remained home to a large Morisco population, and when the Crown tried to suppress their customs, they rose in revolt in 1568, a bitter war that ended with their expulsion from the region. The terraces, irrigation channels and white houses of the villages are the legacy of their skill, and the whole area has a layered, slightly melancholy history.

The road up through the Alpujarras begins here, and it is a good one: a narrow, winding route that climbs through chestnut and almond groves, with views over the valley to the distant sea on clear days. The surface is mostly good, though patched in places, and the bends are tight, with little room for error. Traffic is moderate, with buses and local lorries, and the roads fill with tourists in spring and autumn. In winter, snow can close the highest sections, and in July and August the heat is considerable.

Lanjarón has about four thousand people, with fuel stations, shops and a good choice of cafés and restaurants, and Órgiva, five kilometres to the east, has more. Try the cured ham from the high villages and a plate of local goat or pork, with fried potatoes and a glass of the region's wine. Fill the tank before climbing, as the villages above have little fuel.
t.pampaneira@36.9,-3.4:
Pampaneira is the first of three white villages that cling to the sides of the Poqueira gorge, and it looks like something from the Atlas mountains, which is not an accident. The houses are flat-roofed cubes, whitewashed every year, with chimneys shaped like little pots, and their roofs are made of a grey clay called launa, laid over slate and beams, a building method brought from North Africa by the Moors. The village is steep, with narrow alleys and stepped streets, and the sound of running water from the channels that bring meltwater down the mountainside is everywhere.

The Poqueira gorge is dramatic. The river tumbles from the high peaks of the Sierra Nevada, including Mulhacén, at 3,479 metres the highest mountain in mainland Spain, through a deep, terraced valley that has been farmed for a thousand years. Almond, chestnut and walnut trees cover the slopes, and the terraces are watered by a network of channels called acequias, a system laid out by the Moors. In spring the almond blossom is white and pink, and in autumn the chestnuts turn gold and the villagers gather the nuts.

The village is known for its weaving, and in several shops you can see women making jarapas, the bright, striped rugs of the region, on old wooden looms. Cured ham, sausage and honey are sold in the little shops, and a few small restaurants serve local dishes such as plato alpujarreño, a hearty plate of fried potatoes, ham, eggs and sausage. Above in Bubión stands a Tibetan Buddhist centre, an odd and rather lovely presence on a hillside of whitewashed houses.

The road from Órgiva to Pampaneira is a joy, climbing in bends through terraces and olive groves, with views across the valley. It is narrow and steep in places, with little room to overtake, and coaches and cars come down the other way, so patience is wise. The surface is usually good, but the heat of summer can soften the tarmac in places and winter snow may linger on the higher sections. Parking in the village is limited, so aim for the car park at the entrance and walk. Pampaneira has fuel in none of its streets, so tank up in Órgiva, about seven kilometres away. Spring, for the blossom, and October, for the chestnuts, are the best times.
t.cayoosh pass@50.4,-122.4:
Cayoosh Pass is the high point of the Duffey Lake Road, the stretch of British Columbia Highway 99 that connects the dry, sage-scented interior at Lillooet with the green valleys of Pemberton and the coast. At about 1,275 metres, it is not especially tall, but this road is a rider's favourite, and the pass is an important marker, the place where the road stops climbing and begins its long descent through rock and snow toward the Pacific. The mountains around it are sharp, glaciated and close.

The road was only completed in the 1960s, and it remains a narrow, steep and winding route, with grades that reach thirteen per cent in places and tight bends that follow the creek down from the summit. It crosses the traditional territory of the St'át'imc and Lil'wat peoples, who used trails here for thousands of years, long before the road or the gold rush. Cayoosh Creek, which flows west to east from the pass toward Lillooet, was once the scene of placer gold mining, and Lillooet itself was Mile Zero of the Cariboo Wagon Road in the 1860s.

For a rider, this is a serious and rewarding road. The bends are tight, the gradients are steep, and the surface, while mostly good, has frost heaves, patches and gravel on the corners. Rock falls and avalanches can close the road, especially in spring, and snow can fall on the pass in any month except perhaps July and August. Temperatures change quickly with altitude, and a warm day in Pemberton can be a cold one at the summit. The best season is summer to early autumn, from about late June to September, when the road is dry and snow free, and the best time of day is morning, before the traffic builds.

Wildlife is part of the experience. Black bears and mountain goats are seen along the road, and marmots whistle from the rocks. The landscape has a bleak grandeur, with bare rock, snowfields and stands of subalpine fir, and the air smells cold and clean. The nearby Joffre Lakes, a short walk from the road, require a day-use pass in busy periods, and are worth the walk for the colour of the water.

Pemberton, about twenty-eight kilometres away, is the nearest town, and Lillooet lies further to the east. Fill the tank at either end, bring something to eat, and remember that mobile coverage is poor. A flask of something hot is welcome on a cold day.
t.duffey lake@50.4,-122.3:
Duffey Lake is a long, green-blue lake lying beside the road in a bowl of high mountains, and when the wind drops, it holds a clear mirror image of the peaks. On the far shore the slopes rise in forest and then in grey rock, topped with snowfields and small glaciers, and the whole scene feels remote, though the road runs right beside it. The provincial park at the lake provides a pull-out, a picnic area and a trail, so it is easy to stop and look.

The lake is a landmark on the Duffey Lake Road, between Lillooet and Pemberton, and it sits in the territory of the Lil'wat Nation. The road was built in the 1960s, and for decades it was a rough gravel track, a hard route for logging trucks and the occasional adventurous driver. It has since been paved and improved, and now carries tourists, riders and cyclists in summer, though it remains narrow, with few passing places and steep drops. The peaks above, including Joffre and Matier, are some of the most photographed in the region, with hanging glaciers that gleam in the sun.

The riding along the lake is a pleasure, with curves that follow the shoreline, glimpses of water through the trees, and then a climb away from it into the mountains. The road surface can be rough in places, with frost damage, and in cool weather the shaded sections stay damp. Traffic is generally light, but logging trucks and campers use the road, and they do not always keep to their side on the bends. Allow more time than you expect, since the road has a way of making you stop.

Fishing is popular on the lake, with rainbow trout and char, and in summer you may see people paddling on the water. Black bears feed on the berries on the slopes, and you should treat the area as bear country, keeping food stored and giving animals plenty of room. Mosquitoes can be a nuisance in the still evenings, and the water is cold enough to stop you swimming for very long.

Pemberton, about thirty-seven kilometres to the west, is the nearest town with services, and Lillooet lies a long way to the east. The campsites around the lake fill early in summer, and some are first-come, first-served, so plan accordingly. Early morning, when the lake is calm and the light touches the peaks, is the best time for photographs.
t.puerto de la ragua@37.1,-3.0:
Spain's Sierra Nevada is the southernmost big mountain range in Europe, and the Puerto de la Ragua is the main paved road across it. At 2,041 metres it is not the highest road in the range, since the great summits of Mulhacén and Veleta both lie further west and rise to around 3,400 metres, but it is the easiest to love. It links Guadix, on the high dry plateau to the north, with the villages of the Alpujarras, the steep valleys on the southern side, and the change of scene from one side to the other is abrupt.

The northern approach climbs from the Marquesado del Zenete, a bare, rolling country of ochre earth and scattered pines, past the castle of La Calahorra, a Renaissance fortress with four round corner towers built in the early sixteenth century by a Mendoza nobleman who wanted a palace in the Italian style. You see it from far away, a square block set against the mountains. After that the road tilts upward in long, easy bends, the trees thin out and a few patches of snow may still lie in the hollows in spring. The surface is good, the gradient steady and the traffic light, with the occasional cyclist grinding up toward the top.

On the other side, the road drops into the Alpujarras toward Laroles and Mecina Bombarón, and the landscape turns green and wet with chestnut, poplar and terraced fields watered by Moorish irrigation channels, the acequias, that still carry snowmelt to the hillsides. The villages of whitewashed flat-roofed houses cling to the slopes, a style that passed from the Berbers of the Atlas, and the Moriscos who lived here rebelled against Philip II in the 1560s in a bitter war whose memory remains strong. The descent has plenty of tight bends and some rough patches, so take it with respect.

The nearest town of any size is Guadix, about twenty-three kilometres away, which has stations, supermarkets and a surprising district of cave houses carved into the hillsides, still lived in. In the Alpujarras, the villages have bars and small restaurants serving jamón from Trevélez, which is cured at altitude, along with migas and goat stew. The pass may close in winter after snow, so check conditions if you travel between late autumn and spring.

At the top, the air is thin and dry, and the view stretches over two different worlds. Take a layer, because the wind blows hard.
t.mini hollywood@37.0,-2.4:
Mini Hollywood, officially Oasys, is a Wild West town that happens to be in southern Spain, and it makes a better stop than a cynic might expect. The reason is the land. Around Tabernas, in the province of Almería, the hills are bare, cracked and rust-coloured, rainfall is among the lowest in Europe, and filmmakers realised in the 1960s that the place looked enough like Arizona and Mexico to pass. Sergio Leone shot much of the spaghetti western A Fistful of Dollars out here, and later productions, including an Indiana Jones film, borrowed the same badlands.

The sets that survive have become a theme park of sorts, with wooden saloons, a bank, a gallows, and staged shoot-outs for visitors. It is cheerful, a bit cheesy, and unabashedly proud. If you can ignore the actors in their stetsons, the backdrop of eroded ravines and agave is the real draw. The film industry also left behind a local economy: other former sets nearby offer similar attractions, and the town of Tabernas sells itself as a capital of cinema.

Riding through the desert is a different experience from anywhere else in Spain. Roads such as the A-92 and the old N-340a cross a landscape of dry rambla riverbeds, dusty scrub, and long straights broken by gentle sweeps. The light is hard, the shadows sharp, and in midsummer the heat is considerable, with temperatures that make the engine and the rider equally unhappy at midday. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and early morning gives the best light for photographs. After rain, which is rare but sometimes violent, dry channels can flood, so do not ride into a flooded dip.

The surrounding area, the Tabernas Desert, is generally described as semi-arid rather than a true desert, but it looks plenty desert enough. Plants like esparto grass and wild thyme cling on, and lizards bask on the stones. Not far away, near Tabernas, the Plataforma Solar de Almería uses the reliable sunshine for solar-energy research, a rather logical use for the land.

Fuel is easy in Tabernas, about five kilometres away, and the larger towns of Huércal de Almería and Almería city lie to the south. There is shade and cold drink at the park, but bring a hat and water of your own if you plan to explore on foot.
t.tabernas@37.0,-2.4:
Tabernas is a small white town on the edge of the desert that carries its name, and the first thing you notice is the ruined castle on the hill above. It is a Moorish fortress, later fought over by Christian armies in the Reconquista, and it has been a ruin for a long time. The town itself is a working one, built along the road, with a plaza, a few bars and a feeling of waiting for the next film crew. Cinema made it famous, but farming and travel keep it alive.

Riding in from Almería you cross a surreal landscape. The Tabernas badlands are made of soft marls and clays carved by flash floods into ridges, gullies and little mesas, a miniature Colorado in grey and ochre. Annual rainfall is among the lowest in continental Europe, yet when it comes, it comes hard. t.loch ness view@57.3,-4.4:
Loch Ness is a long way from the postcard idea of a quiet Highland lake. It is a slot in the earth, about thirty-six kilometres of dark water lying along the Great Glen fault, and it is deep enough, over two hundred metres at its worst, that it holds more water than every lake in England and Wales put together. The A82 along the north-west shore is the road you ride here, and it is better than its reputation among tourists in hire cars. It is wide for the Highlands, with decent sightlines, a few fast sweepers and a handful of tight spots where the loch hugs the tarmac. The trouble is traffic. In summer the coaches, caravans and monster-hunters crawl between Fort Augustus and Inverness, so go early in the morning or late in the evening, when the light along the water is lovely and the road is yours. Wind funnels down the glen, usually from the south-west, and can push a loaded bike around on the open stretches.

The history sits mostly a few minutes away at Urquhart Castle, a ruin on a promontory that was blown up in 1692 so the Jacobites could not use it. Older still is the story of Saint Columba, who in the sixth century is said to have faced down a water beast in the River Ness, recorded by his biographer Adomnán. The modern monster industry came much later, in the 1930s, but the loch has never quite shaken it off, and every second shop in Drumnadrochit sells a plush version. Nobody has found anything. The Caledonian Canal, stitched through the glen by Thomas Telford in the early nineteenth century, is the quieter marvel.

For practical matters, Drumnadrochit is a village of about a thousand people and has the basics, including somewhere to eat and a petrol station, but it is the sort of place that fills up fast in the season, so do not leave fuel to chance. Inverness, twenty-odd kilometres away, is the proper town for everything else. t.glen affric forest core@57.3,-5.0:
The tarmac ends, and in a sense so does the modern Highlands. Conservation groups have spent decades fencing, planting and letting the forest regenerate, and you can see the young trees coming up.

t.beauly@57.5,-4.5:
Beauly is pronounced Bew-lee, which tells you something about the layers of language in this part of Scotland. t.newcastle@55.0,-1.6:
The Tyne is crossed by a remarkable set of bridges within a short walk of each other. The Tyne Bridge, a green steel arch opened in 1928, is the one on the postcards, but the High Level Bridge, designed by Robert Stephenson and opened in 1849 with a road below and a railway above, is the older marvel, and the little Swing Bridge, which opens by pivoting on a central pier, comes from the industrial age as well. The Quayside, with its bars and restaurants and the curved Millennium Bridge that tilts to let boats pass, is the lively heart of the town. Up the hill is Grainger Town, a grid of grand Victorian streets in pale stone, designed in the 1830s, and the Castle Keep that gave the city its name. Across the river in Gateshead stands the Angel of the North, Antony Gormley's rust-red figure with a wingspan of fifty-four metres, which watches the A1 from a hill and is best seen at dawn.

From there the wall runs west, and the Military Road, the B6318, follows it for long stretches, a straight and rolling road with views over the Northumbrian hills and the wall itself, stone and turf, running along the crest. Wind and rain come in from the North Sea, so pack layers, and be careful on the damp lanes.

Newcastle's classic comforts are a pie, a pint, a stottie cake with pease pudding and ham, or fish and chips. Locals are friendly and fond of a chat, and a Geordie accent is easier to follow once you have had a pint or two. Leave early, and enjoy the open road beyond the suburbs.
t.glasgow@55.9,-4.2:
Glasgow is a Victorian city that learned to like itself again. In the nineteenth century it was the second city of the British Empire, building ships and locomotives on the Clyde, and the grand sandstone buildings of the Merchant City and the West End are the evidence. In the twentieth century, as the shipyards declined, the city went through hard times, but today it has a thriving music and arts scene, and a reputation for warmth and humour that people from elsewhere often find startling.

The architecture is a pleasure in itself. Charles Rennie Mackintosh's School of Art, on Garnethill, is a masterpiece of the early twentieth century, and the Kelvingrove Art Gallery, with a Spitfire hanging in its hall, is a red sandstone palace. The tenements, with their sandstone closes, define the streets. The subway, nicknamed the Clockwork Orange, is one of the smallest in the world, with a single circle line and little orange trains.

Riding in the city is not difficult, but the grid of one-way streets, bus lanes and tram-free but rail-laden roads takes attention. Rain is common, so watch for slick cobbles and painted lines. The M8 motorway runs through the centre, a dramatic urban trench, and leads east to Edinburgh, which is about seventy-five kilometres away. The long day's ride goes there and back, so you can take the quick road one way and a quieter route through the Lanarkshire or Lothian countryside the other.

Glasgow has nearly six hundred thousand people and plenty of fuel. For a meal, ask locals for a good curry, since the city has a long tradition of South Asian restaurants, or try a proper Scottish breakfast, with square sausage and a tattie scone. Pubs are many, and live music is easy to find. The best light is often in the evening, when the sun breaks through after a wet day and turns the sandstone gold.
t.chuxi tulou cluster@24.6,116.9:
In the mountains of western Fujian the villages are shaped like fortresses, and Chuxi is one of the classic examples. The tulou, or earthen buildings, here are huge rammed-earth rings and squares up to several storeys high, built by Hakka families over the centuries so that a whole clan could live, store grain and defend itself behind one thick wall. The Chuxi cluster, in the Yongding district, is part of the Fujian Tulou World Heritage group, and the buildings sit among terraced fields, bamboo and tea bushes in a valley that is green nearly all year.

Riding here means small mountain roads, narrow and often steep, with sudden bends where a lane squeezes between a stream and a wall of rice terrace. Surfaces are generally paved but patched, and the traffic is a mixture of scooters, small trucks and tourist minibuses, so keep a steady pace and expect the unexpected around blind corners. It is humid country. Mist hangs in the valleys on spring mornings, and summer can bring heavy rain, so waterproofs are worth carrying. Autumn is clearer and cooler, and a good time for photography.

The tulou are the point. Their outer walls can be more than a metre thick and are made of earth mixed with sand, lime and sometimes glutinous rice, then pounded layer by layer. Inside, ring after ring of wooden galleries open around a central courtyard, with a shared well, an ancestral hall and small rooms for each family. Some are still lived in, with washing hanging from the balconies and old men playing cards under the eaves, while others have been turned over to tea sellers and guesthouses. The round ones are the best known, though the square and even oval forms are just as interesting. Try the local Hakka dishes, such as stewed pork, preserved vegetables and tofu stuffed with meat, along with tea grown on the surrounding slopes.

As for practicalities, I cannot name a particular fuel stop at this exact place. The villages are small, and the county towns of the region are the places to find fuel stations, so fill up before heading into the hills. Carry cash, since small shops may not take foreign cards, and check the weather before a long day, because the rural roads in the rain are a different thing altogether.
t.liusheng pagoda@24.8,118.7:
Liusheng Pagoda stands on a hill at the edge of Quanzhou's coastal region in Fujian, and it has watched a lot of ships leave. It is a seven-storey octagonal tower of granite, usually dated to the Song dynasty, and sailors once used it as a landmark and, tradition says, as a bit of spiritual insurance for the sea. Quanzhou was one of the great ports of the medieval world, which Marco Polo and Arab travellers described as a bustling trading city, so a pagoda guarding its approaches fits easily into the picture.

The roads near the coast are well-surfaced and often busy, with trucks and scooters and the usual mild chaos of southern Chinese traffic. The best riding comes when you push inland into the hills, where lanes narrow and climb through litchi and longan trees, and a handful of bends make a welcome change. If you are interested in the sea, the nearby coast has the long Strait of Taiwan on the horizon, usually hazy, with fishing boats working out beyond the surf.

Baiqi, the closest village, is small, so do not rely on it. Look for roadside noodle shops and fish dishes served with local sauces, and have some cash handy. A couple of hours at the pagoda and in the hills makes a gentle, rewarding half day.
t.granada@37.2,-3.6:
Granada lies at the foot of the Sierra Nevada, the highest mountain range on the Spanish mainland, and the snowy ridge is visible from many streets, which is a surprise in a city that is baking hot in August. The Mulhacén, at 3,479 metres, is the highest peak of the Iberian Peninsula, and the summits stay white well into spring. Between the mountains and the plain, the city spreads across three hills, with the red towers of the Alhambra on one side, facing the whitewashed lanes of the Albaicín on another. The two hills look at each other across the river Darro.

The city fell to the Catholic monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492, an event that ended almost eight centuries of Muslim rule in Iberia, and their tomb lies in the Royal Chapel near the cathedral. Tickets for the Alhambra sell out in advance, so book ahead if you wish to go inside. In the evening, the Albaicín's viewpoints, particularly the one at San Nicolás, offer a fine look at the Alhambra glowing in the dusk, with the mountains behind it.

The road south and east climbs into the Sierra Nevada, then into the Alpujarras, a region of deep valleys and white villages on the southern slopes, with hairpin bends, steep gradients and sweeping views. The surface is generally good on the main roads, though narrow and sometimes rough on the minor ones. Traffic in the city is dense, and one-way systems and bus lanes can be confusing. Be careful of cold mornings in winter, with ice on the higher stretches, and the heat of mid-summer afternoons, when the best plan is a long lunch.

Granada has fuel everywhere, and the tradition of free tapas with every drink makes dinner a simple matter: order a beer and the kitchen sends out a small plate. Armilla and Huétor Vega, on the edge of the city, have supermarkets and petrol stations. The best times of day are early morning, with a fresh, clear light, and the evening, when the city comes alive. The air smells of orange blossom in spring and woodsmoke from the hills in winter. You start here with a full tank, a good breakfast and a long climb ahead.
t.abrigo de la fuente de selva pascuala@39:
Villar del Humo is a village of a few hundred people tucked into the folds of the Serranía de Cuenca, a high limestone plateau of pine woods, gorges and rocky cliffs in the east of Castilla-La Mancha, and the surrounding rock shelters hold some of the finest prehistoric paintings in Spain. They belong to what is called Levantine rock art, a style of small, lively red figures painted in shallow shelters across the east of the peninsula, which UNESCO listed in 1998 as the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin. Hunters with bows, running animals and sometimes whole scenes appear on the walls, painted thousands of years ago by people whose names and languages we will never know.

The shelter of the Fuente at Selva Pascuala is one of the group, and it is the sort of place where the paintings appear very small against the large rock face, so that you need to stand still and let your eyes adjust. Protection is strict, with metal barriers or railings and rules about touching or photographing in some sites, so it is worth checking at the village for access and visiting hours. Even at a distance, the figures have a grace and economy that makes the old stone feel crowded with life.

The landscape on the way is part of the experience. The roads in the Serranía are narrow, with plenty of bends, wooded slopes and sudden views across river canyons, particularly of the Cabriel, which runs through a deep gorge nearby. Traffic is light, but the surface can be uneven and there are patches of gravel at the edges. The plateau stands at around a thousand metres, so mornings are cool and winters are cold, with snow on the high ground. Fog and rain can come quickly in autumn. Expect big skies, the smell of pine resin and the sound of cicadas in July.

Fuel is a real concern. Villar del Humo is small, and so are Carboneras de Guadazaón and Cañete, so fill up in a larger town before heading into the mountains. Cuenca, with its hanging houses, is the most convenient large town. Local food is hearty, with roast lamb, migas and a strong cheese, and a bar in a village will often serve something warm. The scenery is rewarding, and the quiet of the place makes the paintings feel nearer than their age would suggest.
t.royal forced labour gaol@38.8,-4.8:
Almadén sits on one of the great mercury deposits of the world, and its history is one of wealth, danger and forced labour. Cinnabar, the red ore from which mercury is extracted, was mined here from Roman times, and for centuries the town produced a large share of the world's supply of the liquid metal. It was vital to the economy of the Spanish empire, because mercury was used to extract silver from ore in the mines of Mexico and Peru, so Almadén in effect fuelled the silver trade. In the sixteenth century the Spanish crown leased the mines to the Fugger banking family of Augsburg, who ran them for a long time and brought German miners to the town.

The Royal Forced Labour Gaol, the Real Cárcel de Forzados, was built in the eighteenth century to house convicts who were sentenced to work in the mines, the most hazardous job in the country. Conditions were hard, and mercury poisoning killed or crippled many. The building, a large square block with an inner courtyard, still stands, and part of it has since been used by the university for its school of mining engineering. UNESCO listed Almadén together with the Slovenian mining town of Idrija in 2012 as the Heritage of Mercury, recognising the way two mines shaped the global trade in the metal for centuries.

The setting is a surprise to many. Almadén lies in a bowl of hills on the southern edge of La Mancha, near the Sierra Morena, in a country of dehesa, rocky ridges and thin soil. The roads leading in are quiet and curving, with gentle gradients and a mix of oak woods and scrub, and the surface is generally fair. Traffic is light, but distances are long and services thin. The weather is hot and dry in summer, and cold in winter, with occasional frosts. In spring the hills are green and covered in wild flowers.

For fuel, rely on Almadén itself, which has stations, a few supermarkets and some bars, and do not rely on the villages around it, which are tiny. A walk around the old mining area gives a sense of the scale of the work, and the mine museum offers tours underground. The air smells of rock dust and rosemary, and the quiet is striking. It is a corner of Spain that few foreign riders visit, and its story is a gripping one.
t.pena del escrito 1@39.9,-1.7:
The name Peña del Escrito means the written rock, and it is exactly that: a sandstone or limestone face in the pine country of the Serranía de Cuenca where prehistoric people painted. The paintings here are small, and often faded, and part of the pleasure is working out what you are seeing: a bull, an archer, a line of dots, a figure that may be a person or may be only a stain. I cannot tell you exactly which motifs are on this panel, but the style of the group is lively, with figures drawn in a few quick strokes, often in red.

The Serranía lies on the high plateau of the Iberian System, where the Cabriel river has carved a gorge through limestone, with cliffs, caves and pine woods, and the area is a refuge for wildlife. The traffic is almost nonexistent, so it is easy to stop at a viewpoint and look at the view for a few minutes. In the Spanish of the time the condition was known as mal de azogue, azogue being the old word for quicksilver. The hospital offered a place of care at a time when few mining towns offered anything.

t.bullring@38.8,-4.8:

t.malaga@36.7,-4.4:
Málaga has been a port for nearly three thousand years, founded by the Phoenicians and later ruled by Romans, Moors and Castilians, and the layers show if you look. At the foot of the hill, a Roman theatre lies right next to the Alcazaba, an eleventh-century Moorish fortress-palace whose gardens and fountains climb the slope. The old port has been turned into a promenade of palm trees and cafes. Spring and autumn bring warm days and clear light, while August can be baking. The smell of Málaga is frying fish, jasmine and warm sea air, and the evenings last long.
t.valencia@39.5,-0.4:
Valencia has a river that is no longer a river. After a catastrophic flood in 1957, the Turia was diverted around the south of the city, and the old riverbed, which runs through the centre in a long curve, was turned into a park, a green ribbon of nearly nine kilometres filled with gardens, sports fields, bridges and playgrounds.
